CONNECTION-MAPIndex · 00-Index

Connection Map — how the library branches

Last updated: 2026-07-31

This is the picture of the brain. Topics are nodes, connects_to links are edges, and frameworks and activities are the shared hubs that make one improvement land in several programmes at once.

GitHub renders the diagrams below. Update them on every ingest.

On this pageThe mapThe shared framework hubsProvenance — which source produced whatReading the mapThe hubs, and why they matterWhy the connections matterWhere the map is thinOther indexes

The map

Topic-to-topic links only. BEWR = Building Effective Work Relationships, CCTE = Creating a Collaborative Team Environment, CSW = Cultural Safety in the Workplace, FR = Future Ready Conflict Resolution. The framework hubs are on their own diagram below, because putting both on one makes neither readable.

The shared framework hubs

The pages more than one topic depends on. Improve one and every connected programme improves.

Provenance — which source produced what

Reading the map

  • Double arrows between topics are connects_to links. They are always two-way: if A links B, B links A
  • Lines to frameworks show which topics share one. FRM-004 sits between three topics, which is exactly why those topics are neighbours
  • Dotted arrows are provenance: which source produced which page
  • FRM-003 STAR touches everything. It is the structural rule, not a topic tool

The hubs, and why they matter

Eleven frameworks are now shared across topics, and they are the proof the structure works:

HubShared byWhy it matters
FRM-018 TuckmanTOP-LEA-003, TOP-LEA-005Both SKILL UP resources carry the same section with different framing. One page holds both lenses. Written twice, it would have drifted apart inside a year

The most reused activity is ACT-013 Start, Stop, Continue. It closes ten topics across three pillars, because all three SKILL UP resources and the Effective Communication workbook put that exact reflection page after every part. One page, ten inbound links.

Three more activities now cross topics: ACT-047 Name It In Ten Seconds serves respect and cultural safety, ACT-063 serves both cultural safety topics, and ACT-032 Stage Moves carries two different header questions for two different programmes.

Why the connections matter

When you ask for a workshop on trust, the library does not hand back one topic page. It hands back the topic, four frameworks, five activities, three neighbouring topics and the source the whole thing came from. That is the difference between a folder and a brain.

Where the map is thin

  • ⚠️ Ice Breaker Games is deliberately not on this map. It is an eighth pillar of sixteen game pages that connect to nothing, which is the whole point of it. The map is a picture of what connects, and games are the one thing in the library that is allowed not to. They link to each other and to their pillar page, and no further. See GAME-INDEX
  • Digital Capability has opened, on 2026-08-02, from a YouTube video pasted in full. It landed connected in three directions immediately — Communication (TOP-COM-006 is the ethics half of the same question), Employment (the CV is its worked example) and Wellbeing (both are about what a machine cannot do for you). One topic is not a pillar, but the node exists and the pillar's own house rules are written
  • Financial Capability is now the only empty pillar in the library, and it is the one with the most obvious neighbours already built. The first payslip sits directly against TOP-EMP-002, 003 and 006, and money pressure is the largest single load on TOP-WEL-001's walls. Financial Capability is now clearly the most urgent, because it is core Zeducation delivery and it has obvious neighbours already built on both sides — the first payslip sits against TOP-EMP-002/003/004, and money pressure is the largest single load on TOP-WEL-001's walls
  • One seed remains: TOP-LEA-001 Leading With Your Strengths. TOP-COM-002 was built out on 2026-08-01 from SRC-007, which supplied the two models it was missing. The Communication pillar is now fully published
  • Employment & Work Readiness has four nodes and is now a real pillar. SRC-010 added the Career Readiness sequence — TOP-EMP-002 → TOP-EMP-003 → TOP-EMP-004 — which is the first chain in the library where the topics run in a deliberate order rather than sitting as neighbours. Its Foundation outcome, write a CV and cover letter, prepare for an interview, had been an empty promise since the pillar was created. It is now covered
  • The EMP ↔ COM bridge is new. TOP-EMP-003 links to TOP-COM-003 (a CV headline is BLUF) and TOP-EMP-004 links to TOP-COM-002 ("tell me about a difficult person" is the most asked interview question). Career readiness turns out to be a communication problem wearing a different hat
  • ⚠️ Two frameworks are now both called STAR. FRM-003 is the session shape, FRM-059 is the interview answer. Both pages carry the warning at the top and the map records the clash as a dotted edge. This is the first genuine collision in the library and it will not be the last
  • Culture & Diversity doubled in one ingest and is now the second-largest pillar. TOP-CUL-001 and TOP-CUL-002 are the first topics created in the pillar rather than moved into it
  • Leadership is now the most densely connected pillar. TOP-LEA-010 links to five other topics and TOP-LEA-001, which had been an orphan seed since the library opened, now has four connections
  • The Leadership ↔ Culture & Diversity bridge is new. Before SRC-009 the two pillars touched only through TOP-LEA-008 and TOP-LEA-009, which had been moved rather than built. FRM-053, FRM-054, TOP-CUL-001 and TOP-CUL-002 now tie them together properly
  • Wellbeing & Identity has opened, on 2026-08-02, from Zeducation's own SKILL UP Building Resilience guide. It was named here as "the sharpest absence". By the end of the same day it had two topics and seven frameworks, the second being TOP-WEL-002 Pepeha from SRC-019 — the first line of its own backlog, answered on the day the backlog was written. Values, stress and the window of tolerance are the named gaps that remain
  • TOP-WEL-002 is the library's widest arrival. It connects to five topics across five pillars on day one — Wellbeing (TOP-WEL-001), Culture & Diversity (TOP-LEA-008 and TOP-CUL-001), Employment (TOP-EMP-005) and Digital (TOP-DIG-001). No other topic has landed touching five pillars, and the reason is structural rather than lucky: identity is the thing every other pillar is standing on
  • The Wellbeing ↔ Employment edge is the one worth naming. TOP-WEL-002 links to TOP-EMP-005 The Jobs Nobody Advertises because that channel runs on people who know you. An introduction whose entire purpose is connection is not a soft skill sitting beside employment — it is the employment skill, and ACT-122 makes the argument in twenty minutes by putting the interview introduction and the pepeha side by side
  • The Digital ↔ Wellbeing edge runs the other way from every other one on this map. TOP-DIG-001 warned that AI is markedly weaker in te reo Māori and answers with the same confidence. TOP-WEL-002 turned that warning into a library-wide house rule: no AI-generated te reo Māori, on any page. It is the first time a topic in one pillar has set a constraint that governs the whole catalogue
  • TOP-WEL-001 landed as a cross-pillar hub immediately. It links to Culture & Diversity (TOP-LEA-008, the same territory from the leader's side), Employment (TOP-EMP-002, because step B of the ABC model is the same move as the skills work) and Communication (TOP-COM-004, because when the load is the problem the answer is a boundary and not more resilience). Three pillars from one new node, which no other topic has managed on arrival
  • FRM-063 and FRM-065 are a bonded pair. Te Whare Tapa Whā and Fonofale are taught together, never one alone, and the map records the edge between them. They also tie the new pillar back to FRM-050 and FRM-036, so Wellbeing & Identity arrived already joined to the te ao Māori and Pacific material rather than sitting on its own
  • Te ao Māori has no page of its own. Whanaungatanga, manaakitanga and hui are named as neighbours on FRM-035 and FRM-036 and none exists. That is the live gap
  • Cross-pillar links have doubled. Creating Culture & Diversity on 2026-08-01 turned four Leadership-internal links into cross-pillar ones (L2↔L8, L4↔L8, L6↔L9) and surfaced a fourth to Communication (T5↔L9). The library is better connected than it looked
  • The Leadership pillar finally has motivation. TOP-LEA-012 was the missing middle: the pillar covered style, decisions and team stages and had nothing on why anybody follows or tries. It landed as a four-way hub immediately — Leadership style, decision styles, team stages, and across to Wellbeing & Identity, because TOP-LEA-012 and TOP-WEL-001 refuse the same move: treating a structural problem as a personal failing
  • Employment & Work Readiness now has two sequences, not one. Career Readiness (CR 1-4) gets somebody a job; Starting Work (SW 1) keeps it. TOP-EMP-006 is the pillar's first topic about what happens after the placement, which is the half MSD actually measures. It is also the first topic in the library built from a research pass rather than an ingested document
  • SRC-013 produced a topic without producing a framework. The hidden job market now has its own 120-150 minute session (TOP-EMP-005) built on FRM-061, FRM-024 and FRM-057 — three frameworks that already existed, assembled rather than copied. That is the architecture doing its job: frameworks live once, topics assemble them, and one page can anchor two different sessions
  • FRM-024 is now a three-topic hub. Granovetter's weak ties reaches TOP-EMP-001 and TOP-EMP-005 directly and TOP-EMP-002 through FRM-061. It is the most reused piece of external evidence in the library
  • Only two framework hubs cross a pillar boundary (FRM-008, and now FRM-033 via FRM-023). The library is now two dense clusters joined by a handful of links. More cross-pillar hubs are what would make it one brain rather than two

FRAMEWORK-INDEXIndex · 00-Index

Framework Index — every tool, model and technique

Last updated: 2026-08-02

Tool = what you use (a model, worksheet, script). Technique = how you do it (listening, "I" statements). Frameworks live once and are linked from every topic that uses them, so improving a framework page improves every programme that draws on it.

On this pageEvery framework carries five or more resourcesBy outcome — what to reach forEvidence ratingsResearched but not yet written upOther indexes

Every framework carries five or more resources

As of 2026-08-02, all 79 framework pages have a "More resources" block of at least five links, mixed between video, article and deeper reading. 523 links in total. Where a video exists from the person who built the model, it is the one listed — Durie on Te Whare Tapa Whā, Ramsden on cultural safety, Masten on ordinary magic, Belbin's own channel, the Co-Active Training Institute on the three levels of listening.

⚠️ How to read these links. Every URL came from a search result, so a search engine has indexed the page. They were not opened and read one by one — this environment's gateway refuses most external hosts, including YouTube. Treat them as a researched starting list, not a checked bibliography. If a link is dead or the content has changed, fix it here rather than working around it, and the whole library gets the fix at once.

➜ Where a framework's resources include the counter-argument, that is deliberate. FRM-054 links the MBTI publisher's own "do not use this for hiring". FRM-061 links a recruiter arguing the hidden job market is a trap. FRM-071 leads with the criticisms of Maslow rather than the pyramid. A resource list that only agrees with the page is not a resource list.

Evidence ratings

  • Strong — peer-reviewed research or meta-analysis behind it
  • Moderate — well documented and widely taught, with mixed or partial research support
  • Practitioner — respected practice wisdom, not formally validated. Teach it as a mirror, not a diagnosis

⚠️ Read this before you pick

Five of these are English spelling and vocabulary games, played at speed, in front of everybody:
GAM-001Scattergories
GAM-002Word Generator
GAM-005Name, Place, Animal, Thing
GAM-009First Letter, Last Letter
GAM-016Articulate

In a room with ESOL learners or low literacy, that is not a warm-up. It is a test, run in public, at speed. A learner exposed in the first ten minutes will not speak again all day.

➜ Every one of those five carries an adaptation. Play it in pairs, allow any language, or drop the elimination. The best fix is "answer in any language", which changes who the expert in the room is. Use it without announcing why.

Three more things the pages flag:
MobilityGAM-011 asks people to get up. There is an arm's-reach version, made the rule for everybody
Homes on cameraGAM-008 and GAM-011 put somebody's living space on screen. Not everybody wants that
DisclosureGAM-006 asks people to say true things about themselves. The passing rule gets said out loud before you start

Games that need no materials at all

GAM-009 First Letter, Last Letter and GAM-015 No Smiling. Both can start in five seconds with nothing prepared and nothing to hand out. Know these two by heart.

Where they came from

All sixteen are from Zeducation's own Online Ice Breaker Games resource, ingested 2026-08-02. The resource supplies the game and the steps. The purpose, the times, what you need, the in-person versions and every warning were added here.

  1. Stories for the Pink Sheets. Twenty-two of the twenty-three sheets carry a real Model, Metaphor and Point, and are placeholder-story. The easiest one to fill is PS-EMP-005 — a graduate who got work through somebody they barely knew, and there will be several. A sheet without a story does not survive a stage. This is by a distance the highest-value gap in the library, and it can only be filled from delivery
  2. ✅ Done. TOP-COM-002 Handling Difficult Conversations was built out on 2026-08-01 from SRC-007, which supplied the staying-steady and going-wrong models it was missing. The Communication pillar now has no seeds left

Rules

  • Lower case, hyphenated. difficult-conversations, not Difficult Conversations
  • Singular unless the thing is naturally plural. boundary is fine, boundaries is what we use — pick one and keep it
  • Tag the subject, not the format. roleplay is a type field, not a subject tag, except on activity pages where it genuinely helps retrieval
  • A tag used five or more times is a signal. Check whether it should become a topic or a module

PIL-COMPillar · Communication

Communication

How people say what they mean, hear what is meant, and handle the conversations that matter. This is the pillar most programmes touch, because every other capability is delivered through a conversation.

Who it serves: frontline workers, emerging leaders, youth, teams under pressure, anyone who has to raise something hard with someone senior.

PS-COM-004Pink Sheet · Communication

Behind every no is a deeper yes

placeholder-story
boundariessaying-noassertivenessworkload

Topic: TOP-COM-004 Boundaries Without Guilt · Module 3

On this pageModel — Yes – No – YesMetaphor — the yes pilePointStudyStoryWhere this sheet branchesRelated sheets

Model — Yes – No – Yes

Three beats. The one in the middle is the one people cannot say, and the two either side are what make it sayable.

Category: how — there is a process to run.

Metaphor — the yes pile

Everything you agreed to in the last fortnight, in one pile on the table. Now take back the three you would agree to again. What is left is not generosity. It is a fortnight of your life allocated by whoever asked first.

Point

Saying yes to everything is not generous. It is a decision handed to whoever asked first.

The reframe underneath it: you are not rejecting the person, you are protecting the promise. A no without a stated yes sounds like rejection. A yes without a no leaves you overloaded and quietly resentful, which costs the relationship anyway, just later and with interest.

Study

WorkSafe New Zealand treats workload as a work health and safety matter, and reports that the most common psychosocial risks for workers in Aotearoa are the pace and quantity of work (WorkSafe: psychosocial risks for all New Zealand workers).

That moves the argument off "learn to say no" as self-help and onto ground a manager has to take seriously: a leader who cannot hold a limit is carrying a hazard.

The model's own source: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No (2007). Ury co-founded the Harvard Program on Negotiation. Practitioner evidence, not trial evidence, and worth saying so.

Story

⚠️ GAP: no Zeducation story yet. This sheet needs a real one before it is used on stage.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner or client who said yes to everything, hit a wall, and changed something specific. The detail that makes it work is what they gave up without deciding to — the second job, the kid's game, the study they dropped — because that is the moment the audience recognises themselves.

Ask at the next Module 3 delivery: "who has a yes they still regret?" Someone in every room does. Get permission before it goes anywhere near a keynote.

Where this sheet branches

The Yes – No – Yes model has three parts, so it will carry at least three more sheets:

Future sheetThe Point it would make
The first YesAn excuse is not a value. "I'm busy" tells them nothing about what you are protecting
The NoIf it can be read as "maybe", you did not say no, you delayed it
The second YesThe door you leave open is what makes the no survivable. Do not offer a door you cannot hold
The Broken RecordYou do not win by arguing better. You win by not needing to argue

About This Topic

Every leader has limits. The skill is knowing how to hold them without damage.

Boundaries protect your energy, your focus and your team. Saying yes to everything is not generous. It leads to burnout, dropped balls and quiet resentment. Clear limits actually build respect, because people learn what you will and will not do, and they stop having to guess.

This is not only a personal problem. WorkSafe New Zealand treats workload as a workplace health issue, and reports that the most common psychosocial risks for workers in Aotearoa are the pace and quantity of work (WorkSafe). A leader who cannot hold a limit is carrying a hazard, not just a heavy week.

Saying no does not have to be harsh. You can acknowledge the request, be clear about your limit, and offer a way forward. You are not rejecting the person, you are protecting what matters and offering an option.

In this module you will learn three tools to do exactly that: a respectful no, a calm way to raise a problem, and a way to hold your ground when someone keeps pushing. None of them require you to be rude or to back down. A respectful no today prevents a bigger problem tomorrow, and the more you practise, the easier it gets.

Key words

WordWhat it means
BoundaryA limit on what you will take on, and what you will accept from others
The Positive NoSaying no to a request by first saying yes to what you are protecting
PushbackSaying no to a request that has already been made, often by someone senior
Broken recordRepeating your answer calmly instead of arguing new points
Psychosocial riskA work hazard that comes from how work is organised, like workload or pressure
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Set a clear workload or role boundary respectfully.
  2. Say "no" without guilt using a structured approach.
  3. Push back on an unreasonable request while preserving the relationship.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Think about the last time you said yes when everything in you was saying no. You did the job. You did it well, probably. And you did it instead of something else, something that mattered to you, that quietly got dropped.

Nobody made that trade. You made it. You just did not get to choose what you gave up, because the person who asked first decided for you.

Statement: Saying yes to everything is not generous. It is a decision handed to whoever asked first.

➜ Facilitator note: run The Yes Pile before you say any of this. Let them build the pile and take back only three. The story lands completely differently when they are looking at the leftovers.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

Framework

The Positive No — Yes – No – Yes

Type: Model · Origin: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No (2007) · Full page: FRM-008

A way to say no without damaging the relationship. Start with a yes to something you care about, give a clear no to the request, then offer another yes as a way forward.

How to read this: the no in the middle is the easy part to write and the hard part to say. The two yeses are what make it possible to say out loud.

StepWhat you doSounds like
YesName the value, priority or person you care about"I really value getting this project right."
NoSay no to the request, not the person. Keep it short"I can't take on the extra report this week."
YesOffer an option so the door stays open"I can help you find someone, or look at it Monday."

Worked examples

  • "I really value getting this project right (Yes). I can't take on the extra report this week (No). I can help you find someone else, or look at it next Monday (Yes)."
  • "Family time on weekends matters to me (Yes). So I won't be able to work this Saturday (No). I'm happy to come in early Monday to catch up (Yes)."
  • "I want our team to hit a high standard (Yes). I can't approve this as it is (No). Let's fix these two points and I'll sign it off (Yes)."

Why it works: leaders cannot say yes to everything. A blunt no creates conflict, and a soft yes leaves you overloaded. Ury's argument is that behind every no there is a deeper yes, to your time, your standards, your family. Naming that yes first turns a refusal into an honest conversation instead of a rejection.

Cultural note: in many Pacific, Māori and migrant families, a direct no to an elder, a minister or an employer can read as disrespect. The third part is what makes this work here. Teach it as clear and respectful, and let learners choose their own words for the middle line.

More resources

  • 📄 William Ury — The Power of a Positive No
  • 📄 Harvard Program on Negotiation — The Power of a Positive No
  • 🎬 TED — Nedra Glover Tawwab: Your 3-step guide to setting better boundaries at work — short and practical, good opener
Framework

DESC — Describe, Express, Specify, Consequences

Type: Model · Origin: Sharon and Gordon Bower, Asserting Yourself (1976) · Full page: FRM-004

A simple script for raising a problem or giving tough feedback calmly. Already taught in Module 1; here it does boundary work, because most boundaries fail before the no, when nobody named the problem.

How to read this: four sentences, written before you speak. Most people manage D and E. The conversation only changes when you do S and C too.

StepExample
Describe"The last three reports came in a day late."
Express"It puts pressure on the whole team to catch up."
Specify"I need them in by Friday noon from now on."
Consequences"If we manage that, we hit our deadlines with no stress."

Second example: "You raised your voice in the meeting today (Describe). It made the room go quiet and people held back (Express). I'd like us to keep feedback calm and one at a time (Specify). That way everyone feels safe to speak up (Consequences)."

Why it works: hard conversations go wrong because people get emotional, vague or accusing. DESC keeps the focus on the behaviour, not the person, and forces you to decide what change you are actually asking for.

More resources

  • 📄 In Equilibrium — the DESC model for assertiveness
  • 📄 NCCMT — DESC for assertive communication
Framework

The Broken Record — Acknowledge, Appreciate, Explain Priorities

Type: Technique · Origin: persistence, from Manuel J. Smith, When I Say No, I Feel Guilty (1975). The three-step form is Zeducation's · Full page: FRM-009

A calm way to hold your ground when someone keeps pushing. Acknowledge what they said, appreciate their position, then explain your priorities and repeat your answer, like a record playing the same line.

How to read this: it is a loop, not a line. Each time round the wrapper changes and the answer does not.

StepWhat you doSounds like
AcknowledgeShow you heard them"I hear that you need it today."
AppreciateValue their point or position"I know this deadline is important to you."
Explain prioritiesYour reason, then repeat your answer"Safety checks come first, so it'll be ready tomorrow morning."

Worked example, pushed twice: "I hear that you need it today. I know this deadline is important to you. My team's safety checks come first, so I can't rush this. I'll have it to you tomorrow morning." (They push again.) "I understand the pressure you're under. I really do want to help. But the checks come first, so it will be ready tomorrow morning."

Customer version: "I get that you'd like a discount (Acknowledge). I appreciate you choosing us (Appreciate). Our price reflects the quality we promise, so the rate stays the same. I'm confident you'll be happy with the result."

Why it works: if you keep arguing new points, you get pulled off track, and every new reason is something else to attack. Repetition takes the argument off the table. The acknowledging is what stops it reading as stonewalling. Clinical de-escalation guidance teaches the same loop of listen, validate, restate, and expects several rounds before it lands (Richmond et al., 2012).

When not to use it: if they are raising something you have not actually considered, stop and listen. This is for pressure, not for new information.

More resources

  • 📄 Psychology Spot — the broken record technique
  • 📄 Richmond et al. (2012) — Verbal De-escalation of the Agitated Patient

Two additions from SRC-008 (2026-08-01)

FRM-042 Why Assertiveness Feels Hard matters more here than anywhere else in the library, because people-pleasing is the barrier this topic exists to solve. A learner who can write a Positive No and still cannot deliver it is not short of a script. Run ACT-080 What's Stopping Me? after the frameworks.

FRM-043 DEAR MAN is the DBT assertiveness script and its Negotiate step is close kin to the third Yes in Yes-No-Yes. Use it when the ask is a refusal: Reinforce becomes what the other person gains from a clear no now, rather than a reluctant yes later.

Self-Assessment

How Well Do I Hold My Limits? — full version and scoring: ACT-016

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I can say no to extra work without apologising three times
2When I turn something down, I say what I am protecting, not just that I am busy
3I offer an alternative when I say no, instead of just closing the door
4⟲ I say yes to things I know I do not have room for
5When someone keeps pushing, my answer stays the same
6I can stay calm when someone is pressuring me
7⟲ I avoid the person rather than have the conversation
8I raise a problem early, before it builds up into resentment
9When I raise a problem, I describe what happened rather than labelling the person
10I ask for one specific change, so people know what to do differently
11⟲ I feel guilty for days after saying no
12People know where my limits are without having to test them
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 4, 7 and 11, flip before adding: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60You hold your limits and keep your relationships. That combination is rareTeach it. Someone on your team is drowning in yeses right now, and you know who
38-49You hold most of the time. It slips with certain people, or when you are tiredWork out who you cannot say no to. Build one Positive No for that person this week
25-37The limit is there, but people have to find it by accidentStart with the middle line. One clear no, one sentence, said out loud before you need it
12-24Being honest here is the first step, and it is the hard onePick one small, low-risk request this week and use all three parts. One. Not a new personality

⚠️ Written by Zeducation to match the house style of How Assertive Am I?. Module 3 of the workbook has no self-assessment of its own. A teaching mirror, not a validated measure.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

Yes – No – Yes Lab · worksheet then roleplay · 25-30 min · pairs

Practises: FRM-008 · Full page: ACT-014

Part 1: build the three lines for a real request you find hard to turn down, then have a partner check the middle line is actually a no. Part 2: roleplay it, with structured feedback from the asker.

Debrief questions

  • Which box was hardest to write? (Usually the first Yes. People reach for an excuse instead of a value.)
  • How did saying the middle line out loud differ from writing it?
  • Askers: what made you accept it?

DESC Rewrite Lab · roleplay · 25-30 min · pairs

Practises: FRM-004 · Full page: ACT-003

Write the four boxes for a real conversation you have been avoiding, sharpen it with a partner, then say it out loud while they push back once.

Debrief questions

  • Which box was hardest? (It is almost always Specify.)
  • What happened to your body when your partner pushed back?
  • When will you have the real conversation?

Hold The Line · roleplay · 25-30 min · pairs or threes

Practises: FRM-009 · Full page: ACT-015

The pressure activity. Person A pushes at least three times. Person B holds one line. With an observer writing down the repeat line each round, because drift is invisible to the person doing it.

Debrief questions

  • At which push did you feel yourself starting to bend?
  • Did anyone's line change? What did it change into?
  • What made the difference between sounding steady and sounding stubborn?
7

Reflection Questions

Notice

  • Which requests do you find hardest to turn down, and who is usually asking?
  • When you say no, do you name what you are protecting, or do you just say you are busy?
  • What happens in your body when someone pushes back on you?

Connect

  • Tell us about a yes you regret. What did it cost, and who paid for it?
  • When has someone said no to you well? What did they do that made it land alright?
  • Where has a boundary you never set turned into resentment you are still carrying?

Apply

  • What is one request this week you will answer with Yes – No – Yes?
  • Which problem have you been sitting on that needs a DESC conversation?
  • Who is going to push back on you, and what is your repeat line going to be?

Commit

  • ❑ I want to start…
  • ❑ I want to stop…
  • ❑ I want to continue…

Full closer activity: ACT-013 Start, Stop, Continue

Facilitator Notes

Suggested run sheet (110 min)

TimeStageWhat happens
0:00SThe Yes Pile, then the story and the statement
0:15RSelf-assessment, run early so they have a reason to listen
0:25TThe Positive No
0:35AYes – No – Yes Lab
1:00TThe Broken Record, demonstrated live with a learner pushing you
1:10AHold The Line
1:35TDESC, briefly. Most groups have met it in Module 1
1:40RStart / Stop / Continue

DESC Rewrite Lab is the activity to drop if you are short on time, or the one to run instead of Hold The Line if the group is raising problems rather than being pushed.

  • Common traps: learners hearing this as permission to be blunt. The whole module is about being clear and keeping the relationship, so watch for anyone whose no has lost its wrapper. Also watch for the third Yes swallowing the no entirely, which is the people-pleaser's escape hatch
  • The strongest sequence is game, then assessment, then tools. The Yes Pile makes the assessment honest, and the assessment makes them want the tools
  • This one gets personal. More than any other module in this workbook, learners bring real situations: a manager who keeps adding work, a family expectation, a church commitment they cannot get out of. Leave room for it and know your referral path
  • Say this out loud early: some people genuinely cannot say no at work. Probation, a visa, an insecure contract, being the only earner. A person in that position is not failing at boundaries, they are managing a real constraint, and the tools here are for the situations where they do have a choice. Without that framing this module can shame the people who need it most
  • Adaptations: for youth, run everything on peer pressure and family scenarios first. For customer-facing teams, agree one shared organisational repeat line as a team output

⚠️ Open gaps: the self-assessment is house-written and unvalidated (flagged above). The Broken Record's three-step form has no published source, only the underlying persistence technique, and the workbook does not credit either. No NZ-specific evidence yet linking boundary-setting to retention or burnout in frontline work.

9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

The Yes Pile · 10-12 min · whole class

Full page: ACT-017

Everyone writes down everything they said yes to in the last fortnight, builds one pile, then takes back only the three they would say yes to again.

The link back: every yes was a no to something else. You just did not get to choose what.

The No Game · 10-15 min · pairs

Full page: ACT-005

The Module 1 opener, and it works even better here now that they have the tools.

The link back: notice how uncomfortable that was, and notice that nobody was even upset with you. That discomfort is what makes people say yes to things they cannot do.

Thirty Seconds of Yes · 3 min · whole class · no materials

In pairs, Person A has thirty seconds to ask for as many things as they can. Person B must say yes to every single one. Then swap. Then ask the room how the yes-sayers feel.

The link back: that flustered, slightly panicked feeling at the end of thirty seconds is what a fortnight of not saying no feels like, just faster.

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

The conversation is won or lost in twenty seconds

placeholder-story
difficult-conversationsconflictde-escalationassertivenesscommunication

Topic: TOP-COM-002 Handling Difficult Conversations · Pillar: Communication

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

Anyone can prepare the first sentence. The conversation is decided in the twenty seconds after the other person reacts, and almost nobody has ever practised that part.

Model

Three things people do in those twenty seconds. Only one of them is a choice.

What you doWhat it teaches them
Take it backReact and it goes away. The most common, and the most expensive
Push harderThis is a fight, so fight
FreezeYou did not mean it
Hold steadyThis is real, and you are safe with me anyway

The move that makes holding steady possible: acknowledge the reaction without conceding the point. "I can see this has landed hard" costs nothing and concedes nothing. Then go back to what you came to say.

And the exit nobody uses: "Let's pause and talk again shortly." Parking is not losing, and the phrasing matters, because it names a return.

Metaphor

A landing, not a takeoff.

Everybody trains the takeoff. You rehearse the opening line in the car, you get the words right, you brace yourself and you get off the ground.

Nobody trains the landing, and the landing is the part that decides whether the flight counted.

(Related to PS-COM-003, which uses the same image for a different point. Do not use both sheets in one session.)

Study

The three reactions are practitioner observation, not research, and should be taught as such.

The evidenced neighbour is Amy Edmondson's psychological safety work, and it is directly on point: people are not testing what you say about openness, they are watching what happened to the last person who was open. In a difficult conversation, you are the last person who was open, and the other person's reaction is teaching them what happens next time. 📄 Edmondson (1999)

⚠️ The de-escalation steps that carry the "hold steady" branch come from SRC-007 with no citation. De-escalation is well evidenced in health and frontline safety and this version is not grounded. Worth fixing.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one, and this is the sheet where it will do most work.

The story to collect: somebody who took it back. Prepared properly, said the thing, watched the other person's face, and heard themselves say "actually, forget it, it's not a big deal." Then what happened over the following months.

That story is extremely common and almost never told, because taking it back feels like kindness at the time and only looks like a mistake later. A facilitator willing to tell their own version of it would open this topic better than anything else available.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any feedback or performance conversation trainingThe half that DESC does not cover
Supervisor and team lead trainingNew supervisors take it back constantly and do not know they do
Conflict resolution programmesPairs directly with the de-escalation module
One-to-one coachingThe three reactions are a fast, honest self-diagnosis

1

About This Topic

A difficult conversation is one where you have something to say that the other person may not want to hear, and where the relationship matters enough that you cannot just say it badly and walk off.

Most people can prepare the words. There are good scripts for that, and this library has them. What derails a difficult conversation is almost never the opening sentence. It is what happens immediately afterwards, when the other person reacts, and you have to decide in about two seconds whether to hold your position, soften it, or abandon it.

That moment is a skill, and it can be practised. It is mostly borrowed from de-escalation: stay calm, keep your body open, let them finish, name what they are feeling, and only then go back to the thing you came to say. If it is too hot to continue, you take a break, on purpose, with a named time to come back.

This matters everywhere, not just at work. The same twenty seconds decide a conversation with a teenager, a landlord, a coach, a sibling and a manager.

Key words

WordWhat it means
DESCA four-part script for raising something: Describe, Express, Specify, Consequences
De-escalationCalming a tense situation before it becomes serious conflict
Taking it backWithdrawing what you said because the other person reacted
Parking itPausing on purpose, with a named time to return. Not the same as dropping it
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Plan and hold a difficult conversation using a structured script.
  2. Stay steady in the twenty seconds after the other person reacts.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Imagine you finally do it.

You prepared. You wrote it down. You practised it in the car on the way in. You sit down, and you say your line, clean and fair, exactly how you rehearsed it.

And she starts to cry.

Or she says "So that's what everyone thinks of me, is it?"

Or she goes completely silent and stares at the table.

Or she says "Right" and walks out.

Ask the room: what happens next? Because that is the part nobody rehearses.

Most of us do one of three things in the next twenty seconds. We take it back: "no, no, it's not a big deal, forget I said anything." We push harder: "well, if you'd just done it properly in the first place." Or we freeze, and fill the silence with words we have not thought about.

Statement: Anyone can prepare the first sentence. The conversation is won or lost in the twenty seconds after the other person reacts.

➜ Facilitator note: ask which of the three they do. Almost everyone knows instantly. Taking it back is the most common and the most expensive, because it teaches the other person that a reaction makes the problem go away. Once someone learns that, you will never get a straight conversation with them again.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-004

The DESC Script

The preparation half, already in the library and taught in full in TOP-COM-001 and TOP-COM-004.

How to read it: DESC gets you to the end of your first sentence in one piece. It says nothing about what happens next, which is why this topic needs the other two frameworks.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-041

De-escalation — six steps

This is the model this topic was missing. Written for conflict that arrives at you, and it works just as well for conflict you started on purpose.

StepActionIn a difficult conversation
1Stay calmYour voice slows. This is the whole first second
2Open body languageUnfold, unclench, keep the distance you had
3Listen activelyLet them finish. Even the unfair part
4Show empathy"I can see this has landed hard."
5Work on a solution together"What would help us move forward?"
6Take a break if needed"Let's pause and talk again shortly."

Step 6 is the answer to "what if it goes wrong". Parking a conversation is not losing it, and the phrasing carries the difference: "let's pause and talk again shortly" names a return. "Let's leave it" does not, and it lands as abandonment.

⚠️ Safety. If someone is threatening, this stops being a communication topic. Leave and get help. Name your workplace's escalation path in the room.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-039

The Compassionate Response

What to actually say in the twenty seconds, so that acknowledging their reaction does not become withdrawing your point.

What you sayWhat it does
"That sounds difficult."Acknowledges without conceding
"I want to hear more about how that made you feel."Buys time and gets information
"I'm sorry if I have offended you in any way."Use only if you actually might have

The distinction this topic turns on: compassion is not agreement. You can say "I can see this has landed hard" to someone whose reaction you think is unfair, and then go back to your point. That is the move that separates staying steady from backing down, and most learners have never seen it demonstrated.

→ Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-079 How Do I Handle Conflict? Ten statements, 1 to 3, out of 30.

The three that belong to this topic are 3, 7 and 9: do you let them finish before you explain, do you stay calm when someone raises their voice, and can you take a break without it feeling like giving up?

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Think of a conversation you have been putting off. What are you afraid will happen when you say it?
  2. Which of the three do you do in the twenty seconds: take it back, push harder, or freeze?
  3. When did someone withdraw something they had said to you because you reacted? What did you learn from that about them?
  4. What does your body do when a conversation turns?
  5. When have you parked a conversation well? What did you say to end it?
  6. Who do you find it hardest to say a hard thing to? Why that person?
  7. What is the difference between acknowledging someone's reaction and agreeing with it?
  8. What is the conversation you will have this week, with whom, and when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min. At 90, cut one of the two openers and run ACT-078 for two rounds instead of three
  • The whole topic is the twenty seconds. If you only have thirty minutes, teach the three reactions from the story and run ACT-078. Everything else is supporting material
  • What usually goes wrong: learners hear "acknowledge their reaction" as "back down". Demonstrate the difference explicitly, out loud, twice. It is the hardest idea on the page
  • The polite roleplay. Pairs will let each other off. Brief the reacting partner to actually push back, and give observers permission to say "that was too easy, run it again"
  • ⚠️ Safety. ACT-078 can surface real experiences of aggression. Let people sit a round out with no explanation, and name the workplace's escalation path before you start
  • The Pink Sheet (PS-COM-002) carries the Point and the metaphor. Its story slot is open, and the story it needs is a facilitator's own account of taking something back

PS-COM-006Pink Sheet · Communication

You are the worst judge of how your own message reads

placeholder-story
digital-communicationtone-in-textemailhybridchannel

Topic: TOP-COM-006 Lead Across The Screen · Module 5

On this pageModel — The Channel-Fit MatrixMetaphor — "Fine."PointStudyStoryWhere this sheet branchesRelated sheets

Model — The Channel-Fit Matrix

Simple messageComplex or sensitive message
Low emotionChatEmail
High emotionQuick callVideo or in person

Two variables, four boxes, ten seconds. The rule that makes it usable when you are torn: go richer.

Category: what — two variables interact.

Metaphor — "Fine."

One word. You meant it was fine. You were on the tools and had one hand free.

They read it three times that evening, showed it to someone else, and came in the next morning ready for a conversation you did not know was happening.

The metaphor is doing something specific: it is not about a rude message, it is about a completely ordinary one. Nobody defends themselves against the version where they were being short. Everyone has sent "Fine."

Point

You are the worst judge of how your own message reads, because you can hear the tone you meant and nobody else can.

The consequence version: when people are unsure of your tone, they do not pick the neutral reading. They assume the worst, and you never find out they did.

Study

Strong, and unusually well matched to the claim. Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng (2005), "Egocentrism over e-mail: can we communicate as well as we think?", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (paper · APA write-up).

Five experiments. People overestimate both their ability to convey tone in email and their ability to read other people's. The mechanism the authors identify is egocentrism: you hear your own message in the tone you intended, and you cannot detach from that when imagining the reader.

That is the Point, stated by a peer-reviewed journal twenty years ago, and almost nobody in any room has heard it.

Supporting, for the video half: Bailenson (2021), Nonverbal Overload, Technology, Mind and Behavior (PDF). Peer-reviewed but explicitly a theoretical argument, so do not oversell it.

Supporting, for the AI half: Hohenstein et al. (2023), Scientific Reports 13:5487 (open access). AI use made people faster, more positive and rated closer, and people were rated more negatively when suspected of using it.

⚠️ What not to use: the workbook's "90% of your warmth comes from voice and face". That is the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule, widely misapplied, and using it on stage in front of anyone who knows the literature costs more than the number is worth. The point survives without it.

Story

⚠️ GAP: no Zeducation story yet. The "Fine." scenario above is a composite written for the topic page, not a real account, and it is labelled as such.

The story to collect: a real one where a short message was misread and it cost something recoverable. The version that lands best is told from the sender's side, by someone who found out weeks later what their message had done, because the audience is full of senders who have never found out.

Ask at the next Module 5 delivery: "has anyone ever discovered, late, that a message of theirs landed completely wrong?" Get permission before it goes near a keynote.

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Today, much of your leading happens through a screen. An email, a chat message, a video call. People form an impression of you from these long before they ever shake your hand. In hybrid work, your digital communication now matters more than a handshake ever did.

The tricky part is that screens strip a lot out. No tone of voice in an email. No body language in a chat. A flat face on a laggy video call. Small things get misread, and a quick message can land far harder than you meant.

This is not just a feeling. Researchers found that people overestimate both how well they convey tone in writing and how well they read other people's, because you hear your own message in the tone you intended and cannot un-hear it (Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng, 2005). Everyone believes they are the exception. Almost nobody is.

In this module you will learn to lead well across the screen. You will choose the right channel for the message, so the important things do not get lost in a chat thread. You will write clear, well-toned digital messages that say what you mean without confusion. You will show a credible presence on video, so people trust the leader they see. And you will work out where your own line sits on using AI, which is now part of how most of us write.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ChannelHow you send it: chat, email, call, video, face to face
Rich channelOne that carries more than words. Tone, face, body language
BLUFBottom Line Up Front. Your main point or ask in the first line
Tone-in-textHow a written message feels to the reader, which is not what you meant
PresenceHow credible and calm you seem on camera, mostly a matter of setup
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Choose the right channel (email, chat, call, video) for the message.
  2. Write clear, well-toned digital messages.
  3. Show credible presence on video.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: You send a one-word reply. "Fine."

You meant it was fine. You were on the tools, you had one hand free, and it was fine.

They read it three times that evening. They showed it to someone else. By the morning they had decided you were annoyed with them, and they came in ready for a conversation you did not know was happening.

Same word. Two completely different messages. You will never find out.

Statement: You are the worst judge of how your own message reads, because you can hear the tone you meant and nobody else can.

➜ Facilitator note: run Read The Room Cold first. Eight ordinary messages, everyone votes on whether the sender is happy or annoyed, and the room splits on every single one. Then tell the story.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

Framework

The Channel-Fit Matrix

Type: Model · Origin: Zeducation house framework, grounded in Media Richness Theory (Daft & Lengel, 1986) · Full page: FRM-013

The same message can land well or badly depending on where you send it. A great message in the wrong channel still fails.

Two questions decide it: how complex is it? (one fact, or many?) and how emotional or sensitive is it? (routine, or will it stir feelings?)

Simple messageComplex or sensitive message
Low emotionChatEmail
High emotionQuick callVideo or in person

How to read this: two questions, four answers. When you are torn between two boxes, go richer.

What each channel carries. Chat is fast but flat, words only, so feelings get lost. Email is clear and gives you a record, but it is slow and easy to misread. A call carries tone of voice. Video and face to face carry tone, face and body language, the full picture.

The golden rule: the harder or more personal the message, the richer the channel. Never deliver bad news, criticism or conflict over text messages.

Why it works: Daft and Lengel's insight was that when a message is open to more than one reading, both people need cues to check they agree, and lean channels do not carry them. Sending a layoff by email is not wrong because email is rude. It is wrong because the message needed cues the channel cannot carry.

More resources

  • 📄 Media richness theory
  • 📄 Channel expansion theory — the main challenge to it
  • 🎬 TED — Tsedal Neeley: 4 ways to make hybrid work better for everyone
Framework

BLUF for Email

Type: Technique · Origin: US Army, formalised in AR 25-50 (1988) · Full page: FRM-005

Once you have chosen email, lead with the bottom line. Most people bury their real ask in paragraph three, and busy readers miss it. BLUF puts your main point or request in the very first line.

Taught in Module 2. In email it matters even more, because people skim. They read the first line, decide if it is urgent, and often stop there. If your ask is at the bottom, it does not exist.

The worked email

Subject: Concrete pour delayed — action needed by 7am Wed Hi Tane, The Level 2 concrete pour is pushed to Thursday. I need the crew re-rostered by 7am tomorrow. ← BLUF The ready-mix supplier can't deliver Wednesday after their truck breakdown, and the slab can't go without it. New delivery is locked in for Thursday 6am. Formwork and steel are already signed off, so we're good to go once the mix lands. ← WHY Please move the pour crew to Thursday and put the framing team on Level 1 Wednesday so no one's standing around. Confirm by 7am. ← ACTION NEEDED Cheers, Pasi

Point at the subject line. It carries the topic and the deadline. Most people would have written "Concrete pour".

More resources

  • 📄 BLUF (communication))
  • 📄 Animalz — the military standard that makes your writing more powerful
Framework

Tone-in-Text

Type: Technique · Origin: Zeducation house framework, grounded in Kruger et al. (2005) · Full page: FRM-014

Text strips out your voice, your smile and your warmth. So the reader supplies their own tone, and when unsure, people assume the worst. A message you meant kindly can read as cold or angry.

How to read this: the middle box does the damage, and you cannot see it from where you are standing.

What goes wrong. A short reply reads as annoyed. A missing "thanks" reads as rude. A full stop after a one-word answer ("Fine.") reads as sharp. ALL CAPS reads as shouting. The reader also brings their own mood, so a neutral message lands badly on someone already stressed.

How to keep tone warm

#Move
1Open with something human before the ask: "Thanks for flagging this."
2Soften instructions: "Could you…" or "When you get a chance…" instead of "Do this."
3Say the positive out loud. The reader cannot see your friendly face
4Re-read it as your most stressed teammate. Could it be misread? Reword it
5Use a name and a sign-off. It makes a message feel personal

Move 4 is the important one, because it is the direct counter to the research finding. You cannot judge your own tone from inside your own head, so read it from somewhere else on purpose.

Reads coldReads warm
"No.""I can't do that one this time, sorry. Could we look at [option] instead?"
"Quick call""Hi Sam, I noticed this isn't done yet, is everything okay? Let me know if you need a hand."
"Fine.""Yep, that works for me, thanks!"

Warm is not longer. "Thanks for flagging this" is four words.

More resources

  • 📄 Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng (2005) — Egocentrism over e-mail (PDF)
  • 📄 APA — E-mails and egos
Framework

The Video Presence Checklist

Type: Tool · Origin: Zeducation house framework, informed by Bailenson (2021) · Full page: FRM-015

On video, people judge your credibility in the first few seconds, before you have said anything worth hearing. The good news: looking calm and capable on camera is mostly setup, not talent.

How to read this: the left branch you fix once. The right branch you practise.

☐ItemWhy
☐Camera at eye level. Raise your laptop on a few booksLooking down at people feels like looking down on them
☐Look at the lens when you speak, not at your own faceThat is how you make eye contact on video
☐Light in front of you, not behind. Face the windowA window behind you turns you into a shadow
☐Quiet, tidy background. Clear the clutter, shut the doorThe background is part of the message
☐Frame head and shoulders, a little space above your headNot too close, not too far
☐Mute when not talkingKills background noise everyone else is straining past
☐Use people's names: "Mere, what's your take?"Quiet people stay quiet on video unless invited
☐Slow down and pauseRushing reads as nervous, pauses read as confident

One more, from the research: hide your own self-view once the call starts. Bailenson's team point out that nobody would work with a mirror held up beside them all day, and that seeing yourself constantly is one of the reasons video calls are so tiring.

More resources

  • 📄 Bailenson (2021) — Nonverbal Overload: causes of Zoom fatigue (PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — four causes of Zoom fatigue and their solutions
Framework

Communicating in the AI Era

Type: Model · Origin: Zeducation house framework, evidenced by Hohenstein et al. (2023) · Full page: FRM-016

AI can now write your emails, summarise your meetings and draft your messages in seconds. Used well, it saves time and sharpens your writing. Used badly, it costs you trust.

The rule: let AI help you think and draft, but you stay the leader.

How to read this: four gates between the draft and the send. Skipping any one of them is where the trust goes.

CheckThe riskWhat you do
VoiceAI writing sounds generic and stiff. If every message sounds like a machine, people stop sensing a real personAlways edit the draft so it sounds like you
TruthAI can be confidently wrong or invent factsCheck anything important before you send. Your name is on it, so you own it
HonestyNever pass off an AI message as something heartfelt, like a condolence or an apologyBe open about routine help. People can tell, and it breaks trust fast
JudgmentAI cannot read the room, weigh someone's feelings, or make the callThat is your job as a leader

The evidence, and both halves of it. A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found that using AI increased speed, increased positive language, and left conversation partners rating each other as closer and more cooperative. It also found people were rated more negatively when their partner suspected AI was involved (Hohenstein et al., 2023).

So the risk is not the tool. It is the gap between what people think you wrote and what you actually wrote.

Good use: "AI, tidy up this long email." Then you cut the stiff bits, add your voice, check the facts, and send. Poor use: copy-pasting an AI-written message of sympathy to a grieving teammate.

More resources

  • 📄 Hohenstein et al. (2023), Scientific Reports
  • 📄 ScienceDaily — social consequences of using AI in conversations

Self-Assessment

How Do I Land On A Screen? — full version and scoring: ACT-028

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I think about which channel a message belongs in before I send it
2⟲ I have delivered bad news or criticism by text or chat
3My subject lines tell the reader the topic and what I need
4My first line contains the main point or the ask
5I re-read a message as the person receiving it before I send
6⟲ People reply to my messages asking what I meant
7I open with something human before the ask
8My camera is at eye level on video calls
9I look at the lens when I speak, not at my own face
10I use people's names on calls to bring quiet people in
11⟲ I have sent an AI-drafted message without editing it into my own voice
12I check the facts in anything AI drafts for me before it goes out
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 2, 6 and 11, flip before adding: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60People get a clear, warm, credible version of you through a screenFix it for your team next. Agree two channel norms with them this month
38-49Strong on some channels, weaker on others. Usually good at email and rough on video, or the reverseFind your weak channel from the item numbers, pick one habit from it
25-37Your messages get there, but they cost the reader effort and sometimes a follow-upStart with item 4. First line, main point, every message, for two weeks
12-24The screen is doing your talking for you and you have not had a say in itPut your camera at eye level today. Two minutes and a couple of books, and it changes every call you make from now on

⚠️ Written by Zeducation to match the house style of How Assertive Am I?. Module 5 of the workbook has no self-assessment of its own. A teaching mirror, not a validated measure.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

This module has five frameworks and five activities, which is more than a single session holds. See the run sheet for which to drop.

Channel Sort · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then small groups

Practises: FRM-013 · Full page: ACT-023

Twelve messages, sorted into chat, email, call or in person. Groups must agree on all twelve, which forces the argument. Three of them are deliberately arguable.

Debrief questions

  • Which ones did your group disagree about?
  • Did anyone choose a channel for the record it leaves rather than the conversation?
  • Which of these have you received in the wrong channel?

BLUF Email Rewrite · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then pairs

Practises: FRM-005 · Full page: ACT-024

Rewrite a rambling steel-order message into the six-part template, subject line included, then do the same to a real email they need to send this week.

Debrief questions

  • What was actually being asked for in the rambler? (Nothing. There is no ask in it at all.)
  • How many of you had to invent the action needed?
  • Whose subject line would you have opened first?

Warm It Up · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then pairs

Practises: FRM-014 · Full page: ACT-025

Twelve cold lines rewritten warm, then a stress test where partners read each other's versions as if already having a terrible day.

Debrief questions

  • Which cold line was hardest to warm up? (Usually the ones with real frustration in them.)
  • Did anyone's warm version lose the message?
  • Partners: what did you catch that they could not?

Video Presence Dry Run · live practice · 20-25 min · pairs or threes

Practises: FRM-015 · Full page: ACT-026

Before shot on the projector, fix the setup, after shot, then 60 seconds of something real.

Debrief questions

  • What surprised you in the before shot?
  • What did hiding your self-view do?
  • Which of these can you fix in the next five minutes?

Make It Human, Draw Your Line · worksheet · 20-25 min · individual then whole class

Practises: FRM-016 · Full page: ACT-027

Humanise a stiff AI draft, draw your own YES/NO line across seven tasks, catch the error in an unverified safety claim, and write your own one-line rule.

Debrief questions

  • What did you cut first? (Almost always "do not hesitate to reach out".)
  • Has anyone received a message they suspected was AI-written? What did it do to how you read it?
  • Whose rule would you steal?
7

Reflection Questions

Notice

  • Which channel do you default to, and is it because it fits the message or because it is easy?
  • What do your messages look like when you are busy? Read the last five you sent
  • If someone only knew you from your messages, what would they think you are like?

Connect

  • When has a message from someone else landed harder than they meant? What did it cost?
  • Have you ever worried about a one-word reply from your boss? What happened?
  • Who on your team have you only ever met through a screen? How well do you actually know them?

Apply

  • Which conversation this week are you having in the wrong channel?
  • What is one message this week you will re-read as your most stressed teammate before you send it?
  • Which video setup fix will you do today?
  • Where is your line on AI, and have you ever said it out loud to your team?

Commit

  • ❑ I want to start…
  • ❑ I want to stop…
  • ❑ I want to continue…

Full closer activity: ACT-013 Start, Stop, Continue

8

Facilitator Notes

This module is overloaded. Five frameworks and five activities is closer to two sessions than one. Two ways to run it:

Option A — one 110 minute session, written channels only

TimeStageWhat happens
0:00SRead The Room Cold, then the "Fine." story and the statement
0:12TThe Channel-Fit Matrix
0:22AChannel Sort
0:40TBLUF for email, using the worked email
0:48ABLUF Email Rewrite
1:05TTone-in-Text, opening with the Kruger finding
1:15AWarm It Up, including the stress test
1:35RSelf-assessment, then Start / Stop / Continue

Video presence and AI move to a second session, or to pre-work.

Option B — two sessions. Session 1 is channel, BLUF and tone. Session 2 is video presence and AI, which is the stronger split because session 2 needs devices and session 1 does not.

  • Common traps: BLUF heard as "be blunt", producing cold emails. Running Warm It Up straight after BLUF fixes this, so keep them adjacent and in that order. Also watch the Channel Sort turning into a twenty-minute argument about edge cases; use "when unsure, go richer" to close it
  • The AI section splits rooms. Some learners use it constantly and some think it is cheating. Lead with the study, because it reports both a real benefit and a real cost, and that keeps the conversation honest instead of tribal. Do not let it become an anti-AI session or a prompting workshop
  • Backgrounds are a class issue. Some learners share a room or have nowhere tidy. Never make a tidy background a standard someone can fail. A plain wall or a virtual background is a fine answer
  • Phone-only groups: the video section works entirely on phones, and propping a phone at eye level against a water bottle is the whole lesson. Do not skip it because there are no laptops
  • Adaptations: for teams from one workplace, the Channel Sort should end with two agreed team norms, which is a real deliverable. For learners writing in a second language, the five tone moves work best as printed sentence-starter cards

⚠️ Open gaps and source corrections

IssueDetail
Self-assessmentHouse-written and unvalidated (flagged above)
"BLUF is from Module 1"The workbook says this. BLUF is taught in Module 2. Fix in the next print run
"90% of your warmth comes from voice and face"A version of the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule, which is widely misapplied. The teaching point survives without the number. Drop it and use Kruger et al. instead. Full explanation on FRM-014
"Stanford research backs this up"Bailenson's work supports the fatigue and nonverbal cost of video calls, not the workbook's claim about decisions. Soften the line or find the study it meant
AI content dates fastRe-check FRM-016 yearly
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

Read The Room Cold · 8-10 min · whole class

Full page: ACT-029

Eight ordinary messages, one at a time. Everyone votes with their hands on whether the sender is happy or annoyed. The room splits on every single one.

The link back: same words, and this room could not agree on one of them. The sender knew exactly what they meant every time. They always do.

Reply In Thirty Seconds · 8 min · pairs

Everyone writes a two-line message asking a colleague for something urgent, in thirty seconds, as they normally would. Swap with a partner who reads it out loud in the flattest, most annoyed voice they can manage.

The link back: nothing in your message stopped them reading it that way. That is not their fault, it is what a lean channel does. Your words are the only tone control you have.

The Subject Line Test · 5 min · whole class · phones

Everyone opens their email and reads out the subject line of the last message they sent. The room votes on whether they would have opened it.

The link back: the most-read and least-written part of any email. Watch how many of them were one word.

From the Ice Breaker Games pillar

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

GameTimeEnergySettingWhy this one here
GAM-008 Spot the Difference8-12 minmediumonline, or in person with imagesBuilt for online, needs no words and no reading
GAM-014 Virtual Pictionary20-30 min🔥 highonline (whiteboard) or in personThe best test there is of whether your channel actually carries what you meant

The trolley was never the problem

placeholder-study
listeningconflictempathycompassioncommunication

Topic: TOP-COM-008 Listen Past The Words · Pillar: Communication

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

People tell you the facts and expect you to hear the values underneath them. Fix the facts, miss the values, and the same conflict comes back next month wearing different clothes.

Nobody is ever as angry as the stated problem justifies. That gap is the actual conversation.

Model

LayerThe question in your headWho usually hears it
Content"What are the facts?"Everyone
Values"What do they care about that is being stepped on?"Almost nobody
Feelings"How is this landing on them?"Some people, guessed at

The middle layer is the one that earns the framework its place. It is the layer that turns a complaint you cannot solve into a conversation you can have.

Metaphor

The iceberg, and it is the source's own.

Only a small portion is visible above the surface. What is showing is the content, the thing they said. The mass underneath is values and feelings, and it is the part that will hole you if you steer by the visible bit alone.

Keep this one. It is the clearest image in the guide and it explains, in one picture, why solving the stated problem so often changes nothing.

Study

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-study. The three layers are Zeducation house content and are not matched to published research.

The nearest evidenced neighbours already in the library: reflective listening in the Carl Rogers lineage (FRM-012) and Egan's active listening (FRM-010).

What to look for: interest-based negotiation, where "listen for the interest behind the position" is the same move under a different name, is the obvious place to ground the values layer properly.

⚠️ And one thing to remove, not add. The source claims "at least 70% of all communication is nonverbal." That is a version of the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule and it does not hold. This is the second Zeducation resource carrying a version of this claim, so it is worth fixing across the whole series. Full note on FRM-014.

Story

The Akanisi case study is the working version and it is house content, not a documented event: asked to lift heavy boxes with no trolley, twice in a week, she arrives furious. Content says trolley. Values say accountability, leadership, safety responsibility. Get her a trolley and she is still not satisfied, because what she said was nobody is looking after us.

⚠️ A collected story would be better. What to look for: a Zeducation facilitator or learner who solved someone's stated problem, watched it come straight back, and found the value underneath on the second attempt. The second attempt is the story.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
The micro-credentialModules 3 and 4. Task 3 is observed and signed
Any frontline or customer-facing trainingThe complaint is rarely about the thing in the complaint
Supervisor and team lead trainingThe single highest-value listening move most managers have never been taught

1

About This Topic

Active listening is a way to hear and respond to another person that increases shared understanding. Improve it and you understand other people's perspectives, emotions and needs better. The ability to hear what another person is actually saying is essential to working through conflict.

Sometimes people's concerns are like an iceberg. Only a small portion is visible above the surface. Listening actively during conflict digs deeper to the root cause, and builds trust between you and the person you are listening to.

Three things stop us listening to the content in the first place. We make assumptions about what they think and what is best for them. We judge, and stop listening because we are busy thinking about how wrong they are. And then we tune out, which is the natural next step. The fix is unglamorous: pay attention, stay focused on the conversation at hand, and put your assumptions aside.

The second half of the topic is what you say back. Most people, having listened well, move straight to fixing. That reads as dismissal however good the fix is.

Compassion literally means "to suffer together." Being compassionate in your response is about connecting what someone said to what they are feeling, out loud, before anything else happens.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ContentThe facts and information. What actually happened
ValuesThe beliefs driving the reaction. Why this one matters so much
Compassion"To suffer together". Feeling moved to relieve someone's difficulty
The icebergThe idea that most of a concern sits below the surface
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Listen for content, values and feelings, and say back what you heard.
  2. Respond to someone's frustration with compassion before offering a solution.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Read this out, angry, the way it would actually be said:

"This company is such a joke! They don't care about our safety or whether someone gets hurt! You should have seen what they told us to do today, lifting and carrying those heavy boxes onto those trucks! Without a single trolley or forklift in sight! Now my back is stuffed, but one of those boxes could have easily fallen over and someone could have been hurt!"

Then ask the room: what does Akanisi want?

Most rooms say a trolley.

Then ask the second question, and let it sit:

If you got her a trolley tomorrow, would she be satisfied?

Statement: People tell you the facts and expect you to hear the values underneath them. Solve the facts and ignore the values, and the same conflict comes back next month wearing different clothes.

➜ Facilitator note: Akanisi is a Fijian name. Say it properly and check with the room. This programme has a whole module about being heard.

5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-038

Powerful Listening — Content, Values, Feelings (house framework)

LayerThe question in your head
1Content"What are the facts here?"
2Values"What do they care about that is being stepped on?"
3Feelings"How is this landing on them?"

How to read it: content is above the water. Values and feelings are underneath, and they are where the conflict actually lives.

The values layer is the one that earns its place, and the one almost no listening training covers. A person furious about a lifting job is usually not angry about boxes. They are angry because they value safety, or fairness, or being treated as though their body matters. A solution built on the value lands. One built on the boxes does not.

Worked example — Akanisi:

LayerWhat you hear
ContentStaff required to lift boxes · second time this week · no trolley or forklift · boxes were heavy
ValuesAccountability · leadership · safety responsibility · organisation
FeelingsAngry, betrayed, frustrated, helpless, hurt

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-039

The Compassionate Response (house framework)

Four sentences that cover most situations:

#What you sayWhen
1"That sounds difficult."Almost always. The safest and most underrated
2"I want to hear more about how that made you feel."You have the facts, not the feelings
3"I'm sorry if I have offended you in any way."You might be part of it
4"Your issue reminds me of a time when I had a similar situation…"You genuinely have one, and briefly

How to read it: the dotted branch is what usually happens. A person who does not feel heard does not stop, they escalate, because escalating is the only tool left.

The permission worth teaching: while it is not about you, reflecting on a time you felt the same way is what lets you say something true rather than something polite. Compassion is a retrieval task, not a personality trait.

⚠️ Response 4 is the risky one. One or two sentences, then hand it straight back: "…but tell me more about yours."

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-010

Active Listening and SOLER

The body half, and it carries the honest critique of the eye-contact instruction that matters for most Zeducation rooms. → Full framework page

⚠️ One correction before you teach Module 4. The source says "most experts agree that at least 70% of all communication is nonverbal." Do not repeat the number. It is a version of the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule, widely misapplied. The true half survives: you communicate with more than words, you are usually unaware of what your body is doing, and in a conflict people read your face before they hear your sentence. Full note on FRM-014.

Self-Assessment

ACT-021 How Well Do I Listen? from Module 4 of the Effective Communication workbook. Already written, already in use, and it covers this territory. No need for a second instrument.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror.

Reflection Questions

  1. What stops you actively listening to others? Be specific about which of the three it is
  2. Think of a time you felt genuinely heard at work. What did the person do?
  3. When did you last solve someone's stated problem and find it did not settle anything?
  4. What do you usually say first when someone comes to you frustrated?
  5. Whose values at work have you never asked about?
  6. What does your face do when you disagree with what you are hearing?
  7. When did someone say "that sounds difficult" to you? What did it change?
  8. Who will you listen to differently this week, and when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min, and ACT-072 needs its full 40. It is the observed assessment
  • The three layers must be filled in one at a time. Learners collapse values and feelings together within a minute
  • ⚠️ Do not fail a learner on eye contact. Item 1 of the observed checklist is culturally loaded. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, direct eye contact with someone senior is disrespectful. Assess presence and attention, and note the adaptation on the sheet
  • What usually goes wrong: the learner names feelings for the other person and calls it listening. "You must be furious" is a guess. "How did that land on you?" is listening
  • Question 3 of ACT-074 can go deep. It asks for a personal experience and it goes to an assessor. Keep it private by default

People follow the one who makes them feel heard
