Topic: TOP-COM-005 Listen To Lead · Module 4

On this pageModel — The 3 Levels of ListeningMetaphor — the two minutes of being ignoredPointStudyStoryWhere this sheet branchesRelated sheets

Model — The 3 Levels of Listening

A ladder, so it builds. Level 1 is not the bottom of a moral ranking, it is the floor everyone starts on. The claim is that leadership happens on the two rungs above it.

Category: why — something builds in stages.

Metaphor — the two minutes of being ignored

Two minutes. Someone you like, looking at their phone while you talk, cutting in, moving you along. Everyone knows the feeling within about fifteen seconds.

The metaphor works because it is not a metaphor, it is an experience you can hand someone in a room. And the thing people report is never "I felt disrespected". It is "I stopped bothering." That is the whole point of the sheet: bad listening does not make people feel bad, it makes them tell you less.

Point

People do not follow the person with the best answers. They follow the person who makes them feel heard.

The consequence version, for when the audience is senior: nobody tells you they have stopped telling you things. They just start giving you the short version, and you find out what was really going on when it is a problem instead of a conversation.

Study

Two, at different strengths, and worth keeping the difference honest:

On de-escalation (moderate). The American Association for Emergency Psychiatry's Project BETA consensus statement names careful listening among its ten domains of verbal de-escalation, and describes the core move as a verbal loop: listen, find something you can genuinely validate, then restate, repeating until it lands (Richmond et al., 2012, Western Journal of Emergency Medicine). Expert consensus, not a trial, and clinical rather than workplace. Say so.

On the model itself (practitioner). The 3 Levels come from Co-Active Coaching (Whitworth, Kimsey-House, Kimsey-House, Sandahl). Widely taught, no trial evidence. Co-Active® is trademarked, so attribute and never imply certification.

The honest critique worth carrying: SOLER, the other framework in this module, was challenged by Stickley (2011) for being taught for thirty years without scrutiny and for producing mechanical behaviour. Using that critique on stage is stronger than hiding it, because it lets you make the cultural point about eye contact without it sounding like a caveat.

Story

⚠️ GAP: no Zeducation story yet. This sheet needs a real one.

The story to collect: a leader who found something out too late, and could name the moment they were told and did not hear it. The detail that makes it land is that they were told, at Level 1, and it did not register.

The alternative, warmer story: a Zeducation learner whose team started telling them things after they changed one habit. Ask in the Module 4 debrief, "has anyone had someone open up to you since we did this?" Collect it with permission.

Where this sheet branches

Future sheetThe Point it would make
Level 1Listening to reply is not a character flaw, it is the default setting. The skill is catching yourself on it
Level 3Noticing is not the same as diagnosing. Level 3 ends in a question, not a verdict
Reflect before you fixA good solution offered too early is heard as not listening
The visible halfListening is invisible. If they cannot tell, it does not count

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

We often think leading is about talking. But the best leaders are the best listeners. People do not follow someone who only waits for their turn to speak. They follow someone who makes them feel heard.

Listening is not just staying quiet. It is paying full attention so you understand the person before you respond. When you really listen, you pick up what matters: the facts, the feelings, and the things left unsaid.

The cost of not doing it is invisible, which is why it goes unfixed. People do not tell you they have stopped telling you things. They just start giving you the short version. By the time you find out what was actually going on, it is a problem rather than a conversation.

In this module you will learn to listen in a way that builds trust. You will use active listening to understand before you respond, instead of jumping in with your own view. You will practise paraphrasing and reflecting, saying back what you heard, so small misunderstandings get caught early. And you will learn to de-escalate tension by listening first, because people calm down once they feel understood, and only then can they hear you.

Listen well, and people open up, trust you, and follow you. It is the quiet skill behind every strong leader.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Active listeningFocusing fully on the person and holding your own reply back
SOLERFive body-language reminders that make your attention visible
ParaphrasingSaying back the content in your own words, to check the facts
ReflectingNaming the feeling you are picking up, to check the emotion
De-escalateBring the heat down, usually by making someone feel heard before you fix anything
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Use active listening to understand before responding.
  2. Apply paraphrasing and reflecting to reduce misunderstanding.
  3. De-escalate tension by listening first.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Think of the person you would go to if something went wrong at work. Not the smartest person you know. Not the most senior. The one you would actually go to.

Now think about what they do. They almost certainly do not have better advice than everyone else. What they have is that when you talk, they stop. They are not waiting for a gap. You can feel the difference, and that feeling is the reason you would pick them.

Statement: People do not follow the person with the best answers. They follow the person who makes them feel heard.

➜ Facilitator note: run Tell It Back before the story, or Bad Listening, Then SOLER if the room needs waking up rather than warming up. Both earn the story better than the story earns itself.

5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

Framework

Active Listening and SOLER

Type: Technique · Origin: Gerard Egan, The Skilled Helper (1975) · Full page: FRM-010

Most people listen to reply, not to understand. Active listening flips that. You give the speaker your full attention so they feel heard, and SOLER is a simple way to show it with your body.

How to read this: SOLER is the body half of listening, the part the other person can see. On its own it is just posture, so it always runs with holding your reply back.

LetterStands forWhat you do
SSquareFace the person, so they have your attention
OOpenOpen posture. No crossed arms, no turning away
LLeanLean in slightly to show interest
EEye contactComfortable eye contact, not a stare
RRelaxStay calm and unhurried, so they feel safe

A note on culture: in some Pacific, Māori and other cultures, direct eye contact can feel disrespectful, especially with elders. Read the person in front of you and adjust.

There is published criticism of SOLER on exactly this ground. Stickley (2011) argued the model had been taught for thirty years without real scrutiny and produces mechanical behaviour rather than genuine attention. His alternative, SURETY, sits at an angle rather than square on, and adds your intuition as a step. Teach SOLER as a starting checklist, and say plainly that a good listener adapts it.

Why it matters for leaders: people share more, trust more, and stay calmer when they feel truly heard. Half of leading is listening well.

More resources

  • 📄 Counselling Tutor — Egan's SOLER model
  • 📄 Stickley (2011) — From SOLER to SURETY
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: 5 ways to listen better (about 8 min) — his RASA sequence works well in session
  • 🎬 TED — Celeste Headlee: 10 ways to have a better conversation (about 12 min)
Framework

The 3 Levels of Listening

Type: Model · Origin: Co-Active Coaching — Whitworth, Kimsey-House, Kimsey-House and Sandahl · Full page: FRM-011

Not all listening is equal. There are three levels, and most of us get stuck on the lowest one.

How to read this: bottom to top. Level 1 is not a failure, it is where everyone starts. Leading happens at 2 and 3.

LevelWhere your attention isYou know you are here when
1 — InternalOn yourselfYou are working out what to say next, or what this means for you
2 — FocusedOn the other personYou forget about yourself for a moment
3 — GlobalOn everything around itYou notice feelings, body language, the energy in the room, the unsaid

Worked example. A worker says they are "fine".

LevelWhat happens
1You take the word and move on, already thinking about your next task
2You hear how they said it, flat and quiet, and you stay with them
3You notice they will not meet your eye, their shoulders are tense, the room has gone quiet. You gently ask if they are really okay

Why it works: Level 1 is normal in a quick chat. But leaders need to move to 2 and 3 in the moments that matter, when someone is upset, unsure, or trying to tell you something hard. Once you can hear yourself sitting at Level 1, you can choose to move.

More resources

  • 📄 Co-Active Training Institute — the three levels of listening
  • 📄 International Coaching Federation — the three layers of listening
Framework

Paraphrasing and Reflecting

Type: Technique · Origin: reflective listening, from Carl Rogers' person-centred counselling · Full page: FRM-012

The fastest way to avoid a misunderstanding is to say back what you heard. These two prove you listened and let the other person correct you if you got it wrong.

How to read this: two moves off the same listening. Most people only ever do the first one.

ParaphrasingReflecting
What you say backThe content, in your own wordsThe feeling you are picking up
What it checksYou understood the factsYou understood the emotion
Sounds like"So the order is delayed and you need a new date by Friday, is that right?""It sounds like that really frustrated you."

This is sometimes called mirroring. The skill behind it is noticing the feeling under the words, in their tone, face and body.

De-escalation rule: when someone is upset, reflect the feeling before you try to fix anything. People cannot hear solutions until they feel heard. "I can see you're really annoyed about this, let's sort it out together."

Worked examples

  • Worker: "I've asked three times and nothing's changed." Paraphrase: "So you've raised this a few times and still nothing's moved." Reflect: "I can hear how frustrating that is."
  • Customer: "This is the second time it's broken." Reflect first: "That's really disappointing, especially twice." Then fix.

Why it works: when people feel understood, they calm down and open up. It also catches mistakes early, before they grow into bigger problems. Clinical de-escalation guidance teaches the same order, listing careful listening among its ten domains and describing a verbal loop of listening, validating and restating (Richmond et al., 2012).

More resources

  • 📄 Richmond et al. (2012) — Verbal De-escalation of the Agitated Patient
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: 5 ways to listen better — the "S" in RASA is summarising, which is paraphrasing under another name

Self-Assessment

How Well Do I Listen? — full version and scoring: ACT-021

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I let people finish before I respond
2⟲ While someone is talking, I am working out what I will say next
3I put my phone down and face the person when it matters
4I say back what I heard, to check I got it right
5I notice when someone's tone does not match their words
6⟲ I jump to solving the problem before the person has finished describing it
7When someone is upset, I name the feeling before I offer a fix
8I ask questions to understand, not to make a point
9⟲ I finish other people's sentences for them
10People tell me things they have not told other people
11I notice what is not being said in a meeting
12I can repeat back what someone told me yesterday
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 2, 6 and 9, flip before adding: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60People feel heard around you, and it is why they tell you thingsNotice which conversations you still rush. Usually the people you find hard
38-49You listen well when you are calm, which is not when it is most neededPick your worst listening moment of the day and do one paraphrase in it
25-37You are hearing the words and missing the restOne move: before you reply, say back what you heard. Just that, for two weeks
12-24Honest scoring here takes more self-awareness than most people havePhone face down for one conversation a day, and let the person finish without interrupting once

⚠️ Written by Zeducation to match the house style of How Assertive Am I?. Module 4 of the workbook has no self-assessment of its own. A teaching mirror, not a validated measure.

Item 10 is the one to point at. It is the only item that measures the result rather than the behaviour, and it is the one that changes people's minds about their score.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

Bad Listening, Then SOLER · paired experience · 15-20 min · pairs

Practises: FRM-010 · Full page: ACT-018

Round 1: Person B listens badly on purpose for two minutes. Round 2: swap, and listen with all five SOLER steps. Then name your strong step and your step to grow.

Debrief questions

  • Speakers in round one: how long before you wanted to stop talking?
  • Did anyone shorten what they were going to say? (That is the real cost. Bad listening changes what people tell you.)
  • Listeners in round one: how easy was it? Be honest.

Which Level Am I On? · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then whole class

Practises: FRM-011 · Full page: ACT-019

Ten statements, sorted into Level 1, 2 or 3. Item 8 is deliberately arguable and the argument teaches more than the answer key.

Debrief questions

  • Which level are you on most of the time at work?
  • What pulls you down to Level 1? (Usually the phone, being busy, or already knowing the answer.)
  • Who do you know who listens at Level 3? What do they actually do?

Reflect Before You Fix · roleplay · 20-25 min · pairs

Practises: FRM-012 · Full page: ACT-020

Paraphrase practice, then reflect-the-feeling practice, then a de-escalation roleplay where Person B must reflect before offering any fix at all.

Debrief questions

  • How long did you last before you wanted to fix it?
  • Upset people: what did the reflect line do to your temperature?
  • Did anyone name the wrong feeling? What happened next? (Being corrected is a good outcome.)
7

Reflection Questions

Notice

  • Which level of listening are you on with the person you work most closely with?
  • What does your body do when you have already decided what you think?
  • Which SOLER step do you do naturally, and which one do you have to remember?

Connect

  • Tell us about a time someone really listened to you. What did they do?
  • When did not listening cost you something at work? What did you find out too late?
  • Has anyone ever stopped telling you things? How did you find out?

Apply

  • Who at work needs you to listen this week rather than solve?
  • Where does someone arrive at you already upset, and what will your first line be?
  • What is one meeting this week where you will listen at Level 3 and say what you notice?

Commit

  • ❑ I want to start…
  • ❑ I want to stop…
  • ❑ I want to continue…

Full closer activity: ACT-013 Start, Stop, Continue

8

Facilitator Notes

Suggested run sheet (110 min)

TimeStageWhat happens
0:00STell It Back, then the story and the statement
0:15ABad Listening, Then SOLER, round one only. Debrief it properly
0:25TSOLER, arriving as the fix for what they just felt
0:32ARound two, then the strong step / step to grow reflection
0:45TThe 3 Levels of Listening
0:55AWhich Level Am I On?
1:10TParaphrasing and Reflecting, including the de-escalation rule
1:20AReflect Before You Fix
1:45RSelf-assessment, then Start / Stop / Continue
  • The single most important sequencing note in this module: run bad listening before teaching SOLER. Every facilitator is tempted to teach the model first. Do not. Being ignored for two minutes is the lesson, and SOLER is only the fix
  • Common traps: learners overacting SOLER and looking unhinged, so say "slightly" and mean it. Learners treating Level 1 as a moral failure, which makes the room defensive and stops the honesty. And learners who leave keen to announce what everyone is feeling, when Level 3 is noticing and asking, not diagnosing
  • The eye contact conversation is not optional. Say the cultural note out loud before the SOLER round, not after. Nobody should sit through this module concluding they listen wrongly because of how they were raised
  • Non-office groups: most of the real listening in these jobs happens side by side, in the ute, at the bench, walking to the car, not sitting square on across a desk. Say so, and use Stickley's sit-at-an-angle point rather than pretending otherwise
  • Adaptations: for phone and contact centre roles, run round two back to back so every SOLER step has to become a voice behaviour. For second-language learners, sentence-starter cards do most of the work in the paraphrasing activity

⚠️ Open gaps: the self-assessment is house-written and unvalidated (flagged above). The 3 Levels model is practitioner material with no trial evidence, and Co-Active® is a registered trademark, so teach with attribution and never imply certification. No NZ evidence yet on listening and aggression or de-escalation in frontline work, which is the gap most worth filling for this module.

9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

Tell It Back · 10-12 min · whole class

Full page: ACT-022

Ninety seconds each in pairs, no notes, then everyone introduces their partner to the room in the first person. The partner gets one sentence to correct anything wrong.

The link back: the corrections were mostly small, because when you actually listen you get it right. Most misunderstandings are not hard problems, they are ninety seconds nobody gave.

Bad Listening, Then SOLER · 15-20 min · pairs

Full page: ACT-018

Doubles as the opener and the first activity. Two minutes of being ignored teaches more about listening than any diagram.

The link back: you already know how to listen. The question is whether the other person can tell.

The Ten-Second Gap · 3 min · whole class · no materials

In pairs, Person A asks a question. Person B must wait a full ten seconds, counted silently, before answering. Then swap. Nobody manages it the first time.

The link back: that itch you felt at about second four is the thing that makes you interrupt. It is not urgency, it is discomfort with silence, and it is costing you the second half of what people tell you.

PS-COM-003Pink Sheet · Communication

The flight is judged on the landing

placeholder-story
clear-messagingblufleadershipteams

Topic: Make Your Message Land · Pillar: Communication · ID: PS-COM-003

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStory

Point

A message is not finished when you have said it. It is finished when it has landed. Which means clarity is not a courtesy you extend to your team. It is the job. If they did not get it, you did not do it.

Model

BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front. One line on top, everything else underneath.

How to read it: if they stop reading after line one, they still know what you need.

Metaphor

The landing. A plane can take off well and fly smoothly, but none of that matters if it cannot land. The whole point of the flight is the landing. A good communicator, like a good pilot, lines up early and brings it down on the runway every time.

The useful extension: pilots do not land well because they are naturally gifted at landing. They land well because it is a trained procedure they run the same way every time, including on the days they are tired. Clear communication works the same way.

Study

BLUF is not a productivity fad. The US Army formalised it in AR 25-50 (1988), and the reasoning in the Army's own writing guidance is blunt: the greatest weakness in ineffective writing is that it does not quickly transmit a focused message. An institution where a missed point can cost a life decided the point goes first (BLUF)).

The same logic sits under NZ workplace safety practice. WorkSafe treats pre-work briefings as a standard way to tell workers what is happening, what the risks are, and whether they are ready (WorkSafe NZ). Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, informing workers of risk is a duty, not a nicety.

Story

⚠️ GAP: story needed. The strongest version is a real one, and this sheet is waiting for it. Collect either:

  • a Zeducation learner whose briefing habit changed something measurable on their site, or
  • Pasi's own story of a message that did not land and what it cost.

Interim version a facilitator can use: run the Whisper Chain and let the room supply the story. The same message goes down two lines, one rambling and one bottom-line-first. Only one arrives. Nobody argues with a message they watched fall apart in their own hands.

Use this sheet for: workshop opener · leadership keynote · LinkedIn post · employer proposal on briefing and safety culture

TOP-COM-003Topic · Communication

Make Your Message Land

✅ publishedCommunicationFoundation90-120 minEffective Communication workbook, Module 2
clear-messagingblufprepbriefingtoolbox-talkwritten-communicationteams

Pillar: Communication · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-COM-003 · Module 2 of the Effective Communication workbook · 🩷 Pink Sheet

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Effective communication is sharing your message in a way that others clearly understand, and listening so you truly understand them too. It is not just talking. It is making sure the meaning lands.

A leader's job is to get things done through people. If your team does not understand the goal, the plan, or what you expect, they cannot follow you. Most problems at work, like missed deadlines, mistakes and conflict, come from poor communication, not lack of skill. When a leader communicates well, the whole team moves faster and trusts more.

What a good communicator looks like. They lead with the main point, so you know what they want straight away. They keep it simple, using plain words everyone understands. They check for understanding instead of assuming. They listen as much as they speak and repeat things back: "So you're worried about the deadline, is that right?" They read the room and adapt to the person in front of them. When they finish, people know what was said, what it means, and what to do next.

The best part is that this is a skill, not a talent. Like landing a plane, it can be learned with practice, which makes it one of the highest-value things any leader can develop.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Bottom lineThe one thing you need the other person to know or do
BLUFBottom Line Up Front. Putting that one thing in your first line
ChannelHow you send it: face to face, phone, email, chat, video call
BriefingA short talk before a job that tells the team what, why and how
Check for understandingAsking, rather than assuming, that the message landed
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Structure a message so the key point lands first.
  2. Give clear instructions and updates with less back-and-forth.
  3. Adapt the message to the audience and the channel.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A plane can take off well and fly smoothly, but none of that matters if it cannot land. The whole point of the flight is the landing.

Your message is the same. You can have a smart idea and the right words, but if it does not land clearly in the other person's mind, it has failed. A good communicator, like a good pilot, lines up early and brings it down on the runway every time.

Statement: A message is not finished when you have said it. It is finished when it has landed.

➜ Facilitator note: run the Whisper Chain before you say any of this. Let them watch a message fall apart, then give them the plane. The story lands harder after the game than before it.

5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

Framework

BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front

Type: Technique · Origin: US Army, formalised in AR 25-50 (1988) · Full page: FRM-005

Put the most important point, your conclusion or your request, right at the start, instead of building up to it at the end.

How to read this: if the reader stops after line one, they still know what you need.

StepWhat you do
1Decide your one key message
2Say it in the first line
3Add the supporting detail underneath
4Close with the action: who, what, by when

Worked example: "I need 4 more labourers on site Monday to hit the concrete pour deadline. We're a day behind from the rain. Can you confirm by Friday so I can book them?"

Why it works: busy people do not have to read to the end to know what you need. It speeds up decisions, cuts confusion, and the opening point is the part people remember. It started in the US military, where people had to act fast and could not waste time digging for the main point.

The quick fix: write the message however it comes out, then look at your last paragraph. Your conclusion is usually sitting there. Move it to the top.

More resources

  • 📄 BLUF (communication) — Wikipedia)
  • 📄 Animalz — the military standard that makes your writing more powerful
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen (10 min, one of TED's most-watched talks)
Framework

PREP — Point, Reason, Example, Point

Type: Tool (structure) · Origin: public speaking practice, taught by Toastmasters International · Full page: FRM-006

A simple way to structure your thinking so people understand you the first time.

How to read this: you start at the conclusion and end at the conclusion. The middle is the evidence.

StepExample
Point"We should hold a safety briefing every morning."
Reason"Most accidents happen in the first hour of work."
Example"Last month a two-minute briefing stopped a forklift near-miss."
Point"So let's make the morning briefing part of every shift."

Why it works: you start with your conclusion instead of building up to it. Busy people get your message straight away, follow your reasoning as you go, and are never left guessing what you mean. It also makes you sound organised and credible, because it shows you have thought your position through.

When to use it: taking a position — a recommendation, feedback, solving a problem, persuading a team. When not to: brainstorming or open chats, where you want to explore ideas rather than push one view.

More resources

  • 📄 Toastmasters International — 90 tips, including PREP
  • 📄 Beverly Landais — tips to PREP for effective communication
Framework

The What-Why-How Briefing Framework

Type: Tool (template) · Origin: Zeducation house framework · Full page: FRM-007

When giving instructions, people need information to be clear and simple. This framework helps leaders explain tasks so the team understands exactly what to do and how to do it safely. It also helps team members follow instructions and ask better questions.

How to read this: the first three are the leader talking. The fourth is the one people skip, and it is the one that turns a presentation into a briefing.

The questionWhy it is there
WhatWhat are we doing today?Clear direction, so everyone knows what they are doing
WhyWhy is this important?Safety, customers, timelines or teamwork. When people understand the why, they are more engaged
HowHow do we do it safely and correctly?The steps, safety requirements, risks and expectations

Briefing plan template

FocusNotes
What? What are we doing today?
Why? Why is this important?
How? How do we do this safely and correctly?
Risks / safety checks. What do we watch out for?
Team input. Questions, concerns, suggestions
Confirmation. Does everyone understand the plan?☐ Yes ☐ Need clarification

Key note: a strong briefing is a team conversation, not a leader presentation.

Worked example (site): "What: we're pouring the slab on the east side today. Why: the weather's clear this morning and the framers can't start until it's cured. How: pump arrives 7:30, Sione and Tama on the screed, everyone else clearing the run first. Hi-vis and boots, nobody walks behind the pump truck. Anything I've missed?"

More resources

  • 📄 WorkSafe NZ — pre-work briefings and inductions
  • 📄 Site Safe NZ — toolbox talks

Self-Assessment

How Clear Am I? — full version and scoring: ACT-012

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I say the main point in the first line of a message
2People do the thing I asked for without needing a follow-up message
3I know what I want to say before I start saying it
4I use plain words instead of jargon my team may not know
5I back up my recommendations with a real example

7I check understanding rather than assuming people got it
8I choose the channel to fit the message
9My messages are short enough that people read all of them
10When I brief a team, other people talk too
11I ask for the specific action I want, with a deadline
12People rarely misunderstand what I meant
Total

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60Your messages land. People know what you mean and what to doTeach it. Fix one team member's briefing habit this month
38-49Clear most of the time, and it slips when you are busyNotice which situations cost you clarity. Rushed messages are usually the culprit
25-37Middle of the road. Your point is in there, but people have to digStart with BLUF. First line, main point, every message for two weeks

⚠️ This instrument was written by Zeducation to match the house style of How Assertive Am I?. Module 2 of the workbook has no self-assessment of its own. It is a teaching mirror, not a validated measure.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

BLUF Rewrite Lab · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then pairs

Practises: FRM-005 · Full page: ACT-007

Part 1: find the buried bottom line in a real message and rewrite it. Part 2: fix a rambling message about a kitchen roster. Part 3: rewrite a real message they need to send this week.

Debrief questions

  • What was the giveaway that told you which sentence was the bottom line?
  • What got cut, and did the message lose anything real?
  • When would opening this directly be the wrong move?

Make It PREP · worksheet · 15-20 min · individual then whole class

Practises: FRM-006 · Full page: ACT-008

Part 1: label the four parts of a worked example. Part 2: build the case for giving new starters a buddy. Part 3: on the spot — 30 seconds to think, then PREP out loud in under a minute.

Debrief questions

  • Which part was hardest to write? (Usually the Example.)
  • What happens to a case with no example in it?
  • Whose PREP would you have said yes to, and why?

Briefing Roleplay — What, Why, How · roleplay · 30-40 min · groups of 4-6

Practises: FRM-007 · Full page: ACT-009

One person leads, everyone else is the crew — and the crew's job is to ask questions, confirm understanding, raise safety concerns and share ideas. Scenarios: starting a task on a busy site, conditions changed before work begins, a new worker joins the shift, a safety risk is identified, equipment or vehicle movement creates hazards.

Debrief questions

  • Leaders: which of the three questions was hardest to fill in?
  • Crew: at what point did you actually understand what you were doing?
  • Who raised something the leader had not thought of?
7

Reflection Questions

Notice

  • Think of a message you sent this week. Where was the main point, first line or last?
  • When you brief someone, do you tell them why, or only what?

Connect

  • When has a message from someone else not landed with you? What did it cost?
  • Who at your work communicates so clearly you never have to check? What do they actually do?
  • When did you last have to send a second message to explain the first one?

Apply

  • What is one message this week you will write bottom line first?
  • Where will you use PREP: a recommendation, a piece of feedback, or a problem you want fixed?
  • Which briefing will you run with What, Why, How, and who will you ask for input?

Commit

  • ❑ I want to start…
  • ❑ I want to stop…
  • ❑ I want to continue…

Full closer activity: ACT-013 Start, Stop, Continue

Facilitator Notes

Suggested run sheet (110 min)

TimeStageWhat happens
0:00SWhisper Chain, then the landing-the-plane story and the statement
0:15TBLUF, rewrite a real message live on the whiteboard
0:25ABLUF Rewrite Lab
0:45TPREP
0:55AMake It PREP, including the on-the-spot round
1:15TWhat-Why-How and the briefing template
1:25ABriefing Roleplay

  • Common traps: learners hearing BLUF as "be blunt" and dropping every greeting. Say early that BLUF is not "no manners", it is the point moving up. Also watch for the briefing roleplay turning into a leader monologue while the crew nods
  • Non-site groups: the briefing framework is written in site language. It works unchanged for a kitchen service, a retail shift change, an aged care handover or a call centre campaign. Swap the scenario, keep the structure
  • The strongest sequence is game first, then story, then tool. Watching a message fall apart earns the theory
  • Adaptations: for low literacy, run the BLUF lab spoken rather than written and use the briefing template as prompts, not a form. For crews with English as a second language, slow down on How and confirm understanding individually rather than as a group

⚠️ Open gaps: the self-assessment is house-written and unvalidated (flagged above). The workbook has no video suggestions of its own, so the ones here are researched additions. No NZ statistic yet on the cost of unclear workplace communication.

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

Whisper Chain — The Message That Didn't Land · 10-12 min · lines of 6-8

Full page: ACT-010

Two rounds of the classic whisper game with the same information: round one rambling, round two BLUF. Round one comes out mangled. Round two survives.

The link back: short, ordered, specific messages survive the trip. Rambling ones were never going to. A message is not finished when you have said it.

Bury the Lede Race · 8-10 min · teams of 3-4

Full page: ACT-011

Teams race to find the one real bottom line in a rambling message. Final round reversed: 60 seconds to write the waffliest possible version of a clear sentence.

The link back: you just did in ten seconds what your reader does in two. If your point is not findable that fast, it is not landing.

The One-Breath Brief · 3 min · whole class · no materials

Everyone gets one breath to explain what they did at work yesterday. When they run out of air, they stop, mid-sentence or not.

The link back: notice who got to the point and who was still setting the scene. Your reader has about that much patience.

PS-COM-009Pink Sheet · Communication

A solution offered too early is an argument

placeholder-study
conflictconflict-resolutionde-escalationproblem-solvingcommunication

Topic: TOP-COM-009 Moving To Resolution · Pillar: Communication

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

A solution offered before someone feels heard is not a solution. It is an argument with a helpful tone, and it will be resisted no matter how good it is.

The order is the method. Everything else is detail.

Model

Gather, then test. Two modes, one at a time.

The five test questions: How would this work? · What will it do for you? · Is it actually possible? · What are the strengths? · What might be the limitations?

And the six steps for when it is too hot to get there at all:

123456
Stay calmOpen body languageListen activelyShow empathySolution togetherTake a break

Steps 1 and 2 are yours. Steps 3 and 4 are load-bearing. Step 6 is the one nobody uses and the most useful when someone is past hearing anything.

Metaphor

Two different tools, and people reach for the wrong one.

Gathering ideas is a net. You want everything in it, including the rubbish, because you cannot tell from the surface which fish is worth keeping.

Testing is a sieve. It only works on what you already caught.

Most people bring the sieve to the netting and wonder why they end up with three ideas, all of them the ones they already had.

Study

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-study. Both frameworks are house content with no citation in the source.

The de-escalation gap is the one that matters. De-escalation is a well developed field across health, mental health services and frontline safety, with real evidence behind it. The six steps here are sensible and uncited. Grounding them properly is worth doing before they are taught as fact, and WorkSafe NZ guidance on managing customer aggression would put it on a local footing.

The gather-then-test half rests on standard divergent-then-convergent problem-solving practice, which is well supported elsewhere and simply not referenced here.

⚠️ A safety note that belongs on the sheet, not just the topic page. De-escalation is not a substitute for leaving. If someone is threatening, the move is to get out and get help. Any teaching of this must name the workplace's escalation path.

Story

The reception desk version is the working one: a guest angry that his room is not ready, met once with a correct explanation delivered at speed while he is still talking, and once with folded arms unfolded, a sentence naming how he feels, and then "what would help most right now?" He asks to leave his bags. Ninety seconds. Nothing about the room changed, only the order of the sentences.

⚠️ It is illustrative, not documented. What to collect: a real one from a Zeducation client in tourism, hospitality or retail, where somebody used step 6 and it worked. Step 6 stories are rare because taking a break feels like losing, and one real example would teach it better than any explanation.

Supervisor trainingThe "ask before you offer" move is the cheapest habit change available

1

About This Topic

This is the last stage, and it only works if the others have happened. When you have named the conflict and actually listened to it, you are ready for a solution, and it is time to gather ideas.

The first move is to encourage others to share what they want and need to resolve the conflict. Ask: "I'd like to hear your thoughts on how you would like this to be resolved." An open question, asked of the person in the conflict, moves them from complaining to problem-solving in one sentence.

Then listen and list every solution, all of them, even the ones that seem silly or impossible. Not every idea will end up being used, and brainstorming only works if everything is considered first. Encouraging creativity generates a wide variety of options, and that prevents everyone from being limited by the dynamics that created the problem in the first place.

Then you test. The key here is being curious, not persuasive.

The topic also carries de-escalation: calming a tense situation before it becomes a serious conflict, by staying calm, listening, and working together to solve a problem peacefully. That is the skill for when it is going wrong in front of you and there is no time for anything else.

Key words

WordWhat it means
BrainstormGathering ideas with no judging, on purpose
De-escalationCalming a tense situation before it becomes serious conflict
TestingGetting to know an idea's strengths and limitations by asking, not arguing
Curious questioningQuestions that get information, rather than opinions with a question mark
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Gather every possible solution without judging any of them, then test each one.
  2. Calm a tense situation using the six de-escalation steps.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A guest is at reception, angry, because his room is not ready. He has travelled all day.

Version one: the staff member explains the booking system. Correctly. At speed. While he is still talking. He gets louder, because being explained at while upset is its own insult.

Version two: she stops. Unfolds her arms. Lets him finish. Says "I understand you're upset, you've travelled all day and the room isn't ready." Then, only then, "What would help most right now?"

He asks to leave his bags and get a coffee. Ninety seconds, no manager needed.

Ask the room: what was different?

Nothing about the room changed. The order of the sentences did.

Statement: A solution offered before someone feels heard is not a solution. It is an argument with a helpful tone.

4

Frameworks Used

IDFrameworkPage
FRM-040Moving to Resolution→

5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-040

Moving to Resolution — gather, then test (house framework)

The five test questions:

#Question
1How would this work?
2What will this do for you if you decide to go with this?
3Is it actually possible to do?
4What are the strengths?
5What might be the limitations?

Why the two halves stay separate: judging while gathering kills the gathering. The moment one idea is criticised, people stop offering unusual ones, and the unusual ones are why you widened the list. Gather with no evaluation, then evaluate with no new ideas.

Worked example — Owairua, who is doing constant overtime and feels he is carrying the team. Solutions listed without filtering include: talk to the team about breaks · ask if he needs time off · review roles and delegate · commit him to leaving on time · ask more questions to check the real issue · ask him what solution he would choose.

Note that two of the six are about understanding the problem better. A brainstorm that produces only actions has usually skipped a step. Then test: "commit him to leaving on time" fails question 3 immediately, because the work still has to be done by somebody. "Review roles and delegate" survives all five.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-041

De-escalation — six steps (house framework)

StepActionWhat it sounds like
1Stay calmTake a deep breath. Speak gently
2Use open body languageRelax your posture. Keep arms uncrossed
3Listen activelyLet them speak. Show you are listening with nods
4Show empathy"I understand you're upset."
5Work on a solution together"What would help us move forward?"
6Take a break if needed"Let's pause and talk again shortly."

How to read it: 1 to 5 are a sequence. Step 6 is an exit available at any point, and using it early is a skill rather than a failure.

Steps 1 and 2 are yours and come first, because you cannot de-escalate anyone while your own heart rate is climbing. Steps 3 and 4 are load-bearing, and most attempts skip from 2 to 5, which reads as "stop being upset so we can move on". Step 6 is the one nobody uses, and the phrasing matters: "let's pause and talk again shortly" names a return.

⚠️ Safety. De-escalation is not a substitute for leaving. If someone is threatening, or there is any risk of harm, the move is to get out and get help. Every workplace teaching this should name its own line and its escalation path.

→ Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-079 How Do I Handle Conflict? Ten statements, 1 to 3. Statements 8 and 9 are this topic's: do you ask how they would like it resolved before suggesting anything, and can you take a break without it feeling like giving up?

Statement 10 is the one almost nobody scores well on: I go back and check whether a resolution actually held. Most people treat a resolved conflict as finished. Going back a fortnight later is rare, cheap, and the reason some resolutions stick.

⚠️ Not validated, and it carries no assessment weight.

Reflection Questions

  1. When did you last offer a solution before the person felt heard? What happened?
  2. What is the difference between asking "what would help?" and offering what you think would help?
  3. Which of the six de-escalation steps disappears first when you are under pressure?
  4. When have you taken a break in a conversation? What made you able to?
  5. Where is your workplace's line between de-escalating and getting help? Do you know it?
  6. Think of a resolution that did not hold. What was missing?
  7. Whose solution have you never asked for?
  8. What is the one technique from this programme you will actually use, with whom, and when?

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min without the capstone filming, which needs its own session
  • Do not run this topic first. The source is explicit that resolution comes after listening, and a room taught to brainstorm before it has been taught to listen will solve the wrong problem confidently
  • ⚠️ Safety, said out loud before the drill. De-escalation is not a substitute for leaving. Name the workplace's escalation path in the room
  • The drill can activate real memories for anyone who has faced aggression at work. Let people sit a round out with no explanation
  • What usually goes wrong in ACT-075: people filter during the five minute brainstorm. It breaks within forty seconds. Remind them mid-timer
  • ⚠️ Open gap: the six de-escalation steps come with no citation in the source, and de-escalation is a well developed field in health and frontline safety. Ground it before it is taught as fact. WorkSafe guidance on customer aggression would put it on a local footing

PS-COM-007Pink Sheet · Communication

Two hours a week is the price of avoiding it

placeholder-story
conflictconflict-resolutionteamscommunication

Topic: TOP-COM-007 Not All Conflict Is The Same · Pillar: Communication

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

Conflict does not cost you two hours a week. Avoiding conflict costs you two hours a week. Dealing with it costs twenty minutes, once.

The bill arrives either way. The only choice is whether you pay it in one instalment or in instalments forever.

Model

TypeAboutSurvivable alone?
TaskThe work itself, and what the goal isYes, and often useful
ProcessWho does what, and howYes, and it drifts fastest
RelationshipThe peopleThis is the destructive one

The dotted arrows are the whole diagram. Left alone, everything becomes relationship conflict, because arguing about who does what is one step from arguing about who someone is.

The diagnostic question: if the work question were settled tomorrow, would these two be fine?

Metaphor

A dripping tap.

Nobody calls a plumber for a drip. It is not an emergency, it does not stop you using the sink, and dealing with it means finding someone and taking an afternoon off.

So you leave it, and it costs you a little every single day, and eventually it is not a tap problem, it is a floor problem.

Study

Two, doing different jobs.

Karen A. Jehn (1995, 1997), Administrative Science Quarterly 40:256-282 and 42:530-557. The three types are hers. She found that task conflict can improve a group's decisions while relationship conflict reliably damages them, and added process conflict in the 1997 paper. 📄 Jehn (1995), full paper PDF.pdf)

⚠️ The Zeducation source teaches the three types and does not name her. Credit her. It is a real research finding rather than a training model, and saying so makes the teaching stronger.

CPP Global Human Capital Report (2008), the 2.1 hours figure, from 5,000 employees across nine countries. 📄 Report

⚠️ Describe it honestly: a large survey commissioned by an assessment publisher, not peer-reviewed research. And the three further statistics the source quotes alongside it, on injury, absence and failed projects, have not been verified and should not be used until they are.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: the small thing left too long. A task or process disagreement that nobody dealt with, which had turned into a relationship conflict by the time anyone looked at it, and what it cost. Every workplace has one and the useful detail is how small it was at the start.

1

About This Topic

The workplace is not immune to conflict. A 2008 survey of 5,000 employees across nine countries found workers spent an average of 2.1 hours a week dealing with it, which is over a hundred hours a year (CPP Global Human Capital Report). Worth knowing what that study is: a large survey commissioned by an assessment publisher, not peer-reviewed research.

The Cambridge Dictionary defines conflict as "an active disagreement between people with opposing opinions or ideas."

But there is another way to look at it, and it is the one this topic is built on:

Conflict is an opportunity to engage in a conversation with someone who has a different viewpoint.

A positive point of view genuinely changes how conflict resolves. That takes a mind shift, because most of us were taught that disagreement is a failure.

The second half of the topic is the diagnosis. Conflict is not one thing. It comes in three kinds and they need different responses, and the most common expensive mistake at work is treating a problem between people as though it were a problem with the process.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Relationship conflictA disagreement about the people. Personality, beliefs, history
Task conflictA disagreement about the work itself, and what the goal is
Process conflictA disagreement about who does what, and how
EscalationA small disagreement turning into a bigger one, usually by being left
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name whether a conflict is about the work, the process or the people.
  2. Describe two things resolving a conflict gets you, and two things avoiding it costs.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask everyone to think of one unresolved thing at work. Not a crisis. The low-level one: the person they route around, the thing that comes up every few weeks and never gets settled, the conversation they keep not having.

Nobody says it out loud. Ask them instead to estimate, privately, how many minutes a week it costs them — thinking about it, working around it, complaining about it, redoing something because of it.

Then take a show of hands by band. Under 15 minutes. 15 to 30. Half an hour to an hour. More.

Nobody puts their hand up for zero.

Statement: Two hours a week is not the price of having conflict. It is the price of not resolving it. Dealt with, it costs twenty minutes once. Avoided, it costs ten minutes a week, forever.

➜ Facilitator note: nobody names a person. Say that before you start.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-037

The Three Types of Workplace Conflict

Origin: Karen A. Jehn, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1995 and 1997. One of the most used typologies in organisational research, and uncredited in the source workbook.

TypeAboutExample
RelationshipThe people. Difference of opinion, experience, personality or beliefs. Carries negative emotion and personal dislikeSomeone said something in a meeting that offended you, you argued, and now you do not speak
TaskThe work. Different views on the content of a decision, and sometimes on what the task even isTwo people disagree on how a project should be done and what the goal should be
ProcessThe how and the who. Division of labour, responsibility, who controls whatSomeone is seen as favoured for a role and is freeriding while the team carries it

How to read it: the dotted arrows are the danger. Task and process conflict are survivable alone. They become destructive when they turn into relationship conflict, and process conflict does this most easily, because arguing about who does what is one step from arguing about who someone is.

Task conflict is not the enemy. Jehn's finding was that disagreement about the work can improve decisions as long as it stays about the work. A team with no task conflict is usually a team where nobody says what they think.

Worked example: two staff argue about how the accident forms are filled in. It looks like task conflict, so the supervisor writes a clearer procedure. It comes back worse a fortnight later. Asked properly, one of them has felt talked down to by the other since a public correction six months ago. The forms were never the problem.

The diagnostic question: if the work question were settled tomorrow, would these two be fine? If no, it is not a task conflict.

More resources:

  • 📄 Jehn (1995), full paper (PDF).pdf)
  • 🎬 How to deal with conflict — the source's own video for this module

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-017

The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team

Lencioni's second layer, fear of conflict, is mostly fear of task conflict, and Jehn explains what avoiding it costs. Useful whenever a room concludes that the goal is a workplace with no disagreement in it. → Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-079 How Do I Handle Conflict? Ten statements, 1 to 3, out of 30. Written fresh: the source guide contains no self-assessment, which was its largest gap.

Statement 1 is the highest-leverage item: I deal with disagreements early, while they are still small. Nearly every case study in this programme became difficult because it was left.

⚠️ Not validated, and it carries no assessment weight.

Reflection Questions

  1. What is the thing at work you keep not dealing with? What has it cost so far?
  2. Which column was easier to fill in, the positives or the negatives? Why?
  3. Think of a conflict that was "solved" and came back. What type was it really?
  4. Which of the three types does your workplace handle worst?
  5. When has a disagreement made something better?
  6. What turns a task conflict into a relationship one? Have you watched that happen?
  7. What does a team look like where nobody ever disagrees?
  8. What is one small thing you will raise this week, while it is still small?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 90 min for the assessed core. 120 with the roleplay
  • Use learners' own examples in ACT-070. Real scenarios are what make the model stick
  • What usually goes wrong: the room concludes task conflict is always good. Jehn's later work and subsequent meta-analyses are more mixed than the 1995 paper alone. Teach "not automatically bad"
  • ⚠️ Statistics caution. The source cites three further figures alongside the 2.1 hours: a third of conflicts leading to attacks or injury, 20% to illness or absence, 10% of projects failing. Those three are unverified against the primary report. Do not read them out as fact. The 2.1 hours figure is the one that checks out
  • Cultural note: where open disagreement with a senior person is a respect issue, task conflict never surfaces as disagreement. It surfaces as silence, or as a safer-sounding process complaint. Watch for that rather than concluding there is no conflict

PS-COM-001Pink Sheet · Communication

Assertive is clear, not loud

complete
assertivenessconflictleadershiptrust

Topic: Speak Up With Confidence · Pillar: Communication · ID: PS-COM-001

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStory

Point

Assertive is not loud. It is clear and respectful at the same time. The people we trust at work are not the ones who talk hardest. They are the ones who say the hard thing kindly, early, before it becomes everyone's problem.

Model

The 4 Communication Styles — two questions decide which of four exits you take under pressure: am I open to communication? and am I considerate of others?

Considerate of othersNot considerate of others
Open to communicationASSERTIVE — I win, you winAGGRESSIVE — I win, you lose
Not open to communicationPASSIVE — I lose, you winPASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE — I lose, you lose

How to read it: only one of the four boxes has two winners in it.

Metaphor

A smoke alarm. Nobody thinks a smoke alarm is aggressive. It is not shouting at you, it is not sulking, and it is not staying quiet to keep the peace. It tells you one clear thing, at the right moment, before the room is on fire. That is what an assertive person does in a team. The alternative is not a peaceful house. It is a house that finds out later.

Study

Assertiveness is taught on the assumption that "I" language lowers defensiveness, and the evidence is real but more modest than the training industry implies. Studies find I-language is less likely to provoke negative emotion and more likely to evoke compassion and cooperative behaviour (Rogers et al., 2018), while reviews outside romantic relationships find phrasing alone does not always change how a message lands (IEEE Professional Communication Society).

So the honest version of the claim is the stronger one to teach: the sentence is not magic. What changes the conversation is that "I" language forces you to work out what you actually want before you open your mouth.

Story

From the Zeducation Effective Communication workbook: the four scenarios learners roleplay are all the same shape. A performance drop nobody mentions. A team rushing and skipping steps. A deadline everyone knows is not real. An experienced worker who says "I've done this for years." In every one of them, the problem was visible to the whole team before anybody said it out loud.

⚠️ GAP: replace this with a real Zeducation learner story once one has been collected with permission. A frontline learner who used an "I" statement with a supervisor and got a different result would be the strongest version of this sheet.

Use this sheet for: workshop opener · leadership keynote · LinkedIn post · employer proposal on psychological safety

  • TOP-COM-001 Speak Up With Confidence — the teaching version
  • FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles — the model page
  • Future sheets off the same model: one per style. The cost of passive · Why aggressive wins twice and loses forever · Passive-aggressive is the most expensive style in a team
TOP-COM-001Topic · Communication

Speak Up With Confidence

✅ publishedCommunicationFoundation90-120 minEffective Communication workbook, Module 1
assertivenesscommunication-stylesconflictboundariessaying-noworkplace-communication

Pillar: Communication · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-COM-001 · 🩷 Pink Sheet

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Assertive communication is the foundation of confident leadership. When you say what you think clearly and respectfully, people trust you, and problems get raised before they grow.

Most of us fall into one of four styles when the pressure comes on. Passive: you hold back and stay quiet, so your ideas go unheard. Aggressive: you push or blame, so you win the moment but lose trust. Passive-aggressive: you say it is fine when it is not, which breeds confusion. Assertive: you say what you mean, clearly and kindly, and you listen too. That is the goal.

Being assertive is not about being loud, pushy or difficult. It is about being clear and respectful at the same time. It is a skill, which means it can be learned, and it gets easier with practice.

This matters everywhere, not just at work. It is the skill that lets you raise a safety issue on site, tell your manager a deadline is not realistic, say no to a shift you cannot cover, ask for help, set a boundary with family, and speak up in a meeting where everyone else is nodding. People who never learn it end up carrying work, resentment and stress that was never theirs.

Key words

WordWhat it means
AssertiveSaying what you think and need, clearly and respectfully, while listening to others
PassiveHolding back, staying quiet, going along with things you do not agree with
AggressivePushing your view onto others, blaming, interrupting, not listening
Passive-aggressiveSaying it is fine on the outside while being upset on the inside
BoundaryA clear line about what is and is not okay for you
"I" statementA sentence that starts with your own experience instead of an accusation
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Speak up with clarity and respect using assertive communication.
  2. Identify your default style under pressure and shift to assertive.
  3. Turn "you" statements into "I" statements under pressure.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Think of a job where something was going wrong and everybody could see it. The order was wrong, the deadline was never going to happen, the shortcut was unsafe. Ask the room: how long did everyone know before anybody said it out loud? Usually the answer is days. Sometimes weeks. Sometimes it took an accident.

Then ask the second question: what would it have cost the person who spoke up first? That is the whole topic in one question.

Statement: Problems do not get bigger because people are careless. They get bigger because nobody wanted to be the one to say it.

➜ Facilitator note: if you have a personal story of a time you stayed quiet and it cost you, use it. Your own story beats any example on this page. If you would rather not, the two questions above will pull three stories out of the room in ninety seconds.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

Framework

The 4 Communication Styles — know your default before you try to change it

Type: Tool (model) · Origin: Zeducation house model · Full page: FRM-001

Your communication style is the way you interact with others. It decides how you speak, act and react in different situations. Two questions place you: are you open to communication, and are you considerate of others?

Considerate of othersNot considerate of others
Open to communicationASSERTIVE — I win, you winAGGRESSIVE — I win, you lose
Not open to communicationPASSIVE — I lose, you winPASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE — I lose, you lose

How to read this: four exits from the same pressure. Only one protects the result and the relationship.

StyleSounds likeThe risk
Passive"It's okay, I guess… I'll manage."People take advantage. Your ideas never get heard
Passive-aggressive"Sure, I'll do it. Just like last time when no one helped me."Confusion, damaged relationships, more stress
Aggressive"You're hopeless at this job."Wins the moment, loses the trust
Assertive"I understand you're busy, but I need this report by 3pm."The healthiest style. The goal

Worked example (NZ workplace): A supervisor asks you to stay late for the third time this week. Passive: "…okay." Aggressive: "You always dump this on me." Passive-aggressive: "Fine. Whatever." Assertive: "I can't stay tonight, I've got my kids. I can start early tomorrow if that helps."

More resources

  • 📄 Positive Psychology — assertive communication styles and techniques
  • 🎬 TED — Adam Galinsky: How to speak up for yourself (15 min) — why low-power people go passive, and what to do about it. Best played after the model
  • 🎬 Assertiveness scenarios in the workplace — short worked scenarios, good discussion trigger
Framework

The Assert Approach & "I" Statements — the sentence that lowers the temperature

Type: Technique · Origin: Zeducation house technique; "I messages" from Thomas Gordon (1960s) · Full page: FRM-002

Name the situation, say how it affects you, say what you need, calmly.

StepWhat you doSounds like
1. Name the situationState the facts. No blame, no "always" or "never""The report came through after 3pm today."
2. Say how it affects youOwn it with "I""I feel stuck, because I can't finish my part without it."
3. Say what you needBe specific and reasonable"I need it by 1pm on Fridays. Can we do that?"

How to read this: three steps said calmly. The calm is not decoration, it is part of the message.

The formula: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. What I need is ___.

Instead of…Say…
"You never listen.""I feel unheard when I'm interrupted."
"You're always late.""When the shift starts late, I'm the one covering. I need us to start at 7."
"You dumped this on me.""I've got three jobs on today. I can do this one tomorrow morning."

Know your rights. You have the right to share your opinion. You have the right to say no without feeling guilty. You have the right to be treated with respect. You have the right to set clear boundaries: "I'm happy to help, but I need 24 hours' notice."

Keep your body language confident. Stand or sit tall. Keep eye contact. Use a calm, steady voice.

Worked example (home / community): Family asks for money you do not have. "I want to help with the fundraising. Money's tight for us this month, so I can't put in cash. I can do the cooking and the setup."

More resources

  • 📄 University of Iowa — I-statements
  • 📄 Rogers et al. (2018) — the benefits of I-language during conflict
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen (10 min, one of TED's most-watched talks) — HAIL: honesty, authenticity, integrity, love
Framework

The DESC Script — for the conversation you have been avoiding

Type: Tool (script) · Origin: Sharon and Gordon Bower, Asserting Yourself (1976) · Full page: FRM-004

Four lines, written down before you speak. Use it when the stakes are higher: a repeated behaviour, a performance issue, pushback from someone senior.

How to read this: most people manage D and E. The conversation only changes when you do S and C too.

StepWhat you sayExample
DescribeThe specific behaviour, facts only"The last three toolbox talks started ten minutes late."
ExpressHow it affects you"I'm concerned, because we end up rushing the safety part."
SpecifyThe one change you want"I'd like us to start at 7 sharp, with the checks done first."
ConsequencesWhat good looks like after"Then we're on the tools by 7:15 and nobody gets pulled up on site."

Worked example (NZ workplace): "The last two Fridays the van's come back without being restocked. I end up doing it Monday before I can start my run. I need it restocked before it's parked up. Then we both start Monday clean and nobody's chasing anybody."

More resources

  • 📄 In Equilibrium — the DESC model for assertiveness
  • 📄 NCCMT — the DESC model for assertive communication
  • 🎬 Indeed — Assertive communication: speak up for yourself — short, career-framed, good pre-work
FrameworkFRM-042

Why Assertiveness Feels Hard (added 2026-08-01)

Everything above is a skill. This section is why the skill does not get used.

Every facilitator has met the learner who can recite DESC perfectly, roleplay it well, and say nothing at all on Monday. Their problem is not the script.

BarrierWhat it sounds like from the inside
Shyness"If I speak, everyone will be looking at me"
People-pleasing"If I say no, they'll think less of me"
Low self-esteem"My needs aren't as important as theirs"
Fear of the reaction"It'll turn into a fight"
Passive-aggressive habit"I'd rather just make it obvious I'm annoyed"
Culture and upbringing"I was raised not to answer back"
Power and safety"It genuinely isn't safe for me to say this here"
Energy and health"I don't have it in me at the moment"

How to read it: Me and Them respond to practice. Here may not be a personal problem at all. Today needs a smaller ask, not a bigger push.

The two that are not skill problems, and both matter in this room:

Culture and upbringing is context, not a defect. A learner raised to defer to elders is not failing at assertiveness. Often the assertive move simply looks different: one to one, at a different time, or through someone trusted. That is a legitimate answer, not a workaround.

Power and safety is sometimes just correct. A person on an insecure visa or a casual contract, whose manager has punished the last three people who raised something, is making an accurate calculation. Teaching them they need more confidence tells them their judgment is a personality flaw. Say out loud that some workplaces are not safe to be assertive in, and the skill there is knowing it and knowing where else to take it.

⚠️ Scope. This names what is in the way so a learner can pick a next step. It is not a diagnosis and a facilitator is not a clinician. Referral options: workplace EAP, their GP, or 1737, call or text.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-043

DEAR MAN (added 2026-08-01)

Origin: Marsha Linehan, from the interpersonal effectiveness module of Dialectical Behavior Therapy. The best-evidenced assertiveness script available, and a close relative of DESC.

DEAR is what you say. MAN is how you hold it when they push back.

LetterWhat you do
DDescribeThe facts. Only what a camera would have seen
EExpress"I feel…"
AAssertThe actual ask. This is the step people skip
RReinforceWhat the other person gets if they agree
MMindfulStay on the point. Do not get pulled onto a side argument
AAppear confidentSteady voice, steady posture
NNegotiateOffer the smaller version. "What would work for you?"

Which script, when: DESC to raise a problem, DEAR MAN to ask for something. DESC ends on consequences; DEAR MAN ends on what they gain, then a negotiation. And MAN works as an add-on to DESC, which is the cheapest upgrade available to this topic, because DESC says nothing about what happens after the other person reacts.

⚠️ "Appear confident" in the standard teaching includes eye contact. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures that reads as disrespect with someone senior. Teach it as steady and let learners choose the form.

→ Full framework page

How Assertive Am I? — full version with all 15 items: ACT-002

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I do not feel guilty when I ask others to do something

Total

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
60+Your beliefs, opinions and actions are those of a very assertive person. You handle most situations well, respecting your own rights and those of the people around youPick the one situation where you still hold back, and go there next
45-59You are fairly assertive, depending on the situation. Respect is a key part of assertiveness: respecting yourself and expecting respect from othersNotice which rooms and which people you drop out of assertive with
30-44Middle of the road. Neither aggressive nor assertiveSpeak out for yourself and take these tools into your next conversation
15-29The first positive step towards being more assertive is being hereListen, learn and apply. Start with one "I" statement this week
6

Apply — Suggested Activities

Four Styles Roleplay · roleplay · 25-35 min · groups of 3-5

Practises: FRM-001 and FRM-002 · Full page: ACT-001

Materials: scenario cards, timer.

How to run it

  1. Each group gets one scenario: performance drop, running behind schedule, unrealistic deadline, or senior worker pushback.
  2. They roleplay the same situation four times, once in each style. 8 minutes to prepare.
  3. They perform to the class without saying which style is which.
  4. The class guesses the style each time.

Debrief questions

  • Which style was hardest to act? Why?
  • What did the assertive version do that the others did not?
  • Which style have you seen at your workplace this month?

DESC Rewrite Lab · structured practice · 25-30 min · pairs

Practises: FRM-004 · Full page: ACT-003

Each learner writes the four DESC lines for a real conversation they have been avoiding, swaps with a partner to sharpen it, then says it out loud while the partner pushes back once.

Debrief questions

  • Which of the four boxes was hardest to fill in?
  • What happened in your body when your partner pushed back?
  • When will you have the real conversation?

Statement Sort — Four Corners · game · 12-15 min · whole class

Practises: FRM-001 · Full page: ACT-004

Twelve real statements, four corners of the room. Learners walk to the style they think each one is. Works as an opener or as a fast recap. See section 6.

Added 2026-08-01: ACT-080 What's Stopping Me? (20-25 min, worksheet, private) and ACT-081 The DEAR MAN Lab (30-35 min). Run ACT-080 after the skill content, not before: the barriers only make sense once someone has tried a script and noticed the gap.

7

Reflection Questions

Notice

  • Which of the four styles is your default when the pressure comes on?
  • Is it the same at work as it is at home? What changes it?

Connect

  • Think of a time you stayed quiet when you should have spoken up. What did it cost you?
  • Who do you find it hardest to be assertive with? What is it about that person?
  • When has someone been assertive with you and you respected them for it?

Apply

  • Where will you use an "I" statement this week? What exactly will you say?
  • What is one boundary you need to set, and who with?
  • Which conversation have you been avoiding? What is the Specify line?

Commit

  • ❑ What are 2-3 things you will do to be more assertive?
  • ❑ Who will you tell, so somebody asks you about it next week?

Full closer activity: ACT-006 Two Things

Facilitator Notes

Suggested run sheet (110 min)

TimeStageWhat happens
0:00SStory and the two questions. One-Word Weather if the room is cold
0:10TThe 4 Communication Styles + Statement Sort game
0:30TThe Assert Approach and "I" statements. Rewrite live on the whiteboard
0:45AFour Styles Roleplay, perform and guess
1:15TThe DESC script
1:30ADESC Rewrite Lab in pairs
1:45RSelf-assessment, then Two Things commitment
  • Common traps: learners labelling each other with the four styles. Set the rule early that the model is for looking at yourself. Watch for "assertive equals blunt" — pair the model with the Assert Approach immediately, never teach it alone
  • The room will go quiet at the DESC lab when people realise the conversation they have been avoiding. That silence is the work. Do not rush it
  • Adaptations: for youth, run everything on group chat, friends and part-time work first. For Pacific and Māori groups, name early that respect for elders and speaking up when something is unsafe are both true. For low literacy, drop the written DESC and use the four-box card with spoken answers
  • Safety: someone will surface a genuinely serious situation (bullying, harassment, safety). Know your referral path before you start

⚠️ Open gaps: none for delivery. Next enrichment: a Pacific or Māori voice on speaking up in a workplace hierarchy, and an NZ statistic on the cost of unraised workplace issues.

9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

Statement Sort — Four Corners · 12-15 min · whole class · 4 signs

Full page: ACT-004

Four signs in four corners: PASSIVE, AGGRESSIVE, PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE, ASSERTIVE. Read a statement in character and learners walk to the corner they think it belongs in. Twelve statements, no talking on the way, ask one person from the biggest and smallest corner to explain.

The link back: the same words can be three different styles depending on tone. Assertive is words plus tone plus intent lining up.

The No Game · 8-10 min · pairs · no materials

Full page: ACT-005

Person A asks for anything for sixty seconds. Person B's only job is to say no every time. Swap. Round two: say no and stay friendly, no apologising, no long excuse.

The link back: most of us do not struggle with the word. We struggle with the guilt after it. Saying no to a request is not saying no to a person.

One-Word Weather · 3 min · whole class · no materials

Everyone gives one word for how they are arriving today. No explaining, no fixing, just the word.

The link back: that took courage from some of you, and it was one word. Everything today is practice at saying the true thing out loud.

PIL-CULPillar · Culture & Diversity

Culture & Diversity

Working well across difference, and building places where people can be themselves. This pillar is about what happens between people and cultures, and what a leader or an organisation does to make that go well.

Who it serves: leaders and teams in culturally mixed workplaces, which in Aotearoa and the Pacific is nearly all of them. Tourism, hospitality, health, aged care, construction, education, and any employer with a Pacific, Māori or migrant workforce.

"Real leadership doesn't take more room, it makes more room."
