About This Topic

This is the third part of career readiness. TOP-EMP-002 worked out what you can do. TOP-EMP-003 got you in the door. This one is what happens when somebody asks you about it.

Four things happen in a session on interviews and they need holding apart.

What it isWhere it lives
The standard questions"Tell me about a time you…" Prepared for, practised, learnableFRM-059 and ACT-099
The one they are dreadingThe gap, the dismissal, the conviction, the visa, the reason somebody like them would not get this jobACT-100, and it needs care
The last five minutes"Do you have any questions for us?" Most people say noFRM-062 and ACT-102
Getting there at allTransport, childcare, clothes, a shift they cannot get out of, no quiet room for a video callACT-103, and it is not a confidence problem

Everybody in the room has one of the second kind. Most of the anxiety about interviews is attached to it, and a session that only teaches the first kind leaves it exactly where it was.

⚠️ Read the whole of ACT-100 before you run this topic. It handles disclosure, and it has rules that are not negotiable.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Behavioural question"Tell me about a time you…" The premise is that what you did before predicts what you will do next
STAR answerSituation, Task, Action, Result. The shape of a good answer to one
ResultWhat actually changed. A number if you have one, a lesson if you do not
PanelTwo or more interviewers together. Standard in government, health and education
Clean SlateNew Zealand law that lets many people, after seven clean years and other criteria, legally answer "no" about convictions
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Build four STAR stories that stretch to cover almost any behavioural question.
  2. Answer out loud with the action as the longest part, and an actual result at the end.
  3. Say your own hardest question in three parts, finishing forward.
  4. Walk in with three questions of your own, and walk out knowing what happens next.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two people are interviewed for the same support worker role, half an hour apart.

The first is asked "tell me about a time you dealt with someone difficult." She talks for two minutes about how the rest home was always short-staffed, and how management never listened, and how some of the families were hard work. Then she stops and says, "so yeah, it was pretty full on."

The second gets the same question. She says: "There was a resident who wouldn't let anyone near her in the mornings. I was on her wing for six weeks. I stopped trying to get her up on our schedule and started coming in fifteen minutes earlier just to sit. On the fourth day she told me she'd fallen in the shower two years ago and never told anyone. I told the RN, we got a shower chair and a second person on her, and after that she got herself up most mornings."

Same job. Same rest home, as it happens. Ask the room: which one has more experience?

The honest answer is that we have no idea. Only one of them told us anything.

Statement: An interview is not a test of your experience. It is a test of whether you can put your experience into a story that has a point.

➜ Facilitator note: read both answers out loud, in character. The first one gets nervous laughter because everybody recognises it, usually as themselves.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-059

The STAR Interview Answer

What it is: a four-part shape that turns "tell me about a time you…" from a panic into a story with a point.

Origin: the behavioural interviewing tradition, from the 1970s on, built on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour better than hypothetical questions do. No single author owns STAR. Evidence: strong, for the underlying method rather than the acronym. Structured behavioural interviews are among the better-validated selection tools available and clearly beat unstructured "have a chat" interviews. The four letters are a memory aid sitting on top of that.

What goes in itHow long
SSituationWhere and when. Enough to picture it1 sentence
TTaskWhat you specifically had to do. Not the team1 sentence
AActionWhat you did, step by step. This is most of the answer3-4 sentences
RResultWhat happened. A number, or a lesson1-2 sentences

How to read it: A is the answer. Most people spend ninety seconds on Situation, run out of nerve, and finish with "so yeah, it worked out." Flip the proportions.

Worked example, a warehouse interview. "Tell me about a time you dealt with pressure."

S: "Last Christmas we were two people down on the night shift for a fortnight." T: "I was the senior on nights, so getting the trucks loaded by six was on me." A: "I split the crew into two teams instead of four so nobody was working alone. I moved the pick order so the biggest customer's pallets got done first, in case we ran out of time. And I rang the day supervisor each morning to tell him exactly what was left, so he wasn't finding out at nine." R: "We got every truck out on time except one, which went an hour late. The day team said it was the first Christmas they hadn't inherited a mess."

➜ The result is not heroic. It contains a failure — one truck went late — and the answer is stronger for it. Perfect results sound rehearsed.

Four stories, not twenty answers. Trying to script every possible question is exactly why people freeze when one arrives worded differently. Build four and let them stretch.

StoryA time you…Covers
1Dealt with a difficult personConflict, customers, teamwork, patience
2Had something go wrong, partly on youAccountability, learning, honesty, pressure
3Worked in a team and did a specific partTeamwork, communication, reliability
4Kept going when it was hardResilience, motivation, workload

⚠️ "I" is genuinely hard for some learners, and it is not shyness. In many Pacific and Māori settings, taking individual credit is poor form. Do not tell anyone their upbringing is wrong. Name the clash and hand them the bridge: "our team did X, and my part was Y." Both true, and comfortable to say.

More resources:

  • 🔗 Tahatū Job Hunters' Workbook teaches the same shape

→ Full framework page

The hard question (house content)

STAR does not cover the question people are actually dreading. That one has its own shape, three parts, and the third is where it turns.

Example
1. Say it plainlyOne sentence. No apology, no long story"I was out of work for two years."
2. What it wasBrief and factual"I was caring for my mum full time until she passed."
3. Turn forwardWhat you did about it, or what you can do now. Land here"I kept my first aid current, and I've just finished my Level 3. I'm ready to be back."

How to read it: most people do 1 and 2 and then stop talking, leaving the silence for the interviewer to fill. Part 3 is the whole thing.

⚠️ On criminal convictions, do not improvise. New Zealand's Criminal Records (Clean Slate) Act 2004 means many people can legally answer "no" about convictions if they meet the criteria. It is specific and it is not guesswork. Send people to real advice: Community Law · Citizens Advice Bureau · their MSD case manager. A facilitator's job is the sentence, not the law.

⚠️ Open gap: the library has nothing on Clean Slate and it comes up constantly with MSD-referred learners. Worth building properly, with legal input, and it is logged as a priority-zero item on the Source Log.

FrameworkFRM-062

The Questions You Ask Them (house model)

What it is: every interview ends with "do you have any questions for us?", most people say no, and it is the only moment in the whole hour where the power in the room is level.

Three things happen when somebody says no. Interest: you did not care enough to think of one. Judgement: you will take a job you know almost nothing about. The last impression: it is the final thing that happens, and it is what they say to each other afterwards.

Take three in, from at least two of these four kinds. Written on paper, and it is fine to read them.

How to read it: question 4 is not optional and it goes last. It is what gets you a date instead of a fortnight of refreshing your email.

KindExamples
The job"What does a normal day look like?" · "What's the hardest part of this job?"
The people"Who would I be working with day to day?" · "How does the team hand over?"
The future"Is there training or a ticket the company puts people through?"
The process"What are the next steps, and when will you be in touch?"

What to ask now, and what waits.

Ask it in the interviewWait until they offer you the job
The shift pattern and rosterWhether you can swap shifts
Whether the pay range in the ad is rightNegotiating the number
Whether there is training or a ticketWhether they will pay for a course you want
Start date and next stepsTime off you have booked, unless it is soon

➜ Pay is allowed. Learners are told constantly that asking about money looks greedy. "The ad said $26 to $28, is that right for this role?" is checking you can afford to take the job. The negotiation is a different conversation and it happens after the offer.

After the interview, two moves and five minutes: a three-line thank-you the same day, naming one thing from the conversation, and one follow-up if the date they gave you has passed. When there is silence it is usually the process, not you. Follow up once, then keep applying.

⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, questioning somebody older or in authority is not straightforward. Do not treat that as a confidence gap to be fixed. Name it, and offer the framing that works: "Can I ask you something about the job?"

→ Full framework page

The day itself (house content, and it is not a confidence problem)

Most interview advice says "have an outfit ready." That sentence assumes a wardrobe, a car, a printer, a quiet room and nobody depending on you.

What actually stops our learners getting to an interview:
Getting thereNo transport, no fare, a bus that does not run on Saturdays
ChildcareAnd nobody asked until the night before
A shiftWhich they cannot get out of without saying why
ClothesNot "which outfit". Whether there is one at all
Online interviewsNo device, no data that holds 45 minutes, no room where nobody walks in

➜ None of that is fixed by wanting the job more, and none of it is a character flaw. It is logistics, it is solvable in a week, and it needs a facilitator who will act on what comes out of ACT-103.

⚠️ Never advise anybody to hide who they are. Cultural dress, taonga and moko are not problems to be managed. An employer who treats them as one has told you something useful early.

FrameworkFRM-061

How Jobs Are Actually Found — why the interview is not the start

What it is: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds.

It belongs in this topic for one reason. The best interview you will ever have is the one where somebody already vouched for you, because you are not a stranger being assessed, you are a known quantity being confirmed.

ChannelWhat the interview feels like
1. Applied coldYou are one of eight, and they are looking for reasons to cut
2. Someone inside handed your CV overYou arrive with credit already on the board
3. Never advertisedOften barely an interview. A conversation and a start date
4. Created for youThey have already decided. This is logistics

➜ So the practical move after this topic is not more interview practice. It is ACT-101 and the sentence: what I'm looking for, what I bring, would you let me know.

→ Full framework page

Self-Assessment

The four ticks (house content, and it is an observer check, not a score).

Inside ACT-099, the observer has one job. Tick what they actually heard:

Heard it?
Situation kept to about a sentence☐
Said "I", not only "we"☐
Action was the longest part☐
There was an actual result at the end☐

Feedback is those four ticks and nothing else. No general opinions, no "that was good". Specific feedback is the only kind that changes anything.

For a written self-check after the session:

Yes / No
Do I have four stories written down, not just in my head?☐
Can I tell each one in under two minutes?☐
Does at least one of them include something going wrong?☐
Does every one finish with what changed?☐
Have I said my hardest answer out loud to another person?☐
Does my hardest answer finish on part 3?☐
Do I have three questions written down, and is one of them about next steps?☐
Do I know how I am getting there, and who is covering what I normally do?☐

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-099 The STAR Answer LabRoleplay40-45 minFRM-059, FRM-057
ACT-102 Three QuestionsWorksheet25-30 minFRM-062
ACT-100 The Hardest QuestionRoleplay30-35 minThe three-part shape
ACT-103 The Day ItselfWorksheet, then one-to-one30-40 minThe barriers, not the nerves
ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?Game20-25 minFRM-061, FRM-024
ACT-013 Start, Stop, ContinueReflection10-12 minCloses the topic

Suggested flow, and it is now two sessions rather than one:
Session 1The two answers in section 3 read aloud → teach FRM-059 → ACT-099 in threes → teach FRM-062 → ACT-102 → close
Session 2Recap → the three-part shape → ACT-100 with the rules said out loud first → ACT-103 → ACT-101 to end forward rather than on the hard question → ACT-013

If it has to be one session: FRM-059 → ACT-099 → FRM-062 → ACT-102 → ACT-101. Give ACT-100 and ACT-103 their own time. Both surface hardship and neither survives being rushed.

⚠️ ACT-099 before ACT-100, always. The standard questions build the confidence that makes the hard one survivable. Reversing them is how a room shuts down.

⚠️ Do not end on ACT-100. Whatever your timing, put something forward-facing after it. ACT-101 is designed to be that.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Which of the two answers in the opening story sounded more like you? Be honest.
  2. Which of the four story boxes was hardest to fill, and what does that tell you?
  3. Where do you catch yourself saying "we" when you mean "I"?
  4. Story 2 was a time something went wrong. How did it feel to tell it? What did telling it do?
  5. What is the question you have been dreading, and what would part 3 of your answer be?
  6. What have you been leaving off your CV entirely because of that question?
  7. What is the difference between explaining and apologising?
  8. When did you last say "no, I think you've covered everything"? What did you actually want to know?
  9. What would you need to sort out this week to get to an interview on Thursday?
  10. Who is the last person you told that you are looking for work? When will you tell three more?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: this topic is now genuinely two sessions. 180 min covers all of it; 150 is tight. Under 120, run FRM-059, ACT-099, FRM-062 and ACT-102, and give ACT-100 and ACT-103 their own time. Both are better as a whole session than as a rushed twenty minutes
  • ⚠️ ACT-103 produces a to-do list for you, not just for the learner. Do not run it unless you can act on what comes out: bus fares, clothes, childcare, a room with wifi. Know your options before you walk in — the programme's own fund, their MSD case manager, a community clothing pool
  • ⚠️ Read ACT-100 in full before delivery. Nobody discloses to the room, pairs are chosen by the learner, anyone can pass at any point with no reason given, and all of that is said out loud before it starts
  • ⚠️ Know your referral options before you walk in. Bereavement, illness, violence, prison and deportation all surface here. Workplace EAP, their GP, 1737 call or text, and their MSD case manager
  • Say which STAR you mean, every single time. Facilitators trained on FRM-003 will use the word by reflex and the room will follow them into the wrong model
  • The cheapest upgrade in this topic: make every ACT-099 roleplay finish with "do you have any questions for us?" Nobody has an answer the first time. After a fortnight everybody does
  • Do not turn ACT-103 into a grooming lecture. No commentary on hair, jewellery, tattoos or how somebody carries themselves. It is logistics, and barriers get named one-to-one, never to the room
  • What usually goes wrong: the twelve-minute Situation. Timebox it out loud during practice or it will happen in the room
  • Push for a story where something went wrong. They are better answers and interviewers know it. Learners will resist, because it feels like handing over ammunition
  • Never tell somebody to lie, and never tell them their honest answer is unsayable. If an answer genuinely will not survive, that is a conversation about which employers to approach, not about becoming a better liar
  • The learner whose hard question is about their name, their age or their race is not describing a gap. That is discrimination, and the answer is not a better sentence. It is FRM-061 and the Human Rights Commission
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on this Pink Sheet yet, and no employer voice. A friendly hiring manager for the last twenty minutes beats any facilitator feedback, and it is the easiest thing on this list to arrange
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • The two answers (6 min, low energy). Read both answers from section 3 in character, then ask which one has more experience. Free, needs no materials, and it opens the whole topic.
  • "And then what happened?" (8 min, medium energy). The facilitator asks a question, takes any answer, and replies only "and then what happened?" until there is a result. Usually three rounds. The single most useful drill in the topic, and it is part 3 of ACT-099.
  • ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know? (20-25 min, medium energy). Best used as the closer here, not the opener.
  • ACT-034 The Two Minute Introduction (20-25 min). "Tell me about yourself" is the first question in almost every interview, and this is where it is practised.

From the Ice Breaker Games pillar

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

GameTimeEnergySettingWhy this one here
GAM-006 Two Truths and a Lie15-25 minmediumonline or in personTelling something convincingly, and watching the room decide whether they believe you
GAM-016 Articulate15-20 minmediumonline or in personA story that will not fit the time is not ready

➜ All sixteen: Ice Breaker Games

Built from SRC-010 Tahatū Career Navigator, ingested 2026-08-01. Tahatū's Job Hunters' Workbook teaches the same STAR shape and is where learners should go for the practice material. The three-part shape for the hard question is Zeducation house content, written because Tahatū does not cover gaps, dismissals or convictions and our learners arrive with them. Both worked examples and both roleplays were written fresh. The Clean Slate section is deliberately a signpost, not advice.

Enriched on 2026-08-01 from SRC-011 Indeed, "How To Prepare for an Interview in 11 Steps". ⚠️ That page could not be read — indeed.com is refused at the network gateway — so it was assessed from search results and not one sentence of it was ingested. Its value was in exposing what this topic was missing: the questions the candidate asks, and getting to the interview at all. Both are house content, written fresh. Where the source says "have an outfit ready", ACT-103 asks the question that has to come first.

⚠️ Name clash — read this before you introduce anything

Two different things in this library are called STAR.

Stands forWhat it is for
FRM-003 STARStory · Tools · Apply · ReflectZeducation's session shape. How a facilitator builds a session
FRM-059 STAR (this topic)Situation · Task · Action · ResultA learner's interview answer. How a candidate tells a story about themselves

Both are genuinely called STAR in the wild. In this topic, say "the STAR answer". Reserve "the STAR session shape" for FRM-003.

PS-EMP-003Pink Sheet · Employment & Work Readiness

Your CV gets seconds, not minutes

placeholder-story
career-readinesscvjob-searchwork-readinessatswriting

Topic: TOP-EMP-003 The CV That Gets Read · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

You are writing for a reader who does not exist.

The reader you imagine has time, interest, and the whole page. The real one is software, then a tired person with a stack. The top third is your entire application. Everything below it only gets read if the top third worked.

Model

Two readers, in this order, wanting different things.

Reads firstWantsBreaks on
1. The softwareAn applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the adColumns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos, image-PDFs
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA fast answer to "can this person do the job?"A personal statement, hobbies, and the licence on page two

B and C are above the fold. Everything else is the evidence file for a decision that has already been made.

And the test that carries the whole thing: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is a duty. Rewrite it as what changed because you were there.

Metaphor

A shop window, not a stockroom.

Nobody walks past a shop and reads the inventory list. They look at the window for about as long as it takes to walk past it, and that decides whether they come in.

Most CVs are a stockroom with the door open. Everything is in there somewhere, in no particular order, and the customer is expected to find it. The window is the top third, and you rearrange it for every person walking past.

Study

⚠️ This is the section where the popular numbers have to be refused.

Two figures circulate constantly and neither is usable:

The claimWhy it is not quoted here
"Recruiters spend six seconds on a CV"Traces to small eye-tracking studies published by a recruitment vendor as marketing. Sample and method are not independently checkable
"75% of CVs are never seen by a human"No traceable source. It is repeated by companies selling CV-optimisation services

What is defensible and enough to teach from:

  • Screening is fast, and at volume it is filtered by software before any person sees it. That is not contested by anyone who hires
  • Tahatū, the Tertiary Education Commission's careers service, publishes free New Zealand CV templates and a CV builder deliberately built plain enough to be machine-readable

Honest limit: the four-sentence letter and the two-readers model are practitioner models. There is no study saying four sentences beats five. What is defensible is that short and specific beats long and generic, and that a letter which gets written beats one that does not.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The forty-one applications, two automated replies, and the Class 2 licence on page two is composite and written for teaching. It is true to what tutors describe. It is not one identified person.

The story to collect: a learner who moved one thing to the top third — a licence, a ticket, a headline — and started getting calls. The shape that lands is the number before and the number after, because it is the same person and the same skills, only visible.

Second story worth collecting: a hiring manager, in their own words, on what they do with a stack of CVs on a Friday afternoon. Thirty seconds of that beats twenty minutes of facilitation, and it is the easiest story on this list to get.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any CV session, in the first five minutesBefore anyone opens a document. It reframes the whole task
One-to-one with somebody who has stopped applyingLook at their top third and nothing else
Employer engagementAsk them to confirm it. They will, and it is more powerful from them
Tutor trainingThe shop-window line is the one staff remember

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-EMP-002 You are not starting from nothingThat sheet fills the container. This one is the container. Always in that order
PS-EMP-004 Four stories, not twenty answersEverything in the top third has to survive being asked about
PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowThe honest counterweight. A perfect CV in channel 1 still has the worst odds

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on the four-sentence cover letter. The Point is already written: sentence 3 is the only one that proves you did not send this to forty employers.

TOP-EMP-003Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

The CV That Gets Read

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation120-150 minCareer Readiness, Part 2
career-readinesscvcover-letterjob-searchwritingwork-readinesstahatu

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-EMP-003 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Career Readiness, Part 2

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

This topic assumes you have already done TOP-EMP-002. That one worked out what you can do. This one is about the container it goes in.

Everybody leaves with a tailored CV and a cover letter for a real job they could apply for that night. Not an exercise. A finished thing, with a date against it. That is the design, and a session that ends with good intentions and no application has failed.

Use Tahatū's CV builder. It is free, it is New Zealand standard, and its templates are plain enough that screening software can read them. A blank Word document is where this work goes to die, and a beautiful Canva design is often worse than useless, because the software that reads it first cannot parse a text box.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ATSApplicant tracking system. Software that reads and filters CVs before any person sees them
The top thirdEverything visible without scrolling or turning the page. Name, headline, skill bullets
HeadlineOne line under your name saying what you are, for this job
DutyWhat you were told to do. Anyone in that role could write the same sentence
AchievementWhat changed because you were there
TailoringRewriting the top third for each job, using that ad's words. Fifteen minutes, not a rewrite
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Rewrite the top third of your CV so a reader knows within seconds what job you are going for.
  2. Turn three duties into three achievements, each with evidence.
  3. Write a four-sentence cover letter for a real job, including one true, specific thing about that employer.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A man has applied for forty-one jobs in four months. He keeps a list. He has had two replies, both automated, and he has started to believe there is no work in Auckland.

His CV is two and a half pages. It is well laid out, in two columns, with a photo and a skills bar chart. Page one is his contact details, a personal statement about being a hardworking team player, and his hobbies. What he can actually do is on page two, under the third job down.

He has a Class 2 licence. It is on page two.

Ask the room: how long do you think somebody spends on a CV before they decide?

Then hand out four real CVs, face down, and give the room seven seconds each.

Statement: Your CV does not get read. It gets scanned by software, then glanced at by a tired person with a stack of them. The top third is your whole application.

➜ Facilitator note: run ACT-096 right here rather than talking about it. The point cannot be argued with once they have been the reader.

4

Frameworks Used

IDFrameworkPage
FRM-058The CV That Gets Read→

5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-058

The CV That Gets Read (house model)

What it is: your CV gets a few seconds and a keyword scan before a person decides anything, so the top third has to do almost all the work.

Two readers, in this order. Most CV advice fails because it optimises for the wrong one.

Reads firstWants
1. The softwareIncreasingly, an applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the job ad
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA quick answer to "can this person do the job?"

⚠️ A beautiful CV the software cannot read is not a CV. Columns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos and PDFs-of-images all break parsers.

The shape:

How to read it: everything above the fold is B and C. That is the whole strategy.

SectionThe rule
ContactPhone, email, suburb. No full street address, no date of birth, no photo. In New Zealand a photo invites discrimination and gives nothing back
HeadlineOne line, rewritten for every job. "Warehouse assistant with forklift F endorsement and four years on nights." Not "hardworking team player seeking opportunity"
Skill bulletsThree to five, in the job ad's words, each with evidence from FRM-057
Work historyWhat changed because you were there, not what you were told to do
TrainingLicences, tickets and endorsements go high if the job needs them. A Class 2 or a Site Safe card can be the entire reason you get called
RefereesNamed, asked first, and briefed on which job it is

Duties versus achievements. The single biggest lift available on most CVs.

Duty, which everyone writesAchievement, which gets read
"Responsible for stock""Cut stock discrepancies from weekly to almost none over six months"
"Customer service""Handled the complaints desk on Saturdays, the busiest shift"
"Cleaning duties""Held the kitchen at an A grade through two council inspections"
"Worked in a team""Trained four new starters, three of whom are still there"

➜ The test: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is still a duty.

Tailoring, which is not optional. One CV sent to forty jobs is why nobody called. Fifteen minutes:

  1. Print the job ad. Highlight every skill word
  2. Rewrite the headline for this job, in its words
  3. Reorder the skill bullets so what it asked for comes first
  4. Check the licence or ticket it names is visible without scrolling

⚠️ Use their words, not your synonyms. If the ad says "forklift licence", do not write "counterbalance certification". Software matches text, not meaning.

⚠️ On the "six seconds" figure. You will see it everywhere, along with "75% of CVs are never seen by a human". Both trace back to recruitment-vendor marketing, not to research anyone can check. Do not quote either as fact. What is not in dispute is that screening is fast and often filtered by software first, and that is enough to teach from.

More resources:

  • 🔗 Tahatū CV templates and Job Hunters' Workbook

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-060

The Four-Sentence Cover Letter (house model)

What it is: four sentences that answer the only four questions a hiring manager has.

SentenceAnswers
1Which job, and one reason you want this one. Name the employer"Why are you writing?"
2The single strongest thing you bring, in the ad's words, with evidence"Can you do it?"
3One specific thing about them. A project, a value, a location, a customer"Do you actually want us?"
4What happens next. Availability, no fuss"What now?"

How to read it: sentence 3 is the one almost nobody writes, and it is the one that proves this was not sent to forty employers. Write it first.

Worked example. Support worker, an Auckland disability provider.

Kia ora Sarah, [1] I'm applying for the support worker role at your Māngere site, because the shifts fit around my study and I've wanted to move into disability support since caring for my grandfather. [2] I've got two years of personal care experience, including medication support and working alongside district nurses, and I've just finished my Level 3 in Health and Wellbeing. [3] I noticed your team runs the community garden programme at that site. That's exactly the kind of support work I want to be part of, rather than only in-home. [4] I'm available from 12 August and can come in for a chat any weekday. My CV is attached. Ngā mihi, Losa

What to cut:

CutWhy
"I am writing to apply for the position advertised on Seek"They know. It wastes the best line on the page
"I am a hardworking team player with excellent communication skills"Everyone writes it, so it says nothing
Retelling the whole CVThe CV is attached. The letter is the reason to open it
An apology for anythingNever apologise for a gap, a career change, or being new

⚠️ Sentence 3 is where people invent. An invented detail is worse than no sentence, because it is checkable and it is a lie in writing.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-057

Transferable Skills — where the content comes from

You cannot write skill bullets out of nothing. Every bullet in the top third comes from the skills work in TOP-EMP-002, and every one carries three parts:

Example
SkillThe employer's words"Cash handling and reconciliation"
WhereThe real setting, however informal"Two years on the till at a family takeaway"
ProofA number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it"Balanced the float nightly. Never short."

⚠️ A learner arriving without this work done cannot do the session properly. If they have not done TOP-EMP-002, run ACT-094 first and accept that you will only get the top third finished.

→ Full framework page

On using AI to write it (house content)

Learners will use it, and pretending otherwise wastes the chance to teach something.

Where AI helpsWhere it fails
Tidying grammar and shorteningSentence 3. It does not know the employer, so it invents something plausible and false
Turning a duty into a shorter sentenceInventing achievements you did not have
Suggesting the employer's word for a skill you haveMaking the whole thing sound like everyone else's

➜ The rule: AI can help you say what is true. It cannot decide what is true. See TOP-COM-006 and ACT-027.

Self-Assessment

The seven-second check (house content, and it is a partner check, not a score).

Swap CVs. Your partner gets seven seconds on the top third, then answers one question:

"What job is this person going for?"

If they cannot say, it is not tailored yet. That is the entire assessment, and it is harder to pass than any rating scale.

For a written self-check, tick honestly:

Yes / No
Is there a headline naming what I am, for this job?☐
Are three to five skill bullets visible without scrolling?☐
Does every bullet have evidence in it?☐
Are the ad's own words in my top third?☐
If the ad names a licence or ticket, is it above the fold?☐
Have I turned at least three duties into achievements?☐
Are my referees named, asked, and told which job?☐
Would a person who replaced me be able to write my bullets?☐ (this one should be no)

⚠️ Not validated, and not a score out of eight. A teaching mirror.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-096 Seven SecondsGame / opener12-15 minFRM-058
ACT-097 The Tailoring LabWorksheet, then live editing40-50 minFRM-058, FRM-057
ACT-098 Four SentencesWorksheet25-30 minFRM-060
ACT-006 Two Things CommitmentReflection10 minCloses with a date

Suggested flow: ACT-096 cold, before any teaching → teach FRM-058 → ACT-097 on a real job ad → break → teach FRM-060 → ACT-098 on the same job ad → ACT-006 to close.

⚠️ The same job ad runs through both worksheets. One application, finished, in two activities. Splitting them across two different jobs halves the value and doubles the work.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. What did you notice about your own CV when you had seven seconds on somebody else's?
  2. What was in the job ad that you have been doing for years and never written down?
  3. Which duty was hardest to turn into an achievement, and why?
  4. What did you find out about the employer that you did not know before?
  5. Did anything you found put you off the job? What does that tell you?
  6. What have you been leaving off your CV, and what is the honest reason?
  7. Who are your three referees, and when did you last ask them?
  8. Which job are you applying for, and when? Write the date.
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable. 120 min works if ACT-096 is kept tight. Under 90, do ACT-096, FRM-058 and ACT-097 only, and set the letter for next session
  • Bring spares of everything. Spare CVs, spare printed job ads, spare pens, and a printed copy of the worked cover letter. Half the room will arrive with none of it, and turning them away is how you lose them
  • Devices and wifi need checking the week before. Sentence 3 cannot be written without looking the employer up
  • What usually goes wrong: somebody spends twenty minutes on fonts and colours. Redirect to step 1 of ACT-097 and say plainly that the software cannot see the design
  • Never let them invent to match the ad. If the ad wants something they do not have, the honest moves are to apply anyway and deal with it in the letter, or to find out what the ticket costs and who pays for it. Not to claim it
  • The gap in somebody's history will come up here, quietly, when they are laying out the work section. That belongs to ACT-100 in TOP-EMP-004. Say it is coming, do not open it in a CV session
  • ⚠️ Do not finish without a date. "I'll do it later" is where this topic goes to die. ACT-006 exists for that one reason
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-096 Seven Seconds (12-15 min, medium energy). Four real CVs, seven seconds each, and the room becomes the reader. Run it before any teaching, because it makes the argument for you.
  • Cut the waffle (10 min, high energy). Hand out one real, bad, five-paragraph cover letter. Groups race to cut it to four sentences. Fast, funny, and it lands hard. Full version is a variation inside ACT-098.
  • Headline round (5 min). Everyone writes their headline on a sticky note. Read them out with no names. The room guesses the job. Good after lunch.

PS-EMP-006Pink Sheet · Employment & Work Readiness

They already decided you can do the job

placeholder-story
work-readinessonboardingstarting-workretentionmistakesreliability

Topic: TOP-EMP-006 The First Two Weeks · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

The interview tested whether you can do the work. The first two weeks tests whether you turn up and whether you are honest.

New starters spend that fortnight trying to look competent, which is the one thing nobody is checking. They already made that call. What they have no evidence about yet is reliability, and the only way to give them any is to be there and to tell the truth fast.

Model

Four moves, in order of what it costs you to skip them.

The moveWhy it is in that position
1Turn upThe only evidence they have. Fifteen minutes early beats on time
2Ask earlyThere is a window where asking is free. It closes about week three
3Own it fastThe mistake rarely ends a job. The four hours of hiding it does
4Learn the unwritten rulesNobody writes them down and everybody is judged on them

And inside move 3, the ten seconds that decide it. Four sentences, no "but":

"I've made a mistake. I've loaded the wrong pallet onto the Whangārei truck. I've stopped the loading and I haven't sent it. What do you want me to do?"

⚠️ Sentence 3 is the one everybody leaves out, and it is what makes somebody sound capable rather than helpless.

Metaphor

A driving test you have already passed, and a licence you are still on probation for.

The interview was the test. You passed it, and nobody is re-testing your three-point turn.

What happens next is the probation period on the licence. Nobody is watching whether you can drive. They are watching whether you show up sober, on time, and whether you tell them when you scrape the wing mirror. You lose a restricted licence for the things around the driving, not for the driving.

Study

Two anchors, and it matters which part each one holds up.

1. What good onboarding consists of. Talya Bauer, published by the SHRM Foundation, identified four elements: compliance, clarification, culture and connection. It is real, it is researched, and it is widely used.

⚠️ But it is written for the employer. It describes what a well-run organisation does to a new starter, and most of our learners are not starting at one. There is a payroll form and somebody saying "just follow Dave around."

➜ The house contribution is the flip: the same four needs, answered by the worker when nobody answers them for you. Bauer gets the credit for the half that is hers.

2. Why it is worth a whole topic. MSD's client outcome measure tracks people who exit a main benefit for employment and do not return to a main benefit for the following six months (MSD Annual Report 2025).

➜ A placement that does not last does not count. That is the business case in one sentence, and it is checkable.

⚠️ What this sheet refuses to say. You will see figures everywhere for how many people quit in the first ninety days. Almost all of them trace to HR-software vendors selling onboarding products. None is quoted here. The MSD measure does the work instead.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The two warehouse starters are written for teaching. They are composite and true to what tutors and employers describe, not identified people.

The story to collect, and it is an easy one: a Zeducation graduate who nearly lost a job in the first fortnight and did not. What lands is the specific moment — the pallet, the phone call, the thing they nearly hid — and what they said instead.

Second story, and it is the higher-value one: an employer describing the last new starter who did not make it past a month. Ask them what actually went wrong. It is almost never the work, and hearing that from an employer rather than a facilitator changes the room.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
The week somebody starts a jobThis is the point. The most time-sensitive material in the library
One-to-one, the day before day oneFifteen minutes. Worth more than the group session eight weeks earlier
Any work-readiness programmeThe full topic, 120-150 min
Employer engagementAsk them to confirm it. They will, and it is far more powerful from them
Supervisor trainingPoint move 3 the other way: what do you do in the first four seconds after somebody tells you they got it wrong? That reaction decides whether it happens again

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowThe long game. This is the first fortnight, that is the first five years
PS-EMP-005 They're not hiding it from youMove 4's "learn names" is how a new workmate becomes the person who tells you about the next job
PS-WEL-001 You only need the next rockBoth are about the small specific action rather than the big intention

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on "Say It Early" alone. The Point is already written: a problem told early is a problem, the same problem found later is a problem and a lie. It is the strongest single idea in the topic and it deserves its own page once there is a real story behind it.

TOP-EMP-006Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

1

About This Topic

Everything else in this pillar is about getting a job. TOP-EMP-002 works out what you can do, TOP-EMP-003 gets you in the door, TOP-EMP-004 is the interview, TOP-EMP-005 is the jobs that never had a door.

This one is about keeping it.

⚠️ And it is the part that gets counted. MSD's client outcome measure tracks people who leave a benefit for work and do not go back on a main benefit for the next six months. A placement that does not last does not count. Getting somebody a job they lose in five weeks helps nobody, least of all them.

Two things make the first fortnight different from every other fortnight:
You are being watched for something other than skillThey already tested whether you can do the job. Now they are checking reliability and honesty, and they have no evidence yet either way
There is a window where asking is freeIn week two nobody expects you to know. It closes around week three, and after that the same question costs something

What this topic is not: a lecture about attitude. "Be keen" is not an action. Fifteen minutes early is. Everything here is specific and doable, and one whole section is information the learner was simply never given.

Key words

WordWhat it means
OnboardingWhat an employer does to get a new person up and running. Most small workplaces do almost none
Unwritten ruleSomething everybody knows and nobody says. Breaking one costs more than breaking a written rule
Trial periodA clause some employment agreements carry, allowing dismissal in the first 90 days without the usual grievance route. See below
EscalateTo tell somebody above you about a problem, early, on purpose
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name the four things that decide whether you are still in the job in six months.
  2. Find out ten unwritten rules in your first week, and say who you will ask.
  3. Tell a supervisor you have got something wrong, in four sentences, with no excuse in them.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two people start at the same warehouse on the same Monday. Both got through the same interview. Both can do the work.

The first one turns up at seven every day. On day two he asks the forklift driver what time smoko actually is, and gets told 9:45, not 10:00. On day four he stacks a pallet wrong, realises at eleven, and goes straight to the supervisor: "I've done these wrong. I've stopped. What do you want me to do?" They fix it in twenty minutes.

The second one is quicker on the gear. But he arrives at 7:05 most days, because he assumed seven meant arrive at seven. He does not ask about anything, because he does not want to look like he does not know. On day four he stacks a pallet wrong too, notices, and thinks he will sort it before anyone sees. It goes out on the truck at three.

One of them is still there at Christmas.

Ask the room: which one, and what actually decided it?

Then the second question, which is the real one: has anyone here seen somebody lose a job in the first month? What actually happened?

Statement: They already decided you can do the job. That was the interview. The first two weeks is them finding out whether you turn up and whether you are honest.

➜ Facilitator note: the second question does the teaching. Every room has a story and it is almost never about the work. Collect two or three, then point that out.

4

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-068

The First Two Weeks (house model)

What it is: four things a new starter can do that decide whether they are still there in six months, especially when the employer does no onboarding at all.

Where it comes from. Talya Bauer, published by the SHRM Foundation, identified four elements of good onboarding: compliance, clarification, culture and connection. It is a real framework with research behind it.

⚠️ But it is written for the employer. It describes what a well-run organisation does to a new starter. Most of our learners are not starting at one. There is a payroll form and somebody saying "just follow Dave around."

➜ So the house model flips it. Same four needs, answered by the worker.

Bauer's CWhat a good employer doesWhat you do if they don't
ComplianceExplains the rules and the paperworkAsk for them. Contract, hours, who you tell when you are sick
ClarificationSets out what good looks likeAsk what a good day looks like, in week one
CultureIntroduces the unwritten normsWatch, and ask. When is smoko really
ConnectionIntroduces you to peopleLearn names, especially whoever has been there longest

How to read it: in order of what it costs you to skip it. Turning up is worth more than being good at the job in the first fortnight, because they already decided you can do the job.

The unwritten rules, which nobody hands you:

The questionWhy it matters
When does the day actually start?"Seven" sometimes means boots on at seven
Who do you ring when you are sick, and how early?Getting this wrong once reads as unreliable, however good the reason
When is smoko, how long, and where?The most common week-one mistake in trades and warehousing
Who has been here longest?Not the manager. The person who knows how things are actually done
How do you ask for a day off?Text, app, in person, two weeks ahead

⚠️ Somebody who has never worked in that setting has no way to guess any of this, and that is not a character problem. It is information they were not given.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-069

Say It Early (house model)

What it is: a problem told early is a problem. The same problem found later is a problem and a lie, and that second thing is what gets people sacked.

How to read it: the branch is the whole thing. The mistake is rarely what ends a job. Which way you go at that fork is.

The four sentences. Ten seconds, and most people have never been given the words.

SayExample
1Name it, plainly"I've made a mistake."
2What happened, factually"I've loaded the wrong pallet onto the Whangārei truck."
3What you've already done"I've stopped the loading and I haven't sent it."
4Ask"What do you want me to do?"

⚠️ No "but" in any of the four. "I've made a mistake, but nobody showed me" lands completely differently, even when it is true. Say that afterwards, not in the first ten seconds.

➜ Sentence 3 is the one everybody leaves out, and it is what makes somebody sound capable rather than helpless.

And the version they will use far more often, for a problem that is not their fault:

"I need to flag something. I'm not going to finish this by three. I've done the priority ones first. Do you want me to keep going or hand it over?"

⚠️ Saying "I'm not going to make it" at eleven instead of at three gives a supervisor four hours they can use. Most people say nothing and hope.

⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, and in many migrant workplaces, going to somebody senior to report your own error cuts against how respect works. That is real and it is not a flaw. Name the clash, and give the bridge: "Can I show you something?" is easier to say, respectful, and gets to the same place.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-021

The Four Professional Habits — the long game

The first fortnight buys you a job. These four keep it, and get you recommended for the next one.

HabitWhat it looks like on a Tuesday
ProfessionalismYou speak to the cleaner the same way you speak to the manager
FeedbackSomeone says you cut people off, and you say thank you instead of explaining why they are wrong
Development mindsetYou ask the experienced person how they do it
Conflict managementYou say something in week one, while it is still small

➜ Taught in full in TOP-EMP-001. Ten minutes here is enough, as the bridge from the first fortnight to the first year.

→ Full framework page

⚠️ Trial periods — signpost, do not advise

A trial period is a real thing and learners should know it exists. Since 23 December 2023, all New Zealand employers can use a 90-day trial period, where previously only employers with fewer than 20 staff could. To be valid it must be in writing, signed before the first day of work, agreed in good faith, and used only with somebody who has not previously worked for that employer.

⚠️ Verified 2026-08-02 by search, not read on the authoritative page. Check before delivery.

⚠️ A facilitator's job here is the four moves, not the law. If a learner is worried about a trial period, or has been let go under one, send them to real advice and do not improvise:
Employment New ZealandAgreements, minimum rights, free mediation
Community LawFree legal help
Citizens Advice BureauFree, everywhere
Their unionIf there is one in that sector

Never advise a learner on their employment rights from a workbook.

Self-Assessment

The first two weeks check (house content, and it is a readiness list rather than a score).

Tick honestly, before you start:

Yes / No
Do I know exactly what time to be there, and how I am getting there?☐
Do I know who to ring if I am sick, and how early?☐
Do I have their number in my phone?☐
Have I got everything I need to bring? Boots, ID, bank number, IRD number☐
Do I know who my supervisor is, by name?☐
Have I got three questions ready to ask in week one?☐
Can I say the four sentences without a "but" in them?☐
Do I know what I will do if I get something wrong on day three?☐

⚠️ Not a score. Every "no" is a thing to fix this week, and most of them take five minutes.

➜ Any "no" on the first four is a logistics problem, not a confidence problem, and it belongs in ACT-103 The Day Itself. Act on it, do not talk about it.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Which of the two people in the story is more like you when you start something new?
  2. Have you seen somebody lose a job in the first month? What actually happened?
  3. Which of the twenty unwritten-rule questions had you never thought to ask?
  4. What stops you asking a question at work? Be honest about which reason it is.
  5. What is the longest you have left something before saying it? What did that cost?
  6. Who was the best person you ever worked with in your first week? What did they do?
  7. Which of the four professional habits will be hardest for you?
  8. What is the one thing you will do differently on your first day, and how will you remember it?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. Under 90, run ACT-112, FRM-068 and ACT-110, and give FRM-069 and ACT-111 their own session. Never cut ACT-112, because it is what makes the rest believable
  • ⚠️ Run it the week somebody starts, not months before. The most time-sensitive topic in the library. A one-to-one version the day before day one is worth more than the whole group session eight weeks earlier
  • ⚠️ Check the trial-period section before you deliver it. It was verified on 2026-08-02 by search, not read on the authoritative page. Employment law changes
  • Do not let it become a lecture on attitude. "Be keen" is not an action. Every move here is specific, and one whole section is information the learner was never given
  • The opening story works because the second question is real. Every room has seen somebody lose a job in the first month and it is almost never about the work
  • ⚠️ Somebody in the room has been sacked for exactly what FRM-069 describes. Keep the teaching on the mechanism, never on character, and never ask anybody for their story
  • Turning up on time for a month is a transport, childcare and sleep problem before it is a motivation problem. Everything in ACT-103 applies here. A learner who cannot get there needs help, not a talk
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on the Pink Sheet. The one to collect is a graduate who nearly lost a job in week one and did not, and your tutors will know several
  • ⚠️ Open gap: Bauer's original SHRM Foundation report was verified through consistent secondary sources rather than read directly. Find the primary PDF and link it

PS-EMP-005Pink Sheet · Employment & Work Readiness

They're not hiding it from you

placeholder-story
career-readinessjob-searchhidden-job-marketnetworkingweak-tieswork-readiness

Topic: TOP-EMP-005 The Jobs Nobody Advertises · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

A lot of jobs are never advertised, and it is not a conspiracy. It is a manager avoiding a fortnight of work.

Writing the ad, paying to post it, reading two hundred applications, shortlisting, ringing, booking a room, interviewing eight people. Or: standing in the smoko room and saying "anyone know someone?"

Once you understand that, you know exactly where to stand. A person who turns up already vouched for is doing that manager a favour, not asking for one.

Model

Four channels. Almost everybody spends almost all their effort in the worst one.

ChannelWhat it isCompetition
1Advertised, applied coldHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering first
2Advertised, someone inside knows youMuch lower. You start as a known quantity
3Never advertisedLow, and most people never see these
4Created for youLowest, and rare

Channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing: people who know you exist. That is what makes it teachable. One habit, not three.

And the tool is one sentence, three parts:

  1. What you're looking for. Specific
  2. What you bring. One thing
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"

⚠️ Never call it networking. The word closes people down and sounds like something other people do in a suit. It is telling people what you are looking for.

Metaphor

Everyone queuing at the front door while the side door is open.

The advertised job is the front door. It is well lit, everybody can see it, and there are two hundred people in the queue. Nobody is doing anything wrong by standing in it.

The side door is not locked and it is not hidden. It just does not have a sign on it, because putting up a sign is the expensive part the manager was trying to avoid. It opens for anybody who knows somebody, or who knocks.

Most people never try it, because they assume a door without a sign is not for them.

Study

Mark Granovetter, "The Strength of Weak Ties", American Journal of Sociology, 1973. He asked 282 men in Massachusetts how they had found their jobs. Casual acquaintances beat close friends, by a lot.

The mechanism is the interesting part: your close circle hears the same news you do. Your best mate and your cousin move in your world and know what you know. The person you have not spoken to in two years moves in a different one, and that is where the information you have never heard lives.

Evidence: strong. The core finding has held up over fifty years and across countries.

⚠️ What this sheet deliberately does not say. You will see "70% of jobs are never advertised" or "80%" quoted everywhere. The figures have no traceable source and they are not used here. Say "many". Say "often".

➜ The better evidence is free and it is in the room. Have people chart every job they have ever had against the four channels and tally it on a board (ACT-109). It is more convincing than a statistic and, unlike a statistic, it is about them.

And the part that matters for our learners: Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That advantage is usually going completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that using it is allowed.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The Wiri distribution centre and Hemi's cousin is composite, written for teaching. It is true to how those roles get filled and it is not one identified person.

The story to collect, and it is an easy one: a Zeducation graduate who got work through somebody they barely knew. There will be several. What lands is the chain — who told whom, and how weak the link was. "My aunty's neighbour's son" is the shape that makes a room laugh and then go quiet.

Second story worth collecting: a hiring manager describing a role they filled without advertising it, in their own words, including how long it took. Thirty seconds from the other side of the table is worth more than the whole framework.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any job-search programmeThe full topic, 120-150 min. Runs any time after TOP-EMP-002
One-to-one with somebody who has stopped applyingSixty applications, no replies, concluded there are no jobs. This is the conversation
Redundancy supportThe channel most useful to somebody with twenty years of contacts they have never used
Employer engagementAsk employers how they filled their last three roles. The answer sells the topic for you
Funder conversationsWhy Zeducation's placement approach is not just CV workshops

⚠️ Where it goes wrong: said carelessly, "it's who you know" tells a learner who already feels shut out that the system is rigged. The employer's-side reason has to come first, every time.

PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowThe same weak-ties evidence, pointed at the job once you have it

The Jobs Nobody Advertises

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation120-150 minCareer Readiness, Part 4
career-readinessjob-searchhidden-job-marketnetworkingweak-tiesdirect-approachwork-readiness

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-EMP-005 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Career Readiness, Part 4

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Most job-search teaching stops at the advertised job: find the ad, tailor the CV, write the letter, prepare for the interview. All of that is in TOP-EMP-003 and TOP-EMP-004, and all of it is worth doing.

But it is the channel with the worst odds, and it is where almost everybody puts almost all of their effort.

This topic is about the other channels. The jobs that get filled before an ad is ever written, and how ordinary people actually reach them.

⚠️ This is not "it's who you know" as an excuse. That sentence, said the wrong way, tells a learner who already feels shut out that the system is rigged and there is nothing to do. Said the right way it is the opposite: you already have a network, it is much bigger than you think, most people never use it, and using it costs nothing.

Two things this topic refuses to do:
Quote a percentageYou will see "70% of jobs are never advertised" everywhere. The figure has no traceable source. Say "many", say "often", and let ACT-109 supply the evidence instead
Call it networkingThe word closes people down and it sounds like something other people do in a suit. It is telling people what you are looking for

Key words

WordWhat it means
Hidden job marketJobs that are filled without ever being advertised publicly
Weak tieSomeone you know a bit but not well. A former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
ReferralSomebody inside an organisation putting your name forward
Cold approachContacting an employer when there is no advertised job
Internal candidateSomebody already in the organisation who moves into the role
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Explain why many jobs are never advertised, from the employer's side.
  2. Map your own network and name at least twenty people in it.
  3. Say the three-part sentence out loud, and approach one employer directly.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A manager at a distribution centre in Wiri needs a storeperson. Here is what happens next.

He does not write an ad. Writing the ad takes an afternoon, HR wants it signed off, it costs a few hundred dollars to post, and then two hundred applications arrive and somebody has to read all of them. Then he has to shortlist, ring people, book a room, and sit through eight interviews to find one person who might not last a month.

So instead he stands in the smoko room and says: "anyone know someone?"

Hemi says his cousin is looking. The cousin starts on Monday.

That job existed. It was real, it was paid, and it was never visible. Not to anybody refreshing Seek. And the reason was not secrecy.

Ask the room: why didn't he advertise it?

Then the second question, which is the real one: who in this room got their job the way Hemi's cousin got that one?

Statement: A lot of jobs are never advertised, and it is not because they are being hidden from you. It is because advertising is expensive and slow, and asking around is free and fast.

➜ Facilitator note: let the room answer the first question themselves. Somebody always gets it, and it lands completely differently coming from them than from you.

4

Frameworks Used

IDFrameworkPage
FRM-061How Jobs Are Actually Found→
FRM-024The Strength of Weak Ties→
FRM-057Transferable Skills→
5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-061

How Jobs Are Actually Found (house model)

What it is: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds, and none into the ones that actually work.

Start with the employer's reason, before the channels. Without it the room hears a conspiracy.

The employer's reasonWhat it actually means
Advertising costs money and timePosting the ad, then reading two hundred applications, then interviewing. That is a fortnight of somebody's work
There is already an internal candidateSomeone in the building who knows how the place runs
Referral programmesThey ask their own staff first, because a workmate's recommendation is a known quantity

➜ Say this out loud: "They are not hiding it from you. They are trying not to do two weeks of work."

⚠️ And the flip side, which follows from the same logic. If the manager is avoiding the work, then a person who turns up already vouched for is doing them a favour, not asking for one.

The four channels:

ChannelWhat it isCompetition
1. Advertised, applied coldSeek, Trade Me Jobs, the company siteHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering first
2. Advertised, with someone insideSame ad, but somebody hands your CV overMuch lower. You start as a known quantity
3. Not advertisedThe manager asks the team "know anyone?"Low, and most people never see these
4. Created for youSomebody meets you and finds work for youLowest, and rare

How to read it: channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing — people who know you exist. That is what makes it teachable. One habit, not three.

Four ways in:

The way inWhat it looks like here
1Tell the people you already knowCousin, neighbour, church, former supervisor, the parent at the school gate
2Ask inside where you already workMany unadvertised jobs are internal. If you are in work and want a change, ask around before you look outside
3Go straight to the employerA walk-in, a phone call, or a short written message to a real named person
4VolunteerUnpaid work where you would like to be paid. It produces referees, referrals and somebody who has seen you turn up on time

And one signal worth watching. A company announcing a new site, a new contract or a new shift is a company about to need people. A distribution centre in Drury, a supermarket fit-out, a rest home wing, a roading contract awarded. Ring then, not three months later.

More resources:

  • 📄 Volunteering New Zealand
  • 🔗 Tahatū — job hunting guidance

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-024

The Strength of Weak Ties

What it is: the job and the opportunity usually come from someone you barely know.

Origin: Mark Granovetter, American Journal of Sociology, 1973. He asked 282 men how they found their jobs. Casual acquaintances beat close friends, by a lot. The finding has held up over fifty years and across countries. Evidence: strong.

Strong tiesWeak ties
WhoFamily, close matesA former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you do not
What they give youSupport and helpInformation and opportunities

How to read it: your close circle hears the same news you do. The dotted line is the valuable one, because it reaches information you do not already have.

➜ This is why the answer is not "ask your best mate". They know what you know. It is the person you have not spoken to in two years who has the thing you have never heard about.

More resources:

  • 📄 Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties (PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — The strength of weak ties

→ Full framework page

The three-part sentence (house content, and it is the whole practical tool)

Not "networking". That word closes people down. Telling people what you are looking for.

PartRule
1What you are looking forSpecific. "Warehouse or storeperson work" beats "anything going"
2What you bringOne thing. "I've got my F endorsement"
3The askSmall. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"
"I'm looking for warehouse or storeperson work. I've got my F endorsement. If you hear of anything, would you flick me a text?"

➜ Said to a cousin, a neighbour, someone at church, a former supervisor, the parent at the school gate. Twenty of those beats sixty online applications, and it is less work.

⚠️ A vague ask gets nothing. "Anything going" is unmemorable, so nobody thinks of you when they hear something. A specific ask is the one people remember three weeks later in a smoko room.

Where part 2 comes from: the skills work in TOP-EMP-002 and FRM-057. If somebody cannot fill part 2, that is the gap, not their confidence.

⚠️ Why this matters more for our learners, not less

Two things are true at once and both should be said in the room.

The good news: Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That is a real advantage and it is usually going completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that using it is allowed.

The hard part: research has found candidates with non-Pākehā names get fewer callbacks from cold applications. Channel 1 is where that bites hardest, because a name on a screen is all there is. Channels 2, 3 and 4 route around it, because somebody has already vouched for you.

⚠️ That is not a reason to hide a name. It is a reason to spend the effort where it pays. Never advise a learner to anglicise their name.

⚠️ Open gap: the New Zealand name-discrimination research is referred to here in general terms because the specific studies have not been verified. Find and cite them properly, or reword to "international and New Zealand research has found", before this is used in a tender. The same gap is logged on FRM-061.

Self-Assessment

ACT-109 Where Did Your Jobs Come From? is the assessment, and it is evidence rather than a score.

Every job the learner has ever had, sorted into the four channels, then tallied on the board for the whole room.
What they findMost of their jobs came through channels 2 and 3
What they realiseAlmost all of their effort this month went into channel 1
The name in Part 4Usually somebody they barely knew, who mentioned it by accident

➜ The board is the instrument. It is more convincing than any statistic and, unlike a statistic, it is about them.

⚠️ Not a score, and nothing is recorded. A learner whose list is entirely channel 1 has not failed anything — that is real, it usually means a small network in this country, and it is exactly who the rest of the topic is for.

A second check, at the end of the session:

Yes / No
Can I say why a job might never be advertised, from the employer's side?☐
Have I written down at least twenty names?☐
Is my three-part sentence specific enough to be remembered?☐
Have I said it out loud to a real person?☐
Do I have three names and three dates?☐
Have I approached one employer directly?☐
6

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-109 Where Did Your Jobs Come From?Assessment, and the opener20-25 minFRM-061, FRM-024
ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?Game20-25 minFRM-061, FRM-024
ACT-108 The Direct ApproachRoleplay35-45 minFRM-061, FRM-024

Suggested flow: the Wiri story → ACT-109 before any teaching, because the board makes the argument for you → teach FRM-061, employer's reason first → teach FRM-024 → ACT-101 to build the list → break → the three-part sentence → ACT-108 with a real list of local employers → ACT-006 to close with three names and three dates.

⚠️ ACT-109 goes first, cold. Teaching the four channels and then asking people to chart their own jobs is backwards, and it wastes the single most persuasive twenty minutes in the topic.

⚠️ Bring a real list of local employers for ACT-108. A room asked to think of three will produce two supermarkets and go quiet.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Why did the manager in the story not write an ad? Would you have, in his position?
  2. What did the board say in ACT-109? Where has your effort actually been going?
  3. Who was the person who told you about a job? How well did you know them?
  4. How many names did you expect to write? How many did you get?
  5. Who is a ★ on your map that you had never thought of as a work contact?
  6. Who is the last person you told that you are looking for work?
  7. What stops you saying the sentence? Be honest about which part is hard.
  8. What is your one direct approach, to whom, and when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. Under 90, run ACT-109, FRM-061 and ACT-101, and give ACT-108 its own session. Never cut ACT-109 — it is what makes the rest believable
  • Where it sits in the pillar: it is Career Readiness Part 4, and it can run any time after TOP-EMP-002. It does not need the CV or interview topics first. A room that is currently out of work and demoralised will often engage with this one before any of the others
  • ⚠️ The single biggest risk in this topic is that it lands as "the system is rigged". The employer's-side reason is the antidote and it has to come first. "They are not hiding it from you, they are trying not to do two weeks of work."
  • Do not quote a percentage. Somebody will ask. The honest answer is that the numbers circulating are unsourced, and that the board in ACT-109 is better evidence anyway
  • Do not call it networking, and do not push LinkedIn. For most Zeducation learners the live network is church, sport, family, marae and former workmates. Naming what they already have beats teaching them to build something new
  • Some learners genuinely have a small map. New migrants, people out of a violent relationship, people recently out of prison. Do not let ACT-101's count become a competition. The room itself becomes part of their map, and saying so out loud matters
  • Do not send anybody to an employer unprepared. Practise in ACT-108 first. A bad walk-in can close a door for the whole programme, and small towns have long memories
  • Do not teach this as a replacement for applying. Advertised jobs are real jobs. It is proportion, not abandonment
  • ⚠️ Open gap: the New Zealand name-discrimination research needs finding and citing properly
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on the Pink Sheet. A graduate who got work through somebody they barely knew is the story this topic needs, and there will be several. Ask your tutors and get permission properly
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-109 Where Did Your Jobs Come From? (20-25 min, medium energy). The best opener in the topic. Nobody is told that most jobs come through people. They prove it to themselves and the tally goes on the board.
  • ACT-035 Six Degrees Of This Room (10-12 min, 🔥 high energy). A string web of what people have in common. Use it when the room needs moving rather than counting.
  • Six degrees to an employer (8 min). Name one local employer. See how few steps it takes for anyone in the room to reach somebody inside it. Usually two or three, and it is startling.
  • Text-it-now (3 min, at the end). Phones out, send the sentence to one person. Beats any amount of good intention.

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

The New Zealand equivalents are in FRM-061 instead.

The evidence underneath it is Granovetter (1973), not the source. No percentage is quoted anywhere in this topic, because the figures that circulate for the size of the hidden job market have no traceable basis. PS-EMP-001Pink Sheet · Employment & Work Readiness

The job comes from the person you barely know

placeholder-story
networkingweak-tiesrelationshipswork-readinessopportunity

Topic: TOP-EMP-001 The People You Work With · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

The people who love you cannot help you find work. The people who barely know you can.

It is not about who cares about you most. It is about who knows something you do not.

Model

Strong tiesWeak ties
WhoFamily, close mates, the people you see every dayA former workmate, a tutor, someone from church, a cousin's friend
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you have never heard
Who they knowRoughly who you knowPeople you have never met
What they give youSupport, help, a place to stayInformation, opportunities, introductions

The closed triangle is your circle. Everybody in it hears the same news. The dotted line is the only one that reaches new information.

Metaphor

A closed circle and a bridge.

Your close friends are a circle. Warm, safe, and completely enclosed. Everyone inside hears the same news at the same time, so no matter how much they love you, they cannot tell you anything new.

A weak tie is a bridge out of the circle. You do not have to live on the bridge. You just have to have built one, and be willing to walk over it occasionally.

Study

Mark Granovetter, "The Strength of Weak Ties", American Journal of Sociology 78(6), 1360-1380 (1973). Granovetter surveyed 282 men in Massachusetts about how they had found their jobs. Casual acquaintances turned out to be more useful than close friends. It became one of the most cited papers in the social sciences.

📄 Full paper (PDF) · 📄 Stanford summary

Honest limit: 282 men, Massachusetts, early 1970s. The finding has held up broadly across fifty years of replication, but say what the original study was.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. This sheet needs a real one and it can only come from delivery.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who got work through a weak tie. The shape that lands is: applications that went nowhere, then one message to someone they had half-forgotten, and the job came from that. Ask tutors and coaches for it. Get permission and get the details right, including how long the gap was since they had last spoken.

Second story worth collecting: a learner who did not think they had a network, until someone walked them through church, sport, family and former workmates and counted it up. That one is more common and probably more useful.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any work-readiness sessionThe line that reframes "networking" for people who hate the word
CV and job search coachingBefore the CV. Most jobs are not found by applying
Employer conversationsWhy they should keep talking to past learners

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-COM-001 Assertive is clear, not loudBoth argue that a workplace skill people think needs confidence actually needs a small repeatable habit

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on the red flags, built on the contrast between building relationships and building them badly. The Point is already there: most damaged reputations started with telling one person, once.

The People You Work With
