Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-EMP-001 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 1

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Success at work is not just about doing your job well. It is also about deliberately building the right relationships, because the people around you can open doors, back you up, and speak well of you when you are not in the room. Or, if you choose badly, they can hold you back and make work harder than it needs to be.

This matters for four reasons. Support: the right relationships help you feel included and confident instead of isolated. Opportunity: strong connections lead to new work, honest feedback, and people who recommend you. Wellbeing: healthy relationships make work more enjoyable and give you people you can trust when things get hard. Influence: without them you have less say over decisions that affect you.

It is your job, not your employer's. Notice who is safe, respectful and growth-minded, and put your time into those people on purpose.

And you do not need to be loud. The shyest person in the room can do this, because it is built out of very small things repeated often.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Weak tieSomeone you know a bit but not well. A former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
SiloSticking to your own small group and not talking to anyone else
ProfessionalismBehaving the same way with everyone, no matter their job title
ConfidentialityKeeping to yourself what you were told in private
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Build a work relationship on purpose, starting with one short conversation with someone outside your immediate team.
  2. Name the behaviours that protect a work relationship and the ones that quietly damage it.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two people start the same job on the same day. Both can do the work.

One of them says good morning to everyone, including the cleaner and the security guard. He asks the experienced guy how he sets out a job. When he is going to miss a deadline he says so early. When he gets pulled up he says "fair enough, I'll fix it."

The other is faster with the tools.

Twelve months later, one of them is being recommended for the next job. Ask the room: which one, and why?

Then the second question, which is the real one: think of someone at your last job who was good at the work but nobody wanted on their team. What was it about them?

Statement: Being good at the job gets you hired. How you are with people is what gets you kept, recommended, and told about the next opportunity.

➜ Facilitator note: the second question does the work. Every room has that person and the answers come fast. Collect three or four, then point out that not one of them was about competence.

4

Frameworks Used

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-021

The Four Professional Habits (house model)

What it is: the four habits that make people want to work with you, over time.

HabitWhat it looks like on a Tuesday
ProfessionalismYou speak to the cleaner the same way you speak to the manager
FeedbackSomeone says you cut people off, and you say thank you instead of explaining why they are wrong
Development mindsetYou ask the experienced person how they do it, and show the new person where things are
Conflict managementYou say something in week one, while it is still small

How to read it: habits, not talents. Every one can be started this week by someone who has never done it.

Worked example: a new warehouse hand makes a point of learning the forklift driver's name and asking how he likes the pallets stacked. Six weeks later, when the new hand needs a favour on a bad day, he gets it. Nothing about that required confidence.

More resources: house content, with no external reading matched to it yet. The gap and what would fill it are recorded on the framework page. → Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-024

The Strength of Weak Ties

What it is: the job and the opportunity usually come from someone you barely know.

Origin: Mark Granovetter, American Journal of Sociology, 1973. He asked 282 men how they found their jobs. Casual acquaintances beat close friends, by a lot.

Strong tiesWeak ties
WhoFamily, close matesA former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you do not
What they give youSupport and helpInformation and opportunities

How to read it: your close circle hears the same news you do. The dotted line is the valuable one.

Worked example: a woman sends forty online applications and gets two replies. Then she messages her tutor from four months ago, just to say what she has been up to. The tutor mentions a former student managing a distribution centre in Wiri who is short-staffed. One message beat forty applications.

More resources:

  • 📄 Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties (PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — The strength of weak ties

→ Full framework page

The six red flags (house content)

Building relationships is powerful. How you build them decides whether they help you.

Red flagWhy it costs you
Oversharing personal informationBlurs boundaries and makes it harder to stay professional
Romantic entanglements and office dramaConflicts of interest, and hard for everyone involved
Being too close to a small groupOthers read it as favouritism or cliques
GossipingIf you talk about others, people assume you talk about them too
Using people only for personal gainShow up only when you want something and people pull away
No clear boundariesRelationships get unprofessional and distract from the work

→ Covered in full on FRM-021. For trust specifically, see FRM-022 The Trust Equation.

The shy starter (house content, and the most important paragraph in this topic)

You don't need to be loud or extroverted to build good relationships.

Three moves, and that is all:

  1. Brief eye contact when you walk past someone
  2. A nod or a small smile, as a simple sign of respect and openness
  3. A short human conversation. "How's your day going?" "How did that meeting go?"

These tiny actions help people feel seen and make the deeper conversations possible later.

Self-Assessment

ACT-030 How Well Do I Build Relationships? Ten statements, scored 1 to 3, out of 30. House content, taken as written from the source workbook.

ScoreWhat it means
24-30You are actively and consistently building healthy professional relationships
18-23A good base, with a few areas to strengthen
10-17Still developing these habits. Start with one or two simple changes

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Who at work would say something good about you if your name came up when you were not there?
  2. Think of a work relationship that has helped you. How did it actually start?
  3. Which of the six red flags have you seen damage someone? What did it cost them?
  4. When did you last talk to someone at work who is not in your usual group?
  5. Who is a weak tie you have not spoken to in six months, and what would it take to send one message?
  6. Are you someone people can tell things to in confidence? How do you know?
  7. Which of the four habits is your weakest right now?
  8. What is one thing you will do differently in the next week, with whom, and when?

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 90 min tight, 120 min comfortable. If you have 60, run ACT-036, FRM-021 and ACT-030
  • The shy starter paragraph is not optional. Half the room decides in the first ten minutes that this topic is for extroverts and switches off. Say it early
  • What usually goes wrong: the red flags land as being told off. Anchor every one in what it costs you, not what you will be in trouble for
  • Do not push LinkedIn. For most Zeducation learners the live network is church, sport, family, marae and former workmates. Naming what they already have beats teaching them to build something new
  • Where this sits in the pillar: TOP-EMP-001 is about the job once you have it. The three Career Readiness topics — TOP-EMP-002, TOP-EMP-003 and TOP-EMP-004 — are about getting it. Either order works, and a room that is currently out of work will engage with those three first
  • The weak-ties teaching now has a home of its own. FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found turns the same evidence into a job-search habit, and ACT-101 makes a learner's own network visible in about eight minutes. Worth borrowing into this session
  • ⚠️ Partly closed: the gap on NZ employability material is now partly filled by SRC-010 Tahatū, which carries New Zealand pay and job-demand data across 800-plus careers. Still open: nothing on what employers say they actually ask for in a Zeducation region. Worth an employer survey, and it would be ours

PS-EMP-002Pink Sheet · Employment & Work Readiness

You are not starting from nothing

placeholder-story
career-readinesstransferable-skillsconfidencework-readinesscv

Topic: TOP-EMP-002 What You Can Already Do · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

"I haven't really got any experience" is almost never true. It means nobody has ever helped you put it into words.

The skill is there. The vocabulary is missing. Those are completely different problems and only one of them is the person's fault, which is neither.

Model

Five sources, one set of skills, one translation.

WhereWhat people countWhat is actually there
Paid work✅ CountedUsually written as duties, not skills
Unpaid and family❌ Never countedBudgeting, logistics, personal care, advocacy
Church, marae, community❌ Never countedEvent organisation, handling money, speaking to a room
Sport and culture❌ Never countedReliability, coaching, being coached, losing well
Study and self-taught❌ Rarely countedAnything learned off YouTube is still learned

Four of the five arrows are ones people leave out. The box on the right is the whole job.

And the rule that stops it becoming a pep talk: every skill gets three parts — the skill in the employer's words, where you did it, and proof. A number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it. Without the third part it is a slogan.

Metaphor

A pantry you have never taken stock of.

You are standing in front of it saying there is nothing to cook. There are four shelves and you have only ever looked at the one at eye level. Everything on the other three is still food. It is just been sitting in packaging you do not recognise, with somebody else's labels on it.

Nobody is asking you to buy groceries. They are asking you to look on the bottom shelf.

Study

No single study proves this one, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. It is a practitioner model. What sits under it:

  • Tahatū, the Tertiary Education Commission's careers service, is built on the premise that a career is not one ladder and that skills carry across a working life. Its 800-plus career profiles are organised so you can enter through skills rather than job titles
  • O*NET, the US occupational database Tahatū's interest quiz derives from, has spent thirty years describing jobs as bundles of skills instead of titles

Honest limit: neither of those is evidence that reframing changes employment outcomes. What this model is, is a translation tool. It should be taught as one, never as a proven intervention.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The section-1 story in the topic — the Māngere woman with the household budget, the school run, the interpreting and the fono catering — is composite and written for teaching. It is true to what tutors describe, and it is not one identified person.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who said "I haven't got any experience", did the skills work, and could then name eight things with evidence. What lands is the before and after sentence — what they said in the first ten minutes and what they said at the end. Get permission properly and get the detail right.

Second story worth collecting: a learner who got a job on the strength of a skill that came from church or family, not from paid work. That one closes the argument for good.

Use it inHow

1

About This Topic

Most job-search teaching starts with the CV. That is the wrong end.

A CV is a container. If you sit down to write one before you know what goes in it, you produce half a page, feel worse about yourself, and stop. This topic is the part that comes first: working out what you can already do, what you are actually drawn to, and who already knows you.

Three questions, in this order.

The questionWhat answers it
1What can I do?FRM-057 Transferable Skills
2What am I drawn to, and what jobs is that?FRM-056 RIASEC, on Tahatū
3How do people actually get work?FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found

This topic uses somebody else's tool on purpose. Tahatū is the New Zealand government's careers site, run by the Tertiary Education Commission. It replaced careers.govt.nz in December 2025. It carries profiles for more than 800 careers with New Zealand pay ranges and job-demand ratings, an interest quiz, and a free CV builder. Zeducation does not have that data and never will. Our job is the teaching around it, not a copy of it.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Transferable skillSomething you can do that carries from one setting to another. Handling money, calming someone down, meeting a deadline
EvidenceThe proof underneath a claim. A number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it
Interest typeOne of six broad kinds of work people are drawn to. See FRM-056
Weak tieSomeone you know a bit, but not well. The person a job usually comes through
Job demandHow many of these jobs New Zealand actually needs right now. Tahatū rates it on every career profile
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name at least eight skills you already have, in the words an employer uses, each with a place you did it and one piece of proof.
  2. Use Tahatū to turn your interests into a list of real New Zealand jobs, with pay and demand attached.
  3. Say out loud, to a real person, what work you are looking for.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A woman sits down for a work-readiness session in Māngere and says the sentence almost everybody says: "I haven't really got any experience."

Here is her actual week. She runs a household on a fixed budget and it balances. She gets three children to two different schools by 8:30 every day, and has done for six years. She translates for her parents at WINZ and at the doctor, which means she handles other people's most stressful conversations in two languages. She did the food for a fono of a hundred and forty people last month, to a budget, and there was enough.

Ask the room: which of those things did not count?

Then the second question, which is the real one: what have you been doing for years that you have never written down anywhere?

Statement: You are not starting from nothing. You are starting from a lot of experience that nobody has ever helped you put into words.

➜ Facilitator note: do not rush past the first question. Let the room answer it. Somebody will say "but that's just being a mum" and that sentence is the whole topic. Write it on the board.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-057

Transferable Skills (house model)

What it is: the skills you built somewhere nobody wrote down, which are the same skills the job ad is asking for, in different words.

Ask most people what they can do and they answer with job titles. Kitchenhand. Caregiver. Mum. Job ads do not ask for job titles. They ask for skills. The gap between those two sentences is where a lot of good people stop applying.

The five places skills come from. Most people count the first one and nothing else.

WhereWhat people miss
Paid workCounted, but usually described as duties rather than skills
Unpaid and familyRunning a household budget. Caring for a parent. Getting three kids somewhere on time
Church, marae, communityOrganising an event for 200 people. Handling money. Speaking in front of a room
Sport and cultureTurning up when you did not feel like it. Coaching. Being coached
Study and self-taughtAnything learned off YouTube counts. Welding, video editing, fixing a car

How to read it: one set of skills, five sources. The arrow on the right is the translation, and it is the actual work of this topic.

The translation. Left column is how a learner says it. Right column is how a job ad says it.

What they sayWhat it is called
"I just helped out at church"Volunteer coordination · event organisation
"I looked after my nana"Personal care · medication support · working with health professionals
"I did the food for the fono"Catering to budget and headcount · food safety
"I ran the till"Cash handling · reconciliation · customer service
"I translate for my parents"Bilingual · interpreting in high-stakes settings
"I got the kids to school every day"Reliability · logistics · time management

➜ Nothing in the right column is a lie. Say that out loud to a room worried about overselling. Naming a skill accurately is not exaggeration. Most people are doing the opposite, and it is costing them work.

The three-part evidence rule. A skill on a CV is a claim, and a claim without evidence is noise.

Example
SkillThe employer's words"Cash handling and reconciliation"
WhereThe real setting, however informal"Two years on the till at a family takeaway"
ProofA number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it"Balanced the float nightly. Never short."

⚠️ The proof column is the one people skip, and it is the one that gets read.

More resources: house model. The reframing comes from Tahatū's skills-not-jobs framing and the skills taxonomies underneath O*NET. → Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-056

RIASEC — Holland's six interest types

What it is: six broad kinds of work people are drawn to. It is the model behind Tahatū's interest quiz, and behind most careers tools in the world.

Nobody is one type. Everybody is a mix, usually described by their top two or three letters.

TypeDrawn toSounds like
RRealisticTools, machines, materials, outdoors, being physical"I like finishing the day and seeing what I built"
IInvestigativeWorking things out, data, diagnosis"I want to know why it broke"
AArtisticMaking, designing, performing, expressing"I'd rather it looked right than be quick"
SSocialTeaching, helping, caring, serving people"The best part of the job is the people"
EEnterprisingPersuading, selling, leading, running things"Put me in front of the customer"
CConventionalOrder, accuracy, systems, records"It should be right, and it should be filed"

How to read it: the six sit in a circle, and neighbours are similar while opposites are not. Realistic and Conventional get on. Realistic and Social pull hard against each other.

⚠️ Be straight about what this is worth. The circular structure has held up across fifty years of studies. The promise attached to it has not. Matching your interests to your job is only weakly linked to being happy in it (r ≈ .17 across 53 studies), and a separate review of 27 studies found no significant link at all. The link to performance is stronger, around .32, which is not the direction most people assume.

➜ The honest line for a room: "This tells you what you're drawn to. It does not tell you what you'd be good at, and it is a weak predictor of whether you'd be happy. What it is genuinely good for is giving you words for something nobody has ever asked you about, and showing you jobs you had never heard of."

More resources:

  • 🔗 Tahatū interest quiz and career profiles
  • 📄 O*NET Interest Profiler

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-061

How Jobs Are Actually Found (house model)

What it is: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds, and none into the one that works.

ChannelWhat it isCompetition
1. Advertised, applied coldSeek, Trade Me Jobs, the company siteHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering first
2. Advertised, with someone insideSame ad, but somebody hands your CV overMuch lower. You start as a known quantity
3. Not advertisedThe manager asks the team "know anyone?" firstLow, and most people never see these
4. Created for youSomebody meets you and finds work for youLowest, and rare

How to read it: channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing, people who know you exist. That is what makes it teachable. One habit, not three.

And say why the job was never advertised, before any of the channels. Advertising costs money and about a fortnight of somebody's time: posting it, reading two hundred applications, interviewing. A manager who already has somebody in mind avoids all of that.

➜ "They are not hiding it from you. They are trying not to do two weeks of work." Without that sentence the room hears that the system is rigged. With it, they can see exactly where to stand.

The move is not "networking". That word closes people down. It is telling people what you are looking for, in one sentence with three parts:

  1. What you are looking for. Specific. "Warehouse or storeperson work" beats "anything going"
  2. What you bring. One thing. "I've got my F endorsement"
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"

➜ Said to a cousin, a neighbour, someone at church, a former supervisor, the parent at the school gate. Twenty of those beats sixty online applications, and it is less work.

And say this part. Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That is a real advantage and it usually goes completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that using it is allowed.

More resources: built on FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties and Granovetter (1973). → Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-095 What's My Code? is the assessment for this topic, and it runs on Tahatū's interest quiz rather than anything Zeducation wrote.

The score is not the point. What the learner leaves with is:
Their top three lettersWords for something nobody has asked them about before
A list of jobsIncluding several they had never heard of
Pay and demand for eachReal New Zealand numbers, not a guess
One job to look into properlyWith a date against it

⚠️ Not a measure of ability. RIASEC describes what someone is drawn to now, and interests move. It should only ever widen a learner's list, never rule anything out. If it is being used to tell somebody what they cannot do, it is being used wrongly.

Suggested flow: open with the story → teach FRM-057 → ACT-094 while the room is warm → break → teach FRM-056 honestly, including the evidence audit → ACT-095 on devices → teach FRM-061 → ACT-101 → ACT-013 to close with a date against a name.

With ACT-108 this becomes two sessions. The direct approach needs 45 minutes of its own and a real list of local employers. Put it at the start of session two, straight after a recap of FRM-061.

⚠️ ACT-095 needs devices and wifi. Check both the week before, and have a paper fallback. Half a room turning up without a phone that will hold a charge is a normal Tuesday.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. What is something you have been doing for years that you had never counted as a skill?
  2. Which of the five places did you get the most from? Which one had you never thought about?
  3. Whose voice is it when you say "that doesn't really count"? Where did that come from?
  4. Which of your three letters surprised you, and which one did you already know?
  5. What job came up on Tahatū that you had never heard of? What made you look twice?
  6. Who is on your map that you had never thought of as a work contact?
  7. Who is the last person you told that you are looking for work?
  8. What is the one thing you will do in the next week, with whom, and when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. If you only have 90, run FRM-057, ACT-094 and ACT-101, and set ACT-095 as homework with a due date
  • The first sentence of section 3 is the whole topic. "I haven't really got any experience." Every room says it. Do not argue with it, and do not reassure. Count out loud instead
  • What usually goes wrong: the RIASEC quiz becomes the session, and everybody leaves with three letters and no jobs list. Budget the second half of ACT-095 for the career profiles, because the profiles are the value and the letters are not
  • Do not let it become a personality-test session. Somebody will ask how it compares to MBTI or a work-style quiz they did once. Answer it honestly using the evidence audit, then move on
  • Interests are shaped by exposure. A young person who has never met an engineer will not test toward engineering. For learners whose working world has been retail, care and warehousing, treat a narrow result as a signal about their exposure, not about them
  • ⚠️ Never advise a learner to anglicise their name. If channel 1 bias comes up, the answer is to spend the effort in channels 2, 3 and 4, not to change who they are
  • ⚠️ Open gap: we have no Zeducation learner story for the Pink Sheet yet. It can only come from delivery. Ask your tutors and get permission properly
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know? (20-25 min, medium energy). Everyone maps their own network and counts it. Most people expect twenty names and write sixty. The count is the lesson, and it works as an opener or a closer.
  • The two-minute version: ask everyone to say one thing they can do that is not on any CV they have ever written. Go round the room. It takes two minutes and it sets up the whole topic.
  • ACT-035 Six Degrees Of This Room (10-12 min, high energy). If you have already run ACT-101 with this group, use this instead.

From the Ice Breaker Games pillar

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

GameTimeEnergySettingWhy this one here
GAM-006 Two Truths and a Lie15-25 minmediumonline or in personSurfaces things about people the room would never have guessed, which is the point of the topic
GAM-016 Articulate15-20 minmediumonline or in personNaming a thing in few words, which is what a skill line has to do

Source Trail

Built from SRC-010 Tahatū Career Navigator, ingested 2026-08-01, and enriched 2026-08-02 from SRC-013 Indeed, "What Is the Hidden Job Market?", which supplied the employer's-side explanation and the direct approach in ACT-108. Its vendor statistic and its US white-collar tactics were excluded on the record. The strategy is take the teaching, point at the tool: Tahatū holds the New Zealand career data, and Zeducation holds the facilitation around it. The story in section 3, the translation table, the three-part evidence rule and all four activities were written fresh. The RIASEC evidence audit was researched separately and is not Tahatū's framing.

GAM-001Game · Ice Breaker Games

Scattergories

Ice Breaker Games10-15 min
ice-breakerword-gamecompetitivequickonline

Time: 10-15 min · Group: 3-20, or breakout rooms above that · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

One letter, five categories, sixty seconds. The trick is that unique answers score more, so the safe obvious word is worth less than the one nobody else thought of.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Fast, competitive and needs almost no preparation. Good for a room that has gone quiet and good as a five-minute filler while you wait for people to arrive.

What you need

  • one letter and five categories, prepared
  • a timer
  • paper and pen each, or the chat box

How it works

  1. Pick one letter and read out five categories. Say them twice
  2. Sixty seconds. Everyone writes one word per category, all starting with that letter
  3. Time up. Go round and read them out, category by category
  4. Score it. A word nobody else has is worth more than one two people share
  5. New letter, new round. Three rounds is usually enough

Example. Category: animals. Letter: C. → cat, cow, cheetah, camel, chicken, chimpanzee, crocodile, crab.

Word lists, categories and questions

Category sets that work:
EasyAnimals · food · a boy's name · something in this room · a colour
NZA town · a rugby team · something at the beach · a bird · a takeaway
WorkA job title · something in an office · a tool · a workplace hazard · a reason someone is late

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This is a spelling and vocabulary game in English. In an ESOL or low-literacy room it stops being a warm-up and becomes a test. Play it in pairs so nobody is exposed, or use the picture categories in the variations
  • Do not argue about whether a word counts. Facilitator decides, instantly, and moves on. The argument is longer than the round
  • Read the categories twice. Half the room will not have caught the fifth one

Variations

  • Pairs: two people per sheet. Takes all the pressure off and it is louder
  • Team version: two teams, one scribe each, scored on the board
  • Spoken version: no writing at all. Go round the room, one category at a time, and anyone who repeats an answer is out
  • Te reo round: one round where every answer is in te reo Māori or a Pacific language. The room teaches each other and it changes who the expert is

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-EMP-003 The CV That Gets ReadFast recall under time pressure, same as a reader giving you seven seconds
TOP-LEA-011 Leader Or ManagerFast, competitive, and somebody always starts organising everybody else

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-005 Name, Place, Animal, ThingThe same game with fixed categories. Run one or the other, not both
GAM-002 Word GeneratorAlso a letters game, but everyone works alone and there is no category to argue about
GAM-009 First Letter, Last LetterIf you want the same feel with zero preparation

GAM-002Game · Ice Breaker Games

Word Generator

Ice Breaker Games8-12 min
ice-breakerword-gamequietquickonline

Time: 8-12 min · Group: any · Energy: low · Where: online or in person

You give a handful of letters. Everybody has two or three minutes to make as many real words from them as they can. Most words wins, and an invented word costs you a point.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Quiet, low pressure and needs no talking. Good for a wary room, a room that has just arrived, or the ten minutes before you actually start. It also works completely fine with people joining late.

What you need

  • a set of seven or eight letters, shown on screen or written up
  • a timer
  • paper and pen each

How it works

  1. Show seven or eight letters. Include three or four vowels or it will not work
  2. Two to three minutes. Everyone writes as many words as they can, using only those letters
  3. Time up. Count. Highest number reads their list out
  4. Anything not a real word costs a point. Facilitator decides, quickly

Example. Letters: A, E, I, O, U, T, S. Player 1: out, sat, tea, toe. Player 2: sea, set, toes, sue, east, tie. Player 2 wins.

Word lists, categories and questions

Letter sets that work: A E I O U T S · A E I R T S N · A E O R T L M · A E I D N R T

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Another English spelling game. In an ESOL or low-literacy room, run it in pairs or skip it. The adaptation matters more than the game
  • Three vowels minimum, or the room sits there with nothing
  • Do not let the scoring dispute run. Facilitator rules on a word in about a second

Variations

  • Pairs: far better for a mixed room, and it gets people talking
  • Longest word only: one word each, longest wins. Thirty seconds and it is over
  • Any language: words in any language count, and the person has to say what it means. Levels the field completely and it is usually the best version
  • Themed: all words must be food, or animals, or something you would find at work

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-DIG-001 Getting A Straight Answer Out Of AILow pressure and quiet, good before a topic that makes people feel behind
TOP-LEA-008 Safe To Be Yourself HereQuiet, no talking, no pressure. The one for a room that has not decided about you yet
TOP-WEL-001 Building ResilienceQuiet and low pressure, for a session that asks a lot of people

GAM-003Game · Ice Breaker Games

Trivia

Ice Breaker Games15-30 min
ice-breakerquizteamsonlineprep-needed

Time: 15-30 min · Group: any, in teams of 3-5 · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

A quizmaster, some questions, teams writing answers. The oldest one in the book and it still works, as long as the questions fit the room in front of you.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Fills a real slot. Good when you have twenty minutes to spend, good for teams who need a reason to talk to each other, and good online because the chat box does the answering for you.

What you need

  • your questions, prepared beforehand
  • a way to keep score
  • the chat box, or paper per team

How it works

  1. Prepare your questions beforehand. This is the whole job. Five or six rounds of five
  2. Split into teams of three to five. Let them pick a team name, it takes ten seconds and it changes the mood
  3. Read a question. Teams confer quietly and write an answer
  4. Online: everyone types the answer into the chat at the same time, on your count of three, so nobody copies
  5. After each round, read the answers out and score
  6. Highest score at the end wins

Word lists, categories and questions

Rounds that work in a Zeducation room:
AotearoaTowns, rivers, the flag, kupu Māori, who is on the money
The IslandsCapitals, flags, languages, food
Music and TVPitch it at the age in the room, not at yours
This programmeQuestions about your own content. Sneaky revision and it works
Guess the staff memberA fact about each tutor. Always the best round

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Trivia rewards whoever went to the best school, unless you write it carefully. Mix the rounds so everybody in the room is an expert at something
  • Teams, never individuals. Individual trivia humiliates somebody within four questions
  • Prepare properly or do not run it. A quizmaster making questions up loses the room fast
  • Keep rounds to five questions. Ten is too many and the energy sags

Variations

  • Team-written: each team writes five questions for another team. Takes longer, and the room owns it
  • Picture round: photos on screen. Works better than text for a mixed-literacy room
  • Music round: ten seconds of a song each. Loudest round every time

Topics it suits

Any of them, and none of them. This one is pure warm-up: no link back to teach, nothing to debrief. Reach for it when a room needs waking up rather than when a topic needs opening.

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-013 Guess That MovieA trivia round that is entirely visual
GAM-005 Name, Place, Animal, ThingIf you have no time to prepare questions
GAM-014 Virtual PictionaryThe other one that fills a whole slot

GAM-004Game · Ice Breaker Games

Charades

Ice Breaker Games15-25 min
ice-breakeractinghigh-energynon-verbalonlineafter-lunch

Time: 15-25 min · Group: 6-30, two teams · Energy: 🔥 high · Where: online or in person

One person acts out a word. No talking, no sound, no props. Their team has a time limit to guess it. Then the other team goes.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

The best thing in this pillar for a flat room after lunch. It gets people out of their seats, it makes the room laugh at itself, and it works just as well on camera as in person.

What you need

  • a list of words or phrases, prepared
  • a timer
  • nothing else

How it works

  1. Two teams. Pick an actor for the first round
  2. Show the actor the word privately. Online, send it in a direct message
  3. Set a timer. Sixty or ninety seconds
  4. The actor acts. Gestures, faces, body. No talking, no noises, no pointing at objects
  5. Their team guesses. Correct inside the time wins a point
  6. Swap teams, new actor. Keep going until you have a winner or you run out of time

Word lists, categories and questions

Word lists that work: films · animals · jobs · things you do at work · everyday actions · NZ things (jandals, hāngī, the Sky Tower, a hongi, a chilly bin).

⚠️ Keep them concrete. "Loyalty" is not actable. "Making a cup of tea" is.

Watch out for

  • Online, the actor should be the only one on camera or pinned, or nobody can see them
  • ⚠️ Some people will not act in front of a room, and that is not shyness to be pushed through. Have the passing rule said out loud before you start, and let them be the timekeeper or the scorer instead
  • Watch for words tied to one culture. If half the room has never seen the film, the round is dead. Ask the room to supply the list and this fixes itself
  • Ninety seconds maximum. A round that drags kills the energy the game is there to create

Variations

  • Room-supplied words: everybody writes two on a slip at the start. Better words, more buy-in, no prep
  • Sound charades: the reverse. Noises only, no movement. Works well for people who will not stand up
  • Team of two acting: takes the pressure off the individual and doubles the comedy
  • Low literacy: show the actor a picture instead of a word

Topics it suits

Any of them, and none of them. This one is pure warm-up: no link back to teach, nothing to debrief. Reach for it when a room needs waking up rather than when a topic needs opening.

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-014 Virtual PictionaryThe drawing version. Same game, different medium
GAM-016 ArticulateThe talking version, for a room that will not act
GAM-015 No SmilingThe other high-laughter one, and it needs no preparation at all

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-005Game · Ice Breaker Games

Name, Place, Animal, Thing

Ice Breaker Games12-20 min
ice-breakerword-gamecompetitivequickonline

Time: 12-20 min · Group: any · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

Pick a letter. Everyone writes a famous person, a place, an animal and a thing that all start with it. Unique answers score, shared answers do not.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Zero preparation, four fixed categories, works anywhere. Good for a room that enjoys a bit of a scrap, and good online because everyone can write at once with no equipment.

What you need

  • a timer
  • paper and pen each, or the chat box

How it works

  1. Choose a letter. Say C
  2. Set a timer. One minute
  3. Everyone writes four things starting with C: a name, a place, an animal, a thing
  4. Time up. Go category by category, everyone reads their answer
  5. Score: unique answer is worth more, an answer somebody else has is worth less, and a blank is worth nothing
  6. New letter, new round. Rotate who picks the letter

Word lists, categories and questions

⚠️ Avoid X, Z and Q unless you want a round where everybody writes nothing.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ A spelling and general-knowledge game in English. Run it in pairs in an ESOL or low-literacy room, and consider the Pacific version in the variations
  • "Place" and "name" quietly favour whoever has travelled or watched a lot of TV. The Pacific version fixes it
  • Rule on disputes in one second flat. Somebody will argue that a fictional character is a name
  • Three rounds maximum. It gets old faster than Scattergories

Variations

  • Pacific and Aotearoa version: the place must be in the Pacific or Aotearoa, the animal must live here, the name must be somebody the room could actually have met. Changes who the expert is and it is the best version for our rooms
  • Add a fifth: a food, or a job, or a song
  • Pairs or teams: takes the exposure off individuals
  • Spoken version: go round the room, one category each. No writing at all

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-CUL-002 What Diversity Actually Buys YouSame four categories, wildly different answers. That is the topic in ten minutes

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-001 ScattergoriesThe same game with categories you choose. Run one or the other
GAM-009 First Letter, Last LetterThe spoken, no-materials version
GAM-003 TriviaIf you want general knowledge with the pressure taken off by teams

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-006Game · Ice Breaker Games

Two Truths and a Lie

Ice Breaker Games15-25 min
ice-breakergetting-to-know-younew-groupstorytellingonline

Time: 15-25 min · Group: 4-15, or breakout rooms above that · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

Everybody says three things about themselves. Two are true, one is not. The rest of the group guesses which is the lie.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

The best one in this pillar for a group who have never met. It surfaces genuinely surprising things about people in about fifteen minutes, and those facts get referred back to for the rest of the programme.

What you need

  • nothing
  • paper and pen if people want to draft first

How it works

  1. Give everyone two minutes to think. Three statements about themselves, two true, one false
  2. Say the rules: you can pass, and you never have to share anything you would rather not
  3. First person reads their three, mixed up so the lie is not obviously last
  4. Everyone else guesses. Online, a show of fingers on camera: one, two or three
  5. They reveal the lie. Correct guessers get a point
  6. Next person. Keep going round

Word lists, categories and questions

Prompts, for a room that goes blank: somewhere you have been · something you can do that nobody would guess · a job you have had · something that happened to you as a kid · a famous person you have met · a food you cannot stand.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Say the passing rule out loud before you start, every time. This game asks people to disclose, and a room where somebody feels cornered is worse off than before you started
  • ⚠️ Some people's true statements are heavy. A prison sentence, a bereavement, a country they left. Handle it warmly, briefly, do not make it the moment, and move on
  • The person who cannot think of anything. Give them a prompt from the list, or let them go last
  • Do not let one person's turn run to five minutes. Everybody gets a turn or the game has failed
  • Above fifteen people, use breakout rooms. Twenty people going round one at a time is forty minutes of waiting

Variations

  • Two truths and a wish: the third one is something they want to do rather than a lie. Warmer, and much safer for a fragile room
  • Team version: the group has to reach agreement before guessing. Slower, and it makes them talk
  • Written version: everyone submits anonymously and the room guesses whose it is
  • Work version: all three must be about work. Narrower and safer, good for a staff day

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-008 Listen Past The WordsReading what somebody is not saying, which is the whole topic
TOP-EMP-001 The People You Work WithSurprising, safe, and it gives people something to talk about afterwards
TOP-EMP-002 What You Can Already DoSurfaces things about people the room would never have guessed, which is the point of the topic
TOP-EMP-004 Tell Them The StoryTelling something convincingly, and watching the room decide whether they believe you
TOP-EMP-005 The Jobs Nobody AdvertisesPeople learn something about each other they had no way of knowing
TOP-EMP-006 The First Two WeeksMade for a group who have never met, which is exactly week one
TOP-LEA-001 Leading With Your StrengthsPeople name something they are good at without it sounding like boasting

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-007 Find Something in CommonThe natural next one. This finds what is unusual, that finds what is shared
GAM-010 What Would You Do?Also builds a group, and nobody has to disclose anything real
GAM-012 Would You Rather?The lower-stakes way into the same territory

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-007Game · Ice Breaker Games

Find Something in Common

Ice Breaker Games20-25 min
ice-breakergetting-to-know-youconnectionbreakout-roomsonline

Time: 20-25 min · Group: 8-40, in groups of 4-6 · Energy: medium · Where: online (breakout rooms) or in person

Small groups have to find five things they all have in common, and the obvious ones do not count. Not "we all live in Auckland". Something they had to dig for.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Builds connection on purpose, which most ice breakers only do by accident. Best used at the start of a programme that is going to run for weeks, because the groups it forms tend to stick.

What you need

  • breakout rooms, or tables
  • a category per group
  • a timer

How it works

  1. Explain the rule: five things you all share, and obvious ones do not count
  2. Split into groups of four to six. Online, breakout rooms
  3. Give each group a category if you want to focus it: food, travel, music, childhood, work
  4. Eight to ten minutes. They talk and write a list
  5. Encourage a story with each one. "We have all broken a bone" is fine, the story of how is better
  6. Back to the whole room. Each group reads their five out
  7. As they read, everyone else notes which ones they also share. The room finds it has more in common than any one group did

Word lists, categories and questions

Categories that work: food you grew up on · a place you have all been · something you are all bad at · a job you have all done · something you all did as a kid · a song you all know the words to.

Watch out for

  • Group size four to six. Three is thin, eight is a group where two people say nothing
  • Online, drop into each breakout room once. A room with no facilitator visit usually stalls at two items
  • "We are all Samoan" is exactly the obvious answer to rule out. Push past the surface, because the point is what they did not already know
  • Watch the group that finishes in three minutes. They took the easy ones. Send them back for two more

Variations

  • Whole-room version: find five things the entire room shares. Much harder and it takes longer
  • Pairs, speed version: three minutes per pair, then rotate. Everyone meets everyone
  • Deliberate mixing: put people together who do not know each other, rather than letting them pick
  • Then the difference: finish by finding one thing that is true of only one person in the group

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-009 Moving To ResolutionFinding the shared thing is what a resolution is built on
TOP-EMP-001 The People You Work WithBuilds the thing the topic is about, in twenty minutes
TOP-EMP-005 The Jobs Nobody AdvertisesWeak ties, literally played. The connection you did not know was in the room
TOP-EMP-006 The First Two WeeksThe fastest way into a room where you know nobody
TOP-LEA-001 Leading With Your StrengthsStrengths turn up in what people have in common more than in what makes them different
TOP-LEA-002 Trust Is Built In Small PromisesThe small shared thing that trust gets built on top of
TOP-LEA-004 Respect In MotionRespect starts with knowing one true thing about somebody
TOP-LEA-005 One Team, Not Us And ThemPuts the two halves of a split room in the same pair on purpose
TOP-LEA-008 Safe To Be Yourself HereBuilds connection on purpose rather than by accident
TOP-LEA-009 Weave Before You DecideThe relational half of talanoa, played

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-006 Two Truths and a LieRun them together. That one finds what is unusual, this finds what is shared
GAM-012 Would You Rather?Also splits and re-forms a room, faster and with less depth
GAM-010 What Would You Do?If you have no breakout rooms available

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-008Game · Ice Breaker Games

Spot the Difference

Ice Breaker Games8-12 min
ice-breakerobservationvisualno-literacyonlinequick

Time: 8-12 min · Group: 4-20 · Energy: medium · Where: online, or in person with images

One person's camera goes off, they change something in their background or on themselves, and it comes back on. The room has to spot what changed.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Made for online and it is genuinely delightful. Needs no words, no reading and no cultural knowledge, so it works in any room. Also very short, which makes it a good filler.

What you need

  • cameras on
  • or a pair of altered images if playing the image version

How it works

  1. Pick a player. Everyone studies their screen carefully for about fifteen seconds
  2. Camera off. They have thirty seconds to change one thing. A hat, a mug moved, a picture turned around, glasses on
  3. Camera on. The room guesses
  4. First correct guess picks next. Three or four rounds is plenty

The image version, which works in person too: put two nearly identical pictures on screen and let the room call out the differences.

Word lists, categories and questions

Ideas for what to change: something worn · something moved · something added to the background · something turned around · hair up or down · a completely different room.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Some people will not want their space looked at closely. A shared bedroom, a car, a room with somebody else in it. Say people can pass, and let anybody use the image version instead
  • Fifteen seconds of studying is enough. Longer and it drags
  • Do not let one person take two minutes to change something. Thirty seconds, called out loud

Variations

  • Image version: two altered photos on screen. Works in person, works with any group, and needs no cameras
  • Whole-room version: everybody changes one thing at once, then people are paired to spot each other's
  • In person: two people leave the room, change one thing about themselves, and come back
  • Team version: teams confer before guessing

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-003 Make Your Message LandNoticing the detail that matters, which is what a reader does to your message
TOP-COM-006 Lead Across The ScreenBuilt for online, needs no words and no reading

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-015 No SmilingThe other short online one, and it needs no preparation either
GAM-011 Scavenger HuntAlso uses whatever is around people. Louder
GAM-013 Guess That MovieThe other visual one, for a longer slot

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-009Game · Ice Breaker Games

First Letter, Last Letter

Ice Breaker Games8-12 min
ice-breakerword-gameno-materialsquickonline

Time: 8-12 min · Group: 4-20 · Energy: low · Where: online or in person

Pick a category. Each person says a word in it, starting with the last letter of the word before. Dog → giraffe → elephant → tiger.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Absolutely no preparation, no materials, and it can start in five seconds. The one to reach for when a session runs short and you need something now.

What you need

  • nothing at all

How it works

  1. Choose a category. Animals, food, countries, towns, jobs
  2. Choose an order. Round the room, or round the Zoom gallery
  3. First person says a word. "Dog"
  4. Next person says a word starting with G. "Giraffe"
  5. Keep the chain going. No repeats
  6. When somebody is stuck, either help them or move on. Set a time limit or a score limit and stop while it is still fun

Word lists, categories and questions

Categories that work: animals · food · countries · NZ towns · jobs · things in this room · kupu Māori.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ English spelling under time pressure, in front of everybody. This is the harshest version of that problem in the pillar. Play it with help allowed and no elimination, or use the te reo or picture version
  • Do not eliminate people. Somebody knocked out in round one sits and watches for ten minutes
  • Words ending in Y, X or E get brutal. Let people pass
  • Stop it early. It is a filler, not a session

Variations

  • Help allowed: anybody can help anybody. Removes the entire problem and it is more fun
  • Te reo or Pacific language round: changes who the expert is
  • Team chain: teams confer, so nobody is alone
  • Category-free: any word at all. Much easier, good for a mixed room

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-005 Listen To LeadYou cannot play at all unless you listened to the last word said
TOP-LEA-002 Trust Is Built In Small PromisesEvery turn is a small promise kept, and one break ends the chain

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-002 Word GeneratorAlso letters, but written and private, so less exposing
GAM-005 Name, Place, Animal, ThingIf you have a minute to prepare and want it scored
GAM-015 No SmilingThe other zero-preparation game

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-010Game · Ice Breaker Games

What Would You Do?

Ice Breaker Games10-20 min
ice-breakerdiscussionimaginationquiet-roomonlineno-literacy

Time: 10-20 min · Group: any · Energy: low · Where: online or in person

One hypothetical question. "What would you do if…" Everybody answers, and there is no right answer.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Gets a quiet room talking without asking anybody to disclose anything real. Also the safest one in the pillar, because nothing anybody says is about their actual life unless they choose it to be.

What you need

  • a few questions, ready

How it works

  1. Ask the question. Make it open and a bit silly
  2. Thirty seconds of thinking time. Say it is fine to be ridiculous
  3. Go round, or take volunteers. Online, hands up or straight into the chat
  4. Ask why. "What made you pick that?" is where it actually gets interesting
  5. New question. Two or three is usually plenty

Word lists, categories and questions

Questions that work:
SillyZombies take over Auckland, what is your plan? · You wake up able to speak every language. What do you do first?
MoneyYou find $50 on the footpath · Somebody gives you $10,000 but you must spend it in a day
WorkYou are the boss for one day · You see a workmate take something
KindYou could fix one thing about your street. What?

Watch out for

  • Keep it away from real dilemmas unless you meant to run a values session. "You see a workmate steal" is a real conversation, so only ask it if you want one
  • No right answers, and say so. The moment somebody feels marked, the room closes
  • The quiet person. Ask if they want to go last rather than putting them first
  • Two or three questions maximum. It is a warm-up

Variations

  • Chat storm: everybody types their answer at once and you read the funniest out. Fast, and it includes people who will not speak
  • Groups first: small groups agree on one answer between them, then report back
  • Room-supplied: everybody writes a question, you draw them out of a hat
  • Two-option version: turn it into GAM-012 if the open question is too open for the room

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-002 Handling Difficult ConversationsHard scenarios talked through without anybody having to disclose a real one
TOP-COM-004 Boundaries Without GuiltRehearses the pause before the answer, which is where a boundary lives
TOP-COM-007 Not All Conflict Is The SameNaming what kind of problem you are looking at before you respond to it
TOP-COM-008 Listen Past The WordsListen for the reasoning under the answer, not just the answer
TOP-COM-009 Moving To ResolutionGather, then test. The game runs the same order
TOP-CUL-001 The Values You Lead WithWhat you would do is where your values actually show
TOP-LEA-006 How You Decide Is What They LearnThe same scenario, decided three different ways
TOP-LEA-007 Helpful Without Burning OutThe scenario where saying yes is the wrong answer
TOP-LEA-010 People, Results, Or BothThe scenario where the task and the person pull in opposite directions
TOP-LEA-011 Leader Or ManagerHalf the scenarios need managing and half need leading, and the room will not agree which
TOP-LEA-012 What Actually Motivates PeopleAutonomy, competence and relatedness all show up in the answers

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-012 Would You Rather?The same idea with two options instead of an open question. Easier for a shy room
GAM-006 Two Truths and a LieWhen you want people to talk about themselves rather than a scenario
GAM-007 Find Something in CommonThe longer connection-building one

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-011Game · Ice Breaker Games

Scavenger Hunt

Ice Breaker Games10-15 min
ice-breakermovementhigh-energyno-literacyonlineafter-lunch

Time: 10-15 min · Group: any · Energy: 🔥 high · Where: online or in person

Somebody calls out an item. Everybody runs and finds one. First back wins the round.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Gets people out of their chairs, which after ninety minutes is worth more than anything they will learn in the next ten. Also brilliant online, because it makes homes and people visible in a way a grid of faces never does.

What you need

  • nothing
  • a list of items if you want to prepare

How it works

  1. Call out an item or a category. "Something red." "Something older than you." "A kitchen utensil"
  2. Go. Everybody gets up and finds one
  3. First person back on screen with it wins the round
  4. Everybody shows what they found. This is the good bit, not the racing
  5. Ask about one or two. "Why have you got that?" produces the best stories in this whole pillar
  6. Somebody else calls the next item. Four or five rounds

Word lists, categories and questions

Items that produce stories: something red · something older than you · something from another country · something that makes you laugh · something you have had since you were a kid · something with a smell · something you should have thrown out.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Mobility. Not everybody can get up and run. Have a seated version ready: something within arm's reach, and make that the rule for everybody rather than singling anyone out
  • ⚠️ Not everybody's home is something they want on camera. Say people can stay seated and find something nearby. Do not comment on anybody's house
  • In person, keep it to the room and the bags in it. People wandering off down a corridor never come back
  • Do not skip the showing. The race is the mechanism, the stories are the point

Variations

  • Arm's reach version: everything must already be within reach. Inclusive and just as fun
  • Story version: one item only, and everybody tells the story of theirs. Slower, warmer
  • Team version: teams collect a list of five, first team with all five wins
  • In person: items from bags and pockets only

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-LEA-003 Every Team StormsA team, a clock, and no agreed way of working. Storming arrives on schedule
TOP-LEA-010 People, Results, Or BothA task, a clock and a team. Whoever forgets the people will show you

Related games

GameWhy
GAM-008 Spot the DifferenceAlso uses what is around people, quieter
GAM-012 Would You Rather?The other one that gets a room moving
GAM-004 CharadesThe other high-energy after-lunch option

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-012Game · Ice Breaker Games

Would You Rather?

Ice Breaker Games15-25 min
ice-breakerdiscussionmovementbreakout-roomsno-literacyonline

Time: 15-25 min · Group: any · Energy: medium · Where: online (breakout rooms) or in person

Two options, pick one, then go and stand with everybody who picked the same. The choice is the warm-up. The conversation afterwards is the actual game.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Splits and re-forms a room repeatedly, so people end up talking to somebody different every round. Easier than an open question for a shy room, because there are only two answers and neither is wrong.

What you need

  • a few either-or questions
  • breakout rooms, or two sides of the room

How it works

  1. Pose the question. Two options. "Beach or bush?"
  2. Everybody picks. No fence-sitting
  3. Split them. In person, two sides of the room. Online, two breakout rooms
  4. Five minutes in the groups. Why did you pick it? What would it actually be like?
  5. Back together. Each side says one interesting thing that came up
  6. New question, re-split. Three rounds and people have talked to most of the room

Word lists, categories and questions

Questions that work: beach or bush · early bird or night owl · always cold or always hot · work from home or work with people · sweet or savoury · summer Christmas or a white one · never use your phone again or never watch TV again · be able to fly or be invisible.

Watch out for

  • Keep the split roughly even. If a question sends nineteen people one way, drop it next time
  • The point is the conversation, not the choice. A round with no talking is just a poll
  • Do not use questions with a socially correct answer. "Money or happiness" makes people perform
  • Online, breakout rooms of two minutes are too short. Five, or do not bother

Variations

  • Spectrum version: a line across the room rather than two sides, and people place themselves. More honest and it makes a better picture
  • Defend it: each side argues their case for two minutes. Louder and more competitive
  • Room-supplied questions: everybody writes one on a slip
  • Silent version: hold up one or two fingers. Good for a room that will not move

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-002 Handling Difficult ConversationsTaking a position out loud and defending it, with the stakes removed
TOP-COM-004 Boundaries Without GuiltChoosing between two things you would rather not choose between, out loud

TOP-CUL-001 The Values You Lead WithEvery choice reveals a value, and nobody has to announce one
TOP-CUL-002 What Diversity Actually Buys YouThe room keeps re-sorting, and the splits are never the ones you expect
TOP-LEA-005 One Team, Not Us And ThemSplits the room a dozen different ways, and never the same way twice
TOP-LEA-006 How You Decide Is What They LearnA decision with no right answer, made in public
TOP-LEA-007 Helpful Without Burning OutChoosing what to give up is the skill, and here it costs nothing
TOP-LEA-009 Weave Before You DecideSplits and re-forms the room, so people talk to somebody they did not arrive with
TOP-LEA-012 What Actually Motivates PeopleWhat people choose when nothing is riding on it says more than a survey

GameWhy

Pillar: Ice Breaker Games · All sixteen: GAME-INDEX · Source: SRC-014

GAM-013Game · Ice Breaker Games

Guess That Movie

Ice Breaker Games15-25 min
ice-breakervisualquizteamsonlineprep-needed

Time: 15-25 min · Group: any · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

Play a short clip or show a still. First person to name the film wins the round. Online, guesses go in the chat.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Good for a group that likes a screen and a bit of noise, and it fills a real slot. The reactions after each answer are usually better than the guessing.

What you need

  • a prepared playlist of short film clips or stills
  • a screen with working sound
  • the chat box

How it works

  1. Build the playlist beforehand. Eight to ten clips, thirty seconds each, recognisable
  2. Mute everybody so the audio is clean
  3. Share screen and play a clip. Check the sound is actually sharing, every time
  4. Guesses go in the chat. First correct one wins the round
  5. Reveal, and let people react. This is where the session actually warms up
  6. Next clip. Keep score if you want to

⚠️ Test your screen share with sound before the session. It fails more often than it works.

Word lists, categories and questions

Round ideas: kids' films · films shot in New Zealand · films from twenty years ago · Pacific and Māori films (Boy, Whale Rider, The Panthers, Three Wise Cousins) · sports films.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Film knowledge is generational and cultural. A playlist of one person's favourites excludes half the room. Mix the eras and include films made here
  • Check the sound share. The single most common failure, and it kills the round
  • Thirty seconds per clip. Longer and people stop guessing and start watching
  • Stills work almost as well as clips and they never break

Variations

  • Stills only: no audio, no sharing problems, and it works in person
  • Guess the song: ten seconds of a track. Louder, easier and usually better
  • Guess the ad: New Zealand TV ads. Surprisingly good and everybody knows them
  • Teams: confer before guessing, so nobody is left out

Topics it suits

Any of them, and none of them. This one is pure warm-up: no link back to teach, nothing to debrief. Reach for it when a room needs waking up rather than when a topic needs opening.

GameWhy

GAM-014Game · Ice Breaker Games

Virtual Pictionary

Ice Breaker Games20-30 min
ice-breakerdrawinghigh-energyteamsonlineafter-lunch

Time: 20-30 min · Group: 6-25, two teams · Energy: 🔥 high · Where: online (whiteboard) or in person

One person draws, their team guesses. No letters, no numbers, no talking. The worse the drawing, the better the game.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Fills a whole slot and it gets loud. The best option when you have twenty-five minutes to spend and a room that has been sitting down too long.

What you need

  • a shared whiteboard, or a flipchart in person
  • a word list, prepared
  • a timer

How it works

  1. Set up the whiteboard and check the drawer can actually draw on it. Test this beforehand
  2. Two teams. Pick the first drawer
  3. Send them the word privately. Direct message, or a slip of paper
  4. Sixty seconds. They draw while their team shouts guesses, or types them in the chat
  5. Correct inside the time is a point. If not, the other team gets one chance to steal
  6. Swap drawer, swap team. Keep score
  7. No letters, no numbers, no talking, no gestures

Word lists, categories and questions

Word lists that work: animals · food · jobs · films · things at work · NZ things (jandals, a hāngī, the Beehive, a chilly bin, gumboots, a tinny house).

⚠️ Concrete nouns only. "Teamwork" produces sixty seconds of a stick figure and no laughs.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Test the whiteboard first. Whether a participant can draw depends on the platform and the settings. This is the most common way this game dies
  • Have a phone-camera fallback: the drawer draws on paper and holds it up. Works every time
  • Nobody has to draw. Let people be scorer or timekeeper. "I can't draw" is usually anxiety and sometimes a real reason
  • Sixty seconds, hard stop. The clock is what makes it funny

Variations

  • Paper and camera: skip the whiteboard entirely. More reliable and just as good
  • Everybody draws: everyone draws the same word at once, then all reveal. No individual on the spot and it is very funny
  • Team relay: three people draw the same word in turn, twenty seconds each
  • In person: flipchart at the front, exactly as it always was

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-006 Lead Across The ScreenThe best test there is of whether your channel actually carries what you meant
TOP-LEA-003 Every Team StormsWatch who takes over, who goes quiet, and how the group sorts itself out

Related games

GameWhy

GAM-013 Guess That MovieThe other screen-based one, for a group that prefers watching
GAM-016 ArticulateThe talking version, and the easiest of the three to run

GAM-015Game · Ice Breaker Games

No Smiling

Ice Breaker Games5-10 min
ice-breakerhumourquickno-materialsno-literacyonline

Time: 5-10 min · Group: any · Energy: 🔥 high · Where: online or in person

Nobody is allowed to smile or laugh. Then you do everything you can to make them. First person to crack loses.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

Five minutes, almost no preparation, and it changes the temperature of a room instantly. The one to use when a session has gone flat and you have no time to set anything up.

What you need

  • a few funny clips, memes or jokes
  • nothing, if the room supplies them

How it works

  1. Announce the rule: nobody smiles, nobody laughs. Straight faces only
  2. Agree the forfeit. Something light. Tell a joke, do a star jump, pick the next game
  3. Now try to break them. Funny clips, a meme, a bad joke, or just look at each other on camera
  4. First to crack is out, or takes the forfeit
  5. Keep going or stop. Five minutes is usually enough, and it is over when everybody is laughing anyway

Online it is better than in person, because everybody's face is on a grid at the same size.

Word lists, categories and questions

What works: the room's own photos · a bad dad joke · a clip everybody has seen · thirty seconds of everyone just staring at each other. The last one is free and it works.

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Keep the content clean and check it yourself first. A meme that lands badly costs more than the game is worth. Never let the room supply unvetted clips on screen
  • Forfeits stay light. Nothing embarrassing, nothing physical, nothing anybody would dread
  • Never make it about one person. If the same person keeps losing, stop the game
  • Five minutes. It is a temperature change, not a session

Variations

  • Just staring: no content at all. Everybody looks at each other on camera. Works every time and needs nothing
  • Try to make me laugh: one person keeps a straight face while the room tries. Volunteers only
  • Teams: last team with a straight face wins
  • The reverse: everybody has to laugh, on purpose, for thirty seconds. Fake laughter turns real fast

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-001 Speak Up With ConfidenceHolding your nerve while everybody looks at you, with nothing at stake
TOP-LEA-004 Respect In MotionFive minutes proving that very small behaviours change a room
TOP-WEL-001 Building ResilienceChanges the temperature of a room in five minutes, which is the point of a reset

GAM-016Game · Ice Breaker Games

Articulate

Ice Breaker Games15-20 min
ice-breakerword-gamespeakingteamsonlinecommunication

Time: 15-20 min · Group: 4-20, or teams · Energy: medium · Where: online or in person

Describe a word without saying the word. Or anything in it. The others guess. One minute, as many as you can get through.

On this pagePurposeWhat you needHow it worksWord lists, categories and questionsWatch out forVariationsTopics it suitsRelated games

Purpose

The most useful game in this pillar, because describing something clearly under time pressure is a real skill and this is the only place it is fun. Good before any session about explaining, briefing or handing over.

What you need

  • a list of ten words per player, prepared
  • a timer

How it works

  1. Give each player a list of ten words, or give the first one a list and rotate
  2. One minute on the clock
  3. They describe a word without saying it, or any part of it. What it does, what it looks like, where you find it
  4. Everybody else guesses. Correct, move to the next word
  5. They can pass, but a pass costs the word
  6. Count how many they got through. Next player
  7. Most words guessed wins

Word lists, categories and questions

Word lists that work: everyday objects · food · jobs · animals · things in a workplace · NZ things.

⚠️ Concrete before abstract. Start with "kettle", not "patience".

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This is a fluent-English game under time pressure, and it is hard work for an ESOL speaker in front of a room. Play it in pairs, or let people describe in any language and have the room guess. The second version is better than the original
  • Nobody is made to take a turn. Timekeeper and scorer are real jobs
  • Watch for the describer who says a word inside the word. "Tea towel" for towel. Ruled out, move on, no argument
  • Sixty seconds, hard. The clock is what makes it work

Variations

  • Pairs: two describers per turn, sharing the list. Removes the exposure entirely
  • Any language: describe it in whatever language you like. Changes who is good at this game and it is worth doing once on purpose
  • Teams: one describer, their team guesses, other team keeps time
  • One word, everybody: the whole room describes the same word one clue at a time, until somebody guesses

Topics it suits

This game stands alone — it needs no topic and teaches nothing on its own. But if you are running one of these, it earns its place.

TopicWhy this game here
TOP-COM-001 Speak Up With ConfidenceDescribing something clearly while a timer runs is the same muscle as speaking up before the moment passes
TOP-COM-003 Make Your Message LandOne idea, few words, a clock running. The whole topic as a game
TOP-COM-005 Listen To LeadThe describer needs the guessers, so both halves have to listen

⚠️ Two house rules

1. Nobody is made to play. Anybody can pass, at any point, without giving a reason. Say it before you start, every time. A game somebody is forced into is worse than no game.
