Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-044

The Blake-Mouton Managerial Grid

Origin: Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton, The Managerial Grid, 1964.

Two dials, five positions. The full page, with the diagram and the warehouse worked example, is at FRM-044.

PositionPeopleResultsThe shorthand
ImpoverishedLowLowAbsent
Produce or perishLowHighNumbers hit, people gone
Middle of the roadMidMidAverage both
Country clubHighLowLovely, unproductive
TeamHighHighDemanding and backed

➜ Teach the middle hardest. Almost everybody plots themselves there and it is the position Blake and Mouton were arguing against.

FrameworkFRM-045

Theory X and Theory Y

Origin: Douglas McGregor, The Human Side of Enterprise, 1960.

Both beliefs are self-fulfilling, and that is the entire teaching point. Full page at FRM-045.

The Theory X loop: you supervise closely → they do the minimum and stop offering → "see, I was right." The Theory Y loop: you set the goal and give room → they take responsibility and raise problems early → "see, I was right."

⚠️ Do not teach X as evil. A new crew on a dangerous site needs direction. The failure is choosing X permanently and never checking.

FrameworkFRM-046

House's Path-Goal Theory

Origin: Robert J. House, 1971, revised 1996. Full page at FRM-046.

StyleUse it when the obstacle is
DirectiveThey do not know how
SupportiveThey are running on empty
ParticipativeThey know something you do not
Achievement-orientedThey are coasting, or they do not believe they are capable
FrameworkFRM-067

Goleman's Six Leadership Styles

What it is: six moves available to one leader, and the finding that the ones getting the best results use most of them in a single week.

Origin: Daniel Goleman, "Leadership That Gets Results", Harvard Business Review, March-April 2000, from research with Hay/McBer across more than 3,000 executives.

⚠️ You will meet these six everywhere without his name on them. "Visionary leadership", "coaching leadership", "pacesetting" — every leadership listicle reproduces this set and almost none credit him, including a Harvard blog. Naming him is what lets anybody check the evidence.

StyleIn one lineWhat it does to the room
1Commanding"Do what I tell you"Works in a genuine crisis. Damaging as a default
2Visionary"Come with me"Sets a direction, lets people find their own way to it
3Affiliative"People come first"Heals rifts. Alone, it lets poor performance slide
4Democratic"What do you think?"Builds buy-in. Slow, and useless in an emergency
5Pacesetting"Do as I do, now"The one that burns teams out
6Coaching"Try this"The long game. Least used, and among the most valuable

How to read it: not six kinds of person. Six moves available to one person.

➜ The line worth saying: "You are not a democratic leader. You are a leader who used a democratic move on Tuesday and a commanding one on Thursday, and the skill is knowing which and when."

Pacesetting is the one to spend time on. It looks like leading from the front and it feels virtuous. The message underneath "watch me do it properly" is that nobody else can, and it is why good performers exhaust their teams without ever raising their voice.

⚠️ The evidence audit, because somebody will ask. The six are a useful teaching set, and the claim that good leaders use several rather than one is the same conclusion Lewin, Blake-Mouton and Path-Goal reach from three other directions. But Goleman's headline figure — that climate accounts for nearly a third of results — comes from Hay/McBer's own consulting data, not peer-reviewed work, and nobody has replicated it. Do not put that number in front of a room. Teach the styles, leave the statistic alone.

⚠️ In a Māori or Pacific room, hold this next to Tū Rangatira. Goleman's six came from a corporate database of mostly Western executives. Neither is the real version of the other.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-047

Likert's Four Systems (optional extension)

Origin: Rensis Likert, 1967. Full page at FRM-047.

Use this only if the room is strong and you have time. Its one contribution is the line between System 2 and System 3: below it people tell you what you want to hear, above it they tell you what is true. Most New Zealand workplaces are System 2 and think they are System 3.

Self-Assessment

ACT-083 What Do You Actually Believe About People? Ten statements, agree or disagree, scored out of 10 toward Theory X.

ScoreWhat it suggests
0-3Leans strongly Theory Y. Watch that trust is not standing in for standards
4-6Mixed. Where most working supervisors land
7-10Leans Theory X. Not a character flaw, and possibly an accurate read of your workplace

Statement 6 is the one to spend time on. "You have to earn trust before you get it." Nearly every room agrees. Then ask whether a new starter begins on zero and earns their way up, or begins with a full tank and spends it. Both are defensible and they produce very different workplaces.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. It is a set of statements written for a classroom, not a psychometric instrument. See FRM-054 for why that distinction is worth being strict about.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Think of the best leader you ever had. Where would you plot them, and where would you plot yourself?
  2. Which axis is easier for you to raise, and what would raising it cost you?
  3. What does your team do because you are watching, rather than because they think it matters?
  4. Which of your team is currently getting the wrong style from you?
  5. When did somebody last tell you something you did not want to hear? What happened to them afterwards?
  6. Is there a situation where being lower on the people axis would be the right call for a week?
  7. Which statement in the self-assessment would you most like to be wrong about?
  8. What is the one thing you will change, with which person, and by when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min. At 90, cut FRM-047 and ACT-058 and set the reflection as homework
  • Run the self-assessment cold. This is the single most important delivery instruction on the page. See section 6
  • What usually goes wrong: the room hears "be a 9,9 leader" and files it as a slogan. Keep coming back to what it costs. A Team-corner leader is demanding, and learners who equate good leadership with being liked find that genuinely surprising
  • Watch the honest Theory X answer. Some learners supervise people they do not trust, sometimes because of the workplace rather than the people. Do not push anyone to recant in the room. Ask what they would need to see to change their mind
  • Status in the room. In a mixed cohort, some learners lead nobody. Reframe throughout: the grid works on a flatmate, a sports team, a church roster
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no NZ video linked. The two TED talks on FRM-048 and FRM-049 are both overseas. A New Zealand supervisor talking about the grid would be worth more than either
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • The two supervisors (5 min). Tell the warehouse story from section 3 and take a vote before any teaching. Cheap, fast, and it sets up everything that follows.
  • Floor grid (10 min). Masking-tape two axes on the floor and have people physically stand where they think they sit. More honest than paper, and the clustering in the middle is visible to everyone at once. This is the physical variation of ACT-082.
  • ACT-050 Whose Call Is It? (12-15 min). Sorts real decisions by who should make them. A good warm-up if the room already knows Lewin.

Topic: TOP-LEA-004 Respect In Motion · Pillar: Leadership

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

"Be more respectful" has never changed anyone's behaviour. "Ask the apprentice before you give your own view" changes it on Monday.

Admiration is common and useless. It only becomes useful at the moment you can name the exact thing the person does.

Model

Each step narrows the last. Stop at W and you have a feeling. Stop at H and you have an intention. The O is the only step that produces behaviour.

The stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."
FromTo
"She's a great leader""She asks the quietest person what they think, by name, before she gives her own view"
"I'll be more respectful""I will open Tuesday's meeting by checking everyone's name and pronunciation"

Metaphor

Tracing paper.

You do not learn to draw by admiring a picture. You learn by laying tracing paper over it and following one line at a time.

W-H-O is tracing paper for behaviour. You are not trying to become the person. You are following one line of theirs until your hand knows it.

Study

Two, and together they cover the whole framework.

Albert Bandura, Social Learning Theory (1977). Most human behaviour is learned by watching others and copying them. Bandura's own words: "most human behavior is learned observationally through modeling." The W and H steps are that process, made deliberate. 📄 Simply Psychology summary

Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38, 69-119. A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests and over 8,000 participants found implementation intentions ("when X happens, I will do Y") produced a medium to large effect on goal attainment, d = 0.65, with a similar effect on the specific failure of never getting started. That is the O step. 📄 Gollwitzer (1999) (PDF)

Worth saying out loud: W-H-O is house content wrapped around two of the better evidenced findings in behaviour change. When someone asks whether it is just a nice exercise, that is the answer.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a learner who named a role model, converted it to a behaviour, did it, and something changed. The aged care example on the topic page is illustrative, not real, and should not be told as though it happened.

The story most likely to be the best one: a learner who told the person they had named. The source's whole premise is that the aunties, coaches and elders who showed us respect become quiet mentors we can call on. Someone going back and saying so is the story this sheet is waiting for.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any leadership session, at the endThe strongest closer Zeducation has. It ends in a dated commitment
Youth and rangatahi programmesThe W step honours family and church role models rather than corporate ones
Values or culture work with a clientThe answer to "how do we make our values real?" You cannot. You can make one behaviour real

Related sheets

SheetRelationship

PS-COM-003 The flight is judged on the landingBoth are about the final step being the one that counts

TOP-LEA-004Topic · Leadership

Respect In Motion

✅ publishedLeadershipFoundation90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 4
respectrole-modelsleadershiphabitscommitmenthouse-contentculture

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-004 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 4

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Respect is not just something we give or earn. It is something we learn and practise. We learn it by watching people who carry themselves with dignity, keep their word, and lift others even when it is inconvenient. Then we turn what we saw into repeatable actions: greet people by name, listen without interrupting, follow through, give clear feedback, protect people's focus time.

Real leadership is respect in motion.

One of the most effective ways to build a behaviour is to name a role model, pull out the specific thing you admire, and commit to doing it yourself. Keep it specific: who, when, where, and why it matters. Over time those choices become your repetition, and your repetition becomes your reputation.

This matters more under pressure than in calm. As the source puts it: when we are under pressure, we do not rise to the level of our intentions, we fall to the level of our habits.

And it works anywhere. The behaviours that earn respect on a building site are the same ones that earn it at home, at church and on the sports field.

"Respect yourself and others will respect you." — Confucius

Key words

WordWhat it means
ModellingLearning a behaviour by watching someone do it
Observable behaviourSomething someone could watch you do. Not a feeling or a quality
Implementation intentionA plan in the form "when X happens, I will do Y"
Role modelSomeone whose behaviour you deliberately copy
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Turn a person you respect into one specific behaviour you can copy this week.
  2. Commit to that behaviour with a time, a place and a person attached.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask everyone to think of one person who taught them what respect looks like. Not told them. Showed them.

Give it a moment. It is rarely a manager. It is an aunty, a coach, a supervisor from years ago, a church leader, a grandparent.

Then ask: what did they actually do?

The room will start with adjectives. Kind. Humble. Fair. Push once more and the real answers arrive, and they are always tiny and specific. She learned how to say my name properly. He asked the apprentice first. He never talked about anyone who wasn't there.

Statement: You cannot copy "respectful". You can copy "asks the apprentice first". Respect is not a value, it is a set of small things somebody does on purpose.

➜ Facilitator note: this opener is warm and it can go deep quickly, especially where the person has died. That is not a problem to manage away. Give it room.

4

Frameworks Used

IDFrameworkPage
FRM-019W-H-O — Who, How, Outcome→
FRM-026Modelling and Social Learning→
FRM-025Implementation Intentions→
5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-019

W-H-O — Who, How, Outcome (house framework)

What it is: pick someone you respect, name one thing they actually do, and commit to doing it yourself this week.

StepThe questionWhat you write
WWHOWho will I mirror?One role model, and why
HHOWHow will I act like them?One observable behaviour
OOUTCOMEWhat outcome will I create?Time, place, person, impact

How to read it: each step narrows the last. Stop at W and you have a nice feeling. Stop at H and you have a good intention. The O is what makes it happen.

The commitment stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."

The house examples:

Example 1Example 2
WMy older brotherChurch youth leader
HGreets people by name and checks pronunciationArrives early and sets the room up for success
OI will open tomorrow's team meeting by confirming everyone's name and pronunciation so that people feel seen and respectedI will arrive 10 minutes early to Thursday's workshop to set up chairs, slides and materials so we start on time and keep momentum

Worked example: a team leader in aged care names her late grandmother as her W. The H is that her grandmother never talked about anyone who was not in the room. Her O: "I will change the subject when the afternoon shift starts talking about Mere, on Tuesday, in the staff room, so that people know this team does not do that." That is a leadership act, on a date, that anyone can picture.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-026

Modelling and Social Learning

Why W-H-O works. Albert Bandura found that most human behaviour is learned by watching other people and copying them. Four conditions have to be present:

ConditionWhere it breaks
1AttentionYou admire someone but have never watched what they specifically do
2RetentionYou noticed once and never put it into words, so it faded
3ReproductionThe behaviour is beyond you today. Pick a smaller one
4MotivationYou do not believe it will work for you

How to read it: a chain, so it breaks at the weakest link. Most people break at Retention, which is exactly what the H step fixes.

The uncomfortable half: you are a model whether you want to be or not. Anyone junior to you is learning how to behave by watching you, including how you talk about people who are not there and what you do when you are wrong.

More resources:

  • 📄 Simply Psychology — Bandura's Social Learning Theory
  • 📄 Albert Bandura — Modeling and Observational Learning

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-025

Implementation Intentions

Why the O step is shaped the way it is. Peter Gollwitzer found that plans in the form "when X happens, I will do Y" dramatically outperform general good intentions. The Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis pooled 94 tests and over 8,000 participants and found a medium to large effect on goal attainment (d = 0.65), with a similar effect on the specific problem of never getting started.

That is why the commitment stem demands a day, a place and a person. Say the number out loud in the room. Learners take the commitment more seriously when they hear it was tested on 8,000 people.

More resources:

  • 📄 Gollwitzer (1999) (PDF)

→ Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-048 Do I Lead By Example? Ten statements, scored 1 to 3, out of 30.

The instrument's last statement is the whole thing in one line: if someone copied how I behave at work this week, would I be happy with that? If it is the lowest number on the page, ignore the total and work on whatever made you circle it.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises

ACT-046 Behaviour, Not AdjectiveGame8-10 minFRM-019, FRM-026
ACT-045 The Respect InterviewRoleplay20-25 minFRM-019

Suggested flow: ACT-047 to open → ACT-046 to train the H skill → teach W-H-O → ACT-045 → ACT-033 to write the real commitment → ACT-048 quietly → close.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Who taught you what respect looks like? What did they actually do?
  2. What would it mean to that person to know you named them today?
  3. Somebody junior to you is already copying something you do. What is it?
  4. What have you picked up from someone you did not admire?
  5. Are you the same person under pressure as you are on a good day? Who would notice the difference?
  6. When did someone last get your name, or something else about you, wrong for a long time? What did that feel like?
  7. Which one behaviour, copied for a month, would change how people experience you?
  8. What is your O? Day, place, person, impact.
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 90 min is enough. 120 lets the W conversation breathe, which is worth it
  • Do the W out loud before anything else. It warms the room and it is what makes the rest work
  • What usually goes wrong: learners write adjectives instead of behaviours, and O statements with no day in them. Both are fixable by a partner asking one question twice
  • Discourage famous role models. It works far better with someone the learner has actually stood next to
  • Follow up. The O is a promise with a date, so it can be checked. Ask next session. A framework nobody follows up teaches people that commitments are optional
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no video teaches W-H-O, because it is house content. A two minute clip of a Zeducation facilitator doing their own W, H and O would be the most useful asset this topic could have
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-047 Name It In Ten Seconds (8-10 min, high energy). The room learns to say each other's names properly. Then: put your hand up if someone at work has been saying your name wrong for over a month.
  • ACT-046 Behaviour, Not Adjective (8-10 min). Shout adjectives, the room converts them into behaviours, and the facilitator rejects anything that is still an adjective.

PS-LEA-002Pink Sheet · Leadership

Nobody remembers breaking your trust

placeholder-story
trustteamspsychological-safetyreliabilityleadership

Topic: TOP-LEA-002 Trust Is Built In Small Promises · Pillar: Leadership

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

Trust is not broken by betrayal. It is broken by twenty small things the other person has already forgotten doing.

Which is also the good news, because that is exactly how it gets rebuilt. No grand gesture is available to you, and none is required.

Model

The ladder, read from the bottom. Each layer rests on the one below, so the weak one at the bottom brings down everything above it.

Most teams try to fix the top. They set better goals and add another meeting, and none of it holds, because the reason nobody speaks up in the meeting is at the bottom.

The repair loop, at the bottom rung:

Metaphor

A bank account nobody tells you the balance of.

Every kept promise is a small deposit. Every missed one is a small withdrawal. Nobody reads you the statement, and you only find out you are overdrawn when you ask for something and the answer is a polite version of no.

The person who overdrew the account is usually the last to know, because from where they stand every single withdrawal was reasonable at the time.

Study

Amy C. Edmondson, "Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams", Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 350-383 (1999).

Edmondson set out to study hospital nursing teams and found something that looked wrong: the teams with the best relationships reported the most errors. They were not making more mistakes. They were the only ones willing to report them.

Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 of its own teams between 2012 and 2016 and found psychological safety was the strongest single predictor of team effectiveness.

📄 The paper · 🎬 Edmondson's TEDx talk

Why this study and not Lencioni: the 5 Dysfunctions is the better teaching model and the weaker evidence. When someone in the room wants proof, use Edmondson.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a supervisor who rebuilt a team's trust with small kept promises rather than a big change. The shape: a team that had stopped bringing them things, three or four weeks of boring reliability, and the specific moment they noticed it had turned. That moment is the story.

The alternative shape, which is often stronger: someone who was on the receiving end. A person who stopped telling their manager things, and what the manager did that changed it back.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any leadership sessionThe opener. It gets past "trust is important" in ninety seconds
Supervisor trainingPaired with Say-Do-Close as the practical week
Client work on cultureThe honest answer to "how long will this take?"

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-COM-001 Assertive is clear, not loudFear of conflict is the second rung of this ladder. That sheet is the skill that gets you past it
PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowSame source workbook. Build the relationship, then make it trustworthy

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on the Close step alone. The Point is already written: silent delivery and no delivery look identical from the outside.

TOP-LEA-002Topic · Leadership

Trust Is Built In Small Promises

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 2
trustteamspsychological-safetyaccountabilityreliabilityconflictleadership

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-002 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 2

On this page1About This Topic2Learning Outcomes3Open With This (Story & Statement)4Frameworks Used5Tools, Techniques & Frameworks6Apply — Suggested Activities7Reflection Questions8Facilitator Notes9Games & EnergisersConnectionsSource Trail
1

About This Topic

Trust is the foundation of every effective work relationship. When people trust each other they feel safe to speak honestly, share ideas, ask for help and admit mistakes without fear of being judged. Work becomes less about protecting yourself and more about solving the problem together.

Teams with high trust move faster, communicate better and handle conflict without damage. When trust is low, people hold back, misunderstandings grow, and simple tasks become stressful.

Building trust is not about being perfect. It is about being consistent, honest and human.

Five things trust gets you: people feel safe to speak up; there is less stress and drama; work gets done faster because there is less second-guessing; people admit mistakes and learn; and good people want to stay.

This matters everywhere, not only at work. The same behaviours build or break trust in a family, a church group, a sports team and a marae committee.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Psychological safetyThe shared belief that it is safe here to ask a question, admit a mistake or disagree
ReliabilityDoing what you said you would do, by when you said it
Self-orientationBeing in it for yourself. The thing that cancels out everything else
Fake yesAgreeing in the room and doing something different afterwards
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Rebuild trust using a small promise, kept on time and closed off with proof.
  2. Respond to bad news in a way that makes the person bring you the next one.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask the room to think of someone at work they do not fully trust. Not a villain. Just someone whose word they have learned to discount.

Then ask: what did they actually do?

The answers are never dramatic. They said they would send it and did not. They agreed in the meeting and something different happened. They told you something in confidence and it came back to you from somewhere else. They were fine with you and different with someone else.

Then the second question, which is the one that lands:

How many of those would that person even remember doing?

Almost none. That is the whole topic.

Statement: Nobody breaks trust in one big moment. They break it in twenty small ones they have already forgotten about, and they rebuild it the same way.

➜ Facilitator note: do not let anyone name a real person out loud. The thinking is private, the answers are general.

4

Frameworks Used

IDFrameworkPage
FRM-017The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team→
FRM-020Say-Do-Close→
FRM-022The Trust Equation→
FRM-023Psychological Safety→
5

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-017

The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team

What it is: five problems that stack, so if the bottom one is weak everything above falls over. Origin: Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (2002).

How to read it: the arrows are causes, not steps. Fix the bottom first. Working on results while trust is broken is wasted effort.

Worked example: a kitchen keeps missing Friday orders. The manager adds a checklist and it does not help. The real cause is that the newest chef cannot read the handwriting on the tickets and has never said so, because the first time he asked a question he got laughed at. A results problem, four layers above its actual cause.

More resources:

  • 📄 Table Group overview (PDF)
  • 🎬 Patrick Lencioni presenting the model

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-020

Say-Do-Close (house technique)

What it is: make a small promise, deliver on time, confirm it is done with proof.

How to read it: one trip round changes nothing. Twenty trips round is a reputation.

The step everyone skips is Close. From the outside, silent delivery and no delivery look identical until somebody checks.

Worked example: a supervisor known for saying "I'll sort it" and not sorting it picks one thing. "I'll get you the roster by Thursday lunchtime." He writes it Wednesday night. Thursday 11am it goes in the group chat: "roster's up, as promised, tell me if I've got your Saturday wrong." Nobody praises him. Three weeks later people start asking him for things again.

The other five house trust tips: Share the Why · Make it Safe · Set Clear Rules · Repair Fast (within 24 hours) · Be Fair and Private. → Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-023

Psychological Safety

What it is: a shared belief that this team is safe for interpersonal risk, so you can ask, admit or disagree without being punished for it. Origin: Amy Edmondson, Harvard, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999. Strongest evidence in this topic.

Her study of hospital nursing teams found the teams with the best relationships reported the most errors. They were not making more. They were willing to report them. Google's Project Aristotle later found the same factor was the strongest predictor of team effectiveness across 180 of its own teams.

Low standardsHigh standards
High safetyComfort zoneLearning zone
Low safetyApathy zoneAnxiety zone

Safety is not softness. It is what makes high standards achievable, because a team that can talk about failure can fix it.

The three leader moves: frame the work as a learning problem · admit your own limits out loud · respond productively to bad news. The third one decides it. People are not testing what you say about openness, they are watching what happened to the last person who was open.

More resources:

  • 📄 Edmondson (1999)
  • 🎬 TEDxHGSE — Amy Edmondson, Building a psychologically safe workplace (about 11 min)

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-022

The Trust Equation

                Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy
Trustworthiness = ───────────────────────────────────
                        Self-orientation

The top three add up, the bottom one divides. It explains the person who is expert, reliable and warm and still not trusted: everyone can tell they are mainly in it for themselves. → Full framework page

How trust gets broken (house content)

Mixed messages · missed promises · hidden information · blame and gossip · favouritism · poor listening · breach of confidence.

Self-Assessment

Step 1 of ACT-031 Fix Your Lowest Pillar is the instrument: rate yourself 1 to 5 on Trust, Conflict, Commitment, Accountability and Results, and circle the lowest. House content, taken as written from the source workbook.

There is no scored band here on purpose. The lowest pillar is the result, and the worksheet turns it straight into a daily action with a trigger.

6

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Think of someone whose word you have learned to discount. What did they actually do?
  2. When did someone last bring you bad news? What did your face do in the first two seconds?
  3. Which of the five pillars is weakest for you personally? For your team?
  4. What is something you agreed to in a meeting and then quietly did differently?
  5. Who on your team has stopped telling you things? When did that start?
  6. Where have you dropped the ball and not repaired it? What would repairing it take?
  7. Whose trust would change your working life most if you rebuilt it?
  8. What is the one small promise you will make, keep and close this week, and to whom?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min for the full flow. At 90, cut ACT-036 and ACT-037
  • Work bottom up, always. If a group rates trust low and results low, only trust is worth working on this month
  • What usually goes wrong: groups love talking about healthy conflict and want to skip there. If trust is not present, encouraging debate produces a fight
  • Cultural note: open disagreement with someone senior is a respect issue, not a comfort issue, in many Pacific and Māori settings. Ask how honest debate actually works in their world before prescribing the meeting-room version
  • ACT-031 and ACT-037 both need a follow-up week. Diary it before you run the session, or you teach the group that commitments made here do not count
9

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-039 The Silent Nod (10-12 min). Three briefed people agree with a mildly bad proposal and the room stays silent. Fake yes, experienced live. The best opener in this topic.
  • ACT-036 Red Flag Or Green Flag? (12-15 min). Use the trust variation: trust-breaking behaviours, asked as "have you seen this?"

PS-LEA-012Pink Sheet · Leadership

Not motivated is not a diagnosis

placeholder-story
leadershipmotivationself-determinationexpectancyevidenceteams

Topic: TOP-LEA-012 What Actually Motivates People · Pillar: Leadership

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

"They're not motivated" is what you say when you have not asked which specific thing has broken.

It sounds like an explanation and it is a shrug. Every person who has stopped trying has stopped for a reason that is findable in about a minute, and the fix is completely different depending on which reason it is.

Model

Two models doing two jobs. What people need, and why they are not trying today.

Three needs — Deci and Ryan. All three, or it does not hold. All three are free.

Three links — Vroom. A chain breaks at its weakest point.

LinkThe questionIf it broke, the fix is
Expectancy"If I try, can I actually do it?"Training, tools, a smaller step. Not encouragement
Instrumentality"If I do it, will the thing actually happen?"Keep a promise. Then another
Valence"Do I even want the thing?"Ask. Most reward schemes fail here and nobody checks

⚠️ Say the pay thing first. Below enough, none of this works. Above enough, pay stops being the lever. A room on low wages will rightly stop listening to anyone who skips that.

Metaphor

A car that will not start.

Nobody says "this car is unmotivated." They ask whether it is the battery, the fuel or the starter, because the fix is different for each and you cannot guess from the outside.

Yet a person who has stopped is routinely diagnosed with a personality. "They're just not motivated" is the mechanic shrugging at the bonnet.

➜ And the most common broken link is the fuel line, not the engine. They tried, it worked, and the thing they were promised did not happen.

Study

Three findings, and it matters which is which.

1. Self-Determination Theory — strong. Deci and Ryan (1985, 2000). Autonomy, competence and relatedness, supported across decades of research in work, school, sport and health. The best-evidenced motivation framework in this library. Cognitive Evaluation Theory, which workbooks name without explaining, is one of its sub-theories.

2. Expectancy Theory — moderate. Vroom (1964). The three components are useful and well established. The multiplicative formula is the weak part and has been revised repeatedly. Teach three questions, not a sum.

3. Maslow's Hierarchy — weak, and it is the famous one.
The pyramid was not Maslow'sHe never drew one. Somebody else added it, and the pyramid is what makes the order look official
Wahba & Bridwell (1976)Reviewed the research and found little support for the hierarchy as described, especially the ordering. Longitudinal tests of the gratification-activation claim found none
What survivesThe list. Five real categories of need. Not the ladder

➜ And the ladder is not a harmless error. It says you cannot think about belonging or dignity until food and housing are sorted, and that has been used to decide what people in hardship are allowed to want. What people actually do is find belonging and pride in the middle of hardship, not after it.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The night-shift picker who was promised a look at team leader and never mentioned again is written for teaching. It is composite, true to what supervisors describe, not one identified person.

The story to collect: a supervisor who found the broken link and fixed it. It will be an instrumentality one — a promise that had not been kept — and what lands is how small the fix was compared to how long the problem had run.

Second story, higher value: somebody who was called unmotivated and could name exactly which of the three had gone. In their own words. That single sentence dismantles the whole shrug.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Supervisor and team-lead trainingThe full topic, 120-150 min
Any time "they're just not motivated" is saidThree questions, about a minute, and it becomes fixable
Reward and incentive designAsk about valence before you design anything
Programme designIt applies to a classroom exactly as it applies to a workplace. A learner who stops in week six has a broken link too
Funder and employer conversationsWhy Zeducation does not treat disengagement as an attitude problem

⚠️ Where it goes wrong: used to argue that pay does not matter. It does. Say so first, every time.

What Actually Motivates People

1

About This Topic

Motivation is the thing every supervisor is expected to produce and almost nobody is taught.

The Leadership pillar has covered style (TOP-LEA-010), decisions (TOP-LEA-006) and team stages (TOP-LEA-003). It has had nothing on motivation at all, which is the gap this topic fills.

Three models, in this order, and the order is the teaching:

ModelWhy it is there
1Maslow's HierarchyBecause they have already met it, and it needs auditing before anything else can land
2Self-Determination TheoryThe one with the evidence. Three needs, all free
3Expectancy TheoryThe diagnostic. Which link broke, for this person, today

⚠️ This topic teaches a famous model and then takes it apart. That is deliberate, and it is the intellectual habit worth more than any of the three models: a model can be useful and not true, and you are allowed to know which.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Intrinsic motivationDoing something because of the thing itself
Extrinsic motivationDoing something for what it gets you
AutonomyHaving some say inside the rules. Not the absence of rules
ValenceHow much somebody actually wants the reward on offer
TaxonomyA useful list of categories. Not the same as a proven order
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Explain why the strict Maslow ladder is not supported by the evidence, and what survives of it.
  2. Name the three needs that motivation runs on, and one free thing you could do for each.
  3. Diagnose which of three links has broken for somebody who has stopped trying.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A supervisor has a picker on nights who used to be the best on the floor. For the last two months he has been slow, quiet, and last out of the truck.

She has tried everything she can think of. She has told him he has potential. She has put him up for employee of the month. She has offered the team a $50 voucher for hitting target. Nothing has moved.

So she asks him.

It turns out that eighteen months ago he was told that if he stuck it out on nights he would be looked at for team leader. He stuck it out. Two team leaders have been appointed since and nobody has mentioned it again.

He is not unmotivated. He tried, it worked, and the thing he was promised did not happen. He has correctly worked out that effort and outcome are not connected here, and he has adjusted.

Ask the room: which of the things she tried would ever have fixed that?

Then the second question, which is the real one: when did somebody last tell you that you were not motivated? Were they right?

Statement: "They're not motivated" is not a diagnosis. It is what you say when you have not asked which specific thing has broken.

➜ Facilitator note: the answer to the first question is none of them. Encouragement, recognition and a voucher all aim at the wrong link. Let the room work that out before you name anything.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-071

Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs — the famous one, audited

What it is: five kinds of human need, drawn as a ladder you climb one rung at a time.

Origin: Abraham Maslow, 1943 and 1954. ⚠️ The pyramid is not his. He never drew one, and the pyramid is what makes the strict-order claim look official.

NeedWhat it covers
5Self-actualisationBecoming what you could be
4EsteemRespect, recognition, being good at something
3BelongingRelationships, being part of something
2SafetyHousing, health, a job that will still be there
1PhysiologicalFood, water, sleep, warmth

⚠️ The audit, and it is not optional. Wahba and Bridwell (1976) reviewed the research and found little support for the hierarchy as Maslow described it, particularly the ordering. Ten factor-analytic and three ranking studies gave only partial support. Longitudinal studies of the "satisfy one level and the next switches on" claim gave none.

What survives is the list. Five real categories of need. The ladder is the part that does not hold.

➜ And this is not an academic quibble. The ladder says you cannot think about belonging or dignity until food and housing are sorted. That sentence has been used to decide what people in hardship are allowed to want. What people actually do is find belonging and pride in the middle of hardship, not after it, and every room can supply an example.

More resources:

  • 📄 Wahba & Bridwell (1976), Maslow reconsidered

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-070

Self-Determination Theory — the one to actually use

What it is: three needs that have to be met before anybody is motivated by anything other than the money, and the money is the weakest lever you have.

Origin: Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan, 1985 and 2000. Evidence: strong, across decades and across work, school, sport and health. Cognitive Evaluation Theory is one of its sub-theories, which matters because that is the name a lot of workbooks use without saying what it belongs to.

How to read it: all three, or it does not hold. Undermine any one and motivation shifts to "because I have to" or goes.

NeedWhat it looks like at workWhat kills it
AutonomyChoosing the order of your jobs. Being asked rather than toldBeing watched. Every decision made for you
CompetenceBeing trained properly. Being told when you did it wellNever being shown. Only hearing when it is wrong
RelatednessBeing known by name. Being missed when you are awayBeing a number on a roster

➜ All three are free. That is why this is the one a supervisor can act on. "I can't pay them more" is usually true and it is not the end of the conversation.

⚠️ But pay does matter, and say so first. Below enough, nothing else works. Somebody who cannot make rent is not going to be moved by autonomy, and a room on low wages will rightly walk out on anybody who suggests otherwise. Above enough, pay stops being the lever.

More resources:

  • 🔗 APA — Self-determination theory

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-072

Vroom's Expectancy Theory — the diagnostic

What it is: people try when they believe effort produces performance, performance produces an outcome, and the outcome is worth having. Break any one and they stop trying, and it is not laziness.

Origin: Victor H. Vroom, Work and Motivation, 1964. Evidence: moderate. The three components are useful and well established; the multiplicative formula is the weaker part and has been revised repeatedly. Do not put the formula on a slide as though it calculates anything.

How to read it: a chain, and a chain breaks at its weakest link.

If this brokeThe fix, and it must match the link
ExpectancyTraining, tools, a smaller first step. Not encouragement
InstrumentalityKeep a promise. Then keep another one. Slowest to repair
ValenceAsk what they actually want. Most reward schemes fail here and nobody checks

⚠️ Instrumentality is the one that matters most in our rooms. For a lot of learners it has been broken repeatedly before they walked in. Told that finishing the course meant a job. Told that working hard meant more hours. Somebody who has stopped believing effort leads to outcomes is not unmotivated. They are accurately describing their own history.

➜ Which is why a small kept promise is worth more than a big one made. Same mechanism as FRM-022 The Trust Equation, from the motivation side.

→ Full framework page

Self-Assessment

ACT-115 Which One Broke? is the assessment, and it is a diagnostic rather than a score.

Everyone starts with their own example — a time they stopped trying at something — and works out which of the three links went.
Their own caseWhich link broke, and what made it that way
Six scenariosDiagnosed in groups, with a fix that has to match the link
One real personSomebody on their team who has stopped trying, and how they would check rather than assume

⚠️ Not validated and nothing is recorded. You cannot see somebody else's expectancy, instrumentality or valence. You can only ask, and "how would I check rather than assume" is the most important line on the sheet.

➜ Take a show of hands on which link broke in people's own examples. It is almost always instrumentality, and that lands harder than any teaching.

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-114 Build The Ladder, Then Knock It DownGame, and the opener20-25 minFRM-071
ACT-113 Three Needs, One TeamWorksheet30-35 minFRM-070
ACT-115 Which One Broke?Assessment25-30 minFRM-072
ACT-006 Two Things CommitmentReflection10 minCloses with a date

Suggested flow: the night-shift story → ACT-114 to build and knock down Maslow → teach FRM-070 while the ground is clear → ACT-113 → break → teach FRM-072 → ACT-115 → ACT-006.

⚠️ Do not run ACT-114 unless you are going to teach SDT afterwards. Knocking down a model and putting nothing in its place is worse than leaving it alone.

⚠️ Part 1 of ACT-113 runs before FRM-070 is taught. The room derives the three needs from their own best and worst jobs, which is far more convincing than being told.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. Which of the supervisor's three attempts in the opening story would ever have worked? Why not?
  2. When did somebody last call you unmotivated? Which of the three had actually broken?
  3. Where have you seen the Maslow ladder logic used to decide what somebody was allowed to want?
  4. Which of the three needs is weakest on your team right now?
  5. Who on your team would not be noticed if they did not turn up? What are you going to do about it?
  6. What have you promised somebody that you have not yet delivered?
  7. What reward have you offered that nobody actually wanted? Did you ask first?
  8. What is one free thing you will do this week, for which need, and when?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable. Under 120, run ACT-114, FRM-070 and ACT-113, and give FRM-072 and ACT-115 their own session
  • ⚠️ Say the pay thing first, before SDT. "Below enough, nothing else works." A room on low wages will stop listening to anybody who seems to be arguing that money does not matter, and they would be right to
  • ⚠️ Do not run ACT-114 without teaching SDT afterwards. Taking a model away and leaving a hole is worse than leaving it alone
  • The order matters. Maslow first because they have met it, SDT second because it works, Vroom third because it is the diagnostic. Reversing it wastes the audit
  • Do not turn the audit into "Maslow was stupid." He gave a good list in 1943 and somebody else drew the ladder. Getting that distinction right is the intellectual habit worth teaching
  • "They're just not motivated" is the sentence to hunt. Every time it is said in the room, ask which of the three, and the conversation becomes fixable
  • ⚠️ A learner will have been on the wrong end of the ladder logic from a service that decided what they were allowed to want. Be on their side about it, briefly, and move on
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation story on the Pink Sheet. The one to collect is a supervisor who found the broken link and fixed it, and it will be an instrumentality one
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-114 Build The Ladder, Then Knock It Down (20-25 min, medium energy). Groups order five cards, produce Maslow without being told, then take it apart from their own lives. The room does the disproving, not you.
  • Best job, worst job (8 min). Two columns, and one question: what was different? It is Part 1 of ACT-113 and it works perfectly well on its own as an opener.
  • The voucher round (5 min). "What reward would actually change your week?" Round the room. The answers are never what management would have guessed, and that is valence in ninety seconds.

From the Ice Breaker Games pillar

Not tied to this topic, and that is the point — they warm a room up, and any of them can open or close the session. These two suit this topic best.

GameTimeEnergySettingWhy this one here
GAM-012 Would You Rather?15-25 minmediumonline (breakout rooms) or in personWhat people choose when nothing is riding on it says more than a survey
GAM-010 What Would You Do?10-20 minlowonline or in personAutonomy, competence and relatedness all show up in the answers

➜ All sixteen: Ice Breaker Games

Source Trail

Built from SRC-017 TWoA Leadership Kōnae Ako 2, ingested 2026-08-02. ⚠️ Record only, no full text — third-party copyright, and this library renders to a shareable site.

What the source contributed was the gap, not the content. Its Lesson 4 asks tauira to apply Hierarchy of Needs Theory, Expectancy Theory and Cognitive Evaluation Theory to a three-and-a-half hour scenario, and then says "you might need to do a bit more research about these models." No Maslow, no Vroom, no Deci and Ryan. No dates, no evidence, no caution.

Everything on this page was researched from scratch: the Wahba and Bridwell audit, the fact that the pyramid is not Maslow's, Deci and Ryan's three needs and the sub-theory relationship, and the weakness of Vroom's multiplicative form. The story, all three activities and the diagnostic table are house content.

PIL-WELPillar · Wellbeing & Identity

Wellbeing & Identity

Hauora, resilience, values and culture. The foundation the other five pillars stand on, and the pillar that decides whether learning sticks.

Who it serves: everyone, and especially learners carrying pressure from work, family and money at the same time.

The boundary: if it is about the learner's own identity and wellbeing, it belongs here. If it is about working across difference, or what a leader builds, it belongs in Culture & Diversity.

PS-WEL-001Pink Sheet · Wellbeing & Identity

You only need the next rock

placeholder-story
wellbeingresiliencehauoraabc-modelactionsetbackshouse-content

Topic: TOP-WEL-001 Building Resilience · Pillar: Wellbeing & Identity

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

Clarity comes from action, not the other way around.

People wait to start until they can see how it ends. That wait is not caution, it is the thing keeping them stuck. You do not need to see every step. You need the next one, and the one after it only becomes visible once you are standing on the first.

Model

ABC. Three steps, and the third is the whole thing.

StepWhat it doesThe failure mode
AAcceptSplits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannotHeard as "get over it"
BBelieveReplaces doubt with evidence, not encouragementSkipped, and it is the step with the research behind it
CCommitOne action, fifteen minutes, with a time and a definition of doneBecomes a project instead of a step

⚠️ Not Ellis's ABC (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), which is a therapy model with the same three letters. Say "the ABC of resilience".

And the frame that has to come first: resilience is ordinary. It is common, it runs on ordinary systems, and it is not a personality trait some people were issued with. Without that framing the tool lands as "try harder", which is worse than teaching nothing.

Metaphor

Crossing a river on stepping stones.

Some people can see the whole line of rocks to the other side. They know each step and they just follow it.

Others can only see the rock right in front of them. That is fine. Step onto it, and the next one shows up.

Different views, same goal. Keep moving.

➜ This is Zeducation's own, straight from the SKILL UP guide, and it is the strongest thing in the resource. It also runs as an activity — ACT-107 puts a paper river on the floor and it takes fifteen minutes.

Study

Two anchors, and it matters which part of the model each one holds up.

1. Resilience is ordinary. Ann S. Masten, University of Minnesota, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development (Guilford, 2nd ed. 2024). Decades of longitudinal work with children exposed to serious adversity. Her finding: resilience is common, and it runs on ordinary adaptive systems — relationships, routines, a functioning body, culture, belief — rather than on rare personal strength. Evidence: strong.

2. Why step B works. "Remember your past wins" is Bandura's mastery experiences, which the self-efficacy literature consistently finds to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief. Direct personal evidence of having done a hard thing beats encouragement from anybody else.

➜ The line: being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can. Remembering that you already did is the strongest.

And the part worth saying in a Zeducation room: Masten's list of ordinary systems is the same list as Te Whare Tapa Whā (Durie, 1984) and Fonofale (Pulotu-Endemann). Three traditions, arrived at separately, one answer. Durie got there forty years earlier.

⚠️ Honest limit: the ABC model itself has no study behind it. Step B does. The other two steps are craft, and they should be presented as craft.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The man on the stepping stones is the resource's own metaphor, told as a teaching story. It is not a real person.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who was stuck waiting to see the whole path, took one small step, and found the next one. What lands is what the step actually was — small enough to sound unimpressive, which is the point — and what became visible afterwards.

Second story worth collecting, and it is the higher-value one: somebody whose confidence moved on the ABC worksheet while nothing about their situation changed. The before and after number, in their own words. That is the proof of the whole model in about fifteen seconds.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any wellbeing or resilience sessionThe full topic, 120-150 min
One-to-one after a knockbackA job rejection, a failed assessment, a fallout at home. Fifteen minutes and a sheet
Team debriefsA lost tender, a bad audit, a restructure. One sheet, whole team
Talks and keynotesThe river stones is the strongest metaphor Zeducation owns. It carries a whole talk
Funder and employer conversationsThe "resilience is ordinary" framing is why Zeducation does not treat circumstances as a motivation problem

⚠️ Where it does not go: grief, trauma, depression, anxiety. This is a tool for a setback. Know the difference, and know the referrals: their GP, 1737 free call or text, workplace EAP.

1

About This Topic

Everyone gets knocked around. A deadline slips, the bills stack up, a relationship strains, a health scare turns up, or somebody dies. The details differ. The feeling is the same: pressure, uncertainty, and the question "what now?"

Resilience is the answer to that moment. It is not about being unbreakable. It is about adapting: steadying yourself, learning from what happened, and taking the next small step.

This topic runs in three moves.

The moveWhy it is in this order
1What resilience actually isBecause half the room has already decided it is a personality trait they do not have
2The whole personTe Whare Tapa Whā and Fonofale. Because "be more resilient" aims at the mind and ignores the four things holding it up
3The toolThe ABC model, on a real setback, leaving with one step

⚠️ Do not skip move 1. A resilience session taught without it becomes a session about trying harder, and for a learner already carrying a heavy load that is worse than teaching nothing.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ResilienceAdapting after a knock. Steadying, learning, taking the next step. Not being unbreakable
HauoraWellbeing, in the whole-person sense. Body, mind, family, spirit, place
PouA post or a pillar. One of the parts holding the house up
AigaFamily, including extended family and anyone you are linked to
SetbackSomething that knocks you off course and that you can do something about. Not the same as a crisis
Self-efficacyYour belief that you can do a particular thing. Built mostly out of having done hard things before
2

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Explain what resilience actually is, and name the ordinary systems it runs on.
  2. Name one thing that needs care in each part of your whare or your fale.
  3. Apply the ABC model to a real setback and leave with one small step, with a time on it.
3

Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A man is crossing a river on stepping stones. He knows the far bank is there, but standing where he is, he can see exactly one rock. The rest is under the glare of the water.

Next to him is somebody who can see the whole line of stones, all the way across. She steps out and walks it in eight seconds.

He waits. He waits because it feels obvious that you should be able to see where you are going before you go. Then eventually he puts one foot on the one rock he can see, and stands on it, and from there the next one is visible.

He crosses. Slower than her, and he still gets to the other side.

Ask the room: which one of them needed the whole plan?

Then the second question, which is the real one: what have you not started, because you cannot see how it ends?

Statement: Clarity comes from action, not the other way around. You do not need to see every step. You need the next one.

➜ Facilitator note: the room will have an answer to the second question and most of them will not say it out loud. That is fine. Let the silence sit for a moment, then move.

Tools, Techniques & Frameworks

FrameworkFRM-066

Resilience Is Ordinary

What it is: resilience is common, not rare, and it runs on ordinary systems around a person rather than on exceptional personal strength.

Origin: Ann S. Masten, University of Minnesota, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development. Decades of work with children exposed to serious adversity. Evidence: strong, and built on longitudinal research rather than one study.

Most people arrive with one of two beliefs and both are wrong.

The beliefWhere it leads
"Resilient people are made differently"Nothing you teach applies to them, because they have decided it is a trait they lack
"Resilience means taking anything"The word becomes a weapon, used to explain why the problem is you and not the load

How to read it: the question is never "are you strong enough?" It is "which of your systems is missing, and can we put it back?"

⚠️ The sentence this framework exists to refuse: "you just need to be more resilient." Said to somebody working two jobs whose car has died, that is not support. It moves a structural problem into a personal failing. The honest version: resilience is real and it can be built, and it is not a substitute for enough hours, a safe house, or somebody to ring.

More resources:

  • 📕 Ann S. Masten, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development, 2nd ed.

→ Full framework page

FrameworkFRM-063

Te Whare Tapa Whā · FRM-065 Fonofale

Teach these two together. Never one alone. A room offered a single model has been told which half of itself counts.

Te Whare Tapa Whā is Sir Mason Durie's, developed at Hui Taumata in 1984 in response to Rapuora, research carried out 1978 to 1980 by the Māori Women's Welfare League into the health barriers Māori were experiencing. It is the framework that got wairua acknowledged in health practice in this country.

How to read it: four walls on one foundation. A whare with three walls does not stand.

Fonofale is Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann's, built across Cook Islands, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Niuean and Tokelauan values. Culture is the roof. Aiga is the floor. Four pou between them, and the whole fale sits inside its environment, its time and its context.

Te Whare Tapa WhāFonofale
FamilyTaha whānau, one of four wallsAiga is the floor. Everything stands on it
CultureCarried through whenua and wairuaThe roof. Named on its own
The fourth elementTaha wairua"Other" — age, gender, sexuality, money
What surrounds itWhenua as the foundationEnvironment, time and context

➜ The "other" pou does something no other wellbeing model here does. It puts money, age, gender and sexuality inside the picture of health instead of outside it.

Why this matters for resilience specifically:

What it gives you when things go wrong
BodySteadies the stress. Sleep and food change what a problem feels like before they change anything else
MindLets you think straight enough to make a decision you will not regret
Family, aigaThe backup. Somebody to ring, somebody who turns up
Spirit, cultureThe reason to keep going when there is no short-term reason
Whenua, contextKnowing who and where you are from, when a setback is telling you that you are nothing

⚠️ Aiga cuts both ways and the room knows it. Family is the strongest support most Pacific learners have, and sometimes also the obligation grinding them down. Do not teach the floor as though it is only a resource.

⚠️ Say whose these models are. Durie by name, 1984. Pulotu-Endemann by name, and he is a living person. Teaching a Māori or Pacific model without attribution is the exact habit this library exists to break.

More resources:

  • 🔗 Mental Health Foundation — Te Whare Tapa Whā
  • 📄 Fonofale Model of Health — Pulotu-Endemann (PDF)

→ Te Whare Tapa Whā · Fonofale

FrameworkFRM-064

The ABC Model of Resilience (house model)

⚠️ Name clash. This is not Ellis's ABC (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), which is what a counsellor or a psychology student will mean. Say "the ABC of resilience" when you introduce it. And it is not Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which shares two of its words and is a clinical therapy delivered by clinicians. This is a workshop tool.

What it is: three steps from spinning your wheels to having one small thing you are going to do.

How to read it: in order, and C is the point. A and B without C is a nice conversation that changes nothing by Friday.

StepWhat it does
AAcceptStops the spinning. Splits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannot
BBelieveReplaces doubt with evidence. Evidence, not a pep talk
CCommitTurns insight into momentum. Fifteen minutes, with a time on it

Worked example. You have been turned down for a job you thought you had.
Accept"They said no. I can't change that. I can control whether I ring and ask why, and whether I apply for the other two this week."
Believe"I got the warehouse job in March and I had less experience then. I've got Mere, who knows people at the DC."
Commit"Tomorrow at 10, I'll ring and ask what would have made the difference. Done means I've asked one question and written the answer down."

➜ Notice what the commitment is not. Not "be more positive", not "get back out there". One action, a time, and a definition of done.

Where the evidence actually sits. Be honest about which part is backed and which is craft.

StepWhat holds it up
AcceptThe control / no-control split. A useful distinction, not a research finding
BelieveThe strongest part. "Remember your past wins" is Bandura's mastery experiences, consistently found to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief
CommitSmall, specific, time-boxed action. The specificity does the work, not the size

➜ The line worth saying out loud: "Being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can do it. Remembering that you already did is the strongest. That is why step B asks for a past win and not a compliment."

More resources:

  • 🔗 Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy

→ Full framework page

⚠️ Where to send someone (house content, and it is not optional)

The ABC model is for a setback. It is not a treatment for depression, anxiety, grief or trauma, and somebody in the room will be carrying one of those.
1737Free call or text, any time, to a trained counsellor
Their GPThe first door for anything that has lasted more than a couple of weeks
Workplace EAPFree, confidential, and most learners in work do not know they have it
Their MSD case managerFor the practical load: money, housing, transport
Healthline 0800 611 11624/7

Say these out loud at the start, not the end. Somebody who needs them will have stopped listening by the end.

Self-Assessment

ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall is the assessment, and both models are on the sheet so the learner picks.

⚠️ There is no score. No total, no rating out of ten, nothing to hand in. One thing per wall that needs care. That is the entire instrument, and somebody will ask what a good result looks like. There is not one.

What the learner leaves with:
One thing per wallNamed, in their own words
The wall holding everything up on its ownUsually obvious once the model gives them the word
The wall they have been letting goUsually tinana. Sometimes wairua
One step on one wallFifteen minutes, with a time and somebody who will know

The ABC worksheet also carries a confidence check, 1 to 10, before and after planning. Also not validated, also not recorded. The movement is the lesson — people routinely go up two or three points in fifteen minutes while nothing about the situation has changed.

⚠️ Never fill either in about a learner. A hauora model used to assess somebody else is doing the opposite of what it was built for.

6

Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises

ACT-105 One Thing Per WallAssessment25-30 minFRM-063, FRM-065

Suggested flow: the river story in section 3 → ACT-104 while the room is settling → teach FRM-066 → teach both wellbeing models → ACT-105 → break, because they have been sitting → ACT-107 to get them up → straight into ACT-106 while they are standing → ACT-006 to close.

⚠️ ACT-107 goes immediately before step C of ACT-106. That is what it is for. Running the game early and the worksheet after lunch loses most of its value.

7

Reflection Questions

  1. What have you not started, because you cannot see how it ends?
  2. Which quote landed fastest, and what does that say about what you already carry?
  3. Which wall or pou has been holding everything up on its own?
  4. Which one have you been letting go, and how long has that been going on?
  5. What have you been spending energy on that belongs in the "cannot control" column?
  6. What is a past win you had stopped counting?
  7. Who is the one person who would turn up for you at 2am? Do they know that is what they are?
  8. What is your next rock, when will you step on it, and who will know that you did?
8

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. Under 90, run FRM-066, one wellbeing model, ACT-107 and ACT-106. Never drop the referral list to save time
  • ⚠️ Read the referral list out at the start of the session, not the end. Somebody who needs it will have stopped listening by the end
  • Teach both wellbeing models, always. Ten minutes each. A Pacific room given only Te Whare Tapa Whā, or a Māori room given only Fonofale, has been told something you did not mean to say
  • Do not comment on which model anybody picks. Some Māori learners will pick Fonofale. Some Pacific learners will pick the whare. It is not a test of identity
  • The ABC worksheet needs a real setback. Not hypothetical. Say at the start that it is fine to pick something small, and that nobody will be asked to share the situation
  • What usually goes wrong: "Accept" is heard as "get over it" or "it was your fault". Say what it means before they write, not after. It is the single most common misfire in the topic
  • Step C will be too big. "Sort my life out" is not a step. Be strict, because this is where the session is won or lost
  • ⚠️ Somebody's setback will turn out to be a crisis. Bereavement, a diagnosis, violence, a relationship ending, losing the house. ABC is not for those. Have the referrals ready before you walk in
  • Come back to the sheets a fortnight later and ask whether the step happened. This is where the tool either becomes real or dies in the room it was taught in
  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on the Pink Sheet yet. It can only come from delivery. Ask your tutors and get permission properly
  • ⚠️ Open gap: FRM-066 rests on US developmental research. New Zealand longitudinal evidence would strengthen it, and the Dunedin and Christchurch studies are the obvious places to look
9

Games & Energisers

Use these to open the session, to reset a flat room after ninety minutes, or to close on something light. The link back is the part that matters — the game is only worth the time if somebody says what it was about afterwards.

  • ACT-107 The River Stones (15-20 min, 🔥 high energy). Two volunteers cross a paper river, one seeing every stone and one seeing only the next. The best fifteen minutes in this topic, and it works as an opener too if the room arrives full of energy.
  • ACT-104 Three Quotes (25-30 min, low energy). The quiet opener. Use this one when the room arrives flat or wary.
  • Two-minute version: ask everyone to say one thing they have got through that they did not think they would. Round the room, no detail required. Two minutes, and it sets up FRM-066 for free.

PS-WEL-002Pink Sheet · Wellbeing & Identity

It is an offer, not a claim

placeholder-story
pepehaidentitywhakapapabelongingte-ao-maoriconnectionhouse-content

Topic: TOP-WEL-002 Pepeha: Why And How Do I Do It · Pillar: Wellbeing & Identity

On this pagePointModelMetaphorStudyStoryWhere it goesRelated sheets

Point

A pepeha is not there to prove you belong. It is there so somebody else can find the thing you share.

Every mistake people make with pepeha comes from getting that backwards. Treat it as a credential and you either say nothing because you are frightened of overstepping, or you borrow one that is not yours because you think you need the full set. Treat it as an offer and both problems disappear.

➜ Zeducation's own line, and it is the sentence the whole topic hangs on: the true essence of a pepeha is much more about connections and creating the potential for connections.

Model

The order is the water cycle, and the order is what decides who says what.

Mau means to catch, to hold. Maunga is the thing that catches and holds the rain and the snow. It runs down into the awa, feeds the people who live along it, and goes back to the sky.

It is a description of a system, running in the direction the system runs. Not a preference, not decoration.

➜ Which answers the question the room is already holding. A maunga in Sāmoa and an awa in Waikato are not in the same water cycle. The sentence would not be describing anything real. So there are two structures, and both of them do the same job.

Māori whānauNon-Māori whānau
Namesmaunga, awa, waka, iwi, hapū, mātua, kāinga, ingoawhakapaparanga mai, engari, whenua tupu, kāinga, nō, noho, mahi, ingoa
Points towhakapapaconnection
Lines119

The word doing the work in the second one is engari. But.

My ancestry is Sāmoan and Irish — engari — Māngere is where I grew up.

Two truths, held at once, in the right order. For most Zeducation rooms that is the line that lands, and it lands hard.

Metaphor

The good short answer.

A woman is eleven years in the country and has an answer ready for where are you from. She built it short on purpose, because she gets asked about twice a month and the short version ends the conversation. That was the design.

Then one morning, at a mihi whakatau, she says a bit more than usual. Afterwards a bloke from the warehouse comes over: my wife's family is from about forty minutes from there.

Eleven years of an answer built to close the subject. And the one time it opened, it opened onto somebody standing four metres away the whole time.

➜ That is the difference between an introduction that gets you through the minute and one that does the job. Both are eight seconds long.

Study

⚠️ There is nothing to measure here and nothing to prove. This is tikanga, not research, and it should be presented that way. What matters instead is who says it, and that part is verified.

Keri Opai — linguist and educator, author of Tikanga: An Introduction to te ao Māori (Upstart Press, 2021) and of Te Reo Hāpai, the glossary of mental health, addiction and disability terms in te reo. The water cycle reasoning and the non-Māori structure are his, set out in "Pepeha for non-Māori" and "A respectfully curious approach" on E-Tangata. The first is an edited extract from the book.

His own words, and read them rather than paraphrasing:

"I believe that it's inappropriate for non-Māori people to use the same pepeha as tangata whenua. It is not a matter of mere opinion, of like or dislike, of right or wrong: it simply doesn't make sense. It is a matter of indigeneity."

➜ The line to sit on: the objection is not that somebody will be offended. It is that the sentence would not be true.

⚠️ Honest limit. Zeducation's template cites both URLs but does not name him. That is fixed on FRM-077 and FRM-079. And both E-Tangata pages are blocked by this environment's gateway — the authorship, the book and the quote are verified through search, but the full articles have not been read, so it is not confirmed which of Opai's two templates this is.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The woman at the mihi whakatau is a teaching story built from the pattern, not a named person.

The story to collect, and it is the one that carries the whole topic: a non-Māori Zeducation learner who spent years saying their name and sitting down, and now has nine lines they can say. The engari line in their own words — the moment they realised they did not have to pick between where their people are from and where they actually grew up.

Second story, different shape: somebody who came in not knowing their maunga, rang an aunty, and found out. What the phone call was like is the story. The answer is not.

⚠️ Where it does not go: this is not a pōwhiri briefing, it does not qualify anybody to run tikanga on a marae, and it is not cultural competency training. It is one form, taught properly.
