Collaborative Overload

modelstrong
collaborationworkloadburnoutboundarieswellbeingsaying-noteams

What it is in one line: the most helpful people in an organisation get asked for the most, and it is quietly burning them out.

Origin: Rob Cross, Reb Rebele and Adam Grant, Collaborative Overload, Harvard Business Review, January-February 2016 (HBR · full PDF on Rob Cross's site). Evidence: strong. Built on network analysis across more than 300 organisations. Best for: the person who is great at their job, says yes to everything, and is about to fall over.

Why this page exists: the Zeducation SKILL UP resource on collaborative teams says "researchers have found three common reasons people get overloaded by collaboration" without naming them. This is who. The three reasons in the workbook map directly onto this research.

On this pageThe findingsThe three reasons we take on too muchWhy it mattersWorked exampleWhat to do about itFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The findings

FindingWhat it means
Most knowledge workers spend 85% or more of their week in email, meetings and on the phoneThere is very little time left for the work itself
20 to 35% of value-added collaboration comes from only 3 to 5% of employeesA tiny group carries most of it
Those same in-demand collaborators show the lowest engagement and career satisfactionBeing the person everyone relies on is not a reward

That last row is the one that stops a room. The people a workplace depends on most are the ones most likely to leave.

The three reasons we take on too much

Straight from the workbook, now with the research behind it.

ReasonWhat it sounds like in your headThe trap
1Desire to help"They need me, and I'm good at this"Your reputation as helpful is exactly what generates the next request
2Need for accomplishment"I'll just knock this off, it'll take five minutes"Small wins for other people crowd out the deep work that is actually yours
3Fear"What if I miss out? What if they think I'm not a team player?"Fear of missing out, fear of losing control, fear of what people will think

How to read it: it is a loop, and it is powered by your best qualities. That is why willpower does not break it and only a decision rule does.

Why it matters

Because it reframes the problem. A person drowning in collaboration usually thinks they have a time management problem or a personal weakness. They do not. They have a demand problem created by being good and being willing, and the organisation has no mechanism to notice it.

It also puts an honest limit on the collaboration message. Everything else in this part of the library argues for more sharing, more input, more connecting. This is the counterweight, and teaching collaboration without it produces exactly the overload the research describes.

Worked example

The most capable person in a service team is the one everyone messages. She knows the systems, she never says no, and she is in every project because she is useful in all of them.

Her own work happens at night. Her performance review says she is a great team player. She is applying for other jobs, and when she leaves everyone will be shocked, because from the outside she looked like the person who was thriving.

Nobody did anything wrong. That is what makes it worth teaching.

What to do about it

The workbook's three habits are the practical response. They are on their own page: FRM-031 The 3 Habits of a Healthy Team Player.

For a leader, the research points at three moves:

  1. Find out who the hubs are. Ask who people go to when they are stuck. The answer is usually two or three names, and they are not always the senior ones
  2. Redistribute, do not just praise. Recognising the helper without reducing the load makes it worse, because it confirms the reputation that generates the requests
  3. Make it structurally cheaper to ask elsewhere. Better documentation, clearer ownership, and people trained up so the hub is not the only route

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. Lead with the three findings. The 3 to 5% statistic does the work
  • Ask "who is the person everyone asks?" In most rooms people name the same person within seconds, and often that person is present and has never heard it said out loud
  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning it into permission to disengage. The finding is about protecting high contributors, not about doing less
    • Aiming it only at individuals. Cross's argument is largely structural. A workshop that tells overloaded people to manage themselves better misses the point
    • Quoting the 85% figure as if it applies to every job. It comes from knowledge work. On a ward, a site or a shop floor the shape is different, though the hub effect still shows up
  • Cultural note: for many Pacific and Māori learners, being the person who carries things for others is not a workplace habit, it is an obligation to family, church and community as well. The load is real and it is not all at work. Say that, or the topic reads as though it is asking them to care less

More resources

Cultural Safety — awareness, competence, safety

modelstrong
cultural-safetycultureleadershipbelonginginclusionmaoripacific

What it is in one line: people can show up as themselves, including their identity, language, values and worldview, without fear of judgment, exclusion or penalty.

Origin: Irihapeti Ramsden (Ngāi Tahu, Rangitāne), a Māori nurse and academic, developed kawa whakaruruhau / cultural safety with Māori nursing students in Aotearoa New Zealand through the 1980s. It was formally incorporated into New Zealand nursing education in 1992, and her 2002 PhD thesis at Victoria University of Wellington, Cultural Safety and Nursing Education in Aotearoa and Te Waipounamu, is the founding text. It has since been adopted by other professions and by health systems in Australia and Canada (the thesis, full PDF · Victoria University record · Irihapeti Ramsden). Evidence: strong. Thirty years of published work, professional adoption and continuing academic development. Best for: any workplace with a culturally mixed team or customer base, which is most of them.

⚠️ Attribution matters here. The Zeducation source workbook teaches this concept without naming its origin (SRC-006). Cultural safety is not a generic HR idea. It is Māori intellectual property from Aotearoa, developed by a named woman, and using it without saying so is exactly the kind of erasure the concept exists to name. Credit Ramsden every time you teach it.

On this pageThe modelThe one thing that makes this different from every other diversity modelAn honest refinement of the ladderHow cultural safety is broken (from the source, and it is a strong list)Worked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

LevelWhat it isWhat the leader does
Cultural awarenessRecognising that people bring different identities, languages, values, histories and norms, and that these shape how they communicate and decideLearn and use correct names and greetings. Notice who speaks and who does not. Ask "what would feel respectful here?" Check your assumptions before acting
Cultural competenceThe practical skill to engage across cultures with care and accuracy. Knowing protocols, adapting behaviour, choosing language that landsPronunciation practice in onboarding. Inclusive meeting rules. Service checklists with cultural protocols. Flexible rosters for prayer or family. Scenario role plays
Cultural safetyThe felt experience of dignity and belonging, where people know they can be themselves without penalty and their voice will be protectedSet norms that guard against jokes, interruptions and mispronunciations. Model them. Intervene early and kindly. Offer confidential feedback and close the loop. Run pulse checks and act on them

How to read it: awareness is what you notice, competence is what you can do, and safety is what the other person experienced. Only the first two are yours to assess.

The one thing that makes this different from every other diversity model

Cultural safety is judged by the person receiving it, not by the person providing it.

That is Ramsden's radical move and it is the part most training loses. You do not get to decide whether you were culturally safe. Your team does. A leader can be well informed, well intentioned, fully trained, and still not safe to work for, and the only way to find out is to ask the people affected and believe the answer.

The source workbook gets this right in its own words: cultural safety is "the felt experience of respect: I'm safe here. I belong here. I can contribute here."

An honest refinement of the ladder

The three-part progression is a useful teaching shape and the research has moved past it. Curtis, Jones, Tipene-Leach and colleagues (2019), in Why cultural safety rather than cultural competency is required to achieve health equity, argue that safety is not simply more competence. Competence frames the problem as a knowledge gap in the practitioner. Safety frames it as a question of power: who decides, who is comfortable, whose norms are the default, and who has to adapt (paper, open access · PubMed).

Their argument in one line: you can be culturally competent and still be unsafe, because you can know all the protocols and still hold all the power.

Teach the ladder, then say this. It stops the topic becoming a checklist, which is the failure mode the source itself warns about.

How cultural safety is broken (from the source, and it is a strong list)

What it looks like
Token invitesPeople are asked to be present but not heard. Input is decoration, not direction
Assumption-led decisionsLeaders guess what is respectful without asking, so well-meant actions still cause harm
Protocol theatreGreetings or ceremonies performed for show while daily behaviour contradicts them
Name and language neglectNames mispronounced, macrons and diacritics dropped, bilingual staff used as unpaid translators without consent
English-only spacesMeetings, signage and guest materials default to one language, signalling other identities are secondary
Culture as a jokeSmall comments, stereotypes or mimicked accents left unchecked, teaching people to hide parts of themselves
Uneven consequencesHigh performers get a pass for disrespect. Those who speak up face subtle penalties
Invisible risksSacred practices photographed, private matters shared, cultural boundaries crossed for convenience

➜ Facilitator tip: protocol theatre and uneven consequences are the two that land hardest, because most rooms recognise both immediately and neither is usually named out loud.

Worked example

A hotel manager mispronounces a new staff member's name on day one. On day two he comes back having learned it properly, macron and all, and uses it from then on.

That is thirty seconds of effort and it is the whole model working. Awareness noticed the name mattered. Competence went and learned it. Safety is what the staff member felt on day two, and only she can say whether it worked.

The opposite version is equally small: an eye roll at an accent, a rushed photo in a no-photo zone. People retreat, and the retreat is invisible until you go looking for it.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes for the three levels and the recipient-judges point. Do not rush the second one
  • Lead with Ramsden. Naming a Māori nurse as the originator changes how a Pacific or Māori room receives the whole topic, and it models the behaviour the topic teaches
  • Common mistakes:
    • Confusing being nice with being safe. The source names this and it is the most common failure in the room. Warmth is not protection
    • Treating it as a tick-box training. Also named in the source. Safety is a daily practice, not a poster
    • Speaking for communities instead of with them. Including in the session itself. If there are people in the room from the culture being discussed, they are not there to be the exhibit
    • Running it as though the facilitator is safe by default. Model asking for feedback on your own impact
  • Watch the load. In any mixed room, the people who have experienced the broken-safety list are doing unpaid emotional work while it is read out. Say so, and never invite anyone to share a story of harm in front of colleagues

More resources

  • 📄 Curtis et al. (2019), Why cultural safety rather than cultural competency is required to achieve health equity
  • 📄 Nursing Praxis Aotearoa — Kawa Whakaruruhau: cultural safety in nursing education
  • 📄 Treaty Resource Centre — Kawa whakaruruhau

  • 📄 Dr Irihapeti Ramsden's powerful petition for cultural safety (PDF) — the political fight it took to get this into nursing training
  • 🔗 Irihapeti Ramsden — Wikipedia — Ngāi Tahu / Rangitāne, 1946-2003. Who she was, in one page

S.A.F.E Leadership — Shape, Apply, Fairness, Educate

modelpractitioner
cultural-safetyleadershiphouse-contentinclusionfairnessculture

What it is in one line: four things a leader does, repeatedly, to turn good intentions about cultural safety into behaviour people can actually feel.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Cultural Safety in the Workplace SKILL UP resource (SRC-006). Evidence: practitioner. It is the house playbook for FRM-033 Cultural Safety, which carries the research. Best for: the leader who agrees with cultural safety in principle and does not know what to do on Monday morning.

On this pageThe modelThe four steps in fullWhy it worksWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

StepWhat it means
SShape the spaceCreate conditions where respect is the norm, not the exception
AApply curiosityLead with questions, not assumptions
FFairness firstMake processes, expectations, opportunities and consequences even, and say so early
EEducate myselfDo the learning so others are not carrying your load

How to read it: a loop, not a course. The E step feeds the next S, which is why it is a practice and not a training day.

The four steps in full

S — Shape the space

Set clear respect norms and expectations at the start of gatherings, not after something has gone wrong. Name the standard: one voice at a time, correct names with diacritics. Make the environment inclusive with visible cues such as dual-language signage and a quiet space for prayer. State consent rules for photos, filming and use of cultural elements before events. Rotate who speaks first and who presents, to equalise visibility. Keep the norms visible so you can point back to them when the room gets hot.

➜ That last clause is the practical heart of it. A norm agreed in advance is something you can refer to calmly. A norm invented mid-conflict is just your opinion.

A — Apply curiosity

Ask what would feel respectful here. Ask people to help you say their names correctly. Stay open to learning about their cultures, histories and motivations.

Resist the pull to jump to conclusions or to take offence. Check intent and impact first. Seek permission before translating or sharing stories or motifs. Make a habit of inviting two quieter voices before you decide.

F — Fairness first

Publish decision criteria and timelines. Apply the same standards to everyone, including friends and stars. Rotate high-visibility tasks and speaking order. Separate behaviour feedback from accent, identity or style.

Keep a simple decision log: the criteria, who was consulted, the final choice, and the why. Share a short summary so people can see fairness rather than being asked to assume it.

E — Educate myself

Learn local protocols, histories and traditions through briefings or trusted resources. Practise pronunciation and correct forms of address. Keep a personal glossary with macrons or diacritics.

Set a cadence: one credible resource a month, and one change you will make because of it. Rehearse respectful responses with short role plays so they are available in busy moments. Ask for feedback on your impact, "did that land respectfully?", and adjust.

➜ The phrase that carries this step is "so others are not carrying your load." In most workplaces the cultural education of the manager is being done, unpaid and unasked, by the staff.

Why it works

Because each letter fixes a different failure, and they are the four that actually happen.

StepThe failure it prevents
ShapeNorms invented after the harm, which always sound like a reaction to a person
ApplyAssumption-led decisions. Well-meant actions that still cause harm
FairnessUneven consequences, where high performers get a pass
EducateMaking your team responsible for teaching you about themselves

Worked example

A supervisor is running a season briefing with a mixed team.

Shape: she opens with the norms, one voice at a time, and says filming is off unless everyone agrees. Apply: she asks two people how to say their names properly and repeats them back. Fairness: she rotates who presents, and says out loud how the shift preferences were decided. Educate: afterwards she notes one thing she got wrong, a form of address, and fixes it before the next briefing.

None of that took extra time. It took different attention, applied at the start rather than after a complaint.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run ACT-064 Before, During, After, which is the source's own worksheet and turns the model into a plan for a real meeting
  • Common mistakes:
    • Doing S and skipping E. Setting norms for other people while learning nothing yourself is the most common version of this framework done badly
    • Fairness as sameness. Treating everyone identically is not the same as fair. Rotating who presents is fair; ignoring that one person always gets talked over is not
    • Curiosity as interrogation. Two questions is curiosity. Twenty is making someone the exhibit
  • Cultural note: this framework was written for a Fiji tourism client, where the mix is iTaukei and Indo-Fijian, and the source's examples reflect that. In an Auckland room the mix will be different. The four steps travel; the examples should be rewritten for the room

More resources

  • 📄 Ramsden (2002), the founding cultural safety text (PDF)
  • 📄 Curtis et al. (2019), why cultural safety rather than cultural competency

⚠️ GAP: S.A.F.E is house content and no external reading is matched to it directly. The evidence sits on FRM-033, which is where to point anyone who asks.

  • 📄 A systematic review of inclusive leadership research — what the evidence actually supports, and what it does not
  • 📄 Inclusive leadership and taking-charge behaviour: psychological safety and thriving at work — the mechanism: it works through psychological safety
  • 📄 The double-edged sword effect of inclusive leadership — the honest counterweight. It is not costless, and this says where it backfires
  • 🎬 Inclusive leadership, and why it's so effective — the behaviours, demonstrated
  • 🎬 Empowering leadership: building an inclusive culture — Shape, Apply, Fairness and Educate under different names

Talanoa — the Pacific relational conversation

techniquemoderate
talanoapacificcultural-safetylisteningleadershipcultureconversations

What it is in one line: an open, relational conversation where people share stories, experiences and hopes in a spirit of trust, and where the relationship comes before the decision.

Origin: Talanoa is a Pacific practice, long-standing across Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, not anyone's invention. It was theorised as a research methodology by Timote M. Vaioleti (Tongan) in Talanoa Research Methodology: A Developing Position on Pacific Research, Waikato Journal of Education 12 (2006) (paper · full text PDF). Vaioleti breaks the word open: tala is to talk or tell, noa is a space without a fixed framework. It is conversation whose shape is not decided in advance.

Evidence: moderate. Two decades of academic use as a Pacific research methodology, and centuries of practice before that. It is not a controlled trial and it was never meant to be.

Best for: the decision that needs the "why" behind a protocol, not just the "what". Anything where you need people to speak in their own voice and at their own pace.

⚠️ Attribution and care. This is Pacific indigenous practice. Zeducation is well placed to teach it and it still deserves saying out loud where it comes from, who theorised it, and that it is not a meeting technique borrowed for efficiency. A talanoa run to extract information faster is not a talanoa.

On this pageThe modelThe questions that workThe metaphor, and it is the source's ownWhy it worksWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

The source's three-part flow, and it is a good one.

StepWhat you do
1Teu le vā — prepare the spaceSet a calm, relational tone first. Welcoming setting, sit in a circle, open with purpose and consent, check names and pronunciation. Agree simple norms, including how filming or sharing will work, so people know their stories are safe
2Ask open questionsGentle, curious prompts that invite story, not short answers. Keep them spacious: how, what, when
3Listen and shareFull attention, mirror back what you heard, one curious follow-up. Invite quieter voices before anyone speaks twice. Check consent in the moment. Close by gifting back what will change

How to read it: the dotted return is not decoration. Coming back having learned the names, and echoing one thing you heard, is what proves the first conversation was real.

The questions that work

Straight from the source, and they are well chosen:

  • "What would feel respectful here?"
  • "What meaning sits behind this practice?"
  • "When has this gone well for you?"
  • "Who else's voice should we include before we decide?"

The last one is the leadership question. It is the difference between consulting and weaving.

The metaphor, and it is the source's own

Think of cultural safety as a woven mat. Shared values are the strong warp threads, and people's lived stories are the weft. Talanoa is the act of weaving those threads so the mat holds.

Keep this. It is the best image in the whole SKILL UP series and it does real work: a mat with only warp threads is not a mat, and neither is one with only weft.

Why it works

Because it inverts the usual order. Most workplace process is decide, then explain, then manage the reaction. Talanoa is relationship first, then understanding, then decisions.

That order is slower at the front and much faster afterwards, because the objections arrived while they could still change something. It also surfaces the why behind a protocol, which is the thing that prevents harm around sacred spaces. Knowing that a place is off-limits stops one incident. Knowing why it is off-limits stops all of them.

For leaders, Vaioleti's framing matters: talanoa produces knowledge through the relationship, not despite it. There is no neutral extraction of information. Who you are to the person shapes what they tell you.

Worked example

A tourism operator wants to add a new site to a tour route. The fast version: check it is legally accessible, add it, brief the guides.

The talanoa version: sit with the local families first, no agenda paper, ask what the place means and when it has gone well before. It emerges that the site is fine to visit but not to photograph, and that a particular month matters. The route goes ahead with two rules nobody would have thought to write, and the guides can now explain the why to guests, which is a better tour.

The relationship produced the information. A survey would not have.

Facilitating it

  • Run it in: 45 to 90 minutes for a real one. It does not compress well, and a rushed talanoa teaches people that the invitation was not sincere
  • Prepare the space physically. A circle, no top table, phones down. The setting is step 1, not admin
  • Common mistakes:
    • Calling a normal meeting a talanoa. If the decision is already made, it is a briefing. Say so
    • Extracting rather than exchanging. Talanoa is reciprocal. The leader shares too
    • No gift back. Closing without saying what will change, by when, and how people will see it, turns it into unpaid consultation. The source is firm on this and it is right
    • Skipping consent. "Is this for us only, or can it be shared?" asked in the moment, not assumed afterwards
  • Cultural note: talanoa is Fijian, Tongan and Samoan practice with local variation, and the word carries different weight in each. In an Aotearoa setting the nearest Māori practice is hui and the two are related but not the same. Do not use the terms interchangeably, and do not present a Pacific concept to a Māori room as though it is theirs

More resources

  • 📄 Vaioleti (2006), Talanoa Research Methodology (Waikato Journal of Education)
  • 📄 Full text PDF, University of Waikato
  • 📄 Anae (2016), Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics (PDF)

⚠️ GAP: the source is written for a Fiji client, and the best-documented talanoa scholarship is Tongan (Vaioleti) and Samoan (Anae). Fijian-authored material on talanoa, and on Sitiveni Halapua's use of talanoa in Pacific dialogue and conflict resolution, would ground this page in the client's own context. Worth commissioning.

  • 📄 Tunufai — Pacific research: rethinking the talanoa methodology (PDF) — a Samoan critique. Read it before claiming to be doing talanoa
  • 📄 Fa'avae, Jones & Manu'atu — talking about talanoa, the dilemmas of a novice — honest about how easily it is done badly
  • 🎬 Talanoa methodology for transformative climate action — talanoa doing real work, outside a research seminar
  • 📄 Reflections on using talanoa to engage Pacific youth in Aotearoa — an honest account of what it takes to do properly

FRM-036Framework · Leadership

Teu le vā — caring for the relational space

techniquemoderate
teu-le-vapacificsamoancultural-safetyrelationshipsleadershipculture

What it is in one line: tend the space between people before you try to do anything in it.

Origin: Teu le vā is a Samoan concept. Vā is the relational space between people, which is understood as real and as something both parties are responsible for. Teu le vā is to tidy, value and nurture that space.

It was brought into education and research ethics in Aotearoa by Melani Anae (Samoan, University of Auckland), whose Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics sets out the idea as a research ethic (PDF), and by Airini, Anae and Mila-Schaaf (2010) in the New Zealand Ministry of Education report Teu Le Va: Relationships across research and policy in Pasifika education (report PDF). It was adopted into New Zealand education guidance in 2010.

Evidence: moderate. Well established in Pacific education and research ethics in Aotearoa, and grounded in much older practice.

Best for: the five minutes before the conversation that actually decides how the conversation goes.

⚠️ This is Samoan knowledge, used here inside a resource written for a Fiji client. That is not wrong, and Pacific concepts do travel, but it should be said rather than blurred. Name the concept's home.

On this pageThe ideaWhat it looks like in practiceWhy it matters for a leaderWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The idea

Western workplace thinking treats the space between two people as empty. Something to be crossed, efficiently, on the way to the transaction.

Teu le vā says the opposite. The space is the thing. It exists, it holds obligations in both directions, and it can be tended or neglected. If it has been neglected, nothing you say across it will land properly, however well you say it.

How to read it: the vā is not a gap between two people. It is a third thing, and both of them are responsible for its condition.

What it looks like in practice

MoveWhat it is
Arrive before the businessGreet properly. Ask about family, travel, the week. This is not small talk, it is the work
Set the room, not just the agendaCircle rather than rows, no top table, phones down. The physical space signals the relational one
Names and pronunciation firstGet them right, out loud, before anything else happens
Consent before contentSay how what is shared will be used, and who will hear it
Repair when you damage itIf you got something wrong, come back to it. An unrepaired vā stays damaged, quietly

Why it matters for a leader

Because most workplace conversations that fail did not fail on content. They failed because someone walked into an untended space and started talking business.

The practical version: the meeting begins before the meeting. A leader who has tended the vā can say a hard thing and be heard. A leader who has not will be resisted for reasons neither party will name, and will usually conclude the other person was being difficult.

It also puts a useful obligation on the leader. The vā is shared, but the person with more power has more responsibility for its condition, because they are the one who can neglect it without consequence.

Worked example

A manager needs to tell a supervisor that a shift pattern is changing.

Untended: message on Friday afternoon. It is accurate, it is clear, and it is received as a decision made about him rather than with him.

Teu le vā: she goes to him in person, asks about his mother who has been unwell, then says what is changing and why, and asks what it will cost him. Same decision. Same words about the roster. Entirely different outcome, because the space it landed in had been tended.

The extra time was four minutes.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes, as step 1 of Talanoa. It rarely stands alone in a session and it is the step people skip
  • The best question to ask a room: "think of a time someone gave you difficult news and it landed well. What had happened before they said it?" The answers are all teu le vā
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating it as a warm-up. A warm-up is something you do to get to the real thing. This is the real thing
    • Performing it. Asking about someone's family while visibly waiting to get to the point damages the vā rather than tending it
    • Using the term without the practice. Naming a Samoan concept in a slide and then running a Western meeting is the protocol theatre that FRM-033 warns about
  • Cultural note: the concept has close relatives across the Pacific, including Tongan vā and vahā'a. The Māori equivalent territory is whanaungatanga, which is related but is its own thing with its own literature. Do not treat the words as translations of each other

More resources

  • 📄 Anae, Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics (PDF)
  • 📄 Airini, Anae & Mila-Schaaf (2010), Teu Le Va, NZ Ministry of Education report (PDF)
  • 📄 Vaioleti (2006), Talanoa Research Methodology

  • 📄 Anae — Teu le va: Samoan relational ethics (journal listing) — the published version in Knowledge Cultures

  • 🎬 Unlocking deeper relationships — the power of whanaungatanga (Māori and Pacific) — short, and it makes the Māori-Pacific link explicit

The Three Types of Workplace Conflict

modelstrong
conflictteamsconflict-resolutiondiagnosisleadershipcommunication

What it is in one line: conflict comes in three kinds, and only one of them is reliably bad for a team.

Origin: Karen A. Jehn, in two papers that founded the field: A Multimethod Examination of the Benefits and Detriments of Intragroup Conflict, Administrative Science Quarterly 40, 256-282 (1995) (full paper PDF.pdf)), and A Qualitative Analysis of Conflict Types and Dimensions in Organizational Groups, Administrative Science Quarterly 42, 530-557 (1997), which added process conflict to the original two. Evidence: strong. Thirty years of replication and one of the most used typologies in organisational research. Best for: the moment a team says "we're not getting on" and cannot say what is actually wrong.

⚠️ The Zeducation source teaches these three types and does not name Jehn (SRC-007). Credit her. It is a real research finding, not a training-industry model, and saying so makes the teaching stronger.

On this pageThe modelWhy it mattersWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

TypeWhat it is aboutThe root of itExample
RelationshipThe peopleDifferences of opinion, experience, perspective, personality or beliefs. Carries negative emotion and personal dislikeSomeone said something in a meeting that offended you, you argued, and now you do not speak
TaskThe workDifferent ideas and views about the content of the decision, and sometimes about what the task even isTwo people disagree about how a project should be done and what the goal should be
ProcessThe how and the whoDisagreement over division of labour, responsibility, roles and who controls whatSomeone is seen as favoured for a role and is freeriding while the rest of the team carries it

How to read it: the dotted arrows are the danger. Task and process conflict are survivable on their own. They become destructive when they turn into relationship conflict, and process conflict does this most easily, because arguing about who does what is one step from arguing about who someone is.

Why it matters

Because it stops a team treating all conflict as one bad thing to be avoided.

Task conflict is not the enemy. Jehn's finding was that disagreement about the work can improve decisions, as long as it stays about the work. A team with no task conflict is usually a team where nobody is saying what they think.

Relationship conflict is the destructive one. It carries personal dislike and negative emotion, which is not only damaging but distracting: people spend their attention managing the relationship instead of doing the job.

Process conflict is the sneaky one. It looks practical, about rosters and roles and who does the tidy-up, and it "shows attributes of relationship conflict too", because who gets which role is rarely felt as a neutral question.

The practical use is diagnostic. Name the type before you pick a response. A task conflict needs a decision. A process conflict needs clarity about roles. A relationship conflict needs a conversation about how people are treating each other, and treating it as a task problem will not touch it.

Worked example

Two staff argue about how the accident forms are filled in. It looks like task conflict, so the supervisor writes a clearer procedure.

It comes back a fortnight later, worse.

Asked properly, it turns out one of them has felt talked down to by the other since a public correction six months ago. The forms were never the problem. That is relationship conflict wearing a task conflict's clothes, and no procedure will fix it.

The diagnostic question: if the work question were settled tomorrow, would these two be fine? If the answer is no, you are not dealing with a task conflict.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run ACT-070 Name That Conflict
  • Use learners' own examples. The source's activity does this, asking for two to four real workplace scenarios to sort. It works far better than invented ones
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating the three as mutually exclusive. They overlap constantly. The question is which one is doing most of the work
    • Concluding task conflict is always good. Jehn's later work and subsequent meta-analyses are more mixed than the 1995 paper alone suggests. Teach it as "not automatically bad", not as "good"
    • Diagnosing someone else's conflict from the outside. The type usually only becomes clear once somebody has asked
  • Cultural note: in settings where open disagreement with someone senior is a respect issue, task conflict may never surface as disagreement at all. It surfaces as silence, or as a process complaint that is safer to raise. Watch for that rather than concluding there is no conflict

More resources

  • 📄 Jehn (1995), A Multimethod Examination of the Benefits and Detriments of Intragroup Conflict (PDF).pdf)
  • 📄 Greer, Jehn & Mannix (2008), Conflict Transformation
  • 📄 UC San Diego — Team Conflict definitions
  • 📄 Jehn, Greer, Levine & Szulanski — the effects of conflict types, dimensions and emergent states (PDF) — the three types, tested
  • 📄 Jehn & Mannix — The dynamic nature of conflict, a longitudinal study (PDF) — the finding worth teaching: process conflict early poisons everything after it
  • 📄 Task conflict, information processing and decision-making — why task conflict stops helping the moment relationship conflict turns up
  • 📄 How team-level and individual-level conflict influences team commitment — the three types tested at two levels at once
  • 📄 Personality, relationship conflict, and teamwork-related mental models — why relationship conflict is the one that does the damage

Powerful Listening — Content, Values, Feelings

techniquepractitioner
listeningconflictconflict-resolutionempathyhouse-contentcommunication

What it is in one line: in a conflict, listen for three things at once, and the two most people miss are the ones that actually resolve it.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007). Evidence: practitioner. The "listen for feelings" step is close to reflective listening in the Carl Rogers lineage, already in the library as FRM-012. Best for: the person who comes to you angry, where the thing they are angry about is not the thing that is wrong.

On this pageThe modelThe iceberg, and it is the source's own imageThe three things that stop content listeningWhy the values layer matters mostWorked example — the house case studyFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

LayerWhat you are listening forThe question in your head
1ContentFacts and information. What actually happened"What are the facts here?"
2ValuesThe beliefs driving the reaction. Why this one matters so much to them"What do they care about that is being stepped on?"
3FeelingsWhat it did to them"How is this landing on them?"

How to read it: content is above the water. Values and feelings are underneath, and they are where the conflict actually lives.

The iceberg, and it is the source's own image

Sometimes people's concerns are like an iceberg. Only a small portion is visible above the surface. Actively listening in times of conflict helps dig a little deeper to the root cause, and builds trust between you and the person you are listening to.

Keep this. It is the clearest thing on the page and it explains why solving the stated problem often does not end the conflict.

The three things that stop content listening

The source is good on this, and they are worth teaching as named traps.

TrapWhat it sounds like inside your head
We make assumptions"I know what they're going to say, and I know what's best for them"
We judgeYou stop listening because you are busy assembling why they are wrong
We tune outHaving assumed and judged, tuning out is the natural next step

The fix, also from the source: pay attention · stay focused on the conversation at hand · put your assumptions aside.

Why the values layer matters most

This is the part of the framework that earns its place, and it is the least common in listening training.

One of the things that often gets overlooked when you're listening is: what values does this person hold that are driving the conflict? When you listen for those, you can often help them find solutions that align with those values.

A person who is furious about a lifting job is often not angry about the boxes. They are angry because they value safety, or fairness, or being treated as though their body matters. A solution that addresses boxes and ignores safety will not land. A solution built on the value will.

Worked example — the house case study

Akanisi is asked to lift heavy boxes into a truck just before lunch, for the second time this week. She comes to you angry: "This company is such a joke! They don't care about our safety... now my back is stuffed, but one of those boxes could have easily fallen over and someone could have been hurt!"

LayerWhat you hear
ContentStaff required to lift boxes. Second time this week. No trolley or forklift. Boxes were heavy
ValuesSafety, accountability, leadership, organisation
FeelingsAngry, betrayed, frustrated, helpless, hurt

The content alone gets you a conversation about trolleys. The values tell you this is about whether anyone is taking responsibility for people's safety, which is a much bigger and more solvable conversation.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run the Akanisi case study (ACT-071) and the observed listening task (ACT-072)
  • Do the layers in order and separately. Learners collapse values and feelings together within about a minute. Make them fill in one column at a time
  • Common mistakes:
    • Naming feelings for the other person and calling it listening. "You must be furious" is a guess. "How did that land on you?" is listening
    • Treating values as corporate values. These are the person's own. Safety, fairness, being respected, providing for family
    • Rushing to the solution once you have the content. That is the failure the framework exists to prevent
  • Cultural note: "most people have been taught not to share their feelings at work", as the source says, and that is more true in some settings than others. Do not read reluctance as absence. The values layer is often a safer route in than the feelings layer, and it gets to the same place

More resources

  • 📄 FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting — the Rogers lineage behind the feelings layer, already in the library

⚠️ GAP: this is house content with no external reading matched to it. The nearest evidenced neighbours are active listening and reflective listening. Worth pairing with published work on interest-based negotiation, where "listen for the interest behind the position" is the same move under a different name.

  • 📄 Animas Coaching — the power of deep listening — the story beneath the story
  • 📄 Simply.Coach — the three levels of listening — how the levels map onto content, values and feelings
  • 📄 Bailey Balfour — active listening and presence in coaching — presence is the part technique cannot fake
  • 📄 Transformation Academy — mastering active listening in coaching — listening for the values a person keeps returning to
  • 🎬 Active listening — the three levels of listening in coaching — content, then feelings, then the whole field

The Compassionate Response

techniquepractitioner
conflictempathycompassionconflict-resolutionhouse-contentcommunicationde-escalation

What it is in one line: connect what they said to what they are feeling, out loud, before you try to fix anything.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007). Evidence: practitioner. Best for: the twenty seconds after someone has told you something that matters to them, which is the moment most conflicts are either defused or doubled.

On this pageThe ideaThe four responsesWhy it worksWhat it does for a workplaceWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The idea

Compassion literally means "to suffer together". It is the feeling that arises when you are confronted with another's suffering and feel motivated to relieve it.

Being compassionate in your response is about connecting content to feelings. When you are listening, paying attention to what they are saying and how that relates to what they are feeling makes a real difference in a conflict.

And the useful permission the source gives: while it is not about you, reflecting on a similar experience, or a time when you felt the same way, can lead you to a compassionate response. You do not have to manufacture empathy from nothing. You have to find the nearest thing you have felt.

The four responses

Four sentences from the source, and they cover most situations.

#What you sayWhen to use it
1"That sounds difficult."Almost always. The safest opener in the set, and the one people underrate
2"I want to hear more about how that made you feel."When you have the facts and not the feelings
3"I'm sorry if I have offended you in any way."When you might be part of it
4"Your issue reminds me of a time when I had a similar situation…"When you genuinely have one, and briefly

How to read it: the dotted branch is what usually happens. A person who does not feel heard does not stop, they escalate, because escalating is the only tool left.

⚠️ Response 4 is the risky one. Used briefly it builds connection. Used at length it takes the conversation off them and puts it on you, which is the opposite of compassion. One or two sentences, then hand it straight back: "…but tell me more about yours."

Why it works

Because unheard feelings do not go away, they get louder. The instinct in a conflict is to move straight to the solution, and that instinct reads as dismissal to the person in front of you, however good the solution is.

Naming the feeling costs one sentence and it changes what the other person is doing. They stop building the case for why this matters and start describing what is actually wrong.

What it does for a workplace

The source lists four byproducts of workplace compassion:

  • Improved interpersonal relationships
  • More loyalty and commitment to work
  • Enhanced customer satisfaction
  • A highly functioning work environment

⚠️ These are presented without a source. They are plausible and they are unevidenced here. Treat them as a claim to be tested rather than a finding, or link them to psychological safety, which covers similar ground with actual research behind it.

Worked example

Owairua comes to you angry about overtime: "I'm sick and tired of staying extra time after work! Our team is getting lazier and lazier... I feel like I'm carrying the team."

Without it: "Let's look at the roster." Accurate, efficient, and he leaves feeling like a scheduling problem.

With it: "That sounds difficult. It sounds like you feel you're carrying it on your own and nobody's noticed. Is that right?" Then the roster conversation, which now has a chance of landing, because the thing he actually came to say has been said back to him.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. Then run ACT-074 Applying A Compassionate Response
  • Practise the sentences out loud. They feel unnatural the first time and available the fourth
  • Common mistakes:
    • "At least…" Any sentence starting with "at least" is the opposite of this framework
    • Response 4 as a hijack. Watch for the learner whose similar situation takes four minutes
    • Compassion as agreement. You can say "that sounds difficult" to someone whose complaint you think is wrong. It is not a concession, it is an acknowledgement
    • Doing it once and moving on. In a real conflict you will do it three or four times before the person is ready for a solution
  • Cultural note: the "sorry if I offended you" construction is conditional and can read as a non-apology in some settings. If you actually got something wrong, say so plainly instead

More resources

  • 📄 FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting — the technique underneath, from the Carl Rogers lineage
  • 📄 Edmondson (1999), psychological safety — the evidenced version of what compassion buys a workplace

⚠️ GAP: house content, no external reading matched directly, and the four workplace byproducts are unevidenced. Worth finding real research on compassion at work.

  • 📄 Dutton, Workman & Hardin — Compassion at Work (PDF) — the review paper. Notice, feel, act — and the act is what makes it compassion rather than sympathy
  • 📄 Lilius et al. — the contours and consequences of compassion at work (PDF) — what it actually looks like on a real work floor
  • 📄 CIPD — the role of compassion in the workplace — the HR profession's own position
  • 📄 MindTools — empathy at work — the practical version: attention, assumptions set aside, acknowledgement, then action
  • 📄 ICMA — supporting a colleague in distress — what to say, and where the line is
  • 🎬 Brené Brown on empathy (RSA Short) — three minutes, animated, and it does more than an hour of explanation. Empathy versus sympathy
  • 🎬 Brené Brown — empathy with boundaries — the counterweight, and the reason compassion does not have to cost you everything

Moving to Resolution — gather, then test

modelpractitioner
conflictconflict-resolutionproblem-solvinghouse-contentleadershipcommunication

What it is in one line: collect every idea without judging any of them, then test each one with curiosity rather than opinion.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007). Evidence: practitioner. Best for: the point where the heat has come out of a conflict and somebody needs to decide what happens now.

The precondition matters. The source is clear that this comes after the listening. Run it too early and you are solving a problem you have not understood, in front of someone who does not yet feel heard.

On this pageThe modelWhy the two halves must stay separateWorked example — the house case studyFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

1. Ask

"I'd like to hear your thoughts on how you would like this to be resolved."

An open question, asked of the person in the conflict rather than answered for them. It is the step that moves someone from complaining to problem-solving, and it takes one sentence.

2. Listen and list

List all the solutions, even ones that seem silly or impossible to you. The source is firm on this and it is the discipline people break first.

Although not every idea will end up as a solution, to use brainstorming effectively all things must be considered initially. Encouraging creativity generates a wide variety of options. This prevents everyone from being limited by the dynamics that created the problem in the first place.

That last line is the reason for the rule. The thinking that produced the conflict will produce the same three solutions unless you deliberately widen it.

3. Test with curiosity

Put every suggestion through the same five questions. The key here is being curious, not persuasive.

#Question
1How would this work?
2What will this do for you if you decide to go with this?
3Is it actually possible to do?
4What are the strengths?
5What might be the limitations?

The point of testing is to get to know each idea's strengths and its limitations, then see which aligns best with the outcome you know is needed.

Why the two halves must stay separate

Because judging while gathering kills the gathering. The moment one idea is criticised, people stop offering the unusual ones, and the unusual ones are the reason you widened the list.

Gather with no evaluation. Then evaluate with no new ideas. Two modes, one at a time.

Worked example — the house case study

Owairua is doing constant overtime and feels he is carrying the team. Solutions listed, without filtering:

  • Talk to team members about coming back late from breaks
  • Ask Owairua if he needs to take time off
  • Review roles and responsibilities, and delegate some of his tasks
  • Commit Owairua to leaving on time
  • Ask more questions to check the real issue has been found
  • Ask Owairua what solution he would choose

Note the last two. Two of the six are about understanding the problem better, and in a real case they are often the right first move. A brainstorm that only produces actions has usually skipped a step.

Then test. "Commit Owairua to leaving on time" fails question 3 fast, because it treats the symptom and leaves the work undone. "Review roles and delegate" survives all five.

Facilitating it

  • Run it in: 20 minutes. Five minutes gathering, the rest testing
  • Time-box the gathering and say nothing during it. The source's own activity sets a five minute timer, and the silence from the facilitator is what makes it work
  • Common mistakes:
    • Evaluating during the gather. Even a face does it. Write, do not react
    • Testing with opinions instead of questions. "That won't work" ends it. "What might the limitations be?" gets the same information from the person who suggested it, which they can hear
    • Skipping straight here from the complaint. The most common failure, and the reason resolutions do not stick
    • The leader supplying the solutions. If you have the answer already, this is a briefing. Say so
  • Cultural note: in many settings people will not offer an idea that contradicts a senior person's. Gathering in writing first, or in pairs before the group, gets you the list you actually wanted

More resources

⚠️ GAP: house content with no external reading matched. The nearest evidenced neighbours are interest-based negotiation and standard divergent-then-convergent problem-solving practice. Worth grounding properly, since the two-modes rule is well supported elsewhere.

  • 📄 SPARC / Anthem EAP — the four steps of interest-based problem-solving — the shortest usable version
  • 📄 Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service — steps in interest-based negotiation (PDF) — worksheets you can run a real session from
  • 📄 Ten steps for an interest-based resolution — the longer form, including the follow-up most processes skip
  • 📄 Beyond Intractability — interests, rights, power and needs frames — why gathering before testing works: interests are negotiable, positions are not
  • 📄 Beyond Intractability — summary of Moore, The Mediation Process — the standard text, summarised
  • 🎬 Five steps to manage conflict between team members — gather, then test, under other names
  • 🎬 Thirteen tools for resolving conflict in the workplace — Dr Jeremy Pollack — a conflict psychologist's own toolkit

De-escalation — six steps

techniquepractitioner
de-escalationconflictconflict-resolutionsafetyhouse-contentcommunicationlistening

What it is in one line: calm a tense situation before it becomes a serious conflict.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the extra resources of the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007). Evidence: practitioner. The steps line up with de-escalation practice taught across health, security and frontline service, and the source cites none of it. Best for: the moment it is going wrong in front of you, with a colleague, a customer or a guest.

De-escalation is the process of calming a tense situation before it becomes a serious conflict. It involves staying calm, listening, and working together to solve a problem peacefully.

Why bother: it reduces workplace tension, improves communication, prevents harm or misunderstanding, and builds a respectful work environment.

On this pageThe six stepsWhy the order mattersWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The six steps

StepActionWhat it sounds or looks like
1Stay calmTake a deep breath. Speak gently
2Use open body languageRelax your posture. Keep arms uncrossed
3Listen activelyLet them speak. Show you are listening with nods
4Show empathy"I understand you're upset."
5Work on a solution together"What would help us move forward?"
6Take a break if needed"Let's pause and talk again shortly."

How to read it: steps 1 to 5 are a sequence. Step 6 is an exit available at any point, and using it early is a skill rather than a failure.

Why the order matters

Steps 1 and 2 are yours, and they come first for a reason. You cannot de-escalate anyone while your own heart rate is climbing. Every later step is delivered through your body and your voice, and those are already broadcasting before you say anything.

Steps 3 and 4 are the load-bearing ones. Most attempts at de-escalation jump from step 2 to step 5 and offer a solution, which reads as "stop being upset so we can move on" and reliably raises the temperature.

Step 6 is the one nobody uses. Taking a break feels like losing. It is the single most useful move when someone is past the point of being able to hear anything, and the phrasing matters: "let's pause and talk again shortly" names a return. "Let's leave it" does not, and it lands as abandonment.

Worked example

A guest is angry at reception about a room that was not ready.

Escalating: the staff member explains the booking system, correctly, at speed, while the guest is still talking. The guest gets louder, because being explained at while upset is its own insult.

De-escalating: she stops, unfolds her arms, lets him finish, and says "I understand you're upset, you've travelled all day and the room isn't ready." Then, only then: "What would help most right now?" He asks to leave his bags and get a coffee. Ninety seconds, no manager needed.

Nothing about the room changed. The order of the sentences did.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. The six steps are easy to teach and hard to do under adrenaline, so the time goes into rehearsal
  • Rehearse until it is automatic. This is the framework in the library that most needs to be available without thinking, because it is used in the worst thirty seconds of someone's shift
  • Common mistakes:
    • Skipping to step 5. The most common failure by a distance
    • "Calm down." Never de-escalated anything in recorded history
    • Treating step 6 as defeat. Teach it as a move, and give people the exact sentence
    • Practising it only for customers. Most of the conflicts people actually face are with colleagues, and the steps are identical
  • Safety note, and say it plainly: de-escalation is not a substitute for leaving. If someone is threatening, if there is any risk of harm, the move is to get out and get help, not to work through six steps. Any workplace teaching this should say where its own line is and what the escalation path is
  • Cultural note: step 2 travels less well than it looks. Sustained eye contact, physical closeness and directness read differently across cultures, and the version taught in most de-escalation training assumes a Western reading. Ask the room what calm looks like where they are from

More resources

⚠️ GAP: the source gives the six steps with no citation and no video that survives extraction. It links this clip, which is listed as its de-escalation video and has not been opened or verified from this session. De-escalation is a well developed field in health and frontline safety, and grounding this page properly is worth doing before it is taught as fact.

⚠️ NZ-specific gap: WorkSafe guidance on managing customer aggression, and health sector de-escalation training, would put this on a local footing.

  • 📄 HSI — conflict de-escalation techniques — a safety-training version, aimed at frontline staff
  • 📄 De-escalation examples: nine scenarios — worked scenarios, good as roleplay prompts

Why Assertiveness Feels Hard — the eight barriers

modelpractitioner
assertivenessbarrierspeople-pleasingself-esteemculturewellbeingcommunication

What it is in one line: the reasons a person who knows exactly what to say still does not say it.

Origin: adapted by Zeducation from SRC-008, an article on brainmanager.io. Two of the source's ten categories were deliberately dropped and one was rewritten. See "What was left out" below. Evidence: practitioner. The categories are recognisable and useful; they are not a validated taxonomy and should not be presented as one. Best for: the second half of any assertiveness session, and the reason the first half did not work.

On this pageWhy this page existsThe eight barriersThe two barriers that are not skill problemsWhat was left out, and why⚠️ Scope, and when to stopFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

Why this page exists

Everything else the library teaches about assertiveness is a skill: the four styles, "I" statements, DESC, the Positive No. TOP-COM-001 says so explicitly: "it is a skill, which means it can be learned."

That is true and it is only half the picture. Every facilitator has met the learner who can recite DESC perfectly, roleplay it well, and then not say a word to their supervisor on Monday. Their problem is not the script.

This framework names what is in the way. It is diagnostic, not therapeutic.

The eight barriers

BarrierWhat it sounds like from the insideThe first move
Shyness"If I speak, everyone looks at me"Smaller rooms first. This is a graded exposure problem, not a courage problem
People-pleasing"If I say no, they will think less of me"Name the cost. It usually comes from genuine kindness, and it leaves people drained and resentful
Low self-esteem"My needs are less important than theirs"One small assertion at a time. Each one is evidence against the belief
Fear of the reaction"It will turn into a fight"FRM-041 De-escalation and TOP-COM-002. The fear is usually of the twenty seconds afterwards
Passive-aggressive habit"I'll just make it obvious I'm annoyed"The frustration is already being expressed, just sideways. Swap the channel, not the feeling
Culture and upbringing"We were raised not to answer back"Not a deficit. See the note below
Power and safety"It is genuinely not safe for me to say this here"Sometimes correct. See the note below
Energy and health"I do not have it in me today"Smallest possible step. "I can't right now" is a complete sentence

How to read it: four families. Me and Them respond to practice. Here may not be a personal problem at all. Today is temporary and needs a smaller ask, not a bigger push.

The two barriers that are not skill problems

These are the ones a facilitator most often gets wrong, and both matter enormously in Zeducation's rooms.

Culture and upbringing

The source puts this well and it is worth keeping close to its words: some people grew up in families where children were "seen, not heard", or in cultures where politeness and harmony mattered more than individual opinions. Those lessons stay.

Do not teach this as a deficit to be corrected. A learner whose culture prizes deference to elders is not failing at assertiveness. The framing that works:

Respecting your roots does not mean silencing yourself. Assertiveness does not erase where you come from, it helps you find your voice within it.

In practice that often means the assertive move looks different: one to one rather than in the meeting, through a trusted third person, or at a different time. That is a legitimate answer, not a workaround. See FRM-033 Cultural Safety for why the Western meeting-room version is not neutral.

Power and safety

Sometimes the reason someone is not speaking up is that they are right. A person on an insecure visa, a casual contract, or with a manager who has punished the last three people who raised something is making an accurate calculation, not a psychological error.

Teaching assertiveness to someone in that position, without acknowledging it, tells them their judgment is a personality flaw. Say it out loud in the room: some workplaces are not safe to be assertive in, and if that is yours, the skill is knowing that and knowing where else to take it.

⚠️ This barrier is not in the source. It was added because the library serves migrant, Pacific and low-wage learners for whom it is frequently the actual answer.

What was left out, and why

Two of the source's ten categories were deliberately not carried into the library.

Left outWhy
Personality type (MBTI)The source frames barriers in Myers-Briggs terms: "Feelers may avoid conflict", "Perceivers may struggle to commit". MBTI has well documented psychometric problems, particularly poor test-retest reliability and weak predictive validity (Pittenger and others · overview of the criticisms). It is also a commercial conflict of interest: the publisher sells MBTI-style tests, and the article closes by linking to them
Attachment stylesReal research territory, and clinical. Attaching an attachment style to a learner in a workshop is diagnosis, and a facilitator is not qualified to do it

Clinical conditions were also rewritten rather than dropped. The source lists depression, social anxiety and Highly Sensitive Person as barrier categories. Those are real, and naming them in a workshop invites a facilitator to identify them in a learner, which is out of scope and can do harm. They are folded into "energy and health" and "shyness", with the referral note below.

⚠️ Scope, and when to stop

A facilitator is not a clinician. This framework names what is in the way so a learner can choose a next step. It does not diagnose, and it must not be used to.

If someone's difficulty is clearly beyond a communication skill, the assertive move is the source's own ninth tip: get support. Know your options before you run the session.

  • Workplace EAP, if the employer has one
  • Their GP
  • 1737 — free national helpline, call or text, any time

The source is right that assertiveness training is used clinically, in Dialectical Behavior Therapy among others. That is a reason to refer, not a reason to attempt it.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, after the skill content rather than before it. The barriers only make sense once someone has tried the skill and noticed the gap
  • Run ACT-080 What's Stopping Me? straight after
  • Common mistakes:
    • Diagnosing the room. These are self-identified, always. Never assign someone a barrier
    • Treating culture as the problem. It is context, not a defect
    • Ignoring power. The most damaging version of this session tells a person in a genuinely unsafe job that they need more confidence
    • Going clinical. If a learner discloses depression or anxiety, that is a referral conversation, not a workshop topic
  • The best single question: "which of these is yours, most of the time?" Asked privately, on paper, never round the room

More resources

  • 📄 APA Dictionary — assertiveness — the definition the source cites, and a good authoritative anchor
  • 📄 MBTI reliability and validity, a critical review (PDF)
  • 📄 1737 — NZ national helpline

⚠️ GAP: no research grounds this eight-category set. It is a teaching aid assembled from a content-marketing article and edited for safety. If it earns a place in delivery, it deserves better foundations, particularly on people-pleasing and self-esteem where real literature exists.

DEAR MAN — the assertiveness script from DBT

modelmoderate
assertivenesssaying-nodbtnegotiationcommunicationboundariesscript

What it is in one line: a seven-part script for asking for something or saying no, where the first four letters are what you say and the last three are how you hold yourself while saying it.

Origin: Marsha M. Linehan, as part of the interpersonal effectiveness module of Dialectical Behavior Therapy. DBT was developed for borderline personality disorder and its skills modules are now taught far beyond that setting (Therapist Aid worksheet · Kaiser Permanente skills handout, PDF). Evidence: moderate. DBT as a whole has strong clinical evidence; DEAR MAN as an isolated skill has much less. One controlled study found the DEAR components produced significantly greater compliance than a control condition (Western Michigan University dissertation). Best for: a prepared ask where the relationship also has to survive it.

Why it is in this library: SRC-008 points out that assertiveness training is commonly delivered as part of DBT, and stops there. This is what it is actually pointing at, and it is the best evidenced assertiveness script available.

On this pageThe modelHow it compares to DESC, which the library already teachesWorked exampleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

DEAR is what you say. MAN is how you say it.

LetterStands forWhat you do
DDescribeThe factsState the situation. Only what a camera would have seen
EExpressHow you feel about it"I feel…". Do not assume they already know
AAssertThe askSay clearly what you want, or say no clearly. This is the step people skip
RReinforceWhy it is worth it for themWhat the other person gets, or what improves, if they agree
MMindfulStay on the pointDo not get pulled onto a side argument. Come back to the ask
AAppear confidentVoice and bodySteady tone, steady posture. Even if you do not feel it
NNegotiateBe willing to give to getOffer alternatives. Ask "what would work for you?"

How to read it: DEAR is the sentence. MAN is what keeps it intact when the other person pushes back, which is the part most scripts leave out.

How it compares to DESC, which the library already teaches

They are close relatives and the library now has both. Use this to choose.

DESCDEAR MAN
OriginAssertiveness training tradition, taught in the Zeducation workbookLinehan, DBT
ShapeDescribe · Express · Specify · ConsequencesDescribe · Express · Assert · Reinforce + Mindful · Appear confident · Negotiate
Ends onWhat happens if nothing changesWhat the other person gains, then a negotiation
ToneFirmer. Good for a standard being missedWarmer. Good where you need the relationship intact
Covers pushback?NoYes, that is what MAN is
Best forRaising an issue, holding a lineAsking for something, saying no, negotiating

➜ The practical rule: DESC to raise a problem. DEAR MAN to ask for something. And DEAR MAN's MAN half works as an add-on to DESC, which is the cheapest upgrade available to TOP-COM-001.

Worked example

A support worker wants to stop being rostered on Sundays, because of church.

Describe: "I've been on the Sunday roster four of the last six weeks." Express: "I feel stretched, and Sunday mornings are when my family are all together." Assert: "I'd like to come off Sundays from next month." Reinforce: "I'm happy to take more Saturdays, which I know is the harder shift to fill." Mindful: when the manager says "everyone has to take a turn", she does not defend herself. She says: "I understand. I'd still like to come off Sundays, and I'll take the Saturdays." Appear confident: steady voice, not apologising for asking. Negotiate: "If Sundays are impossible, could we do one a month instead of three?"

Note that the Reinforce step is what makes it work. She is not asking for a favour, she is proposing a swap.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Seven letters is a lot, so teach DEAR first, run it, then add MAN
  • The letter to spend time on is A for Assert. Learners describe and express fluently and then never actually say what they want. Make them underline the ask in their own script
  • Common mistakes:
    • No Reinforce. Without it the ask is a request. With it, it is an offer
    • Reinforce as a threat. "It'll be better for you because otherwise I'll resign" is Consequences, not Reinforce. That is DESC's job and it is a different conversation
    • Negotiate too early. Offering the compromise before the ask lands means you negotiate against yourself
    • "Appear confident" heard as "fake it". It means voice and posture, not pretending to feel something
  • ⚠️ Cultural note, and it matters here: "Appear confident" in the standard DBT teaching includes eye contact and an upright stance. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, sustained eye contact with someone senior reads as disrespect. Teach it as steady, and let learners choose the form. Same caution as FRM-010 SOLER
  • ⚠️ Say where it comes from, carefully. DEAR MAN is a therapy skill taught outside therapy. That is legitimate and common, and it is worth naming so nobody presents a workshop as treatment. See the scope note on FRM-042

The Blake-Mouton Managerial Grid

modelmoderate
leadershipstylesteamsresultspeoplemanagementself-assessment

What it is in one line: two dials, one for how much you care about the people and one for how much you care about the result, and where you set them is your leadership style.

Origin: Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton, The Managerial Grid: The Key to Leadership Excellence (Gulf Publishing, Houston, 1964). They watched managers at work, found that most of what they did fell into two buckets, and drew the grid (overview · citation record). It was built directly on top of McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y. Evidence: moderate. Sixty years of use in management training, a shortage of hard outcome studies. It is a thinking tool, not a measuring instrument. Treat the position a learner picks as a conversation starter, not a score. Best for: the supervisor who is either everyone's mate or nobody's, and cannot see a third option.

On this pageThe modelWorked example, an Auckland warehouseFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

Two questions, asked separately:

  1. How much do I care about the people?
  2. How much do I care about getting the result?

Blake and Mouton's point is that these are not opposite ends of one dial. You can be high on both. Most people assume you have to trade one for the other, and that assumption is the whole problem the grid exists to break.

How to read it: the middle of this grid is not a safe place. "Middle of the road" gets you average results and people who are not especially bothered either way.

StylePeopleResultsWhat it looks like on the floor
ImpoverishedLowLowHides in the office. Signs things. Nobody knows what they want
Produce or perishLowHighHits the numbers, burns through staff. Rosters are always short
Middle of the roadMediumMediumNever has a disaster, never has a good month either
Country clubHighLowLovely to work for. The job does not get done and everyone else has to cover
TeamHighHighExpects a lot, backs you all the way. Hard to work for and people stay for years

Worked example, an Auckland warehouse

Same shift, same problem: the pick rate is down and two people are off.

StyleWhat the supervisor says
ImpoverishedNothing. Puts the roster up and goes to lunch
Produce or perish"I don't care who's off. The truck leaves at four."
Middle of the road"Do what you can, we'll probably be right."
Country club"Don't stress about it team, have a break, we'll sort it tomorrow."
Team"The truck has to leave at four and there's two of us short. What's the fastest way to do this, and who needs a hand?"

➜ The Team answer is the only one that says both things out loud. That is the whole framework in one sentence.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Draw the axes on a whiteboard, describe the four corners, let the room name the middle
  • Run ACT-082 The Grid Self-Plot after it
  • The best question: "which corner does your current supervisor sit in, and which corner do you sit in?" The gap between those two answers is usually where the session gets interesting
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating "team" as a personality. It is a choice made per situation, not a type of person
    • Hearing "country club" as an insult. For a lot of learners, being the kind supervisor is the only model of good leadership they have seen. The point is that kindness without delivery eventually costs the team, because someone else picks up the work
    • Skipping the middle. Middle of the road is the most common real position and the one people least want to claim
  • ⚠️ Do not turn this into a test. Blake and Mouton sold a whole development programme off the back of the grid. The library uses the picture and leaves the instrument alone. Same caution as FRM-054 Personality Tests At Work

  • 🎬 Blake Mouton managerial grid explained — the two axes and the five positions, in a few minutes

McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y

modelpractitioner
leadershipassumptionsmotivationtrustmanagementmindset

What it is in one line: what you privately believe about whether people want to work decides how you manage them, and they can tell.

Origin: Douglas McGregor, The Human Side of Enterprise (McGraw-Hill, 1960). McGregor was an MIT management professor. He argued that every manager is running on an unexamined theory of human nature, and that most of them are running the wrong one (overview). Evidence: practitioner. It is a proposition about assumptions, not a tested model, and it has never really been measurable. Its influence is enormous anyway: the Blake-Mouton Grid was built on it and most modern engagement thinking descends from it. Best for: the leader who says "I've tried trusting them and it doesn't work" without noticing they have never actually tried.

On this pageThe modelWhy this one matters more than it looksWorked example, a South Auckland kitchenFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

Theory XTheory Y
What you believePeople dislike work and avoid itWork is as natural as rest or play
So they needTo be pushed, watched, and threatenedConditions where they can commit
ResponsibilityPeople avoid it and want to be toldPeople seek it out when the work means something
MotivationMoney and fear of consequencesAchievement, growth, being trusted
So you manage byRules, supervision, checkingGoals, autonomy, asking

How to read it: both loops prove themselves. That is the point. The belief creates the evidence for the belief.

Why this one matters more than it looks

Most leadership models tell you what to do. This one tells you what you are already assuming, and the assumption arrives before the technique does.

A supervisor who believes their team are lazy will run a beautiful DESC conversation and it will still land as an accusation, because the belief leaks through tone, through what gets checked, through who gets asked. Learners read the belief long before they parse the words.

Worked example, a South Auckland kitchen

Two chefs, same problem: prep is running late most mornings.

The Theory X chef puts up a checklist, stands over the section, and starts logging times. Prep gets faster for eight days. Then two people stop flagging when they run out of stock, because flagging gets you a conversation about your times.

The Theory Y chef asks the section what is making mornings hard. Turns out the delivery is landing forty minutes later than it used to and nobody thought it was their place to say. They move the prep order. Prep is faster in a week and stays faster.

➜ The X chef is not a bad person. They are solving the problem they believe they have.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Two columns on a whiteboard, no jargon
  • Run ACT-083 What Do You Actually Believe About People? straight after
  • The best question: "think of the best boss you ever had. Which one were they running? Now the worst." Learners get there faster from experience than from the table
  • Common mistakes:
    • Teaching X as evil and Y as good. McGregor did lean Y, and a new team on a dangerous site genuinely needs direction. The failure is not choosing X, it is choosing X permanently and never checking
    • Confusing Theory Y with no standards. Y is not "let them do what they like". A Theory Y leader can be extremely demanding. See the Team corner of FRM-044
    • Letting people diagnose their manager and stop there. The useful half of this session is always "and which one am I running?"
  • ⚠️ Watch for the honest answer. Some learners supervise people they genuinely do not trust, sometimes for good reasons. Do not push them to declare Theory Y in the room. The question is what they would need to see to change their mind

More resources

  • 📄 Theory X and Theory Y, overview
  • 📖 McGregor, D. (1960). The Human Side of Enterprise. New York: McGraw-Hill. Still in print, and the annotated 2006 edition is the one to buy
  • 📄 Blake and Mouton built the Grid on it
  • 📄 Lumen Learning — McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y — an open textbook chapter, free to reuse
  • 📄 MindTools — Theory X and Theory Y — with the self-fulfilling prophecy made explicit
  • 📄 Theory X and Theory Y: what McGregor got right, and wrong — the counter-view, and worth having in the room
  • 📄 MTD Training — McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y in practice — what each assumption looks like in a real manager's behaviour
