House's Path-Goal Theory

modelmoderate
leadershipstylesmotivationsituationalcoachingteams

What it is in one line: your job as a leader is to clear the path to the goal, and which style you use depends on what is actually blocking it.

Origin: Robert J. House (1971), A path-goal theory of leader effectiveness, in Administrative Science Quarterly, revised and expanded by House in 1996 (chapter summary, SAGE PDF). Evidence: moderate. Wofford and Liska's 1993 meta-analysis supported parts of it, but the theory as a whole is broad enough that testing it properly is difficult, and the research does not support all of its claims. The four styles are useful; the full theory is more than most rooms need. Best for: the leader whose default style is fine for half the team and wrong for the other half.

On this pageThe modelWorked example, one team leader, one shiftFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

House's move was to stop asking "what is the best style?" and start asking "what is in this person's way?" The leader's job is to remove the obstacle, and different obstacles need different leaders.

StyleYou do thisUse it when the obstacle is
DirectiveSay exactly what, how and by whenThey do not know what good looks like. New, unclear, or genuinely complicated
SupportiveBe approachable, notice the person, take the pressure downThe work is boring, hard, or stressful and they are running out of gas
ParticipativeAsk, consult, decide togetherThey know things you do not, and the decision affects their day
Achievement-orientedSet a stretch goal and say plainly you think they can hit itThey are capable and coasting, or they do not believe they are capable

How to read it: the style is chosen by the obstacle, not by your personality. Four people on one team can need four different leaders on the same day.

Worked example, one team leader, one shift

A support-work team leader, four staff, Monday morning.

WhoWhat is in the wayStyleWhat they actually say
New starter, week twoDoes not know the medication processDirective"I'll walk it with you this morning, then you do it and I'll watch."
Staff member whose mum is in hospitalNothing to do with the jobSupportive"How are you doing? What would make this week easier?"
Ten-year veteranThe new roster does not work and she knows whyParticipative"You've seen more rosters than I have. What are we missing?"
Capable, quiet, never puts her hand upDoes not think she is a leaderAchievement"I want you to run the handover on Thursday. You're better at it than you think."

➜ Four conversations, four styles, one leader, one morning. That is Path-Goal.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes. Teach the four styles as four questions, not four labels
  • Run ACT-084 Four Teams, One Leader after it. It is the fastest way to make the switching real
  • The best question: "which of these four is your default, and who on your team is getting the wrong one?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Reading Directive as bossy. Directive is a gift to somebody who has no idea what is expected. Withholding it is not respect, it is abandonment
    • Using Supportive as an all-purpose answer. Being nice to someone who is stuck on how to do the task does not unstick them
    • Participative when the decision is already made. Learners smell fake consultation instantly. See FRM-028 on the same trap
    • Achievement-oriented without the belief. "I know you can do it" from someone who does not mean it is worse than silence
  • ⚠️ Do not teach the full theory. House's model includes follower characteristics, task structure and expectancy motivation. At Level 3 that is noise. Teach the four styles and the question that picks them

Likert's Four Systems of Management

modelpractitioner
leadershipdecision-makingstylestrustconsultationteams

What it is in one line: four rungs on a ladder from "do as you are told or else" to "we decide this together", and most workplaces are further down it than the manager thinks.

Origin: Rensis Likert, The Human Organization: Its Management and Value (McGraw-Hill, 1967). Likert ran the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research and is the same Likert whose name is on every 1-to-5 agree/disagree scale you have ever filled in (overview). Evidence: practitioner. Likert had survey data behind it in the 1960s and the four systems have survived as a description rather than as a tested model. Best for: naming the difference between being asked and being listened to, which is the gap most teams actually feel.

On this pageThe modelThe bit worth the whole frameworkWorked example, a Hamilton retail storeFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

Lewin gives you three styles. Likert splits the middle of that ladder, and the split is where the useful teaching is.

SystemNameWhat it feels like from the floor
1Exploitative authoritative"Do it or find another job." Threat is the motivator. Nobody tells the boss anything true
2Benevolent authoritativeSame control, but there are rewards. People say what they think the boss wants to hear
3ConsultativeYou get asked. Your view is genuinely heard. The boss still decides
4ParticipativeYou are part of the decision. Information moves up, down and sideways

How to read it: the important line is between 2 and 3. Below it, people tell you what you want to hear. Above it, they tell you what is true. Everything else about running a team depends on which side of that line you are on.

The bit worth the whole framework

System 2 is the most common workplace in New Zealand and the most misread.

A System 2 manager is often warm, generous, remembers birthdays, shouts the pizza. They also make every call themselves and have never once been told bad news early. They think they run a happy team. They run a quiet one.

Likert's finding was that people in Systems 1 and 2 filter upward information. They do not lie. They just leave out the parts that will not go down well. So the manager's picture of their own workplace is assembled from edited reports and it is always more positive than the truth.

➜ If you have not been told something you did not want to hear in the last month, you are probably at System 2.

Worked example, a Hamilton retail store

The EFTPOS terminal by the door has been dropping out for three weeks.

  • System 1: nobody mentions it. Last person who raised a problem got asked why they could not just sort it themselves
  • System 2: the team work around it, move customers to the other till, and mention it to the manager in week four when a customer complains
  • System 3: raised in the Monday huddle, day two. Manager asks what people are seeing, then calls the provider
  • System 4: whoever is on the till that morning phones the provider, because the team agreed months ago that anyone can

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes, and only after Lewin. This is the refinement, not the introduction
  • The best question: "when did somebody last tell you something you did not want to hear? What happened to them afterwards?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Selling System 4 as the target for everything. A kitchen at Friday service is System 1 for twenty minutes and that is correct. Likert's point is about the default, not the exception
    • Confusing System 3 with System 4. Most managers who think they are participative are consultative. That is not a failure. Consultative done honestly is a good place to be
    • Running the ladder as a self-assessment. Ask the team, not the manager. The whole finding is that the manager's read is unreliable
  • ⚠️ Careful with System 1. Some learners work in one. Naming it can be a relief or it can be frightening. The follow-up is not "be more assertive", it is FRM-042's power and safety barrier

Transactional and Transformational Leadership

modelstrong
leadershipmotivationchangevisionstylesteamsperformance

What it is in one line: you can get effort by trading for it, or by giving people a reason to care, and the second one outperforms the first almost everywhere it has been measured.

Origin: James MacGregor Burns, Leadership (Harper & Row, 1978), a political scientist writing about political leaders. Bernard M. Bass turned it into something testable for workplaces in Leadership and Performance Beyond Expectations (1985). Evidence: strong, and the strongest of any leadership style model in this library. Judge and Piccolo's 2004 meta-analysis pooled 626 correlations from 87 studies and found transformational leadership correlated .44 with overall leadership effectiveness, .58 with follower job satisfaction, and .64 with leader-rated effectiveness. Contingent reward, the useful half of transactional, came in at .39. Laissez-faire came in at –.37 (Judge & Piccolo, 2004, Journal of Applied Psychology, PDF). Best for: the team leader who has run out of things to offer and cannot work out why nobody goes the extra mile.

On this pageThe modelThe most important thing to teach off this pageWorked example, a Māngere logistics yardFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

TransactionalTransformational
The dealYou do the work, you get the reward. You do not, there is a consequenceYou believe in where we are going, so you bring more than the job description
Runs onRules, targets, incentives, structureVision, example, belief in the person
The leaderManages the exchangeChanges what people think is possible
You getThe job done to standardThe job done, plus ideas, plus people who grow
Fails whenThe reward runs out, or the work needs judgmentThe vision is vague, or the leader does not live it

Bass's four behaviours that make up the transformational half, usually called the four I's:

What the leader actually does
Idealised influenceWalks the talkDoes the thing they ask others to do, including when it costs them
Inspirational motivationGives the whySays where this is going in words people can repeat
Intellectual stimulationAsks, does not tell"How would you do it?" Treats a challenge as useful, not rude
Individualised considerationSees the personKnows what this particular person is working towards

How to read it: this is not a choice. Bass's own finding was that transformational leadership augments transactional. It does not replace it. Nobody is inspired by a mission statement when their timesheet is wrong.

The most important thing to teach off this page

Transactional first, then transformational. In that order.

Zeducation's learners are frequently in low-wage, insecure work. Talking to someone about vision and growth while their roster changes without notice and their last pay was short is not inspiring leadership, it is an insult dressed as one.

➜ Fix the transaction. Then earn the right to the rest.

Worked example, a Māngere logistics yard

The site has a safety walkaround nobody does properly.

Transactional: the supervisor puts a completion bonus on it and audits the sheets. Compliance goes to 100% in a fortnight. The sheets get filled in at the end of the shift from memory.

Transformational: the supervisor tells the yard about the forklift incident at their old site, walks the first one himself every Monday for a month, and asks two of the crew to redesign the sheet because "you two see more of this yard than I do". Compliance goes to 90% and the walkarounds actually happen.

Both together: keep the audit. Keep the standard. And do the other thing as well.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes. Teach the two words, then the four I's, then the "both, in order" rule
  • Run ACT-086 The Vision Test after it
  • The best question: "who is someone you worked harder for than you had to? What did they do?" Every answer that comes back is one of the four I's, and the room works that out for themselves
  • Common mistakes:
    • Hearing transformational as charismatic. It is not about being magnetic. Individualised consideration is mostly just remembering what someone told you last month
    • Skipping the transaction. See above. This is the one that matters in our rooms
    • Vision as wallpaper. A vision nobody can repeat back is not a vision
    • Reading laissez-faire as a mild option. It scored –.37. Being absent is measurably worse than being merely transactional. Worth saying to anyone who thinks hands-off is generous
  • ⚠️ Be honest about the measurement. Most of that meta-analysis rests on followers rating their leader on a questionnaire. People who like their boss rate them high on everything. The effect is real and it is probably smaller than .44

More resources

  • 📄 Judge, T. A., & Piccolo, R. F. (2004). Transformational and transactional leadership: a meta-analytic test of their relative validity (PDF)
  • 📖 Burns, J. M. (1978). Leadership. New York: Harper & Row
  • 📖 Bass, B. M. (1985). Leadership and Performance Beyond Expectations. New York: Free Press

  • 📄 BusinessBalls — the four I's of transformational leadership — idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individual consideration
  • 📄 Michigan State — the four I's of transformational leadership — with what each looks like in practice
  • 📄 Contrasting Burns and Bass — does the paradigm live up to Burns' philosophy? — the honest critique. Burns meant something more moral than what Bass measured

Kotter on Leadership and Management

modelstrong
leadershipmanagementchangeplanningteamsroles

What it is in one line: management is how you cope with complexity, leadership is how you cope with change, and a team that is short of either one is in trouble.

Origin: John P. Kotter, What Leaders Really Do, Harvard Business Review, May–June 1990, reprinted as an HBR classic (HBR · indexed in PubMed · full text, PDF). Kotter was a professor at Harvard Business School. Evidence: strong as a distinction, in the sense that it has held up for thirty-five years and reshaped how organisations describe these two jobs. It is a conceptual argument rather than an experiment. Best for: the newly promoted team leader who has been given a leadership title and a management job, and cannot tell why they feel like they are failing at both.

On this page⚠️ Go to the originalThe modelThe half that gets missedWorked example, a Papakura caféFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

⚠️ Go to the original

This comparison is reproduced in a lot of training material, usually credited to a secondary link rather than to Kotter himself. The original is "What Leaders Really Do", Harvard Business Review, 1990, one of the most cited management articles ever published, and it is worth the twenty minutes. Always follow the name to the source.

The model

Kotter's central claim, and the reason the distinction is worth teaching: these are two different jobs, not two levels of the same job. A manager is not a junior leader. They are doing different work, and both jobs need doing.

MANAGEMENT copes with complexityLEADERSHIP copes with change
Sets the direction byPlanning and budgeting. Steps, timeframes, resourcesSetting a vision and the strategies to reach it
Builds capacity byOrganising and staffing. Structure, roles, who reports to whomAligning people. Communicating the direction until people believe it
Makes it happen byControlling and problem solving. Monitoring, comparing, correctingMotivating and inspiring. Meeting people's need to achieve and belong
AsksWhat, and howWhy, and what if
Time frameThis month, this quarterThis year, next five
ProducesPredictability and order. Budgets hit, deliveries on timeChange, sometimes dramatic. New products, new ways of working

How to read it: same three-step shape, different work at every step. Kotter's argument is that strong management with weak leadership produces a very orderly organisation that cannot change, and strong leadership with weak management produces chaos with a great mission statement.

The half that gets missed

Most retellings of this framework teach it as leadership good, management boring. Kotter did not say that.

He said complexity is real, large organisations genuinely need planning and control, and that most companies are over-managed and under-led — which is a claim about the balance, not a claim that management is a lesser activity. A team leader who cannot build a roster is not compensating for it with vision.

➜ For Zeducation's learners, most of whom are supervisors rather than executives, the management half is usually the one they are actually being paid for, and the leadership half is what would make them promotable.

Worked example, a Papakura café

The owner wants to open a second site.

Management work: costing the fit-out, working out staffing for two sites, building the roster template, setting up stock ordering, deciding who runs which shift, checking the numbers weekly. Without this the second café opens and fails.

Leadership work: telling the team why a second site matters and what it means for them, naming who is going to step up to run site one, convincing the best barista that this is a career and not a job, holding the standard when everything is stretched.

Without this, the second café opens, the good staff leave, and the owner ends up working both sites themselves.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes with the table. Do not read out all twelve rows, pick four
  • Run ACT-085 Leader Or Manager? The Sort as the opener, before you teach it. The sort is more useful when the room has not been told the answers yet
  • The best question: "of everything you did at work last week, how much was management and how much was leadership?" For most supervisors the honest answer is 95/5, and the point of the session is that 5 is not zero
  • Common mistakes:
    • Making management the villain. It insults everyone in the room who is good at it
    • Treating them as two people. In a small NZ business the same person does both, often in the same conversation
    • Teaching "leaders have vision" as a personality trait. Kotter's whole opening move is that leadership has nothing to do with charisma or being born special
  • ⚠️ Watch the status reading. In a room where some learners are supervisors and some are not, this framework can land as "leaders matter more". Say plainly: the person who notices the roster is wrong before Friday is doing something the organisation cannot survive without

More resources

Tikanga Māori in Business — four values that run a workplace

modelpractitioner
tikanga-maorivaluescultureleadershipwhanaungatangamanaakitangakaitiakitanga

What it is in one line: four values from te ao Māori that already describe how good workplaces behave, whether or not anybody in them uses the words.

Origin: tikanga Māori is not a framework and nobody invented it. It is the body of values and protocols that guide how people behave and treat each other, developed over generations and handed down. This particular set of four, applied to a workplace, is how it is commonly taught in New Zealand business contexts, including in SRC-009.

The authoritative written treatment is Sir Hirini Moko Mead, Tikanga Māori: Living by Māori Values (Huia, 2003, revised 2016) (publisher · Royal Society of NZ, Te Takarangi). For the business application specifically, see MBIE's principles from te ao Māori and the Māori enterprise research of Professor Jason Mika (Ngāi Tūhoe, Whakatōhea, Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Kahungunu), whose work is on how Māori businesses hold cultural and commercial goals at the same time (University of Auckland).

Evidence: practitioner, and the wrong question. These are values, not a hypothesis. What is evidenced is that Māori businesses using them describe them as commercially load-bearing rather than decorative. Best for: any room where people are being asked what they stand for and have never been given words for it.

On this page⚠️ Before you teach thisThe modelThe move that makes this work in a mixed roomWorked example, a Māori-owned consultancy going internationalFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

⚠️ Before you teach this

Three things, and they are not optional.

  1. This belongs to Māori. Zeducation can teach it with respect and attribution. Zeducation does not own it, cannot certify anybody in it, and should not present a two-hour workshop as sufficient. Say that in the room
  2. Get pronunciation right or do not use the words. Practise before you deliver. A facilitator mangling manaakitanga while teaching a page about respect has already lost the room. If you are unsure, ask
  3. Do not use it as an icebreaker. These are not four nice words for a poster. Whanaungatanga involves actual obligation

The model

ValuePlain translationIn a workplace it meansYou can see it when
WhanaungatangaRelationship, connection, belongingRelationships are built through shared experience, mutual respect and doing the work together. People belong hereNew starters get introduced properly, not just shown a desk
ManaakitangaHospitality, care, lifting others upYou look after people's mana. Clients, staff, suppliers, the person who walks in the doorNobody is treated differently because of what they can do for you
RangatiratangaLeadership, self-determinationThe leader's job is to weave the group together, not to control it. Everyone is part of the wholeDecisions get made with the people they land on
KaitiakitangaGuardianship, stewardshipYou are looking after something that was here before you and will be here after. Resources, environment, the business itselfThe next person inherits it in better shape

How to read it: these are not four separate policies. Mead's own framing is that all tikanga are underpinned by manaakitanga — nurturing relationships, looking after people, and being careful about how others are treated. The other three are what that looks like in different directions.

The move that makes this work in a mixed room

Zeducation's rooms are Pacific, Māori, migrant, Pākehā and young. Teaching tikanga Māori as the answer to values would be its own kind of disrespect, and it would not land.

Teach it as the worked example, then ask for theirs.

These are Māori values, in Aotearoa, and they are the tangata whenua ones so they come first. Now: what did your family teach you about how you treat people at work? What is the word for it?

What comes back is fa'aaloalo and tautua, alofa, aiga, utang na loob, ubuntu, izzat, "you look after your own", "you don't leave a job half done". Every one of them belongs on the whiteboard next to the four above.

➜ That is the whole session. Not "learn these values", but "you already have values, here are the ones this country runs on, now name yours out loud." See FRM-036 Teu le vā and FRM-035 Talanoa for the Pacific pages that sit alongside this one.

Worked example, a Māori-owned consultancy going international

From SRC-009, and it is the best story in that workbook. Kāhui Tautoko Consulting, a New Zealand company expanding into Canada, considered changing its name because clients might not pronounce it. Mara Andrews, the director, quotes her Aunty Mate:

"Just because you're going overseas, you don't stop being Māori. Don't change who you are for anybody."

They kept the name. Andrews' account is that the Māori identity and values became the reason indigenous communities in Hawai‘i and Canada worked with them.

She also says something more useful for a classroom, about writing the values down:

"If you've been raised with those values, nobody gives you a booklet and says, 'This is how you have to behave!' It's just how you are."

➜ Which is exactly why naming them is hard, and why it is worth doing.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes minimum. This is not a five-minute slide
  • Run ACT-088 The Values You Brought To Work after it
  • The best question: "which of these four does your workplace actually do well? Which one does it talk about and not do?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Translating and moving on. "Manaakitanga means hospitality" is true and nearly useless. Manaakitanga is about somebody's mana, which is a bigger idea than being welcoming
    • Values-as-poster. Almost every workplace has values on a wall that nobody can name. The session is worthless if it produces another set
    • Asking Māori learners to teach the room. Do not put the one Māori person in the group on the spot to explain tikanga. That is your job, and if you cannot do it, get someone in
    • Skipping rangatiratanga because it is political. It is a leadership word here. Use it as one, and know that it carries more than that outside this room
  • ⚠️ Rangatiratanga carries constitutional weight. In te Tiriti o Waitangi, tino rangatiratanga is a guarantee to Māori. Teaching it purely as a workplace leadership word is a simplification. Name that you are simplifying

More resources

  • 📖 Mead, H. M. (2003, rev. 2016). Tikanga Māori: Living by Māori Values. Wellington: Huia (publisher page)
  • 📄 MBIE — Principles from te ao Māori, the Māori worldview
  • 📄 Te Aka Māori Dictionary — the first stop for any word on this page
  • 📄 Jason Mika on supporting Māori entrepreneurship, University of Auckland
  • 📄 Waihanga Ara Rau — Māori concepts lifting workplace culture and safety

Tū Rangatira — seven Māori leadership roles

modelpractitioner
tikanga-maorileadershiprolescultureteamskaitiakitangarangatiratanga

What it is in one line: seven jobs a leader does, named in te reo Māori, and most leaders are strong at two of them and have never thought about the other five.

Origin: Tū Rangatira: Māori Medium Educational Leadership, Ministry of Education, 2010. Developed with experienced Māori-medium principals, advisors, researchers and organisations. It is freely available (Educational Leaders · full document, PDF). The seven roles are called ngā whenu, the strands. Evidence: practitioner. It is a professional framework built from practice and consultation, not a tested instrument, and it does not claim to be one. Best for: a leader who is good at their job and cannot name what the job actually consists of.

On this page⚠️ Always name the sourceThe seven rolesWhy this is worth having next to the Western modelsWorked example, an Auckland team leader in aged careFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

⚠️ Always name the source

These roles circulate widely, and they are often taught as generic "traditional Māori leadership" with no reference attached. Zeducation first met four of them that way.

They are not undifferentiated tradition. They are a named 2010 New Zealand publication, made by identifiable Māori educators, in a specific sector, for a specific purpose. A Māori framework presented as anonymous tradition loses the people who built it, and naming them is part of teaching it properly.

➜ Cite Tū Rangatira, Ministry of Education, 2010. Every time. This page carries all seven roles, not four.

The seven roles

WhenuRoleWhat the leader does
He KaitiakiGuardianBuilds and holds high-trust relationships. Protects the people and the kaupapa
He KaiwhakariteManagerRuns the resources well so the vision is actually reachable
He Kanohi MataraVisionaryThinks and plans ahead. Understands the past well enough to see what is coming
He KaiakoTeacher and learnerTeaches, and stays a learner. Both halves, always
He KaimahiWorkerLeads by doing the work. Builds capability in others by working alongside them
He KaikōtuituiNetworkerContributes beyond their own organisation. Connects people who need each other
He KaiaratakiAdvocateSpeaks up for people. Holds culturally responsive practice, with te Tiriti as the foundation

How to read it: seven strands, not seven stages. You are doing several at once and neglecting several at once. The question is which.

Why this is worth having next to the Western models

Put it beside the rest of this library's leadership pages and something shows up:

What Tū Rangatira hasWhich Western model covers it
He Kaiwhakarite, the managerKotter
He Kanohi Matara, the visionaryTransformational leadership
He Kaimahi, leading by doingModelling
He Kaikōtuitui, the networkerWeak ties
He Kaitiaki, the guardianNothing, really
He Kaiako, permanently a learner as well as a teacherNothing, really
He Kaiarataki, the advocateNothing, really

➜ Three of the seven have no clean equivalent in the mainstream canon. Guardianship, staying a learner, and advocating for your people are not optional extras on the Western models. They are missing from them. That is the argument for teaching this framework, and it is a better argument than "include a Māori model".

Worked example, an Auckland team leader in aged care

One person, one week, all seven.

WhenuWhat it looked like
KaitiakiKept a resident's family complaint away from the new staff member until she had the facts
KaiwhakariteRebuilt the roster after two people went off sick
Kanohi MataraStarted planning for the funding round that closes in March
KaiakoTaught the hoist properly. Learned the correct pronunciation of a resident's name from her mokopuna
KaimahiWorked the Sunday shift nobody would pick up
KaikōtuituiRang the team leader at another facility to ask how they handled night handovers
KaiaratakiTold the manager the new documentation system was not going to work for staff whose first language is not English, and did not drop it

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Say the names properly, give the English, then the worked example
  • Run ACT-089 Seven Roles, One Kaupapa after it
  • The best question: "which two are you strong at, and which one have you never done?" Nearly everyone lands on Kaiarataki or Kaikōtuitui for the second answer
  • Common mistakes:
    • Translating and dropping the reo. The English is a hint, not a replacement. Kaitiaki is not just "guardian"
    • Teaching it as a checklist to be scored. It is a mirror, not an audit
    • Using only the four from the workbook. Kaiako, Kaikōtuitui and Kaiarataki are three of the most interesting, which is a reason to think the four-role version was chosen for space rather than for meaning
  • ⚠️ This was written for kura, not for warehouses. Tū Rangatira is a Māori-medium education framework. Every workplace example on this page is Zeducation's translation, not the Ministry's, and the framework's authors did not write it for a logistics yard. Say so when you teach it

FRM-052Framework · Culture & Diversity

The Three Kinds of Diversity

modelmoderate
diversityteamsculturedecision-makinginclusionevidence

What it is in one line: when people say "diverse team" they usually mean what the team looks like, and two of the three kinds that actually change how a team performs are invisible.

Origin: assembled by Zeducation. The three-way split is standard in the group-composition literature and appears in SRC-009 drawing on Stanford GSB's 1999 summary. The evidence attached to it here is Zeducation's own audit, and it changed one of the claims. Evidence: moderate for the effect on decision quality. See the audit below, because the claim most people make for diversity is the one that does not hold. Best for: the team that ticked the diversity box by hiring and cannot work out why nothing about its decisions changed.

On this pageThe model⚠️ The evidence audit, and it is the point of this pageWorked example, one team, three kindsFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

KindWhat differsExample on one team
DemographicWho people are. Age, gender, ethnicity, disability, where they were bornA crew of five: two Sāmoan, one Māori, one Filipina, one Pākehā, ages 19 to 58
InformationalWhat people know. Education, training, work history, tradeOne trained overseas as an engineer, one has fifteen years on the floor, one just finished school
Values-basedWhat people are for. Goals, priorities, what they think the job is forOne is here to pay a mortgage, one is building a career, one is supporting family back home

How to read it: the bottom of this diagram is the whole framework. Diversity that is present but not heard does nothing. A team can be demographically diverse and informationally identical, or diverse in every way and run by someone who only asks one person.

⚠️ The evidence audit, and it is the point of this page

Diversity training in New Zealand runs on two claims. One of them has fallen over.

The claim that failed: "diverse companies make more money"

The figures everyone quotes are McKinsey's: companies in the top quartile for gender diversity are 15% more likely to outperform their industry median, and for racial and ethnic diversity, 35% more likely (Hunt, Layton & Prince, Why Diversity Matters, 2015). They appear in SRC-009 as settled fact.

They did not replicate. In March 2024, Jeremiah Green (Texas A&M) and John R. M. Hand (University of North Carolina) published McKinsey's Diversity Matters/Delivers/Wins Results Revisited in Econ Journal Watch. McKinsey would not release its data, so they rebuilt the test using S&P 500 firms as at 31 December 2019. They found no statistically significant relationship between McKinsey's diversity measures and industry-adjusted earnings margin, sales growth, gross margin, return on assets, return on equity or total shareholder return across 2015–2019.

➜ Do not use the 15% and 35% figures. Not in a workshop, not in a tender, not on a slide. If a learner brings them up, this is the page that answers them.

What that does not mean. A failed replication of one consultancy's correlation is not evidence that diversity harms performance, and nobody should leave the room thinking it is. It means the profit claim is unproven, and that Zeducation should not have been leaning on it.

The claim that held: "diverse teams think harder"

This one is experimental rather than correlational, which is why it survives.

  • Samuel Sommers (2006) ran mock juries. Racially mixed juries deliberated longer, raised a wider range of facts, and made fewer factual errors than all-white juries. And the white jurors on mixed juries performed better than white jurors on all-white juries, before deliberation even began (APA, PDF)
  • Katherine Phillips (2014) summarised the broader literature in Scientific American: the mechanism is not that minority members bring information, it is that the majority works harder when difference is present
  • Rock & Grant (2016), Why Diverse Teams Are Smarter, HBR, is the accessible summary, though it also repeats the McKinsey figures. Read it for the mechanism, not the numbers

➜ The finding to teach: a diverse team is not smarter because the new person knows more. It is smarter because everybody stops assuming they already agree. Sameness feels like consensus and usually is not.

And say the cost out loud. The same research finds diverse teams feel less comfortable and often rate their own performance lower while objectively doing better. Diversity buys you a harder meeting and a better decision. Learners deserve to know both halves.

Worked example, one team, three kinds

A five-person community health team in Ōtara reviewing why appointment no-shows are high.

  • Demographic diversity working: the Tongan health worker says families are turning up but being turned away at 10 minutes late, and 10 minutes is nothing if you are getting three kids to school first
  • Informational diversity working: the ex-receptionist knows the booking system can hold a 15-minute grace window and nobody has ever switched it on
  • Values diversity surfacing: the clinician thinks the job is to protect clinic throughput. The outreach worker thinks the job is to get people seen. They have never said this to each other and it is the actual disagreement

➜ The demographic difference found the problem. The informational difference found the fix. The values difference is why it had not been fixed already, and it needed to be named before anything could move.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes, and spend most of it on the audit above
  • Run ACT-090 What Kind Of Difference Is This? as the opener, then ACT-091 The Ten Moves Audit
  • The best question: "what does someone on your team know that nobody ever asks them about?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Using the McKinsey numbers. See above. This is the one that matters
    • Making it a business case at all. If diversity is only worth having because it pays, then it stops being worth having the moment somebody produces a spreadsheet saying it does not. Zeducation's position is that people are entitled to be treated properly at work regardless of what it does to the margin. The performance research is a bonus, not the foundation
    • Stopping at demographic. It is the visible one and the least interesting
    • Selling it as comfortable. It is not
  • ⚠️ This subject attracts bad faith from both directions. Some people want the 35% figure because it wins arguments. Some people want the replication failure because it ends them. The honest position is on this page and it satisfies neither. Teach it anyway

More resources

  • 📄 Sommers, S. (2006). On racial diversity and group decision making. JPSP (APA, PDF)
  • 📄 Phillips, K. W. (2014). How Diversity Makes Us Smarter. Scientific American
  • 📄 Rock, D. & Grant, H. (2016). Why Diverse Teams Are Smarter. HBR
  • 📄 Chicago Booth Review — Do diverse leadership teams produce better performance?

FRM-053Framework · Leadership

Belbin's Nine Team Roles

modelmoderate
teamsrolesstrengthscollaborationteam-buildingself-awareness

What it is in one line: nine jobs that need doing in any team regardless of who is on it, and every one of them comes with a matching weakness you are supposed to tolerate.

Origin: R. Meredith Belbin, Management Teams: Why They Succeed or Fail (1981), from nine years of research at Henley Management College running business simulations. Belbin's finding was that teams of the most able individuals routinely lost to mixed teams (Belbin). Evidence: moderate, and contested. Furnham, Steele & Pendleton (1993) attacked the self-perception inventory for low internal consistency and an unclear factor structure. Aritzeta, Swailes & Senior (2007), reviewing 43 studies in the Journal of Management Studies, concluded the model has adequate convergent validity but weak discriminant validity — the roles are real, some of them overlap more than the model admits (review). Belbin's own answer is that it measures behaviour, not personality, and is not a psychometric test. Best for: the team where two people keep colliding and everyone has decided it is personal.

On this pageThe modelThe half of Belbin that is worth more than the nine namesWorked example, a five-person team on a fit-out jobFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The model

Nine roles, in three families.

Action-oriented, they make things move

RoleStrengthAllowable weakness
ShaperDrives, challenges, thrives on pressure. Finds a way throughCan argue, and can bruise people without noticing
ImplementerTurns talk into a plan and then does itSlow to accept a change once the plan is set
Completer-FinisherCatches the errors. Delivers on time, properlyWorries. Reluctant to hand anything over

People-oriented, they hold it together

RoleStrengthAllowable weakness
CoordinatorKeeps the team on the goal, hears everyone, delegates wellCan delegate away their own share of the work
Team WorkerSmooths friction, supports people, keeps the group wholeAvoids the hard conversation
Resource InvestigatorKnows a guy. Brings in contacts, options and resourcesEnthusiasm fades once the novelty does

Thought-oriented, they make it good

RoleStrengthAllowable weakness
PlantThe ideas person. Solves the problem nobody could crackWorks alone, takes criticism badly
Monitor-EvaluatorWeighs it up coldly and accurately. Rarely wrongSlow to decide. Can flatten a room's energy
SpecialistDeep expert knowledge in one narrow thingNot interested in anything outside it

How to read it: nobody plays one role. Most people have two or three they fall into and two or three they never touch. A team missing a whole family is the one that struggles, and it usually struggles in a predictable way.

The half of Belbin that is worth more than the nine names

The allowable weakness.

Belbin's argument is that the weakness is not a defect to be fixed, it is the price of the strength. The Plant who takes criticism badly is the same person who produced the idea. The Completer-Finisher who will not let go is why nothing shipped broken. Trying to remove the weakness usually removes the strength with it.

➜ So the leader's question is not "how do I fix this person?" It is "is this weakness one I can carry, given what I get?" Sometimes the answer is no. But it is a different question and it gets a different conversation.

Worked example, a five-person team on a fit-out job

Behind schedule. Two people are barely speaking.

  • The Shaper has been pushing hard, and told the room on Tuesday that the plan was "useless"
  • The Implementer wrote that plan and has stopped contributing
  • The Team Worker has been quietly patching it up with both of them and telling neither the truth
  • There is no Completer-Finisher, which is why three snags got signed off that should not have
  • There is no Monitor-Evaluator, which is why nobody said the original timeline was optimistic

The read: this is not a personality clash, it is a Shaper and an Implementer doing exactly what those roles do, in a team missing the two roles that would have caught the problem early.

The move: name it out loud. Give the snag list to whoever is closest to Completer-Finisher. Before the next plan is signed off, ask one person to spend ten minutes trying to break it.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Do not read out all nine with all their weaknesses. Teach the three families, then let people find themselves
  • Run ACT-093 Nine Roles, One Table after it
  • The best question: "which role is missing from your team, and what has that cost you?" Better than asking people what they are
  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning it into a personality type. Belbin insists this is behaviour, and behaviour changes with the team you are in. Somebody who is a Shaper at work is often a Team Worker at home
    • Buying the official inventory. The self-perception questionnaire is the part the researchers criticised. The roles are the useful bit and they are free. See FRM-054 for the general position
    • Labelling other people. "You're such a Plant" is not a compliment when it is used to explain away someone's objection
    • Assuming you need all nine. Belbin's teams were larger. A four-person crew covers nine roles between them or does without
  • ⚠️ Be straight about the evidence. If a learner asks whether this is scientific, the honest answer is: the roles are a useful description, the questionnaire has been criticised for thirty years, and it is a conversation tool rather than a measurement

More resources

  • 📖 Belbin, R. M. (1981). Management Teams: Why They Succeed or Fail. Oxford: Butterworth-Heinemann
  • 📄 Aritzeta, Swailes & Senior (2007). Belbin's Team Role Model: Development, Validity and Applications for Team Building. Journal of Management Studies
  • 📄 Belbin's own reliability and validity page — read it knowing who wrote it
  • 📄 A comprehensive review of the method, reliability and validity (Belbin, PDF)
  • 🔗 Belbin — the nine team roles — Belbin's own site. Use this rather than a summary of it
  • 🎬 Belbin team roles video guide — the nine roles walked through on screen
  • 📄 Belbin — do you know your Completer Finishers from your Implementers? — the two roles people most often confuse. The Implementer wants it done; the Completer Finisher wants it right
  • 🎬 The official guide to Belbin team roles, from Belbin HQ — from the source. Team Roles measure behaviour, not personality, and that distinction is the whole point

Personality Tests At Work — what they can and cannot tell you

techniquestrong
personalityassessmentmbtiself-awarenessteamsevidencehiring

What it is in one line: the library's standing position on MBTI, DISC and the rest, written because learners keep asking and facilitators keep guessing.

Origin: Zeducation house page. Written after two consecutive sources taught the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator without qualification: SRC-008, which was selling personality tests, and SRC-009, which was not. Evidence: strong. The psychometric problems with type-based instruments are well documented and not seriously disputed by researchers, whatever the publishers say. Best for: the moment a learner says "my work made us all do one and I'm an ENFJ, is that good?"

On this pageThe position, in one tableWhat is actually wrong with MBTI⚠️ Where the real harm isWhat to say when a learner asksWhat Zeducation uses insteadFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The position, in one table

InstrumentWhat it isUse it forDo not use it for
MBTI (Myers-Briggs)16 types from four either/or pairsNothing Zeducation teaches. If a workplace has already done it, use the vocabulary to talk, not to decideHiring. Team selection. Predicting performance. Explaining someone's behaviour to their face
DISCFour behavioural stylesSame. A shared vocabulary at bestThe same list
Belbin Team RolesNine roles a team needsThe roles as a conversation. See FRM-053The paid self-perception questionnaire, which is the criticised part
Big Five / OCEANFive traits on continuous scalesThis is the one with the research behind it. Still not a Zeducation productAnything with consequences for someone's job, without a qualified practitioner
Strengths inventoriesRanked strengthsStarting a conversation about what someone is good atDeciding what someone is not allowed to do

What is actually wrong with MBTI

Learners deserve the reason, not just the ruling.

1. It splits people in half where no gap exists. MBTI reports you as either Extravert or Introvert. Actual scores on that trait pile up in the middle, like height. Cutting a continuous distribution at the average means most people are sitting a point or two from the boundary and get sorted arbitrarily.

2. Test-retest reliability is poor. Studies have found a substantial share of people get a different type when they retake it weeks later. A measure that changes when the thing it measures has not is not measuring it (Pittenger and others, critical review, PDF · overview of the criticisms).

3. It does not predict job performance. Which is the thing everyone wants it for.

4. It was not built by psychologists. Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers developed it from Carl Jung's theory of types. Jung's typology was itself observational, and he did not intend it as a sorting instrument.

5. It feels accurate for a reason. Type descriptions are written to be flattering and broadly applicable. Nearly everyone reads their profile and recognises themselves, and would also recognise themselves in most of the other fifteen. That effect has a name and it is worth teaching in its own right.

⚠️ Where the real harm is

Not in the fun of doing a quiz. In four specific places:

HarmWhat it looks like
Hiring"We don't think you're the right type for this team." Legally exposed, and it filters out difference while feeling objective
Excusing behaviour"I'm a Thinker, that's just how I give feedback." A type is not a permission slip
Limiting peopleA quiet learner told they are an Introvert and therefore not leadership material. There is no evidence for that and plenty against
Cultural biasThese instruments were normed largely on Western, individualist populations. A learner from a culture where deference to elders is correct behaviour can read as "low assertiveness" on an instrument that has no category for context. Same problem FRM-042 names for assertiveness

What to say when a learner asks

They will, and often they have paid for one or been put through one at work. Do not sneer at it.

Those tests are good for one thing: giving people words to talk about differences they already noticed. They are not good at predicting how someone will do a job, and a lot of people get a different result if they take it again a few weeks later. So use the language if your workplace uses it. Just do not let anyone use it to decide something about you.

➜ That is the whole script. It respects the learner, tells the truth, and does not require them to defend a decision their employer made.

What Zeducation uses instead

Because "don't use that" is only half an answer.

Instead of a typeUse
"What kind of person are you?"FRM-053 Belbin's roles — behaviour, and it changes by team
"What's your leadership style?"FRM-044 The Grid and FRM-028 Lewin — a position you chose, not a type you are
"Why don't you speak up?"FRM-042 Why Assertiveness Feels Hard — self-identified barriers, never assigned
"What are you good at?"Direct observation and asking, which nobody has improved on

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes, and only when it comes up. Do not go looking for the fight
  • The best question: "has a test ever been used to decide something about you?" The answers are usually more instructive than anything on this page
  • Common mistakes:
    • Mocking learners who like their type. Self-knowledge language is genuinely valuable to people who have never had any. Take the instrument seriously as an experience while being straight about the science
    • Overclaiming. MBTI is unreliable. It is not astrology, and saying so makes you look partisan rather than accurate
    • Refusing to engage. If a learner's employer runs on DISC, "that's rubbish" leaves them worse off than they started
  • ⚠️ Never administer one. Zeducation facilitators are not registered psychometricians. If a client wants profiling, that is a referral

More resources

  • 📄 MBTI reliability and validity, a critical review (PDF)
  • 📄 An overview of the validity challenges
  • 📄 Aritzeta, Swailes & Senior (2007) on Belbin's psychometrics
  • 📄 Criteria Corp — four reasons never to use Myers-Briggs for hiring — including the retest problem: about half of people get a different type five weeks later
  • 📄 MBTI USA — MBTI for hiring, the publisher's own position — the publisher says do not do it. The strongest line to have ready
  • 🎬 How bad is the Myers-Briggs personality test? With psych researcher Randy Stein — a researcher, being fair about what it can and cannot do
  • 🎬 Why the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator is garbage — blunter, and useful when a room is attached to their four letters

Accommodating Diversity — ten things a leader can actually do

techniquepractitioner
diversityinclusioncultureleadershippracticalteamsworkplace

What it is in one line: ten concrete moves, most of them free, that turn a diverse team into a team where the difference actually gets used.

Origin: adapted by Zeducation from SRC-009, which offered ten ideas. Four were cut, three were added, and the order was changed so the ones that matter come first. See the bottom of the page. Evidence: practitioner. These are practice moves, not tested interventions, and nobody should claim otherwise. Best for: the leader who agrees with all of it and does not know what to do on Monday.

On this pageWhy this page existsThe ten movesWhat was cut, and whyWhat was added, and whyWorked example, a West Auckland manufacturing teamFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

Why this page exists

FRM-052 makes the case that difference only helps if it gets heard. This is the page about making it heard.

Most diversity training stops at awareness, which is why most of it changes nothing. Awareness without a next action is just a slightly uncomfortable afternoon.

The ten moves

The four that matter most

MoveWhy it is first
1Learn to say everyone's name properly. Ask. Write it down phonetically. Practise it. Then correct other people when they get it wrongIt is the smallest possible act and the one people remember for years. A person who has spent a decade answering to a shortened version of their own name knows exactly what that means
2Ask the quiet ones directly, by name, in advance. "In Thursday's meeting I want your read on the roster. Have a think."The single highest-return move on this list. Difference that is present and never asked is difference you are paying for and not using. See FRM-052
3Be flexible about time. Religious observance, school pickup, a tangi, Ramadan, a court date, a sick kidMost exclusion at work is a rostering decision, not an attitude
4Check the meeting calendar against the actual calendar. Do not schedule the big decision on Eid, Diwali, Christmas week or Sāmoan Independence DayMissing the meeting where it was decided is how people end up outside the team

The six that build on them

MoveWhat it looks like
5Put cultural awareness into induction, not into a one-off workshopA new starter learns how this team works with people in week one, alongside the health and safety
6Share kai, and let people bring their ownPotluck beats catering. It is the cheapest way for someone's background to become an asset in the room rather than a private fact
7Support the ones who are studyingFlexible hours around class. Pair them with someone further along. Zeducation's own learners are usually doing this on top of a job
8Make room for parents and carersSchool holidays, sick children, elderly parents. Say it out loud so people do not have to ask as a favour
9Acknowledge more than one faith, or noneIf there is a Christmas tree, there is room for the other dates too. And do not require anyone to have one
10Ask the team what would make this a better place to work, and then do one thingDoing one is worth more than asking about twenty. Never run this if you are not going to act

How to read it: 1 to 4 are free and immediate. 5 to 9 need a bit of organising. 10 is the one that makes the list yours rather than this page's.

What was cut, and why

Being honest about the editing. The original list was mostly good, and two items did not survive.

CutWhy
Hang a world map and pin everyone's birthplaceWell meant, and it makes migrant staff into exhibits. Some people do not want their origin on a wall in the hallway. Also flattens a Māori or Pacific staff member's relationship to this place into a pin like any other
Count and post the number of languages spokenSame problem. A statistic about people is not the same as valuing them
"Consider dietary needs when catering"Kept, but folded into move 6. As a standalone it is the item organisations do instead of the other nine

What was added, and why

AddedWhy
Move 2, ask the quiet ones by name, in advanceThe source has nothing on this and it is the move that connects accommodation to actual team performance. In advance matters: being put on the spot in a meeting is not inclusion
Move 4, check the calendarThe source has "avoid scheduling meetings on major cultural holidays". Made specific, because "major" is doing a lot of work in that sentence and usually means "ones I already know about"
Move 10, ask and then actThe source's list is entirely things done to a team. Nothing on it asks them

Worked example, a West Auckland manufacturing team

Twenty-two staff. Six languages. The team leader picks three moves for one quarter.

  • Move 1: spends one shift getting every name right, including the four he had been avoiding by saying "mate". Writes them phonetically on the back of the roster
  • Move 3: moves the Friday afternoon toolbox meeting to Friday morning, because three staff go to mosque at lunchtime and had been silently missing half of it for two years
  • Move 10: asks the team what would make the place better. Gets told the safety notices are in English only and two people have been guessing. Gets them translated

Cost: one afternoon and about $200. What changed: near-miss reporting went up, which is what you want, and two people who had never spoken in a toolbox meeting started to.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Do not read all ten aloud, that is a list not a session
  • Run ACT-091 The Ten Moves Audit, which is the whole point of the page, and ACT-092 Say My Name as the opener
  • The best question: "which one of these would your team notice by Friday?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Picking ten. Nobody does ten. Pick two and finish them
    • Doing the easy ones. Kai and a calendar are visible and cheap. Names and asking the quiet ones are the ones that change something
    • Asking without acting. Move 10 done badly is worse than not doing it. A team that gets asked and then sees nothing happen will not answer honestly again
    • Treating it as HR's job. Every move on this list belongs to whoever runs the shift
  • ⚠️ Do not let this replace the harder conversation. Accommodation is about making room. It does not address someone being talked over, passed up, or having their name mocked. That is FRM-033 Cultural Safety, and it is a different session

  • 📄 Waihanga Ara Rau — using Māori concepts to lift workplace culture and safety
  • 📄 Human Rights Commission — your rights at work
  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — flexible working arrangements
  • 📄 UNICEF — a manager's guide to nurturing neurodivergent talent (PDF) — concrete, free, and written for the manager rather than the policy team
  • 🔗 AskEARN — including neurodivergent workers: workspace, schedules and other accommodations — a long list of things that cost almost nothing
  • 📄 Ohio OOD — the employer's reasonable accommodation handbook (PDF) — worked scenarios, and the always ask, never assume rule

RIASEC — Holland's six interest types

modelmoderate
career-readinessinterestsriasecself-awarenessjob-searchwork-readiness

What it is in one line: six broad kinds of work people are drawn to, and the observation that people tend to look for workplaces full of others like them.

Origin: John L. Holland, from 1959, fully set out in Making Vocational Choices (3rd ed., 1997). It is the model behind Tahatū's interest quiz, the US O*NET Interest Profiler, and most careers tools worldwide. Evidence: moderate, and honestly mixed. See the audit below, because the headline claim is weaker than the way it is usually sold. Best for: the learner who has never once been asked what they actually like, and has no words for it.

On this pageThe six types⚠️ The evidence auditFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The six types

Nobody is one type. Everybody is a mix, usually described by the top two or three letters.

TypeDrawn toSounds like
RRealisticTools, machines, materials, outdoors, being physical"I like finishing the day and seeing what I built"
IInvestigativeWorking things out, data, diagnosis, research"I want to know why it broke"
AArtisticMaking, designing, performing, expressing"I'd rather it looked right than be quick"
SSocialTeaching, helping, caring, serving people"The best part of the job is the people"
EEnterprisingPersuading, selling, leading, running things"Put me in front of the customer"
CConventionalOrder, accuracy, systems, records"It should be right, and it should be filed"

How to read it: the six sit in a circle, and neighbours are similar while opposites are not. Realistic and Conventional get on. Realistic and Social pull hard against each other. That circular structure is the part of the theory with the strongest support.

⚠️ The evidence audit

Facilitators will ask whether this is another personality test. It is a fair question and it deserves a straight answer.

What holds up: the structure. Fifty years of studies find the six types really do arrange themselves in that reproducible circle across many populations. That is genuine structural validity and it is far more than MBTI's sixteen types can claim.

What is oversold: the promise. The idea that matching your interests to your job makes you happy is real but small.

ClaimWhat the research actually shows
Interest match → job satisfactionr ≈ .17 (Tsabari, Tziner & Meir, 2005, 53 studies). A separate meta-analysis of 27 studies found no significant overall relationship
Interest match → job performancearound .32. Stronger than the satisfaction link, which is not the direction most people assume
A warning signMethodologically weaker studies produced the strongest results. Discount the headline accordingly

➜ The honest line for a room: "This tells you what you're drawn to. It does not tell you what you'd be good at, and it is only a weak predictor of whether you'd be happy. It is a way of getting words for something you have never been asked about, and a way of finding jobs you had not heard of."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then send them to the Tahatū quiz and let the tool do the work
  • Run ACT-095 What's My Code?
  • The best question: "what does the result make you want to look up?" The list it opens is the value. The letters are not
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating the code as an identity. "I'm an RIC" is the failure mode. It is a description of current interests, and interests move
    • Using it to rule things out. It should only ever widen the list. A learner who tests low on Social can still be a brilliant support worker
    • Skipping the pay and demand check. An interest with no jobs in Auckland is a hobby. Tahatū's career profiles carry the numbers, so use them in the same session
  • ⚠️ Interests are shaped by what you have been exposed to. A young person who has never met an engineer will not test Investigative toward engineering. For learners whose exposure has been narrow, and that is many of Zeducation's, the quiz partly measures their opportunities so far, not their capacity. Say that out loud
  • ⚠️ Watch the gendered pattern. Realistic skews male and Social skews female in most samples, which reflects how people are raised as much as anything innate. Do not let a result quietly steer a young woman away from a trade

More resources

  • 📄 Tahatū Career Navigator — the interest quiz and 800+ career profiles
  • 📄 O*NET Interest Profiler, the US instrument this descends from
  • 📄 Nauta, M. (2010). The development, evolution, and status of Holland's theory (PDF)
  • 📄 Tsabari, Tziner & Meir (2005). Updated meta-analysis on congruence and satisfaction
  • 📄 EBSCO Research Starters — Holland's theory of career choice — the academic summary, and honest about the hexagon's limits
  • 📄 An application of Holland's theory to career interests (PDF, ERIC) — a study using it, so learners can see it tested rather than asserted
  • 🎬 Holland and the RIASEC model — the six types and the hexagon
  • 🎬 Holland's career choice theory — the RIASEC test — how the instrument is meant to be used

Transferable Skills — what you can already do

modelpractitioner
career-readinesstransferable-skillswork-readinesscvconfidencejob-search

What it is in one line: the skills you built somewhere nobody wrote down, which are the same skills the job ad is asking for, in different words.

Origin: Zeducation house model. The reframing comes from Tahatū, whose central idea is that a career is not one ladder and that skills carry across a working life, and from the skills taxonomies underneath O*NET. Evidence: practitioner. This is a translation tool, not a tested model, and it should not be presented as one. Best for: the learner who says "I haven't really got any experience" and has fifteen years of it.

On this pageThe problem this solvesThe five places skills come fromThe translationThe three-part evidence ruleFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The problem this solves

Ask most people what they can do and they answer with job titles. Kitchenhand. Caregiver. Mum.

Job ads do not ask for job titles. They ask for skills. And the gap between those two sentences is where a lot of good people stop applying.

"I've only ever worked in a kitchen." "So you've worked to a deadline every single night, under pressure, in a team, to a health and safety standard, in a second language. Which of those did you think didn't count?"

The five places skills come from

Most people count the first one and nothing else. The other four are where the good material is.

WhereWhat people miss
Paid workCounted. Usually described as duties rather than skills
Unpaid and familyRunning a household budget. Caring for a parent. Getting three kids somewhere on time. This is logistics, budgeting and care work
Church, marae, communityOrganising an event for 200 people. Handling money. Speaking in front of a room. Coordinating volunteers who do not have to turn up
Sport and cultureTurning up when you did not feel like it. Coaching. Being coached. Losing well
Study and self-taughtAnything learned from YouTube counts. Somebody taught themselves to weld, or edit video, or fix a car

The translation

This is the actual work. Left column is how a learner says it. Right column is how a job ad says it.

What they sayWhat it is called
"I just helped out at church"Volunteer coordination · event organisation
"I looked after my nana"Personal care · medication support · working with health professionals
"I did the food for the fono"Catering to budget and headcount · food safety
"I sorted my brother's phone plan"Advocacy · negotiating with providers
"I ran the till"Cash handling · reconciliation · customer service
"I translate for my parents"Bilingual · interpreting in high-stakes settings
"I got the kids to school every day"Reliability · logistics · time management
"I'm the one everyone rings"Trusted point of contact · problem solving under pressure

➜ Nothing in the right column is a lie. That is the whole point, and it is worth saying to a room that is worried about overselling. Naming a skill accurately is not exaggeration. Most people are doing the opposite, and it is costing them jobs.

The three-part evidence rule

A skill on a CV is a claim. A claim without evidence is noise. So each one gets three parts:

Example
SkillThe employer's words"Cash handling and reconciliation"
WhereThe real setting, however informal"Two years on the till at a family takeaway"
ProofA number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it"Balanced the float nightly. Never short."

⚠️ The proof column is the one people skip, and it is the one that gets read.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes, and spend most of it on the translation table
  • Run ACT-094 The Skills You Don't Count
  • The best question: "what do people ring you about?" It gets past modesty faster than anything else, because people will describe a skill happily when it is framed as other people's opinion
  • Common mistakes:
    • Doing the translating for them. They have to say it, or it will not survive an interview
    • Stopping at the list. A list of skills with no evidence is worse than three skills with proof
    • Letting "soft skills" become filler. "Good communicator" on its own is wallpaper. See FRM-058
  • ⚠️ Care with unpaid work, especially for women and for Pacific and Māori learners. Years of caring and community work are real skills, and some employers still discount them. Teach the translation, and be honest that not every employer will value it equally. That is a reason to evidence it harder, not to leave it off
  • ⚠️ Never inflate. There is a line between naming a skill properly and claiming one you do not have, and an interview finds it in about ninety seconds. Anything on the page must survive "tell me about a time you did that"

More resources

  • 📄 O*NET OnLine — the skills taxonomy behind most careers tools
  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — starting work
  • 📄 Indeed — transferable skills: 10 skills that work across industries — the plainest list, and the one a learner will actually finish
  • 📄 Columbia Career Design Lab — the power of transferable skills in career transitions — how to translate one industry's words into another's
  • 📄 TopResume — what are transferable skills, and how to change careers with them — written for somebody with no experience in the field they want
  • 🎬 How to change careers using transferable skills you already have — Indeed — short, and pitched at somebody with no confidence in their own list
  • 🎬 How to identify your transferable skills — National Careers Service webinar — a government careers service running the exercise properly

The CV That Gets Read

techniquepractitioner
career-readinesscvjob-searchwork-readinesswritingats

What it is in one line: your CV gets a few seconds and a keyword scan before a human decides anything, so the top third has to do almost all the work.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written to sit alongside Tahatū's CV templates and Job Hunters' Workbook, which are free, NZ standard, and should be what learners actually type into. Evidence: practitioner. The "six seconds" figure you see everywhere comes from small eye-tracking studies by a recruitment vendor and should not be quoted as fact. What is not in dispute is that screening is fast and often filtered by software first. Best for: the learner who has applied for forty jobs and heard nothing.

On this pageTwo readers, in this orderThe shapeDuties versus achievementsTailoring, which is non-negotiableFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

Two readers, in this order

Most CV advice fails because it optimises for the wrong one.

Reads firstWants
1. The softwareIncreasingly, an applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the job ad
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA quick answer to "can this person do the job?"

⚠️ A beautiful CV that the software cannot read is not a CV. Columns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos and PDFs-of-images all break parsers. Tahatū's templates are safe. A Canva design often is not.

The shape

Everything above the fold is B and C. That is the whole strategy.

SectionThe rule
ContactPhone, email, suburb. No full street address, no date of birth, no photo. In New Zealand a photo invites discrimination and gives nothing back
HeadlineOne line, rewritten for every job. "Warehouse assistant with forklift F endorsement and four years on nights." Not "hardworking team player seeking opportunity"
Skill bulletsThree to five, in the job ad's words, each with the evidence from FRM-057
Work historyWhat changed because you were there, not what you were told to do
TrainingLicences, tickets and endorsements go high if the job needs them. A Class 2 or a Site Safe card can be the whole reason you get called
RefereesNamed, asked first, and briefed on which job it is

Duties versus achievements

The single biggest lift available on most CVs.

Duty, which everyone writesAchievement, which gets read
"Responsible for stock""Cut stock discrepancies from weekly to almost none over six months"
"Customer service""Handled the complaints desk on Saturdays, the busiest shift"
"Cleaning duties""Held the kitchen at an A grade through two council inspections"
"Worked in a team""Trained four new starters, three of whom are still there"

➜ The test: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is a duty. Make it specific to you.

Tailoring, which is non-negotiable

One CV sent to forty jobs is why nobody called. Tailoring is not a rewrite. It is fifteen minutes:

  1. Print the job ad. Highlight every skill word.
  2. Rewrite the headline for this job, using its words
  3. Reorder the skill bullets so the ones it asked for are first
  4. Check the licence or ticket it names is visible without scrolling

⚠️ Use their words, not your synonyms. If the ad says "forklift licence" do not write "counterbalance certification". Software matches text, not meaning.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Then get them into Tahatū's builder rather than a blank Word document
  • Run ACT-096 Seven Seconds to open and ACT-097 The Tailoring Lab to apply
  • Common mistakes:
    • Design over parsing. See the warning above
    • An objective statement. "Seeking a challenging role in a dynamic company" says nothing. Replace it with the headline
    • Listing every job since 2004. Ten to fifteen years is plenty. Anything older is one line
    • Referees "available on request". Just name them. It reads as delay
    • No numbers anywhere. One number changes the whole page
  • ⚠️ Gaps are normal and they are not a scandal. Illness, caring, redundancy, prison, raising kids, a visa. Teach a one-line honest account and move on. The gap is rarely the problem; the panic about it is. See ACT-100
  • ⚠️ Names and discrimination are real. New Zealand research has found candidates with non-Pākehā names get fewer callbacks. Never advise a learner to anglicise their name. Do tell them why networks and referrals matter so much, which is FRM-061

More resources

  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — applying for a job
  • 📄 Human Rights Commission — discrimination in employment

⚠️ GAP: the "six seconds" and "75% of CVs are rejected by software" figures circulate everywhere and both trace back to vendor marketing rather than independent research. This page deliberately does not use them, and neither should a facilitator.

  • 🔗 Work and Income — CVs and cover letters — the New Zealand one, and what MSD-referred learners will already have been shown

  • 🎬 Ten resume writing tips from a recruiter — somebody who reads them for a living

The STAR Interview Answer — Situation, Task, Action, Result

techniquestrong
career-readinessinterviewsstarjob-searchwork-readinessstorytelling
On this page⚠️ Name clash, read this firstThe modelWorked example, a warehouse interviewThe three questions everyone getsFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

⚠️ Name clash, read this first

This is not FRM-003 STAR.

Stands forWhat it is for
FRM-003 STARStory · Tools and techniques · Apply · ReflectZeducation's teaching recipe. How a facilitator builds a session
FRM-059 STAR (this page)Situation · Task · Action · ResultA learner's interview answer. How a candidate tells a story about themselves

Two different things, same four letters, both in this library and both genuinely called STAR in the wild. Say which one you mean, every time. In any session where both could come up, call this one "the STAR answer" and FRM-003 "the STAR session shape".

What it is in one line: a four-part shape that turns "tell me about a time you…" from a panic into a story with a point.

Origin: the behavioural interviewing tradition, which took hold from the 1970s on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour better than hypothetical questions do. No single author owns STAR; it is the standard teaching shape across the recruitment industry, and Tahatū's Job Hunters' Workbook teaches it too. Evidence: strong, for the underlying method rather than the acronym. Structured behavioural interviews are among the better-validated selection tools available, and clearly outperform unstructured "have a chat" interviews. The four letters are a memory aid on top of that. Best for: anyone who freezes, rambles, or answers in the abstract.

The model

What goes in itHow long
SSituationWhere and when. Enough to picture it1 sentence
TTaskWhat you specifically had to do. Not the team. You1 sentence
AActionWhat you did, step by step. This is most of the answer3-4 sentences
RResultWhat happened. A number if you have one, a lesson if you do not1-2 sentences

How to read it: A is the answer. Most people spend ninety seconds on Situation, run out of nerve, and finish with "so yeah, it worked out." Flip the proportions.

Worked example, a warehouse interview

Question: "Tell me about a time you dealt with pressure."

Weak answer: "Yeah I'm pretty good under pressure, we were busy heaps, especially Christmas, and you just get on with it aye."

STAR answer:

S: "Last Christmas we were two people down on the night shift for a fortnight." T: "I was the senior on nights, so getting the trucks loaded by six was on me." A: "I split the crew into two teams instead of four so nobody was working alone. I moved the pick order so the biggest customer's pallets got done first, in case we ran out of time. And I rang the day supervisor each morning to tell him exactly what was left, so he wasn't finding out at nine." R: "We got every truck out on time except one, which went an hour late. The day team said it was the first Christmas they hadn't inherited a mess."

➜ The result is not heroic. It contains a failure — one truck went late — and the answer is stronger for it. Perfect results sound rehearsed.

The three questions everyone gets

Prepare these and most interviews are covered:

  1. Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult person. → the answer lives in TOP-COM-002
  2. Tell me about a time something went wrong. → they want to know if you own it. Never blame the absent
  3. Tell me about a time you worked in a team. → make sure "I" appears, not only "we"

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then straight into practice. This one dies on a slide
  • Run ACT-099 The STAR Answer Lab
  • Prepare four stories, not twenty answers. Four good STAR stories flex to cover most questions. Trying to script every question is why people freeze when one is worded differently
  • Common mistakes:
    • "We" all the way through. The panel cannot hire the team. Make them say "I"
    • No result. The story just stops. Ask "and then what happened?" every single time
    • A twelve-minute Situation. One sentence. Timebox it in practice
    • Only glorious stories. A story where something went wrong and they fixed it is usually better
  • ⚠️ Culturally, "I" is genuinely hard for some learners. In many Pacific and Māori settings, claiming individual credit is poor form and the group comes first. That instinct is right at home and costly in a Pākehā interview room. Do not tell them their upbringing is wrong. Name the clash, and give them the bridge: "our team did X, and my part was Y." Both true, both comfortable. Same territory as FRM-042's culture barrier

  • 📄 Indeed — how to use the STAR interview response technique — with a worked video example
  • 📄 University of Washington Careers — the STAR method of interviewing — a careers service's own handout
  • 📄 The STAR method of behavioral interviewing (PDF) — printable, with question banks to practise against
  • 🎬 STAR method interview: how to answer behavioural questions, with examples — a full worked answer
  • 🎬 22 STAR method interview questions and answers — a bank to practise against
