The Four-Sentence Cover Letter

techniquepractitioner
career-readinesscover-letterjob-searchwritingwork-readiness

What it is in one line: four sentences that answer the only four questions a hiring manager has, which is three paragraphs shorter than what most people send and considerably more likely to be read.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written because cover letters are where learners stall hardest. Sits alongside Tahatū's cover letter templates. Evidence: practitioner. There is no research saying four sentences beats five. What is defensible is that short and specific beats long and generic, and that a letter which never gets written beats nothing at all. Best for: the learner who has been staring at a blank page for two days and has now decided not to apply.

On this pageThe four sentencesWorked exampleWhat to cutFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The four sentences

SentenceAnswers
1Which job, and one reason you want this one. Name the employer"Why are you writing?"
2The single strongest thing you bring, in the ad's own words, with evidence"Can you do it?"
3One specific thing about them. A project, a value, a location, a customer"Do you actually want us?"
4What happens next. "I'm available from the 12th and happy to come in any time""What now?"

Worked example

Job: Support worker, an Auckland disability provider.

Kia ora Sarah, [1] I'm applying for the support worker role at your Māngere site, because the shifts fit around my study and I've wanted to move into disability support since caring for my grandfather. [2] I've got two years of personal care experience, including medication support and working alongside district nurses, and I've just finished my Level 3 in Health and Wellbeing. [3] I noticed your team runs the community garden programme at that site. That's exactly the kind of support work I want to be part of, rather than only in-home. [4] I'm available from 12 August and can come in for a chat any weekday. My CV is attached. Ngā mihi, Losa

Ninety seconds of a manager's time. Every sentence earns its place. Sentence 3 is the one almost nobody writes, and it is the one that shows this was not sent to forty employers.

What to cut

CutWhy
"I am writing to apply for the position advertised on Seek"They know. It wastes the best line on the page
"I am a hardworking team player with excellent communication skills"Everyone writes it, so it says nothing. Replace with evidence
Retelling the whole CVThe CV is attached. The letter is the reason to open it
"Thank you for taking the time to consider my application"Harmless, and it is not a sentence that gets you an interview
An apology for anythingNever apologise for a gap, a career change, or being new

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. The example does most of the work
  • Run ACT-098 Four Sentences
  • The best move: have them write sentence 3 first. It is the hardest and it forces them to actually look the employer up, which is the real skill hiding inside this exercise
  • Common mistakes:
    • No name. "Dear Sir/Madam" on an ad that lists a contact person is a tell. Ring and ask if it is not there
    • Sentence 3 invented. "I've always admired your commitment to excellence" is worse than leaving it out. It must be something real they found
    • Writing it before the CV. Sentence 2 comes straight out of FRM-057. Do the skills work first
  • ⚠️ On using AI to write it: learners will, and Tahatū's own workbook covers it. The honest position is that AI is fine for tidying and terrible at sentence 3, because it does not know the employer and will invent something. Anything it writes must be checked against the truth, and sentence 3 should always be theirs

  • 📄 Enhancv — six short cover letter examples — full worked letters at 100-200 words
  • 📄 Resume.io — eleven short cover letter samples — more examples, by industry

How Jobs Are Actually Found — the four channels

modelmoderate
career-readinessjob-searchnetworkingweak-tieswork-readinesshidden-job-marketdirect-approach

What it is in one line: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds, and none into the one that actually works.

Origin: Zeducation house model. The evidence underneath it is FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties — Mark Granovetter's finding that people hear about jobs far more often through acquaintances than through close friends, because close friends know the same openings you already know about. Evidence: moderate. Granovetter's core finding has held up over fifty years and across countries. The specific percentages people quote for "the hidden job market" are not reliable and this page deliberately gives none. Best for: the learner who has sent sixty online applications, heard nothing, and concluded there are no jobs.

➜ This framework has its own topic. See TOP-EMP-005 The Jobs Nobody Advertises for the full 120-150 minute session built around it.

On this pageThe four channelsWhy the job was never advertisedThe moveFour ways into channels 2, 3 and 4Why this matters more for Zeducation's learners, not lessFacilitating itMore resourcesUsed byRelated frameworks

The four channels

ChannelWhat it isCompetitionEffort per application
1. Advertised, applied coldSeek, Trade Me Jobs, the company websiteHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering firstLow per application, terrible odds
2. Advertised, with someone insideSame ad, but somebody hands your CV over or mentions your nameMuch lower. You start as a known quantityMedium
3. Not advertised, filled by word of mouthThe manager asks the team "know anyone?" before it is ever written upLow, and most people never see theseMedium
4. Created for youSomebody meets you and finds work for youLowest of all, and rareHigh, and slow

How to read it: channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing — people who know you exist. That is what makes this teachable. It is one habit, not three.

Why the job was never advertised

This is the part that stops it sounding like a conspiracy, and it is the question every room asks. Teach it before the channels, not after.

The employer's reasonWhat it actually means
Advertising costs money and timePosting the ad, then reading two hundred applications, then interviewing. That is a fortnight of somebody's work
There is already an internal candidateSomeone in the building who knows how the place runs
Referral programmesEmployers ask their own staff first, because a workmate's recommendation is a known quantity

➜ Say this out loud: "They are not hiding it from you. They are trying not to do two weeks of work."

That reframe does more than any tactic on this page. A learner who thinks the hidden job market is a closed club stays out of it. A learner who understands it is a tired manager taking the easy option can see exactly where to stand.

⚠️ And the flip side, which follows from the same logic. If the manager is avoiding the work, then a person who turns up already vouched for is doing them a favour, not asking for one. That is the whole psychology of channels 2, 3 and 4 in one sentence.

The move

Not "network", which is a word that makes most people close down. Tell people what you are looking for.

Most people do not know what their cousin's boss does, and their cousin's boss does not know they are looking. Both problems are fixed by one sentence, said out loud, to twenty people.

The sentence has three parts:

  1. What you are looking for. Specific. "Warehouse or storeperson work" beats "anything going"
  2. What you bring. One thing. "I've got my F endorsement"
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"

➜ Said to a cousin, a neighbour, the person at church, a former supervisor, the parent at the school gate. Twenty of those beats sixty online applications, and it is less work.

Four ways into channels 2, 3 and 4

The sentence is the main one. These four are how you create chances to say it.

The way inWhat it looks like here
1Tell the people you already knowThe list from ACT-101. Cousin, neighbour, church, former supervisor, the parent at the school gate
2Ask inside where you already workA large share of unadvertised jobs are internal. If you are in work and want a change, ask around other departments before you look outside. Do it discreetly, and be straight with your supervisor once you are actually applying
3Go straight to the employerA walk-in, a phone call, or a short written message to a real named person. Not asking for a job in the first sentence. Practised in ACT-108
4VolunteerUnpaid work in a place you would like to be paid. It produces referees, referrals and somebody who has seen you turn up on time. Most of our learners are already doing this at church, at a club, or on a marae and have never counted it

And one signal worth watching. A company announcing a new site, a new contract or a new shift is a company about to need people. A new distribution centre in Drury, a supermarket fit-out, a rest home wing, a roading contract awarded. That is the moment to ring, not three months later when the ad goes up.

⚠️ Channels 2, 3 and 4 all still run on a name. Direct approaches and online profiles are places where a non-Pākehā name gets fewer callbacks, the same as cold applications. The answer is never to change the name. It is that a person who has met you, or been told about you by somebody they trust, is no longer a name on a screen.

Why this matters more for Zeducation's learners, not less

Two things are true at once and both should be said in the room.

The good news: Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That is a real advantage and it is usually going completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that it is allowed.

The hard part: New Zealand research has found candidates with non-Pākehā names get fewer callbacks from cold applications. Channel 1 is where that bias bites hardest, because a name on a screen is all there is. Channels 2, 3 and 4 route around it, because somebody has already vouched for you.

⚠️ That is not a reason to hide a name. It is a reason to spend the effort where it pays. Never advise a learner to anglicise their name.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes
  • Run ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?
  • The best question: "who is the last person you told that you're looking?" Most rooms go quiet
  • Common mistakes:
    • Quoting a percentage for the hidden job market. The figures circulating are unsourced. Say "most", say "often", do not say "80%"
    • Making it sound like schmoozing. It is one honest sentence to people who already know you
    • Skipping channel 1 entirely. Advertised jobs are real jobs. The point is proportion, not abandonment
    • Teaching the tactics before the reason. The employer's-side explanation is what makes the rest land. Without it the room hears "the system is rigged"
    • Importing advice written for somebody else. Alumni associations, professional bodies, conferences, business cards and informational interviews all assume a white-collar career. The New Zealand equivalents are careers expos, open days, industry training organisations, unions, and the person you already know who works there. See SRC-013
  • ⚠️ Do not let this become "it's who you know, so why bother". For a learner who feels shut out, this framework can land as confirmation the system is rigged. Turn it the other way: you already have a network, you just have not used it, and using it is free

  • 📄 Tahatū — career profiles and job-hunting guidance

The Questions You Ask Them

techniquepractitioner
career-readinessinterviewsquestionsjob-searchwork-readinessfollow-up

What it is in one line: every interview ends with "do you have any questions for us?", most people say no, and it is the only moment in the whole hour where the power in the room is level.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written after SRC-011 showed the library taught how to answer and stopped there. Evidence: practitioner. There is no study saying three questions beats two. What is defensible is that "no, I think you've covered everything" reads as no interest, and that an interview is a two-way decision whether or not the candidate is treating it as one. Best for: the learner who prepares hard for the questions coming at them and has nothing for the last five minutes.

On this pageWhy "no" costs youThe four kinds of questionThe questions that are fine to ask, and the ones that waitThree that do not workAfter the interviewFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

Why "no" costs you

Three separate things happen when somebody says they have no questions.

What the interviewer takes from it
InterestYou did not care enough to think of one
JudgementYou are willing to take a job you know almost nothing about
The last impressionIt is the final thing that happens. It is what they remember at the table afterwards

➜ And a fourth thing, which matters more than all of them: you have just agreed to spend forty hours a week somewhere without asking a single thing about it.

The four kinds of question

Take three in, from at least two different rows. Written down, on paper, and it is fine to read them.

KindExamples
1The job"What does a normal day look like in this role?" · "What would you want me to have got on top of in the first month?" · "What's the hardest part of this job?"
2The people"Who would I be working with day to day?" · "How does the team hand over between shifts?" · "How long has the person doing this job been here?"
3The future"Is there training or a ticket the company puts people through?" · "Where have people gone from this role?"
4The process"What are the next steps, and when will you be in touch?"

⚠️ Question 4 is not optional and it goes last. It is the one that gets you a date instead of a fortnight of refreshing your email.

The questions that are fine to ask, and the ones that wait

This is where learners get bad advice from everywhere at once.

Ask it in the interviewWait until they offer you the job
The shift pattern and the rosterWhether you can swap shifts
Whether the pay range in the ad is rightNegotiating the number
Whether there is training or a ticketWhether they will pay for a course you want
Start date and next stepsTime off you have already booked, unless it is soon

➜ Pay is allowed. Learners are told constantly that asking about money looks greedy. Asking "the ad said $26 to $28, is that right for this role?" is not greed, it is checking you can afford to take the job. The negotiation is a different conversation and it happens after the offer.

⚠️ If you have something already booked in the next few weeks — a funeral, a wedding, a court date, a tangi, a trip home — say it at the end of the interview, not after you start. It is almost always fine, and it is very much not fine as a surprise in week one.

Three that do not work

QuestionWhy it lands badly
"How did I do?"Puts them on the spot and reads as anxious. Ask about the process instead
Anything answered on their websiteIt says you did not look. This is the risk of a memorised list
"What does the company do?"Same problem, larger

After the interview

Two moves, and the whole thing takes five minutes.

WhenWhat
Same dayA short thank-you email or text to whoever arranged it. Three lines. Name one thing from the conversation so it is obviously not a template
After the date they gave youIf the day they named has passed, follow up once. Politely, and once

And when there is silence: it is usually the process, not you. Restructures, an internal candidate, the manager on leave. Follow up once, then put it down and keep applying. The learner who stops applying while waiting on one answer is the one this framework is really for.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The four rows are the whole model
  • Run ACT-102 Three Questions
  • The best move: at the end of every roleplay in ACT-099, make the interviewer finish with "do you have any questions for us?" Nobody has an answer the first time. After a fortnight everybody does
  • Common mistakes:
    • A memorised list, asked regardless. If they answered it during the interview, say so and ask a different one. That is why you take three
    • Questions that are really complaints. "How much overtime is there?" asked in a certain tone is heard as "I don't want to do any"
    • Not writing them down. Under pressure the questions evaporate. Paper is allowed and it looks prepared, not weak
  • ⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, questioning someone older or in authority is not straightforward. Do not treat that as a confidence gap to be fixed. Name it, and offer the framing that works: "Can I ask you something about the job?" Asking permission first makes it comfortable and it costs nothing

More resources

  • 📄 Harvard Business Review — 38 smart questions to ask in a job interview — the best list there is, sorted by what you are trying to find out
  • 📄 Indeed — good questions to ask at the end of an interview — the plain version, with examples
  • 📄 San José State — excellent questions to ask at the end of your next job interview — a careers service's own list
  • 📄 Interview Boss — fifteen questions you could ask at the end of your interview — Australasian, so the tone fits a NZ room
  • 📄 Seven killer questions to ask an interviewer, and three to avoid — the three to avoid matter as much as the seven
  • 🎬 The best questions to ask at the end of your job interview — from a recruiter, with the reasoning for each
  • 🎬 Ten best questions to ask in an interview — worked delivery, so learners hear the tone as well as the words

FRM-063Framework · Wellbeing & Identity

Te Whare Tapa Whā

modelstrong adoption, practitioner outcomes
wellbeinghauorate-whare-tapa-wharesiliencemaoriidentityholistic

What it is in one line: wellbeing as a wharenui with four walls and a foundation, where letting any one wall go weakens the whole house.

Origin: Sir Mason Durie, developed at Hui Taumata in 1984. It was a response to Rapuora, research carried out between 1978 and 1980 by the Māori Women's Welfare League into the health barriers Māori were actually experiencing. Evidence: it is a model, not an intervention, so the honest word is not "proven". What is true is that it is the standard wellbeing framework across New Zealand health, education and social services, and that it is the framework that got wairua acknowledged in health practice in this country. See the audit below. Best for: any room where wellbeing is being taught, and especially the learner who thinks wellbeing means going to the gym.

On this pageThe whareWhy it matters for resilience specifically⚠️ The evidence auditFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The whare

How to read it: four walls on one foundation. A whare with three walls does not stand, and that is the whole argument.

PouWhat it holdsWhat "needs care" looks like on a Tuesday
Taha wairuaSpirit, purpose, faith, what makes life mean somethingYou have not been to church, to the moana, or anywhere quiet, in a month
Taha hinengaroMind, emotions, how you think and feelYou are snapping at people and cannot say why
Taha tinanaThe body. Sleep, food, movement, healthFour hours a night and takeaways since Tuesday
Taha whānauFamily, relationships, the people you belong toYou have not rung your mum in three weeks
Taha whenuaConnection to place, land, roots, where you are fromYou have been in Auckland eight years and never been home

⚠️ Whenua is the foundation, not a fifth wall. It sits underneath the other four, which is the point. Somebody disconnected from where they are from is standing on a floor that moves.

Why it matters for resilience specifically

Each pou does a different job when you get knocked around.

PouWhat it gives you when things go wrong
TinanaSteadies the stress. Sleep and food change what a problem feels like before they change anything else
HinengaroLets you think straight enough to make a decision you will not regret
WhānauThe backup. Somebody to ring, somebody who turns up
WairuaThe reason to keep going when there is no short-term reason
WhenuaKnowing who you are and where you are from, when a setback is telling you that you are nothing

➜ This is why "just be more resilient" is bad advice. It aims at hinengaro alone and ignores the four things holding it up.

⚠️ The evidence audit

Facilitators get asked whether this is evidence-based. Answer it straight.

What is true: it is the most widely adopted wellbeing framework in Aotearoa. It is used by the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand, the Mental Health Foundation, schools under the New Zealand Curriculum's hauora concept, ACC and most social services. It has been in continuous use for over forty years.

What is not the claim: nobody has run a randomised trial on "using Te Whare Tapa Whā". It is a way of organising what wellbeing consists of, not a treatment. Asking whether it is proven is a category error, in the same way you would not ask for a trial on the food pyramid's shape.

What it genuinely did: before it, spiritual wellbeing was not something a New Zealand health practitioner was expected to ask about. After it, it was. That is a real change and it is traceable.

➜ The honest line for a room: "This is not a therapy. It is a picture of what a whole person is made of, built out of Māori women's research into their own communities, and it has held up for forty years because it describes something true."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Draw the whare on the board as you talk. Do not use a slide
  • Run ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall
  • The best question: "which wall have you been letting go?" Most rooms answer honestly and fast, because the model gives them a word for something they already knew
  • Pair it with FRM-065 Fonofale. Offering only one model to a mixed room tells half of it which half counts. Teach both, let people choose
  • Common mistakes:
    • Scoring the walls out of ten. It turns a picture into a test. One thing per wall that needs care is all it is for
    • Treating wairua as religion. For some people it is. For others it is the moana, music, a garden, or their kids. Do not narrow it
    • Skipping whenua because it is awkward for migrants. It is not awkward, it is often the most important pou in the room. Ask about where they are from, not where they live
    • Using it as a checklist for someone else. It is a self-check. Never fill one in about a learner
  • ⚠️ Say whose it is. Durie's name, 1984, Hui Taumata, and the Māori Women's Welfare League research underneath it. Teaching a Māori model without attribution is exactly the habit this library exists to break

More resources

  • 🔗 Mental Health Foundation — Te Whare Tapa Whā
  • 🔗 Healthify — Te whare tapa whā and wellbeing
  • 🔗 Te Ara — Māori health: te whare tapa whā model
  • 📄 Health Quality & Safety Commission — Te Whare Tapa Whā resource (PDF)
  • 🎬 Overview of Te Whare Tapa Whā — Ministry of Health NZ — Sir Mason Durie explaining his own model. Play this rather than describing it
  • 🎬 The significance of Te Whare Tapa Whā — Ministry of Health NZ — Durie on why it was needed and what it changed
  • 📄 Stuff — four walls of the whare: recognising our health beyond the physical — a newspaper version, pitched at anyone

The ABC Model of Resilience — Accept, Believe, Commit

techniquepractitioner, with a strong anchor under step B
wellbeingresilienceabc-modelsetbacksself-efficacyhouse-contentaction
On this page⚠️ Name clash, read this firstThe modelWorked exampleWhere the evidence actually isThe confidence checkFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

⚠️ Name clash, read this first

This is not Ellis's ABC, which is the one a counsellor, a psychology student or a Google search will mean.

Stands forWhat it is
FRM-064 ABC (this page)Accept · Believe · CommitZeducation's house tool for getting moving after a setback
Ellis's ABC (1950s, REBT)Activating event · Belief · ConsequenceA therapy model about how beliefs, not events, produce feelings

Same three letters, different models. Say "the ABC of resilience" when you introduce it, and if somebody in the room names Ellis, they are right and it is a good moment rather than an awkward one.

⚠️ And a second one to know about. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) shares "accept" and "commit" as its two anchors. It is a clinical therapy delivered by clinicians. This is a workshop tool. Do not let the resemblance turn a facilitator into a therapist.

What it is in one line: three steps that take you from spinning your wheels after a setback to having one small thing you are actually going to do.

Origin: Zeducation house model, from the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide. Evidence: practitioner overall, but step B has a genuinely strong anchor and it is worth knowing which part of this is doing the work. See below. Best for: the moment after something goes wrong, when somebody has been going over it for three days and nothing has moved.

The model

How to read it: in order, and C is the point. A and B without C is a nice conversation that changes nothing by Friday.

StepThe questionWhat it does
AAcceptWhat actually happened, and what can I control?Stops the spinning. Splits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannot
BBelieveWhen have I got through something like this before?Replaces doubt with evidence. Evidence, not a pep talk
CCommitWhat is one small thing I will do, and when?Turns insight into momentum. Fifteen minutes, with a time on it

Worked example

Situation: you have been turned down for a job you thought you had.
Accept"They said no. I can't change that. I can control whether I ring and ask why, and whether I apply for the other two this week."
Believe"I got the warehouse job in March and I had less experience then. I've got Mere, who knows people at the DC."
Commit"Tomorrow at 10, I'll ring and ask what would have made the difference. Done means I've asked one question and written the answer down."

➜ Notice what the commitment is not. It is not "be more positive" or "get back out there". It is one action, with a time, and a definition of done. That is what makes it a commitment instead of an intention.

Where the evidence actually is

Be honest about which part of this is backed and which part is craft.

StepWhat holds it up
A · AcceptThe control / no-control split is old, practical and uncontroversial. Not a research finding, a useful distinction
B · BelieveThe strongest part. "Remember your past wins" is exactly Bandura's mastery experiences, which the self-efficacy literature consistently finds to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief. Direct personal evidence of having done a hard thing beats encouragement from anyone else, every time
C · CommitSmall, specific, time-boxed action is standard behavioural practice. The specificity is what does the work, not the size

➜ The line worth saying out loud: "Being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can do it. Remembering that you already did is the strongest. That is why step B asks for a past win and not a compliment."

⚠️ What this is not. It is not a treatment for depression, anxiety, grief or trauma. It is a tool for a setback. Know the difference and know where to send somebody: their GP, 1737 to call or text free, or a workplace EAP.

The confidence check

The house worksheet asks for confidence out of 10 before planning and after. Keep it.

  • It is a teaching mirror, not a measure. Nothing is validated and nothing should be recorded against anyone
  • The movement is the lesson. People routinely go from a 3 to a 6 in fifteen minutes without anything about the situation changing, which is the most persuasive demonstration of the model available
  • If it does not move, that is information too, and it usually means step C is still too big

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes with one worked example
  • Run ACT-106 The ABC Worksheet
  • The best move: do the whole thing on a real, current, small setback from the room rather than a hypothetical. It has to be somebody's actual week or it stays theoretical
  • Common mistakes:
    • Accept heard as "get over it". It is not. It is naming the facts so you can stop arguing with them and start on the part that moves. Say that explicitly, because the word does real damage otherwise
    • A step C that is a whole project. "Sort out my CV" is not a step. "Open the file and rewrite the top three lines, Tuesday 7pm" is
    • Skipping B. It is the step that gets rushed and it is the one with the research behind it
    • Using it on something too big. A bereavement is not a setback to ABC your way through
  • ⚠️ Somebody's "setback" will turn out to be much bigger than a setback. Have your referrals ready before you run it, and never push a learner to share the situation itself

More resources

  • 📄 Gollwitzer — Implementation Intentions (PDF) — the evidence for step C. A plan with a when and a where beats a good intention
  • 📄 Masten — Ordinary magic: resilience processes in development (PDF) — the framing that has to come before the tool: resilience is common, not rare
  • 📄 Simply Psychology — Bandura's social learning theory and self-efficacy — the evidence for step B. Mastery experiences beat encouragement
  • 📄 Positive Psychology — Albert Ellis's ABC model (REBT) — ⚠️ the name clash. A different ABC, from therapy. Read it so you can tell the room which one this is not
  • 📄 Implementation intention — Wikipedia — the if-then plan, and where it stops working
  • 🎬 Resilience is a skill, not a trait — Vikram Rai, TEDx — the framing that has to come before the tool
  • 🎬 Resilience: a trainable skill, not an innate trait — short, and it makes the same argument in a workplace register

Fonofale — the Pacific model of health

modelstrong adoption, practitioner outcomes
wellbeinghauorafonofalepacificresilienceidentityholistic

What it is in one line: wellbeing as a fale, where culture is the roof, aiga is the floor, four pou hold it up, and the whole house sits inside its environment, its time and its context.

Origin: Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann, developed in the New Zealand context and drawing on Cook Islands, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Niuean and Tokelauan values. It has been accepted by the Mental Health Commission as a standard for Pacific mental health. Evidence: a model, not an intervention, so the same honesty applies as with FRM-063. What is true is that it is the standard Pacific wellbeing framework in this country and has been for decades. Best for: any Zeducation room, and non-negotiable in a Pacific one.

On this pageWhy this page existsThe faleFonofale and Te Whare Tapa Whā side by sideWhy it matters for resilienceFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

Why this page exists

The SKILL UP Building Resilience guide teaches Te Whare Tapa Whā and stops there. It is a good model and it is not the only one.

➜ A room that is offered only one model is being told which half of itself counts. Teach both, side by side, and let people work in the one that is theirs.

The fale

How to read it: the roof and the floor are not optional extras. Culture shelters the whole house, and aiga is what everything stands on. That is a different claim from a Western model that starts with the individual.

PartWhat it holds
Roof · cultureYour beliefs and value system. What protects and shelters the rest
Floor · aigaFamily. Not only immediate. Extended, and anyone you are linked to by partnership or agreement
Pou · spiritualFaith, religious belief, connection with the sacred. Self-awareness, identity and purpose
Pou · physicalThe body. Healthy behaviours, managing illness
Pou · mentalEmotions, thinking, communication, the motivation to get somewhere. Not only mental illness
Pou · otherAge, gender, sexuality, socioeconomic status. The things that shape your wellbeing whether anyone names them or not
Environment, time, contextWhere you are, when this is, and what is going on around it

⚠️ The pou are continuous and interactive. They connect the roof to the floor and each other. Working on one moves the others, which is the same argument Te Whare Tapa Whā makes.

Fonofale and Te Whare Tapa Whā side by side

Not the same model, and the differences are the interesting part.

Te Whare Tapa WhāFonofale
ShapeWharenui, four wallsFale, roof and floor and four pou
FamilyTaha whānau, one of four wallsAiga is the floor. Everything stands on it
CultureCarried through whenua and wairuaCulture is the roof. Named on its own
The fourth elementTaha wairua"Other" — age, gender, sexuality, money
What surrounds itWhenua as the foundationEnvironment, time and context as a circle around the whole fale

➜ The "other" pou is the one that does something no other wellbeing model here does. It puts money, age, gender and sexuality inside the picture of health instead of outside it. For a learner who is broke, or young, or takatāpui, that is the difference between a model that describes them and one that does not.

Why it matters for resilience

PartWhat it gives you when things go wrong
AigaThe floor. In practice this is who feeds you, who has your kids, who lends you the money
CultureThe roof. What tells you who you are when a setback is telling you that you are nothing
The four pouThe same four jobs the whare's walls do
ContextPermission to say "this is hard because of what is going on around me", which is often the truest thing in the room

⚠️ Aiga cuts both ways and the room knows it. Family is the strongest support most Pacific learners have, and it is sometimes also the obligation that is grinding them down. Do not teach the floor as though it is only a resource. Ask the honest question.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, alongside Te Whare Tapa Whā, not instead of it
  • Run ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall, which carries both models on one sheet and lets people choose
  • The best question: "which part of your fale has been holding everything up on its own?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating it as the Samoan version of Te Whare Tapa Whā. It is not a translation. It was built across six Pacific nations and it makes different claims
    • Skipping the "other" pou because it raises money and sexuality. It is the most useful pou for the learners who need the model most
    • Assuming every Pacific learner will pick Fonofale. Some will not, and some Māori learners will pick it. Let people choose and do not comment on the choice
    • Getting the words wrong. If you are not confident with pronunciation, say so and ask the room. They will help, and asking is better than avoiding
  • ⚠️ Say whose it is. Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann, by name. He is a living person and this is his work

More resources

FRM-066Framework · Wellbeing & Identity

Resilience Is Ordinary

modelstrong
wellbeingresilienceevidencemythshauorasystemshouse-content

What it is in one line: resilience is common, not rare, and it runs on ordinary systems around a person rather than on exceptional personal strength.

Origin: Ann S. Masten, Regents Professor of Child Development at the University of Minnesota, in Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development (Guilford Press; second edition 2024). Her central finding, across decades of work with children exposed to serious adversity, is that resilience depends on ordinary adaptive systems inside and around a person: relationships, routines, a functioning body, culture, community, belief. Evidence: strong. This is one of the better-supported findings in developmental psychology and it is built on longitudinal work rather than a single study. Best for: the ten minutes before you teach any resilience tool, because it decides how the tool gets heard.

On this pageWhy the framing matters more than the toolWhat "ordinary adaptive systems" actually meansThe sentence this framework exists to refuseWhat this does to how you teach the ABC modelFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

Why the framing matters more than the tool

Most people arrive at a resilience session with one of two beliefs, and both are wrong.

The beliefWhere it leads
"Resilient people are made differently." They are tougher, and I am notNothing you teach will apply to them, because they have already decided it is about a trait they do not have
"Resilience means being able to take anything." Keep absorbing, keep goingThe word becomes a weapon. It is used to explain why the problem is you and not the load

Masten's finding takes both apart at once.

How to read it: if resilience runs on ordinary systems, then the question is never "are you strong enough?" It is "which of your systems is missing, and can we put it back?"

What "ordinary adaptive systems" actually means

The systemWhat it looks like for a Zeducation learner
Close relationshipsOne adult who has your back. A partner, an aunty, a coach, a tutor
Routines and structureSomewhere to be at 9am. This is a large part of why a programme itself works
A body that functionsSleep, food, health. Nothing else works well underneath a body that does not
Belief and meaningFaith, culture, purpose. A reason that outlasts a bad week
Community and cultureChurch, marae, club, aiga. Belonging that does not depend on performing
A sense of agencyHaving done a hard thing before, and knowing you did it

➜ Read that list against Te Whare Tapa Whā and Fonofale. It is the same list. Durie in 1984 and Pulotu-Endemann named these systems from within Māori and Pacific knowledge; Masten's research arrived at them from the outside. Three traditions, one answer, and that is worth saying out loud in a room that has been taught to treat Western research as the real version.

The sentence this framework exists to refuse

⚠️ "You just need to be more resilient."

Said to somebody working two jobs, whose car has died and whose landlord has given notice, it is not support. It relocates a structural problem into a personal failing.

The honest version: "Resilience is real and it can be built. It is also not a substitute for enough hours, a safe house, or someone to ring. If the load is the problem, the answer is not more strength."

⚠️ A facilitator who cannot say that sentence should not teach resilience. It is the difference between a wellbeing session and a compliance one.

What this does to how you teach the ABC model

Without this framingWith it
"Here is a tool for bouncing back""Here is one of the ordinary systems, written down so you can use it on purpose"
The learner who fails to bounce back has failedThe learner who cannot use it is telling you a system is missing, and that is the useful information
Resilience is a personal qualityResilience is a set of things that can be protected, and some of them are not in the learner's control

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 6 minutes, before FRM-064. It is framing, not a session of its own
  • The best question: "who is the one person who would turn up for you at 2am?" Then: "that is not luck. That is the biggest single predictor in the research."
  • Run ACT-107 The River Stones after it, so the room moves before it thinks too hard
  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning "resilience is common" into "so this should be easy for you". It means the opposite: it is common because the systems are common, and somebody without them is not weak
    • Quoting a number. There is no clean percentage and this page deliberately gives none
    • Treating it as a licence to skip the tool. The framing is not the session. It is the ten minutes that make the session land
  • ⚠️ Somebody in the room will not have the systems. No safe adult, no routine, no house. Notice it, do not name it publicly, and know where to send them

More resources

  • 📕 Ann S. Masten, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development, 2nd ed. (Guilford Press)

⚠️ GAP: no New Zealand replication is cited on this page. Masten's work is US-based and developmental. What would strengthen it: New Zealand longitudinal evidence, and the Dunedin and Christchurch studies are the obvious places to look. Worth a proper research pass.

  • 📄 Masten — Ordinary magic: resilience processes in development (PDF) — the 2001 paper that named it, free
  • 📄 MinnPost — children's natural resilience is nurtured through 'ordinary magic' — an interview, and the plainest version of the argument
  • 🔗 Ann S. Masten — Wikipedia — Project Competence, and the 2024 Grawemeyer Award for this idea
  • 📄 Routledge — Ordinary Magic, second edition — contents and chapter list, if you want to know what is in it before buying
  • 🎬 Ann Masten — Ordinary Magic on the Developmental Road to Resilience — Masten's own keynote. University of Minnesota
  • 🎬 Ann Masten — is resilience born or built? — under a minute, and it answers the question the room always asks

FRM-067Framework · Leadership

Goleman's Six Leadership Styles

modelmoderate, and the headline number is not usable
leadershipstylesgolemansituationalclimateemotional-intelligenceuncredited-framework

What it is in one line: six ways to lead, and the finding that the leaders who get the best results use most of them in any given week rather than picking one.

Origin: Daniel Goleman, "Leadership That Gets Results", Harvard Business Review, March-April 2000, drawing on research with the consulting firm Hay/McBer across more than 3,000 executives. Evidence: moderate for the styles as a teaching set. The headline statistic is not usable and the emotional-intelligence framing underneath it is contested. See the audit below, because a facilitator will be asked about both. Best for: the leader who has decided they are one kind of leader, and treats that as a fixed fact about themselves.

On this page⚠️ Why this page existsThe sixTwo that need a warning⚠️ The evidence auditFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

⚠️ Why this page exists

You will meet these six everywhere, almost always without Goleman's name on them. "Visionary leadership", "coaching leadership", "pacesetting" — every leadership listicle on the internet reproduces this set. Most do not credit him, including a Harvard blog.

Knowing whose they are means you can check the evidence. That is the whole reason for the page.

The six

StyleIn one lineWhat it does to the room
1Commanding (coercive)"Do what I tell you"Works in a genuine crisis. Damaging as a default
2Visionary (authoritative)"Come with me"Sets a direction and lets people find their own way to it. Generally the most positive
3Affiliative"People come first"Builds harmony and heals rifts. Alone, it lets poor performance slide
4Democratic"What do you think?"Builds buy-in through participation. Slow, and useless in an emergency
5Pacesetting"Do as I do, now"Sets a very high bar and models it. Exhausting, and it quietly says nobody else is good enough
6Coaching"Try this"Develops people for the long term. The least used and, Goleman argued, among the most valuable

How to read it: not six kinds of person. Six moves available to one person. Goleman's actual finding was that the leaders getting the best results used most of these in a single week, switching as the situation asked for it.

➜ The claim to carry, and it is the useful one: "You are not a democratic leader. You are a leader who used a democratic move on Tuesday and a commanding one on Thursday, and the skill is knowing which and when."

Two that need a warning

Why
CommandingReal in a crisis: a safety incident, a deadline that will genuinely sink the business. Used as a default it produces a team that stops thinking, which is the same thing Theory X predicts and Likert's System 1 describes
PacesettingLooks like leading from the front and often feels virtuous. It is the one that burns teams out, because the message underneath "watch me do it properly" is that nobody else can. Fine in short bursts with a strong, experienced team

⚠️ The evidence audit

Be straight about this one, because Goleman is quoted more than almost anyone in leadership training and the quality of the evidence does not match the volume of the quoting.

What is defensible:

  • Leaders who get the best results use several styles, not one. This is the same conclusion Lewin (1939), Blake-Mouton (1964) and Path-Goal (1971) reach from three different directions. Four traditions, one answer, and that convergence is worth more than any single study
  • The six are a genuinely useful teaching set. They give a room language for something it can already see happening

What is not usable:

The claimWhy it is not quoted here
"Climate accounts for nearly a third of results"It comes from Hay/McBer's internal consulting research, not from peer-reviewed work, and there is no independent replication anyone can check. Do not put this number in front of a room
The emotional-intelligence foundationGoleman derives the six from components of EI. Salovey and Mayer, who originated the term and from whom Goleman took it, are critical of how broadly he applies it. His mixed model blends cognitive ability, personality and motivation, which makes it hard to measure against an objective standard and hard to falsify

➜ The honest line for a room: "These six are a good set of words for things you already do. The number attached to them comes from a consulting firm's own data and nobody has replicated it, so we teach the styles and leave the statistic alone."

⚠️ This is the same call the library made on the McKinsey diversity figures (retired after Green & Hand, 2024), the "six seconds on a CV" figure on FRM-058, and the hidden-job-market percentages on FRM-061. A famous number is not a checked number.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes. The six-row table and the two warnings are the whole thing
  • Where it goes: TOP-LEA-010 People, Results, Or Both, as the practical layer over Blake-Mouton's two axes
  • The best question: "which of these did you use this week, and which one have you not used in a year?" The unused one is usually coaching, and that is the conversation
  • Run ACT-084 Four Teams, One Leader and read its scenarios against these six as well as against Path-Goal
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating them as personality types. "I'm a visionary leader" is the failure mode, and it is the same error FRM-054 warns about. Six moves, one leader
    • Quoting the 30% figure. It is the most repeated thing in the article and the least defensible
    • Ranking them. Commanding is not wrong, it is wrong as a default. A safety incident needs it
    • Skipping the attribution. Naming Goleman takes four seconds and it is what lets anyone check
  • ⚠️ In a Māori or Pacific room, hold this next to Tū Rangatira. Goleman's six were drawn from a corporate database of mostly Western executives. Tū Rangatira names leadership roles from within te ao Māori. Neither is the real version of the other

More resources

  • 📄 Daniel Goleman, "Leadership That Gets Results", HBR, March-April 2000
  • 📄 Full text (PDF, NHS Leadership Academy)
  • 📄 Six emotional leadership styles — choosing the right style for the situation (PDF) — a printable one-pager, NZ-hosted
  • 📄 AAPL — six common leadership styles, and how to decide which to use when — the when is the part most summaries skip
  • 📄 Torrens University — the six different leadership styles — a short academic write-up with the climate argument intact
  • 🎬 The six Goleman leadership styles, and when to use them — all six with the climate effect of each
  • 🎬 Goleman's Leadership That Gets Results — a walkthrough of the original HBR article

FRM-068Framework · Employment & Work Readiness

The First Two Weeks

modelpractitioner, on a researched foundation
work-readinessonboardingstarting-workretentionreliabilityhouse-content

What it is in one line: four things a new starter can do in their first fortnight that decide whether they are still there in six months, especially when the employer does no onboarding at all.

Origin: Zeducation house model. It is the worker-side flip of Talya Bauer's Four Cs — compliance, clarification, culture and connection — published by the SHRM Foundation as what good employers do when somebody starts. Evidence: practitioner, on a researched foundation. The four needs are Bauer's and they hold up. Answering them yourself is ours, and there is no study saying that works. Best for: the learner who has just got the job, and everybody who has watched somebody lose one in the first month.

On this pageWhy the flipThe modelThe unwritten rules, which nobody hands you⚠️ Where this sits against the lawFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

Why the flip

Bauer's Four Cs describe what a well-run organisation does to a new starter: paperwork sorted, role explained, culture introduced, people met.

⚠️ Most of our learners are not starting at a well-run organisation. A small business, a labour-hire placement, a night shift, a subcontractor. There is a payroll form and somebody saying "just follow Dave around."

➜ So the question is not what good onboarding looks like. It is what you do when there isn't any.

Bauer's CWhat a good employer doesWhat you do if they don't
ComplianceExplains the rules, the paperwork, the safety briefingAsk for them. Contract, hours, who you tell when you are sick
ClarificationSets out the role and what good looks likeAsk what a good day looks like, in week one, while asking is still free
CultureIntroduces the unwritten normsWatch, and ask. When is smoko really. How early is early
ConnectionIntroduces you to peopleLearn names. Especially the person who has been there longest

The model

How to read it: in order of how much they cost you if you skip them. Turning up is worth more than being good at the job for the first fortnight, because they already decided you can do the job.

The moveWhat it actually looks likeWhy it decides things
1Turn upEvery day, on time, for the first month. Fifteen minutes early beats on timeThey hired you on a guess. This is the only evidence they have
2Ask early"Can I check how you want this done?" Before you guess wrongThere is a window where asking is free. It closes around week three
3Own it fast"I've made a mistake, can I show you?"See FRM-069. This is the one that separates people
4Learn the unwritten rulesWho to tell when you are sick. Where you do and do not sit. What "start at seven" really meansEvery workplace has them, nobody writes them down, and breaking one costs more than breaking a written rule

➜ The line for a room: "They already decided you can do the job. That was the interview. The first two weeks is them finding out whether you turn up and whether you are honest. That is all it is."

The unwritten rules, which nobody hands you

Most first-month trouble is here, not in the work.

The questionWhy it matters
When does the day actually start?"Seven o'clock" sometimes means boots on at seven, and sometimes means arrive at seven
Who do you ring when you are sick, and how early?Getting this wrong once reads as unreliable, however good the reason
When is smoko, how long, and where?The most common week-one mistake in trades and warehousing
Who has been here longest?Not the manager. The person who actually knows how things are done
What do people wear?Especially for anyone who has never worked in that sector
Is your phone allowed out?Varies enormously and assumptions are expensive
How do you ask for a day off?Text, app, in person, two weeks ahead

⚠️ Somebody who has never worked in that setting has no way to guess any of this, and that is not a character problem. It is information they were not given.

⚠️ Where this sits against the law

A trial period is a real thing and learners should know it exists. Since 23 December 2023, all New Zealand employers can use a 90-day trial period, where previously only employers with fewer than 20 staff could. To be valid it must be in writing, signed before the first day of work, agreed in good faith, and used only with somebody who has not previously worked for that employer.

⚠️ Verified 2026-08-02 by search, not read on the authoritative page — every New Zealand government site is blocked from this environment. Check before delivery.

➜ A facilitator's job here is the four moves, not the law. If a learner is worried about a trial period or has been let go under one, send them to real advice: Employment New Zealand · Community Law · Citizens Advice Bureau · their union.

Never advise a learner on their employment rights from a workbook.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes. The four moves and the unwritten-rules table are the whole thing
  • Run ACT-110 The Unwritten Rules Hunt
  • The best question: "who here has seen somebody lose a job in the first month? What actually happened?" It is almost never the work. It is turning up, or hiding a mistake
  • Common mistakes:
    • Teaching it as a lecture on attitude. It is not. It is four specific, doable things, and the fourth one is information the learner was never given
    • "Just be keen." Useless. Keen is not an action. Fifteen minutes early is
    • Skipping the unwritten rules because they seem obvious. They are only obvious to somebody who has worked in that setting
    • Letting it become "don't be lazy". Most people who lose a job in the first month were not lazy. They guessed instead of asking, or went quiet when something went wrong
  • ⚠️ Barriers, again. Turning up on time for a month is a transport, childcare and sleep problem before it is a motivation problem. Everything in ACT-103 The Day Itself applies here, and a learner who cannot get there needs help, not a talk

More resources

  • 🔗 SHRM Foundation — onboarding new employees, Talya Bauer
  • 🔗 Employment New Zealand — trial periods, agreements, minimum rights

⚠️ GAP: Bauer's original SHRM Foundation report was not read directly, only verified through consistent secondary sources. Find the primary PDF and link it.

  • 🎬 IMD's The First 90 Days: five questions for your new role — the five questions, which work just as well at week one

FRM-069Framework · Employment & Work Readiness

Say It Early

techniquepractitioner
work-readinessmistakesaccountabilitytruststarting-workhouse-contentescalation

What it is in one line: a problem told early is a problem. The same problem found later is a problem and a lie, and that second thing is what actually gets people sacked.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written for TOP-EMP-006. Evidence: practitioner. There is no study behind the four sentences. What is not in dispute is that concealment costs more than the original error, which every supervisor will confirm and every learner already knows from their own life. Best for: the new starter who has just got something wrong and is deciding, right now, whether to say so.

On this pageThe whole modelThe four sentencesThe same shape, for a problem that is not your faultWhen it is hard, and whyFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The whole model

How to read it: the branch is the whole thing. The mistake itself is rarely what ends a job. Which way you go at that fork is.

Told earlyFound later
What it isA problemA problem and a concealment
Who owns itThe teamYou, alone
Cost to fixUsually smallUsually large, because it has been running
What they learn about youYou are honest under pressureThey cannot rely on what you tell them

➜ The line for a room: "Nobody gets sacked in week two for breaking something. People get sacked for the four hours between breaking it and mentioning it."

The four sentences

The whole technique. It takes about ten seconds and most people have never been given the words.

SayExample
1Name it, plainly"I've made a mistake."
2What happened, factually"I've loaded the wrong pallet onto the Whangārei truck."
3What you have already done"I've stopped the loading and I haven't sent it."
4Ask"What do you want me to do?"

⚠️ No excuse in any of the four. "I've made a mistake, but nobody showed me" is a different sentence and it lands completely differently, even when it is true.

➜ Sentence 3 is the one people leave out, and it is the one that changes how it is heard. It is the difference between bringing a problem and bringing a problem you have already started containing.

The same shape, for a problem that is not your fault

Most of what a new starter needs to raise is not a mistake. It is something not going to plan.

SayExample
1Name it"I need to flag something."
2What is happening"I'm not going to finish this by three."
3What you have done"I've done the priority ones first."
4Ask"Do you want me to keep going or hand it over?"

⚠️ The most valuable thing a new person can do is say "I'm not going to make it" at eleven o'clock instead of at three. That is four hours a supervisor can use. Most people say nothing and hope.

When it is hard, and why

Naming this out loud matters more than the technique does.

Why people go quietThe honest answer
"I'll get in trouble"You will get in more trouble later, and it will be about honesty rather than about a pallet
"They'll think I can't do it"In week two they expect you not to be able to do it yet. That is what week two is
"I'll fix it before anyone notices"Sometimes this works. When it does not, you have spent the credibility you had
"Where I'm from you don't correct or contradict people above you"⚠️ Real, and not a flaw. See below

⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, and in a lot of migrant workplaces, going to somebody senior to report your own error cuts against how respect works. Do not treat that as a confidence problem to be trained out.

➜ Name the clash, and give the bridge: "Can I show you something?" is easier than "I've made a mistake", it is respectful, and it gets you to the same place. Ask permission first, then say it.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. The fork diagram and the four sentences
  • Run ACT-111 I Got It Wrong
  • The best question: "what is the longest you have ever left something before saying it? What happened?" Do not make anybody answer out loud. Ask it and let it sit
  • Common mistakes:
    • Teaching it as honesty being the right thing to do. It is, and that is not the argument that lands. The argument is that it costs less. Learners who have been in trouble before need the practical case, not the moral one
    • Skipping sentence 3. It is what makes the person sound capable rather than helpless
    • Letting an excuse in. Practise the version with no "but" in it, out loud, until it is sayable
    • Only practising the mistake version. The "I'm not going to make it" version gets used far more often
  • ⚠️ Somebody in the room has been sacked for exactly this, and knows it. Keep the teaching about the mechanism, not about anybody's character, and never ask for the story

More resources

  • 📄 Center for Creative Leadership — how leaders build psychological safety at work — why people stay quiet, and what changes it
  • 📄 Calm — how to support a speak-up culture at work — includes the part this framework is about: how to speak up when you are nervous, starting small
  • 📄 Arinite — psychological safety at work: why staff stay silent — more than a third of workers do not feel safe asking for help
  • 📄 Harvard Business School Online — how to build psychological safety in the workplace — the leader's half of the same problem
  • 📄 Speaking up and taking action: psychological safety and joint problem-solving — the research, in a safety-critical setting
  • 🎬 Amy Edmondson — building a psychologically safe workplace (TEDxHGSE) — the reason saying it early is possible at all, and why it usually is not
  • 🎬 Amy Edmondson defines psychological safety — two minutes, for the top of a session

FRM-070Framework · Leadership

Self-Determination Theory — autonomy, competence, relatedness

modelstrong
leadershipmotivationself-determinationautonomycompetencerelatednessteams

What it is in one line: three needs that have to be met before anybody is motivated by anything other than the money, and the money is the weakest of the levers you have.

Origin: Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan, from 1985 and set out fully in 2000. It is a family of theories rather than one model, and Cognitive Evaluation Theory is one of its sub-theories — which matters, because that is the name a lot of workbooks use without saying what it belongs to. Evidence: strong, and it is the best-supported motivation framework in this library. Decades of studies across work, school, sport and health. Best for: the supervisor who has tried everything, cannot afford a pay rise, and has concluded that people just do not care.

On this pageThe three needsWhy this is the one to teachWhere the money fitsFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The three needs

How to read it: all three, or it does not hold. Undermine any one and motivation shifts to "because I have to" or disappears.

NeedWhat it meansWhat it looks like at workWhat kills it
AutonomySome say over what you do and howChoosing the order of your jobs. Being asked rather than toldBeing watched. Every decision made for you
CompetenceGetting better at something, and knowing itBeing trained properly. Being told when you did it wellNever being shown. Only hearing when it is wrong
RelatednessBelonging, and mattering to peopleBeing known by name. Being missed when you are awayBeing a number on a roster

⚠️ Autonomy does not mean no rules. It means having some say inside the rules. A warehouse hand who chooses which end of the run to start at has autonomy. It costs nothing.

Why this is the one to teach

Because it is the one a supervisor can actually act on. All three are free.

The excuseWhat SDT says
"I can't pay them more"Pay was never the strongest lever. All three needs cost nothing
"They just don't care"Somebody who has never been trained properly cannot feel competent. That is not caring, that is a competence need going unmet
"It's a boring job"Probably. Boring plus no say plus nobody knows your name is a different thing entirely

➜ The claim to carry: "You cannot make anybody motivated. You can only build a place where the motivation people already have does not get squashed."

Where the money fits

Pay matters, and it matters differently from how people assume.

  • Below enough, nothing else works. Somebody who cannot pay rent is not going to be moved by autonomy, and telling them otherwise is insulting
  • Above enough, pay stops being the lever. More money does not produce more of the motivation that lasts
  • ⚠️ Rewards can undermine it. This is the specific finding of Cognitive Evaluation Theory: a reward attached to something somebody was already enjoying can reduce the motivation to do it. The effect is real and it is often overstated, so teach it as a caution rather than a law

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Three needs, three questions
  • Run ACT-113 Three Needs, One Team
  • The best question: "think of the best job you ever had, and the worst. Which of the three was present, and which was missing?" Every room answers this correctly without being taught the model first, which is the fastest way to prove it
  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning autonomy into "let them do whatever." It is having some say inside the rules
    • Using it to excuse low pay. ⚠️ The theory does not say money does not matter. Somebody using this to justify not paying properly is misusing it, and a room will spot that instantly
    • Only teaching it to managers. It works just as well as a self-check. Which of my three is missing right now?
  • ⚠️ Relatedness is not the same as everyone being friends. It is being known and mattering. A quiet team where everyone knows your name has it; a loud one where nobody notices you are away does not

  • 🔗 Simply Psychology — Self-Determination Theory
  • 🔗 TheoryHub — Self-Determination Theory

Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs

modelweak for the hierarchy, useful as a taxonomy
leadershipmotivationmaslowevidencemythsteamsuncredited-framework
On this page⚠️ Read the audit before you teach thisThe five needs⚠️ The evidence auditWhy the ladder claim actually matters hereFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

⚠️ Read the audit before you teach this

This is the most-taught idea in workplace training and the evidence does not support it as a hierarchy. It is on this page because learners will meet it everywhere and need to be able to place it, not because it is the best model here. For that, see FRM-070 Self-Determination Theory.

What it is in one line: five kinds of human need, drawn as a ladder you climb one rung at a time.

Origin: Abraham Maslow, 1943 and 1954. ⚠️ The pyramid is not his. He never drew one; the pyramid was added by others later and it is the pyramid that carries the claim most people object to. Evidence: weak for the hierarchy, useful as a taxonomy. See below. Best for: a room that has already met it, so they can hold it accurately instead of half remembering it.

The five needs

NeedWhat it covers
5Self-actualisationBecoming what you could be
4EsteemRespect, recognition, being good at something
3BelongingRelationships, being part of something
2SafetyHousing, health, a job that will still be there next month
1PhysiologicalFood, water, sleep, warmth

How to read it: as five categories that all matter, not as five rungs in a fixed order. The dotted line is the part the research does not back.

⚠️ The evidence audit

Be straight, because this comes up in every leadership room in the country.

What does not hold: the hierarchy.

  • Wahba and Bridwell (1976) reviewed the research and found little support for the hierarchy as Maslow described it, particularly the ordering
  • Ten factor-analytic and three ranking studies gave only partial support for the concept
  • Longitudinal studies testing the gratification-activation claim — that satisfying one level activates the next — gave no support at all
  • Cross-sectional studies showed no clear evidence for the deprivation-domination claim, except around self-actualisation

What does hold: the taxonomy. Maslow identified real categories of human need, and having words for them is genuinely useful.

And the pyramid, which is the bit everyone pictures, was not Maslow's. It was imposed on his work afterwards, and it is the pyramid that makes the strict-order claim look official.

➜ The honest line for a room: "Maslow gave us a good list and somebody else turned it into a ladder. The list is useful. The ladder has been tested for fifty years and it does not hold up."

Why the ladder claim actually matters here

This is not an academic quibble for a Zeducation room. The strict ladder says you cannot think about belonging or esteem until food and housing are sorted.

⚠️ That is a sentence with consequences. It has been used to argue that people in hardship should be given only the basics, and that anything about dignity, purpose or belonging is a luxury for later.

What people actually do is find belonging, purpose and pride in the middle of hardship, not after it. Anybody who has spent time on a marae, in a church, or in a family under real pressure has watched it happen.

➜ So teach the categories, refuse the ladder, and say why.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes, and always with the audit. Teaching it without is how the ladder claim keeps spreading
  • Teach it before FRM-070, not instead of it. Maslow is the one they have heard of; SDT is the one that works
  • The best question: "has anyone here found belonging or pride while things were genuinely hard?" The room answers yes, and that is the ladder disproved from inside the room
  • Common mistakes:
    • Drawing the pyramid without saying it is not his. Four seconds, and it changes the status of the claim
    • Using it to sequence support. "We'll deal with housing first, then look at goals" sounds sensible and is not what the research supports
    • Presenting it as settled science. It is 1943, and it has been tested hard since
  • ⚠️ A learner will have been on the receiving end of the ladder logic, from a service that decided what they were allowed to want. Be careful, and be on their side about it

More resources

  • 📄 Wahba & Bridwell (1976), Maslow reconsidered: a review of research on the need hierarchy theory
  • 📄 University of Birmingham — critical analysis of Maslow's hierarchy of need (PDF)
  • 📄 Reconsidering Maslow and the hierarchy of needs from a First Nations' perspective — Aotearoa New Zealand Social Work, and the version to read before teaching this here
  • 📄 What I got wrong: revisions to my post about the Blackfoot and Maslow — an author correcting their own viral claim. Model this, not the claim
  • 📄 The Blackfoot wisdom that inspired Maslow's hierarchy — the contested account, presented so learners can weigh it themselves
  • 🎬 Criticisms of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs — play this one, not a straight explainer. The room already thinks it knows the pyramid
  • 🎬 Maslow's hierarchy of needs — the standard version, for the half of the room who have not met it

Vroom's Expectancy Theory

modelmoderate
leadershipmotivationexpectancyvroomteamseffortfairness

What it is in one line: people try when they believe effort will produce performance, performance will produce an outcome, and the outcome is worth having. Break any one of the three and they stop trying, and it is not laziness.

Origin: Victor H. Vroom, Work and Motivation, 1964. Evidence: moderate. The three components are well established and useful. The multiplicative formula is the weaker part and has been repeatedly revised since. See the audit. Best for: the supervisor looking at somebody who has visibly stopped trying and wants to know which of three specific things has broken.

On this pageThe three questionsWhy instrumentality is the one that matters most here⚠️ The evidence auditFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The three questions

How to read it: a chain, and a chain breaks at its weakest link. All three have to be a yes.

TermThe question in plain wordsWhen it is broken
EExpectancy"If I put the effort in, can I actually do this?"Never trained. Broken gear. Impossible target
IInstrumentality"If I do it well, will the thing they promised actually happen?"Promises not kept before. The same person always gets picked
VValence"Do I even want what is on offer?"A pizza voucher offered to somebody who needs hours

➜ The diagnostic question, and it is the whole value of the model: "which of the three has broken for this person?" Because the fix is completely different for each one.

If this brokeThe fix
ExpectancyTraining, tools, a smaller first step. Not encouragement
InstrumentalityKeep a promise. Then keep another one. This is the slowest to repair
ValenceAsk what they actually want. Most reward schemes fail here and nobody checks

Why instrumentality is the one that matters most here

For a lot of Zeducation's learners, instrumentality has been broken repeatedly before they walked in.

Told that if they finished the course there would be a job. Told that if they worked hard they would get more hours. Told the restructure would not affect them.

⚠️ Somebody who has stopped believing that effort leads to outcomes is not unmotivated. They are accurately describing their own history. Treating that as an attitude problem is both wrong and insulting.

➜ And it is why a small kept promise is worth more than a big one made. Instrumentality is rebuilt by evidence, not by assurance. This is the same mechanism as FRM-022 The Trust Equation, from the motivation side.

⚠️ The evidence audit

What holds: the three components are a genuinely useful diagnostic, and they have been applied and supported across a range of work settings.

What is weaker:

  • The multiplicative formula — motivation = E × I × V — is the part that has attracted most criticism, and versions of the model have been revised repeatedly since 1964. Do not put the formula on a slide as though it calculates anything
  • The theory is hard to test cleanly, because all three terms are somebody's private beliefs. It is used far more than it has been rigorously validated

➜ The honest line: "Treat it as three questions, not as a sum. The questions are excellent. The multiplication is decoration."

What the multiplication does get right, and it is worth keeping as an idea rather than an equation: a zero anywhere gives you zero. A great reward nobody believes they will get is worth nothing.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Three questions and the diagnostic table
  • Run ACT-115 Which One Broke?
  • The best question: "think of a time you stopped trying at something. Which of the three had gone?" Most people can answer immediately, and it is almost always instrumentality
  • Common mistakes:
    • Putting the formula up. It looks rigorous and it is the least defensible part
    • Assuming valence. The most common management error in the model. Somebody assumes everyone wants the same reward and never asks
    • Fixing the wrong link. Encouragement aimed at a broken expectancy does nothing. The person needs training, not belief
    • Using it only on other people. It works as a self-check on your own flat week
  • ⚠️ "They're just not motivated" is the sentence this framework exists to replace. Every time it is said, ask which of the three, and the conversation becomes fixable

More resources

  • 📄 Victor H. Vroom, Work and Motivation (1964)
  • 📄 Lunenburg — Expectancy theory of motivation (PDF)
  • 🔗 Institute for Manufacturing, Cambridge — Vroom's expectancy theory
  • 🎬 Vroom's expectancy theory — valence, instrumentality and expectancy — the formula explained on screen
  • 📄 Positive Psychology — Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of motivation — with worked examples of each link breaking
  • 📄 Toolshero — Vroom's expectancy theory of motivation — a diagram version, good for a slide

The Four-Part Prompt — Role, Context, Command, Format

techniquepractitioner
digital-capabilityaipromptingtechniquetools

What it is in one line: four things to put in every prompt, and the quality of what comes out will never be better than what you put in.

Origin: SRC-018, a monetised YouTube video. The four-part structure is his and it is good. The examples, the cautions and everything about privacy are ours. Evidence: practitioner. No study says four parts beats three. What is not in dispute is that a one-line prompt produces a one-line-quality answer, and every person who has used these tools can confirm it. Best for: the learner who typed one sentence, got something generic, and concluded AI is useless.

On this pageThe four partsWorked example, and the difference is the pointGive it far more than you thinkFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The four parts

PartWhat it doesExample
1RoleNarrows the whole thing down to one kind of expertise"Act like a New Zealand careers adviser who works with school leavers."
2ContextEverything it needs. This is where almost everybody stops shortThe job ad, your CV, what you have already tried, who it is for
3CommandExactly what you want done. Make the implicit explicit"Rewrite the top third of this CV for this job ad."
4FormatWhat it should look like coming out"A table. Three columns. Under 150 words."

➜ Most people write a command and nothing else. That is a text message, not a prompt.

Worked example, and the difference is the point

What most people type:

"Help me write a CV."

The four-part version:

[Role] Act like a New Zealand recruiter who hires warehouse staff. [Context] Here is the job ad. Here is my current CV. I've got a Class 2 licence and an F endorsement, four years on nights, and I've applied for eleven of these and heard nothing. [Command] Rewrite the top third only. Use the ad's own words. Turn the three work-history lines into achievements with a number in each. [Format] Give it back as plain text I can paste straight in. No headings I have to delete.

⚠️ Notice how much of that is context. That is the part people skip, and it is the part that does the work.

Give it far more than you think

The video's line is that you can give it "two or three books worth" before it answers. Directionally right, and the actual limit depends entirely on which tool and which plan you are on.

⚠️ Check your own tool. Verified 2026-08-02 and it moves constantly.

What to put in context: the job ad · your CV · the email you are replying to · what you have already tried · who the reader is · anything you have written before that sounded right.

⚠️ And what never to put in. See FRM-075 and the privacy section of TOP-DIG-001. A public AI tool is not a private notebook.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The four parts, then the before-and-after example
  • Run ACT-116 Same Question, Four Ways
  • The best move: put the bad prompt and the good prompt side by side on the same screen, live. Nobody argues with it after that
  • Common mistakes:
    • Skipping context. The single biggest one. Role and command are easy, context is work
    • A vague command. "Make it better" is not a command
    • Forgetting format, then spending ten minutes deleting headings
    • Treating the role as magic words. It narrows the search. It does not make the tool an expert
  • ⚠️ Do not teach this without teaching FRM-075. A better prompt produces a more confident answer, and a more confident wrong answer is more dangerous than an obviously bad one

More resources

  • 📄 Google Cloud — what is prompt engineering? — the vendor-neutral overview of the same four parts
  • 📄 Anthropic — prompting best practices — the clarity test is the best thing on this page: if a colleague would be confused by your prompt, the model will be too
  • 📄 OpenAI — best practices for prompt engineering — be specific about context, outcome, length, format and style
