Pull, Not Push — let it ask you the questions

techniquepractitioner
digital-capabilityaipromptingtechniquequestions

What it is in one line: instead of writing a perfect prompt, give it the outcome and say "ask me all the questions you need." Then answer them.

Origin: SRC-018. The push/pull framing and the GPS metaphor are his, and both are good. Evidence: practitioner. Best for: everybody, and beginners most of all. It is the single highest-leverage move in this pillar and almost nobody knows it.

On this pagePush versus pullThe move, in three linesWhy this is the one to teach a beginnerFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

Push versus pull

PushPull
What you doWork out every instruction, then write it all downSay what you want to end up with, and let it interview you
Who does the thinkingYou, then it does the last bitIt works out what it needs to know
The metaphorA mate giving directions: "left at the dairy, right at the church, red mailbox"A GPS. You give the destination
Fails whenYou did not know what to include, which is most of the timeRarely, and you can always ask for more questions

How to read it: push needs you to already know what matters. Pull does not, which is why it works for somebody who has never done the task before.

The move, in three lines

  1. Role and context, as usual. Who it should be, and what the situation is
  2. The outcome you want. Specific. "I need a cover letter for this job that would make this employer ring me"
  3. The line that does the work:
"Ask me all the questions you need to do this properly, then give it back to me as [format]."

Then answer the questions. Use voice-to-text if there are a lot, which there usually are.

Not right yet? "Ask me more questions to make it more relevant." It will.

Why this is the one to teach a beginner

Push prompting requires you to already know what a good answer needs. A learner who has never written a cover letter does not know that the employer's name, the shift pattern and their own strongest evidence all matter.

➜ Pull prompting means they do not have to know. The tool asks, they answer in their own words, and the answering is where the actual thinking happens.

⚠️ That is the hidden benefit and it is worth naming. Being asked seven good questions about your own situation is useful even if you never read the output. For a lot of our learners that is the real value.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 6 minutes. The GPS metaphor, then the one line
  • Run it live, in front of the room, on a real task somebody in the room has. It takes four minutes and it is more convincing than any explanation
  • The best question: "which of the questions it asked you had you not thought about?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Answering the questions in three words. The answers are the context. Short answers, generic output
    • Not asking for more questions when the first round was thin
    • Using it for something trivial. Pull is for a real piece of work, not for "what's a synonym"
  • ⚠️ The questions will sometimes ask for things you must not share. Names, health information, somebody else's situation. You are allowed to say "I'm not giving you that, work with what you have." Teach that line explicitly

More resources

  • 📄 Anthropic — prompting best practices — the same principle from the other side: give it what it needs before it has to guess
  • 📄 Google Cloud — prompt engineering guide — on iteration, which is what pull-not-push actually is
  • 📄 Prompt engineering basics, 2026 — clarity, context, structure, constraints, iteration
  • 📄 Infomineo — prompt engineering techniques and examples — includes asking the model to interrogate you first
  • 📄 Best practices in prompt engineering, part 3 — the iterate-and-refine loop written out
  • 🎬 Prompt engineering essentials: getting better results from LLMs — the iterate-and-refine loop, demonstrated

What AI Actually Does — and why it makes things up

modelstrong for the mechanism, practitioner for the rules
digital-capabilityaihallucinationprivacycheckingsafetyhouse-content

What it is in one line: it predicts the next likely word, very well, which is why it is fluent and confident whether or not it is right.

Origin: the token-prediction explanation comes from SRC-018 and it is a good one. Everything after it is house content, because the source explains the mechanism and never draws the consequence. Evidence: the mechanism is well established. The rules are practitioner. Best for: every learner, before they are taught a single prompting technique.

On this pageThe mechanism, in one pictureWhat follows, and this is the part the source leaves outThe three rulesFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The mechanism, in one picture

All the text it was trained on, broken into pieces, and a very good guess at what comes next.

Say "twinkle, twinkle, little…" and it says star.

How to read it: it is answering "what would a good answer sound like", not "what is true." Most of the time those land in the same place. When they do not, it does not know.

➜ The line that matters: "It is not lying to you. It has no idea it is wrong. It is producing the shape of a right answer."

What follows, and this is the part the source leaves out

1. ⚠️ It will invent things, confidently

Names, dates, statistics, court cases, references, quotes, NZ law, prices, whether a course exists. It will produce them fluently and it will not flag them.

Where it bites for our learners
A CV or cover letterInvents an achievement or a detail about the employer. Checkable, and a lie in writing
An assessmentInvents a source. Markers check
Anything legal or moneyMinimum wage, tenancy, Clean Slate, WINZ entitlements. Confidently wrong and it costs somebody money
A pepeha or a mihiAI is markedly weaker in te reo Māori and Pacific languages and will still answer. A learner can be handed something wrong and have no way to know

⚠️ The te reo one deserves saying out loud in every room. The tool does not hesitate more when it knows less. Ask a person.

2. ⚠️ It is not a private notebook

Anything you type into a public AI tool has left your control. Treat it like posting on a noticeboard in the foyer.

Never put in:
A learner's or client's name, and their situation
Health information about anybody
Anything from a file you would not email to a stranger
Someone else's contact details
Passwords, bank details, IRD numbers

➜ How to still get the help: take the names out. "A 24-year-old with a two-year gap in their CV" gets you the same answer as a real name and puts nobody at risk.

⚠️ For Zeducation this is not optional. We hold learner records at a registered PTE. A tutor pasting a learner's file into a chat window is a privacy breach, however good the intention.

3. It sounds like everybody else

It writes what the average of its training data sounds like. That is why AI writing has a recognisable texture — long dashes, "delve", "it's not just X, it's Y", relentless enthusiasm.

⚠️ The source claims the dashes are because humans like them and it is copying us. Plausible, not established. Either way it is now a real editing problem, and it is why the house voice already bans dashes as sentence punctuation in learner copy.

The three rules

Short enough to put on a wall.
1Check anything checkable. A name, a number, a date, a law, a place. If it can be wrong, look it up
2Never put in what you would not put on a noticeboard. No names, no health, no files
3You sign it, so you own it. It does not matter that AI wrote it. Your name is on the CV

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, before any prompting technique. A better prompt makes a more confident answer, and a confident wrong answer is more dangerous than an obviously bad one
  • Run ACT-118 Catch The Mistake
  • The best demonstration: ask it something about your own town, your own organisation, or a New Zealand rule, live, in the room. It will get something wrong within about three questions and the room will see it happen
  • Common mistakes:
    • Teaching prompting first. Backwards, and the reason so many people trust these tools too much
    • "It's usually right so it's fine." It is usually right, which is exactly what makes the wrong one slip through
    • Making it a scare session. These tools are genuinely useful. The point is checking, not avoiding
  • ⚠️ Someone in the room has already submitted something AI wrote without checking it. Keep it about the habit, not about them

More resources

  • 📄 Nature — evaluating large language models for accuracy incentivises hallucinations — the key finding for a classroom: the way these systems are scored rewards confident guessing over saying I don't know
  • 📄 Large language models hallucination: a comprehensive survey — why next-token prediction produces invention, not lying
  • 📄 Keylabs — large language models explained: how LLMs work — the plain-English mechanism, for a room with no technical background
  • 📄 Engineering of hallucination in generative AI: it's not a bug, it's a feature — the argument that invention is inseparable from the thing that makes it useful
  • 📄 Mitigating hallucination in LLMs — a survey on RAG, reasoning and agentic systems — what is actually being done about it, so nobody thinks it is solved

The Master Prompt — introduce yourself once

techniquepractitioner
digital-capabilityaipromptingcontextreusetechnique

What it is in one line: one document about you, written once, pasted in at the start of anything, so you stop retyping your own situation every single time.

Origin: SRC-018. His idea and his phrase, built for founders with a role per company. Adapted here for learners and tutors, who mostly need one. Evidence: practitioner. Best for: anybody whose AI answers come back generic, which is almost everybody.

On this pageThe problem it fixesWhat goes in oneHow to build one, in four minutesTwo things worth changing from the source⚠️ What does not go in oneFacilitating itMore resourcesWhere it goesRelated frameworks

The problem it fixes

If the answer sounds like anybody could have got it, it is because you never introduced yourself.

Context is the part of a prompt people skip (FRM-073, part 2), because typing your whole situation every time is tedious. So write it once.

What goes in one

Keep it to a page. Longer is not better.

SectionWhat to put
Who I amName, where, what you do, how long
What I'm working onThe current job, course, or search
Who I'm doing it forYour learners, your employer, your whānau
What I already haveTickets, licences, experience, qualifications
What I'm trying to get toThe actual goal
How I want it to sound"Plain words. New Zealand English. No dashes. Short sentences. Do not oversell."
What to never assume"I'm not in the US. Don't quote US law, US pay or US job titles."

⚠️ That last row earns its place immediately. These tools default to American everything, and a learner will be handed a US resume format or US employment law without either party noticing.

How to build one, in four minutes

Use pull prompting. Do not write it yourself.

  1. Say: "I want to make a master prompt about me, so I never have to explain my situation again. Ask me all the questions you need, one at a time."
  2. Answer the questions. Voice-to-text if there are a lot
  3. Read it and fix it. "You've got that wrong, I'm not a manager, I'm a storeperson"
  4. Save it. A note on your phone is fine. It does not need to be a PDF

➜ Then paste it in at the top of anything that matters.

Two things worth changing from the source

The sourceFor our rooms
One master prompt per role — "Dan CEO", "Dan Father"One is enough for most people. Several is a founder's problem
Save as a PDF on a hard driveA note on a phone. Most of our learners do not have a laptop and will not open a PDF to copy from it

⚠️ What does not go in one

A master prompt is a document you will paste into a public tool many times.

Never: your address · your IRD or bank details · health information · anybody else's name or situation · anything about a learner or client.

➜ You can say "I work with young people leaving school in South Auckland" without naming one of them. See FRM-075.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 5 minutes. The problem, then build one live
  • Run ACT-117 Build Your Master Prompt
  • The best move: get one learner to build theirs in front of the room using pull prompting, then run the same question with and without it. The difference is obvious and nobody needs convincing afterwards
  • Common mistakes:
    • Writing it by hand. Slower and worse. Let it interview you
    • Making it five pages. A page. It is context, not a biography
    • Never updating it. Ten minutes every few months
    • Forgetting the "how I want it to sound" line, which is the one that stops the output reading like a press release
  • ⚠️ Check what a learner has put in one before they start pasting it everywhere. People over-share when a machine asks politely

FRM-077Framework · Wellbeing & Identity

The Water Cycle — why a pepeha runs in that order

modeltikanga, not a study
pepehaidentitywhakapapate-ao-maoritikangawater-cycleindigeneity

What it is in one line: a pepeha names maunga, then awa or moana, then iwi, hapū and marae because that is the order water travels, and the order is what decides who can say which lines.

Origin: Keri Opai — linguist and educator, author of Tikanga: An Introduction to te ao Māori (Upstart Press, 2021) and of Te Reo Hāpai. Set out in his E-Tangata pieces "Pepeha for non-Māori" and "A respectfully curious approach", and reached this library through Zeducation's own pepeha template. Evidence: tikanga, not a study. There is nothing to measure here and nothing to prove. It is an explanation of why a form is shaped the way it is, from somebody qualified to explain it. Best for: the two minutes before anybody writes a pepeha. It answers the question the room is already holding.

On this pageThe orderWhy that answers the question about non-MāoriThe line that has to come with itHow to teach itWhat this framework does not settleMore resourcesRelated frameworksUsed bySource

The order

It is a cycle, not a list. The maunga catches the rain and the snow. The water runs down into the awa, or out into the moana. It feeds the people who live along it. It goes back up into the sky, and it starts again.

➜ The word carries it too. Mau means to catch, to capture, to hold. Maunga is the thing that catches and holds.

So the sequence in a pepeha is not a preference or a tradition in the weak sense of the word. It is a description of a system, running in the direction the system runs.

Why that answers the question about non-Māori

The question comes up in every room that meets a pepeha: can I have one?

The short answer is yes. The longer answer is that it has to be built differently, and the water cycle is the reason.

The moveWhy it does not work
A maunga in Scotland, an awa in WaikatoThose two are not in the same water cycle. The mountain does not feed that river. The sentence describes a system that does not exist
Claiming iwi and hapū you do not whakapapa toIwi and hapū are descent groups. You are in one or you are not
Picking a maunga in Aotearoa you happen to likeThe maunga in a pepeha is not the one you liked the view of. It is the one your people come from

➜ Opai's own words, and they are worth reading out rather than paraphrasing:

"I believe that it's inappropriate for non-Māori people to use the same pepeha as tangata whenua. It is not a matter of mere opinion, of like or dislike, of right or wrong: it simply doesn't make sense. It is a matter of indigeneity."

That last line is the one to sit on. The objection is not that somebody will be offended. It is that the sentence is not true. Tangata whenua means people of the land, and the pepeha is the form that says so. Somebody whose people arrived four generations ago saying it in that form is making a claim about origin that their own history does not support.

And nothing about that is a rejection. There is a structure that works, it is on FRM-079, and it does the same job.

The line that has to come with it

From Zeducation's own template, and it is the sentence that stops the whole thing turning into a compliance exercise:

The true essence of a pepeha is much more about connections and creating the potential for connections.

A pepeha is an offer, not a credential. It is not there to prove you belong. It is there so that somebody in the room can say my grandmother is from there too — and now there are two of you who know something you did not know a minute ago.

➜ Teach the purpose before the form. A room that learns the form first hears an exam. A room that learns the purpose first hears an invitation.

How to teach it

Two minutes, standing up, before anybody sees a template.

  1. Draw the cycle on the whiteboard. Mountain, arrow down, river, arrow to people, arrow back up.
  2. "That is the order. It is not decoration, it is the water."
  3. "Which is why, if your maunga is in Sāmoa or Sichuan or Skye, you cannot then name an awa in Aotearoa. Those two are not connected. It is not about permission, it is that the sentence would not be true."
  4. "So there are two structures. Both of them do the same job, which is connection."

Then split the room by which template they are using, and nobody has to ask. That is the practical reason to teach this first — it turns an awkward question into a diagram.

What this framework does not settle

⚠️ Open gap: pepeha varies by rohe, and this page teaches one pattern. Some iwi lead with waka. Some name moana rather than awa. Some include tūpuna the template here does not. The template is a starting point for people who have none, not a correction to anybody who already has theirs.

If somebody in the room already has a pepeha from their marae, theirs is right and this page is not. Say that out loud before you hand the sheet out.

  • 📄 Auckland Newsroom — what is a pepeha? A complete guide to Māori introductions — a plain overview for somebody meeting the form for the first time
  • 📄 Keri Opai — Pepeha for non-Māori (E-Tangata) — the source of this reasoning. An edited extract from Tikanga
  • 📄 Keri Opai — A respectfully curious approach (E-Tangata) — the companion piece
  • 🎬 How to say your pepeha: tikanga explained — the tikanga, not just the words. The right video for this framework
  • 🎬 How to say your pepeha — Speak Māori — structure and pronunciation together

FRM-078Framework · Wellbeing & Identity

Pepeha for Māori Whānau — the template

tooltikanga, not a study
pepehaidentitywhakapapate-ao-maorimaoriintroductionshouse-content

What it is in one line: eleven lines that walk from the maunga down to your own name, and say who you are by saying who and where you come from.

Origin: Zeducation's own template (SRC-019), page 03. The resource cites pepeha.nz, Tākai, Māori Tourism and Mihi — introductions, Māori ki Te Whare Wānanga o Ōtākou, University of Otago. Evidence: tikanga, not a study. Best for: a learner who whakapapa Māori and has never had their pepeha written down.

On this pageWhy pepeha points to whakapapaThe templateThe three lines people get stuck onIf somebody already has their pepeha⚠️ The rule that governs this pageMore resourcesRelated frameworksUsed bySource

Why pepeha points to whakapapa

Zeducation's own framing, from the resource:

For Māori, pepeha points to whakapapa (ancestry). Whakapapa speaks to relationships and links with the land, the sea, the environment, our world and the universe. The idea of pepeha is universal.

The order is the water cycle — see FRM-077. Maunga first because the maunga catches and holds the water; then the awa that carries it; then the people it feeds.

The template

Reproduced exactly as published. Do not paraphrase it and do not let anything generate an alternative version.

Te reoEnglish
Tēnā koutou katoaGreetings
Ko . . . . . te maunga. . . . . is the mountain
Ko . . . . . te awa. . . . . is the river
Ko . . . . . te waka. . . . . is the canoe
Ko . . . . . tōku iwi. . . . . is my tribe
Ko . . . . . tōku hapū. . . . . is my sub tribe / clan
Ko . . . . . tōku matua. . . . . is my father
Ko . . . . . tōku whaea. . . . . is my mother
Ko . . . . . tōku kāinga. . . . . is where I live
Ko . . . . . tōku ingoa. . . . . is my name
No reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tatou katoa.Therefore, greetings, greetings, greetings to us all

⚠️ One thing for a reo speaker to check, not for a facilitator to fix. The last line as published reads "No reira" and "tēnā tatou katoa". Both words normally carry macrons — nō reira, tātou. Every other word on the page is macronised correctly (tōku, hapū, kāinga), so this looks like a typesetting slip. It is reproduced as published above. Ask somebody who knows, then fix it on the original — do not fix it from a search result, and do not ask a model.

The resource also writes "whanau" without the macron in its page headings, while using "whānau" correctly in the body. Same note applies.

The three lines people get stuck on

LineWhy it stallsWhat to say
Te maunga"I don't know mine."That is the normal answer, not a failure. It is a question for a parent, an aunty, a nan. ACT-119 is the homework, and its whole point is that the asking is the exercise
Te wakaMany people never learnt theirsIt is fine to leave a line out. A short true pepeha beats a long guessed one
Tōku matua / whaeaA parent who is absent, unknown, or not safe to nameNobody has to say a name they do not want to say. Skip the line. There is no rule in this room that says otherwise

➜ The rule that covers all three: say what you know, leave what you don't, and go and ask.

If somebody already has their pepeha

Theirs is right and this page is not. Pepeha varies by rohe. Some lead with waka, some name moana rather than awa, some carry tūpuna this template does not mention. This template is a starting point for people who have nothing written down — never a correction to somebody whose marae gave them theirs.

Say that before you hand the sheet out, not after somebody has spotted the difference.

⚠️ The rule that governs this page

No AI-generated te reo. A model asked to fill in a maunga, an awa or an iwi will produce one immediately, fluently, and often wrongly — see FRM-075. A pepeha built that way names a mountain that has nothing to do with the person saying it, in front of a room that may well include somebody who knows the difference.

A pepeha comes from whānau. Ask a person.

FRM-079Framework · Wellbeing & Identity

Pepeha for Non-Māori Whānau — the template

tooltikanga, not a study
pepehaidentitybelongingte-ao-maorimigrantspakehapacific

What it is in one line: nine lines that let somebody whose people are not from here introduce themselves in te reo without claiming a maunga or an awa they have no whakapapa to — and still do the one job a pepeha exists to do.

Origin: Keri Opai, set out in "Pepeha for non-Māori" (E-Tangata, an edited extract from Tikanga: An Introduction to te ao Māori, Upstart Press, 2021). It reached this library through Zeducation's own template, page 02, which cites the article but does not name him. Evidence: tikanga, not a study. Best for: Pākehā, Pacific, Asian, African, Middle Eastern and every other learner in a Zeducation room whose people arrived here — which, in most Zeducation rooms, is most of the room.

On this pageWhat it is solvingThe templateThe word doing the work is engariWhat it deliberately leaves out, and why that is the pointHow to run it⚠️ Open gap: this is one authority's structure, not a national standardMore resourcesRelated frameworksUsed bySource

What it is solving

Read FRM-077 The Water Cycle first. The short version:

Maunga → awa → iwi → hapū → marae is the water cycle. A person whose mountain is in Sāmoa or Guangdong or Gisborne-by-way-of-Glasgow cannot then name a river in Aotearoa, because those two are not part of the same system. The sentence would not be describing anything real.

➜ So this template does not name a maunga or an awa at all. It names ancestry, the place you grew up, home, where you are from, where you live now, what you do, and your name.

Zeducation's own framing of what that buys:

This pepeha template for our non-Māori whānau satisfies the needs of making possible connections with people in the audience but does so without misappropriating any Indigenous ties to land, water and air. Keep in mind that the true essence of a pepeha is much more about connections and creating the potential for connections.

The template

Reproduced exactly as published.

Te reoEnglish
Tēnā koutou katoaGreetings
Ko . . . . . te whakapaparanga mai. . . . . is my ancestry
(engari)(but, however)
Ko . . . . . te whenua tupu. . . . . (place name) is where I grew up
Ko . . . . . te kāinga. . . . . (place) is my home
Nō . . . . . auI'm from (place) . . . . .
Kei . . . . . au e noho anaI am living in (place) . . . . .
He . . . . . au i . . . . .I am a (job title) at (name of work / organisation)
Ko . . . . . auI am (name)
Tēnā tātou katoaGreetings to one and all

The word doing the work is engari

"But." It is the hinge of the whole structure, and it is worth ten seconds in the room.

My ancestry is Sāmoan and Irish — engari — Māngere is where I grew up.

Two truths, held at once, in the right order. Where your people came from, and where your life actually happened. Neither one cancels the other, and the second one is not a lesser claim.

➜ For a lot of learners this is the first time anybody has given them a form that does that. The usual question is "where are you really from", which forces one answer. This gives both, and it is the reason this template lands harder than the Māori one does in most Zeducation rooms.

What it deliberately leaves out, and why that is the point

Not in this templateBecause
MaungaNot in the same water cycle. See FRM-077
Awa / moanaSame
Iwi, hapūDescent groups. You whakapapa to them or you do not
MaraeWhere a hapū stands. You can be welcomed onto one without it being yours

None of that is a demotion. The pepeha exists to create the potential for connection, and this template creates plenty: ancestry, a suburb, a hometown, a job. Any one of those can be the thing somebody in the room shares with you.

➜ The line to say if the room goes quiet: "You are not getting a smaller version. You are getting the one that is true. A true introduction connects. A borrowed one just gets through the minute."

How to run it

  1. Purpose first, always — connection, not credential.
  2. The water cycle, two minutes on the whiteboard.
  3. Both templates on one sheet, and the learner picks (ACT-120). Do not sort the room by who looks Māori to you. Nobody gets handed a version based on your guess about their whakapapa.
  4. Say it out loud (ACT-121). Written and never spoken, it is a worksheet.

⚠️ Open gap: this is one authority's structure, not a national standard

Opai gives two versions in the article — a basic one and a more detailed one. It could not be confirmed which of the two this is, or whether any line was changed, because the E-Tangata articles are blocked by this environment's gateway (HTTP 403) and were assessed through search only.

Some marae, iwi and workplaces do it differently. If a host organisation has its own way, theirs wins in their whare. This template is for a learner who has been asked to introduce themselves and has nothing.

And the pronunciation is not optional. Handing somebody a te reo template and no practice sets them up to be embarrassed in public. ACT-121 exists for exactly that reason.

ACT-002Activity · Communication

How Assertive Am I?

10-15 minassessment
assertivenessself-assessmentself-awareness

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it practises: self-awareness against FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles

Materials: the printed assessment, a pen. Nobody collects it. Say that clearly before they start.

On this pageThe instrumentScoringDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

The instrument

Read each statement and answer honestly. Score each one: 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I do not feel guilty when I ask others to do something
2If I do not want to do something someone has asked me to do, I can say "no" without feeling guilty
3I have no problem speaking to large groups of people or audiences
4I am able to express myself openly and honestly to my superiors
5I am able to verbally express my feelings of anger, tension, stress and frustration openly
6When sitting in a large group, I am able to speak up confidently
7If I disagree with a decision in a meeting, which goes against the majority, I am able to stay focused and stick to my opinion
8I openly acknowledge my mistakes
9If somebody's behaviour bothers me, I tell them
10I do not use a blaming tone of voice when I express my anger
11I am able to meet new people in different environments confidently and at ease
12I do not label other people's opinions as senseless, stupid or irrational when we disagree
13I believe in myself and feel confident when doing something for the first time
14I believe in live and let live. My needs are just as important as everyone else's
15I assume people are honest, reliable and trustworthy, and I am not hesitant about delegating to others
Total

Scoring

ScoreWhat it meansYour next step
60+Your beliefs, opinions and actions are those of a very assertive person. You handle most situations well, respecting your own rights and the rights of people around youPick the situation where you still hold back, and go there next
45-59You are fairly assertive, depending on the situation. Remember that respect is a key part of assertiveness: respecting yourself and expecting respect from othersNotice which rooms and which people you drop out of assertive with
30-44You are in the middle of the road. Neither aggressive nor assertiveSpeak up for yourself and take the tools from this course into your next conversation
15-29The first positive step towards being more assertive is being hereListen, learn and apply. Start with one "I" statement this week

Debrief

  • Which statements did you score lowest on? Is there a pattern?
  • Is your score different at work than it is at home?
  • Which one statement, if it moved from a 2 to a 4, would change the most for you?

The point to land: this is a snapshot, not a label. Assertiveness is situational and it is trainable. The lowest scores are the training plan.

Variations

  • Youth: reword items 4 and 15 to school, coach and part-time work settings
  • Low literacy: read each statement aloud and have learners hold up fingers 1-5
  • Online: a form with auto-scoring, results shown only to the learner
  • Repeat measure: run it again at the end of the programme and compare. Good evidence for funders and for the learner

Watch out for

  • Never have learners read their score out. Ask what they noticed, not what they scored
  • Some people score themselves harshly. Reframe: a low score means the tools have somewhere to work
  • Do not turn this into a diagnosis. It is a mirror

Source: Zeducation Effective Communication workbook.

ACT-012Activity · Communication

How Clear Am I?

10-12 minassessment
self-assessmentclear-messagingself-awarenessblufbriefing

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it practises: self-awareness against BLUF, PREP and What-Why-How.

⚠️ Note: Module 2 of the workbook has no self-assessment. This one was written to match the house instrument in ACT-002 — same 1-5 scale, same band structure, same tone. It is Zeducation's, not from an external source, and has not been validated. Treat it as a teaching mirror, not a measure.

On this pageThe instrumentScoringDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I say the main point in the first line of a message
2People do the thing I asked for without needing a follow-up message
3I know what I want to say before I start saying it
4I use plain words instead of jargon my team may not know
5I back up my recommendations with a real example
6When I give instructions, I explain why the task matters, not just what to do
7I check understanding rather than assuming people got it
8I choose the channel to fit the message (a call for something sensitive, a message for something simple)
9My messages are short enough that people read all of them
10When I brief a team, other people talk too
11I ask for the specific action I want, with a deadline
12People rarely misunderstand what I meant
Total

Scoring

ScoreWhat it meansYour next step
50-60Your messages land. People know what you mean and what to do, and you check rather than assumeTeach it. Fix one team member's briefing habit this month
38-49You are clear most of the time, and it slips when you are busy or under pressureNotice which situations cost you clarity. Rushed messages are usually the culprit
25-37Middle of the road. Your point is in there, but people have to dig for itStart with BLUF. First line, main point, every message for two weeks
12-24Being here is the first step. This is a skill, not a talent, and it moves fast with practicePick one message a day. Write it, then move your last line to the top

Debrief

  • Which statements did you score lowest on? Is the pattern in your writing, your speaking, or your briefings?
  • Is your score different for messages up the chain versus down the chain?
  • Which single one, if it moved from a 2 to a 4, would save you the most time in a week?

The point to land: clear communication is a habit stack, not a personality. Every low score on this page has a tool attached to it that you learned today.

Variations

  • Repeat measure: run it again at the end of the programme and compare. Useful evidence for funders and for the learner
  • 360 version: ask a team member to score the same 12 statements about you. The gap is the real conversation
  • Low literacy: read each statement aloud, learners hold up 1-5 fingers
  • Online: a form with auto-scoring, results visible only to the learner

Watch out for

  • Never have learners read scores aloud. Ask what they noticed, not what they scored
  • Item 12 depends on other people, so some learners will not know. Tell them to answer on their best guess and talk about that uncertainty in the debrief
  • This is a mirror, not a diagnosis

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this.

5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I can say no to extra work without apologising three times
2When I turn something down, I say what I am protecting, not just that I am busy
3I offer an alternative when I say no, instead of just closing the door
4⟲ I say yes to things I know I do not have room for

Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 4, 7 and 11, flip your answer before adding it up: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60You hold your limits and keep your relationships. That combination is rareTeach it. Someone on your team is drowning in yeses right now, and you know who
38-49You hold most of the time. It slips with certain people, or when you are tiredWork out who you cannot say no to. It is usually one or two people, not everyone. Build one Positive No for that person this week
25-37The limit is there, but people have to find it by accidentStart with the middle line. Write one clear no, one sentence, and say it out loud before you need it
12-24Being honest here is the first step, and it is the hard onePick one small, low-risk request this week and use all three parts: Yes, No, Yes. One. Not a new personality, one sentence

Facilitating it

  • Run it before teaching the frameworks, so learners have a reason to listen, or after, as the reflection. Both work. Before is stronger for groups who think this is not their problem
  • Say clearly that nobody hands it in
  • The reverse-scored items catch the people-pleaser pattern. If you have a group that scores high on everything except 4, 7 and 11, that is your teaching point for the day
  • Do not read scores out. Ask instead: "which single statement did you least want to be honest about?"

Watch out for

  • Some learners genuinely cannot say no at work: probation, a visa, an insecure contract, or being the only earner. A low score here is a circumstance, not a character flaw. Say that out loud before people score themselves, or the instrument does harm
  • Item 11 can surface real distress. Know your referral path before the session

RangeWhat it meansYour next step

Facilitating it

  • Best run after ACT-018 Bad Listening, Then SOLER. People score themselves far more honestly once they have felt what bad listening does
  • Item 10 is the useful one. It is the only item that measures the result rather than the behaviour, and it is the one that changes people's minds about their score
  • Say clearly that nobody hands it in
  • Optional and powerful: ask learners to also guess how the person they work most closely with would score them. The gap is the conversation

Watch out for

  • Overconfidence. Nearly everyone rates themselves a good listener. If the whole room scores 50+, do not argue with them, go back to item 10 and to the round-one experience instead
  • Learners in noisy, fast, high-interruption jobs (kitchens, sites, wards, contact centres) will score low on items 1 and 9 for reasons that are about the job, not about them. Name that

Where Is My Team Right Now?

12-15 minassessment
teamsteam-developmentself-assessmentleadershipdiagnosis

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: which stage of FRM-018 Tuckman your team is actually in. Unlike most instruments here it is not scored on a scale. You tick what is true and count the columns.

⚠️ Not validated. It is a teaching mirror, not a measure. Fine for the room, not for reporting.

On this pageHow to run itReading itFacilitator notesUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

Tick every statement that is true of your team right now. Be honest rather than hopeful. Then count the ticks in each block.

Block F

  • ☐ People are still polite and careful with each other
  • ☐ Most decisions come from the person in charge
  • ☐ I am not completely sure what some people's jobs are
  • ☐ Nobody has really disagreed with anyone yet

Block S

  • ☐ There is tension about who does what
  • ☐ People agree in the meeting and complain afterwards
  • ☐ Small groups have formed and they do not mix much
  • ☐ Someone has said, or nearly said, "that's not my job"

Block N

  • ☐ People say "we usually do it like this"
  • ☐ New people get shown how things work here without being told to
  • ☐ Someone can raise a problem without it becoming an argument
  • ☐ We have sorted out most of who does what

Block P

  • ☐ People disagree openly and it does not damage anything
  • ☐ Work gets done when the boss is away
  • ☐ People step in for each other without being asked
  • ☐ We talk about the result, not about whose fault it is

Block A

  • ☐ This work is ending or the team is changing soon
  • ☐ People are talking about what comes next
  • ☐ Nobody has said anything about what we achieved together

Ticks: F ___ S ___ N ___ P ___ A ___

Reading it

ResultWhat it meansYour first move
One block clearly highestThat is your stageGo to that row in ACT-032 Stage Moves and pick one action
F and S both highVery common, and usually means the team is storming quietlyThe work is making it safe to disagree out loud. Start with psychological safety
N and P both highGood position. The risk is coastingWrite the norms down before the next person joins or leaves
Spread evenly across allUsually means different parts of the team are in different placesAsk who is in which. It is often the newest people in Forming while everyone else has moved on
A ticked at allSomething is ending, and it is probably not being handledSay something out loud about what the team did. It costs nothing and people remember it for years

Facilitator notes

  • There is no good or bad stage. Say that before people start, or Forming and Storming get read as failure and the answers stop being honest
  • The most useful follow-up question: "would your team give the same answers?" Most learners are rating the team they wish they had
  • Watch for the person rating a team they have just left. Let them. It is often the most honest reading in the room, and it usually explains why they left
  • Use it twice. Once now, once in three months. The movement is more informative than the reading

The question that matters

Statement 10 is the whole instrument in one line. If it is the lowest number on your page, ignore the total and work on whatever made you circle it.

Ask it the other way round too: somebody junior to you is already copying something you do. What is it? Most people can answer that, and the answer is not always comfortable. That is the honest start of this topic.

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statements 4 and 9 are confronting and people will not answer honestly if they think it is going to be read out

  • Statement 9 is the one to discuss as a group, in general terms. Everybody is respectful when things are calm. Respect under pressure is the only kind that counts, and the framework's own line covers it: under pressure we do not rise to the level of our intentions, we fall to the level of our habits

What's My Default Style?

12-15 minassessment
decision-makingleadershipself-assessmentstylescollaboration

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: which of Lewin's three styles you fall back on, especially under pressure.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. Written in house to match the other Zeducation instruments.

On this pageThe instrumentReading itQuestion 7 is the real resultFacilitator notesUsed byRelated activities

The instrument

For each situation, tick the response closest to what you actually do, not what you would like to do.

#When…ABC
1A decision needs making and time is shortI decide and tell peopleI grab two people for a quick viewI let whoever is closest to it decide
2Someone asks "what do you reckon we should do?"I tell themI ask what they reckon firstI say "up to you"
3The team disagrees with a call I madeI explain why it standsI ask what I have missedI let them change it
4A new person is unsure how to do a taskI show them the way we do itI show them, then ask what they would changeI let them work it out
5Something has gone wrongI sort it, then tell peopleI get the people involved togetherI leave it with the people involved
6I am planning next month's workI plan it and share the planI draft it and ask for input before finalisingI ask the team to plan it
7Under real pressure, my instinct istake controlpull people inget out of the way

Count your ticks: A ___ B ___ C ___

Reading it

MostlyYour defaultWhat it gets youYour risk
AAutocratic, "my way"Speed and clarity. People always know where they standPeople stop bringing you things. You end up the only one thinking
BDemocratic, "our way"Ownership and better decisionsSlower. If overused you can read as unable to decide alone
CLaissez-faire, "your way"Space for capable people to growConfusion and silos if roles and goals are not already clear
Even spreadYou are already choosing per situationThis is the goalCheck question 7. Under pressure most people still have one default

Question 7 is the real result

Everything above question 7 is what you do when things are calm. Question 7 is what you do when they are not, and that is the style your team actually experiences, because pressure is when leadership gets noticed.

If your answers to 1 to 6 are spread and question 7 is a hard A, you are a democratic leader who becomes autocratic under load. That is extremely common, it is not a character flaw, and it is worth telling your team so they can read you.

Facilitator notes

  • There is no winning column. Say it before people start. Lewin found democratic produced the best outcomes overall, and question 1 has a right answer that is not democratic
  • The most useful follow-up: "what would your team say your default is?" Ask people to guess, then to actually go and ask someone. The reports back are the best material in this topic
  • Do not have people share their letters in front of their manager. Column A is easy to read as a criticism
  • Pair it with ACT-050 Whose Call Is It?, run first. People assess themselves more honestly once they have seen that all three styles are legitimate

10-16Your load looks manageable and your yeses are mostly deliberateLook at statement 7. Being the only one who knows something is a risk that builds quietly
17-23You are carrying more than your share, and it is probably invisible to everyone including youDo ACT-060 The Yes Audit. Pick one thing to hand over this month
24-30You are the person everyone relies on, and the research says that is the group most likely to burn out and leaveThis is not a personal failing and you will not fix it alone. Take the audit to your manager as a workload conversation, not a complaint

The top band is deliberately worded that way. In this instrument a high score is not a good result, and learners who are used to being praised for exactly these behaviours need that said plainly.

Which driver is yours?

StatementsDriverWhat helps
2, 8Desire to helpHabit 1, the helpful no. Offer something smaller instead of everything
3, 4Need for accomplishmentHabit 3. Check it against your goals before you answer
6, 9FearName it. Fear of missing out, of losing control, of what people will think
5, 7, 10You have become the bottleneckHabit 2. Delegate and grow others. This is the most urgent one

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statements 6 and 8 are personal
  • The 3 to 5% statistic first. Give people the research before the instrument, or a high score reads as a personal weakness rather than a predictable outcome of being good and willing
  • Statement 10 is the leader's question. If a whole team scores high on it, the organisation has a design problem, not ten individual problems
  • If someone is clearly not coping, this is a conversation, not a worksheet. Know your referral options before you run it: EAP if the workplace has one, their GP, or 1737, the free national helpline, call or text
  • Do not use this with an intact team where the manager will see individual results

PatternWhat it usually meansWhere to go
Awareness high, Competence and Safety lowThe most common profile. You can see it and you have not built anythingFRM-034 S.A.F.E, the S and E steps

Facilitator notes

  • Statement 16 is the trap, and it is deliberate. "Team members say they can be themselves here without penalty." You cannot answer that. Only they can. Ramsden's whole point is that cultural safety is judged by the recipient. Say this out loud when people reach it, and treat any high score on 16 that is not based on someone actually saying so as a guess
  • Nobody shares scores. Especially not in front of their own team
  • The best follow-up is a real one: run statement 17 for a week. "Did you feel respected today?" Then compare what you hear with what you scored
  • ⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. Fine for the room, not for reporting, and definitely not for assessing whether an organisation is culturally safe
  • Watch the room. In a mixed group, people who have been on the receiving end of the failures in this instrument are doing unpaid emotional work while their manager fills it in. Do not ask anyone to help their manager score it

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: what you actually do when conflict turns up, across the four things this programme teaches: noticing, listening, responding and resolving.

⚠️ Not validated, and written fresh. The Future Ready: Conflict Resolution guide (SRC-007) contains no self-assessment, which was the largest gap in it. This instrument was written in house to match the Zeducation shape. It is a teaching mirror, not a measure.

On this pageThe instrumentScore chartWhat the questions map toThe two statements worth talking aboutFacilitator notesUsed byRelated activities

The instrument

Circle the number that best describes you.

#StatementNot really meSometimes meUsually me
1I deal with disagreements early, while they are still small123
2I can tell the difference between a problem with the work and a problem with the person123
3When someone is upset with me, I let them finish before I explain123
4I ask what matters to the other person, not just what happened123

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move
24-30You handle conflict deliberately rather than by reflexPick your lowest single statement. It is probably 5, 8 or 10
18-23A good base, and some of it disappears when the pressure goes upLook at statements 3, 6 and 7 together. That cluster is what goes first
10-17Conflict is mostly happening to you rather than being handledStart with statement 1. Dealing with one small thing early is the cheapest change on this page

What the questions map to

QuestionsWhat they measureWhere to go
1, 2Noticing and naming. Do you know what kind of conflict you are in?FRM-037 The Three Types
3, 4, 5Listening past the words. Content, values, feelingsFRM-038 Powerful Listening
5, 6, 7, 9Staying steady and respondingFRM-039, FRM-041 De-escalation
8, 10Resolving, and checking it heldFRM-040 Moving to Resolution

The two statements worth talking about

Statement 1 is the highest-leverage item in the instrument. Nearly every conflict in this programme's case studies became difficult because it was left. It is also the one people score themselves generously on, so ask the follow-up: what is the thing you are currently not dealing with?

Statement 10 is the one almost nobody scores well on, and it is invisible. Most people treat a resolved conflict as finished. Going back a fortnight later and asking "did that actually work?" is rare, cheap, and the reason some resolutions hold and others quietly do not.

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statement 7 in particular is personal
  • Run it early, not late. It works better as a map at the start of the programme than as a verdict at the end. If you have time, run it twice and let people see the movement
  • Watch for the low scorer reading it as a character verdict. Every item is a behaviour, and the lowest band names the smallest possible first step on purpose
  • Statement 7 can be heavy for anyone who has faced real aggression at work. It is a skill question, not a courage question, and the answer for genuine aggression is to leave and get help. See the safety note on FRM-041
  • This is not part of the micro-credential. It carries no assessment weight and should not be uploaded as evidence

What Do You Actually Believe About People?

20 minassessment
leadershipassumptionstrustmotivationself-assessmentmindset

Type: self-assessment · Time: 20 min · Group: individual, then whole room · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-045 McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y.

⚠️ Run it before you teach the framework, not after. If people know which answers are the "right" ones, they will give you those and learn nothing.

On this pageThe statementsHow to run itStatement 6 is the interesting oneDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The statements

Tick agree or disagree. First reaction. Do not think about it.

StatementAgreeDisagree
1Most people would rather be told what to do than take responsibility☐☐
2If you don't check, it doesn't get done☐☐
3People are mostly here for the money☐☐
4Most people want to do a good job☐☐
5Given the chance, people will take on more than you asked☐☐
6You have to earn trust before you get it☐☐
7If someone is underperforming, they usually know why☐☐
8Most problems at work are people problems☐☐
9If you give people freedom, most will use it well☐☐
10The best way to get performance is clear consequences☐☐

Scoring. Give yourself one point for each agree on 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 10. Give yourself one point for each disagree on 4, 5, 7, 9.

Your score: ____ out of 10

ScoreWhat it suggests
0-3You lean strongly Theory Y. Watch that you are not confusing trust with an absence of standards
4-6Mixed, which is where most working supervisors land. Worth knowing which statements pushed you which way
7-10You lean Theory X. That is not a character flaw and it may be an accurate read of your workplace. It is worth knowing you are running it

How to run it

  1. Statements first, cold (5 min). No framing, no theory, no context. "Just tick"
  2. Score it (2 min). Do not reveal what the scale is yet
  3. Now teach Theory X and Theory Y (7 min). The room works out what they just scored, and the recognition is the moment the session works
  4. The two questions (6 min). Individually, in writing:
    • Which single statement would you most like to be wrong about?
    • What would you have to see to change your mind on it?

Statement 6 is the interesting one

"You have to earn trust before you get it."

Most rooms agree with it almost unanimously, and it sounds like plain common sense. Then ask:

Your new starter walks in on day one. Do they start on zero and earn their way up, or do they start with a full tank and spend it?

Both are defensible. But a leader who starts everyone on zero has to be told everything twice before they believe it, and their team learns that fast. This one statement usually generates more discussion than the other nine combined.

Debrief

Ask these to the room, not to individuals.

  • Which statement did the room split on most?
  • Think of a workplace where Theory X was the correct read. What made it correct?
  • Has anyone ever had a manager decide you were a Theory X employee? What did that do?
  • The real one: does your team think you are running X or Y? Would they be right?

Variations

  • Two-corners version: read each statement aloud and have people physically move to the agree wall or the disagree wall. Faster, more honest, and you can see the splits
  • Team version: the whole team fills it in anonymously about the workplace, not about themselves: "around here, it is assumed that…". The result is a culture reading
  • Manager and team version: the leader predicts their team's average score, then the team scores it. The gap is the finding, and it is usually a big one
  • Low literacy: read the statements aloud, thumbs up or thumbs down, eyes closed

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This is not a test with a right answer, and learners will assume it is. Say so before and after. McGregor leaned Theory Y, and a high X score is information, not a verdict
  • ⚠️ Some learners supervise people they genuinely cannot trust. Sometimes for good reasons, sometimes because of the workplace rather than the people. Do not push them to recant in the room
  • The socially acceptable score. Once anyone works out which way the scale runs, the answers get nicer. This is why the statements come first
  • Do not let it become a diagnosis of an absent manager. Fun, useless. Bring it back to "and which one am I running?"

What's My Code?

30-40 minassessment
career-readinessriasecintereststahatujob-searchwork-readiness

Type: assessment, on the real tool · Time: 30-40 min · Group: individual, with devices · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-056 RIASEC, using Tahatū's interest quiz.

⚠️ This activity uses somebody else's tool on purpose. Zeducation does not have 800 career profiles with New Zealand pay and demand data, and never will. Tahatū does, it is free, and it is kept current. Our job is the twenty minutes either side of the quiz, which is where the value is.

On this pageBefore the sessionHow to run itStep 4 is the whole activityDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Before the session

  • [ ] Check the devices and the wifi. This activity dies without them
  • [ ] Run the quiz yourself and know your own code, so you can go first
  • [ ] Have a plan for anyone without a device: pair them up, no comment
  • [ ] Read FRM-056's evidence audit so you can answer "is this like those Facebook quizzes?" honestly

How to run it

1. Frame it before anyone opens a laptop (5 min). This sentence decides whether the activity helps or harms:

"This tells you what you're drawn to. It does not tell you what you'd be good at, and it's only a weak guide to whether you'd be happy. What it's actually good for is giving you words, and showing you jobs you've never heard of. Nobody in here is going to be defined by four letters."

2. Take the quiz (10 min). tahatu.govt.nz · Everyone works alone. Quiet room.

3. Write down three things (5 min):
My top letters______
One job on my list I had never heard of______________________
One job on my list that surprised me______________________

4. Go to the career profiles (10 min). This is the part that matters. Pick one job from the list and find:

  • What it actually pays in New Zealand
  • What you need to get in — a ticket, a licence, a qualification, or nothing
  • Whether anyone is hiring

5. Pairs (5 min). Tell your partner the job you looked up and one thing that surprised you.

6. Close (5 min). "What do you want to look up tonight?"

Step 4 is the whole activity

The quiz is a doorway. The career profiles are the room.

A learner who leaves knowing their code has got a souvenir. A learner who leaves knowing that a diesel mechanic apprenticeship pays what it pays, and takes what it takes, has got something they can act on.

➜ If time is short, cut the quiz, not step 4. Have them search a job they are already curious about.

Debrief

  • Who got a result that felt wrong? What did it miss?
  • What is one job on the list nobody in here had heard of?
  • Did anyone's list have something they have always wanted to do and never said?
  • The important one: what would you have to find out to take that seriously?

Variations

  • No devices: print six type descriptions, put them in six corners, have people stand in the one that sounds most like them, then second-most. Crude, fast, and it still opens the conversation
  • Whānau version: homework is to have a family member guess your code before you tell them. The gap is usually interesting
  • Employer version: with a group already in work, run it as "what part of your current job do you actually like?" rather than as career change
  • Youth version: the surprise job is the hook. Run step 4 as a race to find the strangest real job with a real salary

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never let a code become a verdict. "I'm not a Social so I shouldn't do support work" is the failure mode, and it can steer somebody away from a career they would be good at. Interests are not ability
  • ⚠️ Interests are limited by exposure. A learner who has never met an engineer will not test toward engineering. For people whose exposure has been narrow, the quiz partly measures what they have been shown. Say so
  • ⚠️ Watch the gendered pull. Realistic skews male, Social skews female, mostly because of how people are raised. Do not let a result quietly move a young woman away from a trade or a young man away from care work
  • ⚠️ Somebody's result will land badly, especially anyone who has been out of work a long time, or whose list is full of jobs needing study they cannot afford. Have the next step ready: what is on the list that needs a ticket rather than a degree?
  • The learner who says "it's rubbish". Sometimes they are right and the quiz missed them. Agree, and go to step 4 with a job they choose themselves

Where Did Your Jobs Come From?

20-25 minassessment
career-readinessjob-searchhidden-job-marketnetworkingweak-tieswork-readinessevidence

Type: assessment, and the best opener in the topic · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found.

Do not tell the room that most jobs come through people. Let them prove it to themselves in eleven minutes. The tally on the board is more convincing than any statistic, and unlike a statistic it is about them.

On this pagePart 1 — every job you have ever had (8 min, individual)Part 2 — put each one in a channel (5 min)Part 3 — the room tally (7 min, whole room)Part 4 — one name (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — every job you have ever had (8 min, individual)

All of them. Paper runs, the weekend job at the takeaway, the two weeks fruit picking, cash jobs, the family business. Especially the first one.

#The jobHow did you actually hear about it?
1
2
3
4
5
6

⚠️ "How did you hear about it" is the question, not "how did you apply". Plenty of people saw an ad only after somebody told them to look.

Part 2 — put each one in a channel (5 min)

ChannelMark it
1I saw an ad and applied cold. Nobody knew me
2There was an ad, and somebody inside knew me or handed my name over
3It was never advertised. Somebody told me, or I was asked
4It was made for me. They met me and found work

My totals: 1 ▢▢▢ 2 ▢▢▢ 3 ▢▢▢ 4 ▢▢▢

Part 3 — the room tally (7 min, whole room)

Four columns on the board. Take a show of hands per channel and count.

Channel 1Channel 2Channel 3Channel 4
This room

➜ Then ask the question that does the work:

"Now, where have you been putting all your effort this month?"

Almost always the answer is channel 1, and almost always the board says channels 2 and 3 got them most of their jobs. Let the room sit with that for a moment before you say anything.

Part 4 — one name (5 min)

Look back at your channels 2, 3 and 4 rows.

Who was the person? Write their name.

The jobThe person who told me

Two questions:

  1. Did you ask them, or did they just happen to mention it? (Usually the second.)
  2. How well did you know them? Close friend, or somebody you barely knew?

⚠️ Most people find it was somebody they barely knew, who mentioned it by accident. That is FRM-024 weak ties, demonstrated on their own life. Do not explain it before they find it.

Debrief

  • What did the board say? What surprised you?
  • Where has your effort been going?
  • Who was the person in Part 4? Have you spoken to them since?
  • Whose first job came through family? (Most hands.) So we already know how this works.
  • What would change if you gave channels 2 and 3 half the time you give channel 1?

Variations

  • Whānau version: ask about a parent's or an uncle's jobs too. Widens the sample and gets stories
  • Employer version: ask a hiring manager how they filled their last three roles. The same tally from the other side of the table, and it is even more persuasive
  • Long version: add a fifth column for "how long did it take". Channel 1 jobs are usually the slowest, which nobody expects
  • Quick version: last three jobs only, straight to the board. Ten minutes
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken, facilitator tallies on the board as people call theirs out. Works just as well and it is often livelier

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not quote a percentage. The figures that circulate for the hidden job market are unsourced and this activity does not need them. The board is the evidence
  • ⚠️ "So it's who you know" can land as proof the system is rigged, especially for learners who already feel shut out. Turn it immediately: you have a network, it is bigger than you think, and using it is free. Pair this with the employer's-side reason from FRM-061
  • The learner with no jobs yet. School leavers, new migrants, somebody out of prison. Use family members' jobs instead, or the room's, and say up front that a short list is not a short future
  • The learner whose list is all channel 1. It happens. It is real, and it is usually somebody with a small network in this country. Do not argue with their sheet
  • Do not let the tally become a competition about how many jobs people have had

Which One Broke?

25-30 minassessment
leadershipmotivationexpectancydiagnosisteamsfairness

Type: assessment, and a diagnostic · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then groups · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-072 Vroom's Expectancy Theory.

"They're just not motivated" is the sentence this activity exists to replace. Three questions, and it usually takes about a minute to find which link has actually broken.

On this pageThe three questions, on the boardPart 1 — your own (8 min, individual)Part 2 — six scenarios (12 min, groups)Part 3 — one real person (8 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The three questions, on the board

The questionIf it is broken, the fix is
E — Expectancy"If I try, can I actually do it?"Training, tools, a smaller step. Not encouragement
I — Instrumentality"If I do it, will the thing actually happen?"Keep a promise. Then another. Slowest to repair
V — Valence"Do I even want the thing?"Ask what they actually want

⚠️ A zero anywhere gives you zero. A great reward nobody believes they will get is worth nothing.

Part 1 — your own (8 min, individual)

Think of a time you stopped trying at something. Work, school, sport, a course, anything.

What was it? ______________________________________________

Was this a yes or a no?What made it that way
Could I actually do it if I tried?
If I did it, would the thing happen?
Did I want the thing?

Which one broke first? ______________

➜ Most people say instrumentality, and it is worth taking a show of hands. They were told something would happen and it did not.

⚠️ Nobody has to share what the situation was. Only which of the three.

Part 2 — six scenarios (12 min, groups)

For each one: which link is broken, and what is the fix? The fix has to match the link.

#ScenarioBrokenFix
1Tane has been asked to run the stocktake. He has never been shown how. He keeps finding other jobs to do
2The team was told that whoever hit target would get first pick of the summer roster. Last year that was promised and the roster went to whoever asked loudest
3Mere has been offered a $50 voucher for perfect attendance. Mere needs more hours, not a voucher
4The new picking target is 40% higher than anyone has ever achieved. The team has stopped trying to reach it
5Sione is told he will be considered for team leader "down the track". He has heard that for two years
6A learner stops submitting work in week six. They passed everything up to week five

➜ Scenario 6 is deliberately about your own programme. Ask the room to answer it honestly.

Answers, for the facilitator: 1 expectancy · 2 instrumentality · 3 valence · 4 expectancy · 5 instrumentality · 6 could be any of the three, and that is the point — you have to ask.

Part 3 — one real person (8 min)

Somebody on your team, or in your class, who has stopped trying.
Which of the three do I think has broken?
How would I check, rather than assume?
What is the fix, and does it match the link?
When will I ask them?

⚠️ "How would I check rather than assume" is the most important line on this sheet. You cannot see somebody else's expectancy, instrumentality or valence. You can only ask.

Debrief

  • Which of the three broke in your own example? Show of hands
  • Why is instrumentality the most common one?
  • What happens when you aim encouragement at a broken expectancy? (Nothing. Sometimes worse than nothing)
  • Scenario 6. What is actually going on with a learner who stops in week six?
  • Who has been called unmotivated when one of these three had broken?

Variations

  • Reward-design version: for managers, run it on an existing incentive scheme. Most fail at valence and nobody ever checked
  • Two sides: half the room diagnoses as the supervisor, half as the person who stopped trying. Compare. The gap is usually large
  • Real scenarios: the room supplies them instead of the cards. Better, and it needs trust
  • Self-check version: run it on your own flat week rather than somebody else's
  • Low literacy: scenarios read aloud, answered by discussion, no writing

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Somebody who has stopped believing effort leads to outcomes is not lazy. They are accurately describing their own history. Say that out loud. For a lot of learners, instrumentality has been broken repeatedly before they walked in, and treating that as an attitude problem is both wrong and insulting
  • The room that diagnoses everybody as valence. "They just don't want it." Push back. Valence is the easiest to blame and the least often the real one
  • Do not let it become a tool for judging people. It is a tool for finding a fix. If somebody leaves with a diagnosis and no action, it has failed
  • Do not skip Part 3. The scenarios are practice; the real person is the point
  • ⚠️ Scenario 6 may get personal for a learner in the room. Keep it about the mechanism

ACT-118Activity · Digital Capability

Catch The Mistake

25-30 minassessment
digital-capabilityaihallucinationcheckingsafetycritical-thinkingte-reo

Type: assessment · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs at devices, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-075 What AI Actually Does.

Do not tell the room that AI makes things up. Make it happen in front of them. It takes about three questions and the room never forgets it.

⚠️ This activity has to come after the prompting ones, because a better prompt produces a more confident answer, and that is exactly the risk.

On this pagePart 1 — ask it about home (10 min, pairs)Part 2 — how sure did it sound? (5 min)Part 3 — the te reo one (5 min, whole room)Part 4 — the three rules (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — ask it about home (10 min, pairs)

Ask it things you can check. Local, specific, New Zealand.

#Ask itThen check
1Something about your own suburb or town — what is on the main street, what the local school is calledYou already know
2Something about Zeducation — what we do, where we are, what we offerYou already know
3The current New Zealand minimum wage, and when it last changedLook it up
4Whether a specific local course or provider existsLook it up
5A short mihi or pepeha, if anybody in the pair is comfortable asking⚠️ Ask a person, not the internet

Write down anything it got wrong:

______________________________________________

➜ Most pairs find something inside three questions. Some find nothing, and that is worth discussing too.

Part 2 — how sure did it sound? (5 min)

The finding that matters is not that it was wrong.

Yes / No
Did it say it was unsure about the thing it got wrong?☐
Did it sound different when it was wrong than when it was right?☐
Could you have told, without checking?☐

⚠️ Almost always no, no and no.

It is not lying to you. It has no idea it is wrong. It is producing the shape of a right answer.

Part 3 — the te reo one (5 min, whole room)

⚠️ Facilitator-led. Do not make anyone do this in a pair.

Ask it something in te reo Māori, or about tikanga, where somebody in the room actually knows the answer.

➜ It will answer. Fluently. And it does not hesitate more when it knows less.

The line: "It will never say 'I'm not the right one to ask about this.' A person would."

So the rule: for te reo Māori, Pacific languages, tikanga and anything about your own people, ask a person. Use it to practise, never to be the authority.

Part 4 — the three rules (5 min)

Write them down. They go on the wall.
1Check anything checkable. A name, a number, a date, a law, a place
2Never put in what you would not put on a noticeboard. No names, no health, no files about other people
3You sign it, so you own it. It does not matter that AI wrote it. Your name is on the CV

Then, one line each:

The thing I'm most likely to use AI for is: ______________________________________________

The thing in that I will always check is: ______________________________________________

Debrief

  • What did it get wrong? How fast?
  • Did anybody find nothing wrong? What does that tell you?
  • Could you have spotted it without checking?
  • Where would getting this wrong actually cost you something? (CV, assessment, money, a rule)
  • Who has already sent or submitted something AI wrote without checking?

Variations

  • Sector version: ask it about their trade. Site rules, tickets, a machine, a medication. Wrong answers there have real consequences and the room knows it
  • The reference test: ask it for three sources on a topic, then try to find them. Very effective, and slower
  • Two tools: ask the same question in two different tools and compare. Where they disagree, at least one is wrong
  • Staff version: ask it about NZQA rules, unit standards, or funding. Run this before any tutor uses AI for assessment material
  • Low tech: the facilitator does it on one screen while the room calls out what to check

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not turn it into a reason not to use AI. These tools are genuinely useful and the room will use them anyway. The point is the checking habit, not avoidance. Say that at the start and again at the end
  • ⚠️ Part 3 needs care. If nobody in the room is confident in te reo, do not stage a test somebody could feel exposed by. Use a tikanga question the facilitator knows the answer to
  • ⚠️ Somebody has already submitted something AI wrote without checking, and may realise it during this activity. Keep it about the habit, never about them, and do not ask
  • The pair that cannot find a mistake. Genuinely happens. Give them the minimum wage question and a harder local one, and note out loud that usually-right is exactly what makes the wrong one slip through
  • Do not let it become an argument about whether AI is good. It is a checking session

ACT-004Activity · Communication

Statement Sort — Four Corners

12-15 mingame
icebreakerenergisercommunication-stylesassertiveness

Type: game / energiser · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class · Energy: high

What it practises: recognising FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles in real language

Materials: four A4 signs — PASSIVE, AGGRESSIVE, PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE, ASSERTIVE — one in each corner of the room. The statement list below.

On this pageSet upHow to run itThe statementsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

Put the four signs up before the session starts. People will read them on the way in, which is half the teaching done already.

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in the middle.
  2. Read a statement out loud, in character.
  3. Learners walk to the corner they think it belongs to. No talking on the way.
  4. Once they are in corners, ask one person from the biggest corner and one from the smallest: what made you pick that?
  5. Give the answer, then read the next one. Twelve statements takes about ten minutes.

The statements

#StatementStyle
1"It's fine… I'll just do it myself."Passive-aggressive
2"You never do this right, I have to fix it every time."Aggressive
3"I can't take on extra work today, but I can help tomorrow."Assertive
4"Whatever you think… it doesn't matter to me."Passive
5"We need to follow the safety checks before starting."Assertive
6"Hurry up! You're slowing everyone down."Aggressive
7"I'd like to finish what I'm saying before we move on."Assertive
8"It's okay, I guess… I'll manage."Passive
9"You're hopeless at this job."Aggressive
10"I understand you're busy, but I need this report by 3pm."Assertive
11"Sure, I'll do it. Just like last time when no one helped me."Passive-aggressive
12"Oh, don't worry about me… I'm used to picking up the slack."Passive-aggressive

Facilitator: read them with the tone. Number 1 said flatly is passive-aggressive; said with genuine warmth it is not. That is the whole lesson and it lands better if they hear it than if you say it.

Debrief

  • Which ones split the room? Why?
  • How much of your decision was the words, and how much was my tone?
  • Which of these have you heard this week? Which have you said?

The point to land: the same words can be three different styles depending on how they are said. Assertive is not a script you memorise, it is words plus tone plus intent lining up.

Variations

  • Small room / online: four zoom reactions, or hold up 1-4 fingers instead of moving
  • Youth: swap in text messages and group chat lines
  • Competitive version: teams score a point per correct corner, best of twelve
  • Closer, not opener: run it again at the end of the session and see how much faster the room is

Watch out for

  • Do not let it become "which corner is the smart one". Every corner is a real thing people do
  • Nobody gets singled out for standing in the wrong corner. Ask for reasoning, not defence
  • Watch mobility. Offer the fingers version to anyone who would rather stay seated

ACT-005Activity · Communication

The No Game

8-10 mingame
icebreakerenergiserboundariessaying-noassertiveness

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: pairs · Energy: high Materials: none. Nothing to print, nothing to set up.

What it practises: the second assertive right — saying no without guilt. Warms up FRM-002 The Assert Approach.

On this pageHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

How to run it

  1. Pairs. Person A asks Person B for anything at all: a lift home, their phone, their lunch, a weekend shift, their car.
  2. Person B's only job is to say no. Every time. Sixty seconds, as many asks as A can fire out.
  3. Swap. Sixty seconds the other way.
  4. Round two: same thing, but B has to say no and stay friendly. No apologising, no long excuse, no "maybe". Just a warm, clear no. Sixty seconds each.

Expect noise and laughter. That is the point.

Debrief

  • Which round was harder? Almost everyone says round two.
  • What did you notice yourself doing to soften it? (Apologising, explaining, going quiet, laughing.)
  • What did a good no sound like when you heard it?
  • Who in your real life do you find it hardest to say no to? Why that person?

The point to land: most of us do not struggle with the word. We struggle with the guilt that comes after it. Saying no to a request is not saying no to a person, and a clear no now saves an apology, a rushed job or a resentment later.

Variations

  • Youth: the asks get funnier and more outrageous, which is fine. It works better that way
  • Frontline: use real workplace asks — cover my shift, sign this off, come in Saturday
  • Online: breakout rooms in pairs, same timing
  • Extension: round three, B says "no, and here is what I can do instead". This is the bridge straight into the Assert Approach
  • Cultural adaptation: in groups where a direct no to an elder is not appropriate, run round three only and focus on the "no to the request, yes to the relationship" wording

Watch out for

  • Keep it fast. It dies if pairs start negotiating
  • Some learners genuinely cannot get the word out in round one. That is useful information for them, not a failure. Name it gently and move on
  • Do not let asks get personal or target something someone actually needs
