ACT-010Activity · Communication

Whisper Chain — The Message That Didn't Land

10-12 mingame
icebreakerenergiserclear-messaginglistening

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: lines of 6-8 · Energy: high

What it practises: why a message has to be built to survive the trip. Sets up FRM-005 BLUF.

Materials: two message cards, written out beforehand.

On this pageHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

How to run it

  1. Two lines of 6-8 people. Everyone faces forward.
  2. Give the person at the front of each line the same message card, written down. They read it, then whisper it once to the next person. No repeats, no questions.
  3. Last person says out loud what they received.
  4. Read out the original.

Round 1 message (the rambler):

"Hey, so the boss reckons the delivery might come Thursday instead of Wednesday, but only if the weather holds, and if it doesn't, we'll need someone to stay back Friday, probably Sione, but check with him first."

Round 2 message (BLUF):

"Delivery moved to Thursday. If it rains, Sione stays back Friday. Confirm with Sione today."

Round 1 comes out mangled. Round 2 usually survives almost intact. That contrast is the entire teaching point and you do not have to explain it, they will see it.

Debrief

  • Which round survived? Why?
  • What got lost first in round one? (Usually the action, which is buried at the end.)
  • Where does this happen for real at your work?
  • Whose job is it to make sure the message lands, the sender or the receiver?

The point to land: a message is not finished when you have said it. It is finished when it has landed. Short, ordered and specific messages survive the trip. Rambling ones do not, and they were never going to.

Variations

  • Small group: one line, run both messages through the same line
  • Online: private chat one person to the next, same rules, no copy and paste
  • Harder: add background noise, which is closer to a real site anyway
  • Extension: groups rewrite round one's message so it would have survived, then test it on the other line

Watch out for

  • Someone will try to repeat or clarify. That is the game working, not a rule break. Note it and hold the rule, then raise it in the debrief: asking for a repeat is exactly what people do not do at work
  • Keep the messages work-relevant, not silly sentences. The point is a real message failing
  • Do not single out whoever "broke" the chain. Nobody broke it. The message did

ACT-011Activity · Communication

Bury the Lede Race

8-10 mingame
icebreakerenergiserblufclear-messaging

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: teams of 3-4 · Energy: high

What it practises: spotting the bottom line fast. Warms up FRM-005 BLUF.

Materials: four to six long, rambling messages printed on cards. Real ones from your own inbox work best, with names removed.

On this pageHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

How to run it

  1. Teams of 3-4. Each team gets the same card face down.
  2. On "go", they turn it over, find the one sentence that is the real bottom line, and one person stands up and reads only that sentence.
  3. First team standing with the correct sentence wins the round.
  4. Five rounds, keep score.
  5. Final round, reversed: give every team the same bare bottom line and 60 seconds to write the most buried, waffliest version of it they can. Read them out. This one gets the biggest laugh and makes the point harder than any of the serious rounds.

Debrief

  • What were you scanning for? (Most people say a verb, a deadline or a name.)
  • How long did it take you to find it? Now imagine 60 unread messages
  • In the reverse round, what were the tricks you used to bury it? Do you do any of those for real?

The point to land: you just did in ten seconds what your reader does in two. If your point is not findable that fast, it is not landing. And notice how easy it was to bury it on purpose. Most buried messages are not written to confuse, they are written by someone thinking out loud.

Variations

  • Youth: use group chat messages and captions
  • Frontline: use real site emails, notices and text messages
  • Online: messages in chat, teams race in breakout rooms, first to post the sentence
  • Quiet groups: teams write the sentence on a card and hold it up instead of standing

Watch out for

  • Use real messages, but scrub names, companies and anything identifiable. Never use a message from someone in the room
  • Keep rounds short. It dies if teams start debating
  • The reverse round can tip into mocking a particular writing style. Keep it about the message

ACT-017Activity · Communication

The Yes Pile

10-12 mingame
boundariessaying-noworkloadicebreakeropener

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, works from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-008 The Positive No and the whole of TOP-COM-004.

Materials: a stack of sticky notes or scrap paper per person, pens.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Write the yeses (3 min). Everyone writes down one thing per note that they have said yes to in the last two weeks. Work, home, church, sport, family, friends. Anything they agreed to do. Push for volume: "keep going, one per note, don't think too hard."
  2. Build the pile (2 min). Everyone puts their notes in a single pile in the middle of the table, or up on the wall. It gets big fast, and that is the point.
  3. Take back three (3 min). Everyone retrieves three of their own notes: the three they would still say yes to if they could start the fortnight again.
  4. Look at what is left (2 min). Point at the pile still on the table. "That is the stuff you did anyway."

The link back

Every one of those was a yes you gave to something, which means it was a no you gave to something else. You just did not get to choose what.

Saying yes to everything is not generous. It is a decision made by whoever asked first. The rest of this module is about making that decision on purpose.

Then go straight into the module opener: every leader has limits, the skill is holding them without damage.

Debrief

  • What kind of thing ended up in the leftover pile? (Watch for the pattern: the leftovers are usually the things asked for in person, at short notice, by someone hard to refuse.)
  • Who was asking, for the ones you would take back?
  • Did anyone struggle to pick only three?

Variations

  • Small groups (under 6): skip the pile, just lay the notes out and count them
  • Online: a shared whiteboard with sticky notes, or everyone types their list in the chat but does not send until you say go, then the wall of text lands all at once. That works surprisingly well
  • Low literacy: run it spoken. Go round the room, each person names one thing they said yes to, keep going round until people run out. The count is the point, not the writing
  • Teams from one workplace: run it on work commitments only. The leftover pile becomes a real conversation about workload that a manager can act on

Watch out for

  • It can get heavy. Some people will look at that pile and see their whole life. Keep the pace up and land the point quickly rather than sitting in it
  • Do not let it become a moan about the boss. The point is that a yes is a choice, including the ones that felt like they were not
  • Nobody reads out anyone else's note. Say so before you build the pile

ACT-022Activity · Communication

Tell It Back

10-12 mingame
listeningparaphrasingicebreakeropenerempathy

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, works from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting and the whole of TOP-COM-005.

Materials: none.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Pair up (30 sec). Everyone pairs with someone they do not know well.
  2. Ninety seconds each (3 min). Person A tells Person B something true about themselves: how they got into this work, the best thing about their weekend, who taught them something that stuck. Then swap. No note-taking. No questions. Just listening.
  3. Introduce your partner (5 min). Go round the room. Everyone introduces their partner to the group, in the first person: "I'm Mere, and I got into this work because…" Speaking as them, not about them.
  4. One correction each. After each introduction, the person being introduced gets one sentence to correct anything that was wrong.

The link back

Notice what happened. You did not need a notepad. You needed to actually be there for ninety seconds.

Then the two points that open the module:

  • The corrections were mostly small. Because when you actually listen, you get it right. Most workplace misunderstandings are not hard problems, they are ninety seconds nobody gave
  • Being introduced accurately feels good. That feeling is what people mean when they say a leader makes them feel heard. It is not a personality trait, it is a thing you just did

Then go into the module opener: we think leading is about talking, but the best leaders are the best listeners.

Debrief

  • How did it feel to hear yourself described by someone else?
  • Who got a detail right that they were not told directly? (Someone always picks up a feeling or an emphasis rather than a fact. That is Level 3 listening, and you can name it later.)
  • What did you notice yourself doing while your partner was talking? Were you listening, or getting ready to remember?

Variations

  • Groups who already know each other: the topic becomes "something about you that most people here do not know", which is a better icebreaker anyway
  • Online: works well in breakout rooms, then introductions in the main room. Ask people to turn cameras on for the introduction of their partner
  • Very shy groups or low literacy: drop the first-person framing, which is the part that raises the stakes. "Tell us about your partner" is enough
  • Large rooms (over 20): do introductions in groups of six rather than to the whole room, or it takes twenty minutes

Watch out for

  • The remembering trap. Some learners will concentrate so hard on memorising that they stop listening. That is a gift for the debrief. Ask who did it, and connect it to Level 1 listening: your attention was on your own performance
  • Nobody shares anything real if the room is cold. Model it first with your own ninety seconds, and make it specific
  • Consent. Say before you start that they should only share what they are happy to have repeated to the room. Then hold that line

Read The Room Cold

8-10 mingame
digital-communicationtone-in-texticebreakeropenerhybrid

Type: game / opener · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, works from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-014 Tone-in-Text and the whole of TOP-COM-006.

Materials: eight short messages on cards, or written up on the whiteboard one at a time.

On this pageThe messagesHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The messages

Short, ordinary, and genuinely ambiguous. These work:

#Message
1"Fine."
2"Can you come see me when you get in."
3"Interesting."
4"Thanks."
5"Noted."
6"K"
7"We should talk about the report."
8"Sure, whatever works."

How to run it

  1. Show one message (10 sec). One at a time, on the board or held up.
  2. Everyone votes with their hands. Three options, called out fast:
    • One hand up = they are happy or neutral
    • Two hands up = they are annoyed
    • Arms crossed = something is wrong and I would be worried
  3. Look around the room. Do not discuss. Just look at the split, then move to the next one.
  4. Run all eight in about four minutes. Pace matters. It should feel like a quiz, not a seminar.

The room will split badly on almost every message, and the splits are the whole game.

The link back

Same words. Same eight messages. And this room could not agree on a single one of them.

Then the point that opens the module:

  • The sender knew exactly what they meant every time. They always do. What they did not know is that half of you would read it the other way
  • Kruger and colleagues (2005) tested this properly: people overestimate both their ability to send tone in writing and their ability to read it. You hear your own message in the tone you meant, and you cannot un-hear it
  • When people are unsure, they assume the worst. Watch how many hands went up for "annoyed" on perfectly innocent messages

Then go into the module opener: screens strip out a lot, and a quick message can land far harder than you meant.

Debrief

  • Which message had the biggest split?
  • Item 6, "K": ask who reads that as rude. Then ask them how old they are. The age split on this one is usually visible across the room and it is a good, light way into the point that the reader brings their own rules
  • Has anyone here misread a message from their boss and worried about it for a day? (Someone always has. Item 2 is the one that does it.)
  • What extra information would have settled it? (Tone of voice. Their face. Knowing what kind of day they were having. All the things text removes.)

Variations

  • Real messages: ask three learners to volunteer a genuinely ambiguous message they have received. More powerful, but check they are comfortable before it goes on the board
  • Online: run the vote through the reactions or a poll. The split shows as a number, which is even clearer than hands
  • Team version: use messages in the team's actual style, from their actual channel. The splits get uncomfortable in a productive way
  • Youth: group chat messages, read receipts and one-word replies. They will have strong opinions and a lot of evidence

Watch out for

  • It turning into a session about one person's boss. Keep it on the cards
  • Do not let anyone identify who sent a real message if you run that variation
  • Pace. Ten seconds per message. If you discuss each one as you go, the cumulative effect is lost, and the cumulative effect is the point

ACT-035Activity · Employment & Work Readiness

Six Degrees Of This Room

10-12 mingame
networkingweak-tiesicebreakeropenerrelationshipswork-readiness

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: high

What it sets up: FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties. It makes the group's own hidden network visible, which is far more convincing than the research.

Materials: a ball of string or wool if you want the picture. It works without.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in a circle (1 min).
  2. First person holds the end of the string and names something specific about themselves: a suburb they grew up in, a job they have had, a sport, a church, a school, a country their family is from.
  3. Anyone who shares it puts a hand up. The first person throws the ball to one of them, keeping hold of their end. The catcher now names something new about themselves.
  4. Keep going for six or seven minutes. The web builds across the circle. Do not let people only throw to their mates. If nobody puts a hand up, they name something else.
  5. Stop and look at it. Everyone holds their string tight so the web is visible.

The link back

Ask two questions, in this order.

"Put your hand up if you learned something about someone you already knew."

Most hands go up.

"Now look at the string. How many of those lines go to someone you would call a close friend?"

Almost none of them.

Then land it:

Those lines are weak ties, and they are the most useful thing in this room. Not because they are deep, but because each one goes somewhere you cannot get to on your own. Somebody here knows somebody who is hiring. You just do not know which one yet.

Then go into the research: Granovetter, 1973, 282 men, and the finding that the job came from the acquaintance far more often than the close friend.

Debrief

  • What surprised you about who you had something in common with?
  • Which connection in this room could actually be useful to you, and for what?
  • Who in your life is a weak tie you have not spoken to in six months?

That last question is the one to close on, because it leads straight into a real action.

Variations

  • No string: run it as "stand up if". Same effect, less picture, and it works with 30 people
  • Small groups (under 8): each person names three things, and the group counts the overlaps
  • Online: use the chat. Each person types one thing, others react with an emoji if they share it. The overlap is visible in the reaction counts
  • Low literacy: it is spoken already. No change needed
  • Work teams: restrict it to work history and previous employers. The web that appears is effectively the team's real professional network, and it is usually much bigger than anyone thought

Watch out for

  • Do not let it get personal. Keep prompts to places, jobs, sports, schools, food. Not family circumstances, not health, not money
  • The person nobody connects to. It happens, and it stings. Have a couple of broad prompts ready ("who has ever worked a weekend shift?") so everyone is in the web before you stop
  • Untangling the string takes longer than you think. Budget two minutes or take a photo and drop it

ACT-036Activity · Employment & Work Readiness

Red Flag Or Green Flag?

12-15 mingame
relationshipsboundariesprofessionalismgossipicebreakeropenertrust

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: high

What it sets up: the red flags half of FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits, and it works just as well as a trust opener for FRM-022 The Trust Equation.

Materials: a RED FLAG sign on one wall and a GREEN FLAG sign on the other. Or just point.

On this pageHow to run itThe situationsThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Explain it (1 min). You read out a situation. Everyone walks to the wall that matches what they think. No standing in the middle.
  2. Read a situation. Everyone moves.
  3. Ask two people why, one from each wall. Never argue with an answer. Just get the reasoning out.
  4. Move on quickly. Ten situations in ten minutes. Pace is what keeps the energy up.

The situations

The good ones are the ones the room splits on. Six of these are designed to split.

#SituationWhere it usually lands
1A workmate tells you something personal about another workmateRed, and fast
2You add your new supervisor on InstagramSplits. This is the best one in the list
3You only ever eat lunch with the same three peopleSplits. Most people say green until someone names cliques
4Someone messages you out of the blue asking for a job reference, and you have not heard from them in two yearsSplits
5You tell your team leader you are struggling with the workloadGreen, though shy learners often say red
6A senior person tells you about their divorce on your second dayRed, but people find it hard to say why
7You say yes to every after-work drink because you want to fit inSplits
8You share something a colleague told you in confidence, with one other person you trustRed. The "just one person" is the whole lesson
9You ask the most experienced person on the crew to show you how they do itGreen
10You vent about your manager in the group chatSplits, and it usually splits by age

The link back

After the last one:

Nearly every red flag in that list started as something normal. Nobody sets out to be the gossip. They just told one person, once.

Then go to the six red flags in the topic: oversharing, romantic entanglements and drama, being too close to a small group, gossip, using people, and no clear boundaries. Most of the room has just argued their way to all six on their own, which is a far better way to arrive at them than a slide.

Debrief

  • Which one did the room split on hardest? Why do you think that is?
  • Has anyone been on the wrong end of number 8?
  • Where is the line between being friendly and oversharing? (There is no clean answer. The disagreement is the value)
  • Number 3 is the interesting one. When does a close group become a clique?

Variations

  • Seated version: thumbs up or thumbs down. Lower energy, works with limited mobility, and nobody is exposed by standing alone
  • Online: poll per situation, then ask one person from each side to unmute
  • Trust version (TOP-LEA-002): swap the list for trust-breaking behaviours from the topic. Mixed messages, missed promises, hidden information, blame, favouritism, poor listening, breach of confidence. Ask "have you seen this happen?" instead of "is this a red flag?"
  • Team version: run it with an intact team and the conversation afterwards becomes a de facto team charter

Watch out for

  • Never let it become about a real person. If someone starts describing an actual colleague, thank them and move to the next situation
  • The lone person at a wall. Go to them second, not first, and be warm about it. Then move on quickly
  • Do not correct people. There is no answer key. Situation 2 genuinely does not have one
  • Number 6 can be raw for someone going through it. It is in the list because oversharing is usually well-meant, not malicious. Keep it light

The Silent Nod

10-12 mingame
trustpsychological-safetyconflicticebreakeropenerteamsstorming

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: fear of conflict, the second layer of FRM-017 The 5 Dysfunctions, and FRM-023 Psychological Safety. It also works as the storming opener for FRM-018 Tuckman.

The point: the group experiences fake yes happening to them, live, in about four minutes.

On this pageHow to run itProposals that workThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Brief three people quietly before the session, or in the corridor at the break. Their job: whatever the facilitator proposes, agree with it enthusiastically and quickly. Nobody else knows.
  2. Propose something mildly bad (3 min). A plan with an obvious flaw. Suggestions below. Present it confidently, as though it is already decided.
  3. The three plants agree fast. "Yeah, that makes sense." "Sounds good."
  4. Ask the room: "Anyone got any concerns?" and then wait. Do not fill the silence. Count to ten in your head. It will feel very long.
  5. Usually nobody says anything. Occasionally one person does, and that is even better material.
  6. Stop the game. Explain what you did.

Proposals that work

  • "We'll finish forty minutes late today so we can get through everything. That's fine with everyone?"
  • "New rule: the team WhatsApp gets checked before 7am so we can start on time."
  • "We'll do the presentations in alphabetical order, and everyone presents alone, no notes."

Pick something with a real flaw that affects them, not an absurd one. Absurd gets laughed at. Mildly unreasonable gets nodded at, which is the lesson.

The link back

Three people in this room were told to agree with me. That was enough. Nobody else said anything, and most of you had a concern.

Then the point:

That is fake yes. It is not that you are cowards, it is that agreement looked like the consensus and disagreeing would have cost something. Now imagine that happening in a real meeting, about a real decision, with your actual manager in the room.

Then land it on the model: this is why Lencioni puts fear of conflict directly on top of absence of trust. And it is why a leader asking "any concerns?" and getting silence should never read that as agreement.

Debrief

  • Who had a concern and did not say it? (Hands go up. Lots of them)
  • What stopped you? Collect the reasons: did not want to be first, thought it was decided, thought it was just me, did not want to hold everyone up
  • What would have made it easier to speak?
  • What does this mean about the last meeting you sat in?

Variations

  • No plants: it often works without them, just from the facilitator's confidence and the framing "so that's decided". Slightly less reliable, and completely honest
  • Small groups: brief one plant instead of three
  • Online: it works better online, not worse. Silence on a call is heavier, and the plants can agree in the chat where everyone sees it
  • Intact teams: be careful. It exposes something real about that team and you need time to deal with what surfaces
  • The fix version: rerun the proposal afterwards, with the facilitator explicitly saying "I want two problems with this before anyone agrees." Watch how fast the room changes

Watch out for

  • Do not humiliate the plants. Name them as helpers and thank them
  • Do not let it become "you all failed". They behaved exactly like everyone does. That is the finding, not a fault
  • The one person who did speak up should be acknowledged carefully, not held up as a hero, or the rest of the room feels judged
  • Never run this with a proposal that touches something genuinely sensitive such as pay, rosters people actually depend on, or anything that could be believed for the rest of the day. Debrief quickly so nobody leaves thinking it was real

Build It Fast, Then Talk

20-25 mingame
teamsteam-developmenticebreakeropenerstormingnormscollaboration

Type: game / opener · Time: 20-25 min · Group: teams of 4-6 · Energy: high

What it sets up: FRM-018 Tuckman's Stages. A team cannot discuss Forming and Storming honestly from memory. This makes them do both in ten minutes, in front of each other, and then debrief what just happened.

Materials per team: 20 sticks of spaghetti, a metre of tape, string, and one marshmallow. Or a cheaper version: a stack of newspaper and a roll of tape.

On this pageHow to run itThe debrief, which is the actual lessonThe link backDebrief extrasVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. The task (1 min). Build the tallest free-standing tower you can in ten minutes. The marshmallow must be on top. It must stand on its own for ten seconds.
  2. No talking about process. Do not tell them to plan. Do not tell them to assign roles. The whole value is in what they do without being told.
  3. Ten minutes. Call the time at 5, 2 and 1 minutes.
  4. Measure. Brief celebration.
  5. Now the real activity: the debrief (10 min).

The debrief, which is the actual lesson

Ask these in order. Do not rush them.

  1. "What happened in the first sixty seconds?" Nearly every team describes Forming: polite, nobody wanted to take charge, a lot of looking at the materials and not much doing.
  2. "When did someone take over? How did that happen?" This is Storming, and it usually happened without a word being said.
  3. "Did anyone have an idea they didn't say?" Hands go up in most teams. Ask why not.
  4. "Which team talked about how they'd work before they started building?" Usually none. Ask what that cost them.
  5. "What rule would you set if you did this again?" Their answers are a team charter, invented by them, in ninety seconds.

The link back

You just did Forming and Storming in ten minutes, with people you already know, on a task with no real consequences. Now think about a team that has to do it over six months, with people they did not choose, on work that pays their rent.

Then name the finding: teams that skip the "how will we work?" conversation do not save time. They spend it later, in the Storming stage, and usually with more damage.

Debrief extras

  • Who ended up leading? Was that decided or did it just happen?
  • What would have been different if you had spent two of your ten minutes planning?
  • Did anyone get quieter as it went on? What made that happen?

Variations

  • The planning contrast: give half the teams two extra minutes with a rule that they may only talk, not touch the materials. Compare results. This is the strongest version
  • Cheap version: newspaper and tape. Works just as well and costs almost nothing
  • Seated / accessible version: build the tallest tower flat on the table as a structure, or use a paper chain for length rather than height
  • Online: each person builds separately from what is in their room, and the team has to agree a shared design first over video. The forming and storming happens in the design conversation
  • Low literacy: no reading or writing involved at any point

Watch out for

  • The debrief is the activity. If you are short on time, cut the build to seven minutes rather than cutting the debrief
  • Competitive groups can get heated. Keep the prize meaningless
  • The person who got talked over may not want to say so publicly. Ask question 3 as "put your hand up if" rather than asking someone to name it
  • Do not let a team blame one person for taking over. They took over because nobody had agreed how to decide, which is a team problem

Behaviour, Not Adjective

8-10 mingame
respectrole-modelsicebreakeropenerleadershipfeedback

Type: game / opener · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the H step of FRM-019 W-H-O, and the Retention condition in FRM-026 Modelling.

The point: admiration is useless until you can say the exact thing the person does. This game makes that difficulty obvious in about four minutes, which is why it belongs before the worksheet.

On this pageHow to run itThe adjectivesWhat good answers sound likeThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Call out an adjective. "Respectful."
  2. The room shouts behaviours. Anything someone could actually watch you do. Take five or six fast.
  3. Reject the ones that are still adjectives. "Considerate" is not a behaviour, it is another adjective. Say so, cheerfully, and ask again. This is the game.
  4. Move to the next adjective. Six or seven of them, thirty to sixty seconds each.

The adjectives

Humble · Reliable · Respectful · A good listener · Fair · Approachable · A good leader

The last one is deliberately the hardest and it should be last.

What good answers sound like

AdjectiveNot a behaviourA behaviour
Humble"Doesn't big-note himself""Asks the apprentice what he thinks before giving his own view"
Reliable"You can count on her""Turns up ten minutes early, every time"
Respectful"Treats people well""Learns how to say your name properly and keeps using it"
A good listener"Really hears you""Puts the phone face down when you start talking"
Fair"Doesn't have favourites""Gives the good jobs out in rotation, and says so"
Approachable"Easy to talk to""Says 'got a minute?' back, instead of 'what is it?'"
A good leaderanything vaguewhatever they land on, and it will take the longest

The link back

Every single one of those adjectives is useless to you. You cannot copy "humble". You can copy "asks the apprentice first".

Then go straight into W-H-O and ACT-033 Who Is Someone You Respect?. The room has just practised the exact skill the H step needs.

Debrief

  • Which adjective was hardest to turn into a behaviour? (Usually "a good leader", and that is worth sitting with for a moment)
  • What does that tell you about the feedback people usually get at work?
  • If someone told you "you're a great team player", would you know what to keep doing?

That last question is the one that lands. Most praise is adjectives, which means most praise teaches nobody anything.

Variations

  • Reverse version: call out a behaviour, the room names the adjective it earns. Quicker and lighter
  • Pairs version: one person says an adjective, their partner has ten seconds to produce a behaviour. Rotate. Higher energy, everyone talks
  • Feedback version: for teams, use it to fix how they praise each other. Everyone rewrites a compliment they have given recently into a behaviour
  • Online: chat storm. Everyone types behaviours, the facilitator reads out the good ones and gently rejects the adjectives
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken already

Watch out for

  • Keep the rejections light. "Nice try, that's still an adjective" with a grin. If it feels like being marked wrong, the room stops shouting
  • Do not let it slow down. Sixty seconds per adjective. The pace is what makes it a game rather than an exercise
  • Do not let people describe a real colleague negatively. Keep it to the positive adjectives on the list

Name It In Ten Seconds

8-10 mingame
respecticebreakeropenernamescultureleadership

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: high

What it sets up: the house example in FRM-019 W-H-O: greets people by name and checks pronunciation. The source uses it as an example of a respect behaviour. This turns it into something the room does rather than reads.

Why it matters more than it looks: for a lot of Pacific, Māori and migrant learners, having their name said properly, or not, is the most repeated respect experience of their working life. This game names that without making a speech about it.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in a circle.
  2. Round one, the mess (2 min). Go round. Everyone says their own name once, quickly. No repeating, no help. Then ask the room to name five people. They cannot.
  3. Round two, properly (4 min). Go round again. This time each person says their name twice, slowly, and the person to their left says it back. If they get it wrong, the owner corrects them and they try again until it is right. Nobody moves on until it is right.
  4. Round three, the test (2 min). Point at people at random. The room says the name together.
  5. Stop and ask the question below.

The link back

Ask, quietly:

Put your hand up if someone at work has been saying your name wrong for more than a month.

In most Zeducation rooms a lot of hands go up. Then:

Now put it up if you have ever corrected them.

Far fewer. Then land it:

That is what respect looks like at ground level. Not a value on a wall. Ten seconds of effort, from the person who has the easier job in that exchange.

Then go to W-H-O and the house example about greeting people by name and checking pronunciation.

Debrief

  • How did it feel to have the room say your name correctly?
  • Why do people stop correcting others? (Answers: did not want to make it awkward, gave up, it felt rude, it happens too often to keep doing it)
  • Whose job is it to get someone's name right?
  • What else is like this? What other small thing signals respect or its absence?

Variations

  • Meaning version: each person says their name and one line about where it comes from or who gave it to them. Slower, considerably warmer, and excellent with Pacific and Māori groups. Budget 15 minutes and never require it
  • Seated version: works fine around a table
  • Existing teams: run it with people who have worked together for years. The discovery that someone has been mispronouncing a colleague's name for three years is the whole lesson, delivered for free
  • Online: works well. Everyone says their name, the next person repeats it. Also fix the display names while you are there, which is a real and lasting outcome
  • Low literacy: nothing is read or written

Watch out for

  • Never single out one person's name as the difficult one. Everyone goes through the same process, including the facilitator and including the shortest, most familiar names
  • The facilitator goes first, and gets their own name repeated back. It sets the tone and it stops the exercise feeling like it is aimed at anyone
  • Do not let anyone laugh at a name. Shut it down immediately and without heat
  • Some people have chosen an easier "work name" because of exactly this problem. If it comes up, it is a good conversation, not a failure. Let them keep whichever name they want

Whose Call Is It?

12-15 mingame
decision-makingleadershipicebreakeropenercollaborationstyles

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-028 Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles.

Materials: three signs on three walls. MY WAY (autocratic), OUR WAY (democratic), YOUR WAY (laissez-faire).

On this pageHow to run itThe decisionsThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Teach the three styles first, in three minutes. No more than that.
  2. Read a decision. Everyone walks to the wall for the style they think fits it best.
  3. Ask one person from each wall why. Never correct them. Some of these have no right answer.
  4. Ten decisions, eight minutes. Keep it fast.

The decisions

#The decisionUsually
1Someone is working at height without a harnessMy way, immediately
2What we call the new team chatYour way. It does not matter, so let them have it
3Changing the weekend rosterOur way, and this is the one people get wrong
4A customer is being abusive to a staff member right nowMy way
5How the team splits up the end-of-day jobsOur way, or your way if the team is solid
6Which supplier we use, when finance has set the budgetSplits. Often my way dressed up as our way
7Whether to change the shift start time by 30 minutesOur way. It is their lives
8How an experienced person does a job they have done for ten yearsYour way. Stop supervising them
9Cutting the team's overtime budgetSplits. The decision may be made, but the how is theirs
10What the team's values should beOur way, and only our way. Handed-down values are wallpaper

The link back

Two points, after the last one.

Nobody in this room has one style. You used all three in the last ten minutes, and you chose correctly most of the time. The skill is not having a favourite, it is choosing on purpose.

Then the harder one, on numbers 6 and 9:

The most damaging thing a leader can do is run a "our way" process on a "my way" decision. If the budget is already cut, do not ask people what they think about cutting the budget. Ask them how to do it. Fake consultation costs more trust than a straight decision ever does.

Debrief

  • Which one did the room split on most?
  • Number 6: have you ever been consulted about something that was already decided? What did that do to your trust?
  • What is your default style when you are under pressure and short of time?
  • Which of these decisions does your manager get wrong?

Variations

  • Seated version: hold up one, two or three fingers. Same effect, lower energy, and it works with limited mobility
  • Their own decisions: each person writes a real decision on a card and the room sorts it. This is the best version with an intact leadership team
  • Time pressure round: rerun three of them with "and you have four minutes to decide". Watch how many people move to My Way, then talk about what urgency does to consultation
  • Online: three-way poll per decision, then unmute one person per option

Watch out for

  • The room learning that democratic is the right answer. It is not, and if that is what they take away the game has failed. Numbers 1, 4 and 8 exist to prevent it
  • Do not correct answers. Say "that's a defensible read" and ask why. Most of these genuinely depend on the team
  • Do not let it become about a real manager's failings. One or two examples are fine, then move on

The Us And Them Hunt

10-12 mingame
collaborationsilosicebreakeropenerteamsblame

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-030 Collaborative vs Siloed Teams, and specifically the fastest diagnostic in it: the word "they".

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Ask a simple question (2 min). "What is one thing that makes your job harder than it needs to be?" Take five or six answers around the room. Do not comment on them, just collect them.
  2. Write them on the board as people say them, in their own words. Exactly their words. This matters.
  3. Now go back and circle every "they", "them" and "that lot". In most rooms it is most of the board.
  4. Count them out loud.
  5. Ask the question below.

The link back

Six answers, and we circled nine "theys". Not one person here is difficult and nobody said anything unfair. That is just what it sounds like from inside a silo.

Then the question that does the work:

Who is the "they" in this room, for somebody else?

Sit in the silence. Someone will eventually say it: every team is somebody else's "they". Head office is the regions' "they". The regions are head office's. Night shift and day shift are each other's.

Then land it on the framework: a siloed team is not a team that dislikes another team. It is a team that has stopped having reasons to talk to them, so all that is left is the times something went wrong.

Debrief

  • Which "they" on the board would change if you actually spoke to them next week?
  • When did you last have a conversation with that team about something that was not a problem?
  • What do they say about us?
  • What information do we have that they would find useful, that we have never sent?

That last question usually produces a real action, and it is often something that takes five minutes.

Variations

  • The week-long count: send everyone away to count how often they hear "they" about another team. Report back next session. More honest than any engagement survey
  • Both sides in the room: run the same question in two groups, head office and regional, separately, then show each group the other's board. Handled well it is the most useful ten minutes in the programme. Handled badly it starts a fight, so only do it with a group that has some trust
  • Swap version: each person has to argue the "they" side of one item on the board. Uncomfortable and effective
  • Online: collect the answers in the chat, then paste them into a doc and highlight the pronouns live

Watch out for

  • Do not let anyone be named. Teams and departments only. Stop it immediately if a person's name goes on the board
  • Do not make people feel caught out. The framing is "this is what a silo sounds like", never "look how negative you all are". Say explicitly that nobody said anything unreasonable
  • Some "theys" are legitimate. Sometimes another team genuinely is not doing its job. The point is not that the complaint is wrong, it is that the complaint is being made in the wrong room
  • If the group is one intact team with a real grievance, this can open something bigger than the session can hold. Have somewhere for it to go before you start

Who Does Everyone Ask?

10-12 mingame
workloadcollaborationburnouticebreakeropenerteamsnetworks

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-032 Collaborative Overload. It makes the hub effect visible in about six minutes, using the room's own answers.

The finding it demonstrates: 20 to 35% of value-added collaboration comes from 3 to 5% of people. Rooms rediscover this on their own, fast.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Everyone gets three sticky notes (1 min).
  2. Three questions, one per note (3 min). Write a name on each. Roles, not real names, if the group is mixed.
    • Who do you go to when you are stuck on something?
    • Who do you go to when you need something done quickly and properly?
    • Who do you go to when something has gone wrong and you need advice?
  3. Stick them all on the wall (2 min).
  4. Group the duplicates out loud. The same two or three names will stack up.
  5. Stand back and look at the shape.

The link back

Nine people, twenty-seven notes, and four names. That is what the research found across three hundred organisations. A small number of people carry most of it.

Then the question that changes the room:

Now: how do you think those four people are doing?

And the finding: the leaders rated by colleagues as the most in-demand collaborators had the lowest engagement and career satisfaction scores. The people everyone relies on are the ones most likely to be quietly looking for another job.

Debrief

  • Is anyone's own name up there? What is that like?
  • Why those people? (Answers: they know things, they always say yes, they never make you feel stupid)
  • What would happen to your workplace if the top name left tomorrow?
  • What would it take for one of those questions to have a different answer?
  • Whose job is it to fix this?

That last question matters. Most rooms answer "the hub's" and the honest answer is the organisation's.

Variations

  • Anonymous version: roles instead of names. Essential if the hubs are in the room and it might embarrass them
  • Intact team version: genuinely revealing and it needs care. Done well it produces a real redistribution conversation. Done badly it publicly labels one person as the bottleneck
  • The leader's version: managers map their own team. Most discover two people carrying it and are surprised, because the hubs never complain
  • Online: three polls, or a shared board. The stacking effect is just as visible
  • Low literacy: spoken. Ask the three questions and tally names on the whiteboard as people call them out

Watch out for

  • The hub in the room. Seeing your own name eleven times can feel like praise or like an accusation, depending on the day. Frame it explicitly as a load problem the organisation created, never as "look how indispensable you are"
  • Do not let it become a popularity chart. The questions are about reliance, not regard, and saying so up front keeps it clean
  • Never leave the notes up after the session
  • The person whose name appears nowhere. It is not a status ranking, and in a room of eight some people will not be named. Say that before you start, lightly

Small Thing, Big Signal

12-15 mingame
cultural-safetycultureicebreakeropenerinclusionleadership

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the "how cultural safety is broken" list in FRM-033 Cultural Safety, and the point underneath it: nearly every breach is small, defensible in isolation, and read instantly by the person on the receiving end.

On this pageHow to run itThe situationsThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Read a situation (30 seconds each).
  2. Everyone rates it 1 to 5 on their fingers, held at chest height. 1 = no big deal. 5 = serious.
  3. Look at the spread. Do not average it. The spread is the lesson.
  4. Ask two people at different numbers why. Never adjudicate.
  5. Eight situations, ten minutes.

The situations

#The situation
1A manager has been saying a staff member's name slightly wrong for six months. Nobody has corrected him
2A team photo is posted online. One person had said they would rather not be in it, and were in it anyway
3A meeting invite goes out for 6pm on a night when two staff have a regular church commitment
4Someone does an impression of a customer's accent in the break room. Everyone laughs, including the person the accent belongs to
5A bilingual staff member is asked to translate for a guest, for the fourth time this week, on top of her own job
6A cultural performance is added to the season launch. None of the staff from that culture were asked about it first
7The high performer makes a comment about someone's clothing. It is let go, because he is the high performer
8A visitor photographs a sacred site after being told not to. The guide says nothing, because the visitor is a paying customer

The link back

Two moves, in this order.

First, point at the spread:

Look at the range on number 4. Some of you said 1 and some said 5. Now think about which of those people is more likely to be the one it happens to.

Then the finding:

Every single one of those is small. Every one of them is defensible if you argue about it on its own. And every one of them teaches somebody that a part of who they are is a problem here. That is how cultural safety breaks. Not with a scandal, with eight small things nobody wrote down.

Then go into the eight named breaches on the framework page: token invites, assumption-led decisions, protocol theatre, name and language neglect, English-only spaces, culture as a joke, uneven consequences, invisible risks. Most of the room has just argued their way to all eight.

Debrief

  • Which one split the room most?
  • Number 4: does it change anything that the person laughed? (This is the hardest question in the set. Laughing along is often the safest available response, not agreement)
  • Number 5: what would it take to fix that one? (It is usually the easiest to fix and the least often noticed)
  • Number 7: whose job is it to say something?
  • Which of these has happened where you work in the last month?

Variations

  • Two-rating version: rate it twice. Once as the manager, once as the person it happened to. The gap between a person's own two numbers is the whole topic, delivered privately
  • Add your own: each table writes one situation from their own workplace. Strongest version, and it needs a room with trust
  • Online: poll per situation, show the distribution, then discuss the split ones
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken. Nothing is read or written by participants

Watch out for

  • Never ask anyone to speak as the target. People from the affected culture in the room are not there to validate the exercise or to tell their story. If someone volunteers, that is theirs to choose
  • Do not adjudicate the ratings. The moment the facilitator supplies the "right" number, the room stops being honest and starts guessing
  • Number 4 can sting if something like it happened recently in that workplace. Keep the pace up and land the point rather than dwelling
  • Watch for the room deciding the low raters are bad people. They are not. Most breaches are invisible from the side that is not experiencing them, which is exactly why the list exists

The Woven Mat

12-15 mingame
talanoapacificcultural-safetyicebreakeropenerculturebelonging

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the source's own metaphor for FRM-035 Talanoa, made physical:

Cultural safety is a woven mat. Shared values are the strong warp threads, people's lived stories are the weft, and talanoa is the act of weaving those threads so the mat holds.

Materials: strips of paper or ribbon in two colours, about 20 of each. Or bring a real woven mat and use it, which is better if you can do it respectfully and it belongs to someone in the room who is happy to explain it.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Lay the warp (4 min). Hold up the first colour. These are the shared values, the things this team says it stands for. Ask the room to name them and write one per strip. Respect. Safety. Manaakitanga. Whatever they actually say. Lay them out parallel on a table or the floor.
  2. Look at it. It is not a mat. It is a set of parallel lines that falls apart if you lift it. Lift one end and let it come apart. This is the moment.
  3. Add the weft (5 min). Second colour. These are people's lived stories and knowledge. Ask each person for one thing about how they do things, where they are from, or what they know that the team relies on. One per strip. Weave each one across the warp.
  4. Lift it again. Now it holds.

The link back

The values on their own were a poster. They did not hold anything, and you could see it. What made it a mat was people's actual stories going across them. Talanoa is the weaving. It is not a nice conversation you have if there is time. It is the thing that turns your values into something that can carry weight.

Then go into the three-part flow: teu le vā, ask open questions, listen and give back.

Debrief

  • Which values went down first? Who named them? (Often the most senior person, and that is worth noticing out loud)
  • Whose story is not in the mat yet?
  • What happens to a mat when one thread is pulled out and never replaced?
  • Where does your workplace have plenty of warp and almost no weft?

That last question is the one to close on. Most organisations have values in abundance and have never asked anyone for a story.

Variations

  • Keep the mat. Photograph it, or leave it on the wall for the rest of the programme and add to it. It becomes a record of the room
  • Repair version: partway through, quietly remove one weft strip. Later, ask what changed. Good for talking about people leaving, or being excluded
  • Real mat version: if someone in the room has a mat, a tīvaevae, a tapa or a korowai and is willing to bring it and speak to it, that is far better than paper. Ask, do not assume, and do not put anyone on the spot in front of colleagues. Ask privately, in advance, and accept no easily
  • Online: a shared board with two colours of note. It works, and it loses the physical moment where the parallel strips fall apart, which is most of the value
  • Low literacy: say the values and stories aloud, facilitator writes the strips

Watch out for

  • Handle the metaphor with care, not decoration. Weaving is a real practice with real meaning across the Pacific and in te ao Māori. Name where the metaphor comes from, credit the source, and do not turn a taonga into a craft activity
  • Never ask someone to be the cultural exhibit. The weft strips are about everyone's knowledge, including the person who has worked there longest and knows how the till jams
  • Do not let the values list get long. Six or seven warp strips is plenty. Twenty makes a mess and weakens the point
  • If you use a real mat, it does not go on the floor unless the person who brought it says so

Two Hours A Week

10-12 mingame
conflictconflict-resolutionicebreakeropenerteamscommunication

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the cost of unresolved conflict, and the reframe that opens TOP-COM-007.

On this pageHow to run itThe numberThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Ask everyone to think of one unresolved thing at work. Not a crisis. The low-level one: the person they route around, the thing that comes up every few weeks and never gets settled, the conversation they keep not having. Nobody says it out loud.
  2. Ask them to estimate, privately, how many minutes a week it costs them. Thinking about it, working around it, talking to someone else about it, redoing something because of it. Write the number down.
  3. Hands up by band. Under 15 minutes. 15 to 30. 30 to 60. More than an hour. More than two.
  4. Look at the room.
  5. Then give them the research.

The number

Across nine countries and 5,000 employees, the CPP Global Human Capital Report (2008) found workers spent an average of 2.1 hours a week dealing with conflict. That is over a hundred hours a year, per person.

📄 CPP Global Human Capital Report: Workplace Conflict (2008)

⚠️ Say what the study is. It is a large survey commissioned by CPP, a publisher of assessment tools, not a peer-reviewed study. The figure is widely cited and it is a vendor report. Learners trust you more, not less, when you say that.

⚠️ The source workbook also cites three further statistics from the same report: that a third of conflicts have led to attacks or personal injury, 20% to illness or absence, and 10% of projects have failed. Those three have not been verified against the primary report and should not be read out as fact until they are. The 2.1 hours figure is the one to use.

The link back

Nobody in this room put their hand up for zero. And most of you were thinking about one thing.

Then the turn, which is the actual opener for the topic:

Here is the part that matters. That two hours is not the cost of having conflict. It is the cost of not resolving it. Conflict that gets dealt with takes twenty minutes once. Conflict that gets avoided takes ten minutes a week, forever.

Then the reframe from the source: conflict is "an opportunity to engage in a conversation with someone who has a different viewpoint."

Debrief

  • Was your number higher than you expected?
  • What is the thing you keep not dealing with? (Nobody answers out loud. Just let them sit with it)
  • What would it take to resolve it? Is it actually that big?
  • What has it cost so far, beyond the time?

Variations

  • Sticky note version: everyone writes their number on a note, all notes go on the wall anonymously. The spread is more striking than the show of hands
  • Team version: with an intact team, add up the room's total and convert to days a year. The number is usually startling and it is the version managers remember
  • Cost version: for a commercial audience, multiply by an hourly rate. Blunt, effective, and it makes conflict resolution a business case rather than a soft skill
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken and by show of hands

Watch out for

  • Nobody names the person. Say it clearly at step 1. This goes wrong fast if someone starts describing a colleague
  • The room that says zero. Occasionally a group insists there is no conflict anywhere. That is worth a gentle question about whether nobody disagrees, or whether nobody says so, which is fear of conflict and a better opener than the one you planned
  • Do not oversell the statistic. One verified number, honestly described, is worth more than four dramatic ones

Leader Or Manager? The Sort

12-15 mingame
leadershipmanagementopenergamesortingteams

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room, or teams of 4-5 · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-049 Kotter on Leadership and Management.

⚠️ Run this before you teach the framework. The argument is the activity. If people already know the answers there is nothing to argue about and nothing sticks.

On this pageThe cardsThe intended sortHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The cards

Eighteen tasks. Cut them up. Teams sort into two piles: LEADERSHIP and MANAGEMENT.

Task
1Building next month's roster
2Telling the team why the new system is coming
3Checking the timesheets
4Deciding the shop will open on Sundays from March
5Ordering stock
6Sitting with someone who is thinking about leaving
7Working out how many staff the second site will need
8Being the first one to follow the new rule
9Running the Monday huddle
10Deciding which two of the five ideas the team will actually chase
11Fixing the till that keeps dropping out
12Telling the manager the documentation will not work for the night crew
13Writing the health and safety procedure
14Asking a quiet staff member what they think, by name, in advance
15Comparing this month's numbers to last month's
16Deciding the team is going to stop doing something it has always done
17Approving leave
18Noticing that the best person on the team is bored

The intended sort

Do not hand this out. It is for you.

Management (coping with complexity)Leadership (coping with change)
1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 172, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18

But the point is the arguments, not the score. Three cards reliably split a room:

  • Card 9, the Monday huddle. Running it is management. What you choose to say in it is leadership. Same meeting
  • Card 7, staffing the second site. It is a spreadsheet, and deciding to open a second site at all was the leadership act it depends on
  • Card 12, telling the manager the system will not work. Learners often file it as neither, because "that's not my job". It is card 12 that makes it worth running this game

How to run it

  1. Teams of 4-5, cards face down (1 min). No teaching yet
  2. Sort, 5 minutes, timed. Every card has to go in a pile. No "both" pile. The refusal is the engine of the activity
  3. Compare (3 min). Which cards did teams disagree on? Only discuss those
  4. Now teach Kotter (5 min). The room already has the distinction. You are giving it a name and a source
  5. The closing question: "which pile is most of your week in?"

Debrief

  • Which card caused the biggest argument in your team?
  • Did anyone want a "both" pile? What was on it?
  • Look at the management pile. What happens to a team with none of it?
  • Now look at the leadership pile. What happens to a team with none of that?
  • The real one: if you disappeared for a month, which pile would nobody pick up?

Variations

  • Human sort: two sides of the room, read cards aloud, people walk to a side. Faster, louder, and you can see who is unsure by who hesitates
  • Add your own: each team writes two cards from their own job before you start. These are always the best cards
  • Rank instead of sort: put all eighteen in order of "what my team would miss most if I stopped". Slower, and it goes somewhere different
  • Manager version: with actual supervisors, tally what they did last week against the two piles. Most get 90/10, and the 10 is the conversation
  • Low literacy: read every card aloud, work as one group, sort physically on a table

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not let management become the losing pile. The framing that "leadership is the good one" insults everyone in the room who is good at the other thing and it is not what Kotter said. Say explicitly: a team with no management fails faster than a team with no leadership
  • Teams that finish in two minutes. They have not argued. Send them back with the three splitting cards
  • The "it depends" defence. True, and it stalls the game. Rule: pick a pile, then say what it depends on
  • Status in the room. If some learners supervise and some do not, watch that the sort does not turn into a ranking of people. Sort the tasks, not each other

What Kind Of Difference Is This?

12-15 mingame
diversityteamsopenergamesortinginclusion

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-052 The Three Kinds of Diversity.

The trick of this game is that it is rigged. Learners sort statements into demographic, informational and values-based, and discover that most of what actually matters on a team is in the two piles nobody thinks about.

On this pageSet upThe statementsThe three moments the game exists forHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Set up

Three corners of the room, or three columns on a whiteboard:

DEMOGRAPHICINFORMATIONALVALUES
who we arewhat we knowwhat we're for

The statements

Read one at a time. The room moves, or points, or calls it out.

StatementAnswer
1"I'm 19, everyone else here is over 40"Demographic
2"I trained as a nurse in the Philippines"Informational (and people say demographic first)
3"I'm the only woman on the crew"Demographic
4"I've been doing this job for 22 years"Informational
5"I'm here to pay off my mum's house"Values
6"I use a wheelchair"Demographic
7"I want to be running my own crew in three years"Values
8"I'm the only one who's ever worked night shift"Informational
9"English is my third language"Both — demographic and informational. See below
10"I think the customer comes before the schedule"Values
11"I did a health and safety rep course last year"Informational
12"I don't want a promotion, I want my weekends"Values
13"I grew up here, everyone else moved in"Both
14"I think this whole approach is wrong"Values

The three moments the game exists for

Statement 2, the Filipino nurse. Rooms sort this as demographic almost every time, because they hear "Philippines". It is informational: this person has clinical training nobody else has. That mis-sort, live, in front of the room, is the best teaching moment in the activity.

➜ "You just heard where she's from and stopped listening to what she knows. That happens at work every day."

Statement 9, third language. Both, and it is worth sitting with. Someone who speaks three languages is demographically different and carries information the team does not have, and the workplace usually treats it purely as a deficit in the first language.

Statement 14, "this whole approach is wrong". Values diversity, and the room usually goes quiet because it does not feel like diversity at all. It feels like a difficult person. That is exactly the point: values diversity is the kind that produces the useful argument and the kind teams are least willing to call diversity.

How to run it

  1. Three corners, no teaching (1 min). Just the three headings
  2. Read the statements (8 min). People move. Do not correct immediately, ask why first
  3. Land the three moments above. Do not rush past statement 2
  4. Then teach FRM-052 (5 min), and the evidence audit that goes with it

Debrief

  • Which pile did you find easiest? Which one did you never think of as diversity?
  • Statement 2: what did you assume, and how fast?
  • Which kind of diversity does a hiring process usually look at?
  • Which kind actually changes what a team decides?

Variations

  • Own-statement round: everyone writes one true statement about themselves on a card, unsigned. Shuffle, read out, sort. Much stronger and it needs a group that already trusts each other
  • Team version: an intact team maps itself. Where are we diverse? Where are we all the same? Most teams discover they are informationally identical
  • Fast version: just statements 2, 9, 10 and 14. Four minutes, and it still works
  • Low literacy: entirely read aloud, hands up or move to a corner. Nothing needs reading

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Nobody discloses anything they did not plan to. The printed statements are about hypothetical people. The own-statement variation changes that, so only run it with a group you know, and make it genuinely optional
  • ⚠️ Statement 6 and disability. The library's Culture & Diversity pillar currently has almost nothing on disability and accessibility. Do not improvise a session on it off the back of one card. Acknowledge and move on
  • The "everything is demographic" room. If people are sorting everything into the first column, slow down and do statement 4 and statement 11 back to back
  • Turning it into a game of gotcha. The wrong answers are the content. Never make anyone feel caught out, especially on statement 2
  • Skipping to the evidence. The sorting has to happen first. If you teach the model before the game, the game is pointless

Say My Name

10-12 mingame
openernamesinclusiondiversityculturebelongingicebreaker

Type: opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole room, up to about 20 · Energy: medium

What it practises: move 1 of FRM-055 Accommodating Diversity, and it is the fastest way into FRM-050 Tikanga Māori in Business.

The best opener in this library for a culture session, because it costs nothing, takes ten minutes, and something real happens in almost every room.

On this pageHow it runsWhy the "say it back" step is not optionalWhat tends to happenDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How it runs

Round the circle. Each person says three things:

  1. My name, the way it should be said.
  2. Where it comes from, if you know. Who gave it to you, what it means, who else has it
  3. What people usually get wrong, if anything

Then the room says it back. Together, out loud. If it is not right, the person says it again and the room goes again. Up to three times.

That is the whole activity.

Why the "say it back" step is not optional

Without it, this is a nice sharing exercise and nothing changes. With it, twenty people have physically practised somebody's name and got it wrong in front of them and been corrected and tried again.

➜ That is the lesson. Getting it wrong is fine. Not trying is the problem. Learners who have been quietly answering to a mangled version of their name for fifteen years watch the room work at it, and that is a different experience from being asked about it politely.

What tends to happen
Somebody's real name comes outPeople who have gone by a shortened, anglicised or nickname version at work for years sometimes give their actual name. Do not make a thing of it. Just use the name they gave you, for the rest of the programme
"It's fine, just call me…"The most common response, and it is worth one gentle push: "I'd rather learn it, if that's alright." If they say no, that is their call and drop it
A Pākehā learner says they have a boring nameOften untrue. Ask who they were named after. There is usually a grandparent in it
Somebody criesOccasionally. It means more than people expect

Debrief

Short. Do not overwork it.

  • Who has had their name shortened at work without being asked?
  • How long did you let it go?
  • What does it cost to ask?
  • The closing line: "Right. For the rest of this programme, we say each other's names properly. Including mine."

Variations

  • Write it phonetically: everyone writes their name as it sounds on a card, and the cards stay on the table for the session. Enormously helpful, and it de-loads people's memory
  • Facilitator goes last: better than going first. The room hears everyone else before they hear you, and you have to have been paying attention
  • Roll-call round two: at the start of the next session, the facilitator names everyone from memory. Get it right. If you cannot, do not attempt it
  • Team version: with an intact team who already know each other, the round is "what do you actually want to be called at work, and is that what happens?" Different activity, same nerve
  • Large groups: tables of six rather than one circle. Loses some of the effect and still works
  • Big Zeducation cohorts: this pairs naturally with a mihi or pepeha round if that is appropriate to the group and the facilitator is confident. It is not a substitute for one

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ The facilitator has to go first at getting it wrong. Model being corrected, cheerfully, at least once. If the facilitator is precious about it, nobody else will risk it
  • ⚠️ Never make anyone explain their heritage. The question is about the name, not about ethnicity. "Where does it come from" is answerable with "my nan" and that is a complete answer
  • ⚠️ Do not push someone who declines. Some people have complicated reasons for the name they use at work. A trans learner, someone estranged from family, someone who changed it to get interviews. Offer once, accept the answer
  • Do not turn it into a pronunciation test. Nobody is being marked. Three attempts and move on
  • Then actually use the names. All programme. The activity is worthless if the facilitator reverts to "mate" on day two

Seven Seconds

12-15 mingame
career-readinesscvopenergamejob-searchwork-readiness

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-058 The CV That Gets Read.

Learners write CVs for a reader who does not exist: somebody with all the time in the world and a warm interest in them. This activity puts them in the actual reader's chair for ninety seconds and the point lands without anyone having to make it.

On this pageSet upHow to run itWhat happens⚠️ On the seven secondsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Set up

Print four sample CVs for the same fictional job. Make them deliberately different:

CVWhat is wrong or right with it
ABeautiful two-column design, photo, skills as little bar charts. Says almost nothing
BPlain, a wall of grey text, ten jobs since 2004, no headline
CPlain, a clear headline, four skill bullets with numbers, ticket listed at the top
DGood content, but the relevant licence is on page two

Do not label them. Nobody knows which is meant to be the good one.

How to run it

  1. Hand out all four to each small group, face down (1 min)
  2. "You are the hiring manager. You have forty CVs and a shift to run. You get seven seconds each."
  3. Timer. Seven seconds per CV. Then, immediately: "Yes pile or no pile?" No going back
  4. Count the room's verdicts on a whiteboard (3 min)
  5. Now give them two minutes with CV D and ask what they missed the first time
  6. Teach FRM-058 (5 min). The room has already worked out most of it

What happens

Nearly every room does the same thing:

  • A gets rejected, and people are surprised, because it is the one that looks like effort
  • B gets rejected in about two seconds
  • C wins, and nobody expected the plainest one to win
  • D splits the room, which is the useful result. Two minutes later everyone can see it was a decent candidate, and in seven seconds it was invisible

➜ The line to land it: "D wasn't a bad candidate. D was a bad top third."

⚠️ On the seven seconds

Say this out loud, because somebody will look it up:

"Seven seconds isn't a real measurement. The figures you see online come from recruitment companies selling something. What is true is that the first look is fast, and that software often reads it before a person does. We're using seven seconds to make a point, not to state a fact."

The library does not use unsourced statistics, and modelling that in front of learners is worth the thirty seconds it costs.

Debrief

  • What made you put one in the yes pile? Be specific
  • What did the pretty one actually tell you?
  • CV D: what would you move, and where?
  • The turn: how long do you think somebody spent on your CV last time you applied?

Variations

  • Their own CVs, anonymised: far more powerful, and only for a group that trusts each other. Collect them the week before, strip names, run the same game
  • Software round: read the four out loud in a flat voice with no formatting, the way a parser sees them. CV A becomes gibberish. Excellent and slightly cruel
  • Real ads: use a genuine Seek ad for the sector the group is heading into. Better than any fictional job
  • Two minutes instead of seven seconds: run the whole thing slow first, then fast. The change in verdicts is the lesson

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never use a learner's real CV without their consent, and never one from this room identifiably. Anonymise properly or use samples
  • The room that defends CV A. Let them. Then run the software round
  • Deflation. Somebody will realise their CV is a B or a D. Move straight into ACT-097 so they leave having fixed it, not just having learned it was wrong
  • Do not moralise about design. A learner who made a lovely CV in Canva did the work. The problem is the reader, not their effort

Who Do You Already Know?

20-25 mingame
career-readinessnetworkingweak-tiesjob-searchwork-readinesshidden-job-market

Type: game · Time: 20-25 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found and FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties.

Nearly everybody underestimates their own network by an order of magnitude. This activity makes it visible in about eight minutes, and most rooms are genuinely surprised.

On this pagePart 1 — the map (8 min, individual)Part 2 — count (2 min)Part 3 — the second question (6 min)Part 4 — the sentence (6 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the map (8 min, individual)

Big sheet. Your name in the middle. Then names, not categories.

CircleWho goes in it
FamilyIncluding cousins, in-laws, and the ones you only see at Christmas
Church, marae, communityEveryone whose name you know
Sport, club, culture groupTeam-mates, coaches, the parents on the sideline
School and studyOld classmates, tutors, people from this programme
Every job you have hadSupervisors, workmates, regular customers
Neighbours and aroundThe dairy, the barber, the school gate

Rule: write the name, even if you have not spoken in five years. Especially then.

Part 2 — count (2 min)

How many names? ______

Most people expect twenty and write sixty or more. Take a show of hands by range and put the spread on the board. The spread is the lesson.

Part 3 — the second question (6 min)

Now go back through and mark:

MarkWho
★Anyone who works somewhere, anywhere. Not a good job, any job
?Anyone whose workplace you could not describe

➜ Every ★ is a doorway into a workplace. Every ? is a five-minute conversation you have never had.

Part 4 — the sentence (6 min, pairs)

Say it out loud to your partner. Three parts, no more.

  1. What I'm looking for. Specific
  2. What I bring. One thing
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"
"I'm looking for warehouse or storeperson work. I've got my F endorsement. If you hear of anything, would you flick me a text?"

My sentence: ______________________________________________

Then the commitment: "Who are three people you'll say that to this week, and when?"

WhoWhen

Debrief

  • How many names did you expect? How many did you get?
  • Who has a ★ they had never thought of as a work contact?
  • The one that lands: who is the last person you told that you're looking?
  • What stops you saying the sentence?

Variations

  • Room version: everyone says their sentence to the whole room, and anyone who knows something says so on the spot. Jobs genuinely come out of this, and it is worth the ten minutes
  • Six degrees: pick a target employer. See how few steps it takes for anyone in the room to reach somebody inside it. Usually two or three, and it is startling
  • Text-it-now: three minutes at the end, phones out, send the sentence to one person. Beats any amount of intention
  • Employer mapping: for a group heading into one sector, map employers instead of people, then work out who knows somebody at each
  • Low literacy: draw it, use first names only, or do it entirely spoken in pairs

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ "It's who you know" can land as confirmation the system is rigged, especially for learners who already feel shut out. Turn it firmly the other way: you already have a network, it is bigger than you thought, and using it costs nothing. That is the whole point of doing the count before the sentence
  • ⚠️ Some people genuinely have a small map. New migrants, people out of a violent relationship, people recently out of prison. Do not let the count become a competition. The room version helps, because the room itself becomes part of their map
  • Do not call it networking. The word closes people down. It is telling people what you are looking for
  • The sentence that is too vague. "Anything going" gets nothing. Push for specific, because a specific ask is the one people remember when they hear something
  • No date, no action. Part 4's table is the point. A sentence nobody says is worth nothing
