ACT-107Activity · Wellbeing & Identity

The River Stones

15-20 mingame
wellbeingresilienceopenergameactionmetaphorhouse-content

Type: game · Time: 15-20 min · Group: whole room · Energy: 🔥 high

What it practises: step C of FRM-064 The ABC Model, and the metaphor the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide closes on:

Some people can see the whole path across. Others can only see the rock in front of them. That's fine. Step onto it, and the next one shows up.

The metaphor was doing nothing on the last page of a PDF. This puts it on the floor, and it takes fifteen minutes.

On this pageSet upRound 1 — the whole path (4 min)Round 2 — one stone at a time (8 min)Round 3 — the question (5 min)The line to land it onDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Set up

Lay out eight to twelve sheets of paper across the floor in a wandering line. That is the river. Tape them down if the floor is slippery, because somebody will be moving with their eyes covered.

⚠️ Clear the space properly. Chairs, bags, cables. Check the floor is not wet.

Round 1 — the whole path (4 min)

One volunteer crosses the river. They can see every stone. They walk across. It takes eight seconds and it is completely boring.

Ask the room: "how did that feel to watch?" Somebody will say "easy". Good.

Round 2 — one stone at a time (8 min)

Second volunteer. Eyes covered, standing at the first stone.

A partner stands beside them and does one thing only: names the next stone.

"There's one about half a metre ahead, slightly to your left."

No route. No plan. No "then you'll go right twice." One stone, then the next, and only after the first foot lands.

⚠️ Hand on the elbow the whole way. Physical safety first, every time. Anyone can stop at any point and nobody explains why.

Do it twice so two people get the feeling.

Round 3 — the question (5 min)

Ask the person who went second:

  • "How far ahead could you see?" (One stone.)
  • "Did you get across?" (Yes.)
  • "When did you know the second stone was there?" (After they had stood on the first.)

Then to the room:

"So which one of them actually needed the whole plan?"

The line to land it on

Say it exactly like this, and then stop talking:

You don't need to see every step. You need the next one. Clarity comes from action, not the other way around.

➜ Go straight into step C of ACT-106 while the room is still standing up. Do not let them sit down first.

Debrief

  • Who in here has been waiting until they can see the whole path before they start?
  • What is the thing you have been not-starting because you cannot see how it ends?
  • Round 2 needed a partner naming the next stone. Who does that for you?
  • What did it feel like to move without the plan?

Variations

  • No blindfold: for a room where covering someone's eyes is a step too far, have them look at the ceiling and rely entirely on the partner. Same lesson, nobody uncomfortable
  • Silent version: the partner may only point, not speak. Harder, funnier, and it makes the point about needing people even sharper
  • Named stones: write a real step on each sheet. The room walks their own path across an actual goal
  • Chairs version: for a room that cannot move around, do it as a thought exercise with two volunteers describing what they would need. Weaker, and still worth doing
  • Outdoor version: if you have a courtyard and some chalk, this is much better outside

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Mobility, balance, vision and pregnancy. Ask for volunteers rather than picking anyone, and never single somebody out. Have a seated role ready, because the partner naming the stones is the more interesting job anyway
  • ⚠️ Being blindfolded is not neutral for everyone. For some people it is a trauma trigger. Offer the no-blindfold version first and let people choose without saying why
  • The partner who plans the whole route. They will. Stop them, restart, and let the room see the difference. That correction is the activity
  • Do not over-explain before you run it. The game makes the point. A facilitator who explains the metaphor first has spent it
  • Do not let it become a trust-fall session. It is about the next step, not about trust. Keep it moving

ACT-112Activity · Employment & Work Readiness

The Question You Didn't Ask

15-20 mingame
work-readinessonboardingquestionsopenerstarting-workgame

Type: game / opener · Time: 15-20 min · Group: whole room, in teams · Energy: 🔥 high

What it practises: moves 2 and 3 of FRM-068 The First Two Weeks.

Do not tell the room that asking early is free. Let them guess instead, get it wrong, and find out what guessing costs. It takes fifteen minutes and it makes the whole session land.

On this pageSet upPart 1 — build it (6 min)Part 2 — mark it (4 min)Part 3 — the two lists (6 min, whole room)The line to land it onDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Set up

Teams of three or four. Each team gets the same simple build task and instructions with three things missing.

The build can be anything: a paper aeroplane to a spec, a tower from newspaper, a shape from Lego, folding a stack of tea towels "the way we do it here". Keep it trivial — the task is not the point.

What the instructions leave out (and you do not mention this):

MissingExample
A standardIt does not say how tall, how many, or which way up
A ruleIt does not say you cannot use tape
A whenIt does not say there is a deadline

⚠️ You know the answers. You are sitting at the front. You say nothing unless somebody asks.

Part 1 — build it (6 min)

Hand out the instructions. Say exactly one thing:

"Here's the job. You've got six minutes. I'm right here."

Then sit down and do not offer anything.

Most teams will start building immediately. Usually one team asks a question, sometimes none do.

Part 2 — mark it (4 min)

Now apply the three standards nobody was told.

  • "These needed to be twenty centimetres. This one's twelve."
  • "You've used tape. You weren't supposed to use tape."
  • "And they were due at four minutes, not six."

The room will object. Loudly, and correctly. Let it run for about thirty seconds.

Then ask the only question that matters:

"Who could you have asked?"

➜ Point at yourself. "I was right here the whole time and I'd have told you."

Part 3 — the two lists (6 min, whole room)

On the board, in two columns:

What it cost us to guessWhat it would have cost to ask
Six minutes of workAbout four seconds
Doing it twiceLooking like we did not know for four seconds

Let the room fill both. The right-hand column stays almost empty, and that is the whole game.

Then the real question:

"So why didn't you ask?"

The answers are always the same, and they are the honest content of this activity:

  • "I didn't want to look stupid"
  • "I thought I'd work it out"
  • "Everyone else was already going"
  • "I didn't want to be the one holding it up"

➜ Write them on the board. Then: "which of those is going to be true in your first week on a new job?"

The line to land it on

In week two, nobody expects you to know. They expect you to ask. The window where asking is free closes about week three. Use it.

Debrief

  • Who nearly asked and did not? What stopped you?
  • Which of the three missing things would have been worst to get wrong at a real job?
  • What is the difference between asking in week one and asking in month six?
  • Who has guessed at work and got it wrong? What did it cost?

Variations

  • Real task version: use something from your own sector. Folding, stacking, labelling, PPE. The closer to their work the harder it lands
  • The plant: brief one person beforehand to ask a good question two minutes in. Their team wins easily, and the contrast does the teaching for you
  • Round two: run it again with a different task and watch the questions come immediately. Worth the extra five minutes because the room feels the change
  • Silent version: teams may only ask in writing. Shows how much harder it is when asking is awkward
  • Low literacy: give the instructions verbally, once, quickly. Same effect and arguably more realistic

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This game works by setting people up, so land it properly. The moment the marking happens, the room needs to see that the facilitator was the problem, not them. If anybody leaves feeling foolish rather than clear, it has failed
  • Do not let the objection phase run past thirty seconds. It turns into a real argument about fairness and you lose the point
  • Never single out the team that did worst. Mark all of them against all three
  • The room where somebody does ask immediately. Great. Say so, loudly, and use them as the worked example. The game still works
  • Do not use a task anybody could fail at for a real reason — nothing needing dexterity, reading speed or eyesight. The task must be trivial

ACT-114Activity · Leadership

Build The Ladder, Then Knock It Down

20-25 mingame
leadershipmotivationmaslowevidencemythsopenercritical-thinking

Type: game / opener · Time: 20-25 min · Group: whole room, in groups · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-071 Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, and it clears the ground for FRM-070.

Half the room has already met Maslow. Rather than pretend otherwise, build it with them, then let them take it apart from their own lives. The room does the disproving, not the facilitator.

On this pagePart 1 — build it (7 min, groups)Part 2 — knock it down (10 min, whole room)Part 3 — why it matters (6 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — build it (7 min, groups)

Hand each group the five needs on cards, shuffled, no order given:
Food, water, sleep, warmth
Housing, health, a job that will still be there
Relationships, belonging, being part of something
Respect, recognition, being good at something
Becoming what you could be
"Put these in the order you think they go."

Every group produces the same order, whether or not they have heard of Maslow. Put it on the board as a ladder.

Now name it. Abraham Maslow, 1943.

⚠️ And say the first thing straight away: "He never drew the pyramid. Somebody else added that later, and the pyramid is what makes it look like a law."

Part 2 — knock it down (10 min, whole room)

One question, and then stop talking.

"Have you ever found belonging, or pride, or purpose, while things were genuinely hard? While money was short, or the house wasn't safe, or you were sick?"

➜ The room says yes. Marae. Church. A sports team. Family. Prison, sometimes. Take three or four answers and write them on the board next to the ladder.

Then:

"So did you climb the ladder in order?"

That is the teaching. The room has just disproved a fifty-year-old model from their own lives, and it will stay disproved.

Now give them the research, briefly, so they know it is not just their opinion:

  • Wahba and Bridwell (1976) reviewed the studies and found little support for the hierarchy as described, especially the ordering
  • Longitudinal studies of the "satisfy one level and the next switches on" claim found no support at all
  • What survives is the list. Five real categories of need. The ladder is the bit that does not hold

Part 3 — why it matters (6 min)

This is not an academic argument. Ask:

"If you believed the ladder was true, and you were running a service for people doing it hard, what would you do first? And what would you leave until later?"

➜ The room gets there: you would deal with food and housing and leave dignity, purpose and belonging for once things were sorted.

⚠️ That is the ladder logic, and a lot of people in the room will have been on the receiving end of it. Let that land. It is the reason the audit matters.

Then the turn: "So what would you use instead?" → straight into FRM-070 and ACT-113.

Debrief

  • Who had met Maslow before? Where?
  • Did anybody's group put them in a different order? (Occasionally somebody does, and it is interesting.)
  • What was your example of finding belonging or pride while things were hard?
  • Where have you seen the ladder logic used on people?
  • What do you do with a model that is useful and not true?

Variations

  • Straight to Part 2: if the room has definitely met Maslow, skip the building and go to the question. Ten minutes
  • Two models side by side: build Maslow's five and Te Whare Tapa Whā's four on the board together. Four walls, no order. Five rungs, an order that does not hold. A good conversation and it is not a competition
  • Written version: everyone writes their own example on a sticky note. Anonymous, and for a room that will not speak
  • Research round: groups get five minutes and phones to find out whether Maslow drew the pyramid. They enjoy finding out he did not
  • Low literacy: cards with pictures instead of words, entirely spoken

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Part 2 asks about hard times. Keep it light, take volunteers only, never ask anybody directly, and do not follow up on detail in the room. The examples can stay general and the point still lands
  • ⚠️ Somebody has been on the wrong end of the ladder logic from a service that decided what they were allowed to want. Be on their side about it, briefly, and move on
  • Do not turn it into "Maslow was stupid." He gave us a good list in 1943. Somebody else built the ladder, and fifty years of testing did the rest. Getting that distinction right is the intellectual habit worth teaching
  • The room that wants to keep the ladder because it feels right. Fine. Ask what would change their mind, then show them Wahba and Bridwell. That is the lesson, not the model
  • Do not run it if you are not going to teach SDT afterwards. Knocking down a model and putting nothing in its place is worse than leaving it alone

ACT-116Activity · Digital Capability

Same Question, Four Ways

20-25 mingame
digital-capabilityaipromptingopenerpracticegame

Type: game / opener · Time: 20-25 min · Group: whole room, in pairs at devices · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-073 The Four-Part Prompt and FRM-074 Pull, Not Push.

Nobody believes prompting matters until they watch the same question get four different answers. Twenty minutes, one shared task, four rounds, and the room proves it to itself.

On this pageSet upRound 1 — the way everybody does it (4 min)Round 2 — add a role (4 min)Round 3 — the full four parts (7 min)Round 4 — let it ask you (6 min)The board at the endDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Set up

One real task, the same for everybody. Put it on the board.

Good ones: write a cover letter for this job ad · explain KiwiSaver to somebody starting their first job · plan a 90-minute session on teamwork · write a text to a boss asking for Friday off.

Pairs, one device between two. ⚠️ Check wifi and accounts the week before. Have a paper fallback.

Round 1 — the way everybody does it (4 min)

Type the task as one short line. Nothing else.

"Write me a cover letter."

Read what comes back. One word each round the room: how would you describe it?

➜ You will get "generic", "boring", "American", "not me". Write those on the board.

Round 2 — add a role (4 min)

Same task. Add one line at the front.

"Act like a New Zealand recruiter who hires warehouse staff."

Better? How? Usually sharper, still not theirs.

Round 3 — the full four parts (7 min)

Role · Context · Command · Format. Context is the work. Give it the ad, the CV, what they have tried, who it is for.

"...Give it back as plain text under 150 words, no headings."

Read it out. ➜ The jump between rounds 2 and 3 is the biggest in the activity and it is all context.

Round 4 — let it ask you (6 min)

Wipe the prompt. Start again with the outcome and one line:

"I need a cover letter for this job that would make this employer ring me. Ask me all the questions you need to do this properly, then give it back as plain text."

Answer its questions. Voice-to-text if the room is not typists.

Then the question that matters:

"Which of the questions it asked you had you not thought about?"

⚠️ That is the real finding. Being asked seven good questions about your own situation is worth something even if you throw the output away.

The board at the end

RoundWhat we gave itWhat came back
1A text messageGeneric
2+ a roleSharper
3+ context and formatUsable
4An outcome, and it askedOurs
The quality of what comes out will never beat the quality of what goes in.

Debrief

  • Which round made the biggest difference? (Almost always 2 to 3)
  • What did it ask you in round 4 that you had not thought of?
  • Did anything it produced sound like you? What would you have to change?
  • Did it say anything you would need to check before sending? (Bridge to ACT-118)
  • What did it assume about you that was wrong?

Variations

  • Real tasks: each pair uses their own job ad or their own problem. Better, and harder to run
  • One device, facilitator drives: for a room without devices. Still works, and the room calls out what to add
  • Bad prompt hall of fame: collect the worst round-1 outputs and read them out. Funny, and it makes the point without anybody feeling got at
  • Staff version: the shared task is a real Zeducation one — a funding paragraph, a session plan
  • Low tech: print four pre-generated outputs from the four rounds and have the room match them to the prompts. No devices needed and it still teaches

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Devices and wifi. Check both the week before, and have the low-tech version ready. Half a room turning up without a working device is normal
  • ⚠️ Somebody will paste in something private in round 3 when you ask for context. Say the rule before the round, not after: no names, no health information, no files about other people
  • Do not use a task with a right answer. Anything factual sends the room into checking, which is the next activity, not this one
  • The learner who is already good at this. Make them the demo for round 4
  • Do not let round 3 run to fifteen minutes. Timebox it out loud

ACT-006Activity · Communication

Two Things — Reflection & Commitment

10-12 minreflection
reflectiongoal-settingcommitmentstar

Type: reflection · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the R in FRM-003 STAR. A generic closer that works for any topic, not just this one.

Materials: the learner's journal or the reflection page in the workbook, a pen.

On this pageHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

How to run it

  1. Review (2 min). Put the learning outcomes back on the screen. Ask one learner to say the purpose of the session in their own words. Not you. Them.
  2. Write (5 min). Silent. Everyone answers, in writing:
    • What is the one thing from today you will remember tomorrow?
    • What are 2-3 things you will do to be more assertive? (swap in the topic's skill)
    • Who will you use it with, and when?
  3. Share (3 min). Pairs read one of their commitments to each other. Reading it out loud to another person is what makes it real.
  4. Close (2 min). Invite two or three to share with the room. Never force it.

Debrief

  • What made you choose that particular commitment?
  • What is likely to get in the way of it?
  • What would make it easier? Who could help?
  • How will you know it worked?

The point to land: a session you enjoyed and a session that changed something are different things. The difference is written down in front of you.

Variations

  • Follow-up: photograph the page, or have learners text their commitment to themselves. Open the next session by asking who did it
  • Low literacy: voice note it on their phone instead of writing
  • Online: private chat to the facilitator, then volunteers share aloud
  • Team version: the group agrees one shared commitment and writes it on the wall
  • Programme version: collect the commitments each week. They become the evidence in the end-of-programme report

Watch out for

  • Vague commitments ("be more confident") do nothing. Push for a person, a situation and a week
  • Do not skip this because you ran over time. It is the part that transfers
  • Never read someone's page without asking

ACT-013Activity · Communication

Start, Stop, Continue

10-12 minreflection
reflectiongoal-settingcommitmentstar

Type: reflection · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the R in FRM-003 STAR. Topic-agnostic. Works as a closer for any session.

Materials: the reflection page, a pen.

On this pageHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

How to run it

  1. Review (2 min). Learning outcomes back on the screen. Ask one learner to say the purpose of the session in their own words.
  2. Write (5 min). Silent. Three boxes:
I want to start…something you are not doing yet
I want to stop…a habit that is costing you
I want to continue…something you already do well, name it so you keep it
  1. Share (3 min). Pairs read one box to each other. Most people find "stop" the hardest to say out loud, which is usually the sign it is the right one.
  2. Close (2 min). Two or three share with the room. Never force it.

Debrief

  • Which box was hardest to fill in?
  • What makes the "stop" one hard to say out loud?
  • What is likely to get in the way of the "start" one?
  • Who will notice if you actually do it?

The point to land: most people only ever write the start list. The stop list is where the time comes from, and the continue list is what stops you throwing away something that already works.

Variations

  • Follow-up: photograph the page. Open the next session by asking who did their "start"
  • Team version: the group agrees one shared start, stop and continue and writes it on the wall
  • Low literacy: voice note it instead of writing
  • Online: private chat to the facilitator, volunteers share aloud
  • Programme version: collect them weekly. They become the evidence in the end-of-programme report

Watch out for

  • Vague entries ("stop being unclear") do nothing. Push for a specific behaviour in a specific situation
  • The "continue" box gets rushed. It is the one that builds confidence, so protect the time for it
  • Do not read someone's page without asking

ACT-076Activity · Communication

Conflict Resolution Presentation

5 min per learner, plus prepreflection
conflictconflict-resolutionassessed-taskhouse-contentpresentingreflectioncommitment

Type: filmed presentation, assessed · Time: maximum 5 minutes per learner, plus prep · Group: individual · Energy: medium

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), where it is Task 6.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify conflict resolution techniques and describe how they can improve leadership skills in the workplace". The facilitator films it and uploads it.

It is also the capstone of the whole micro-credential, and the only task where the learner speaks for themselves rather than filling in a box.

On this pageThe briefHow to run itThe structure to give themWhy item 1 is not just adminMarking guidanceWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The brief

Make a short video, maximum 5 minutes, presenting on conflict resolution. It must include:

  1. You, introducing yourself: your name, where you were born, and your ethnicity
  2. Your role title at work, and what you do
  3. Two things you have learnt during the training
  4. One conflict resolution technique you have learnt, and how you will use it in the workplace

Items 1 and 4 are named twice in the source as mandatory. Make sure both are in.

How to run it

  1. Give the brief at the start of the programme, not the end. Learners who know the capstone is coming pay differently to everything before it.
  2. Prep time, 15 minutes. Notes are fine. Reading a script to camera is not what is being assessed and it produces the worst videos.
  3. Film somewhere quiet, one at a time. Not in front of the group unless the learner wants that.
  4. One retake offered as standard. Most people's second take is much better and nobody should have to ask.

The structure to give them

SectionTimeWhat to say
Who I am45 secName, where you were born, ethnicity, your role and what you do
What I learnt90 secTwo things. Be specific: name the framework, not "communication"
The technique2 minOne technique. What it is, and the actual situation at work where you will use it
Close30 secWhen you will use it. A day, a person, a place

➜ Facilitator tip: the single biggest quality lift is insisting on a real, named situation in part 4. "I'll listen better" is not evidence. "When Sione comes to me about the roster on Monday, I'm going to use the three layers and ask what matters to him before I offer anything" is.

Why item 1 is not just admin

Asking learners to name where they were born and their ethnicity, at the front of a presentation about conflict, is a deliberate choice and worth understanding rather than treating as a form field. Conflict is read differently across cultures, and a programme delivered to Pacific, Māori and migrant learners that never asks who is in the room would be teaching one culture's conflict norms as neutral.

See FRM-033 Cultural Safety for why that matters.

Marking guidance

There is no rubric in the source. This is a suggested one, and it is not part of the official assessment.

EnoughNot yet
Technique namedA specific framework from the programme"Communication" or "listening"
ApplicationA real situation, person and timeA general intention
UnderstandingExplains why the technique worksDescribes the steps only
Leadership linkSays what changes for the people around themOnly about themselves

Watch out for

  • Camera fear is real. For many learners this is the hardest part of the micro-credential by a wide margin. Offer the retake before they ask, let them hold notes, and film against a plain wall rather than in front of peers
  • Five minutes is a maximum, not a target. A tight three minute video that names a real situation beats five minutes of padding
  • Consent and storage. The video goes to an assessor and contains the learner's name, birthplace and ethnicity. Tell them where it goes, who sees it, and how long it is kept, before you film
  • Do not let it become a thank-you speech. Redirect to the technique
  • Accessibility: if a learner cannot present to camera, ask the assessor what alternative evidence is acceptable before the day, not on it

ACT-087Activity · Leadership

Your Leadership Legacy

15-20 minreflection
leadershipreflectionlegacyvaluesself-awarenessgoal-setting

Type: reflection · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then optional pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the closing reflection for any leadership session. Pairs especially with FRM-048 and FRM-049.

The idea, from SRC-009: your leadership legacy has very little to do with your numbers. It is what people keep doing because they worked with you. And the test of it is what survives after you leave.

On this pageThe reflection sheetHow to run itQuestion 3 is the whole activityDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The reflection sheet

1. Think about a leader you worked for who is no longer in your life.

What do you still do, at work, because of them? ______________________________________________

What did you stop doing the moment they left? ______________________________________________

➜ The gap between those two answers is their real legacy. Not what they said. What stuck.

2. Now your own team.

If you left on Friday, what would they keep doing? ______________________________________________

What would go back to how it was within a month? ______________________________________________

3. The hard one.

What is one thing your team currently does because you are watching? ______________________________________________

4. What would have to change for that thing to survive you? ______________________________________________

5. Finish this sentence. One line. No jargon.

When people talk about what it was like to work with me, I want them to say ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Question 1 first, alone (5 min). Working from someone else's legacy before your own is easier and it produces a better answer
  2. Questions 2 and 3 (5 min). Silent
  3. Questions 4 and 5 (5 min). Question 5 gets rewritten at least twice by most people
  4. Optional pairs (5 min). Share only question 5

Question 3 is the whole activity

"What does your team do because you are watching?"

Everyone has an answer and nobody enjoys it. The gloves that go on when you walk into the yard. The sign-off sheet that gets filled in properly on the days you are in.

That is not a failure of character in your team. It is Theory X showing up as a habit, and it means the standard belongs to you rather than to them. A standard that belongs to you leaves when you do.

They writePush with
"Nothing, my team are good""What happened the week you were on leave?"
"Wearing PPE properly""Do they know why, or do they know you check?"
"Filling in the sheets""Who else would notice if they stopped?"

Debrief

Room level. Nobody reports their own answers.

  • Did anyone's answer to question 1 surprise them?
  • What is the difference between a habit your team has and a rule you enforce?
  • Whose legacy is easier to build: a manager's or a leader's? Which one lasts?
  • Question 5: how many of you wrote something about results? How many about people?

Variations

  • End-of-programme version: run it on day one and again on the last day. People keep both sheets. The change in question 5 is usually the best evidence of learning in the whole programme
  • Six-month letter: question 5 becomes a letter to yourself, sealed, and the facilitator posts it in six months. Needs an address and a promise you will actually keep
  • Team version: the leader answers question 2, then the team answers it about them, anonymously. Powerful, and only for a team that is already in decent shape
  • Whakataukī opener: open with Ki te kāhore he whakakitenga ka ngaro te iwi, "without foresight or vision the people will be lost", attributed to Kīngi Tāwhiao. Then ask what they want people to see
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in pairs, one person scribes for the other, or record it on a phone

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Not everyone in the room leads anyone. Reframe for them: what will the people you work beside keep doing? A legacy does not require a title
  • Grandiosity. Question 5 attracts mission statements. Push for something a real person would actually say about them in a smoko room
  • The learner who realises they have no legacy. Usually someone new, sometimes someone who has been coasting. The answer is that question 5 is a decision, not a report
  • Do not force the pairs share. Question 5 is more personal than it looks

ACT-122Activity · Wellbeing & Identity

Two Introductions

20-25 minreflection
pepehaidentitybelongingintroductionsreflectionemploymentte-ao-maori

Type: reflection · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs, then whole room · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-077 The Water Cycle — specifically the part that says a pepeha is an offer of connection, not a credential.

➜ The whole activity is one comparison. Introduce yourself the way you would at a job interview. Then introduce yourself with your pepeha. Notice what each one is for.

On this pageRound 1 — the interview version (5 min)Round 2 — the pepeha version (5 min)Round 3 — the four questions (10 min)What usually comes out — and the point of the activityThe turn — and do not skip thisLast question (2 min)Facilitator notesRelated activitiesUsed by

Round 1 — the interview version (5 min)

Pairs. Thirty seconds each, standing or sitting, no notes.

"Tell me about yourself."

That is it. Same words an employer opens with. Let them do what they would actually do.

Round 2 — the pepeha version (5 min)

Same partner. Read the pepeha they built in ACT-120.

Round 3 — the four questions (10 min)

Individually, on paper. Then pairs, then three or four to the room.
1In the first one, who were you talking about? In the second one, who were you talking about?
2Which one told the other person something they could connect to?
3Which one felt like proving, and which one felt like offering?
4If a stranger heard both, which one would they remember tomorrow?

What usually comes out — and the point of the activity

The interview version is a list of things you have done. It talks about you alone. It is trying to demonstrate that you are enough. It is a credential.

The pepeha is a list of people and places you are connected to. It talks about you inside something. It is not trying to prove anything. It is an offer.

➜ The line to land it:

One of those is you making a case. The other is you opening a door. Both are useful. They are not the same tool, and most people have only ever been taught the first one.

The turn — and do not skip this

This is not "the interview version is bad." Some learners will get there and it is the wrong conclusion.

Ask the room:

Where would each one actually work?
The interview versionThe pepeha version
A job interview, a funder, a first meeting with a clientA pōwhiri, a mihi whakatau, a first day, a hui, a new team
Where somebody is deciding about youWhere somebody is deciding whether to open up to you

And the thing worth naming: the second one is what the hidden job market actually runs on. Jobs get found through people who know you. A form of introduction whose entire purpose is connection is not a soft skill sitting to one side of employment — it is the employment skill, and most people have never been taught it as one.

Last question (2 min)

Written down, kept:

One place in the next month where I could use the second one.

Facilitator notes

  • Order matters. Interview version first, always. Doing the pepeha first makes the interview version feel like a failure, and it is not.
  • Do not let Round 3 become a discussion about how bad interviews are. Two minutes, then Round 4.
  • Watch for the learner who says both felt fake. That is worth a private word rather than a room discussion — it usually means the pepeha has blanks in it that they do not want to talk about.

ACT-094 The Skills You Don't CountSame discovery — you were already carrying something you were not counting
ACT-006 Two Things CommitmentThe close, if this is the last activity of the session

ACT-001Activity · Communication

Four Styles Roleplay

25-35 minroleplay
assertivenessroleplaycommunication-styles

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-35 min · Group: 3-5 per group · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles and FRM-002 The Assert Approach

Materials: one scenario card per group, a timer.

On this pageSet upHow to run itThe scenariosDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

Groups of 3-5, spread around the room so they can rehearse without being overheard. Each group gets one scenario. Say up front: there is no perfect way to do this. The goal is to practise, learn and improve.

How to run it

  1. Each group takes or is given one scenario (below).
  2. As a group, they roleplay the same situation four times, once in each style: passive, aggressive, passive-aggressive, assertive. 8 minutes to prepare.
  3. Each group performs to the class. They do not say which style is which.
  4. The rest of the class guesses the style after each version.
  5. Debrief the assertive version: what exactly made it assertive? Words, tone, or body language?

The scenarios

#SituationGoal
1Performance drop — a team member's work has slipped recently and it is affecting the teamHave a supportive conversation and reset expectations
2Running behind schedule — the team is behind and people are rushing and skipping stepsReset the team and give direction
3Unrealistic deadline — your manager asks for something that may not be realistic in the time givenCommunicate honestly about what is possible and discuss options
4Senior worker pushback — an experienced worker ignores the process and says "I've done this for years"Address it respectfully and maintain standards

Debrief

  • Which style was easiest to act? Which was hardest? Why?
  • What did the assertive version do that the others did not?
  • Which style did you recognise from your own workplace?
  • What changed in the room's body language between versions?

The point to land: assertive was not the loudest version. It was the clearest one. Clear and respectful at the same time is a skill, and it is trainable.

Variations

  • Youth: swap in scenarios about group chats, a friend borrowing money, a coach, a part-time job
  • Frontline / low literacy: read the scenario aloud, no written prep, straight into acting
  • Online: breakout rooms to prepare, perform in the main room with cameras on
  • Large group: each group performs only one assigned style, class assembles the full set
  • Short on time: run scenario 1 only, all groups, four styles

Watch out for

  • The aggressive roleplay can get personal if a group is acting out a real situation with a real person in the room. Set the rule: no naming, no impressions of anyone here
  • Some learners will not want to perform. Give them the observer role: they call the style and explain what gave it away
  • Keep the passive-aggressive version short. It is funny for about 30 seconds, then it is just uncomfortable

ACT-003Activity · Communication

DESC Rewrite Lab

25-30 minroleplay
assertivenessdescdifficult-conversationspractice

Type: roleplay / structured practice · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-004 The DESC Script, built on FRM-002 "I" statements

Materials: a four-box card per learner (Describe / Express / Specify / Consequences), pens.

On this pageSet upHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

Pairs. Everyone brings one real, low-to-medium-stakes conversation they have been avoiding. Set the boundary early: nothing involving harassment, safety or anything that belongs with HR. Those are real conversations, but they need support, not a practice room.

How to run it

  1. Write (8 min). Each learner fills the four boxes for their own situation. Silent work.
  2. Swap and sharpen (5 min). Partners read each other's card and check three things:
    • Is Describe facts only, with no labels or "always"?
    • Is Specify one clear change the other person could actually do?
    • Are Consequences positive first, not a threat?
  3. Say it out loud (8 min). Partner A delivers their script to Partner B, who plays the other person and pushes back once, reasonably. Then swap.
  4. Round two (5 min). Rewrite the line that did not land, and say it again.

Debrief

  • Which of the four boxes was hardest to fill in? (It is almost always Specify.)
  • What happened to your body when your partner pushed back?
  • What is different about hearing your own words out loud versus reading them?
  • When will you have the real conversation?

The point to land: you do not need to be braver, you need to be more prepared. Four lines written down beforehand is what turns avoiding into handling.

Variations

  • Youth: provide the situation rather than asking for a real one. Group chat left them out, a friend borrowing money and not paying it back, a coach not playing them
  • Frontline / low literacy: facilitator writes one shared example on the board, everyone practises the same script, then changes only the Specify line
  • Online: shared doc with the four boxes, breakout rooms in pairs
  • Advanced: partner pushes back twice, second time emotionally, to practise holding the line

Watch out for

  • Someone will bring a genuinely serious situation. Have a quiet word, and know your referral path before the session starts
  • Pairs drift into venting about the person. Redirect to the card
  • Do not let anyone leave with a script they have written but never said aloud. Saying it is the activity

ACT-009Activity · Communication

Briefing Roleplay — What, Why, How

30-40 minroleplay
briefingtoolbox-talksafetyroleplayteamsclear-messaging

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-40 min · Group: 4-6 per group · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-007 The What-Why-How Briefing Framework

Materials: one briefing plan template per group, the scenario list.

On this pageSet upHow to run itThe scenariosDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

Groups of 4-6. One person is the leader, everyone else is a crew member. Make the crew's job explicit before you start, because this is where most briefing practice falls over: the crew must contribute. They ask questions, confirm understanding, raise safety concerns, and share ideas.

Say the key line up front: a strong briefing is a team conversation, not a leader presentation.

How to run it

  1. Each group picks a scenario.
  2. The leader takes 5 minutes with the briefing plan template: What, Why, How, Risks, Team input.
  3. The leader delivers the briefing to their crew. 3-4 minutes.
  4. The crew does its job: questions, concerns, suggestions, confirming understanding.
  5. Swap the leader and run a second scenario, so more than one person practises.

The scenarios

#Situation
1Starting a task on a busy work site
2Conditions have changed before work begins
3A new worker joins the shift
4A safety risk is identified
5Equipment or vehicle movement creates hazards

Debrief

  • Leaders: which of the three questions was hardest to fill in?
  • Crew: at what point did you actually understand what you were doing?
  • Who raised something the leader had not thought of? What was it?
  • What would have happened on a real site if the Why had been left out?

The point to land: the Why is the part that gets skipped and the part that decides whether people adapt correctly when reality does not match the plan. And if nobody but the leader spoke, it was a presentation, not a briefing.

Variations

  • Non-site industries: swap in a kitchen service, a retail shift change, a call centre campaign, an aged care handover. The structure does not change
  • Youth: briefing a team for a sports game or a community event
  • Online: breakout rooms, leader shares the template on screen
  • Harder version: give one crew member a hidden card — they know a hazard the leader does not, and will only mention it if genuinely asked
  • Assessment version: use the template as evidence of competency for a health and safety unit

Watch out for

  • Crews going passive and just nodding. If it happens, stop and reset the expectation
  • Leaders who read the template out like a form. It is prompts, not a script
  • Do not let "any questions?" be asked while walking away. Ask it standing still, and wait through the silence

TOP-COM-003 Make Your Message LandCommunicationTOPIC.md

Source: Zeducation Effective Communication workbook, Module 2. Aligns with WorkSafe NZ pre-work briefing guidance.

ACT-014Activity · Communication

Yes – No – Yes Lab

25-30 minroleplay
boundariessaying-noassertivenesspracticeworkload

Type: worksheet then roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-008 The Positive No

Materials: a three-box card per learner (Yes / No / Yes), pens.

On this pageSet upPart 1 — Build your own (10 min)Part 2 — Roleplay (12 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

Pairs. Everyone brings one real request they find hard to turn down. Keep it to workload, shifts, favours and family asks. Anything involving bullying, safety or harassment is a real conversation that needs support, not a practice room.

Part 1 — Build your own (10 min)

Silent work. Each learner fills in three boxes for their own situation.

BoxPrompt
The requestWhat are you being asked to do?
YesWhat do you care about that makes this hard? The value, the priority, the person
NoYour clear limit. One sentence
YesA way forward you can genuinely offer

Then partners swap cards and check three things:

  • Is the middle line actually a no? Read it on its own. If it could be read as "maybe", it is not done
  • Is the first Yes a value, not an apology? "Sorry, I'm just really busy" fails this
  • Is the last Yes something you can really do? A broken alternative costs more than the original no

Part 2 — Roleplay (12 min)

Person A is the asker. Pick one:

  • "Can you cover my shift this weekend?"
  • "I need you to take on this extra project, you're the only one who can."
  • "Can you stay back late again tonight?"

Person B answers using Yes – No – Yes.

Then the asker gives feedback:

#Question
1Did the no feel clear?
2Did you still feel respected?
3One thing to improve

Then swap roles.

Debrief

  • Which box was hardest to write? (Usually the first Yes. People reach for an excuse instead of a value.)
  • How did it feel to say the middle line out loud, compared with writing it?
  • Askers: what made you accept it? What would have made you push?
  • Whose third Yes would you actually have taken?

The point to land: you are not rejecting the person, you are protecting something. Say what that something is and the no stops feeling like an insult, to them and to you.

Variations

  • Youth: provide the request rather than asking for a real one. A friend asking for money, a lift, homework, or to cover for them
  • Frontline / low literacy: build one shared example on the board, everyone practises the same three lines, then changes only the middle one
  • Online: shared doc with the three boxes, breakout rooms in pairs
  • Advanced: the asker does not accept the first answer. That is ACT-015, and it works well run straight after this one

Watch out for

  • Long explanations. Learners pad the no with three reasons. One is enough. Time them if you have to
  • The third Yes becoming the whole answer. Some learners will offer so much alternative that they have effectively said yes. Point at the middle line and ask what they actually declined
  • Someone will bring a situation where the honest answer is that they cannot refuse, because of immigration status, a probation period, or money. Do not push them to practise a no they cannot afford. Shift them to a lower-stakes example and name plainly that this is a real limit, not a personal failure

ACT-015Activity · Communication

Hold The Line — Broken Record Roleplay

25-30 minroleplay
boundariessaying-noassertivenesspressurepracticecustomer-service

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-009 The Broken Record

Materials: a three-box card (Acknowledge / Appreciate / Explain priorities), pens.

On this pageSet upPart 1 — Build your own (8 min)Part 2 — Roleplay (15 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Set up

This is the pressure activity. It works best straight after ACT-014 Yes – No – Yes Lab: they have just built a no, now someone refuses to accept it.

Demonstrate first. Ask a learner to push you three times while you hold one line. They need to see a calm third repetition before they will believe it is possible.

Part 1 — Build your own (8 min)

Think of a time someone kept pushing you to change your answer.

BoxPrompt
The situationWhat were they pushing for?
AcknowledgeSay back what they asked for
AppreciateValue their point or position, genuinely
Explain prioritiesYour reason, then your repeat line

The repeat line is the important box. One sentence. Write it down and underline it, because it is the thing that must not change under pressure.

Part 2 — Roleplay (15 min)

Person A is the pusher. Pick one, and keep pushing at least three times:

  • A customer demanding a discount
  • A teammate wanting you to rush a job
  • Someone pressuring you to say yes to extra work

Person B holds the line using the Broken Record. Stay calm, keep acknowledging, repeat the answer.

Feedback from Person A:

#Question
1Did Person B stay calm?
2Did the answer stay clear each time?
3Did they sound reasonable, not stubborn?

Then swap.

With an observer (threes): the third person's only job is to write down the repeat line each time it is said. Reading back the three versions is the most useful feedback in the activity, because drift is invisible to the person doing it.

Debrief

  • Pushers: what did you feel when the answer did not move? Did you give up, or get more creative?
  • Holders: at which push did you feel yourself starting to bend?
  • Did anyone's line change? What did it change into? (It almost always softens into a time or a condition.)
  • What made the difference between sounding steady and sounding stubborn?
  • Where in your week will someone push you like this?

The point to land: you do not win by arguing better. You win by not needing to argue. The acknowledging is what keeps it respectful; the repetition is what keeps it yours.

Variations

  • Customer-facing teams: everyone holds the same organisational line (the price, the lead time, the policy). Agreeing one shared repeat line as a team is a genuinely useful output
  • Youth: peer pressure scenarios. Someone wanting a lift, wanting them to skip class, wanting their homework
  • Online: breakout rooms in threes with the observer role, which works better on video than pairs
  • Advanced: the pusher gets emotional on the third push, or brings a new argument that sounds reasonable. That is the real test, and it sets up the "when not to use it" conversation

Watch out for

  • It gets loud. That is fine, but keep an eye on pairs where the pushing is landing personally. Call time early on any pair that has stopped playing
  • Learners using it on a fair point. Debrief this deliberately: if the other person is raising something you have not considered, the right move is to stop and listen, not to repeat. Holding a line you should have changed is not assertive
  • Sarcastic acknowledging. "I hear you" with an edge undoes the whole technique. Name it if you hear it

ACT-018Activity · Communication

Bad Listening, Then SOLER

15-20 minroleplay
listeningactive-listeningbody-languagepracticeempathy

Type: paired experience · Time: 15-20 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-010 Active Listening and SOLER

Materials: none. This is the best activity in the module and it costs nothing.

On this pageWhy it goes firstHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Why it goes first

Run this before you teach SOLER, not after. Being ignored for two minutes teaches more about listening than any diagram. The framework then arrives as the fix for something they have just felt.

How to run it

Round 1 — Bad listening (2 min)

Person A talks about their week. Person B listens badly on purpose: looks away, checks their phone, interrupts, changes the subject, hurries them along.

Give Person B the instruction privately or on a card if you can, so Person A gets the full effect.

Then talk (2 min): how did that feel for the speaker?

Round 2 — SOLER listening (4 min)

Swap. Now Person B listens using all five SOLER steps. No interrupting at all.

Then talk (3 min): what felt different?

Reflect (3 min)

Which SOLER step do you do well? Which one do you need to work on?

My strong step: _____________ My step to grow: _____________

Debrief

  • Speakers in round one: how long did it take before you wanted to stop talking?
  • Did anyone shorten what they were going to say? (This is the real cost. Bad listening does not just feel bad, it changes what people tell you.)
  • Listeners in round one: how easy was it? Be honest. Most people find it uncomfortably familiar
  • In round two, what did the speaker do that they did not do in round one?
  • Where do you listen like round one without meaning to?

The point to land: you already know how to listen. The question is whether the other person can tell. Listening is invisible unless you show it.

Variations

  • Cultural adaptation, and say this out loud: in many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, direct eye contact can be disrespectful, especially with elders. Offer the alternative from Stickley's SURETY critique: sit at an angle rather than square on, and rely on presence and stillness rather than eye contact. Nobody should leave thinking they listen wrongly because of how they were raised
  • Phone-based roles: run round two on the phone, back to back so they cannot see each other. Every SOLER step has to be translated into voice, which makes the point sharply
  • Online: works fine in breakout rooms. Round one is easier to fake convincingly on video, which is itself worth debriefing
  • Large or noisy rooms: threes with an observer, so the observer can report what they saw the listener's body doing

Watch out for

  • Round one goes too far. Two minutes, hard stop. Some pairs get genuinely hurt if it runs long, especially if the speaker chose something that mattered
  • Do not let anyone use round one on a topic that is actually sensitive. Say "your week" and keep it light. If someone starts sharing something real, stop the round early
  • Overacting in round two. Learners lean in like they are about to headbutt each other. Say "slightly" twice
  • Always debrief round one before running round two. Skipping that conversation wastes the activity

TOP-COM-005 Listen To LeadCommunicationTOPIC.md
ACT-020Activity · Communication

Reflect Before You Fix — Paraphrasing and De-escalation

20-25 minroleplay
listeningparaphrasingreflectingde-escalationpracticecustomer-service

Type: paired practice then roleplay · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting

Materials: sentence-starter cards. Two lines are enough: "So what you're saying is…" and "It sounds like you felt…"

On this pagePart 1 — Paraphrase practice (5 min)Part 2 — Reflect the feeling (5 min)Part 3 — De-escalation roleplay (7-10 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Part 1 — Paraphrase practice (5 min)

Person A talks for one minute about something on their mind. Person B replies with one paraphrase: "So what you're saying is…" Person A says whether it was right, or fixes it.

Was it accurate? ☐ Yes ☐ Close ☐ Off

Swap.

Part 2 — Reflect the feeling (5 min)

Person A shares something that annoyed or worried them. Person B names the feeling: "It sounds like you felt __________." Check whether it landed.

The feeling I named: _____________

Swap.

Part 3 — De-escalation roleplay (7-10 min)

Person A plays an upset customer or teammate. Pick one:

  • "I've been waiting all week and no one's called me back."
  • "You changed the roster again without asking me."

Person B must reflect the feeling first, before offering any fix. Stay calm.

This is harder than it sounds. The instinct to jump straight to the solution is strong, especially in people who are good at their jobs.

Feedback from Person A:

#Question
1Did you feel heard before they tried to fix it?
2One thing that helped

Then swap.

Debrief

  • Part 1: how many paraphrases came back "off"? What got lost?
  • Part 2: how did it feel to have your feeling named by someone else? Did anyone get it wrong, and what happened when they did? (Being corrected is a good outcome. It means the other person is engaged and you now have better information.)
  • Part 3: how long did you last before you wanted to fix it?
  • Upset people: what did the reflect line do to your temperature?
  • Where in your job does someone arrive already upset?

The point to land: people cannot hear a solution until they feel heard. Reflecting first is not being soft, it is the fastest route to actually solving it. Clinical de-escalation guidance teaches the same order for exactly this reason.

Variations

  • Contact centres and reception: drill the opening reflect line until it is automatic. Ten repetitions of the first sentence is worth more than one full roleplay
  • Second-language learners: the sentence-starter cards do the heavy lifting. Let them use the same two openers every time. The skill is the noticing, not the phrasing
  • Advanced: the upset person does not settle after the first reflection. Person B has to reflect a second time without repeating the same words. This is where it connects to ACT-015 Hold The Line
  • Online: works well, though reading feeling on video is harder. Debrief that as a finding, it sets up TOP-COM-006

Watch out for

  • Parroting. Repeating exact words back sounds like a script and people hate it. Insist on their own words
  • Reflect-then-fix in one breath. "That sounds frustrating, anyway what I'll do is…" is not reflecting, it is a speed bump. Make them pause and let it land
  • Confident wrong labels. "You're angry" when someone is embarrassed makes it worse. Teach the tentative form: "it sounds like…", "am I right that…"
  • Part 3 can get real if someone picks a live grievance. Keep them on the two scripted scenarios

Video Presence Dry Run

20-25 minroleplay
digital-communicationvideo-presencehybridmeetingspractice

Type: live practice · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-015 The Video Presence Checklist

Materials: a phone or laptop each. A projector helps a lot. The printed checklist.

On this pageWhy it has to be livePart 1 — The before shot (5 min)Part 2 — Fix it (7 min)Part 3 — Say something (8 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Why it has to be live

Reading a checklist about video presence changes nothing. Seeing your own frame on a big screen changes everything, and it takes about four seconds.

Part 1 — The before shot (5 min)

Everyone joins a call from wherever they are sitting, with no adjustments at all. Whatever the device is doing right now.

Put two or three volunteers up on the projector. Ask the room, not the person:

  • Where is the camera compared with their eyes?
  • Where is the light coming from?
  • What can you see behind them?
  • How much of them is in frame?

Facilitator: be the first volunteer, with a deliberately bad setup. Nobody critiques a colleague's kitchen until you have shown them yours.

Part 2 — Fix it (7 min)

Everyone runs the setup half of the checklist on their own device.

☐Item
☐Camera at eye level. Books under the laptop, or prop the phone
☐Light in front, not behind. Turn to face the window
☐Quiet, tidy background. Whatever you can reasonably control
☐Head and shoulders in frame, a little space above your head
☐Hide your own self-view

Then the same three volunteers go back on the projector. The before-and-after is the activity.

Part 3 — Say something (8 min)

In pairs or threes on a call, each person delivers 60 seconds of something real: a project update, a safety brief, an introduction of themselves to a new client.

They practise the four during-the-call habits:

☐Item
☐Look at the lens when you speak
☐Mute when not talking
☐Use a name to bring someone in
☐Slow down and pause

Partner feedback, two questions only:

#Question
1Did it feel like they were looking at you?
2One thing that would make them easier to listen to

Debrief

  • What surprised you in the before shot?
  • Who had a light behind them and had never noticed?
  • What did hiding your self-view do? (Most people report they relaxed. That is Bailenson's mirror anxiety, and naming it lands well.)
  • Speakers: what did looking at the lens feel like? (Unnatural. Say so, and say it looks completely natural from the other end. That gap is the reason nobody does it.)
  • Which of these can you fix in the next five minutes?

The point to land: people judge your credibility in the first few seconds, before you have said anything worth hearing. Almost all of what they are judging is setup, not talent. Fix it once, and it is fixed for every call.

Variations

  • Phone-only groups: entirely fine and more realistic for many learners. Propping a phone against a water bottle at eye level is the whole lesson
  • From a vehicle or a site: for learners who genuinely take calls from a ute, work the problem rather than skipping it. Park facing away from the sun, use the headrest, do not take the important one while driving
  • Interview prep: run the 60 seconds as an interview answer. Very strong for Employment & Work Readiness groups
  • No devices: if the room has no equipment, run the checklist as a discussion and demonstrate all four states yourself on one laptop and the projector. Weaker, but it works

Watch out for

  • Backgrounds are a class issue. Some learners share a room, live with several families, or have nowhere tidy. Never make a tidy background a standard people can fail. Say plainly: control what you reasonably can, and a virtual background or a plain wall is a perfectly good answer
  • The gear conversation. Somebody will want to talk about ring lights and microphones. Redirect: books, a window, and a wall
  • Critiquing the person instead of the setup. Keep every comment about the frame, the light and the angle. Never about how someone looks
  • Do not put a learner on the projector without asking them first

The Two Minute Introduction

20-25 minroleplay
networkingrelationshipswork-readinessroleplaypracticeconfidence

Type: roleplay / live practice · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs, rotating · Energy: medium

What it practises: starting a conversation with someone you do not know, which is the one skill that turns FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties from an interesting fact into something you can use. Also the shy-starter practice in FRM-021.

Materials: a timer, and the scenarios below on a slide or read out.

On this pageHow to run itThe scenariosThe three moves to teach firstDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Set it up (3 min). Everyone gets two minutes to start a conversation with a stranger and find one thing they have in common and one thing they could help each other with. Two minutes only. That is the constraint that makes it work.
  2. Round one (2 min + 2 min debrief). Pairs, scenario 1. Swap who starts.
  3. Rotate. New partner, new scenario. Run three or four rounds.
  4. Keep the timer strict. When it goes off, they stop mid-sentence. That is realistic.

The scenarios

#Where you areWho they are
1Waiting for the induction to start on your first daySomeone else who is also new
2At a family functionYour cousin's friend, who works somewhere you would like to work
3Smoko room, you have been there three weeksSomeone from a different department you have never spoken to
4A community or church eventSomeone twenty years older who runs their own business
5A course or training dayThe tutor, in the ten minutes before it starts

The three moves to teach first

Give them this before round one. Two minutes is not long enough to improvise.

  1. Open with where you both are. "Have you done one of these before?" beats "so, what do you do?" because it needs no courage and no preparation.
  2. Ask a question that cannot be answered with one word. "How did you get into that?" is the best one in the language. People like telling that story.
  3. Leave a door open. "I'd be keen to hear how that goes" or "who should I talk to about that?" That last question is how a single conversation becomes an introduction.

Debrief

  • Which opening line actually worked? Collect the good ones on the board
  • What did it feel like at the ten second mark, before anything was flowing?
  • Who found something in common they would never have guessed?
  • Which of the five scenarios would you avoid in real life? Why?

Variations

  • Confidence-first version: run round one as pairs who already know each other, playing the scenario. It takes the sting out and nobody has to be brave twice
  • Online: breakout rooms of two, two minutes each, and the facilitator drops the scenario into the chat before each round
  • Low literacy: read the scenarios out. Nothing needs to be read or written
  • Advanced: add a difficult partner. One person is distracted, checking their phone, giving short answers. Debrief on what the other person did about it
  • Employer-facing groups: replace the scenarios with real ones from the industry they are entering

Watch out for

  • This is genuinely hard for some learners, and it can be the most confronting thing in the session. Name that at the start. Say that two minutes is deliberately short so nobody is stuck
  • The pair that just chats. Bring them back to the two goals: one thing in common, one thing you could help each other with
  • Do not force anyone to perform in front of the room. Everyone works in pairs at the same time. There is no audience, and that is the point
  • Watch for the rotation excluding someone. Count the pairs before you start

Bad News First

25-30 minroleplay
trustpsychological-safetyroleplayleadershiplisteningfeedback

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: the third leader move in FRM-023 Psychological Safety, responding productively to bad news. It is the move that actually decides whether a team is safe, and almost nobody practises it.

Materials: the five scenarios below, on cards or a slide.

On this pageHow to run itThe scenariosThe three moves to teachDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Set it up (4 min). Say the finding plainly: people are not testing what you say about openness. They are watching what happened to the last person who was open. This session is that moment, practised.
  2. Round one, deliberately badly (5 min). Person A brings the bad news. Person B reacts the way people actually react: sighs, asks why they did not catch it sooner, starts problem-solving over the top of them. Debrief for two minutes: how likely is A to bring the next one?
  3. Teach the three moves (3 min). Thank them first. Ask a question before you react. Separate the news from the person who brought it.
  4. Round two, properly (5 min). Same scenario, same pair, swapped roles.
  5. Debrief (8 min).

The scenarios

#The bad newsBrought by
1"I've made a mistake on the order and it's already gone out"A staff member, on their fourth week
2"The team don't trust the new roster and they've been talking about it"Someone senior, who nearly did not tell you
3"I don't think we're going to hit Friday"A team lead, three days out
4"I saw someone skip the safety check"Someone reporting on a workmate they like
5"Honestly? The way you spoke in that meeting put people off"Someone giving you feedback about yourself

Scenario 5 is the hardest and the most valuable. Save it for the end, and only run it in a group where trust is already reasonable.

The three moves to teach

  1. Thank them, first, before anything else. "Thanks for telling me." Four words, said before your face has time to do anything else.
  2. Ask before you react. One question. "What happened?" or "How did you find it?" It buys you the three seconds that stop the sigh.
  3. Separate the news from the messenger. Deal with the problem later. Right now the only thing happening is whether this person brings you the next one.

Debrief

  • In round one, what did B do that made A want to stop talking? Collect the specific behaviours
  • What was the hardest to hold back?
  • Scenario 4: what happens in a workplace where nobody reports what they saw?
  • Think of a time you brought someone bad news and it went badly. What did you do differently the next time? (This is the question that produces the real stories)

Variations

  • Observer version: threes, with one person watching only B's face and body for the first five seconds. That five seconds is the whole activity
  • Phone version: run it as a call, so tone carries everything. Good for contact centre teams
  • Online: breakout rooms of two. Note that on video the first-five-seconds effect is even stronger, because the face fills the screen
  • Low literacy: read the scenarios out. Nothing needs to be written

Watch out for

  • Round one can sting if someone is playing a version of their real manager. Keep it short and move to the teaching quickly
  • Do not let B defend themselves in the debrief. The question is not whether their reaction was fair, it is what it taught A
  • Scenario 5 needs a safe room. If you are unsure, cut it. Running it badly does more damage than not running it
  • Nobody roleplays a real named person. Say so at the start

Storming On Purpose

30-35 minroleplay
teamsconflictstormingroleplayleadershipnorms

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: threes, two in role and one observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: running a Storming conversation instead of avoiding it (FRM-018), and landing it on an agreement (FRM-027 Team Charter).

Why it exists: Tuckman tells you storming is normal and then says nothing about what to do while you are in it. This is the missing half.

On this pageHow to run itThe four movesThe scenariosDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Set it up (4 min). The goal is not to win the disagreement. It is to get the team to an agreement they will both keep. That is what moves a team from Storming to Norming.
  2. Teach the four moves (4 min). Below.
  3. Round one (7 min). Two in role, one observing against the four moves.
  4. Observer feedback (3 min). Which moves happened? Which got skipped?
  5. Rotate roles and scenarios. Run two or three rounds.
  6. Whole class debrief (8 min).

The four moves

#MoveWhat it sounds like
1Name the stage, not the person"I think we're just working out how this team runs, rather than you and me having a problem"
2Make it about the work"The thing I actually need is to know who's locking up"
3Ask for their version before you argue yours"How are you seeing it?" and then be quiet
4Land on a rule, not a truce"So from Monday, whoever's on late shift locks up and messages the group. Yes?"

Move 4 is the one that separates this from an argument that goes quiet. A truce lasts until next week. A rule survives it.

The scenarios

#The disagreementThe complication
1Who is responsible for the end-of-day cleanOne of you has been doing it for a month without being asked
2A new person is doing the job "wrong"Their way is actually faster, just different
3Someone keeps changing the roster in the group chatThey have a genuine reason and never explained it
4Two shifts blame each other for what gets left undoneNeither has ever spoken to the other directly
5You and a peer both think you are leading the projectNobody ever said who was

Debrief

  • Which of the four moves was hardest?
  • Did anyone land a rule, or did most pairs end on a truce? (Most end on a truce. That is the finding)
  • What happened when someone asked for the other version first? Did it change the conversation?
  • Scenario 5: whose job is it to sort that out?
  • What is the cost of leaving any of these for another three months?

Variations

  • Difficult partner: brief one person to get defensive early. Realistic and much harder
  • Leader version: a third person plays the supervisor who has to step in. Practises the presence move from Tuckman's storming row
  • Cross-team version: for TOP-LEA-005, make the two roles head office and a regional site, and run it with 3C instead of the four moves
  • Online: breakout threes. The observer keeps their camera on and the two in role do the talking
  • Low literacy: read the scenario to each three rather than handing out cards

Watch out for

  • Real disputes leaking in. If two people in the room have this exact argument in real life, do not pair them. Check before you form the threes
  • The polite roleplay. Some pairs will agree in ninety seconds to avoid discomfort, which teaches nothing. Give the observer permission to say "that was too easy, run it again with more push"
  • Winning. Remind them there is no winner. There is a rule at the end or there is not
  • Do not let it become a complaint about a real manager. Redirect to the scenario

The Respect Interview

20-25 minroleplay
respectrole-modelsleadershiplisteningpracticereflection

Type: roleplay / paired practice · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: the W and H of FRM-019 W-H-O, with someone else doing the digging. It is much easier to name a behaviour in someone else's role model than in your own, and this activity uses that.

It also quietly practises listening, because the interviewer's only job is to ask and listen.

On this pageHow to run itThe four questionsThe interviewer's rulesDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Pairs. One interviewer, one interviewee (2 min set-up).
  2. The interviewer asks the four questions and takes notes. Eight minutes. They may not tell their own story, offer advice, or say "oh yeah, my uncle was like that too."
  3. Swap. Eight minutes.
  4. Hand the notes over. Each person now has their own W and H, written by someone else.
  5. Whole class debrief (5 min).

The four questions

#QuestionWhat it is doing
1Who is someone you respect?The W
2Tell me about a time you saw them do something you admired.Forces a story, and behaviours live in stories
3What exactly did they do? What did they say?The H. Ask it twice if you have to
4What would it look like if you did that on Monday?The bridge to the O

Question 3 is the whole activity. The interviewer keeps asking until they have something they could watch someone do.

The interviewer's rules

Say these out loud before you start. They are what make it work.

  • You are not in this conversation. No stories of your own
  • Silence is allowed. After question 2, wait. People find the story in the pause
  • Ask "what did they actually do?" as many times as it takes. Three is normal
  • Write down their words, not your summary of their words

Debrief

  • What did it feel like to have someone genuinely interested for eight minutes? (This is often the answer people remember, and it is a listening lesson arriving free)
  • Interviewers: how many times did you have to ask question 3?
  • Did anyone's partner surprise them with who they named?
  • Did having someone else write it down make the behaviour clearer?

Variations

  • Threes with an observer who watches only whether the interviewer stayed out of it. Most do not, and finding that out is useful
  • Written handover: the interviewer writes the partner's W and H formally on the ACT-033 worksheet and hands it over. Nice artefact to leave with
  • Team version: interview each other about someone respected inside the organisation. The behaviours collected become a genuine leadership profile for that workplace
  • Online: breakout pairs, notes typed and pasted into the chat for the partner
  • Low literacy: the interviewer can record on their phone rather than writing, with permission

Watch out for

  • Interviewers who take over. It happens within about ninety seconds. Name it before you start and it mostly does not
  • Grief. Question 2 often brings up someone who has died. It is usually welcome rather than distressing, but give the pair space and do not hurry them into question 3
  • Pairs that finish in three minutes. They stopped at the adjective. Send them back to question 3
  • Do not make anyone share with the whole room. The debrief is about the process, not the content

The Helpful No

25-30 minroleplay
boundariessaying-nocollaborationworkloadroleplaypractice

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: habit 1 of FRM-031 The 3 Habits of a Healthy Team Player, using the script from FRM-008 The Positive No.

The distinction to hold on to: a helpful no is not a refusal. It is a counter-offer.

On this pageThe three movesHow to run itThe requestsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The three moves

From the source, and they are the whole activity:

  1. Explain what you already have on your plate. Information, not an excuse
  2. Ask which task is the priority. The strongest of the three, because it hands the trade-off back to the person allowed to make it
  3. Offer a smaller way to help. "I can show you how" instead of doing all of it

How to run it

  1. Set it up (3 min). Say the finding from FRM-032 Collaborative Overload first: 3 to 5% of people generate 20 to 35% of the collaboration, and they are the least satisfied people in the organisation. This is not about doing less. It is about not collapsing.
  2. Round one, automatic yes (3 min). Person A makes the request. Person B says yes, the way they normally would. Then B says out loud what that yes will actually cost them this week.
  3. Teach the three moves (3 min).
  4. Round two (6 min). Same request, helpful no. Swap.
  5. Round three, the hard one (6 min). Use the requests from someone senior or from family.
  6. Debrief (8 min).

The requests

#The requestFrom
1"Can you just jump on this project? You're the only one who really gets it"A peer
2"I need you on the working group. It's only an hour a fortnight"Your manager
3"Can you do the report? You do them so much better than me"Someone who could learn to do it
4"We need someone to run the social club"The whole team, in a meeting
5"Can you help me out this weekend?"Family, church or community
6"You did such a good job last time, can you do it again?"Someone senior enough that no feels risky

Requests 5 and 6 are the ones that matter most for Zeducation learners and they are the hardest. Leave time for them.

Debrief

  • What did the automatic yes actually cost you? (Round one is designed to make this concrete)
  • Which of the three moves felt most possible? Which felt rude?
  • Did asking "which is the priority?" change anything? (It usually surprises people. Often the asker did not know they were asking you to drop something)
  • Request 5: is that even the same skill? (Good question. Often it is not, and the answer may be a genuine yes)
  • Who in your life do you never say no to? What does that cost?

Variations

  • Persistent asker: the requester does not accept the first no. Practises FRM-009 Broken Record
  • Written version: rewrite three real messages you have said yes to. Good for people who mostly get asked by chat and email
  • Manager version: the person receiving the no is the leader, practising taking it well. Just as important and almost never taught
  • Online: breakout pairs. Also run one round in chat only, since that is where most requests actually arrive
  • Low literacy: read the requests aloud, one pair at a time

Watch out for

  • Turning it into "say no more". The framing is "stop saying yes without thinking". Much easier to accept and much more accurate
  • Cultural weight. For many Pacific and Māori learners, saying no to someone senior or to family is a relational act with real cost, not a workload decision. The helpful no works precisely because it protects the relationship. Lead with that or the topic reads as telling them to care less
  • The person who cannot do it at all. Some learners will find every version impossible. That is useful information for them and it should not be exposed to the room
  • Do not roleplay a real named person
