The Other Team's Shoes

30-35 minroleplay
collaborationcross-teamroleplaysilosempathypractice

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-029 The 3C Framework, run across a silo.

The twist that makes it work: everyone plays the other team first. You cannot argue your own side until you have argued theirs.

On this pageHow to run itThe scenariosWhat usually happensDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Set it up (3 min). Explain the twist. People play the team they normally complain about.
  2. Preparation, in role (5 min). In their assigned role, each person writes three sentences: what my team's day actually looks like, what I need from them, and what I think they do not understand about us.
  3. Round one, no framework (5 min). Have the conversation cold. It usually goes badly, which is the point.
  4. Teach or revisit 3C (3 min).
  5. Round two, with 3C (8 min). Same pair, same scenario. Connect, Clarify, Commit, in order.
  6. Debrief (10 min).

The scenarios

#Team ATeam BThe friction
1Head officeA regional siteReports keep arriving late
2Day shiftNight shiftEach says the other leaves things undone
3KitchenFront of houseOrders and timing
4FinanceFrontline teamPurchase approvals take too long
5TrainersOperationsStaff keep getting pulled out of training

Use scenario 1 with any group where head office and regions is the live issue. Use 2 or 3 with hospitality or shift-based groups.

What usually happens

Round one goes badly in a predictable way, and naming it in advance ruins it, so do not. Debrief it afterwards:

  • Both sides open with the problem already diagnosed
  • Both explain why it is not their fault
  • Both leave with the same view they arrived with

Round two, the Clarify step nearly always turns up a constraint the other side did not know about. That discovery is the lesson, and it happens by itself if you make people ask real questions.

Debrief

  • What did you find out in Clarify that you did not know before?
  • Playing the other team: what surprised you about their day?
  • What did round one sound like from the outside? (Ask the observers)
  • Did you land a real Commit, with a name and a date?
  • In real life, whose job is it to start this conversation?

Variations

  • Real teams, real friction: with an intact organisation, use their actual silo. Powerful and it needs a facilitator who can hold a room if it gets warm
  • Swap halfway: partway through round two, call "swap" and people argue the opposite side. Very effective at breaking a stuck position
  • Written version: each person writes the email they would send, before and after 3C. The contrast on paper is stark and it makes a good takeaway
  • Online: breakout pairs. Give each person their role brief privately so they cannot see the other side's
  • Low literacy: brief the roles verbally, one at a time, out of earshot of the partner

Watch out for

  • People playing the other team as idiots. Stop it early. The brief is to play them as competent people with a different set of pressures, because that is what they are
  • Round one being too polite. If pairs are being nice, they will learn nothing from round two. Tell them to argue their side properly
  • Real grievances arriving. If two people in the room are actually on opposite sides of scenario 1, that is either the best or the worst pairing in the room. Decide before you pair them
  • Do not let a Commit be vague. Name and date, or run it again

Three Leaders, One Task

30-35 minroleplay
decision-makingleadershiproleplaystylesteamscollaboration

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: teams of 4-6 · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-028 Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles.

Why it works: this is a small re-run of Lewin's original 1939 experiment, where the researchers rotated leaders using different styles through the same groups of boys. The room feels all three styles from the inside, which no explanation achieves.

Materials: any short team task, run three times. Plan a staff social event. Design a shift handover. Build the tallest paper tower. Keep it the same task each round so only the leadership changes.

On this pageHow to run itThe three briefsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Form teams of 4-6. Pick three volunteers per team to lead one round each.
  2. Brief the three leaders privately, out of earshot. Give each a written brief.
  3. Round one, autocratic (5 min). Then thirty seconds of silent note-taking: how did that feel?
  4. Round two, democratic (7 min). Same note-taking.
  5. Round three, laissez-faire (5 min). Same.
  6. Debrief (12 min). This is the activity.

The three briefs

StyleThe brief you hand the leader
AutocraticDecide everything yourself. Tell people what to do. Do not ask for opinions. Be pleasant but do not consult. If someone offers an idea, say "thanks, we're doing it this way"
DemocraticAsk for ideas first. Listen to everyone, including the quiet ones. Then make the call yourself and say which ideas shaped it. You still decide
Laissez-faireSet the task, then step back. Do not direct. Answer questions if asked, but offer nothing. Let them sort it out

The democratic brief must say "you still decide". Otherwise it drifts into consensus and the round takes fifteen minutes.

Debrief

Ask in this order.

  1. Which round got the most done? Often the autocratic one, and the room needs to sit with that.
  2. Which round did you want to be in? Almost always democratic.
  3. What happened in the laissez-faire round? Usually one of two things: it drifted, or the loudest person quietly took over. Lewin found the same, and it is worth naming.
  4. Who stopped contributing, and when? In the autocratic round people go quiet in about ninety seconds and do not come back.
  5. If that leader ran your team for a year, what would happen?

Question 5 is the one to land on. Autocratic looks efficient over five minutes. Over a year it produces a team that waits to be told, which is exactly the finding.

Variations

  • Secret briefs: do not tell the team which style is coming. Let them work it out. Much better, and the guesses in the debrief are revealing
  • Same leader, three styles: one person leads all three rounds. Harder for them and it proves these are choices, not personalities
  • Add a crisis: in one round, introduce an urgent problem halfway. Watch which style suddenly becomes appropriate
  • Online: works in breakout rooms. The laissez-faire round online is even more uncomfortable, which is instructive
  • Low literacy: brief the leaders verbally. No reading required by anyone else

Watch out for

  • Protect the autocratic leader. They are following a brief. Say so clearly in the debrief, or people leave thinking that person was bossy
  • The laissez-faire round can feel like a waste of time. That is the finding, not a failure of the activity. Do not rescue it
  • Do not let anyone play a real manager. These are briefs, not impressions
  • Keep the task trivial. If the task matters, people focus on the output instead of the experience

Intervene Early, Kindly

30-35 minroleplay
cultural-safetyroleplayleadershipinterventionculturepractice

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: threes, two in role and one observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: the hardest single behaviour in FRM-033 Cultural Safety: intervene early and kindly on jokes, interruptions or mispronunciations. Everyone agrees with it. Almost nobody has practised the actual sentence.

Why it matters: the eight ways cultural safety breaks are all small, and all of them survive because the person who could have said something in the moment said nothing. This is that moment, rehearsed until it is available.

On this pageHow to run itThe four movesThe scenariosDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Name the problem (3 min). Ask: "who has watched something small happen at work and said nothing, then thought of the perfect line in the car?" Every hand. That gap is what this fixes.
  2. Teach the four moves (4 min). Below.
  3. Round one (6 min). Threes. One does the small thing, one intervenes, one observes.
  4. Observer feedback (3 min). Did it stay light? Did the other person get defensive?
  5. Rotate and rerun with a new scenario. Two or three rounds.
  6. Debrief (10 min).

The four moves

#MoveWhat it sounds like
1Interrupt the moment, not the person"Hold on, let's go back, Ravi hadn't finished"
2Assume good intent out loud"I know you don't mean anything by it, and"
3Name the standard, not the offence"In here we get names right, so let's get it right" beats "that's offensive"
4Move on fastSay it, then carry on with the meeting. Length turns a correction into a punishment

Move 4 is the one that makes it repeatable. A ten second intervention can be done fifty times. A five minute one gets done once and then avoided forever.

Then, privately: check in with the person it landed on. "Was that alright? Anything you'd want me to do differently?" That second conversation is where you find out whether you helped.

The scenarios

#What happensWho you are
1A colleague keeps mispronouncing a new starter's name in a meetingA peer, same level
2Someone does an impression of a guest's accent in the break roomThe supervisor
3The same person is talked over for the third timeChairing the meeting
4A workmate says "we should just do it in English, it's faster"A peer
5A senior manager makes a joke about someone's food at lunchYou are junior to them
6A guest is about to photograph somewhere they were asked not toThe guide, with the customer right there

Scenarios 5 and 6 are the hard ones. Save them for the last round.

Debrief

  • Which move was hardest to actually say out loud?
  • Scenario 5: what stopped you? (Answers are always about power, and naming that is the point)
  • Scenario 6: how do you protect the site and the customer relationship at the same time?
  • What happened when someone got defensive? What worked?
  • What is the ten second version you would actually use on Monday?

Collect the best lines on the board. A room-generated list of usable sentences is the single most valuable thing this activity produces.

Variations

  • The defensive partner: brief the first person to push back with "it was just a joke". Realistic, and much harder
  • The bystander version: add a fourth person who says nothing, then debrief what the silence taught the room
  • Repair version: run the scenario where the facilitator got it wrong, and practise coming back the next day having learned the name. The source's own example
  • Online: breakout threes. Also run one round in a group chat, since a lot of this now happens in writing where a screenshot lasts forever
  • Low literacy: brief scenarios verbally

Watch out for

  • Nobody plays a real named colleague. Say it at the start
  • Do not cast a person from the affected culture as the target. Ever. Assign roles deliberately rather than letting groups sort themselves
  • The heroic intervention. Some learners produce a speech. Push them back to ten seconds. The point is a move you can make fifty times, not one you make once and dine out on
  • This activity can surface real incidents. Have somewhere for that to go, and know before you start whether the organisation actually acts on complaints. If it does not, be careful what you promise the room

Run A Talanoa

45-60 minroleplay
talanoapacificcultural-safetylisteningleadershippracticeculture

Type: live practice · Time: 45-60 min · Group: circles of 5-8 · Energy: low

What it practises: the full three-part flow of FRM-035 Talanoa, including FRM-036 Teu le vā.

This is not a roleplay in the usual sense. Nobody plays a character. The group holds a real talanoa about a real question, and the practice is in how it is opened, asked and closed. A pretend talanoa teaches the opposite of the point.

Time is the material. This does not compress. If you have 25 minutes, teach the framework and run ACT-068 instead, and come back to this when you have an hour.

On this pageSetting upHow to run itChoosing the questionDebrief (after the circle, 10 min)VariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Setting up

  • Chairs in a circle. No table, no top of the room, no screen
  • Phones away, visibly, including the facilitator's
  • One facilitator per circle if you can. Otherwise nominate a host in each

How to run it

1. Teu le vā — prepare the space (10 min)

The host opens. In order:

  • Welcome and purpose. Why we are here, and what will happen to what is said
  • Consent. "Is this for us only, or can anything be shared? Nothing leaves unless we agree"
  • Names. Every person says their name, and the person to their left says it back until it is right. Nobody moves on until it is right
  • Norms. One voice at a time. No fixing, no advice, no interrupting

Do not rush this. Ten minutes on the space is not preamble. It is step one.

2. Ask open questions (20-25 min)

The host asks one question and then gets out of the way. Use the source's own prompts:

  • "What would feel respectful here?"
  • "What meaning sits behind this practice?"
  • "When has this gone well for you?"
  • "Who else's voice should we include before we decide?"

Rules for the host: invite the quieter voices before anyone speaks twice. Ask one curious follow-up rather than moving on. Say nothing yourself until at least four other people have spoken.

3. Listen and share, then give back (10-15 min)

  • The host mirrors back what they heard. Not a summary of conclusions, the actual things people said
  • Check consent again: "is any of this not for outside this circle?"
  • Gift back: what will change, by when, and how people will see it. This is not optional. A talanoa that ends without a gift back is extraction

Choosing the question

The question decides whether this works. Good ones are real, open, and belong to the group.

GoodWhy
"What would make someone new feel welcome in their first week here?"Real, everyone has an answer, and it produces actions
"What do we do here that we have never explained to anyone?"Surfaces the why behind protocols, which is the point
"When has this workplace got respect right?"Starts positive, which a first talanoa needs
BadWhy
"How can we improve engagement scores?"A management question wearing a talanoa costume
"What's wrong with our culture?"Opens something an hour cannot hold
Anything already decidedThe fastest way to teach a group that the invitation was not sincere

Debrief (after the circle, 10 min)

  • What did the ten minutes at the start do?
  • Hosts: how hard was it to stay quiet?
  • What did you learn that a survey would not have found?
  • What was gifted back? Is it real?
  • What would have happened if we had opened with the question and skipped step 1?

Variations

  • Real decision version: use an actual pending decision. Much better, and only run it if the decision is genuinely open
  • Two circles, then weave: two groups talanoa separately, then one person from each carries what they heard to the other. Good for cross-team work
  • Follow-up talanoa: run a second one a month later, opening by pronouncing names correctly and echoing one insight from last time. The source names this and it is what makes the practice real
  • Online: possible and weaker. Cameras on, no chat, and the host must name people to invite them in. Say out loud that the setting is a compromise

Watch out for

  • A talanoa with a hidden agenda is worse than a meeting. People can tell, and you will not get a second one
  • The host who talks. The most common failure. Give hosts an explicit rule: nothing until four others have spoken
  • No gift back. The second most common failure, and the one that damages trust rather than just wasting time
  • Do not label a normal meeting a talanoa because it was in a circle. Naming a Pacific practice and then not doing it is the protocol theatre the cultural safety topic warns about
  • Facilitator honesty: if you are not Pacific, say so, say where the practice comes from, name Vaioleti, and hold it with care. The room will respect that far more than a confident performance

Demonstrate Active Listening (observed)

30-40 minroleplay
listeningconflictassessed-taskhouse-contentroleplayobservationfeedback

Type: roleplay, observed and signed off · Time: 30-40 min · Group: threes · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-038 Powerful Listening and the visible half of FRM-010 SOLER.

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), where it is Task 3.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Demonstrate active listening skills". It is the library's only observed and verifier-signed activity, which makes it the model for how a practical competency gets evidenced.

On this pageThe three rolesThe observer checklistHow to run itThe three items that decide itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The three roles

RoleJob
Person 1 — ListenerPractise the active listening skills. This is the person being assessed
Person 2 — Team memberTalk to the listener about an issue, based on your chosen scenario
Person 3 — ObserverUse the checklist, tick as they happen, then give feedback and sign

The observer checklist

Listener name: ______________________ Observer name: ______________________

Tick each box as the listener performs it.

  1. ☐ The listener maintained good eye contact
  2. ☐ The listener actively showed interest
  3. ☐ The listener asked effective questions where appropriate
  4. ☐ The listener gave feedback by repeating or summarising the problem in their own words
  5. ☐ The listener gave feedback by acknowledging the team member's personal values
  6. ☐ The listener gave feedback by acknowledging the feelings of the team member

Signature of verifier (observer): ______________________

How to run it

  1. Teach the three layers first. Items 4, 5 and 6 are content, values and feelings. Say that out loud so the checklist reads as the framework rather than a list of manners.
  2. Form threes and assign roles (2 min).
  3. The speaker picks a scenario (2 min). Either a real low-stakes issue of their own, or the Akanisi or Owairua case study from this module.
  4. Listen, 5 to 7 minutes. The observer says nothing and ticks.
  5. Observer feedback, 3 minutes. Which boxes were ticked, and what specifically earned each one.
  6. Rotate twice, so everyone is listener once.

The three items that decide it

Items 1 to 3 are easy and nearly everyone gets them. Items 4, 5 and 6 are the assessment, and they fail in a predictable order:

ItemWhat usually goes wrong
4 — summarise in own wordsThe listener repeats it back almost verbatim. Parroting is not summarising
5 — acknowledge valuesSkipped entirely. Most people never name what the other person cares about
6 — acknowledge feelingsAttempted as a guess. "You must be angry" instead of "how did that land?"

➜ Facilitator tip: give observers a sentence stem to listen for on item 5: "it sounds like what matters to you here is…". Once learners have that sentence, the box gets ticked honestly.

Debrief

  • Listeners: which box was hardest?
  • Speakers: when did you feel actually heard? This is the most valuable question in the activity, because it comes from the only person who can answer it
  • Observers: what did the listener do with their body that helped or hurt?
  • What is the difference between item 4 and item 5?

Variations

  • Conflict version: the speaker brings a live frustration rather than a case study. More real, and only with a group that has trust
  • Phone version: run it back to back so there is no eye contact, and item 1 is replaced by voice signals. Good for contact centre and support roles
  • Online: breakout threes, cameras on. Note that item 1 works differently on video and say so
  • Low literacy: the observer ticks and signs. Nothing needs to be written by the listener

Watch out for

  • Eye contact as a checkbox. Item 1 is culturally loaded, and FRM-010 carries the full critique: in many Pacific, Māori and other cultures direct eye contact with someone senior reads as disrespectful. Do not fail a learner on item 1 for a cultural norm. Assess presence and attention, and note the adaptation on the sheet
  • The speaker who gives nothing. A listener cannot demonstrate item 6 against three flat sentences. Brief speakers to bring something they actually have feelings about
  • Observer as critic. The job is to tick what happened and say what earned it, not to grade the person
  • Assessment integrity: the observer signs. That signature means they watched it

De-escalation Drill

30-35 minroleplay
de-escalationconflictconflict-resolutionroleplaypracticesafetycommunication

Type: roleplay, run as a drill · Time: 30-35 min · Group: threes · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-041 De-escalation, the six steps, under enough pressure that they have to be available without thinking.

Why a drill and not a discussion. De-escalation is used in the worst thirty seconds of somebody's shift, with adrenaline up. A framework you can explain is not the same as one you can perform. This runs short, repeats, and gets faster.

Materials: the six steps up on a wall where everyone can see them. That is deliberate. Nobody is being tested on memory.

On this pageHow to run itThe scenariosWhat the observer watches forDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Teach the six steps (8 min). Stay calm · open body language · listen actively · show empathy · work on a solution together · take a break if needed.
  2. Round 1, slow (5 min). The escalating person starts at about a 4 out of 10. The de-escalator works through the steps, referring to the wall. Observer watches which steps happened.
  3. Feedback, 2 min. Observer names which steps landed.
  4. Rotate. Round 2, faster, starting at a 6.
  5. Rotate. Round 3, starting at an 8, and the escalating person does not calm down easily.
  6. Debrief, 10 min.

Nobody goes above an 8. Say so, and mean it. See the safety note.

The scenarios

#The situationWho is escalating
1A guest's room is not ready and they have travelled all dayCustomer
2A colleague has just found out you reported a safety issue involving themWorkmate
3Someone's shift was changed without being asked, for the third timeTeam member
4A team member is being blamed in front of others for something that was not theirsTeam member
5A customer is angry about a charge, and is loud, in front of other customersCustomer
6Someone you supervise has just accused you of favouritismDirect report

Scenario 6 is the hardest, because the de-escalator is the subject of the complaint. Run it last, and only with a group that has warmed up.

What the observer watches for

StepDid it happen?The tell
1 Stay calm☐Their voice slowed, or it did not
2 Open body language☐Arms, shoulders, distance
3 Listen actively☐Did the other person get to finish a sentence?
4 Show empathy☐An actual sentence naming the feeling
5 Solution together☐A question, not an offer
6 Break if needed☐Did they use it? Did they need to?

Debrief

  • Which step disappeared first when the pressure went up? (It is almost always step 3)
  • Who used step 6? What made you reach for it?
  • Escalators: what did the other person do that actually changed how you felt?
  • What is the difference between step 5 as a question and step 5 as an offer?
  • Where is your workplace's line? At what point do you stop de-escalating and get help?

That last question is the most important one on the page.

Variations

  • Two-minute version: as a warm-up in later sessions, run one 90 second round cold. Drills work by repetition over weeks, not by one long session
  • Phone version: back to back so there is no body language. Steps 1, 3 and 4 carry everything. Essential for contact centre roles
  • The one that does not work: occasionally brief an escalator not to de-escalate at all, so the learner has to use step 6 for real. Valuable, and debrief it carefully so it does not read as failure
  • Low literacy: scenarios briefed verbally, six steps shown as icons on the wall

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Safety, and say this before you start. De-escalation is not a substitute for leaving. If someone is threatening, or there is any risk of harm, the move is to get out and get help. Name your workplace's escalation path in the room. A drill that teaches people to stay and keep trying is a dangerous drill
  • This can activate real memories, particularly for anyone who has been on the receiving end of aggression at work. Say at the start that people can sit a round out with no explanation
  • Do not let escalators enjoy it too much. Cap the intensity, name the cap, and stop a round early if it tips
  • Never roleplay a real named person or a real recent incident
  • The heroic de-escalator. Some learners will produce a speech. The steps are short. Six sentences, not six paragraphs

ACT-084Activity · Leadership

Four Teams, One Leader

30-35 minroleplay
leadershipstylessituationalroleplaypracticecoaching

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: groups of 3 · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-046 House's Path-Goal Theory.

The point is switching, not performing. Same leader, four people, four styles, one morning. Most learners can name all four styles and use exactly one.

On this pageThe four scenario cardsHow to run itCard 3 is where the session happensDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The four scenario cards

Print and cut. Each group works through all four, rotating who leads.

CARD 1 · The new starter

Week two. She has to do the stock count on her own tomorrow and has never done one. She says "yeah, no, I'll be fine" and will not ask a question in front of anyone. What is in her way: she does not know how.

CARD 2 · The one who is running on empty

Reliable for six years. Last three weeks he has been late twice and quiet. You know his mum is unwell. His work is still fine. What is in his way: nothing to do with the job.

CARD 3 · The veteran who is right

Fifteen years here. The new roster you built is not going to work and she has told you so, in front of two other staff, in a tone you did not love. What is in her way: you.

CARD 4 · The quiet one who is better than she thinks

Three years in. Does excellent work. Has never applied for anything, never volunteers, and told you once that she is "not really a leader type". What is in her way: what she believes about herself.

How to run it

  1. Teach the four styles (10 min). Directive, Supportive, Participative, Achievement-oriented. Teach them as four questions, not four labels
  2. Groups of three. One leads, one plays the staff member, one observes
  3. Card 1, three minutes. Then the observer gives one sentence: "which style did they use?"
  4. Rotate. New leader, new card. Four rounds, everybody leads at least once
  5. Whole room (8 min). Which card was hardest?

Card 3 is where the session happens

Almost every room gets cards 1, 2 and 4 broadly right and falls apart on card 3.

The veteran is right, she said it badly, and both of those are true at once. The instinct is to deal with the tone. Path-Goal says the obstacle is that you built a roster without asking someone who knows more than you, and the style is Participative.

The trapWhat it sounds likeWhy it fails
Defend the roster"There were reasons for that"The roster is still wrong tomorrow
Deal with the tone first"I need you to raise that with me privately"True, and it buries the actual information
Cave"Fine, we'll go back to the old one"You have taught the team that volume works

➜ The move: take the information first, deal with the delivery second, and separately. "You're right and I should have asked you. Let's fix it. And I do want to talk about how that landed in front of the others, but not now."

That is one sentence and it is the hardest sentence in this activity.

Debrief

  • Which style is your default? Did you use it on all four cards?
  • Which card felt least natural?
  • Who has a card 3 in real life right now?
  • Card 2: how many of you tried to solve a problem that was not yours to solve?

Variations

  • Wrong-style round: deliberately run card 1 with a Supportive style and card 2 with a Directive one. Fast, funny, and the failure is instructive
  • Real cards: learners write their own card 5 about someone on their actual team, anonymised. Then swap. Much better than the printed set if the group trusts each other
  • Two-minute version: just card 3, whole room, volunteers. If you only have ten minutes this is the one to run
  • Observers get a job: give the observer the four style names on a card and have them hold up the one they are hearing. Instant feedback without interrupting
  • Low literacy: read the cards aloud. Nothing on them needs reading

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Card 2 can land close to home. Someone in the room is looking after a sick parent right now. Say before you start that anyone can pass on a card, no reason needed
  • Directive played as bossy. Card 1 needs someone to actually teach her the stock count. That is kindness. Learners often soften it into uselessness
  • Achievement-oriented played as pressure. Card 4 is not "you need to step up". It is "I am putting you on Thursday's handover because you are better at it than you think"
  • The observer who says nothing. Give them one job and one sentence. See variations
  • Groups that debate instead of playing. Two minutes of discussion, then someone has to actually say the words out loud

ACT-086Activity · Leadership

The Vision Test

25-30 minroleplay
leadershipvisionmotivationchangeroleplaytransformational

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-048 Transactional and Transformational Leadership.

The test is simple and brutal: after you have explained the change, can the other person say back why it matters, in their own words? If not, you have announced something. You have not led anything.

On this pageThe scenarioRound one, transactional onlyRound two, add the transformational halfThe rule this activity exists to teachDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The scenario

Everybody gets the same one.

The change. Your workplace is moving to a new system on the first of next month. Everyone has to log their jobs on a tablet as they finish them, instead of writing them on the sheet at the end of the shift. Most of the team hate the idea. Two of them are not confident with the tablet. One has been here eleven years and says the sheet has always worked fine. What you actually know. The reason for the change is that the paper sheets get filled in from memory at 4pm and about a third of the job times are wrong. The company has lost two contracts in a year because it could not prove what it had done. If it loses a third, there will be redundancies. Your job: get the team to actually use it.

Round one, transactional only

Five minutes. In pairs. The leader may only use rewards, rules and consequences.

Typical: "It's compulsory from the first. There's training Tuesday. If it's not logged it doesn't get paid."

Then the test. The staff member says, in their own words, why the change is happening.

Most cannot. That is the finding, and you should let the room feel it before you explain it.

Round two, add the transformational half

Teach the four I's (5 min). Then run the same conversation again, swapping roles.

The leader has to actually do this
Idealised influenceSay what you will do yourself. "I'm logging mine on the tablet from Monday, in front of you, and I'll be rubbish at it for a fortnight"
Inspirational motivationGive the real reason in plain words. The lost contracts. Say it
Intellectual stimulation"You've been here eleven years. What's going to go wrong with this that I haven't thought of?"
Individualised considerationName the two who are not confident, privately, beforehand. Not in the meeting

Then the test again. Can they say why?

The rule this activity exists to teach

You still need round one.

If the training is not booked, the tablets are not charged, and nobody has been told what happens if it does not get logged, then the vision is a speech. Bass's own finding was that transformational leadership augments transactional, it does not replace it.

➜ Ask the room at the end: "which round would you drop?" The answer is neither, and it takes them about ten seconds to get there once they have played both.

Debrief

  • Round one: how did it feel to be told? How did it feel to do the telling?
  • What is the actual reason your workplace last changed something? Do you know it?
  • Who here has had a change announced with no reason given? What did you assume the reason was?
  • The eleven-year veteran: is she an obstacle or is she the most useful person in the room?
  • Which of the four I's is hardest for you?

Variations

  • Real change round: learners use a change actually happening at their work. Far better, and it needs a group that will not use it to slag off their employer
  • Bad news version: the change is a genuine cut, and there is no upside. Tests whether the four I's survive when you cannot promise anything. They mostly do, and honesty becomes the whole tool
  • Observer version: third person holds the four I's on a card and ticks the ones they hear
  • Written version: everyone writes the two-sentence "why" and reads it out. Ruthless and fast. Most first drafts are policy, not reason
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken. Read the scenario aloud twice

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ The redundancy detail is real for people. Some learners have lived it. Check the room, and offer the alternative scenario (a new safety procedure) if it is too close
  • Vision as waffle. "This is about our journey to excellence" fails the test as badly as a rule does. Push for the specific reason: two contracts, a third would mean job losses
  • Skipping the transaction. Learners who love round two sometimes drop the training and the deadline. Ask what happens on the first of the month
  • The eleven-year veteran played as a villain. She is usually right about something. Intellectual stimulation means asking her, and meaning it
  • Fake consultation. If the decision is made, do not roleplay asking permission. Ask about how, not whether. Learners spot the difference instantly and so do real teams

The STAR Answer Lab

40-45 minroleplay
career-readinessinterviewsstarpracticestorytellingwork-readiness

Type: roleplay · Time: 40-45 min · Group: groups of 3 · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-059 The STAR Interview Answer.

⚠️ This is the interview STAR — Situation, Task, Action, Result. Not FRM-003, which is Zeducation's session shape. Say which one you mean when you introduce it.

Build four stories, not twenty answers. Four good ones flex to cover almost any question. Trying to script every possible question is exactly why people freeze when one comes out worded differently.

On this pagePart 1 — build the stories (15 min, individual)Part 2 — run it (20 min, groups of 3)Part 3 — the "and then what happened?" round (8 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — build the stories (15 min, individual)

Four boxes. Fill them from real life, including outside paid work.

StoryA time you…
1Dealt with a difficult person
2Had something go wrong, and it was partly on you
3Worked in a team and did a specific part of it
4Kept going when it was hard

For each, four lines. Watch the proportions.

Words
SWhere and when1 sentence
TWhat you had to do1 sentence
AWhat you did, step by step3-4 sentences
RWhat happened. A number, or a lesson1-2 sentences

Part 2 — run it (20 min, groups of 3)

Interviewer · Candidate · Observer. Rotate so everyone does all three.

The interviewer picks a question card. The candidate answers using one of their four stories, out loud, no notes.

Question cards
Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer or colleague
Tell me about a time something went wrong at work
Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team
Give me an example of when you had to learn something quickly
Tell me about a time you had too much to do
Tell me about a time you had to follow a rule you did not agree with
Tell me about a time you helped somebody
Tell me about a time you took responsibility for something

The observer has one job

Tick what they hear:

Heard it?
Situation kept to about a sentence☐
Said "I", not only "we"☐
Action was the longest part☐
There was an actual result at the end☐

Feedback is those four ticks and nothing else. No general opinions, no "that was good".

Part 3 — the "and then what happened?" round (8 min)

Whole room. The facilitator asks a question, takes an answer, and whatever the candidate says, replies only: "And then what happened?"

Keep going until there is a result. Usually three rounds.

➜ This is the single most useful drill in the activity, because the missing result is the most common failure and one repeated question fixes it permanently.

Debrief

  • Which box was hardest to fill?
  • Who caught themselves saying "we"?
  • Whose story got better when they had to say what happened at the end?
  • Story 2 was a time something went wrong. How did it feel to tell it? What did it do for you?

Variations

  • Real job version: everyone uses the job ad from ACT-097, and the interviewer asks about the skills that ad names
  • Panel version: three interviewers, one candidate, for anyone heading into government or healthcare where panels are standard. Considerably more nerve-racking and worth doing once
  • Recorded version: phone on a tripod. People find their own filler words faster than anyone can tell them
  • Curveball round: the interviewer asks a question the candidate has not prepared, to prove the four stories still stretch
  • Low literacy: skip the written boxes. Build the four stories by telling them to a partner who prompts with S, T, A, R

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ "I" is genuinely hard for some learners, and it is not shyness. In many Pacific and Māori settings taking individual credit is poor form. Do not tell anyone their upbringing is wrong. Name the clash and give them the bridge: "our team did X, and my part was Y." Both true, and it is comfortable to say
  • ⚠️ Story 2 can surface something real. A time something went wrong might be a dismissal, an accident, or a serious mistake. Let people choose a smaller one. Nobody has to use the big story
  • The twelve-minute Situation. Timebox it out loud in practice, or it will happen in the room
  • Perfect stories only. Push for one where something went wrong. They are better answers and interviewers know it
  • Observers giving general praise. Hold them to the four ticks. Specific feedback is the only kind that changes anything

The Hardest Question

30-35 minroleplay
career-readinessinterviewsgapsdisclosureconfidencework-readiness

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: the questions STAR does not cover, and the one that actually keeps people awake.

Everybody in the room has a question they are dreading. For most it is not "tell me about a time you worked in a team." It is the gap, the dismissal, the conviction, the visa, or why somebody with their background thinks they can do this job.

⚠️ This activity handles disclosure. Read the whole page before you run it.

On this pageThe shape of a good answerHow to run itWorked examples, for teaching only⚠️ On criminal convictionsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The shape of a good answer

Three parts, in this order, and the third is where it turns.

Example
1. Say it plainlyOne sentence. No apology, no long story"I was out of work for two years."
2. What it wasBrief and factual"I was caring for my mum full time until she passed."
3. Turn forwardWhat you did about it, or what you can do now. Land here"I kept my first aid current, and I've just finished my Level 3. I'm ready to be back."

➜ Most people do 1 and 2 and then stop talking, leaving the silence for the interviewer to fill. Part 3 is the whole activity.

How to run it

  1. Teach the three parts (7 min). Use one worked example, not a personal one from the room
  2. Everyone writes their own answer, silently (8 min). Nobody shares what the question is
  3. Pairs (12 min). The partner asks only "can you tell me about the gap in your CV?" or whatever wording the person has asked for. Answer. Swap
  4. Room debrief (6 min). General only. Nobody discloses

⚠️ The learner writes their own question. The facilitator never guesses what somebody's hard question is, and never asks.

Worked examples, for teaching only

Use these rather than anything from the room.

The questionA good answer
A two-year gap"I was out of work for two years caring for my mum. She passed in March. I kept my licence and first aid current, and I've just finished my Level 3. I'm ready to be back."
Left after three months"That role wasn't the right fit and I left at three months. I learned to ask better questions before I take a job, which is why I asked you about the shift pattern."
No experience in this field"I haven't worked in aged care before. I've done four years of customer service on the front counter, which is the same job in a different building: reading people, staying calm, keeping to a standard."
Made redundant"The whole night shift went in the restructure. Nineteen of us. I've used the time to get my forklift F endorsement."

⚠️ On criminal convictions

This will come up. Do not improvise.

  • New Zealand's Criminal Records (Clean Slate) Act 2004 means many people can legally answer "no" to questions about convictions, if they meet the criteria. It is specific, and it is not guesswork
  • Send people to real advice: Community Law · Citizens Advice Bureau · their MSD case manager
  • A facilitator's job here is the sentence, not the law. Practise how to say it. Never advise on whether it has to be said

⚠️ GAP: the library has nothing on this and it comes up constantly with MSD-referred learners. Worth building properly, with legal input.

Debrief

Room level. Nobody reports their own answer.

  • How did it feel to say it out loud instead of dreading it?
  • Who finished on part 3? Who trailed off after part 2?
  • What is the difference between explaining and apologising?
  • Who has been leaving a job off their CV entirely because of this?

Variations

  • Written only: for a room that will not speak. They write the answer, read it back to themselves, and nobody shares. Still worth doing
  • The 30-second version: practise until the whole answer takes under thirty seconds. Length is what makes an answer sound guilty
  • Facilitator as interviewer: for a confident group, take the questions yourself. Only if trust is high
  • Employer panel: a friendly employer takes real questions and says what they would actually think. Powerful, and it needs the right employer

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Nobody discloses to the room. Ever. Pairs only, chosen by them, and anyone can pass at any point with no reason given. Say all of that before you start
  • ⚠️ This can bring up grief, shame, or trauma. Bereavement, illness, violence, prison, deportation. Know your referral options before you run it: workplace EAP, their GP, 1737 call or text, and their MSD case manager
  • ⚠️ Never tell somebody to lie, and never tell them their honest answer is unsayable. If an answer genuinely will not survive, that is a conversation about which employers to approach, not about becoming a better liar
  • Do not let it become a group therapy session. It is interview practice with a hard question. Keep it moving, keep it forward-facing
  • The learner whose question is about race, age or a name. That is discrimination, not a gap, and the answer is not a better sentence. It is FRM-061 and the Human Rights Commission

The Direct Approach

35-45 minroleplay
career-readinessjob-searchhidden-job-marketdirect-approachcold-callingnetworkingwork-readiness

Type: roleplay · Time: 35-45 min · Group: pairs, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: channels 2, 3 and 4 of FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found.

Going to an employer before there is a job. Most learners have never done it, most assume it is not allowed, and it is the single least-competed way into work.

On this pagePart 1 — why it works (6 min, whole room)Part 2 — the sixty-second version (8 min, individual)Part 3 — three ways, three rounds (18 min, pairs)Part 4 — the list, and the date (8 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — why it works (6 min, whole room)

Put the employer's reason on the board first. Without this, the room hears "beg".

Advertising a job costs money and about a fortnight of somebody's time. Posting it, reading two hundred applications, sitting through interviews. A manager who already has somebody in mind avoids all of that.

Then the question that flips it:

"So when you turn up before the ad goes out, are you asking them for a favour, or doing them one?"

➜ Let the room answer. This is the whole activity.

Part 2 — the sixty-second version (8 min, individual)

Four parts. Sixty seconds. You are not asking for a job.

Example
1. Who you areName, and one line"I'm Sione, I've just finished my Level 3 in Health and Wellbeing."
2. Why themOne real, specific thing"I noticed you've opened the new wing on Massey Road."
3. What you bringOne thing, with proof"I've done two years of personal care, including medication support."
4. The ask, which is smallNot a job. A conversation, or their process"I'm not expecting there's anything right now. Could I leave my CV, and would you let me know if something comes up?"

Mine: ______________________________________________

⚠️ Part 4 is where people overreach. "Have you got any jobs?" invites a no and ends it. "Would you let me know if something comes up?" is almost impossible to refuse and it puts your name in their head.

Part 3 — three ways, three rounds (18 min, pairs)

Same sixty seconds, three deliveries. Swap after each.

Round A — the walk-in

Standing up, both of you. The partner is behind a counter and busy. They are not rude, they are just mid-task.

⚠️ Cover this before the round: ask for the right person, do not interrupt somebody serving a customer, and if it is a bad time, ask when a good time is and come back.

Round B — the phone call

Back to back, so nobody can read a face. Far harder, and closer to real.

The partner answers as a receptionist first: "Kia ora, who were you after?" Getting past that sentence is half the skill.

Round C — the message

Written, not spoken. Email, a form, or a message. Six lines maximum. Swap and read each other's.

Partner checks☐
Is there a real, specific thing about the employer?☐
Is the ask small enough to say yes to?☐
Would this fit on a phone screen?☐
Is there a name on it, not "To whom it may concern"?☐

Part 4 — the list, and the date (8 min)

EmployerHow I'll approachWho I'll ask forWhen

⚠️ Bring a real list of local employers. A room asked to think of three will produce two supermarkets and go quiet.

Debrief

  • Which was hardest, the walk-in, the phone or the message? Why?
  • What did it feel like when your partner was busy?
  • Who has done this before? What happened?
  • What is the worst realistic outcome? (Usually: nothing. Which is where they already are.)

Variations

  • The volunteering route: same sixty seconds, different ask. "Could I do a day unpaid to see what the work's like?" It produces referees and a foot in the door, and for some employers it is a much easier yes
  • Real calls: ten minutes at the end, phones out, one actual call each with the facilitator in the room. Terrifying and the single most effective version. Do it only with a group that has practised first
  • The new-site round: the facilitator brings three real local news items — a distribution centre, a fit-out, a contract awarded. Groups work out who to ring and when
  • Employer in the room: a real hiring manager takes three walk-ins and says what they would actually think. Twenty minutes, and worth the rest of the session
  • Low literacy: rounds A and B only. The written message can be scribed by a partner

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ "It's who you know" landing as proof the system is rigged. Part 1 exists to stop that. The employer's-side reason has to come first
  • ⚠️ A non-Pākehā name gets fewer callbacks on cold applications, and learners know it. The honest answer is that the direct approach is the fix, not the problem: once somebody has met you, you are not a name on a screen. Never suggest anybody change their name
  • Do not send anybody to an employer unprepared. Practise first. A bad walk-in can close a door for the whole programme, and small towns have long memories
  • The learner who will not do the phone round. Phone anxiety is real and common. Let them do the message round twice, then come back to the phone next session
  • Do not teach this as a replacement for applying. Advertised jobs are real jobs. This is proportion, not abandonment
  • No date, no action. Part 4 is the point

I Got It Wrong

30-35 minroleplay
work-readinessmistakesaccountabilitystarting-workpracticetrust

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-069 Say It Early.

Nobody gets sacked in week two for breaking something. People get sacked for the four hours between breaking it and mentioning it. This activity is those ten seconds, practised until they are sayable.

On this pagePart 1 — the fork (5 min, whole room)Part 2 — the four sentences (6 min)Part 3 — three rounds (16 min, pairs)Part 4 — the supervisor's four seconds (5 min, whole room)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the fork (5 min, whole room)

Put it on the board and let the room fill in the right-hand side.

Told earlyFound later
What it isA problem?
Who owns itThe team?
What they learn about you??

➜ Somebody will say "a problem and a lie" without being prompted. That is the whole teaching and it lands better from them.

Part 2 — the four sentences (6 min)

On the board, and they stay there for the rest of the session.

SayExample
1Name it, plainly"I've made a mistake."
2What happened, factually"I've loaded the wrong pallet onto the Whangārei truck."
3What you've already done"I've stopped the loading and I haven't sent it."
4Ask"What do you want me to do?"

⚠️ No "but" in any of the four. "I've made a mistake, but nobody showed me" is a different sentence and it lands completely differently, even when it is true. You can say that afterwards. Not in the first ten seconds.

➜ Sentence 3 is the one everyone leaves out, and it is what makes you sound capable instead of helpless.

Part 3 — three rounds (16 min, pairs)

One is the new starter, one is the supervisor. Swap after each round.

Round A — small, and clearly yours

You've put the wrong price labels on a whole shelf. Nobody has bought anything yet. You've sent a text to the wrong customer. You've broken a cup. It was the boss's cup.

Easy. Get the four sentences out cleanly, that is all.

Round B — bigger, and it has been a couple of hours

You realised at 10am that you'd been stacking the pallets wrong all morning. It is now midday. You forgot to pass on a phone message yesterday. The customer has just rung back, annoyed.

⚠️ Here the temptation to explain arrives. The partner should notice every "but" and say so.

Round C — not your fault, and you need to flag it

You are not going to finish by three. A machine is making a noise it did not make yesterday. You have been given two jobs by two different people and both said now.

Same four sentences, different first line: "I need to flag something."

➜ Round C is the one they will use most often, and almost nobody practises it.

The supervisor has one job

Tick what you heard:

☐
They named it in the first sentence☐
There was no "but"☐
They said what they had already done☐
They asked, rather than waiting☐

Feedback is those four ticks and nothing else.

Part 4 — the supervisor's four seconds (5 min, whole room)

Flip it.

"You are the supervisor. Somebody has just told you they got it wrong. What do you do in the first four seconds?"

➜ That reaction decides whether it ever happens again. Worth doing with any group who supervise, and worth saying to learners too, because it explains why some workplaces never hear about problems until they are enormous.

Debrief

  • Which round was hardest?
  • Who caught themselves adding a "but"?
  • What is the longest you have left something before saying it? Do not answer out loud.
  • What made it hard? Was it the boss, or the room, or something else?
  • Round C, the "I'm not going to make it" one — who has ever said that at work?

Variations

  • The bad supervisor round: the partner reacts badly. Only with a confident group, and debrief it properly, because the point is that saying it early is still right and the workplace may be the problem
  • Text version: write it as a message instead of saying it. How most of our learners will actually do it, and it is harder to get the tone right
  • Real ones: the room supplies the scenarios from their own work. Better material, and it needs trust
  • Tutor version: practise telling a tutor you have not done the assessment. Same muscle, and it is happening in your building right now
  • Low literacy: no cards. The facilitator reads each scenario aloud

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Somebody in the room has been sacked for exactly this and knows it. Keep the teaching on the mechanism, never on character, and never ask anyone for their story
  • ⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, and in many migrant workplaces, going to somebody senior to report your own error cuts against how respect works. That is real and it is not a flaw. Name it, and give the bridge: "Can I show you something?" gets to the same place and is comfortable to say. Practise that version too
  • Do not moralise. The argument is not that honesty is right. The argument is that it costs less, and learners who have been in trouble before need the practical case
  • The pair who make it funny. Fine in round A. Pull it back for round B
  • Do not skip round C. It is the one that gets used weekly

Say It Out Loud

30-40 minroleplay
pepehaidentityintroductionspronunciationconfidencete-ao-maoripractice

Type: graduated practice · Time: 30-40 min · Group: pairs → threes → the room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-078 and FRM-079, spoken.

➜ A pepeha that only ever gets written is a worksheet. The whole form exists to be said standing up, to people. This activity is the difference between a learner who has one and a learner who has a piece of paper.

⚠️ And handing somebody a te reo template with no practice sets them up to be embarrassed in public. That is the risk this activity removes, and it is why it is not optional.

On this pageBefore you start — the two things that unlock the roomRound 1 — say it to one person, sitting down (8 min)Round 2 — say it again, paper down (10 min)Round 3 — pronunciation, and only now (10 min)Round 4 — standing, to the room (10 min)Record itFacilitator notesRelated activitiesUsed by

Before you start — the two things that unlock the room

1. Name the fear, out loud, first.

Most people's worry here is not the words. It is saying them wrong in front of somebody who knows them properly. That is a completely reasonable worry and everybody in here has it, including me.

2. Then say the thing that fixes it.

Getting it wrong while trying is normal and it is how everybody who can say it got there. The only version that offends anybody is the one said carelessly. Careful and wrong is fine.

Round 1 — say it to one person, sitting down (8 min)

Pairs. Sitting. Paper in hand. Read it straight off the sheet.

Listener's only job: listen. No corrections.

Swap. Both people go before anybody moves on.

Round 2 — say it again, paper down (10 min)

Same partner. Sheet face down on the table. Get through as much as you can from memory.

Stuck is fine — pick the sheet up, find the line, put it down, keep going.

Now the listener gets one job:

"The line you sounded most sure about was ..."

➜ Sure, not correct. You are building the thing that lets somebody stand up, and that is confidence, not accuracy. Accuracy is Round 3.

Round 3 — pronunciation, and only now (10 min)

Threes. Everybody says theirs once more. Now the group may help with pronunciation — and only with pronunciation.

The five vowels, on the whiteboard, before this round starts:

as in
acar
epeg
isee
opore
umoon

And the rule that does most of the work: a macron means hold the vowel longer. Not louder, not different. Longer. Māori, not Mao-ri.

⚠️ If nobody in the three is confident, they leave it and it goes on the list. Do not have a group of three guessers agree on a pronunciation and move on — that is how a wrong version gets locked in.

⚠️ And if there is a reo speaker in the room, ask them first whether they want this job. Being the designated Māori in a Pākehā-run session is a load, and it is not fair to assign it by surprise. If they say yes, brilliant. If not, that is the end of it.

Where to actually check: Te Aka Māori Dictionary has audio. A kaumātua, a kaiako, the local marae. Not a model — FRM-075.

Round 4 — standing, to the room (10 min)

Volunteers only. Never go round the room in order.

Four or five people. Standing up. Paper allowed.

The room's job: listen, then "tēnā koe" at the end. No clapping, no coaching, no feedback.

➜ If nobody volunteers, you go first, and the facilitator's pepeha needs to be as unpolished as everybody else's. If you are non-Māori, use FRM-079 and let them see you use it. That single move does more for this topic than anything you can say about it.

Record it

Last two minutes. Everybody records themselves on their phone, once, whichever round they got to.

Two reasons: it is the version they can practise against before the day they actually need it, and in three months they will not believe how nervous they sounded.

Facilitator notes

  • The order of the rounds is the activity. Sitting → paper down → pronunciation → standing. Skipping to standing loses half the room and they do not come back.
  • Nobody is made to stand. Round 4 is volunteers and it stays volunteers.
  • Somebody may cry. For a learner who has just found out their maunga after thirty years of not knowing, saying it out loud is not a language exercise. Let it happen, do not make it a moment, keep going.
  • Watch the clock on Round 3. Pronunciation will eat the session if you let it, and Round 4 is where the value is.

ACT-007Activity · Communication

BLUF Rewrite Lab

15-20 minworksheet
blufclear-messagingwritten-communicationpractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-005 BLUF

Materials: the worksheet below, a pen.

On this pagePart 1: Spot the bottom linePart 2: Fix the ramblerPart 3: Your ownDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Part 1: Spot the bottom line

Read the message. Underline the one sentence that is the real bottom line.

"Hi team, hope you all had a good weekend. There's been a bit going on with the schedule. I need everyone to submit their timesheets by Wednesday at 3pm. Payroll closes early this month, so anything late won't be paid until next cycle. Let me know if you have questions."

The real bottom line is: ______________________________________________

Now rewrite it BLUF style, with that point in the first line: ____________________________________________________________________ ____________________________________________________________________

Facilitator answer: the bottom line is "I need everyone to submit their timesheets by Wednesday at 3pm." Everything before it is warm-up. A good rewrite opens with the deadline and keeps the payroll reason underneath as the why.

Part 2: Fix the rambler

This message rambles and buries its point. Rewrite it the BLUF way.

"Hi, hope you're well. So I've been thinking, and the kitchen keeps getting messy, people leave mugs around, I had a chat with a couple of folks, and anyway maybe we could look at some kind of cleaning roster, if that's okay?"

First line (the bottom line): _______________________________________

Supporting detail: _________________________________________________ ____________________________________________________________________

Facilitator note: this one is harder, because the writer is being tentative rather than just disorganised. The interesting discussion is what all the hedging ("maybe", "if that's okay") does to the message, and how it links straight back to the four communication styles.

Part 3: Your own

Take a real message you need to send this week. Write the bottom line first, then the detail.

Debrief

  • What was the giveaway that told you which sentence was the bottom line?
  • What got cut in your rewrite, and did the message lose anything real?
  • When would opening this directly be the wrong move?

The point to land: the reader decides in one line whether this needs them. Give them that line first. It is not blunt, it is respect for their time.

Variations

  • Frontline: use radio calls and text messages instead of emails
  • Youth: use a message to a boss asking for a shift change
  • Online: shared doc, everyone rewrites the same message, compare the versions on screen
  • Advanced: give them a message with two competing bottom lines and let them discover it needs to be two messages

Watch out for

  • Rewrites that strip out the greeting entirely and read as cold. BLUF is not "no manners". Keep the hello, move the point up
  • People who rewrite it shorter but still bury the ask. Check the first line specifically

Make It PREP

15-20 minworksheet
prepclear-messagingpersuasionpractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then whole class · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-006 PREP

Materials: the worksheet below, a pen.

On this pagePart 1: Label the partsPart 2: Build the casePart 3: On the spotDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

Part 1: Label the parts

Read each statement. Label it P, R, E or P.

StatementWhich one is it?
"We should hold a short safety briefing every morning."
"Most accidents happen in the first hour of work, when people aren't switched on yet."
"Last month a two-minute briefing caught a forklift parked in a walkway before anyone got hurt."
"So let's make the morning briefing part of every shift."

Facilitator answers: Point, Reason, Example, Point. Worth noting out loud that the four sentences together take about fifteen seconds to say.

Part 2: Build the case

Here is a point. Fill in the rest.

Point: "We should give new starters a buddy for their first week."

Reason (why is this a good idea?): ___________________________________ ____________________________________________________________________

Example (a real or likely example): __________________________________ ____________________________________________________________________

Point (restate it to close): _________________________________________

Part 3: On the spot

Facilitator calls out a topic. Learner has 30 seconds to think, then delivers PREP out loud in under a minute. Suggested topics: the smoko room roster · starting meetings on time · phones on site · how new people get trained · the best way to give feedback.

Run three or four. It gets noticeably better by the third.

Debrief

  • Which part was hardest to write? (Usually the Example.)
  • What happens to a case with no example in it?
  • Whose PREP would you have said yes to, and why?

The point to land: the reason is the argument, the example is the picture. People say yes to pictures. And restating the point at the end is what turns an explanation into an actual ask.

Variations

  • Youth: topics they care about — a rule they disagree with, a change they want at home or school
  • Frontline: run Part 3 as a 60-second toolbox pitch to the crew
  • Online: Part 3 in breakout pairs, then two volunteers to the main room
  • Advanced: the room pushes back after each PREP and the speaker responds with a second PREP

Watch out for

  • Weak examples ("for example it could cause problems"). Push for something specific that happened, or specifically would
  • People who drop the final Point. Without it the message trails off and nobody acts
  • Do not run Part 3 cold with a nervous group. Do Parts 1 and 2 first so they have the shape

Which Level Am I On? — The 3 Levels Sort

15-20 minworksheet
listeningactive-listeningself-awarenesspractice

Type: worksheet then discussion · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then whole class · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-011 The 3 Levels of Listening

Materials: the printed sheet, pens.

On this pageThe instructionsThe sheetFacilitator answer keyDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

The instructions

Read each line. Write which level of listening it shows.

  • Level 1 — focused on yourself, your own thoughts
  • Level 2 — focused on the speaker's words and meaning
  • Level 3 — picking up feelings, tone, body language, and what is unsaid

The sheet

#StatementWhat level?
1"Yeah, yeah, anyway, here's what I would do…"
2"So what I'm hearing is the new system is slowing your team down."
3"You say you're fine, but your voice dropped just then, what's really going on?"
4(While they talk, you're thinking about what to say at the next meeting.)
5"Let me check I've got this, you need the figures by Thursday, not Friday?"
6"The room went quiet when you said that, and I noticed a few people look down. How's the team feeling?"
7"Mm-hm… sorry, what did you say? I was reading this email."
8"It sounds like the deadline is the part that's worrying you most."
9"You're smiling, but your shoulders are tense. Is something sitting heavy with you?"
10"Hold on, that reminds me of something that happened to me last week…"

Facilitator answer key

#LevelWhy
11Waiting for a gap to give advice
22A paraphrase of the content
33Picked up the voice drop, the thing not said
41Attention on your own agenda
52Checking the facts, a clean paraphrase
63Reading the room, not just the speaker
71Not listening at all
82 or 3Deliberately arguable. It names a feeling, but from what was said rather than what was unsaid. Use this one for the discussion
93Body language over words
101Their story became your story

Item 8 is the useful one. Let the room argue it. The argument teaches the difference between hearing meaning and hearing what is underneath it better than the answer does.

Debrief

  • Which level are you on most of the time at work? Be honest, everyone lives at Level 1 some of the day
  • When did you last catch yourself at Level 1 in a conversation that mattered?
  • What pulls you down to Level 1? (Usually: your phone, being busy, already knowing the answer, or having something you want to say.)
  • Who do you know who listens at Level 3? What do they actually do that others do not?
  • Which conversation this week deserves Level 2 or 3?

The point to land: Level 1 is not a failure, it is the default. The skill is noticing you are there and choosing to move.

Variations

  • Whole-room version: read each line out and have people hold up 1, 2 or 3 fingers. Faster, more energy, and the split on item 8 is visible instantly
  • Card sort: print the statements on cards and have groups sort them into three piles. Better for low literacy and for groups that have been sitting too long
  • Make your own: groups write two more statements each, one for each level, and test them on another group
  • Youth: rewrite the statements for a conversation with a parent, a coach, or in a group chat

Watch out for

  • The moral ranking trap. Learners hear "Level 1 = bad person". Say early that Level 1 is normal and necessary. If the room gets defensive they will stop being honest, and honesty is the whole point
  • Faking Level 3 afterwards. Someone always leaves keen to announce what everyone is feeling. Level 3 is noticing and asking, not diagnosing. Land that in the debrief
  • Do not spend more than three minutes on the answer key. The debrief is worth more than the marking

Channel Sort — Where Does This Message Belong?

15-20 minworksheet
digital-communicationchannelemailhybridpractice

Type: worksheet then group sort · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then small groups · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-013 The Channel-Fit Matrix

Materials: the printed sheet, or the twelve messages on cards for a physical sort.

On this pageThe instructionsThe sheetFacilitator guideHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed by

The instructions

For each message, write the best channel and why.

Channels: chat · email · call · video or in person

The sheet

#MessageChannelWhy
1Telling the crew the start time moved 30 minutes
2Giving a worker feedback about turning up late three times
3Sending the signed variation order to keep on record
4Telling someone their hours are being cut
5A quick "great effort clearing that site today"
6Explaining a complex new safety procedure to the team
7Asking what time the concrete truck is booked
8Letting the team know a workmate has had a family loss
9Confirming next week's full roster
10A near-miss happened and you need to talk it through
11"Can you grab more screws on your way in?"
12Two team members had a heated argument on site

Facilitator guide

There is a defensible answer for each, and three of them are worth arguing about.

#Best channelWhy
1ChatOne fact, no feelings, needs to travel fast
2In personPersonal and sensitive. Never a written message
3EmailSimple, but the record is the whole point
4In personThe highest-stakes message on the sheet
5Chat, or in person⚡ Arguable. Chat is fine and fast. In person is better, because praise in a channel disappears. Good discussion
6Video or in personComplex, and you need to see that they understood
7ChatOne fact
8In person, then written⚡ Arguable. Tell people face to face, then follow up in writing so nobody who was off that day finds out by accident. Two channels, in order
9EmailDetail people need to refer back to
10In personEmotional and complex. Also likely to need a record afterwards
11ChatThe easiest one on the sheet
12In person, separately then together⚡ Arguable. Nobody sensible does this in one meeting. Worth ten minutes on its own

Run the arguable ones deliberately. Items 5, 8 and 12 are where the thinking happens. The matrix gives an answer in seconds; these three show what judgement adds on top of it.

How to run it

  1. Individually (5 min). Everyone fills in the sheet.
  2. Small groups (7 min). Groups of three or four compare. They must agree on all twelve, which forces the argument.
  3. Whole room (5 min). Take only the ones groups disagreed on. Skip the easy ones entirely.

Debrief

  • Which ones did your group disagree about? Why?
  • Did anyone choose a channel because of the record it leaves, rather than the conversation?
  • Which of these have you actually received in the wrong channel? How did it land?
  • Item 4: has anyone here been told something like that by message? (Ask gently. Someone usually has, and it is the most persuasive thing that will be said all session.)

The point to land: a great message in the wrong channel still fails. Two questions, ten seconds, and when you are torn between two boxes, go richer.

Variations

  • Physical card sort: four sheets of A3 on the wall labelled Chat / Email / Call / In person, and groups stick the twelve messages up. Faster, more energy, and disagreements are visible instantly
  • Their own messages: ask each learner to add two real messages they sent this week and sort those. This is the version that changes behaviour
  • Office and non-site groups: the twelve are written in site language and translate directly. Swap the concrete truck for a client deadline, keep the structure
  • Teams from one workplace: run it against their actual tools and end with two agreed team norms. That is a real deliverable a manager can use on Monday

Watch out for

  • Endless edge-case debate. Some messages genuinely sit on a line. Use "when unsure, go richer" to close it and move on
  • Reading it as anti-email. Email is the right answer four times on this sheet
  • Learners whose workplace forces a channel on them ("everything goes in the group chat"). Their real question is how to push back on that, which is TOP-COM-004 territory

ACT-024Activity · Communication

BLUF Email Rewrite

15-20 minworksheet
digital-communicationemailblufwritten-communicationpractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-005 BLUF, applied to email

Materials: the printed six-part template, pens.

Different from ACT-007 BLUF Rewrite Lab: ACT-007 teaches finding the buried bottom line in any message. This one drills the six-part email structure, including the subject line, which is where most emails are actually lost.

On this pageThe worked example firstThe taskPart 2 — Your own (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worked example first

Show this before they write anything.

Subject: Concrete pour delayed — action needed by 7am Wed Hi Tane, The Level 2 concrete pour is pushed to Thursday. I need the crew re-rostered by 7am tomorrow. ← BLUF The ready-mix supplier can't deliver Wednesday after their truck breakdown, and the slab can't go without it. New delivery is locked in for Thursday 6am. Formwork and steel are already signed off, so we're good to go once the mix lands. ← WHY + DETAIL Please move the pour crew to Thursday and put the framing team on Level 1 Wednesday so no one's standing around. Confirm by 7am. ← ACTION NEEDED Cheers, Pasi

Point at the subject line. It carries the topic and the deadline. Most people would have written "Concrete pour".

The task

Take this rambling message and rewrite it using the six-part template.

The rambler:

"Hi, hope you're well. Bit of a long story but the steel order has had some issues at the supplier end, something about their transport, and it's looking like it won't arrive when we thought, so I guess we'll need to think about what the framing crew does, anyway let me know your thoughts."

Rewrite it:

PartYour version
Subject
BLUF
Why
Detail
Action needed
Sign-off

Check: can someone read your first line and know what to do? ☐ Yes ☐ Not yet

Part 2 — Your own (5 min)

Everyone rewrites one real email they need to send this week using the same six parts. This is the part that transfers.

Debrief

  • What was actually being asked for in the rambler? (It never says. There is no ask in it at all, which is why "let me know your thoughts" is doing all the work. Someone will notice this and it is the best moment in the activity.)
  • How many of you had to invent the action needed? What does that tell you about the original?
  • Whose subject line would you have opened first?
  • What did you cut, and did the message lose anything real?
  • Pairs: read your partner's first line only. Do you know what to do?

The point to land: people skim. They read the first line, decide if it is urgent, and often stop there. If your ask is at the bottom, it does not exist.

Variations

  • Their inbox, live: learners open a real email they received that was badly structured and rewrite it. Sharper than any invented example
  • Reply version: rewrite a reply rather than a fresh email. Harder, because the BLUF has to answer a question that may have been buried too
  • Low literacy: do it as a group on the whiteboard, then individuals change only the subject line and the BLUF
  • Advanced: a 40-word limit on the whole email. Constraint does more teaching than instruction

Watch out for

  • BLUF heard as "be blunt". Learners strip every greeting and produce something cold. BLUF is the point moving up, not manners moving out. Run this alongside ACT-025 Warm It Up and the balance takes care of itself
  • The subject line skipped. It is the most-read and least-written part of any email. Make them do it first, not last
  • Detail creeping back to the top. If their first line starts with "As you know…", it is not a BLUF
