Warm It Up — The Tone-in-Text Rewrite

15-20 minworksheet
digital-communicationtone-in-textemailwritten-communicationpractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-014 Tone-in-Text

Materials: the printed sheet, pens.

On this pageOpen with the researchThe taskThe five moves to useFacilitator examplesPart 2 — The stress test (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Open with the research

Before they write anything, give them the finding. It takes thirty seconds and it changes how the room works.

Kruger and colleagues (2005) ran five experiments on email tone. People overestimate both how well they send tone and how well they read it. The reason is that you hear your own message in the tone you meant it, and you cannot un-hear it. You are the worst judge of how your own message reads.

Everyone in the room believes they are the exception. That is the point.

The task

Rewrite each so it reads warm and clear. Warm does not mean longer.

#ColdWarm
1"No."
2"Why isn't this finished?"
3"See attached."
4"We need to talk."
5"That's wrong."
6"Did you even read my email?"
7"Just do it the way I said."
8"Fine."
9"This is the third time I've asked."
10"Not my problem, ask someone else."
11"You're late again."
12"Make sure it doesn't happen again."

The five moves to use

#Move
1Open with something human before the ask
2Soften instructions: "Could you…" / "When you get a chance…"
3Say the positive out loud. They cannot see your face
4Re-read it as your most stressed teammate
5Use a name and a sign-off

Facilitator examples

Do not hand these out. Use them if a table is stuck.

#One warm version
1"I can't do that one this time, sorry. Could we look at Thursday instead?"
4"Have you got 10 minutes today? Want to go over the roster with you, nothing to worry about."
6"Hi Sam, I might have buried this in my last email, so flagging it again: the figures by Thursday?"
8"Yep, that works for me, thanks!"
11"Hi Joe, that's a couple of late starts this week, everything alright? Give me a heads up if something's going on."

Note what item 11 does: it stays a real message about lateness. Warm is not the same as avoiding it.

Part 2 — The stress test (5 min)

Pairs swap sheets. Read your partner's warm version as if you were already having a terrible day. Mark any line that could still be read badly. Rewrite those.

This is move 4, done properly, and it is the whole activity. Learners cannot do it to their own writing, which is exactly what the research predicts.

Debrief

  • Which cold line was hardest to warm up? (Usually 9 and 11, because there is genuine frustration in them and learners think warm means pretending there is not.)
  • Did anyone's warm version lose the message? Read one out and check the ask is still in it
  • Partners: how many lines did you flag on the stress test? What did you catch that they could not?
  • Which of these twelve have you sent this month?

The point to land: text strips out voice, face and timing, so the reader supplies their own tone, and when they are unsure they assume the worst. Warm is not soft. Warm is clear plus human.

Variations

  • Their own sent folder: learners find one message they sent that could have read cold. Most confronting and most useful version
  • Team norms: groups agree two or three shared conventions. Do we sign off? Is a thumbs-up enough? Removes a surprising amount of guesswork
  • Low literacy / second language: provide the five moves as sentence-starter cards and work through six items instead of twelve
  • Youth: run it on group chat and social media messages, where the stakes feel real to them

Watch out for

  • Warm becoming waffle. Cap it. No warm version may be more than one sentence longer than the cold one. This constraint does most of the teaching
  • Emoji as the fix. A 👍 does not repair a cold message, and it reads differently across ages and cultures. Words
  • Softening item 11 into nothing. "No worries if you're late!" is not warm, it is a manager avoiding a conversation. If it stops being a message about lateness, it has failed
  • Someone will say this is fake or "walking on eggshells". Take it seriously and answer with the research: the tone you meant is not the tone that arrives. Adjusting for that is accuracy, not performance

Make It Human, Draw Your Line — The AI Activity

20-25 minworksheet
digital-communicationaiethicstrustwritten-communicationdigital-capability

Type: worksheet then discussion · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then whole class · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-016 Leading Communication in the AI Era

Materials: the printed sheet, pens. No devices needed, though they make Part A more interesting.

On this pageOpen with the researchPart A — Make it human (7 min)Part B — Draw your line (5 min)Part C — Catch the error (4 min)Part D — Your rule (3 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Open with the research

A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found both halves of this. Using AI made people faster, more positive and rated as closer and more cooperative by their conversation partner. And people were rated more negatively when their partner suspected AI was involved. So the risk is not the tool. The risk is the gap between what people think you wrote and what you actually wrote.

That framing keeps the room honest. Most of them already use it.

Part A — Make it human (7 min)

This stiff AI draft needs your voice. Rewrite it so it sounds like a real person. Like you.

"Dear team, I am writing to inform you that the site induction scheduled for Monday has been rescheduled to Wednesday at 8am. Please adjust your plans accordingly. Should you have any questions, do not hesitate to reach out. Regards."

My version:

_______________________________________________________________________

_______________________________________________________________________

Part B — Draw your line (5 min)

Circle YES where AI can help. Circle NO for what you should always do yourself.

Task
YES / NOTidying up a long update email
YES / NOA message of sympathy to a worker who lost a family member
YES / NOSummarising a long safety report
YES / NOA personal thank you to someone who went above and beyond
YES / NODrafting a routine roster notice
YES / NOApologising to a customer after a serious mistake
YES / NOTranslating a notice for a worker whose first language isn't English

The pattern to draw out, not to hand out: AI is fine for the routine and the structural. The moment the message is the relationship, write it yourself.

The translation one is the interesting row. Most people circle YES, and they are right, but it needs a second step: have it checked by someone who speaks the language. Getting a safety notice subtly wrong in Samoan is worse than not translating it.

Part C — Catch the error (4 min)

Why is it risky to send this AI-written line without checking?

"Our safety record shows zero incidents across all 14 sites this year."

The risk: _______________________________________________________________

Facilitator: the answer they usually reach is "it might not be true". Push one step further. If it is wrong, you have put a false safety claim in writing under your own name. Every real incident it overlooks becomes a bigger problem than the email was ever worth, and in a regulated industry that is not just embarrassing.

Part D — Your rule (3 min)

Write your own one-line rule for using AI without losing trust.

"I will use AI to ________________________________________________, but I will always ______________________________________ myself."

Go round the room and have people read theirs out. This is the best three minutes of the activity.

Debrief

  • Part A: what did you cut first? (Almost always "do not hesitate to reach out". Ask why that phrase is a tell.)
  • Whose version sounded most like a real person? What made it sound real?
  • Part B: which row did the room disagree on?
  • Has anyone here received a message they suspected was AI-written? What did it do to how you read it?
  • Part D: whose rule would you steal?

The point to land: let AI help you think and draft. You stay the leader. The judgement, the room reading, and anything that should come from your own hand, that part does not delegate.

Variations

  • With devices: learners generate the stiff draft themselves, then humanise it. Sharper, because they see how confidently generic the first output is
  • Team policy version: groups draft three shared rules for their workplace. A genuinely useful output, and some organisations have nothing written down
  • Workplaces with an AI policy: run Part B against the actual policy. Interesting when the policy and the room disagree
  • Low digital confidence: Part A works with any stiff formal letter, no AI needed. The skill is writing like a person
  • Youth: add a row to Part B for schoolwork and one for a message to a friend

Watch out for

  • It becomes an anti-AI session. The study found real benefits. A blanket ban is not a leadership position, it is avoiding one
  • It becomes an AI training session. People will want to talk about prompts. This is about trust
  • Judging the users. Most of the room already uses it. If they feel judged they will stop being honest and Part D becomes worthless
  • This page dates fast. Check the framework page's evidence before teaching this in a year

ACT-031Activity · Leadership

Fix Your Lowest Pillar

20-25 min, then 5 daysworksheet
trustteamsself-assessmentcommitmenthabitshouse-contentaccountability

Type: worksheet + self-rating + a five day practice · Time: 20-25 min in the room, then five days · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-017 The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team, and the trigger step is a textbook implementation intention.

This is house content, taken as written from the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004).

This worksheet doubles as the topic's self-assessment. Step 1 is the instrument.

On this pageHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

1. Pick your lowest pillar

Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each, where 1 is weak and 5 is strong. Circle the lowest.

PillarMy rating (1-5)
Trust — do I admit mistakes and ask for help?
Conflict — do I say the hard thing, or fake yes?
Commitment — am I clear about what I have signed up to?
Accountability — do I call it when someone slips?
Results — do I put the team's result above my own?

2. One sign

Write one thing you did, or did not do, that shows this is weak.

3. One tiny action, done daily

Keep it small and clear. Under two minutes. The source gives a sentence stem for each pillar, and they are good ones:

PillarThe line to say
Trust"I need help with ______."
Conflict"One concern I have is ______ because ______."
Commitment"I'm doing ______ by ______."
Accountability"Status is green, yellow or red. Next step is ______."
ResultsDo one task that moves our team metric.

My tiny action: ________________________________

4. Trigger

When will you do it? Link it to something already in your day. Start of stand-up, 9am, smoko, the Friday handover.

My trigger: ____________________________________

5. Track five days, then review

MonTueWedThuFri
☐☐☐☐☐
  • What got in the way? ______________________
  • What improved? __________________________
Reminder: small, honest actions build trust. Do one thing, every day.

The link back

Step 4 is the step people skip, and it is the one with the research behind it. Say so:

A commitment with no time attached is a wish. Gollwitzer tested this across 94 studies and more than 8,000 people. Plans in the form "when X happens, I will do Y" beat good intentions by a wide margin. That is the whole reason there is a trigger box on this page.

Debrief

  • Which pillar did most people circle? (Conflict and Accountability usually win by a distance)
  • Was your lowest pillar the one you expected?
  • Whose trigger is actually going to happen? Test each other's in pairs
  • What would your team say your lowest pillar is?

Variations

  • Pairs check-in: everyone swaps triggers with a partner and they message each other on day three
  • Intact teams: collect the ratings anonymously and show the team's shape. Powerful, and only do it if trust is high enough to survive it
  • Online: the table works as a form. The five day tracker works better as a recurring calendar reminder
  • Low literacy: run steps 1 and 3 spoken, in pairs. The stems can be said rather than written

Watch out for

  • Rating the team instead of themselves. Step 1 is about you. People slide into rating their manager within about ninety seconds
  • A tiny action that is not tiny. "I will be more open" is not an action. Push until it is a sentence they could say out loud
  • No follow-up. If you never ask about the five days, you have taught the group that commitments in this room do not count. Diary it before you run the session

Stage Moves — what you do at each stage

20-25 minworksheet
teamsteam-developmentleadershiphouse-contentcollaborationnorms

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: small groups of 3-4, then whole class · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-018 Tuckman's Stages of Team Development.

This is house content. Both SKILL UP resources carry this page as a blank grid. The learner fills it in. That blankness is deliberate and it is the best part of the design, so do not hand out a completed version.

Two lenses. The question at the top of the grid changes depending on the topic:

TopicThe question in the header
TOP-LEA-003 Every Team StormsWhat can you do to build relationships in this stage?
TOP-LEA-005 One Team, Not Us And ThemHow do you encourage collaboration in these phases?
On this pageThe gridHow to run itWhat good answers look likeDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The grid

Tuckman stageWhat I can actually do here
Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
Adjourning

How to run it

  1. Teach the five stages first (10 min). The grid is worthless without them.
  2. Individually, fill in the stage your team is in right now (4 min). Only that one. Concrete actions, not principles.
  3. In threes, fill in the rest (8 min). Groups get further than individuals here, because somebody in every three has been through a stage the others have not.
  4. Collect the best line for each stage on the board (5 min). One per stage. The board version is what people photograph.

What good answers look like

Learners write principles first and actions second. Push them to the second column.

StagePrinciple (what they write first)Action (what you want)
Forming"Be welcoming""Introduce every new person to three people by name in week one"
Storming"Handle conflict well""Get the two of them in a room on Tuesday and make it about the roster, not about them"
Norming"Agree how we work""Write the five rules down and put them in the group chat"
Performing"Don't take it for granted""Keep the Monday check-in even though we don't feel like we need it"
Adjourning"Celebrate""Name what each person did, out loud, before the last day"

Debrief

  • Which stage was hardest to fill in? (Adjourning, every time. Almost nobody has been taught to end things well)
  • Which stage is your team actually in?
  • Whose job is the Storming row? (Watch for everyone assuming it is the manager's)
  • What is one thing on this page you could do this week?

Variations

  • Collaboration lens: swap the header question and run it for cross-team work. The Storming row becomes about silos forming, which is the sharpest version of this exercise
  • Intact teams: fill in only the current stage, together, and turn the answers into a team charter
  • Online: a shared doc with five rows. Works well
  • Low literacy: spoken in threes, facilitator writes the board version

Watch out for

  • Answers that are only about the leader. Ask "what could you do if you were not in charge?" Every row has an answer for that, and it is the more useful one for most learners
  • Skipping Adjourning because it feels irrelevant. It is the row Pacific and Māori learners often value most, and the one most workplaces do worst. Spend time on it
  • Treating the grid as an exam. There is no answer key. The value is in the argument inside the threes

Who Is Someone You Respect?

20-25 minworksheet
respectrole-modelsleadershipcommitmenthouse-contentreflection

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-019 W-H-O, the house framework.

This is house content, taken as written from the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004).

The purpose, in the source's words: move from talking about respect to practising one specific behaviour this week.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itThe house examplesDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

W — WHO | Who will I mirror?

Name one role model you respect, and why.

  • Name: ______________________________________
  • Relationship (whānau / colleague / coach / leader): ______________________
  • Why I respect them, in one sentence: ______________________________________________

H — HOW | How will I act like them?

Choose one observable behaviour to copy this week.

  • Behaviour (make it visible and measurable): ______________________________________________
  • What it looks or sounds like in action (be concrete): ______________________________________________

O — OUTCOME | What outcome will I create?

State time, place, person or team, and impact. Use the stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."
  • My commitment: ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Do the W out loud first (6 min). In pairs, each person names their role model and says why. Do not rush this. It is often the warmest part of the whole programme and it is what makes the rest work.
  2. The H, in pairs (6 min). The partner's only job is to ask "but what do they actually do?" until an adjective becomes a behaviour. Keep asking. It usually takes three rounds.
  3. The O, individually (4 min). Written, using the stem. No stem, no commitment.
  4. Read the O out to the partner (3 min). Saying it aloud to one person roughly doubles the chance it happens.
  5. Collect them. Or have people photograph their own. Follow up next session.

The house examples

Give these before people start. They set the level.

Example 1Example 2
WMy older brotherChurch youth leader
HGreets people by name and checks pronunciationArrives early and sets the room up for success
OI will open tomorrow's team meeting by confirming everyone's name and pronunciation so that people feel seen and respectedI will arrive 10 minutes early to Thursday's workshop to set up chairs, slides and materials so we start on time and keep momentum

Debrief

  • Who did people name? (Watch the pattern. It is rarely a manager. It is usually family, church, a coach or an old supervisor)
  • What made the H hard to pin down?
  • Whose O is definitely going to happen? Test a few
  • What would it mean to someone if you told them they were your W? (This question sometimes changes the room. Some people go and do it)

Variations

  • Tell them version: learners contact the person they named and tell them. Optional, never required, and the reports back are the best material a facilitator will ever get
  • Negative version, for advanced groups: name a behaviour you picked up from someone you did not admire. Confronting and very effective. Only with a group that has trust
  • Team version: everyone names a behaviour they admire in someone in the room. Powerful, and it needs a facilitator who can make sure nobody is left out
  • Online: works fine. Breakout pairs for W and H, individual writing for O
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in pairs. The facilitator writes the O on a card for those who want one

Watch out for

  • Adjectives instead of behaviours. "He's humble" is not an H. This is the single most common failure and the partner's job is to fix it
  • An O with no day in it. Push until there is a day and a person
  • Famous people. Works far worse than someone the learner has actually watched. Redirect gently: "who in your own life is a bit like that?"
  • It can get emotional, especially where the role model has died. That is not a problem to manage away. Give it room, keep moving when the person is ready
  • No follow-up makes it a nice exercise. Ask next session. The O is a promise with a date, which means it can be checked

Say It, Do It, Close It

15 min, then one weekworksheet
trustreliabilitycommitmenthabitspracticehouse-content

Type: worksheet + one week practice · Time: 15 min in the room, then a week · Group: individual, reported back in pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-020 Say-Do-Close.

On this pageHow to run itThe cardThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Explain the loop (3 min). Say a small promise. Do it on time. Close it with proof. The Close is the step everyone skips.
  2. Everyone writes one promise (5 min). In the room, on a card. It must have a person, a thing and a day.
  3. Shrink it (3 min). In pairs, each person reads their promise out and the partner's only job is to ask "could you make that smaller?" Twice. Most promises need shrinking twice.
  4. Write the close (2 min). How exactly will they confirm it is done? Text, in person at smoko, in the group chat, on the whiteboard.
  5. Do it during the week.
  6. Report back next session (5 min). Did you say it, do it and close it? Which of the three failed?

The card
SAY — who I am promising, what, and by when
DO — when I will actually do the work
CLOSE — how they will know it is done

The link back

Nobody builds trust with a speech about being trustworthy. You build it by being boring and reliable about small things, twenty times in a row.

Then name the trap: most people in the room will do the work and not close it. From the outside, silent delivery and no delivery look exactly the same.

Debrief

  • Which of the three steps failed? (It is nearly always Close)
  • How did it feel to close it? Did it feel like showing off? (It usually does, and it is not)
  • Did anyone's promise turn out to be too big? What did that tell you?
  • Who could you use this on where trust is currently low?

Variations

  • Repair version: everyone picks a person whose trust in them has slipped, and makes the promise to that person. Much more powerful and considerably harder
  • Upwards version: the promise must be made to your own manager. Learners are often surprised how quickly this gets noticed
  • Team version: the whole team runs it for a fortnight and counts the closes. Cheap and it changes the feel of a team fast
  • Online: the card is a message to yourself in the chat, and the close happens in the same channel so it is visible
  • Low literacy: spoken. Say the promise to a partner, who writes it if needed

Watch out for

  • Promises that are really tasks they were doing anyway. That is not a promise, it is a to-do list. Ask "would anyone notice if you didn't?"
  • The person who promises something huge to prove a point. Shrink it. A kept small promise beats a broken big one every time
  • No report back. This activity is worthless without the following week. If you cannot follow up, pair people so they follow each other up

Name The Stage

15-20 minworksheet
teamsteam-developmentsortpracticeleadership

Type: worksheet / sort · Time: 15-20 min · Group: pairs or threes · Energy: medium

What it practises: reading a team against FRM-018 Tuckman's Stages. Knowing the five stages is easy. Recognising which one you are standing in is the actual skill.

On this pageHow to run itThe scenariosThe three that teach the mostDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

How to run it

  1. Teach the five stages first.
  2. In pairs, label each scenario F, S, N, P or A. Twelve of them, eight minutes.
  3. Compare answers as a class. Some are contested on purpose. The argument is the learning.
  4. Finish on the last question: which of these is your team?

The scenarios

#What is happeningUsually
1Everyone agrees with the supervisor in the meeting and complains in the car parkStorming, hiding as Forming
2Two people are openly arguing about who owns the tidy-upStorming
3Nobody needs to ask who does what. It just happensPerforming
4A new person joined on Monday and the team has gone polite againForming, and the point is it went back
5The crew has a running joke about how they do handovers, and new people get taught itNorming
6Everyone is being very careful not to upset anyoneForming
7The project finished and nobody has said anything about itAdjourning, done badly
8People disagree hard in the meeting and go for lunch together afterwardsPerforming. This is the one people get wrong
9The manager left and the team is arguing about how things should be done nowStorming, triggered by change
10People are talking about "the old team" and how it used to beAdjourning, unfinished
11Someone said "we usually do it this way" to a new starterNorming
12The team is hitting its numbers but three people are job huntingTrick question. Looks like Performing, is not

The three that teach the most

  • Number 8 splits the room. Open disagreement gets labelled Storming, because people equate conflict with dysfunction. It is the opposite. A team that can argue and then eat lunch together is as high as this model goes
  • Number 4 is the whole point of the dotted arrows. One new person can send a Performing team back to Forming, and nobody has done anything wrong
  • Number 12 has no clean answer. Results are not the same as health, which is where Tuckman ends and Lencioni starts

Debrief

  • Which one did you argue about most?
  • Number 8: is conflict a sign a team is broken or a sign it is working? What decides which?
  • Which scenario is closest to your team right now?
  • Number 12: what would you actually do?

Variations

  • Cards on tables: print the twelve, sort them physically into five piles. Better energy
  • Add your own: each group writes one scenario from their own workplace and the other groups label it. This is the strongest version with intact teams, and it needs trust
  • Online: poll per scenario, then discuss the split ones
  • Low literacy: read each scenario aloud, groups hold up fingers, 1 to 5, for the stage

Watch out for

  • The answer column is "usually", not "correct". Say that before you start, or you will spend the debrief defending a key that does not deserve defending
  • Number 12 can go quiet in a room where someone is job hunting. Keep it brief and general
  • Do not let people diagnose a colleague. The unit is the team, not the person

Collaborative Or Siloed?

15-20 minworksheet
collaborationsilosteamsdiagnosishouse-contentreflection

Type: worksheet / diagnostic · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then small groups · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-030 Collaborative vs Siloed Teams.

This is house content, taken as written from the Creating a Collaborative Team Environment SKILL UP resource (SRC-005).

The source's framing is the part worth reading out: "A collaborative team is not just about people liking each other. You can see it in what they do each day."

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

Read both lists. Circle the one that sounds more like your team.

A collaborative team looks like

  • ☐ People share information without being asked
  • ☐ Teams talk early, not just when things go wrong
  • ☐ Problems are discussed openly, not hidden
  • ☐ Wins are celebrated as "our result", not "my result"

A siloed team looks like

  • ☐ Information is kept to yourself or your department
  • ☐ Teams only talk when they have to
  • ☐ People blame "them" when things go wrong
  • ☐ Wins are claimed by one team, not shared

Reflection

  1. What is one sign that your team is already collaborative? ______________________________________________
  2. What is one sign that silos might be forming? ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Individually, tick honestly (4 min). Both lists. People can tick across both, and most do.
  2. Answer the two reflection questions (4 min). Question 2 is the one that matters.
  3. In threes, share question 2 only (6 min). Not question 1. Question 1 is comfortable and question 2 is where the work is.
  4. Collect the signs of silo forming on the board (4 min). Do not attribute them to anyone.

The link back

Nobody in the room set out to build a silo. Silos are not built by bad people, they are built by busy people who stopped talking to each other because there was no reason to.

Then point at the tick pattern. Almost everyone ticks boxes in both lists, which is the honest finding: teams are not collaborative or siloed, they are collaborative about some things and siloed about others. The useful question is which.

Debrief

  • Which single box was hardest to tick honestly?
  • The wins row: when something goes well here, who gets named?
  • What is the "they" in your workplace? Every organisation has one. Who is it?
  • What is one thing that would move one box from the right list to the left?

Variations

  • Both teams in the room: run it with head office and regional staff together, in mixed threes. Much harder to arrange, far more valuable, and it is the version that actually changes something
  • The "they" count: ask the group to count how many times they hear the word "they" about another team over the next week, then report back. A more honest audit than any survey
  • Intact team: collect the ticks anonymously and show the shape. Only if trust is decent
  • Online: a poll per box, then breakout threes for the reflection
  • Low literacy: read both lists aloud, people raise a hand for each box that is true

Watch out for

  • It becomes a complaint session about the other department within about four minutes if you let it. The redirect is always: "what do we do that makes it worse?"
  • Only one side in the room gives you a confident and partial picture. Say so out loud rather than letting the group conclude it has diagnosed the other team
  • The manager present. Question 2 goes quiet. If you cannot change that, run question 2 in writing and collect the sheets

Plan A Real 3C Conversation

15-20 minworksheet
collaborationconversationscross-teamhouse-contentpracticecommitment

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-029 The 3C Framework.

This is house content, taken as written from the Creating a Collaborative Team Environment SKILL UP resource (SRC-005).

The rule that makes it work: it must be a real conversation the learner actually needs to have. Not a hypothetical. The framework is thin as theory and strong as a plan for Thursday.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itWhat good looks likeDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

Think of a real conversation you need to have with another person or team.

Who is it with, and what is it about? ______________________________________________

1. Connect — how will I open the conversation?

______________________________________________ ______________________________________________

2. Clarify — what is one key question I will ask to understand their view?

______________________________________________ ______________________________________________

3. Commit — what is one clear next step we can agree on together?

______________________________________________ ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Everyone names the conversation first (3 min). If someone cannot think of one, prompt: who do you avoid emailing? Which team do you complain about? That is the conversation.
  2. Write the three boxes (7 min).
  3. In pairs, read them out and stress-test (7 min). The partner asks three questions, one per box:
    • Connect: does that sound like you, or does it sound like a script?
    • Clarify: is that actually a question, or is it your opinion with a question mark on it?
    • Commit: who does what, by when?
  4. Fix and rewrite. Most people rewrite the Clarify box.

What good looks like

BoxWeakStrong
Connect"Hi, hope you're well""Thanks for making time, I know Fridays are your worst day. I think we're both trying to fix the same thing"
Clarify"Don't you think it would be better if you sent them earlier?""Help me understand what your Friday actually looks like. When does the data you need land?"
Commit"We'll stay in touch""So we move the deadline to Monday midday and I'll chase finance to send Thursday. I'll confirm by Wednesday"

The weak Clarify example is the one to dwell on. It is a statement wearing a question mark, and the other person hears it as a complaint every time.

Debrief

  • Whose Clarify question survived the pair check? (Usually about half)
  • What did you assume about the other team that you have not actually checked?
  • What has stopped you having this conversation until now?
  • When exactly are you having it? (Get a day. A plan with no day is a wish)

Variations

  • Straight into roleplay: run ACT-055 The Other Team's Shoes immediately after, using each learner's own planned conversation
  • Both sides in the room: pairs from the two teams that actually need to talk, planning the same conversation from both ends. Excellent and it needs a confident facilitator
  • Online: the worksheet as a form, then breakout pairs for the stress test
  • Low literacy: planned aloud in pairs, with the partner writing the three lines down

Watch out for

  • Hypothetical conversations. They produce polished nonsense. Push for a real one, even a small one
  • A Connect that is a trap. A warm opener followed by an ambush is worse than no opener. If the partner senses a technique, say so
  • Commit with no name and no date. The most common failure, and the reason good conversations change nothing
  • Do not require anyone to name the person out loud if the conversation is sensitive. "Someone in another team" is enough

Practising Democratic Decision-Making

20-25 minworksheet
decision-makingleadershipcollaborationhouse-contentpractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then threes · Energy: low

What it practises: the democratic style in FRM-028 Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles.

This is house content, taken as written from the Creating a Collaborative Team Environment SKILL UP resource (SRC-005).

Goal, in the source's words: use a real situation to practise involving others in a decision in a collaborative way.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itThe trap to name before they startDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

1. Decision

Decision I need to make: ______________________________________________

Who will this decision affect? ______________________________________________

2. Involving others

People or teams I should involve: ______________________________________________

Questions I can ask to get their ideas:

  1. ______________________________________________
  2. ______________________________________________
  3. ______________________________________________

3. Decision and collaboration

What decision will we make after hearing everyone's input? ______________________________________________

How will involving others in this decision help build collaboration? ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Each person names a real decision they are facing (3 min). Real, current, and theirs to make.
  2. Fill in sections 1 and 2 (8 min).
  3. In threes, test the three questions (6 min). The others ask: is that a genuine question, or have you already decided? This is the whole activity.
  4. Finish section 3 individually (4 min).
  5. Set a date. When are you asking these people? Write it on the sheet.

The trap to name before they start

Say this out loud at the top:

There is one way to do this badly, and it does more damage than not asking at all. Ask for input, then make the decision you had already made, and never mention what anyone said. Do that twice and nobody in your team will ever give you a real answer again.

So section 3 has a hidden fourth question, and it is the important one: how will you tell them what their input changed? Add it to the sheet if it is not there.

Debrief

  • Whose questions were real questions? (In most rooms, about half had already decided)
  • Which decision in the room should actually be autocratic? (There is usually one. Safety, urgency or a decision that is not theirs to share)
  • What is the cost of consulting on something you have already decided?
  • Who is the person you did not think to involve?

Variations

  • Style-matching version: before filling this in, each person decides whether their decision should be autocratic, democratic or laissez-faire, and says why. Stops the worksheet implying democratic is always right
  • Team version: the leader brings a genuine decision and the team designs the consultation together. Real output, real buy-in
  • Follow-up session: learners report back on what happened when they asked. The best material in this topic comes from that
  • Online: works as a form, with breakout threes for step 3
  • Low literacy: done aloud in threes, one person scribing

Watch out for

  • Decisions that are not theirs. Some learners will pick something their manager decides. Redirect to something inside their own control, however small
  • Questions that are statements. "Don't you think we should…" is not consultation
  • The worksheet implying democratic is always correct. Lewin's own finding favoured democratic, but a leader who consults on everything reads as unable to decide. Say that
  • No date. Without one this is a nice sheet of paper

The Yes Audit

20-25 minworksheet
workloadcollaborationboundariesdelegationprioritisationwellbeing

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: habits 2 and 3 of FRM-031 The 3 Habits of a Healthy Team Player, against the research in FRM-032 Collaborative Overload.

The point: most people trying to fix their workload start with time management. This starts one step earlier, with what they agreed to and why.

On this pageThe gridHow to run itThe three questions that do the workDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The grid

List everything you have said yes to that is not your core job. Meetings, working groups, favours, projects, jobs you inherited, things you volunteered for. Aim for eight to twelve rows.

What I said yes toHours a weekAm I the best person, or the most available?Could someone else do it and learn?Keep / hand over / stop

How to run it

  1. Fill the first column, fast (5 min). Volume matters more than accuracy. Push people to keep going past the obvious ones.
  2. Add the hours (3 min). Real hours, including the thinking and the messages, not just the meeting slot. Then total them.
  3. The total is the moment. Let people sit with it. Most people underestimate by half.
  4. Columns 3 and 4 (6 min). These are the two questions from habit 3 and habit 2.
  5. Last column (3 min). Every row gets one of the three.
  6. In pairs, defend your keeps (5 min). The partner's only job is to ask "why you?"

The three questions that do the work

ColumnThe questionWhat it exposes
3Am I the best person, or just the most available?Most rows come back "most available", and that is the finding
4Could someone else do it and learn from it?Turns a workload problem into someone else's development opportunity
5Keep, hand over or stopForces a decision. Without this column it is just a list

Debrief

  • What was your total? (Nobody has to say it out loud. Just ask who was surprised)
  • How many rows came back "most available" rather than "best person"?
  • What is the one thing you are going to hand over, and to whom?
  • What did you say yes to for a reason that no longer exists? (Almost everyone has one. It is often years old)
  • Which of the three reasons put you there: wanting to help, wanting the quick win, or fear?

Variations

  • Hand-over version: everyone leaves with one named person they will offer a job to, and a date. This is the version that actually changes something
  • Team version: the whole team audits together and redistributes in the room. Requires a manager who can handle what surfaces, and it is the only version that fixes the structural problem
  • Manager version: a leader audits what their team has said yes to. Usually reveals two people carrying most of it
  • Online: a shared spreadsheet. The totals column doing its own arithmetic adds to the effect
  • Low literacy: spoken in pairs, partner writes the list

Watch out for

  • The person whose list is genuinely all essential. Sometimes true. More often it is the fear reason wearing a disguise. Ask what would actually happen if one row stopped
  • Handing over only the rubbish. Habit 2 says give people work they can learn from. Offloading the tedious jobs is not development and people spot it instantly
  • This is a structural problem for some people. If someone is carrying a team, the audit helps them survive it, it does not fix it. Say so rather than implying it is their fault
  • Do not ask people to share their totals. For some the number is genuinely distressing

Before, During, After — Respect in Action

20-25 minworksheet
cultural-safetyleadershiphouse-contentpracticecommitmentinclusion

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-034 S.A.F.E Leadership, applied to one real meeting, shift or decision.

This is house content, taken as written from the Cultural Safety in the Workplace SKILL UP resource (SRC-006).

The rule: it must be a real meeting, shift or decision that is actually coming up. The worksheet is a plan, not an exercise.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itWhat good looks likeDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

The meeting, shift or decision this is for: ______________________________

1) Before — set up the space (2 minutes)

  • What will respect look like today? ______________________________________________
  • Names and protocols to get right, including diacritics: ______________________________________________
  • Who must be heard? List names: ______________________________________________

2) During — ask and equalise (live)

  • Curiosity prompt I'll use: ______________________________________________
  • Fairness move (one-voice rule, round-robin, rotate first speaker): ______________________________________________
  • Consent check needed? (photos, filming, language): ______________________________________________

3) After — learn and lock in (3 minutes)

  • One thing I learned or need to learn (protocol, pronunciation, history): ______________________________________________
  • What changed because of feedback: ______________________________________________
  • My action by [date and time]: ______________________________

How to run it

  1. Everyone names a real upcoming thing (3 min). A team meeting, a shift briefing, a decision, a guest interaction.
  2. Fill in "Before" (5 min). The hardest box is "who must be heard", because it forces names. Push for names, not roles.
  3. Fill in "During" (5 min).
  4. In pairs, test the plan (5 min). The partner asks three questions:
    • Is your curiosity prompt a real question, or your view with a question mark on it?
    • What happens if the person you named does not speak? What is your actual move?
    • Who is not on your list who should be?
  5. "After" gets filled in afterwards, for real. Set the date in the room.

What good looks like

BoxWeakStrong
What will respect look like"Everyone treated equally""Nobody gets talked over, and I use Losana's name properly the first time"
Who must be heard"The team""Losana and Ravi. Neither spoke last time"
Curiosity prompt"Any thoughts?""What would feel respectful here when we do the site briefing?"
Fairness move"Be fair""Round-robin, and I speak last"
Action by"Soon""Thursday 9am, I confirm the pronunciation guide is in the induction pack"

Debrief

  • Whose "who must be heard" list had actual names on it?
  • What consent check did people realise they had never made?
  • Which is harder for you, Before or After? (Most people find After harder, because it needs them to have asked for feedback)
  • What is the one thing you now need to go and learn?

Variations

  • Run it live: fill in Before, hold the meeting, come back and fill in After the same day. This is the version that changes behaviour
  • Team version: a team fills in the Before boxes together, which produces a set of shared norms in about fifteen minutes
  • Guest-facing version: for tourism, retail and hospitality, run it on a guest interaction rather than a meeting. The consent box becomes the most important one
  • Online: works as a form. Add a box for "who is on mute and why"
  • Low literacy: done aloud in pairs, partner scribes

Watch out for

  • Hypothetical meetings. They produce a tidy sheet and nothing else
  • Skipping the After. It is the S.A.F.E "Educate myself" step and it is the one that stops this being a one-off
  • A "who must be heard" list that is really a list of the people who already speak. Ask who was quiet last time
  • Do not require anyone to name a person they have a live conflict with. Keep the room safe while teaching safety

Positives & Negatives to Workplace Conflict

15-20 minworksheet
conflictconflict-resolutionhouse-contentassessed-taskreflection

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then whole class · Energy: low

What it practises: the reframe at the heart of TOP-COM-007, that conflict is not automatically a bad thing.

This is house content and an assessed task. Taken as written from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), where it is Task 1.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify personal perspectives to workplace conflict and the different types of conflict in the workplace". All parts must be completed, scanned and uploaded.

On this pageThe worksheetFacilitator answer bankHow to run itThe link backDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

In the boxes below, write in your own words:

  • 2 positive outcomes to resolving conflict in the workplace
  • 2 negative outcomes to not resolving conflict in the workplace
Positives
Negatives

Name: ______________________________

Facilitator answer bank

The source supplies these. Use them to prompt a stuck learner, not as a list to copy.

PositivesNegatives
CreativityBad mental health
Better problem-solvingWork disruptions
Healthier and stronger relationshipsAbsenteeism
Improved productivity once a solution is foundHigh staff turnover
Personal growth and insightPhysical fights
Allows vulnerability to be heardWork termination
Teaches us to listenDecreased productivity
Practises communication skillsEmotional stress

How to run it

  1. Open with the video (5 min). The source links this clip and asks learners to note any tips for dealing with conflict. Its own summary: step back and ask why the conflict exists, what is important, what your priorities are, whether your view lines up with the objective, and whether you are being true to your values. Then: keep emotions out, focus on a win-win, and remember conflict can be beneficial.
  2. Individually, fill the two boxes (6 min). Own words. That is an assessment requirement, not a style preference.
  3. Collect on the board (5 min). The positives column is always slower to fill. Let that silence sit before you prompt.

The link back

The negatives came fast and the positives took work. That is the whole reason this module exists. Most of us have been taught that conflict is a failure, so we avoid it, and avoiding it is what turns a task disagreement into a relationship one.

Then the source's reframe, which is worth reading out as written:

Conflict is "an opportunity to engage in a conversation with someone who has a different viewpoint."

Debrief

  • Which column was easier? Why do you think that is?
  • Have you ever seen a conflict make something better? What happened?
  • What does a workplace look like where nobody ever disagrees?
  • What has not resolving something cost you?

Variations

  • Pairs first, for groups who go quiet in a whole-class setting
  • Real-example version: each positive and negative must come from something they have actually seen. Better material, and it needs a room with trust
  • Low literacy: spoken, facilitator scribes onto the board and the learner copies their own two and two. The assessment needs their words, not their handwriting

Watch out for

  • It becomes a list of grievances about a current workplace. Redirect to outcomes rather than incidents
  • "Keep emotions out" needs a caveat. It is in the source's video notes, and FRM-038 Powerful Listening and FRM-039 both teach the opposite: feelings fuel conflict and naming them is how it resolves. Teach "do not be driven by emotion", not "do not have any"
  • Assessment integrity: if you have shown the answer bank, the words on the sheet are not theirs

Name That Conflict

25-30 minworksheet
conflictconflict-resolutiondiagnosishouse-contentassessed-taskteams

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-037 The Three Types of Workplace Conflict (Jehn, 1995 and 1997).

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), combining its "Conflict Types in your Workplace" activity with Task 2.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify personal perspectives to workplace conflict and the different types of conflict in the workplace".

On this pagePart A — your own workplacePart B — Task 2 quizHow to run itThe teaching moment is question 7DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part A — your own workplace

What types of conflict do you commonly see where you work? Write down 2 to 4 real scenarios and identify each one.

Workplace conflict exampleRelationship, task or process?

The source's worked examples:

ExampleType
Tension between two co-workersRelationship
Not agreeing on the way something should be done on the floorTask
Not filling out accident forms properlyTask
Not agreeing with a co-worker being promoted to team leader because he does not work as hard as youProcess

Part B — Task 2 quiz

Fill the gaps using this word bank: task · negative · process · relationship · relationship · process · positive · task

  1. ____________ conflict is a disagreement between two or more people, for example amongst work colleagues.
  2. People in a team having different opinions on work project goals and what needs to be completed is an example of ____________ conflict.
  3. Disputing roles and responsibilities in a work project is an example of ____________ conflict.
  4. ____________ conflict can be seen in both ____________ and task conflict, and can often be destructive or disrupting to work performance.

True or false:

  1. Being offended by what someone said to you is an example of relationship conflict. (True / False)
  2. Task conflict is less destructive when it does not connect to relationship conflict. (True / False)
  3. Your personality clashing with someone else in your team is an example of process conflict. (True / False)

Name: ______________________________

<details> <summary>Answer key (facilitator only)</summary>

  1. Relationship · 2. Task · 3. Process · 4. Relationship, process · 5. True · 6. True · 7. False — a personality clash is relationship conflict, not process. </details>

How to run it

  1. Teach the three types first (10 min). The quiz is meaningless without them.
  2. Part A individually (8 min). Real examples from their own workplace. This is the part that makes the model stick.
  3. In pairs, compare and argue (5 min). Disagreement here is good. Most real scenarios have two types in them.
  4. Part B individually (5 min). Closed book.

The teaching moment is question 7

It is the only one most rooms get wrong, and the mistake is the useful one. A personality clash feels like a process problem because it usually surfaces in an argument about roles or workload. It is relationship conflict, and treating it as process is exactly the error the framework exists to prevent.

Debrief

  • How many of your Part A examples had more than one type in them?
  • Which type is most common where you work?
  • Which type does your workplace handle worst?
  • Think of a conflict that was "solved" and came back. What type was it really?

Variations

  • Card sort: print the source's four examples plus the room's own on cards, sort into three piles
  • Escalation version: for each Part A example, ask what would turn it into relationship conflict. This is the highest-value version for supervisors
  • Low literacy: Part A spoken in pairs with the facilitator scribing. Part B read aloud, answered verbally, scribed. Assessment needs their answers, not their writing

Watch out for

  • Real people getting named. Part A is about situations. Say so before they start, and do not let a sheet go to assessment with a colleague's name on it
  • The room deciding relationship conflict is the only real one. Task and process conflict cost teams a great deal and are far easier to fix
  • Question 7 being marked harshly. Getting it wrong is the point. Teach from it

Case Study — Akanisi

20-25 minworksheet
listeningconflictconflict-resolutionhouse-contentcase-studyempathy

Type: worksheet / case study · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then threes · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-038 Powerful Listening, all three layers.

This is house content, taken as written from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007).

On this pageThe scenario — Lifting Boxes ComplaintThe worksheetFacilitator answer bankHow to run itThe teaching momentDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The scenario — Lifting Boxes Complaint

Akanisi is frustrated.

She, and a few employees in her department, were asked to lift heavy boxes from the office into a truck just before their lunch break. This is the second time in the past week they have been asked to do such a task.

She comes to you to vent:

"This company is such a joke! They don't care about our safety or whether someone gets hurt! You should have seen what they have told us to do today, lifting and carrying those heavy boxes onto those trucks! Without a single trolley or forklift in sight! Now my back is stuffed, but one of those boxes could have easily fallen over and someone could have been hurt!"

The worksheet

Your answer
Facts & information (Content) — what actually happened?
Values driving the conflict — what does she care about that is being stepped on?
Feelings being felt — what is this doing to her?

Facilitator answer bank

From the source. Use to prompt, not to hand out.

Layer
ContentStaff required to lift boxes into a truck · second time this week · Akanisi is not happy · the boxes were heavy for some staff to lift
ValuesAccountability · leadership · safety responsibility · organisation
FeelingsAngry, betrayed, frustrated, grumpy, confused, embarrassed, helplessness, hurt, outraged

How to run it

  1. Read it out loud, in role, with the frustration in it (2 min). Read flat and the feelings layer disappears.
  2. Individually, fill the three rows (8 min). One row at a time, in order. Do not let people jump to values before they have the facts down.
  3. In threes, compare (6 min). The content row will match. The values row will not, and that disagreement is the activity.
  4. Whole class on values only (5 min). Collect them on the board.

The teaching moment

Ask the room:

If you fixed the trolley problem tomorrow, would Akanisi be satisfied?

Most rooms say yes, then reconsider. She might well not be, because the trolley is content and her values row says accountability and leadership. What she is actually saying is nobody is looking after us. A trolley does not answer that. A supervisor saying "you're right, we got that wrong, here is what I'm changing" does.

That gap between the stated problem and the driving value is the whole point of the framework, and this case study is the cleanest demonstration of it in the library.

Debrief

  • Which row was hardest?
  • Did anyone hear a value nobody else did?
  • What is the difference between "my back is stuffed" as content and as feeling?
  • Who in your workplace comes to you like this? What do you usually do first?

Variations

  • Roleplay extension: one person plays Akanisi, one responds using the compassionate response. Runs straight into ACT-074
  • Your own case: learners bring a real complaint they have received and run the three rows on it. Best version with supervisors
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in threes, facilitator scribes the board version

Watch out for

  • Do not let the room dismiss her. "She's overreacting" surfaces in some groups. The response is that the reaction is data, not a verdict on her, and the reaction is exactly what tells you which value is in play
  • Health and safety is real here. Manual handling without equipment is a genuine WorkSafe issue, not just a feelings problem. If a room goes there, that is a legitimate and useful direction
  • Names and pronunciation. Akanisi is a Fijian name. Say it properly, and check with the room. It is a small thing and this library has a whole topic about it

Body Language Reflection

15-20 minworksheet
body-languageconflictlisteninghouse-contentde-escalationself-awareness

Type: worksheet · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then whole class · Energy: medium

What it practises: step 2 of FRM-041 De-escalation, and the visible half of FRM-010 SOLER.

This is house content, from the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007).

The premise: your gestures and non-verbal language convey both positive and negative messages. You are often unaware of your own.

On this pageThe worksheet⚠️ Correct one thing before you teach thisHow to run itThe ones that split a room, and shouldDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

First, before the list: what body language do you think you have during conversations? ______________________________________________

Then mark each gesture below as positive (✓) or negative (✗):
☐ Tapping fingers or feet☐ Rolling of eyeballs☐ Watching the clock
☐ Avoiding eye contact and looking elsewhere☐ Rubbing your forehead☐ Looking down
☐ Smiling with purpose☐ Sigh breathing☐ Frowning
☐ Looking people directly in the eyes☐ Yawning☐ Putting head down on hands
☐ Arms folded with intent☐ Folding legs☐ Covering ears
☐ Leaning back☐ Leaning forward

⚠️ Correct one thing before you teach this

The source says "most experts agree that at least 70% of all communication is nonverbal."

Do not repeat that number. It is a version of the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule, one of the most misquoted findings in communication training. Mehrabian's experiments were about single spoken words where the words and the tone conflicted, and he has said publicly that the ratios do not generalise (background). The full note is on FRM-014 Tone in Text.

This is the second Zeducation resource to carry this claim. The Effective Communication workbook has a version of it too. It is worth fixing across the whole series at once.

The teaching point survives without the number, and it is the true half: you communicate with more than words, you are usually unaware of what your body is doing, and in a conflict people read your face before they hear your sentence. Say that instead.

How to run it

  1. Ask the opening question first, before the list (3 min). What do you think you do? Written down before they see the options, or the list contaminates the answer.
  2. Mark the gestures (5 min).
  3. Compare in pairs (4 min). Several are genuinely contested.
  4. Whole class on the contested ones (5 min).

The ones that split a room, and should

GestureWhy it is not obvious
Folding legsUsually just comfortable. Marking it negative is over-reading
Leaning backRelaxed, or disengaged, entirely depending on context
Looking people directly in the eyesMarked positive in the source. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures it is disrespectful with someone senior. The single most important adaptation on this page
Rubbing your foreheadTired, thinking, or exasperated. You cannot tell from the gesture
Sigh breathingCould be the person calming themselves down, which is de-escalation step 1

➜ Facilitator tip: the lesson is not the answer key. It is that gestures are read, and read wrongly, which is why checking beats assuming in both directions.

Debrief

  • Which gesture do you do without knowing?
  • Has anyone ever misread your body language? What did they think you meant?
  • Which of these would you notice most if someone did it while you were upset?
  • What does your body do when you are trying not to show you disagree?

Variations

  • Mirror round: in pairs, one person talks for a minute while the other deliberately does three negative gestures. Debrief on what it felt like to be on the receiving end
  • Film it: with consent, record a two minute conversation and let people watch their own hands. Uncomfortable and by far the most effective version
  • Culture round: ask the room which of these mean something different where they are from. Often the best conversation on the page
  • Low literacy: read the list aloud, thumbs up or down

Watch out for

  • Do not hand out an answer key. Half of these depend on context, and a key teaches learners to read gestures as a code, which is the actual error
  • Do not let it become amateur lie-detection. Reading body language "accurately" is far less reliable than training material suggests
  • Eye contact needs the cultural note every single time. It is on the sheet as a positive and for a lot of learners in this room it is not

Applying a Compassionate Response — Owairua

20-25 minworksheet
conflictcompassionempathyhouse-contentassessed-taskcase-study

Type: worksheet / case study · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-039 The Compassionate Response.

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), where it is Task 4.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify ways to respond to workplace conflict".

On this pageThe scenario — Working OvertimeThe worksheetFacilitator answer bankQuestion 3 is the whole activityHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The scenario — Working Overtime

Owairua has come to you and expressed his frustrations with how much overtime he is working:

"I'm sick and tired of staying extra time after work! Our team is getting lazier and lazier by the day. Some of them are coming in to work late and taking their time coming back from breaks. I feel like I'm carrying the team, working my butt off to get the orders done before shift is done. This is getting all too much!"

The worksheet

1. Identify two facts or statements (content) in the scenario.

  • ______________________________________________
  • ______________________________________________

2. Identify two feelings Owairua may be experiencing.

  • ______________________________________________
  • ______________________________________________

3. Choose one of those feelings and share, in at least two sentences, a time when you have felt that same way (at work or in your personal life).

  • Feeling chosen: ______________________
  • Experience: ______________________________________________

Name: ______________________________

Facilitator answer bank

From the source
ContentOwairua is working overtime · staff not returning from breaks on time · he is doing additional work because team members are not doing enough
FeelingsAngry · frustrated. Also available: resentful, unappreciated, exhausted, taken for granted

Question 3 is the whole activity

Questions 1 and 2 are warm-up. Question 3 is the framework, and it is doing something specific that is worth naming out loud:

While it's not about you, reflecting on a similar experience, or a time when you felt the same way, can lead you to a compassionate response.

Compassion is not a personality trait you either have or do not. It is a retrieval task. You find the nearest thing you have felt, and that is what lets you say something true instead of something polite.

➜ Then close the loop: having found their own experience, ask each learner to write the one sentence they would actually say to Owairua. That sentence is the deliverable, and the source does not ask for it. It should.

How to run it

  1. Read the scenario in role (2 min). With the frustration in it.
  2. Questions 1 and 2 individually (6 min).
  3. Question 3 individually and privately (6 min). This one is personal. Nobody is required to share it with the room.
  4. In pairs, share only the sentence they would say to Owairua (5 min).
  5. Collect the best sentences on the board (4 min).

Debrief

  • Was it easier to find the facts or the feelings?
  • Did having your own experience change what you would say to him?
  • What would happen if you went straight to "let's look at the roster"?
  • Is Owairua right about his team? Does it matter for your first response? (It does not, and this is the hardest idea in the topic)

Variations

  • Roleplay extension: deliver the sentence out loud to a partner playing Owairua, who says whether it landed
  • The wrong responses round: first collect what people would normally say. "Have you spoken to them?" "Everyone's busy." Then compare
  • Real case: learners bring a complaint they have actually received
  • Low literacy: spoken in pairs throughout, facilitator scribes question 3 for the assessment

Watch out for

  • Question 3 can go deep. People choose real experiences and some are heavy. It is private by default. Never ask anyone to read it out, and be aware it goes to an assessor
  • Compassion read as agreement. You can acknowledge Owairua's feelings without accepting that his team is lazy. The room will need that said explicitly
  • The learner with no comparable experience. Ask for the closest feeling rather than the closest situation. Everyone has felt unappreciated
  • Pronunciation. Owairua is a Māori name. Get it right and check with the room

Finding Solutions to Conflict

25-30 minworksheet
conflictconflict-resolutionproblem-solvinghouse-contentassessed-task

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-040 Moving to Resolution.

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), combining its "Finding Solutions to Conflict" activity with Task 5.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify ways to respond to workplace conflict".

On this pagePart A — the five minute listPart B — Task 5, the Owairua scenarioPart C — test themThe two teaching momentsDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part A — the five minute list

Think about a conflict happening right now, at work, at home, or in the world.

Set a timer for five minutes and write down as many solutions as you can. All of them. Do not filter, do not judge, do not stop to decide whether one is any good.

______________________________________________ ______________________________________________ ______________________________________________

The source's own examples: talk to the person instigating the conflict and find a solution · take a breather from the environment · speak with leaders · try to understand the other person's perspective · understand the facts and feelings of the situation.

Part B — Task 5, the Owairua scenario

"I'm sick and tired of staying extra time after work! Our team is getting lazier and lazier by the day. Some of them are coming in to work late and taking their time coming back from breaks. I feel like I'm carrying the team, working my butt off to get the orders done before shift is done. This is getting all too much!"

Write down three solutions you think may help Owairua resolve this conflict:

  1. ______________________________________________
  2. ______________________________________________
  3. ______________________________________________

Name: ______________________________

Facilitator answer bank

  • Talk with team members about coming back late from breaks
  • Ask Owairua if he needs to take time off
  • Review roles and responsibilities and delegate tasks away from Owairua
  • Commit Owairua to leaving work on time
  • Ask Owairua more questions to make sure the real issue has been found
  • Ask Owairua what solution he would consider

Part C — test them

Take each of your three and run it through the five questions. This is the half the source describes and does not give a worksheet for, so it is here.

Solution 1Solution 2Solution 3
How would this work?
What will it do for him?
Is it actually possible?
Strengths?
Limitations?

The two teaching moments

1. Two of the six answers in the bank are not solutions at all. "Ask more questions to make sure the real issue is found" and "ask Owairua what solution he would consider" are about understanding the problem better. Point this out. A brainstorm that produces only actions has usually skipped a step, and in a real conflict those two are often the correct first move.

2. Test "commit Owairua to leaving work on time" out loud as a class. It sounds caring and it fails question 3 immediately: the work still has to be done by somebody, so you have moved the problem rather than solved it. It is the clearest demonstration of why the testing half exists.

Debrief

  • How many solutions did you get in five minutes? Did the good ones come early or late?
  • Which of your three survived the five questions?
  • Which solution would Owairua choose? Did anyone ask him?
  • What is the difference between a solution that fixes the work and one that fixes how he feels?

Variations

  • Silent brainstorm: everyone writes for five minutes with no talking, then pool. Produces more and more varied options than a group discussion
  • Worst idea first: deliberately generate three terrible solutions before the real ones. Loosens a room up fast and often surfaces a good idea sideways
  • Pairs test each other's: you cannot test your own idea as honestly as someone else can
  • Low literacy: spoken in pairs, partner scribes. Part C works well as a spoken round

Watch out for

  • People filtering during Part A. It is the whole discipline and it breaks within about forty seconds. Remind them mid-timer
  • Solutions that are punishments. "Report them to the manager" appears in most rooms. Run it through the five questions rather than ruling it out
  • Skipping Part C. Without it this is a wish list. The testing is where the learning is
  • Doing this before the listening. Say it plainly: if you have not done ACT-071 and ACT-074 first, you are solving a problem you have not understood

What's Stopping Me?

20-25 minworksheet
assertivenessbarrierspeople-pleasingself-esteemreflectionwellbeing

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then optional pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-042 Why Assertiveness Feels Hard.

Run it after the skill, never before. The barriers only mean anything once someone has learned a script, tried it, and noticed the gap between knowing it and using it.

⚠️ Private by default. Nothing on this sheet is shared with the room unless the learner chooses to. Say that before pens come out.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itGetting question 4 small enoughDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

1. Think of one thing you have not said, to one person. You do not write who.

What would you say, if you were going to say it? ______________________________________________

2. What stops you? Tick everything that is true. Most people tick more than one.

BarrierWhich sounds like you
☐Shyness"If I speak, everyone will be looking at me"
☐People-pleasing"If I say no, they'll think less of me"
☐Low self-esteem"My needs aren't as important as theirs"
☐Fear of the reaction"It'll turn into a fight, or they'll be upset"
☐Passive-aggressive habit"I'd rather just make it obvious I'm annoyed"
☐Culture and upbringing"I was raised not to answer back"
☐Power and safety"It genuinely isn't safe for me to say this here"
☐Energy and health"I don't have it in me at the moment"

3. Circle the one that is most true, most of the time.

4. What is the smallest version of this you could do? Not the conversation. The smallest step towards it. ______________________________________________

5. When? A day, and a place. ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Teach the eight barriers first (8 min). Read them out. Do not elaborate on each one, let people find their own.
  2. Question 1, individually (4 min).
  3. Questions 2 and 3, individually and silently (5 min). No talking. This is the part that needs quiet.
  4. Questions 4 and 5 (5 min). The smallest version is the whole point. Push people down, not up.
  5. Optional pairs (5 min). Share only question 4, the smallest step. Never question 2.

Getting question 4 small enough

Learners write the whole conversation. The job is to shrink it until it is almost embarrassingly easy, because that is the version that actually happens.

They writePush them to
"Talk to my manager about my workload""Ask my manager for ten minutes on Thursday"
"Tell my sister how I feel""Text my sister and say I want to talk about something this weekend"
"Speak up in team meetings""Say one thing in Monday's meeting, even if it's agreeing with someone"
"Stop saying yes to everything""Say 'let me check and come back to you' once this week"

➜ Facilitator tip: the most useful sentence in this whole activity is "let me check and come back to you." It is not a no, it costs nothing, and for a people-pleaser it is often the first time they have ever broken the automatic yes.

Debrief

Ask these to the room in general terms. Nobody reports their own answers.

  • Which barrier do you think is the most common in workplaces? (People-pleasing wins nearly always)
  • What is the difference between "I can't say this" and "I don't want to"?
  • Barrier 7 is on the list on purpose. When is not speaking up the right call?
  • What would have to change for the thing you wrote in question 1 to become sayable?

Variations

  • Anonymous tally: collect ticks on slips and show the room's shape without any names. Powerful, and it tells learners they are not the only one
  • Team version: with an intact team, run only question 2 anonymously. The pattern is a culture diagnosis, and it will tell you more than a survey
  • Pair with the script: run straight into ACT-081 The DEAR MAN Lab so people leave with both the barrier named and the sentence written
  • Low literacy: read the eight aloud, tick by show of hands with eyes closed, then do questions 4 and 5 spoken in pairs

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never assign someone a barrier. These are self-identified. A facilitator who says "that sounds like people-pleasing to me" has just diagnosed a learner in front of their colleagues
  • ⚠️ Barrier 7 is real and must not be argued with. If someone says it is not safe to speak up at their work, believe them. The response is not more confidence, it is: who else can this go to, and is this a job worth staying in? See the power and safety note on FRM-042
  • ⚠️ Culture is not a defect. If a learner ticks barrier 6, the answer is not to override their upbringing. Often the assertive move simply looks different: one to one, or through someone trusted. That is a legitimate answer
  • ⚠️ This can surface real distress. Question 1 sometimes brings up a situation that is not a communication problem at all. Know your referral options before you run it: workplace EAP, their GP, or 1737, call or text. A facilitator is not a clinician
  • Do not let question 4 stay big. A large step is a step that does not happen
