The DEAR MAN Lab

30-35 minworksheet
assertivenessdbtscriptsaying-nopracticeboundariescommunication

Type: worksheet, then paired practice · Time: 30-35 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-043 DEAR MAN, the DBT assertiveness script.

Use a real ask. Ideally the one the learner named in ACT-080. A hypothetical produces a tidy script nobody ever uses.

On this pageThe templateHow to run itThe A row is the whole activityThe R row is what makes it landDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The template

What I want to ask for, or say no to: ______________________________

DEAR — what you say

Your words
DDescribe the facts. Only what a camera would have seen
EExpress how you feel. Start with "I feel…"
AAssert the actual ask. Say it plainly
RReinforce what they get if they agree

MAN — how you hold it

Your plan
MMindful. They will raise something else. What is your one sentence to come back to?
AAppear confident. What will your voice and posture do?
NNegotiate. What is the smaller version you would accept?

How to run it

  1. Teach DEAR only (8 min). Four letters. Do not introduce MAN yet.
  2. Write the DEAR half (7 min).
  3. Pairs: read it out and get one check (5 min). The partner's only job is to ask "what exactly are you asking for?" If the answer is not already in the A row, the script is not finished.
  4. Teach MAN (5 min).
  5. Write the MAN half (5 min).
  6. Pairs: run it live (8 min). The partner pushes back once, mildly, and the speaker uses their M sentence. Swap.

The A row is the whole activity

Learners describe and express fluently, then never say what they want. In most rooms half the scripts have no actual ask in them on the first pass.

Not an askAn ask
"I just wanted to raise it""I'd like to come off Sundays from next month"
"It's been a bit much lately""I need one of these three jobs taken off me"
"I was wondering if maybe…""Could you confirm the roster by Wednesday?"

➜ Make them underline the sentence that is the ask. If they cannot underline one, they have not written one.

The R row is what makes it land

Reinforce is the step that separates this from DESC. Without it, you have made a request. With it, you have made an offer.

Worked example. A support worker asking to come off the Sunday roster:

D: "I've been on the Sunday roster four of the last six weeks." E: "I feel stretched, and Sunday mornings are when my family are all together." A: "I'd like to come off Sundays from next month." R: "I'm happy to take more Saturdays, which I know is the harder shift to fill." M: manager says "everyone takes a turn". She replies: "I understand. I'd still like to come off Sundays, and I'll take the Saturdays." N: "If that's impossible, could we do one Sunday a month instead of three?"

⚠️ Reinforce is not a threat. "It'll be better for you because otherwise I'll resign" is Consequences, which belongs to DESC and is a different conversation.

Debrief

  • How many of you had to rewrite the A row?
  • What did your partner's pushback do to your script?
  • Which is your situation: DESC or DEAR MAN? (Raising a problem, or asking for something?)
  • What is the smallest version you would accept, and is it actually acceptable?

Variations

  • DESC comparison round: write the same situation both ways and compare. The clearest way to teach when to use which
  • Saying-no version: the ask is a refusal rather than a request. Reinforce becomes what the other person gains from a clear no now rather than a reluctant yes later
  • Harder pushback: the partner refuses twice. Practises M properly, and pairs with FRM-009 Broken Record
  • Low literacy: built spoken in pairs, partner scribes the seven rows

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ "Appear confident" is culturally loaded. The standard DBT teaching includes eye contact and an upright stance. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, sustained eye contact with someone senior reads as disrespect. Teach it as steady, and let learners choose the form. Do not mark anyone down for it
  • Say where it comes from, and where it stops. DEAR MAN is a therapy skill used outside therapy. That is normal and it is worth naming, so nobody mistakes a workshop for treatment
  • Negotiating too early. Some learners lead with N. They have negotiated against themselves before the ask has landed
  • The script that is really a complaint. If the D row has adjectives in it, it is not describing facts

The Grid Self-Plot

20-25 minworksheet
leadershipstylesself-assessmentresultspeoplereflection

Type: worksheet · Time: 20-25 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-044 The Blake-Mouton Managerial Grid.

Two dots, not one. That is the whole design of this activity. Where you sit, and where the best leader you ever had sat. The gap is the session.

On this pageThe worksheetHow to run itThe middle is the findingDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The worksheet

Draw the grid on the sheet, or print it. Both axes run 1 to 9.

HIGH  9 |  Country club                          Team
      8 |
      7 |
   P  6 |
   E  5 |              Middle of the road
   O  4 |
   P  3 |
   L  2 |
   E  1 |  Impoverished                    Produce or perish
LOW     +--------------------------------------------------
          1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9
        LOW            RESULTS                        HIGH

1. Think of one real team you lead, or one you are part of. Not a hypothetical.

2. Plot yourself. One dot. Answer these two before you place it:

Score 1-9
Concern for results. How much of your attention goes on whether the work actually gets done, to standard, on time?
Concern for people. How much of your attention goes on how the people are doing, what they need, whether they are alright?

3. Plot the best leader you ever had. Different colour. Same two questions about them.

4. Plot the worst. If you have the stomach for it.

5. Answer these three:

  • What is the distance between your dot and the best leader's dot? Which axis is it on?
  • What would you have to stop doing to move one point on that axis?
  • What would it cost you?

How to run it

  1. Teach the grid first (10 min). Four corners and the middle. Do not skip the middle
  2. Individual plotting (7 min). Silent. People need to be honest and they will not be with an audience
  3. Pairs (5 min). Share only your own dot and what you would have to stop doing. Never share the "worst leader" dot, because in a workplace cohort that person may be down the corridor
  4. Room question (3 min): "hands up who put themselves in the middle." Usually most of the room, and that is the conversation

The middle is the finding

Almost everybody plots themselves around 5,5 the first time. Push on it.

They sayAsk
"I'm balanced""Balanced, or avoiding both?"
"It depends on the day""What did last Tuesday look like?"
"I care about both equally""When they conflicted last month, which one won?"

➜ Blake and Mouton's argument is that the middle is not the sensible compromise. It is the position that produces average results and people who are not especially committed. Say it plainly and let people argue with it.

Debrief

  • Who moved their own dot while they were writing? What changed your mind?
  • Which axis is easier for you to raise, and why?
  • Is there anyone here whose team needs them lower on one axis?
  • What is a job where produce-or-perish is the right call for a week?

Variations

  • Team version: with an intact team, everyone plots the team leader anonymously. Collect and show the spread. The spread itself is the message, and it is often wider than anyone expects
  • Pair with Theory X/Y: run ACT-083 first. The belief usually explains the position
  • Before-and-after: plot where you are, then plot where the team needs you next quarter. One dot becomes a goal
  • Low literacy: run it as a physical floor grid. Masking tape two axes on the ground and have people stand where they think they are. More honest than paper and considerably more fun
  • No-leadership-experience version: plot a teacher, a coach, or a parent

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Nobody plots the "worst leader" dot in a room where that person works. Say this before pens come out. If the cohort is one workplace, cut step 4 entirely
  • The heroic self-plot. Some people put themselves at 9,9 immediately. Ask what their team would say. Usually reframes it
  • Treating a corner as an identity. The grid is a position you are currently occupying, not a type you are. People move
  • The learner who realises they are impoverished. It happens, and it stings. The move is forward: which single axis, which single point, by when

The Values You Brought To Work

30-35 minworksheet
tikanga-maorivaluescultureidentityleadershipworksheetbelonging

Type: worksheet, then whole-room build · Time: 30-35 min · Group: individual, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-050 Tikanga Māori in Business.

This is not a values-poster exercise. The room ends up with a wall of words in several languages, and the activity works only if the facilitator genuinely does not know in advance what will be on it.

⚠️ Prepare the pronunciation before you deliver this. All of it. If you cannot say whanaungatanga, manaakitanga, rangatiratanga and kaitiakitanga properly, do not run this session until you can.

On this pagePart 1, the four (10 min, facilitator-led)Part 2, the worksheet (10 min, silent)Part 3, the wall (10 min, whole room)Part 4, the question that closes itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1, the four (10 min, facilitator-led)

Teach FRM-050. Say the words, give the plain meaning, give one workplace example each. Write all four on the board with room underneath.

Then say, out loud, the thing that makes this activity work:

These are Māori values. We are in Aotearoa, so they come first, and they belong to Māori. Now I want to know what you brought.

Part 2, the worksheet (10 min, silent)

1. Think of one person who taught you how to treat people. A parent, a grandparent, a coach, an aunty, a pastor, a first boss. You do not have to write who.

2. What did they teach you? Write it however it comes out. A sentence, a saying, one word. ______________________________________________

3. Is there a word for it in your family's language? If there is, write it. If you are not sure of the spelling, write it how it sounds. ______________________________________________

4. Where do you see it at work? One concrete thing you do, or wish you did. ______________________________________________

5. Where does it cost you? Every real value costs something. ______________________________________________

Part 3, the wall (10 min, whole room)

Anyone who wants to adds their word to the board, underneath the four. Nobody has to.

The board fills up with things like:

WordOften described as
Fa'aaloalo (Sāmoan)Respect, especially to elders and to the relationship
Tautua (Sāmoan)Service. You lead by serving first
Alofa (Sāmoan) / 'ofa (Tongan)Love, in the sense of obligation to people
'Aiga / kāinga / whānauFamily, and the fact that it is bigger than the household
Utang na loob (Filipino)The debt of gratitude you carry and repay
Ubuntu (southern African)I am because we are
Izzat (South Asian)Honour, and not bringing shame on the family
"You finish what you start"No word for it, and it counts anyway

➜ The last row matters. Plenty of people, including plenty of Pākehā New Zealanders, have strong values and no vocabulary for them. Do not let the activity imply that only people with a heritage language have culture.

Part 4, the question that closes it

Look at the board. How much of this shows up in how your workplace actually runs?

That is the end of the session. Do not answer it for them.

Debrief

  • Which word on the board would your workplace most benefit from?
  • Question 5: which value of yours costs you something at work? What does it cost?
  • Has anyone ever had to leave one of these at the door to fit in at a job?
  • What is the difference between a value your workplace has on a poster and one it actually runs on?

Variations

  • Team version: an intact team builds the wall together, then picks two words to write into a team charter. This is the version that changes something
  • Whakataukī open: open with Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou, ka ora ai te iwi — with your food basket and my food basket, the people will thrive. It is exactly what the board becomes
  • Photograph the wall. Print it. Put it up. A wall that gets taken down at the end of the session says the session was the point
  • Written-only version: for a room that will not speak, everyone writes on a card and the facilitator reads them out anonymously
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken. Facilitator writes on the board as people call words out

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never ask the Māori learner to explain tikanga to the room. Teaching part 1 is the facilitator's job. If a Māori learner offers, that is different and it is theirs to offer
  • ⚠️ Same for every other culture in the room. Nobody becomes the representative of their ethnicity for the afternoon. Invite, never call on
  • ⚠️ Do not correct anyone's spelling or usage of their own family's word. Ever
  • The learner who says "I don't have a culture." Very common, usually Pākehā, sometimes young. Answer: what did your family teach you about work? That is the culture, and it is invisible to you because it is the default around here
  • Values as performance. If the room starts producing impressive-sounding words for the facilitator, go back to question 5. What it costs is the honest bit
  • Wrapping up too fast. This activity generates something. Leave time for the room to sit in it

Seven Roles, One Kaupapa

25-30 minworksheet
tikanga-maorileadershiprolesself-assessmentcultureteams

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-051 Tū Rangatira, the seven Māori leadership roles from the Ministry of Education's 2010 framework.

⚠️ Say where the framework comes from. Every time. It is Tū Rangatira: Māori Medium Educational Leadership, 2010, made by named Māori educators. It is not anonymous tradition, and the workbook Zeducation met it in presented it as though it were.

On this pageThe sheetWhat usually comes backHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The sheet

For each role: how often do you do this? Then: when did you last do it? The second column is the one that tells the truth.

WhenuThe leader who does this…Often / Sometimes / NeverLast time
He Kaitiaki guardianProtects the people and the kaupapa. Holds relationships built on trust
He Kaiwhakarite managerRuns the resources well. Roster, budget, gear, time
He Kanohi Matara visionaryThinks past this month. Knows what is coming
He Kaiako teacher and learnerTeaches others. And is still learning something
He Kaimahi workerDoes the work alongside people. Leads by doing
He Kaikōtuitui networkerConnects beyond this team. Knows who to ring
He Kaiarataki advocateSpeaks up for people. Holds culturally responsive practice

Now answer these.

1. Which two are you strongest at? ______________________________________________

2. Which one have you genuinely never done? ______________________________________________

3. What would doing it once look like this month? Small. Specific. A day. ______________________________________________

4. Who on your team is already strong at the one you are weakest at? ______________________________________________

What usually comes back

Run this enough times and a pattern shows up.

StrongWeak
Kaimahi. Almost everyone. New Zealand supervisors lead by working harder than everyone elseKaiarataki. Speaking up for your people to someone more senior. It carries risk and most people avoid it
Kaiwhakarite. It is what they are paid forKaikōtuitui. Nobody has time, and nobody has been told it is part of the job
Kaiako, second half. People teach constantly. Ask when they last learned something from someone junior to them and the room goes quiet

➜ Question 4 is the useful one. It moves this from a self-assessment to a team design question. You do not have to be all seven. The team has to be.

How to run it

  1. Teach the seven (12 min). Say the names properly. Give the workplace example for each. Do not rush the reo
  2. Fill the sheet (7 min). Silent. Both columns
  3. Questions 1 to 4 (6 min)
  4. Pairs (5 min). Share only question 3, the small specific thing

Debrief

  • Which role did the room score lowest on?
  • He Kaiako says a leader is a learner too. When did you last learn something from someone you supervise?
  • He Kaiarataki: what stops people advocating for their team?
  • What does this framework have that the Western leadership models we looked at do not?

That last question is the one worth the session. Guardianship, staying a learner, and advocacy do not have clean equivalents in Kotter or Blake-Mouton. That is not a gap in the Māori framework.

Variations

  • Team mapping: the team fills it in about each other, anonymously. Where are all seven covered? Where is nobody? Better than the individual version for an intact team
  • Pick one, one month: everyone commits to the role they scored lowest on, for one month. Review at the next session. The only version that changes behaviour
  • Compare version: run alongside ACT-093 Nine Roles, One Table (Belbin). One is Māori and about leadership, one is British and about team composition. The comparison teaches more than either alone
  • Low literacy: read the seven aloud with the examples, hands up for often / sometimes / never, questions 2 and 3 spoken in pairs

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This framework was written for kura, not for warehouses. The workplace examples are Zeducation's translation. Say that out loud, and do not present it as though the Ministry wrote it for a logistics yard
  • ⚠️ Pronunciation. Practise before the session. Kaikōtuitui and Kanohi Matara are the two facilitators most often mangle
  • ⚠️ Do not have the room score each other's cultural competence. This is about leadership behaviour, not about who is Māori enough
  • The seven-out-of-seven self-score. Ask for the "last time" column. It sorts it out
  • Treating the English translation as the meaning. Kaitiaki is not simply "guardian" and rangatiratanga is not simply "leadership". Say the reo and let it be bigger than the gloss

The Ten Moves Audit

25-30 minworksheet
diversityinclusionleadershipaction-planningauditworkplace

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-055 Accommodating Diversity.

This is the activity that stops a diversity session being an awareness session. Everybody leaves with two things to do and a day to do them on. Nobody leaves with ten.

On this pageThe auditNow the part that mattersGetting the actions small enoughHow to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The audit

For each move: does your workplace do this? Be honest, and answer about what actually happens rather than what the policy says.

MoveYesSort ofNoNot my call
1Everyone's name is said correctly, and people get corrected when they get it wrong☐☐☐☐
2The quiet ones get asked directly, by name, before the meeting☐☐☐☐
3Rosters flex for religious observance, tangi, school pickup, court, a sick kid☐☐☐☐
4Big meetings are not scheduled on major cultural or religious dates☐☐☐☐
5New starters learn how this team works with people, in week one☐☐☐☐
6Food gets shared, and people bring their own☐☐☐☐
7Staff who are studying get flexed around it☐☐☐☐
8Parents and carers are accommodated without having to ask as a favour☐☐☐☐
9More than one faith is acknowledged, and no one is required to have one☐☐☐☐
10Someone has asked the team what would make this a better place to work, and then done something☐☐☐☐

Now the part that matters

1. Pick TWO. Not five. Not ten. Two.

The moveWhat I will actually doBy when
A
B

2. For each one, answer: who will notice, and how will they know it was deliberate? ______________________________________________

3. What is the one you ticked "not my call" that you could raise with someone who can? ______________________________________________

Getting the actions small enough

Same discipline as everywhere else in this library. Learners write ambitions. Push them down to something that could happen on Tuesday.

They writePush them to
"Improve our culture around names""Ask the four people whose names I avoid, this week, and write them down phonetically"
"Be more inclusive in meetings""Text Sione on Wednesday: I want your view on the roster on Friday, have a think"
"Look at our rostering""Ask the two who go to mosque at lunchtime whether Friday afternoon works"
"Do a team survey""Ask three people one question each, in person, and write down what they say"

➜ Move 10 done badly is worse than not done. If they pick it, the commitment is not the asking. It is the doing something afterwards.

How to run it

  1. Teach the ten (10 min). Do not read them all out. Teach moves 1 to 4 properly and list the rest
  2. Audit, silent (7 min). The "not my call" column is important. Learners who supervise nobody still have moves 1, 2 and 6
  3. Pick two, write the actions (7 min). This is where the facilitator earns their money. Circulate and shrink things
  4. Pairs (5 min). Read your two out loud to one person. Saying it out loud is most of the commitment

Debrief

  • Which move did the room mostly answer "no" to?
  • Which one surprised you by being already done?
  • Move 1: how many of you have had your own name mangled at work? For how long?
  • Who picked move 2? What are you expecting to hear?

Variations

  • Team version: the whole team audits together and picks two as a team. The strongest version, and it needs someone with authority in the room
  • Follow-up session: collect the sheets, hand them back in a month. Did A and B happen? This is the single highest-value thing a facilitator can do with any action-planning activity
  • Manager and team split: managers audit, team audits, compare. The gap between the two answers on move 3 is usually large and instructive
  • Add your own eleventh: each learner writes a move that is missing from the list. The best ones get added to FRM-055
  • Low literacy: read the ten aloud, hands up per move, then do the "pick two" spoken in pairs

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not let anyone commit to move 10 without a plan for the answers. Asking a team what would make it better and then doing nothing damages trust more than never asking
  • ⚠️ "Not my call" is often true. Do not shame people who do not control the roster. Question 3 is there for exactly them
  • Picking the easy two. Kai and the calendar are cheap and visible. Names and asking the quiet ones are the ones that change something. Say so if a whole room drifts to 6 and 4
  • Turning the audit into a complaint session about the employer. Ten minutes of that is fine and useful. Then back to "which two are yours"
  • The learner who ticks yes to everything. Ask for the evidence on move 2. It is nearly always the one nobody actually does

Nine Roles, One Table

25-30 minworksheet
teamsrolesstrengthscollaborationself-awarenessteam-building

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then team · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-053 Belbin's Nine Team Roles.

⚠️ This is not the Belbin inventory. The official self-perception questionnaire is a paid product and it is the part researchers have criticised for thirty years. This activity uses the roles as a conversation, which is the useful and freely available half. See FRM-054 for why that distinction matters.

On this pageThe sheetThe teaching point is Part 2How to run itDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

The sheet

Part 1. Which of these sounds like you at work? Tick as many as are true. Most people tick three or four.

RoleSounds like
☐Shaper"Let's just get on with it." Pushes, challenges, thrives when it is tight
☐Implementer"Right, here's the plan." Turns talk into steps and then does them
☐Completer-Finisher"Has anyone checked this?" Catches what everyone else missed
☐Coordinator"What does everyone think?" Keeps the group on the goal, shares the work out
☐Team Worker"Are you alright?" Smooths it over, keeps people together
☐Resource Investigator"I know someone." Finds the gear, the contact, the option
☐Plant"What if we did it completely differently?" The ideas
☐Monitor-Evaluator"Hang on. Will that actually work?" Weighs it up cold
☐Specialist"That's my area." Deep knowledge of one thing

Part 2. Now the price. For each one you ticked, the matching weakness:

RoleThe weakness that comes with itDoes this sound like you?
ShaperCan argue, can bruise people
ImplementerSlow to accept a change to the plan
Completer-FinisherWorries, will not hand over
CoordinatorDelegates away their own share
Team WorkerAvoids the hard conversation
Resource InvestigatorEnthusiasm fades once it is not new
PlantWorks alone, takes criticism badly
Monitor-EvaluatorSlow to decide, flattens the energy
SpecialistNot interested in anything outside it

Part 3. Your team.

  1. Which roles are covered on your team? ______________________
  2. Which are missing? ______________________
  3. What has the missing one cost you? Name one actual thing that went wrong ______________________
  4. Who could cover it, even partly? ______________________

The teaching point is Part 2

Belbin called these allowable weaknesses, and the word "allowable" is doing all the work.

The weakness is the price of the strength, not a fault to be trained out. The Completer-Finisher who will not let go is why nothing has shipped broken. Try to fix the weakness and you usually lose the strength as well.

➜ So the leader's question changes from "how do I fix this person?" to "is this weakness one I can carry, given what I get?" Sometimes the answer is genuinely no. But it is a better question and it produces a different conversation.

How to run it

  1. Teach the three families first (10 min). Action, People, Thought. Do not read all nine with all their weaknesses, the room glazes over
  2. Part 1, individually (4 min)
  3. Part 2, individually (4 min). This is the part people go quiet for
  4. Part 3 (7 min). With an intact team, do this together on a whiteboard. With a mixed group, individually then pairs
  5. Room question: "which role is missing from most of your teams?" Monitor-Evaluator and Completer-Finisher win nearly always

Debrief

  • Which weakness did you recognise fastest? Was it the one attached to your strongest role?
  • Question 3: what did the missing role actually cost?
  • Has anyone here been told to fix something that was the price of what they are good at?
  • Do you play the same roles at home as you do at work?

That last one is the best test of whether the room has understood that this is behaviour and not personality. Most people play very different roles at home.

Variations

  • Team mapping, the best version: an intact team maps itself on a whiteboard. Names under roles. The gaps become visible in about four minutes and nobody argues with them
  • Peer nomination: instead of self-ticking, each person is told by two colleagues which roles they see. Frequently different from the self-assessment, and the difference is the interesting bit
  • The conflict read: take a real friction between two people on the team. Which roles are they playing? Often reframes a personality clash as two people doing their jobs. See FRM-018 Tuckman
  • Compare with Tū Rangatira: run alongside ACT-089 Seven Roles, One Kaupapa. One British and about team composition, one Māori and about leadership. The comparison teaches more than either alone
  • Low literacy: read the nine descriptions aloud, hands up. Part 3 spoken

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never assign someone a role. Same rule as everywhere in this library. Self-identified only, or peer-nominated with consent
  • ⚠️ "You're such a Plant" is not a compliment when it is used to dismiss an objection. Watch for the language becoming a way to avoid taking someone seriously
  • ⚠️ Be straight about the evidence if asked. The roles are a useful description, the questionnaire has been criticised since 1993, and this is a conversation tool. Do not oversell it
  • Ticking all nine. Ask for the weaknesses. It sorts itself out
  • Small teams. A four-person crew cannot cover nine roles. The point is not to have all nine, it is to know which one nobody is doing

The Skills You Don't Count

30-35 minworksheet
career-readinesstransferable-skillswork-readinessconfidencecv

Type: worksheet · Time: 30-35 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-057 Transferable Skills.

The activity exists for one sentence: "I haven't really got any experience." Most people who say it have fifteen years of it and no words for any of it.

On this pagePart 1 — the five places (12 min, individual)Part 2 — the translation (10 min, pairs)Part 3 — evidence (8 min, individual)Part 4 — the one lineHow to run itThe prompts that workDebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the five places (12 min, individual)

Do not write skills yet. Write what you have done. Two or three things in each box, however small.

WhereWhat have you done?
Paid work. Any job, any length, cash jobs count
Unpaid and family. Caring, budgeting, running a household, raising kids
Church, marae, community. Events, money, organising, speaking, cooking for numbers
Sport and culture. Playing, coaching, kapa haka, a band, a team you turned up for
Study and self-taught. Courses, and anything you learned off YouTube

Part 2 — the translation (10 min, pairs)

Swap sheets. Your partner reads yours and writes the skill name next to each thing. It is easier to see somebody else's skills than your own, which is the whole reason this part is done in pairs.

They wroteYou write the skill
"Did the food for the fono"Catering to budget and headcount · food safety
"Look after my nana"Personal care · medication support · working with nurses
"Ran the till"Cash handling · reconciliation · customer service

Use the full table on FRM-057 if you get stuck.

Part 3 — evidence (8 min, individual)

Pick your best five. Each one needs three parts, and the third is the one that gets read.

SkillWhereProof: a number, an outcome, or who would confirm it

⚠️ No proof, no bullet. A skill you cannot back up will not survive the interview, so it should not go on the CV.

Part 4 — the one line

Write your five best skills as one sentence you could actually say to somebody.

______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Teach FRM-057 first (12 min). The translation table does the heavy lifting
  2. Part 1, silent (12 min). Circulate. The prompt that unsticks people is "what do people ring you about?"
  3. Part 2, pairs (10 min). Insist they swap. Self-assessment produces a much shorter list
  4. Part 3 (8 min). Push hard on the proof column
  5. Part 4 (3 min). A few read theirs out if they want

The prompts that work

Modesty is the obstacle, not memory. These get past it:

Instead ofAsk
"What are your skills?""What do people ring you about?"
"What experience do you have?""What would fall over if you stopped doing it?"
"What are you good at?""What do you do that other people find hard?"
"Any leadership experience?""Who have you taught to do something?"

Debrief

  • What did your partner name that you would never have written yourself?
  • Which box was hardest to fill? Which was fullest?
  • Whose list surprised them?
  • What is one skill you have been leaving off applications?

Variations

  • Job ad version: bring a real job ad. Highlight every skill it asks for, then find where in your life you already did that. This is the version for a group close to applying
  • Whānau version: the homework is to ask one family member what they think you are good at. The answers are consistently better than the self-assessment
  • Three-column race: speed round on the translation table only. 10 minutes, for a group who have done the thinking already
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in pairs. Partner scribes. Nothing in this activity needs to be written by the person it is about

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Unpaid work is where the shame sits. Some learners, particularly women and particularly those out of paid work for years, will resist counting caring and community work. Be firm that it counts, and be honest that some employers discount it, which is why the evidence column matters
  • ⚠️ Do not inflate. There is a line between naming a skill accurately and claiming one you do not have. Everything written here has to survive "tell me about a time you did that"
  • The empty sheet. Somebody will freeze. Start them on the sport or church box, never paid work
  • The partner who is too polite. Give the translating partner permission to be generous. Their job is to find skills, not to moderate

The Tailoring Lab

40-50 minworksheet
career-readinesscvtailoringjob-searchwork-readinesspractice

Type: worksheet, then live editing · Time: 40-50 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-058 The CV That Gets Read.

Everyone leaves with a CV tailored to a real job they could apply for tonight. Not an exercise, a finished thing. That is the whole design.

On this pageBefore the sessionStep 1 — mine the ad (10 min)Step 2 — the headline (7 min)Step 3 — reorder (10 min)Step 4 — duties into achievements (10 min)Step 5 — the check (5 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Before the session

  • [ ] Ask everyone to bring their current CV and one real job ad they would actually go for
  • [ ] Bring spares of both. Half the room will not have them
  • [ ] Devices and wifi if you are using Tahatū's CV builder, which beats a blank Word document

Step 1 — mine the ad (10 min)

Highlight the job ad. Three colours, or three symbols.

MarkWhat to look for
Must-havesLicences, tickets, endorsements, legal requirements. "Class 2", "F endorsement", "must pass drug test"
Skill wordsEvery skill or task named. Write them exactly as the ad writes them
Their wordsPhrases the company repeats. "Safety-first", "whānau", "fast-paced"

Now list them:

The ad asks forWhere I have done itIs it on my CV now?
☐ yes ☐ no
☐ yes ☐ no
☐ yes ☐ no
☐ yes ☐ no
☐ yes ☐ no

⚠️ Any "no" in column three is the reason you did not get called.

Step 2 — the headline (7 min)

One line. What you are, for this job, in their words.

"Warehouse assistant with F endorsement and four years on nights."

My headline: ______________________________________________

Test it against three questions:

  • Does it use words from the ad? ☐
  • Would it be wrong for a different job? ☐ (if it fits any job, it is too vague)
  • Is the must-have in it, if there is one? ☐

Step 3 — reorder (10 min)

Your skill bullets, in the ad's order of importance, not yours.

#Skill bullet, with evidence
1
2
3
4

Step 4 — duties into achievements (10 min)

Take three lines off your current CV and rewrite them.

Line as it is nowRewritten with what changed

The test: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is still a duty.

Step 5 — the check (5 min, pairs)

Swap. Your partner has seven seconds on the top third, then answers one question:

"What job is this person going for?"

If they cannot say, it is not tailored yet.

Debrief

  • How many "no"s did you have in step 1?
  • What was in the ad that you have been doing for years and never wrote down?
  • Whose headline worked in seven seconds?
  • What is the job you are applying for, and when?

Variations

  • Two ads, one CV: tailor the same CV to two different jobs. Fastest way to make tailoring concrete
  • Do it in the tool: work directly in Tahatū's CV builder so they leave with a saved file, not a marked-up printout
  • Employer in the room: if you can get a real hiring manager for the last twenty minutes, do it. Beats any facilitator feedback
  • Short version: steps 1, 2 and 5 only. Twenty minutes and still worth doing
  • Low literacy: work in pairs throughout, one reads the ad aloud while the other marks. The headline can be spoken and scribed

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never invent to match the ad. If it asks for something they do not have, the honest moves are to apply anyway and address it in the cover letter, or to find out what it takes to get it. Not to claim it
  • ⚠️ Somebody's ad will need a ticket they do not have. That is useful information, not a failure. Turn it into the next step: what does that licence cost, and who pays for it?
  • The learner with no CV at all. Do not send them away. Start them at ACT-094 and have them build the top third only. That is a real morning's work
  • Design drift. Somebody will spend twenty minutes on fonts. Redirect to step 1
  • Do not let them finish without a date. "I'll do it later" is where this activity goes to die

Four Sentences

25-30 minworksheet
career-readinesscover-letterwritingjob-searchwork-readiness

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-060 The Four-Sentence Cover Letter.

Use the same job ad as ACT-097. One application, finished, in two activities.

On this pageWrite them out of orderNow read it back (5 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Write them out of order

Sentence 3 first. It is the hardest, it needs research, and once it is done the rest take five minutes.

3. Why them (10 min, and you will need a device)

Find one real, specific thing about this employer. A project, a site, a value they actually act on, a programme, who their customers are.

Where to look: their website's About page · their Facebook · the ad itself · Tahatū's profile of the industry · someone you know who works there.

What I found: ______________________________________________

Sentence 3: ______________________________________________

⚠️ It must be true and it must be specific. "I admire your commitment to excellence" is worse than leaving the sentence out.

1. Which job, and why this one (4 min)

Name the job. Name the employer. One honest reason.

______________________________________________

Honest reasons that are fine to write: the shifts fit around study · it is close to home · you have wanted to move into this work · somebody who works there told you about it.

2. What you bring (6 min)

The single strongest thing, in the ad's words, with evidence. Straight off your CV from ACT-097.

______________________________________________

4. What happens next (2 min)

Availability, and no fuss. "I'm available from the 12th and can come in any weekday."

______________________________________________

Now read it back (5 min, pairs)

Read your four sentences aloud to your partner. They answer three things:
Could this have been sent to any other employer?☐ yes ☐ no
Did sentence 2 have proof in it?☐ yes ☐ no
Would you ring this person?☐ yes ☐ no

A "yes" on the first question means sentence 3 is not doing its job.

Debrief

  • What did you find out about the employer that you did not know?
  • Who found something in sentence 3 that changed how they feel about the job?
  • What did you cut that you would normally have written?
  • Did anyone find out something that put them off? That is useful too

Variations

  • Cut-the-waffle round: hand out a real, bad, five-paragraph cover letter. Groups cut it to four sentences. Fast, funny, and the point lands hard
  • Cold-call version: the same four sentences, spoken, for ringing an employer who has not advertised. Pairs with FRM-061
  • AI round: have them ask an AI to write the letter, then mark it against the four sentences. It usually nails 1, 2 and 4 and invents something false for 3. Best possible demonstration of where AI helps and where it lies
  • Low literacy: all four spoken and scribed by a partner, then typed later. The thinking is the activity, not the typing

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Sentence 3 is where people invent. Be strict. An invented detail is worse than no sentence, because it is checkable and it is a lie in writing
  • ⚠️ Some learners will not be able to find anything about a small employer. That is fine. The fallback is something about the work itself or the location, honestly stated
  • The letter that becomes the CV again. If sentence 2 turns into a paragraph, cut it back. The CV is attached
  • Apologising. Watch for "although I don't have much experience" and take it out. Never open with a weakness
  • "Dear Sir/Madam" when the ad names a person. Small, and it reads as not paying attention

Three Questions

25-30 minworksheet
career-readinessinterviewsquestionsjob-searchwork-readinessfollow-up

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-062 The Questions You Ask Them.

Every interview ends with "do you have any questions for us?" Most people in the room have said no to that at least once. This activity means they never do it again.

On this pagePart 1 — the cost of "no" (5 min, whole room)Part 2 — build your three (12 min, individual)Part 3 — the ones that wait (5 min, whole room)Part 4 — say them out loud (8 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the cost of "no" (5 min, whole room)

Ask it straight: "who has said 'no, I think you've covered everything'?" Most hands go up.

Then put the three columns on the board and let the room fill them in:

What they meantWhat the interviewer heard
"I'm nervous and I can't think of anything"
"I didn't want to be a nuisance"
"I'll take whatever you give me"

➜ Nobody needs convincing after this. Move on quickly.

Part 2 — build your three (12 min, individual)

Four kinds. Take three in, from at least two different kinds.

1 · The job

What does a normal day look like? · What would you want me on top of in the first month? · What's the hardest part of this job?

Mine: ______________________________________________

2 · The people

Who would I be working with day to day? · How does the team hand over between shifts? · How long has the person doing this job been here?

Mine: ______________________________________________

3 · The future

Is there training or a ticket the company puts people through? · Where have people gone from this role?

Mine: ______________________________________________

4 · The process — always ask this one, and ask it last

What are the next steps, and when will you be in touch?

Now test each one:

Q1Q2Q3
Is the answer already on their website?☐☐☐
Could I ask this of any employer at all?☐☐☐
Would I actually want to know the answer?☐☐☐

A tick in the first two rows means rewrite it. A blank in the third means you picked it to sound good, and it will sound like it.

Part 3 — the ones that wait (5 min, whole room)

Read out eight things and have the room call NOW or AFTER THE OFFER.

Answer
The shift pattern and rosterNOW
Whether the pay range in the ad is rightNOW
Whether I can swap shifts with peopleAFTER
Whether there's training or a ticketNOW
Whether they'll pay for a course I want to doAFTER
The start dateNOW
A week off I already booked in three weeksNOW, at the end
Negotiating the numberAFTER

⚠️ Pay is allowed. Half the room will get this one wrong and it is the most useful correction in the activity. "The ad said $26 to $28 — is that right for this role?" is checking you can afford to take the job, not being greedy.

Part 4 — say them out loud (8 min, pairs)

The partner plays the interviewer and says one line only:

"Great — do you have any questions for us?"

Ask all three. Out loud, from the paper, in a normal voice. Swap.

The partner answers one thing: did that sound like interest, or like a list?

Debrief

  • Which of your three did you actually want to know the answer to?
  • Who found something on the employer's website while writing these? What was it?
  • What surprised you in Part 3?
  • Who has been in an interview and never asked what happens next? How long did you wait afterwards?

Variations

  • Real employer version: everyone uses the employer from ACT-097 and ACT-098. Best version by a distance, and it makes the whole sequence one application
  • Bolt-on: stop using this as a standalone and just make every ACT-099 roleplay finish with "any questions for us?" Cheaper and it builds the reflex faster
  • Employer panel: a real hiring manager takes the room's questions and says which ones they would actually rate. Twenty minutes, and worth more than the rest of the activity
  • The follow-up round: add ten minutes and write the three-line thank-you message as well. Phones out, drafted, saved
  • Low literacy: all spoken, scribed by a partner. Three questions held in the head is the goal, not three questions written neatly

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, questioning an elder or someone in authority is not straightforward. Do not treat it as a confidence problem to be fixed. Name it, and offer the opener that makes it comfortable: "Can I ask you something about the job?"
  • The memorised list asked regardless. If they covered it during the interview, say so and use a different one. That is the whole reason for taking three
  • Questions that are really complaints. "How much overtime is there?" is fine. Said in a certain tone it is heard as "I don't want to do any". Practise it out loud in Part 4
  • "How did I do?" Somebody will write it. It puts the interviewer on the spot and reads as anxious. Redirect them to question 4
  • Do not let anyone leave with fewer than three. Two is not enough when one gets answered

The Day Itself

30-40 minworksheet
career-readinessinterviewsbarrierslogisticswork-readinessequityonline-interviews

Type: worksheet, then practical problem-solving · Time: 30-40 min · Group: individual, then one-to-one · Energy: low

What it practises: the part of interview preparation that is not about confidence at all.

Most interview advice on the internet says "have an outfit ready". That sentence assumes a wardrobe, a car, a printer, a quiet room and nobody depending on you. Plenty of people in a Zeducation room have none of those, and it is why they do not get to the interview, not why they do badly in it.

⚠️ This activity produces a to-do list for the facilitator, not just for the learner. Do not run it unless you are prepared to act on what comes out.

On this pagePart 1 — the walk-through (12 min, individual)Part 2 — what to wear, honestly (6 min)Part 3 — if it is online (8 min, and it is a different set of problems)Part 4 — what goes in the bag (4 min)Part 5 — the ask (10 min, one-to-one)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the walk-through (12 min, individual)

Start at the interview and work backwards. Write the actual times.

Mine
InterviewDay, time, and where exactly
ArriveTen minutes early. What time is that?
Leave homeHow, and how long does it take?
Get readyWhat time do you need to start?
Night beforeWhat has to be done by then?

Now the questions underneath it:

✅ / ⚠️
Do I know exactly where it is? Have I looked at the door, not just the street?
How am I getting there? Bus, ride, drive, walk?
If it is a bus, do I know the actual times on that day?
Do I have the fare or the petrol?
Who is picking up the kids, and have I asked them yet?
Am I rostered to work? Have I sorted it?
Do I have their phone number, in my phone, in case something goes wrong?
Is my phone going to be charged and have credit?

⚠️ Any ⚠️ is a real problem with a real solution. It is not a character flaw and it does not get fixed by wanting the job more.

Part 2 — what to wear, honestly (6 min)

Not "have an outfit ready". The actual question:

Do you have something to wear? Yes or no.

If no, that is the most useful thing you will say all week, and it is fixable by Thursday. Options that work: a family member's, a community or church clothing pool, Dress for Success or an equivalent, the programme's own kit if you have one, a good op shop.

The standard, and it is lower than people think:
Clean, tidy, and one step smarter than the jobWarehouse interview: a collared shirt. Office: a bit more
Comfortable enough to sit in for an hourNew shoes are a mistake
Whatever you can be yourself inIe faitaga, a tapa print, a taonga. Do not tell anyone to take off who they are. If an employer holds that against somebody, the problem is the employer and it is worth knowing early

⚠️ A facilitator's job here is to solve the problem, not to inspect anyone. Never comment on somebody's clothes in front of the room.

Part 3 — if it is online (8 min, and it is a different set of problems)

✅ / ⚠️
Do I have a device that will do video, and is it charged?
Do I have data or wifi that will hold for 45 minutes?
Do I have a room where nobody will walk in?
Have I clicked the link before the day to check it works?
Do I know what is behind me on camera?
Do I have their phone number for when it drops out?

➜ "I'll use my phone on the bus" is the answer that ends the interview. If there is no room and no data, the programme's own space is often the answer. Say so, and book it.

Part 4 — what goes in the bag (4 min)
Two printed copies of the CVThey lose them, or there is a second interviewer
Your three questions, written downFrom ACT-102
Licence, tickets, endorsements — the actual cardsNot a photo of them
Referees' names and numbers on paperSo it is not "I'll have to text you"
A penSomebody always needs one
WaterAnd a snack if it is a panel

Part 5 — the ask (10 min, one-to-one)

Everyone with a ⚠️ talks to the facilitator before they leave the room. Not later.

My ⚠️What would fix itWho I'll askBy when

Debrief

Room level, and keep it practical.

  • What was the thing you had not thought about at all?
  • Who has missed an interview for a reason that had nothing to do with being able to do the job?
  • What is the one thing you need to sort this week?

Variations

  • Do it for a real interview: if anybody in the room has one booked, do the whole thing on theirs and let everyone watch. Ten times better than the hypothetical
  • The dry run: for a first interview, actually travel to the address beforehand. Some programmes do it as a group trip and it removes an enormous amount of fear
  • Online-only version: for a rural or remote group, Part 3 is the whole activity. Give it forty minutes
  • Employer's version: ask a hiring manager what actually goes wrong. Late, no ID, no referees, camera off, dropped out and never rang back. It lands harder from them
  • Low literacy: do it as a conversation with a scribe. The checklist is a prompt sheet for the facilitator, not a test

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This will surface hardship. No money for the bus, no clothes, no childcare, unsafe housing, no device. Do not run it unless you can act on it. Know your options first: the programme's own fund if there is one, their MSD case manager, a community clothing pool, Work and Income's transition to work support
  • ⚠️ Nobody's barriers get named in front of the room. Part 5 is one-to-one. Say that at the start
  • Do not turn it into a grooming lecture. No commentary on hair, jewellery, tattoos, or how somebody carries themselves. That is not this activity and it is not our business
  • Never advise anybody to hide who they are. Cultural dress, taonga and moko are not problems to be managed. An employer who treats them as one has told you something useful
  • "I'll be fine" from the learner who will not be fine. The walk-through in Part 1 is designed to make it concrete without anyone having to admit anything. Let the times do the work
  • Do not skip the phone number. Being twenty minutes late and able to ring is survivable. Being twenty minutes late and silent is not

Three Quotes

25-30 minworksheet
wellbeingresilienceopenervaluesstrengthsreflectionhauora

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the framing in FRM-066 Resilience Is Ordinary, and it surfaces the strengths a learner already has before anybody teaches them a tool.

Straight from the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide. The house note underneath it is the best paragraph in the resource and it is kept word for word in spirit: the quotes you chose are not random.

On this pagePart 1 — find three (10 min, individual)Part 2 — the note that matters (5 min, read it out)Part 3 — name the strength (7 min, pairs)Part 4 — the small step (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — find three (10 min, individual)

Three quotes about resilience. Or mindset, perseverance, hope, courage, getting up again.

Bring your own, search for some, or use the sheet. A line from a song counts. A whakataukī counts. Something your nana says counts.

QuoteWhat it means to me. Why it stood out, or a story it connects to

⚠️ Do not hand out a list of famous quotes and skip the searching. The looking is part of it. Have a printed sheet as a backup for anyone without a phone, and do not make a thing of who needs it.

Part 2 — the note that matters (5 min, read it out)

Read this to the room, slowly.

The quotes you chose are not random. They landed because they connect to your values, your experiences and your strengths. That pull you felt is a signal: you already have resilience to build on. Maybe a line reminded you of a time you kept going. Maybe it put words to something you believe about courage, or hope, or asking for help. Resilience grows out of what is already there. Notice it, name it, build on it.

Part 3 — name the strength (7 min, pairs)

Read one quote to your partner and say why it landed. Then they answer one question:

"What does that tell me about you?"

Write down what they say. In their words, not yours.

The quoteThe strength my partner named in me

➜ This is the part people remember. Being handed a word for something you did not know showed is worth more than any amount of self-reflection.

Part 4 — the small step (5 min)

One sentence.

A strength I already have is: ______________________________________________

One place I could use it this week: ______________________________________________

Debrief

  • Which quote came fastest? What does that say?
  • Did anyone pick something in a language other than English? Read it to us
  • What did your partner name in you that you would not have said about yourself?
  • Whose voice is in your quote? Who taught you that?

Variations

  • Whakataukī and Pacific proverbs only. Far better in a Māori or Pacific room, and the room will supply them. Ask before you assume nobody has any
  • Song lyrics version: for a young group, lyrics beat quotes every time. Phones out, play one
  • Wall version: everyone writes their strongest quote on a big sheet and it stays on the wall for the rest of the programme. Cheap, and it keeps working for weeks
  • One quote version: ten minutes, one quote, straight to Part 3. Good as an opener when time is short
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken. Say a line you carry, say why. Nothing is written except the strength in Part 4

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ A quote can bring somebody's whole situation into the room. Grief, illness, a person they lost. Let it be brief, be warm, and do not turn it into the session. Know your referrals: 1737 to call or text free, their GP, workplace EAP
  • Do not correct anyone's choice. If somebody picks something from a movie or an influencer, that is fine. What it means to them is the activity, not the quality of the source
  • The learner who says "I couldn't find any". Usually means "I don't want to". Give them the backup sheet and let them pick three without explaining. They will still do Part 3
  • Do not let the search become twenty minutes on the phone. Timebox it out loud
  • Skipping Part 2. The read-aloud note is what turns a nice warm-up into the actual point

One Thing Per Wall

25-30 minassessment
wellbeinghauorate-whare-tapa-whafonofaleself-assessmentresilienceidentity

Type: self-assessment · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-063 Te Whare Tapa Whā and FRM-065 Fonofale.

Both models are on the sheet and the learner picks. That is the design, and it is not a small detail. A room offered only one model has been told which half of itself counts.

⚠️ This is not a score. There is no total, no rating out of ten, and nothing to hand in. One thing per wall that needs care. That is the entire instrument.

On this pageBefore you start — say this out loudPart 1 — pick your house (2 min)Part 2A — Te Whare Tapa Whā (12 min)Part 2B — Fonofale (12 min)Part 3 — the two questions (6 min)Part 4 — one wall, one step (5 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Before you start — say this out loud

Nobody sees this but you and whoever you choose to show it to. There is no score. You are not being assessed on your wellbeing. We are naming what needs care, that is all.

Part 1 — pick your house (2 min)
☐ Te Whare Tapa WhāThe wharenui. Four walls on the whenua
☐ FonofaleThe fale. Culture on top, aiga underneath, four pou between

Either is fine. Both is fine. Nobody comments on anybody's choice.

Part 2A — Te Whare Tapa Whā (12 min)

One thing per pou that needs care so you can bounce back better. Not a life plan. One thing.

PouOne thing that needs care
Taha wairuaSpirit, purpose, faith, what makes it mean something
Taha hinengaroMind and emotions
Taha tinanaBody. Sleep, food, movement, health
Taha whānauFamily, the people you belong to
Taha whenuaConnection to place, land, where you are from

Part 2B — Fonofale (12 min)

PartOne thing that needs care
Roof · cultureYour beliefs and values. What shelters everything
Floor · aigaFamily, immediate and extended, and anyone you are linked to
Pou · spiritualFaith, the sacred, identity and purpose
Pou · physicalThe body
Pou · mentalEmotions, thinking, motivation
Pou · otherAge, gender, sexuality, money, status
Around it allEnvironment, time, what is going on right now

Part 3 — the two questions (6 min)

1. Which one has been holding everything up on its own?

______________________________________________

2. Which one have you been letting go?

______________________________________________

➜ Most people answer both fast, because the model gives them a word for something they already knew. That is what a good model does.

Part 4 — one wall, one step (5 min, pairs)

Pick one. Not five.
The wall I'm working on
One thing I'll do, 15 minutes or less
When
Who will know

Say it to your partner. They write down what you said and read it back. That is all they do.

Debrief

Whole room, and general only.

  • Which house did people pick? (Take a count, do not ask anyone why)
  • Which wall does this room let go of most? (Usually tinana. Sometimes wairua)
  • What was easier, naming what needs care or naming what is holding you up?
  • Who found the "other" pou useful? (Only if the room raised it first)

Variations

  • Drawn version: everyone draws their own whare or fale, sized by how each wall is going. A tall strong wall, a short thin one. Far more revealing than writing and it works for any literacy level
  • Whānau version: do it for the household rather than the individual. Powerful for a room of parents
  • Team version: a team fills one in for the team. Works well, and it needs a facilitator who will hold the line on it staying about the team and not about individuals
  • Revisit version: run it in week one and again in week eight. Do not compare scores, because there are none. Compare what has moved
  • Ten-minute version: Part 1, one wall, Part 4. Still worth doing

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never fill one in about a learner. It is a self-check. A hauora model used to assess somebody else is doing the opposite of what it was built for
  • ⚠️ Do not turn it into a score. Somebody will ask what a good result looks like. There is not one. Say so
  • ⚠️ This will surface real things. Isolation, grief, illness, money, an unsafe house. Have your referrals ready before you run it: their GP, 1737 to call or text free, workplace EAP, their MSD case manager
  • Whenua and migrants. Somebody will say "I'm not from here". That is not a problem with the model, it is the most important pou in their sheet. Ask about where they are from, not where they live
  • Wairua and religion. For some it is church. For others it is the moana, music, a garden, their kids. Do not narrow it and do not assume
  • Aiga is not only a resource. For some learners family is the load. If somebody writes that, do not correct it
  • The learner who fills in all five with big problems. Bring them back to Part 4 and one wall. Then talk to them afterwards

The ABC Worksheet

30-40 minworksheet
wellbeingresilienceabc-modelsetbacksactionself-efficacyhouse-content

Type: worksheet · Time: 30-40 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-064 The ABC Model of Resilience.

Taken close to the original from the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide, including the confidence check, which is the part that proves the model in front of the room.

⚠️ Use a real, current, small setback. Not a hypothetical. The activity does nothing on an invented example, and it does a lot on somebody's actual week.

On this pageMy situationA — AcceptB — BelieveC — CommitThe confidence checkPart 2 — say the step out loud (8 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

My situation

What happened? ______________________________________________

⚠️ You will not be asked to share this. Write enough that you know what you mean.

A — Accept

What are the facts? Just what happened. No interpretation, no blame, no story.

______________________________________________

I can controlI cannot control

➜ Accept does not mean "get over it" and it does not mean it was fine. It means naming the facts so you can stop arguing with the part that will not move, and start on the part that will.

B — Believe

A past win. A time you got through something like this. Anything counts, and it does not have to be big.

______________________________________________

What did you do then that you could do again?

______________________________________________

Strengths I'll use:

☐ courage ☐ planning ☐ asking for help ☐ persistence ☐ creativity ☐ humour ☐ faith ☐ patience

☐ other: ________________

Who is in my corner? Name people, not categories.

______________________________________________

⚠️ This is the step people rush, and it is the one with the research behind it. Being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe it. Remembering that you already did is the strongest.

C — Commit

One small step. Fifteen minutes maximum.

______________________________________________
When
Done means

Test it:

Yes / No
Could I do this in 15 minutes?☐
Is there a day and a time on it?☐
Would somebody else be able to tell whether I did it?☐

A "no" anywhere means it is still too big. Cut it down.

The confidence check
Confidence before I started this sheet___ / 10
Confidence now I have a plan___ / 10

⚠️ Not a score of anything and nobody records it. It is a mirror.

➜ The movement is the lesson. Most people move two or three points in fifteen minutes and nothing about the situation has changed. Point that out. It is the most persuasive thing that happens in the session.

If it did not move, that is useful too, and it usually means step C is still too big. Go back and cut it in half.

Part 2 — say the step out loud (8 min, pairs)

You say only your step C, not the situation. Your partner asks three questions and nothing else:

  1. "When?"
  2. "What does done look like?"
  3. "Who will know you did it?"

Then swap.

⚠️ The partner does not give advice, does not ask what happened, and does not fix anything. Say that before you start, because everybody will want to.

Debrief

  • Did your confidence move? By how much? Did anything about the situation change?
  • What went in the "cannot control" column that you have been spending a lot of energy on?
  • Which past win did you use? When did you last think about it?
  • Whose name went in "who is in my corner"? Do they know?

Variations

  • Team version: one sheet, a shared setback. A lost tender, a bad audit, a restructure. Works well and the "cannot control" column is where the useful argument happens
  • Coaching version: one-to-one, spoken, no sheet. The three columns as three questions
  • The fortnight-later version: bring the sheets back out. Did the step happen? This is where the model either becomes real or does not, and skipping it is why most tools die in the room they were taught in
  • Whiteboard version: the facilitator does one live, on a real setback offered by the room. Best possible teaching of step C, because everyone watches a big step get cut into a small one
  • Low literacy: spoken with a scribe, or the three headings as three sticky notes

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Somebody's "setback" will be much bigger than a setback. A bereavement, a diagnosis, a relationship ending, a job loss that means the rent. ABC is not for those. Say so plainly at the start, tell them it is fine to pick something smaller for today, and know where to send them: their GP, 1737 to call or text free, workplace EAP, their MSD case manager
  • ⚠️ Nobody has to share their situation. Ever. Part 2 is the step only. Anyone can pass
  • "Accept" heard as "it was your fault" or "get over it". The single most common misfire. Say what it means before they write, not after
  • Step C that is a whole project. "Sort my life out" is not a step. "Ring the doctor at 9am Tuesday" is. Be strict, because this is where the activity is won
  • A past win that gets dismissed. "That wasn't really anything." Push back once, gently. It counts
  • The empty "who is in my corner" line. That is real information. Do not let it pass unnoticed, and follow it up afterwards rather than in the room

The Unwritten Rules Hunt

25-30 minworksheet
work-readinessonboardingstarting-workunwritten-rulesquestionsretention

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: move 4 of FRM-068 The First Two Weeks.

Every workplace has rules nobody writes down. Breaking one costs more than breaking a written rule, and somebody who has never worked in that setting has no way to guess any of them.

On this pagePart 1 — the room already knows (8 min, whole room)Part 2 — the twenty questions (10 min, individual)Part 3 — who do you ask (5 min, pairs)Part 4 — the three you will actually ask (5 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the room already knows (8 min, whole room)

Ask it straight:

"What is something you only found out about a job after you got it wrong?"

Collect them on the board. You will get twenty in five minutes and they will be things like:

  • smoko is 9:45 not 10:00, and it is fifteen minutes not twenty
  • you text the supervisor, not the office, and before 6am
  • that chair is somebody's chair
  • boots on at seven means boots on, not arriving at seven
  • you do not go home until the truck is loaded, whatever the roster says

➜ Do not teach anything yet. The board is the teaching.

Part 2 — the twenty questions (10 min, individual)

The things to find out in week one. Tick the ones you would not have thought to ask.

#The question☐
1What time does the day actually start?☐
2Who do I tell when I am sick, how, and how early?☐
3When is smoko, how long, and where do people go?☐
4Where do I park, and is it free?☐
5What do people wear? Is there anything I need to buy?☐
6Is my phone allowed out? When?☐
7Who has been here longest?☐
8Who do I ask when my supervisor is not here?☐
9How do I ask for a day off, and how far ahead?☐
10When do I get paid, and how often?☐
11Do I get a break if I work through?☐
12Where is the first aid kit and who is the first aider?☐
13What do I do if I finish my job early?☐
14Is there anything I am not allowed to touch or do yet?☐
15What does a good day look like here?☐
16What is the thing new people usually get wrong?☐
17Do people eat together, or separately?☐
18Is overtime expected, offered, or neither?☐
19How will I know if I am doing okay?☐
20Who signs my timesheet, and by when?☐

⚠️ Questions 15 and 16 are the two most valuable on the sheet and almost nobody asks them. "What's the thing new people usually get wrong?" is a gift to a supervisor, because they get to tell you instead of correcting you later.

Part 3 — who do you ask (5 min, pairs)

Not everything goes to the supervisor. Sort five of your questions:

Ask the supervisorAsk a workmateWatch and work it out

➜ Most of the twenty go to a workmate, and the person who has been there longest is the best source in the building. That is question 7 doing its work.

Part 4 — the three you will actually ask (5 min)

My questionWho I will askWhen

Say the first one out loud to your partner. Practise the wording, because "what time do we actually start?" sounds different from "sorry, um, what time was it again?"

Debrief

  • How many of the twenty had you not thought of?
  • Which one would have caused you the most trouble?
  • Who has got one of these wrong before? What happened?
  • Why do you think nobody writes these down?
  • Which one is hardest to ask, and why?

Variations

  • Real job version: if somebody in the room starts a job next week, do the whole thing on theirs and let the room help. Best possible version
  • Sector sets: build a separate twenty for construction, care, retail and warehousing. The rules are genuinely different and your tutors know them
  • Employer answers: send the twenty to a friendly employer and bring their answers back. Powerful, and it takes one email
  • The other side: for a supervisors' group, ask which of the twenty they actually tell people, and watch them realise it is about four
  • Low literacy: whole thing spoken, facilitator scribes on the board, learners take a photo

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not let it become a list of things learners are expected to already know. The whole point is that nobody is told these and everybody is judged on them. Say that out loud at the start
  • The room that says "that's just common sense". It is common sense once you have worked somewhere. It is invisible if you have not
  • Somebody who has been sacked over one of these. Likely. Keep it about the mechanism, do not ask for the story, and do not let the room laugh at a real one
  • Do not add a twenty-first about attitude. This sheet is information, not character

Three Needs, One Team

30-35 minworksheet
leadershipmotivationself-determinationautonomycompetencerelatednessteams

Type: worksheet · Time: 30-35 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-070 Self-Determination Theory.

The room already knows this model. They have lived both sides of it. This activity gets it out of them before it is taught, then hands them the words.

On this pagePart 1 — best job, worst job (10 min, individual)Part 2 — the three, on a real team (12 min)Part 3 — one free thing (8 min, pairs)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — best job, worst job (10 min, individual)

Do this before any teaching.

The best job you have hadThe worst job you have had
What was it?
Did you get any say in how you did the work?
Did you feel like you were getting good at something?
Did people know your name and notice if you were away?
What was the pay like?

➜ Now the room reads the pattern back to you. Almost always the best job scored yes on the middle three and not necessarily better on pay. That is the whole model, discovered rather than taught.

Only now put the three needs on the board: autonomy, competence, relatedness.

Part 2 — the three, on a real team (12 min)

Pick one real team you are in or lead. Score nothing. Just answer.

Autonomy — some say inside the rules

Where does somebody on this team get to choose something?

______________________________________________

Where do they get no say at all, and does that need to be true?

______________________________________________

Competence — getting better, and knowing it

How does somebody on this team learn the job properly?

______________________________________________

When did anyone last get told they had done something well, specifically?

______________________________________________

Relatedness — known, and missed when away

Who on this team would not be noticed if they did not turn up?

______________________________________________

⚠️ That last question is the sharpest on the sheet. Sit with the answer.

Part 3 — one free thing (8 min, pairs)

All three needs cost nothing. Find one move for each that requires no budget and no permission.

NeedOne thing I could do this weekWhen
Autonomy
Competence
Relatedness

Say them to your partner. They ask one question only: "does that cost anything?" If it does, find another one.

➜ Examples that cost nothing: letting somebody choose the order of their jobs · showing one person one thing properly · learning how to say a name correctly · saying what somebody did well, specifically, in front of one other person.

Debrief

  • What did the best job and worst job comparison show?
  • Which of the three is weakest on your team? Which is strongest?
  • Who would not be missed? What are you going to do about it?
  • Which one is hardest to give people in your workplace, and is that a real constraint or a habit?
  • Where did pay actually sit in your two jobs?

Variations

  • Self-check version: run the whole thing on yourself rather than a team. Which of my three is missing right now? Works well in a wellbeing session
  • Learner version: run it on this programme rather than a workplace. Brave, useful, and your tutors will learn something
  • Team version: the whole team fills it in and compares. Needs trust and it is the most honest version
  • Two-column version: for a supervisors' group, ask them to answer once as themselves and once as they think their team would answer. The gap is the conversation
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in pairs, facilitator captures the free moves on the board

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not let it become an argument that pay does not matter. It does. Below enough, nothing else works, and a room on low wages will rightly walk out on anybody who says otherwise. Say that first, out loud
  • "I can't give them autonomy, it's a factory." Push gently. Autonomy is some say inside the rules, and there is almost always a choice available somewhere
  • The person who realises they are the one who would not be missed. It happens. Handle it warmly and follow up afterwards, not in the room
  • Do not score it. There is no total and no benchmark
  • The supervisor who blames their own manager. Often fair. Bring them back to what is inside their own reach, which is Part 3

Build Your Master Prompt

30-35 minworksheet
digital-capabilityaipromptingcontextreusepractice

Type: worksheet · Time: 30-35 min · Group: individual, at devices · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-076 The Master Prompt, built using FRM-074 pull prompting.

Everybody leaves with a saved document about themselves that makes every AI answer they get from now on about their actual situation. Not an exercise. A thing they keep.

On this pagePart 1 — the rule, before anybody types (4 min)Part 2 — let it interview you (12 min)Part 3 — check it has these seven rows (8 min)Part 4 — save it, and prove it works (8 min)DebriefVariationsWatch out forUsed byRelated activities

Part 1 — the rule, before anybody types (4 min)

⚠️ Say this first, every time.

You are going to paste this into a public tool, many times. So it must not contain: your address · your IRD or bank number · health information · anybody else's name or situation · anything about a learner, client or patient. "I work with young people leaving school in South Auckland" is fine. A name is not.

Part 2 — let it interview you (12 min)

Do not write it yourself. Type this:

"I want to make a master prompt about me, so I never have to explain my situation every time I ask you something. Ask me all the questions you need, one at a time."

Answer the questions. ➜ Use voice-to-text. There will be a lot and most people will not type them.

If it asks something you should not answer: "I'm not giving you that. Work with what you have." ⚠️ Practise saying that once, out loud, before Part 2 starts.

Part 3 — check it has these seven rows (8 min)

Read what it gave you. Anything missing, tell it to add.

Row☐
1Who I am — name, where, what I do☐
2What I'm working on right now☐
3Who I'm doing it for☐
4What I already have — tickets, licences, experience, quals☐
5What I'm trying to get to☐
6How I want it to sound☐
7What to never assume☐

Rows 6 and 7, use these words if you have not got better ones:

6. "Plain words. New Zealand English. Short sentences. No dashes. Don't oversell me." 7. "I'm in New Zealand. Don't use US law, US pay rates, US job titles or US spelling."

⚠️ Row 7 earns its place in the first five minutes. These tools default to American everything and a learner will get handed a US resume format without either of you noticing.

Fix anything wrong by talking to it: "You've got that wrong, I'm not a manager, I'm a storeperson."

Part 4 — save it, and prove it works (8 min)

Save it. ➜ A note on your phone is fine. It does not need to be a PDF.
Where I saved it
What I called it

Now the test. Ask the same question twice:

  1. In a brand new chat, ask something real. "What should I do next about getting work?"
  2. New chat again. Paste your master prompt first, then the same question

What changed? ______________________________________________

➜ This is the moment the room stops needing convincing.

Debrief

  • What did it ask you that you had not thought about yourself?
  • What did it get wrong about you first time?
  • What is different between the two answers in Part 4?
  • Did anybody nearly put something in that they should not have?
  • When will you next use it, and for what?

Variations

  • Job-search version: narrow the whole thing to looking for work. Sharper for a work-readiness group
  • Tutor version: staff build one about their teaching role. Do this before you run it with learners so you know what it feels like
  • Whānau version: one about their household, for budgeting, school, appointments. Useful, and the privacy rule matters even more
  • Zeducation house version: ⚠️ one about the organisation — who we serve, our voice, our rules — so staff outputs stay consistent. Worth building properly
  • Low tech: the seven rows filled in on paper, typed up later. The thinking is the activity

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ People over-share when a machine asks politely. Walk the room during Part 2. Check what learners have put in before they start pasting it everywhere
  • ⚠️ Devices, wifi and accounts. Check the week before. Age limits apply on some tools and a learner without an account cannot do Part 2
  • The five-page master prompt. One page. It is context, not a biography
  • Row 4 will be thin for anybody who has not done TOP-EMP-002. That is useful information, and the fix is that topic, not this one
  • Do not skip Part 4. The before-and-after is what makes them actually use it
