Find Your Places

20 min in the room, then a weekworksheet
pepehaidentitywhakapapabelonginghomeworkwhanaute-ao-maori

Type: worksheet with homework · Time: 20 min in the room, then a week · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-077 The Water Cycle, and it is the step before FRM-078 or FRM-079.

➜ This is the activity the resource does not have, and it is the one that decides whether anybody finishes. Hand out a pepeha template cold and roughly half the room stops on line two. Not because it is hard, but because they do not know the answer and have never been given permission to say so.

On this pageBefore you start — say this out loudPart 1 — what you already know (10 min)Part 2 — who to ask (5 min)Part 3 — how to ask (5 min)The homeworkBringing it back⚠️ Do notRelated activitiesUsed by

Before you start — say this out loud

Not knowing your maunga is not a gap in you. It is a gap in what got passed down, and that happened to a lot of families for reasons that were not their fault. The answer is not on Google. It is with somebody in your whānau, and the asking is the whole exercise.

Part 1 — what you already know (10 min)

Fill in only what you are sure about. Leave the rest blank. Blank is data.

I know itI think I know itNo idea
Where my mother's people are from☐☐☐
Where my father's people are from☐☐☐
The town or village☐☐☐
Maunga (if you whakapapa Māori)☐☐☐
Awa or moana☐☐☐
Waka☐☐☐
Iwi☐☐☐
Hapū☐☐☐
Marae☐☐☐
The place I grew up☐☐☐
The place I call home now☐☐☐

Most people fill in the bottom two and not much else. Say that in the room, before anybody looks sideways at their neighbour's sheet.

Part 2 — who to ask (5 min)

Write down one name and one way to reach them. Not three. One.
The person who knows............................................
How I'll ask☐ phone ☐ in person ☐ text ☐ next time I see them
When............................................

Who usually knows: a nan or a koro, an aunty, the one cousin who did the family tree, the person who does the whaikōrero at tangi. It is rarely a parent — it is usually a generation further back or one sideways.

If there is nobody: that is a real answer and it is not rare. Write "nobody" and go on. There are other routes — a marae office, an iwi register, Te Puni Kōkiri, Archives NZ, a birth certificate with a place on it — but they take longer than a week and none of them is homework.

Part 3 — how to ask (5 min)

The ask is one sentence. Practise it on the person next to you.

"I'm doing something at course where I write my pepeha. Can you tell me where our people are from?"

Then stop talking. Most people who know this will talk for forty minutes and you will get far more than you asked for.

➜ Record it if they say yes. Voice memo on your phone. Names and places do not survive being remembered.

⚠️ Two things to expect. Some people will not want to talk about it, and that is theirs to decide, not yours to push. And some answers come back contested — two aunties, two different maunga. That is normal. Write down both and ask a third person.

The homework

One conversation. One week. Bring back whatever you got, including nothing.

Bringing it back

Ten minutes at the top of the next session. Do not go round the room in order — ask who wants to share, take three or four, and move on.

Ask for the thing they did not expect, not the list of place names. That is where the stories are, and it is what makes the next person want to ask their own aunty.

⚠️ Do not

  • Do not ask a model. AI will invent a maunga, an awa and an iwi, immediately and confidently, and it is markedly weaker in te reo Māori than in English — FRM-075. A pepeha built that way names a mountain with no connection to the person saying it.
  • Do not require it. Nobody is assessed on whether their whānau answered the phone.
  • Do not make the blanks visible. No reading out, no comparing sheets, no wall display.

ACT-120Activity · Wellbeing & Identity

Fill In The Template

25-30 minworksheet
pepehaidentitywhakapapabelongingintroductionste-ao-maorihouse-content

Type: worksheet · Time: 25-30 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-078 Pepeha for Māori Whānau and FRM-079 Pepeha for Non-Māori Whānau.

Both templates are on one sheet and the learner picks. That is the design and it is not a small detail — it is the same rule as ACT-105 in this pillar.

⚠️ Nobody gets handed a version based on your guess about their whakapapa. You do not know who in the room is Māori by looking at them, and being sorted by somebody else's guess is exactly the experience this topic is trying not to repeat.

On this pageBefore you startPart 1 — pick your template (2 min)Part 2 — fill it in (15 min)Part 3 — read it to one person (8 min)Part 4 — the one line (5 min)Facilitator notes⚠️ Do notRelated activitiesUsed by

Before you start

FRM-077 The Water Cycle is taught first. Two minutes, whiteboard, the diagram. If the room has not had that, they will read two templates and assume one of them is the real one and the other is the consolation prize.

And say this:

If you already have your pepeha — from your marae, from your kura, from your nan — yours is right and this sheet is not. Pepeha differ by rohe. Use this only if you have nothing written down.

Part 1 — pick your template (2 min)
☐ Māori whānauMaunga, awa, waka, iwi, hapū, mātua, kāinga, ingoa
☐ Non-Māori whānauWhakapaparanga mai, engari, whenua tupu, kāinga, nō, noho, mahi, ingoa

Some people will be unsure and that is allowed. Somebody whose mother is Māori and whose father is Tongan is not doing this wrong. Do one, then do the other, and see which one sounds like you.

Part 2 — fill it in (15 min)

Use whatever you brought back from ACT-119. Pencil, not pen, if it helps.

Rules for this part, and say all three:

  1. Blank lines are allowed. A short true pepeha beats a long guessed one.
  2. Nobody has to name a parent they do not want to name. Skip the line. No explanation owed.
  3. Do not fill a gap with something that sounds right. If you do not know your awa, leave the awa.

Part 3 — read it to one person (8 min)

Pairs. Read it out once each. The listener's only job is to say one thing back:

"The bit I want to know more about is ..."

No corrections, no pronunciation coaching, no advice. That is Part 3 of the next activity, and doing it here kills the room.

Part 4 — the one line (5 min)

Write, at the bottom of the sheet:

The connection I am hoping somebody makes with this is ...

➜ That line is the point of the whole exercise. A pepeha is an offer, not a credential. If a learner writes "nothing, I just have to do it", the purpose did not land and it is worth two more minutes on FRM-077.

Facilitator notes

  • This sheet does not get collected, marked, or displayed. It goes home with them.
  • Expect the non-Māori template to land harder than you think. The engari line — my ancestry is X, but I grew up in Y — is the first time a lot of migrant and second-generation learners have been handed a form that lets both be true. Leave space for that.
  • If somebody says they do not want to do it at all, that is fine and it is not a discipline matter. Give them the sheet to take home.
  • Macrons matter and this is a worksheet, not a test. If a learner writes one wrong, leave it. Pronunciation is ACT-121.

⚠️ Do not

No AI on this sheet. Not to fill a gap, not to check the reo, not to "tidy it up". A model will complete a pepeha instantly and confidently and it is markedly weaker in te reo Māori than in English — FRM-075. Ask a person.

READMEpage · README.md

Zeducation Content Library

The place every piece of Zeducation teaching content lives, in a shape you can build from.

Content arrives raw — a YouTube video, an article, a workbook, a transcript, notes off a whiteboard. It gets dissected, written up to one standard, connected to everything related, and indexed. Later, when you need to build a workshop, a module or a student workbook, you pull the pieces back out instead of starting from a blank page.

Managed by the zeducation-content-organiser skill. Say "add this to the library" with any content attached, or "what have we got on feedback?", or "build me a 90 minute workshop on assertiveness".

On this pageBrowse it, don't read itStart hereHow it is organisedEvery topic looks the sameThree rules that keep it working

Browse it, don't read it

The whole library is also a clickable page: _site/index.html. Download it and open it in any browser. Search box, nav rail down the side, and every link between topics, frameworks and activities works. It is one self-contained file, so you can email it or drop it on a USB stick for a facilitator.

Rebuild it after adding content:

python3 .claude/skills/zeducation-content-organiser/scripts/build_site.py

How it is organised

Content-Library/
├── 00-Index/        how anything gets found
├── 01-Pillars/      the six content domains, each holding topics
├── 02-Frameworks/   one page per framework, shared across topics
├── 03-Activities/   one page per roleplay, game, assessment, reflection
├── 04-Sources/      Raw/ the original material · Notes/ what we took from it
├── 05-Builds/       workshops and workbooks assembled from the library
└── _templates/      the page templates

The seven pillars:

CodePillarCovers
LEALeadershipSelf-leadership, leading others, mindset, coaching, teams
COMCommunicationAssertiveness, listening, feedback, difficult conversations, presenting
FINFinancial CapabilityBudgeting, debt, saving, KiwiSaver, money mindset
DIGDigital CapabilityDigital basics, online safety, AI at work, digital communication
EMPEmployment & Work ReadinessCVs, interviews, workplace expectations, career direction
WELWellbeing & IdentityHauora, resilience, values, your own identity, stress
CULCulture & DiversityCultural safety, talanoa, working across difference, inclusion
ICEIce Breaker Games⚠️ The odd one out. Sixteen warm-ups that teach nothing and belong to no topic

⚠️ Ice Breaker Games works differently from the other seven. It holds game pages, not topics: no learning outcomes, no frameworks, no STAR, no self-assessment. Just the game, the purpose, what you need, how long it takes and how it works. A warm-up that has to justify itself against a learning outcome stops being a warm-up. See GAME-INDEX.

Every topic looks the same

Eight sections, every time, so a topic can be lifted straight into a student workbook:

  1. Topic name + the story a facilitator opens with
  2. 1-2 learning outcomes
  3. About this topic — what it is, why it matters, in plain words
  4. 2-3 frameworks, tools and techniques — with diagrams, tables, articles and popular videos
  5. Apply — roleplays and activities that practise them
  6. Self-assessment for students
  7. Reflection questions facilitators can ask
  8. Fun openers — games to introduce the topic

Alongside it sits a 🩷 Pink Sheet: the one-page IP snapshot of the idea (Point, Model, Metaphor, Study, Story) for talks, posts and proposals.

Built on Zeducation's STAR teaching framework — Story, Tools & Techniques, Apply, Reflect.

⚠️ Two different frameworks in here are called STAR. FRM-003 is the session shape above. FRM-059 is Situation · Task · Action · Result, the interview answer taught in Employment & Work Readiness. Both pages carry the warning. Say which one you mean.

Three rules that keep it working

  1. Nothing is invented. Every framework, statistic and video link is real and cited. Missing evidence is marked ⚠️ GAP, never filled with a guess.
  2. Everything connects. No page stands alone. Frameworks and activities live once and are linked from every topic that uses them, so a change improves every programme at once.
  3. Raw is kept. The original source is never rewritten, so any claim can be traced back.
